### 12.2 Model answers (exam-style, marks-proportioned)

**Q1 (3m) — Main classes of biomolecules with one function each.**
Answer: Biomolecules are the organic and inorganic compounds that make up living cells. (i) **Carbohydrates** — main energy source and structural material (cellulose). (ii) **Proteins** — growth, repair, catalysis (enzymes) and defence (antibodies). (iii) **Lipids** — concentrated energy storage (9 kcal/g) and membrane structure. (iv) **Nucleic acids** — storage and transmission of hereditary information (DNA, RNA). (v) **Enzymes** — protein catalysts that speed up metabolism. (vi) **Minerals and water** — regulate osmotic balance, act as cofactors and provide the reaction medium. *(Write definition + 4–6 classes + one clear function each; ½–½ marks per class with function.)*

**Q2 (3m) — Structure of a nucleotide and its role in DNA.**
Answer: A nucleotide has three components: (1) a **pentose sugar** — deoxyribose in DNA; (2) a **nitrogenous base** — purine (adenine/guanine) or pyrimidine (cytosine/thymine); (3) a **phosphate group**. Sugar + base = nucleoside; adding phosphate makes a nucleotide. In DNA, nucleotides join by **phosphodiester bonds** into long polynucleotide chains; the sequence of bases stores genetic information, and complementary base pairing (A=T, G≡C) allows exact replication and transmission of heredity.

**Q3 (4m) — Salient features of the Watson–Crick model.**
Answer: (1) DNA consists of two polynucleotide chains wound into a right-handed **double helix**; (2) the chains run **antiparallel** (5′→3′ and 3′→5′); (3) sugar–phosphate backbones lie **outside**, bases **inside**; (4) bases pair specifically — **A with T (2 H-bonds), G with C (3 H-bonds)** — a purine with a pyrimidine; (5) the strands are **complementary**, permitting semiconservative replication; (6) one turn = 3.4 nm with 10 base pairs; helix diameter 2 nm. *(Keywords: double helix, antiparallel, complementary, hydrogen bonds, 3.4 nm.)*

**Q4 (3m) — Enzymes: chemical nature and biocatalysts.**
Answer: Enzymes are chemically **proteins** (globular proteins; a few are catalytic RNAs). They are called **biocatalysts** because they are produced by living cells and accelerate biochemical reactions enormously — without being consumed or permanently changed — by lowering the activation energy, under mild conditions of temperature and pH.

**Q5 (3m) — Temperature and pH effects + immobilised enzymes.**
Answer: **Temperature:** enzyme activity rises with temperature up to an optimum (~37 °C in humans) because molecules collide more often; above the optimum, heat denatures the protein's tertiary structure and activity collapses. **pH:** each enzyme has a narrow optimum (pepsin ~2, trypsin ~8); at extreme pH the ionic charges of the active site change, the substrate no longer fits, and the enzyme is denatured. **Advantage of immobilised enzymes:** they are fixed to an inert support so they can be **reused many times**, recovered easily from products, and used continuously in industrial bioreactors — cheaper and cleaner.

**Q6 (2m) — Classify carbohydrates with one example each.**
Answer: (1) **Monosaccharides** — single sugar unit — glucose; (2) **Disaccharides** — two units — sucrose; (3) **Oligosaccharides** — 3–10 units — raffinose; (4) **Polysaccharides** — many units — starch/cellulose.

**Q7 (3m) — Saturated vs unsaturated fatty acids; why bilayers form.**
Answer: **Saturated** fatty acids have only C–C single bonds, carry maximum hydrogen, are straight, pack tightly and are solid at room temperature (ghee, palmitic acid). **Unsaturated** fatty acids have one or more C=C double bonds, are bent (kinked), pack loosely and are liquid oils at room temperature (mustard oil, oleic acid). **Phospholipid bilayers:** phospholipids are **amphipathic** — hydrophilic phosphate heads and hydrophobic fatty-acid tails. In water the heads face outward toward water while the tails hide from it, so two layers arrange tail-to-tail, forming the stable bilayer that is the basis of all cell membranes.

**Q8 (2m) — DNA vs RNA.**
Answer: DNA has **deoxyribose**, is **double-stranded**, uses **thymine**, is very **stable**, and **stores heredity**; RNA has **ribose**, is usually **single-stranded**, uses **uracil**, is **less stable**, and helps in **protein synthesis** (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA).

### 12.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Calling lipids "true polymers" — they are not; fatty acids are not repeated monomers.
2. Writing "RNA has thymine" — RNA uses **uracil**.
3. Confusing **nucleoside** (sugar + base) with **nucleotide** (sugar + base + phosphate).
4. Saying enzymes "provide energy" — they only **lower activation energy**; they never supply energy or change equilibrium.
5. Forgetting that denaturation does **not** break peptide bonds.
6. Reversing A=T (2 bonds) and G≡C (3 bonds) hydrogen-bond counts.
7. Saying the camel's hump stores water — it stores **fat** (which yields metabolic water when oxidised).
confusion: **Lipid vs carbohydrate as "polymer":** carbohydrates, proteins and nucleic acids are true polymers of repeated monomers; triglycerides are NOT — glycerol and fatty acids are different molecules, not repeated units. NEB loves this trap.
**Nucleoside vs nucleotide:** nucleoside = sugar + base only; nucleotide = sugar + base + phosphate. Only the nucleotide is the true monomer of nucleic acids.
**Denaturation vs digestion:** denaturation (heat, pH) destroys 3-D shape but leaves peptide bonds intact; hydrolysis (digestion) actually breaks peptide bonds into amino acids.

**Starch vs glycogen vs cellulose:** all are glucose polymers, but starch (plants, α-1,4/1,6), glycogen (animals, more highly branched), cellulose (β-1,4, indigestible). Same monomer, different bonds = different biology.
**Competitive vs non-competitive inhibition:** competitive inhibitors bind the active site and can be overcome by more substrate; non-competitive inhibitors bind an allosteric site and cannot.
**Enzyme vs hormone:** enzymes are catalysts (not consumed, act locally on substrates); hormones are chemical messengers (consumed after action, transported by blood to distant targets).
**DNA "contains protein":** DNA is pure nucleic acid; chromosomes contain DNA + histone protein. DNA itself has no protein.
**Saturated fat vs cholesterol:** saturation describes fatty-acid bonds; cholesterol is a steroid (derived lipid), a separate thing — both raise heart-disease risk but are chemically different.

practiceQuestions: **Short answer (2m): Define biomolecules. Give two examples.** — Biomolecules are the organic and inorganic compounds that constitute living cells and take part in all life processes. Examples: glucose (carbohydrate), haemoglobin (protein); also lipids, nucleic acids, water, minerals.

**Short answer (2m): What is a peptide bond?** — The covalent bond (−CO−NH−) formed between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next by condensation, releasing water; it links amino acids into polypeptides.

**Short answer (2m): Why is water called the universal solvent?** — Because its polar molecules form hydrogen bonds and hydration shells around ions and polar compounds, dissolving more substances than any other liquid; this makes blood, cytoplasm and sap possible.

**Short answer (2m): What are coenzymes? Give one example.** — Small organic, non-protein cofactors (often vitamin derivatives) required by some apoenzymes for activity. Example: NAD, FAD, coenzyme A.

**Long answer (5m): Describe the classification of carbohydrates with examples and state their functions.** — Full answer: definition + general formula; four classes (mono-, di-, oligo-, polysaccharides) each with definition, examples and significance; storage vs structural polysaccharides (starch/glycogen vs cellulose/chitin); functions — energy (4 kcal/g), storage, structure, transport (sucrose), cell recognition, nucleic-acid sugars. Structure the answer as: definition → classification table → functions list.

**Long answer (5m): Describe the structure of DNA according to the Watson–Crick model.** — Double helix of two antiparallel strands; sugar–phosphate backbone outside, bases inside; complementary pairing A=T (2 H-bonds), G≡C (3 H-bonds); purine–pyrimidine pairing keeps 2 nm diameter; 10 bp/turn, 3.4 nm/turn; complementarity explains semiconservative replication and Chargaff's rule. Include a labelled diagram.

**Long answer (5m): What are enzymes? Explain the factors affecting enzyme activity.** — Definition + protein nature + active site + ES complex + activation-energy lowering. Factors: temperature (optimum then denaturation), pH (narrow optimum), substrate concentration (saturation plateau), enzyme concentration (proportional rise), inhibitors (competitive vs non-competitive). Draw rate-vs-temperature and rate-vs-pH curves.

**Conceptual (3m): "Structure determines function." Justify this statement with two biomolecule examples.** — (1) Starch vs cellulose: identical glucose monomers, but α vs β glycosidic bonds make one digestible and the other structural fibre. (2) Haemoglobin: one amino-acid substitution in the β-chain (sickle-cell anaemia) changes the quaternary shape and destroys O₂-carrying efficiency. In both cases the 3-D arrangement — not the composition alone — decides the biological role.

**Conceptual (3m): Why are enzymes called biocatalysts but not "sources of energy"?** — Enzymes only lower the activation energy so reactions reach equilibrium faster; they are not consumed and they supply no energy themselves — the energy comes from the substrate's chemical bonds. A catalyst changes rate, never the ΔG or the equilibrium position.

**Application (3m): A patient's blood test shows low haemoglobin and an enlarged thyroid. Which minerals are deficient, and why?** — Low haemoglobin → **iron** deficiency (Fe²⁺ is the central atom of haem, the O₂-binding prosthetic group of haemoglobin) → anaemia. Enlarged thyroid → **iodine** deficiency (iodine is required to synthesise thyroxine; without it TSH keeps stimulating the thyroid, causing goitre).

**Application (2m): Why is sucrose, not glucose, the sugar transported in plant phloem?** — Sucrose is non-reducing and chemically inert, so it neither reacts with, nor is consumed by, the cells it passes through during long-distance transport; glucose would be metabolised or react en route.

originalContent.summary: Biomolecules — carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, plus minerals, enzymes and water — are the chemical basis of life. Monomers join into polymers by condensation (water out) and are split by hydrolysis (water in). Carbohydrates (Cₓ(H₂O)ᵧ) supply quick energy and structure; proteins (amino acids + peptide bonds, four structural levels) do the cell's work; lipids (water-insoluble, 9 kcal/g) store concentrated energy and build the amphipathic phospholipid bilayer of all membranes; nucleic acids (nucleotides, A=T/G≡C pairing) store and express heredity. Minerals act as structural materials, cofactors and electrolytes, while water — polar, hydrogen-bonded, 70–90% of the cell — is the solvent, reactant and temperature buffer in which all life chemistry happens. Enzymes, protein catalysts that lower activation energy with high specificity, control the speed of every one of these reactions.

mcs.question: Which biomolecule is NOT a true polymer?
mcs.explanation: Triglycerides are esters of one glycerol with three fatty acids — different molecules, not repeated identical monomers. Proteins, starch and DNA are true polymers of amino acids, glucose and nucleotides respectively.

mcs.question: How many hydrogen bonds join guanine to cytosine in DNA?
mcs.explanation: G≡C pairing forms 3 hydrogen bonds; A=T forms only 2. More G≡C content makes DNA more heat-stable.

mcs.question: The bond joining two amino acids is the:
mcs.explanation: Peptide bond (−CO−NH−), formed by condensation between −COOH of one amino acid and −NH₂ of the next. Glycosidic = sugars, ester = glycerol–fatty acid, phosphodiester = nucleotides.

mcs.question: A polypeptide of 200 amino acids contains how many peptide bonds?
mcs.explanation: A chain of n amino acids has (n − 1) peptide bonds; 200 amino acids → 199 bonds and 199 water molecules released.

mcs.question: Which sugar is transported through plant phloem and why?
options: Glucose — it is a reducing sugar
Sucrose — it is non-reducing and chemically inert
Fructose — it is the sweetest sugar
mcs.explanation: Sucrose's glycosidic bond locks both anomeric carbons, so it does not react with (or get consumed by) tissues during transport.

mcs.question: The induced-fit model of enzyme action was proposed by:
mcs.explanation: Koshland (1959) proposed that the active site is flexible and moulds around the substrate; Fischer (1894) proposed the rigid lock-and-key model; Sumner crystallised urease.

mcs.question: Which test distinguishes a reducing sugar from sucrose?
mcs.explanation: Benedict's/Fehling's gives a brick-red Cu₂O precipitate with reducing sugars (free aldehyde/ketone group) and is negative with sucrose.

mcs.question: Phospholipids form bilayers in water because they are:
mcs.explanation: Each phospholipid has a hydrophilic phosphate head and hydrophobic fatty-acid tails; in water the heads face outward and tails hide inward, self-assembling a bilayer.

mcs.question: Which of the following is a conjugated protein?
mcs.explanation: Haemoglobin = globin (protein) + haem (iron-containing prosthetic group), so it is a chromoprotein — conjugated. Albumin, keratin and collagen are simple proteins.

mcs.question: Ice floats on water because water has:
mcs.explanation: Water reaches maximum density at 4 °C; below that, hydrogen bonding forms an open ice lattice that is less dense, so ice floats and insulates aquatic life.

importantConcepts: **Condensation/hydrolysis cycle** — the universal build-and-break chemistry of every biomolecule.

**Activation energy lowering** — the single correct explanation of enzyme catalysis.
**Energy density hierarchy** — fat (9) > protein = carbohydrate (4) kcal/g, because lipids are more reduced (less oxygen per carbon).

subtopics.name: The four classes at a glance
points: Carbohydrates: immediate energy and structure
Proteins: catalysis, transport, structure, defence
Lipids: energy storage, membranes, hormones
Nucleic acids: information storage and transfer

subtopics.name: Why each class exists
points: Carbohydrates are easily oxidised, giving rapid ATP without oxygen debt
Proteins are the only class that catalyses reactions, so they carry regulation
Lipids store the most energy per gram and form the only barrier that makes a cell a cell
Nucleic acids are the only class that can be copied with high fidelity

subtopics.name: Minerals and water
points: Macro-minerals are needed in gram quantities; micro-minerals in milligram or microgram quantities
Deficiency diseases map to specific minerals: iodine -> goitre, iron -> anaemia, calcium -> rickets
Water makes up the majority of protoplasm and is the solvent for all metabolism

subtopics.name: Metabolic interconnection
points: Excess carbohydrate converts to glycogen, then to fat — the classes interconvert
Amino acids can enter respiration as keto acids after deamination
Nucleotides are built from amino acid, sugar and phosphate precursors

**Cell theory and cell types — classified**

| Item | Statement / feature | Author / example |
|---|---|---|
| Cell theory 1 | All organisms are made of one or more cells | Schleiden and Schwann (1838-39) |
| Cell theory 2 | The cell is the basic unit of life | Schleiden and Schwann |
| Cell theory 3 | Cells arise only from pre-existing cells | Virchow (1855) — omnis cellula e cellula |
| Prokaryote | Naked DNA, 70S ribosomes, peptidoglycan wall | Bacteria, cyanobacteria, mycoplasma |
| Eukaryote | True nucleus, 80S ribosomes, organelles | Protists, fungi, plants, animals |
| Boundary exception | Virus — not cellular at all | Only replicates inside a host cell |
Basic cell components: plasma membrane, cytoplasm (cytosol + organelles), genetic material, and (in prokaryotes) cell wall, capsule, pili, flagella.

Cells are classified into two types — prokaryotic and eukaryotic — based on the nature of the nucleus and cell organelles and the complexity of the genetic material (terms introduced by Chatton, 1925; dichotomy proposed by Dougherty, 1957; popularised by Stanier and van Niel, 1962).
Prokaryotic Cell: A prokaryotic cell is a primitive cell that lacks organized nucleus and membrane-bound cell organelles.
They have the following properties:
It lacks a definite nuclear membrane, membrane-bound organelles, a mitotic apparatus, nucleoli, and flagella with a (9+2) pattern of fibril arrangement.
It bears a naked circular DNA that fold into nucleoid.
Cell wall is composed of carbohydrates and amino acids, with murein or peptidoglycan.
Prokaryotes lack mitochondria: respiratory electron transport occurs across the plasma membrane (mesosomes, once described as respiratory sites, are now known to be fixation artifacts).

Chlorophylls are located in lamellae rather than in membrane-enclosed chloroplasts.

**Deep dive — the exceptions that prove the rule.** Mycoplasma has no cell wall at all (the smallest known cells, penicillin-proof for that reason). Cyanobacteria photosynthesise without chloroplasts — their thylakoid lamellae run free in the cytoplasm. Both show that 'prokaryote' is defined by architecture, not by chemistry: the reactions of respiration and photosynthesis are identical, only the housing differs.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Inside the Eukaryotic Cell

Topic 2 established *that* eukaryotic cells have membrane-bound organelles; this topic opens every compartment and explains *how each one is built and what it does*. The syllabus names the full inventory: **cell wall, cell membrane, mitochondria, plastids, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi bodies, lysosomes, ribosomes, nucleus, chromosomes, cilia, flagella and cell inclusions**.

- **Why it matters:** every disease, drug, hormone and metabolic process acts at some organelle. Antibiotics hit ribosomes; cyanide hits mitochondria; cholesterol drugs hit the ER.
- **Study method:** for each organelle learn the same five questions — **structure (membranes?), location, chemistry, function, and the evidence/interesting fact**. NEB questions are almost always built from these five.
- **Connection:** the phospholipid bilayer from Topic 1 is the universal building unit of every structure below.

## 2. Cell Wall — The Outer Armor of Plant Cells

**Definition:** the rigid, non-living outer layer **outside the plasma membrane**, found in plants, fungi, bacteria and algae (absent in animals).

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Chemistry | Plants: **cellulose** (microfibrils in a matrix of hemicellulose and pectin). Fungi: chitin. Bacteria: peptidoglycan |
| Layers | **Middle lamella** (pectin, cements adjacent cells) → **primary wall** (thin, extensible, growing cells) → **secondary wall** (thick, rigid, lignified, mature cells) |
| Functions | Shape and rigidity; protection against mechanical injury and pathogens; prevents bursting in hypotonic water (turgor pressure); plasmodesmata allow transport between cells |

**Key concept:** the wall is **fully permeable** — it is *not* the selective barrier; the membrane is. Water moves freely through the wall; osmosis is decided by the membrane.

## 3. Cell Membrane (Plasma Membrane) — The Selective Barrier

### 3.1 Structure — the fluid-mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972)

- A **phospholipid bilayer** ~7–8 nm thick: hydrophilic heads face the aqueous inside and outside; hydrophobic tails form the interior.
- **Proteins** float like icebergs in the lipid sea: **integral (intrinsic) proteins** span the membrane (channels, carriers, pumps); **peripheral (extrinsic) proteins** sit on the surfaces (enzymes, anchors).
- **Cholesterol** in animal membranes stabilises fluidity across temperatures.
- **Glycoproteins and glycolipids** on the outer face form the glycocalyx — cell recognition.
- The membrane is **fluid** (lipids and proteins move laterally) and a **mosaic** (patchwork of proteins) — hence the name.

### 3.2 Functions

1. **Selective permeability** — decides what enters and leaves (small non-polar molecules diffuse freely; ions need channels/pumps).
2. **Transport** — passive (diffusion, osmosis, facilitated diffusion) and active (ATP-driven pumps, e.g. Na⁺/K⁺ pump).
3. **Endocytosis and exocytosis** — bulk transport in vesicles (phagocytosis, pinocytosis).
4. **Recognition and signalling** — receptors for hormones; glycoprotein identity markers.
5. **Compartmentalisation** — the same bilayer principle builds every organelle.

**Historical models (short-answer favourite):** Robertson (unit membrane, 1950s) → Singer & Nicolson (fluid mosaic, 1972). Also recall: Overton (lipid nature), Gorter & Grendel (bilayer from RBC lipids, 1925), Davson–Danielli (protein sandwich).

## 4. Mitochondria — The Powerhouse

### 4.1 Structure

- **Double-membraned organelle**, 0.5–1.0 µm wide, rod or sausage shaped ("chondriosome" — granules seen by Kölliker, 1880s; named by Benda, 1898).
- **Outer membrane:** smooth, permeable to small molecules (porins).
- **Inner membrane:** folded into **cristae** — folds that hugely increase surface area; studded with **oxysomes (F₁ particles)** where ATP is made. Cristae density reflects the cell's energy demand (heart muscle: very dense).
- **Matrix:** contains enzymes of the **Krebs cycle**, circular **mitochondrial DNA**, **70S ribosomes**, tRNA and enzymes of fat/protein oxidation.
- Semi-autonomous: mitochondria divide by fission like bacteria (endosymbiotic evidence).

### 4.2 Function

- **Aerobic respiration:** pyruvate → Krebs cycle (matrix) → electron transport chain + oxidative phosphorylation (inner membrane) → ~36 ATP per glucose.
- Stores and releases Ca²⁺; synthesises some lipids and amino acids; generates heat (brown fat).

**NEB 2022 asked it directly:** the mitochondrion is the "powerhouse of the cell" because it carries out aerobic respiration and produces most of the cell's ATP.

## 5. Plastids — The Plant-Only Organelles

Plastids are double-membraned, DNA-bearing organelles found **only in plants and algae**, classified by pigment:

| Type | Pigment | Colour | Function | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Chloroplast** | Chlorophyll a, b + carotenoids | Green | Photosynthesis | Mesophyll cells |
| **Chromoplast** | Carotenoids (carotene, xanthophyll) | Yellow/orange/red | Pigmentation, attract pollinators and seed dispersers | Tomato fruit, carrot root, petals |
| **Leucoplast** | No pigment | Colourless | Storage: amyloplast (starch), elaioplast (oil), aleuroplast (protein) | Potato tuber, castor seed |

### 5.1 Chloroplast structure (draw this in exams)

- Oval, 4–10 µm; **double membrane** envelope.
- Inside: colourless **stroma** (enzymes of the Calvin cycle, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes) and **grana** — stacks of disc-like **thylakoids** holding chlorophyll in their membranes (light reaction site). Grana are connected by **stroma lamellae**.
- Semi-autonomous like mitochondria — own DNA and ribosomes (endosymbiosis).

**Functions:** photosynthesis (light reaction on thylakoids, carbon fixation in stroma); stores starch temporarily.

## 6. Endoplasmic Reticulum — The Intracellular Highway

**Definition:** a network (reticulum) of membrane-bound tubules, vesicles and flattened sacs (**cisternae**) running from the nuclear envelope outward. Discovered by Porter, Claude and Fullam (1945) in cultured cells.

| Type | Structure | Ribosomes? | Main role | Where abundant |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Rough ER (RER)** | Flattened cisternae, studded with ribosomes | Yes (80S) | Synthesis and folding of proteins destined for membranes, lysosomes or secretion | Protein-exporting cells: pancreatic acinar cells, plasma cells |
| **Smooth ER (SER)** | Tubular network, no ribosomes | No | Lipid and steroid synthesis; detoxification of drugs; Ca²⁺ storage | Steroid-secreting cells, liver, muscle (as sarcoplasmic reticulum) |

**Functions:** synthesis and transport of materials; the ER lumen connects to the nuclear envelope and Golgi — part of the **endomembrane system**; provides surface for enzyme attachment; in muscle, the sarcoplasmic reticulum releases Ca²⁺ for contraction.

## 7. Golgi Apparatus — The Packaging and Dispatch Department

- Discovered by **Camillo Golgi (1898)** in nerve cells (silver stain).
- Structure: stacks of 4–8 curved, flattened membrane sacs (**cisternae**) with a convex **forming (cis) face** receiving vesicles from the ER and a concave **maturing (trans) face** shipping vesicles outward.
- **Functions:**
  1. **Modification** of proteins and lipids arriving from the ER (glycosylation — adding sugars).
  2. **Packaging** into secretory vesicles, lysosomes and membrane-bound granules.
  3. **Secretion** — dispatch to the cell surface (exocytosis).
  4. **Source of lysosomes** and of the **cell plate** during plant cytokinesis.
  5. **Complex sugar synthesis** (mucopolysaccharides, plant cell-wall matrix).

**Conceptual flow to memorise:** RER (make protein) → vesicle → Golgi cis face (modify) → trans face (package) → vesicle → destination (membrane / lysosome / secretion).

## 8. Lysosomes — The Suicide Bags

- Discovered by **Christian de Duve (1949/1955**, Nobel 1974): single-membraned sacs (~0.2–0.8 µm) packed with ~50 **acid hydrolases** (digestive enzymes active at acidic pH ~5).
- **Why they don't digest the cell:** the inner membrane's H⁺-pump keeps the lumen acidic while the cytosol stays near pH 7.2, where the enzymes are inactive — compartmentalisation in action.
- **Forms:** primary lysosome (fresh enzymes) → secondary lysosome (fusing with food vacuole = digestive vacuole) → residual body (undigested waste, expelled by exocytosis).
- **Functions:** intracellular and extracellular digestion; digestion of worn-out organelles (**autophagy**); destruction of engulfed pathogens (in white blood cells); **autolysis** — rupture releases enzymes and digests the cell itself, hence "suicide bags" (e.g. tadpole tail reabsorption during metamorphosis, uterine wall breakdown at menstruation).

**Organelle address book — who does what, where (highly classified)**

| Organelle | Membranes | Core job | Marker enzyme / feature |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mitochondrion | Double (cristae inside) | ATP by aerobic respiration | Own circular DNA + 70S ribosomes |
| Chloroplast | Double (grana inside) | Photosynthesis | Chlorophyll in thylakoids; own DNA |
| Rough ER | Single, ribosome-studded | Protein synthesis + transport | Ribosomes on cytosolic face |
| Smooth ER | Single, no ribosomes | Lipids, detox, Ca2+ store | Abundant in liver and muscle cells |
| Golgi apparatus | Stacked cisternae | Modify, package, dispatch | cis (receiving) vs trans (shipping) faces |
| Lysosome | Single vesicle | Intracellular digestion | Acid hydrolases working at pH ~5 |
| Ribosome | No membrane | Protein synthesis | 80S; free or ER-bound |
| Nucleus | Double envelope with pores | Stores genome; transcription | Nucleolus makes ribosome subunits |

## 9. Ribosomes — The Protein Factories

- Discovered by **Palade (1953**, Nobel 1974) — dense granules ~15–20 nm, made of **rRNA + proteins**, **no membrane**.
- Two subunits: **eukaryotic 80S = 60S + 40S**; prokaryotic/organelle **70S = 50S + 30S**.
- Occur **free in the cytosol** (making proteins used inside the cell) or **attached to RER** (making secretory/membrane proteins). Several ribosomes on one mRNA form a **polyribosome (polysome)**.
- **Function:** site of protein synthesis (translation) — they read mRNA codons and link amino acids by peptide bonds. Because of the 70S/80S difference, antibiotics (streptomycin, tetracycline) can block bacterial ribosomes without stopping ours.

## 10. Nucleus — The Control Centre

### 10.1 Structure

- Discovered by **Robert Brown (1831)**. Usually one per cell (multinucleate cells exist — coenocytes); absent in mature RBCs and sieve tubes.
- **Nuclear envelope:** double membrane with **perinuclear space**; perforated by **nuclear pores** (complex of proteins) that regulate traffic of mRNA out and proteins in.
- **Nucleoplasm:** nucleic acids + proteins + enzymes.
- **Nucleolus:** dense, rounded, membraneless region of rRNA genes — the **ribosome factory**.
- **Chromatin:** DNA + histones in two forms — **euchromatin** (loose, active transcription) and **heterochromatin** (condensed, inactive).

### 10.2 Chromosomes — the packaged genome

- Chromatin condenses into visible **chromosomes** during division. Each chromosome has two **chromatids** joined at the **centromere (primary constriction)**; some carry a secondary constriction with a **satellite**.
- Nucleosome organisation: DNA wound around histone octamers ("beads on a string").
- **Chromosome types by centromere position:** metacentric (middle), submetacentric (off-middle), acrocentric (near end), telocentric (at end).
- **Karyotype** = the ordered photograph of all chromosomes of a species.
- **Functions of the nucleus:** controls all cell activities through gene expression; stores hereditary information; ribosome production; cell division distributes its DNA.

**Deep dive — the endosymbiont clue.** Mitochondria and chloroplasts each carry their own circular DNA, their own 70S ribosomes and a double membrane — the signature of bacteria that moved inside larger cells and stayed. The inner membrane corresponds to the original bacterial membrane; the outer one is the host's engulfing vacuole. NEB loves this as a link between cell structure and evolution: organelle anatomy is fossil evidence you can see in every cell.

## 11. Cilia and Flagella — The Motors

| Basis | Cilia | Flagella |
|---|---|---|
| Size | Short (5–10 µm), numerous | Long (100–200 µm), one or few |
| Movement | Oar-like, coordinated beating | Whip-like, undulating |
| Examples | Paramecium surface, tracheal epithelium | Sperm tail, Euglena |
| Organisation | Both arise from basal bodies and have the **9+2 axoneme**: 9 fused microtubule doublets around a central pair, wrapped in a membrane | Same 9+2 arrangement |

**Function:** locomotion of unicellular organisms; movement of fluid/mucus over tissues; in humans, cilia sweep mucus in the airway — smoking destroys them (real-life link).

## 12. Cell Inclusions — The Non-Living Contents

**Cell inclusions** are non-living, non-membrane-bound deposits in the cytoplasm — stored food or waste:

| Inclusion | Nature | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Starch grains | Stored carbohydrate (plants) | Potato tuber |
| Glycogen granules | Animal storage carbohydrate | Liver, muscle |
| Fat droplets | Stored lipid | Adipose cells, oil seeds |
| Protein crystals (aleuroplasts) | Stored protein | Castor/Aleurites seeds, aleurone layer of grains |
| Pigment granules | Melanin etc. | Skin, hair cells |
| Mineral crystals | Calcium oxalate (raphides), silica | Plant cells |
| Vacuoles (with tonoplast) | Sap, water, dissolved salts/food/wastes | Plant central vacuole — turgor, storage, digestion |

**Vacuole concept:** in plants the central vacuole is a dominant, tonoplast-bound compartment storing water, salts, sugars, pigments and wastes, and maintaining **turgor pressure** that keeps non-woody plants upright.

## 13. Master Comparison Tables

### 13.1 Double-membraned vs single-membraned vs non-membraned organelles

| Membranes | Organelles | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Double | Nucleus (envelope), mitochondria, chloroplasts | Enclose their own DNA/ribosomes; semi-autonomous (endosymbiotic origin) |
| Single | ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vacuoles, microbodies (peroxisomes, glyoxysomes) | Part of the endomembrane system; exchange by vesicles |
| None | Ribosomes, centrioles, nucleolus, cytoskeleton, inclusions | Assembled directly in cytoplasm |

### 13.2 Mitochondria vs chloroplast (guaranteed comparison)

| Basis | Mitochondria | Chloroplast |
|---|---|---|
| Occurrence | All aerobic eukaryotes | Only plants and algae |
| Pigment | None | Chlorophyll a, b, carotenoids |
| Internal folds | Cristae (tubular/sheet infolds of inner membrane) | Thylakoids stacked into grana suspended in stroma |
| Reaction carried out | Respiration — releases energy as ATP | Photosynthesis — traps light to make glucose |
| Gases | Consumes O₂, releases CO₂ | Consumes CO₂, releases O₂ |
| Common features | Double membrane, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, divide by fission | Same — evidence of common endosymbiotic origin |

### 13.3 Rough ER vs smooth ER

| Basis | RER | SER |
|---|---|---|
| Ribosomes | Present on outer surface | Absent |
| Shape | Flattened cisternae | Tubular network |
| Synthesises | Proteins (for secretion/membranes) | Lipids, steroids; detoxifies drugs |
| Continues as | Connected to nuclear envelope; feeds Golgi | Often continuous with RER |
| Special form | — | Sarcoplasmic reticulum in muscle (Ca²⁺ store) |

### 13.4 Organelle discovery quick table

| Organelle | Discoverer | Year |
|---|---|---|
| Cell | Robert Hooke | 1665 |
| Nucleus | Robert Brown | 1831 |
| Golgi apparatus | Camillo Golgi | 1898 |
| Mitochondria (named) | Benda (seen by Kölliker) | 1898 |
| ER | Porter, Claude & Fullam | 1945 |
| Ribosome | Palade | 1953 |
| Lysosome | Christian de Duve | 1949–55 |
| Fluid-mosaic model | Singer & Nicolson | 1972 |

## 14. Conceptual Relationships

- **Topic 1 → here:** every organelle is built from the biomolecules — phospholipid membranes, protein machines, DNA in nucleus/mitochondria/chloroplast.
- **Here → Topic 4:** chromosomes organise for division; the cell plate from Golgi separates plant daughter cells.
- **Here → respiration/photosynthesis (later units):** mitochondria and chloroplasts are the two energy organelles whose chemistry powers the biosphere.
- **Here → health:** lysosome storage diseases, mitochondrial myopathies, cilia damage from smoking, and antibiotic action on 70S ribosomes.
- **Here → ecology:** chloroplasts capture the solar energy that flows through every food chain.

## 15. Exam Orientation

### 15.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

| Year | Unit | Topic | Question | Marks | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2078/2022 | Biomolecules & Cell Biology | Mitochondria | Why is the mitochondrion called the powerhouse of the cell? | 2 | Reasoning |

*(This unit's bank carries one direct question here, but this topic supplies the organelle knowledge behind many unit-1 questions — organelle structure is the most diagram-tested area.)*

### 15.2 Common examination mistakes

1. Drawing chloroplast grana without **stroma lamellae** connecting them, or omitting **stroma**.
2. Writing "lysosomes digest the cell" without the suicide-bag mechanism (**autolysis** after rupture).
3. Confusing **cristae** (mitochondria) with **thylakoids/grana** (chloroplasts).
4. Saying ribosomes have a membrane — they are **non-membranous**.
5. Forgetting that the **cell wall is fully permeable** and the membrane is the selective one.
6. Mixing up **cis** (forming, receives from ER) and **trans** (maturing, ships out) faces of the Golgi.
confusion: **Cell wall vs cell membrane:** the wall is outside, rigid, fully permeable, non-living; the membrane is living, selective, and the true gatekeeper of the cell.
**Cristae vs thylakoids:** cristae are folds of the mitochondrial *inner membrane*; thylakoids are separate flattened discs *inside* the chloroplast stroma, stacked into grana.
**Lysosome vs vacuole:** lysosomes are single-membraned enzyme sacs for digestion; the plant central vacuole is mainly storage/turgor, though it also contains hydrolases.
**RER vs SER:** ribosomes on the surface define RER and protein synthesis; smooth tubules without ribosomes make lipids and detoxify.
**Cilia vs flagella:** same 9+2 axoneme, but cilia are short, numerous and beat like oars; flagella are long, few and undulate.
**Nucleolus vs nucleus:** the nucleolus is a membraneless sub-region of the nucleus that makes rRNA/ribosomes — not a separate organelle.
**Inclusions vs organelles:** inclusions (starch, fat, crystals) are non-living, non-membrane-bound deposits; organelles are living, organised functional structures.

practice:
Why does a liver cell contain more SER than a muscle cell, but a pancreatic cell more RER?

**Answer.** **Structure follows chemistry.** The **liver** is the body's detox and lipid-chemistry plant: it modifies drugs and poisons, synthesises lipoproteins and steroid precursors — all **SER jobs**, so hepatocytes are packed with smooth tubules. The **pancreatic acinar cell** is an export factory for **digestive enzymes** — proteins destined for secretion, which must be synthesised on **RER ribosomes**, threaded into the cisternae, glycosylated in the Golgi and packaged into zymogen granules — so it is stuffed with RER. A **muscle cell** needs little of either: its business is contraction, so its ER specialisation is the Ca²⁺-storing sarcoplasmic reticulum instead.

Why don't lysosomal enzymes digest the lysosome's own membrane first?

**Answer.** Three safeguards:

1. **Membrane composition** — the lysosomal membrane is unusually rich in heavily **glycosylated (sugar-armoured) proteins** (e.g. LAMP proteins) that present no protein backbone to the proteases and resist digestion.
2. **pH separation** — the enzymes are **acid hydrolases**, active only at **pH ~5** maintained by a proton pump; the cytosol is pH ~7.2, where they are nearly inert. If a little leaks out, cytosolic enzymes neutralise it.
3. **Compartmentalisation** — substrates are delivered *into* the lysosome (by phagocytosis, autophagosome fusion), so the enzymes meet their targets inside, not outside.

Only when the membrane is ruptured — damage or programmed death — does the system fail, and that failure is precisely the 'suicide bag' function.

A student draws a chloroplast with grana but no stroma DNA. Which features did they miss and why do they matter?

**Answer.** **Missed features:** the **circular DNA** (nucleoid region), the **70S ribosomes** and the **starch grains** in the stroma — and often the **stroma lamellae** connecting the grana.

**Why they matter:**
- The **DNA + 70S ribosomes** are the evidence that the chloroplast is **semi-autonomous** — an endosymbiotic cyanobacterium that still makes some of its own proteins and divides by fission.
- **Starch grains** show the stroma is where the **Calvin cycle** stores the fixed carbon.
- **Stroma lamellae** are structurally real: grana are not free-floating stacks but connected units of one continuous thylakoid system.

A chloroplast without stroma DNA is drawn as a bag of membranes — missing the organelle's evolutionary story and its biochemistry.
universalFacts: Membrane thickness ≈ 7–8 nm; mitochondrion ≈ 0.5–1 µm; ribosome ≈ 15–20 nm.
About 50 acid hydrolases are packed in lysosomes.
The 9+2 axoneme arrangement is universal in motile eukaryotic cilia and flagella.
examples: **Pancreatic acinar cell** — RER-rich; exports digestive enzymes.
**Liver cell (hepatocyte)** — SER-rich; detoxifies drugs and alcohol.
**Muscle cell** — sarcoplasmic reticulum stores Ca²⁺ for contraction; mitochondria dense between myofibrils.
**Potato tuber amyloplast** — leucoplast storing starch.
**Tomato chromoplast** — carotenoid pigments colour the ripe fruit.
**Tracheal ciliated epithelium** — cilia sweep mucus; destroyed by smoking.
practiceQuestions:
**Short answer (2m):** Why is the mitochondrion called the powerhouse of the cell?

**Answer.** Because it runs **aerobic respiration**: the **Krebs cycle** in the matrix oxidises food derivatives, and the **electron transport chain + ATP synthase on the cristae** convert that energy into most of the cell's **ATP** — the universal energy currency. Muscle, liver and nerve cells, the biggest energy spenders, are packed with mitochondria.

**Short answer (2m):** Distinguish RER and SER (two points).

**Answer.** 1. **Ribosomes:** RER bears **ribosomes** on flattened **cisternae**; SER **lacks ribosomes** and forms **tubules**.
2. **Function:** RER synthesises **proteins for secretion and membranes**; SER synthesises **lipids and steroids, detoxifies drugs and stores Ca²⁺** (sarcoplasmic reticulum in muscle).

**Short answer (2m):** What are cell inclusions? Give two examples.

**Answer.** **Non-living, non-membrane-bound cytoplasmic deposits** of stored food or waste material — not organelles, just stored material.

**Examples:** **starch grains** (potato tuber), **fat droplets** (adipose tissue); also glycogen granules, protein crystals and pigment granules.

**Short answer (2m):** State the fluid-mosaic model in one sentence and name its proposer.

**Answer.** The membrane is a **fluid phospholipid bilayer** carrying a **mosaic of embedded integral and peripheral proteins** (plus cholesterol and surface glycocalyx) that can move laterally — proposed by **Singer and Nicolson (1972)**.

**Long answer (5m):** Describe the structure of a chloroplast with a labelled diagram.

**Answer.** **Structure:**

1. **Double envelope** — outer permeable membrane + inner selective membrane, with a narrow intermembrane space.
2. **Stroma** — the protein-rich fluid matrix holding **Calvin-cycle (CO₂-fixation) enzymes**, plus **circular DNA, 70S ribosomes and starch grains** (semi-autonomous).
3. **Grana** — stacks of disc-shaped **thylakoids**; the thylakoid membranes carry **chlorophyll a, b and accessory pigments** with the light-reaction complexes (photosystems, ETC, ATP synthase).
4. **Stroma lamellae** — flattened membranes connecting the grana.

**Functions:**
- **Light reaction** on the thylakoid membranes: light energy → ATP + NADPH, O₂ released from water splitting.
- **Dark reaction (Calvin cycle)** in the stroma: CO₂ fixed into sugar using that ATP and NADPH.
- **Temporary starch storage** as grains in the stroma.

*Labelled diagram:* envelope (double), stroma, one granum of stacked thylakoids, stroma lamella, starch grain, DNA region.

**Long answer (5m):** Describe the structure and role of the Golgi apparatus.

**Answer.** **Structure:** stacks of **curved, flattened membrane cisternae** (3–8 per stack) with **vesicles budding off** at the edges. The stack is polarised:
- **cis (forming) face** — receives transport vesicles from the **RER**;
- **trans (maturing) face** — dispatches finished products.

**Roles:**
1. **Modification** — glycosylation of proteins and lipids (making glycoproteins/glycolipids).
2. **Packaging and sorting** — routing materials to their destinations in vesicles.
3. **Secretion** — packaging export proteins (enzymes, hormones, mucus) for release.
4. **Lysosome formation** — budding off the enzyme-filled lysosomes.
5. **Cell-plate formation** — in plant cells the Golgi supplies the material that becomes the middle lamella during cytokinesis.
6. **Complex polysaccharide synthesis** (pectin, hemicellulose).

*Flow diagram:* RER → (vesicle) → cis-Golgi → modified through cisternae → trans-Golgi → vesicles → secretion / lysosome / membrane.

**Conceptual (3m):** Why is the cell membrane called selectively permeable while the cell wall is not?

**Answer.** The **membrane is a lipid bilayer with specific proteins** — channels, carriers and pumps — so it **discriminates**: small non-polar molecules (O₂, CO₂) diffuse through freely, water crosses via aquaporins, but ions and sugars pass only through **controlled** protein routes. It decides what enters and leaves.

The **cellulose wall is an open mesh**: its microfibril pores are large, so **water and dissolved solutes pass freely** — it is **fully permeable**. Its job is **support and shape**, not selection. Selection is the membrane's job.

**Conceptual (3m):** "Lysosomes are suicide bags." Justify.

**Answer.** Lysosomes contain **acid hydrolases** — enzymes able to digest **every class of biomolecule** (proteases, lipases, nucleases, glycosidases). In life, the membrane isolates them and the cytosol's pH ~7.2 keeps the enzymes (which need pH ~5) nearly inactive. But when a cell is **badly damaged or programmed to die**, the lysosomal membrane ruptures, the enzymes flood the cytoplasm, drop the local pH and **digest the cell from within — autolysis**.

Useful examples: resorption of the **tadpole's tail** at metamorphosis, breakdown of the **menstrual endometrium**, dissolution of webbing between digits in development, and self-destruction of injured cells. The cell carries its own digestion kit in a bag — hence the name.

**Application (3m):** A patient's ciliated airway epithelium is destroyed by years of smoking. What functional loss follows?

**Answer.** The **mucus escalator is lost**. Beating cilia normally sweep the mucus blanket — loaded with trapped **dust, pollen and microbes** — upward to the pharynx to be swallowed or spat. With the cilia destroyed, mucus **stagnates**: pathogens and particles accumulate, causing chronic irritation, repeated chest infections and the persistent **smoker's cough** — the body compensating with a cough reflex for the transport the cilia no longer perform. Prolonged stasis also exposes the epithelium to carcinogens longer, raising cancer risk.
keyPoints: Cell wall: cellulose (plants), chitin (fungi), peptidoglycan (bacteria); middle lamella → primary → secondary; fully permeable.
Membrane: fluid-mosaic model (Singer & Nicolson 1972) — phospholipid bilayer + integral/peripheral proteins + cholesterol + glycocalyx; selective permeability, transport, signalling.
Mitochondria: double membrane, cristae with oxysomes, matrix with Krebs enzymes + circular DNA + 70S ribosomes; aerobic respiration → ATP ("powerhouse").
Plastids: chloroplast (photosynthesis), chromoplast (colour), leucoplast (storage: amylo/elai/aleuroplast); grana = thylakoid stacks in stroma.
RER: ribosome-studded cisternae — protein synthesis for export; SER: tubules — lipids, steroids, detox, Ca²⁺ (sarcoplasmic reticulum).
Golgi (Golgi 1898): cis face receives from ER, modifies (glycosylation), trans face ships — vesicles, lysosomes, cell plate.
Lysosomes (de Duve): acid hydrolases at pH ~5; digestion, autophagy, autolysis — "suicide bags".
Ribosomes (Palade 1953): rRNA + protein, no membrane; 80S = 60S+40S (eukaryote), 70S = 50S+30S (prokaryote/organelles); polysomes; translation.
Nucleus (Brown 1831): double envelope + pores, nucleolus (rRNA factory), chromatin (eu- vs heterochromatin) → chromosomes with centromere; metacentric/submetacentric/acrocentric/telocentric.
Cilia/flagella: 9+2 microtubule axoneme from basal bodies; cilia short/numerous/oar-like, flagella long/few/undulating.
Inclusions: starch, glycogen, fat droplets, protein crystals, pigments, crystals — non-living stores; plant central vacuole maintains turgor.
data.summary: The eukaryotic cell is a city of membrane-bounded departments. The cellulose cell wall (with middle lamella, primary and secondary layers) gives shape but is fully permeable; the fluid-mosaic plasma membrane (Singer & Nicolson, 1972) is the selective gatekeeper. Mitochondria (cristae, matrix, own DNA, 70S ribosomes) run aerobic respiration and supply ATP; plastids — chloroplasts with grana-bearing thylakoids in stroma, chromoplasts and leucoplasts — are the plant's photosynthetic and storage organs. The endoplasmic reticulum (rough = protein synthesis, smooth = lipid/detox), the Golgi apparatus (cis receives, trans dispatches) and lysosomes (acid hydrolases, autolysis) form the endomembrane production line, while non-membranous ribosomes (80S) build proteins. The nucleus — envelope with pores, nucleolus, chromatin condensing into centromere-joined chromosomes — stores and expresses heredity. Cilia and flagella share the 9+2 axoneme for movement, and non-living inclusions (starch, glycogen, fat, crystals, vacuolar sap) fill the cytoplasm's storage needs.

mcqs.question: Which organelle is bounded by a double membrane and contains cristae?

mcqs.explanation: Eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S = 60S + 40S; 70S = 50S + 30S belongs to prokaryotes and organelles.

mcqs.question: Which face of the Golgi apparatus receives vesicles from the ER?
mcqs.explanation: The convex cis (forming) face receives ER vesicles; the concave trans (maturing) face ships modified products out.

mcqs.explanation: SER makes lipids and steroids and detoxifies drugs — abundant in steroid-secreting (and liver) cells. Protein-exporting cells are RER-rich.

mcqs.explanation: The cellulose wall is an open mesh — water and solutes pass freely; all membranes listed are selective barriers.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Inside the Eukaryotic Cell

Topic 2 established *that* eukaryotic cells have membrane-bound organelles; this topic opens every compartment and explains *how each one is built and what it does*. The syllabus names the full inventory: **cell wall, cell membrane, mitochondria, plastids, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi bodies, lysosomes, ribosomes, nucleus, chromosomes, cilia, flagella and cell inclusions**.

- **Why it matters:** every disease, drug, hormone and metabolic process acts at some organelle. Antibiotics hit ribosomes; cyanide hits mitochondria; cholesterol drugs hit the ER.
- **Study method:** for each organelle learn the same five questions — **structure (membranes?), location, chemistry, function, and the evidence/interesting fact**. NEB questions are almost always built from these five.
- **Connection:** the phospholipid bilayer from Topic 1 is the universal building unit of every structure below.

## 2. Cell Wall — The Outer Armor of Plant Cells

**Definition:** the rigid, non-living outer layer **outside the plasma membrane**, found in plants, fungi, bacteria and algae (absent in animals).

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Chemistry | Plants: **cellulose** (microfibrils in a matrix of hemicellulose and pectin). Fungi: chitin. Bacteria: peptidoglycan |
| Layers | **Middle lamella** (pectin, cements adjacent cells) → **primary wall** (thin, extensible, growing cells) → **secondary wall** (thick, rigid, lignified, mature cells) |
| Functions | Shape and rigidity; protection against mechanical injury and pathogens; prevents bursting in hypotonic water (turgor pressure); plasmodesmata allow transport between cells |

**Key concept:** the wall is **fully permeable** — it is *not* the selective barrier; the membrane is. Water moves freely through the wall; osmosis is decided by the membrane.

## 3. Cell Membrane (Plasma Membrane) — The Selective Barrier

### 3.1 Structure — the fluid-mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972)

- A **phospholipid bilayer** ~7–8 nm thick: hydrophilic heads face the aqueous inside and outside; hydrophobic tails form the interior.
- **Proteins** float like icebergs in the lipid sea: **integral (intrinsic) proteins** span the membrane (channels, carriers, pumps); **peripheral (extrinsic) proteins** sit on the surfaces (enzymes, anchors).
- **Cholesterol** in animal membranes stabilises fluidity across temperatures.
- **Glycoproteins and glycolipids** on the outer face form the glycocalyx — cell recognition.
- The membrane is **fluid** (lipids and proteins move laterally) and a **mosaic** (patchwork of proteins) — hence the name.

### 3.2 Functions

1. **Selective permeability** — decides what enters and leaves (small non-polar molecules diffuse freely; ions need channels/pumps).
2. **Transport** — passive (diffusion, osmosis, facilitated diffusion) and active (ATP-driven pumps, e.g. Na⁺/K⁺ pump).
3. **Endocytosis and exocytosis** — bulk transport in vesicles (phagocytosis, pinocytosis).
4. **Recognition and signalling** — receptors for hormones; glycoprotein identity markers.
5. **Compartmentalisation** — the same bilayer principle builds every organelle.

**Historical models (short-answer favourite):** Robertson (unit membrane, 1950s) → Singer & Nicolson (fluid mosaic, 1972). Also recall: Overton (lipid nature), Gorter & Grendel (bilayer from RBC lipids, 1925), Davson–Danielli (protein sandwich).

## 4. Mitochondria — The Powerhouse

### 4.1 Structure

- **Double-membraned organelle**, 0.5–1.0 µm wide, rod or sausage shaped ("chondriosome" — granules seen by Kölliker, 1880s; named by Benda, 1898).
- **Outer membrane:** smooth, permeable to small molecules (porins).
- **Inner membrane:** folded into **cristae** — folds that hugely increase surface area; studded with **oxysomes (F₁ particles)** where ATP is made. Cristae density reflects the cell's energy demand (heart muscle: very dense).
- **Matrix:** contains enzymes of the **Krebs cycle**, circular **mitochondrial DNA**, **70S ribosomes**, tRNA and enzymes of fat/protein oxidation.
- Semi-autonomous: mitochondria divide by fission like bacteria (endosymbiotic evidence).

### 4.2 Function

- **Aerobic respiration:** pyruvate → Krebs cycle (matrix) → electron transport chain + oxidative phosphorylation (inner membrane) → ~36 ATP per glucose.
- Stores and releases Ca²⁺; synthesises some lipids and amino acids; generates heat (brown fat).

**NEB 2022 asked it directly:** the mitochondrion is the "powerhouse of the cell" because it carries out aerobic respiration and produces most of the cell's ATP.

## 5. Plastids — The Plant-Only Organelles

Plastids are double-membraned, DNA-bearing organelles found **only in plants and algae**, classified by pigment:

| Type | Pigment | Colour | Function | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Chloroplast** | Chlorophyll a, b + carotenoids | Green | Photosynthesis | Mesophyll cells |
| **Chromoplast** | Carotenoids (carotene, xanthophyll) | Yellow/orange/red | Pigmentation, attract pollinators and seed dispersers | Tomato fruit, carrot root, petals |
| **Leucoplast** | No pigment | Colourless | Storage: amyloplast (starch), elaioplast (oil), aleuroplast (protein) | Potato tuber, castor seed |

### 5.1 Chloroplast structure (draw this in exams)

- Oval, 4–10 µm; **double membrane** envelope.
- Inside: colourless **stroma** (enzymes of the Calvin cycle, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes) and **grana** — stacks of disc-like **thylakoids** holding chlorophyll in their membranes (light reaction site). Grana are connected by **stroma lamellae**.
- Semi-autonomous like mitochondria — own DNA and ribosomes (endosymbiosis).

**Functions:** photosynthesis (light reaction on thylakoids, carbon fixation in stroma); stores starch temporarily.

## 6. Endoplasmic Reticulum — The Intracellular Highway

**Definition:** a network (reticulum) of membrane-bound tubules, vesicles and flattened sacs (**cisternae**) running from the nuclear envelope outward. Discovered by Porter, Claude and Fullam (1945) in cultured cells.

| Type | Structure | Ribosomes? | Main role | Where abundant |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Rough ER (RER)** | Flattened cisternae, studded with ribosomes | Yes (80S) | Synthesis and folding of proteins destined for membranes, lysosomes or secretion | Protein-exporting cells: pancreatic acinar cells, plasma cells |
| **Smooth ER (SER)** | Tubular network, no ribosomes | No | Lipid and steroid synthesis; detoxification of drugs; Ca²⁺ storage | Steroid-secreting cells, liver, muscle (as sarcoplasmic reticulum) |

**Functions:** synthesis and transport of materials; the ER lumen connects to the nuclear envelope and Golgi — part of the **endomembrane system**; provides surface for enzyme attachment; in muscle, the sarcoplasmic reticulum releases Ca²⁺ for contraction.

## 7. Golgi Apparatus — The Packaging and Dispatch Department

- Discovered by **Camillo Golgi (1898)** in nerve cells (silver stain).
- Structure: stacks of 4–8 curved, flattened membrane sacs (**cisternae**) with a convex **forming (cis) face** receiving vesicles from the ER and a concave **maturing (trans) face** shipping vesicles outward.
- **Functions:**
  1. **Modification** of proteins and lipids arriving from the ER (glycosylation — adding sugars).
  2. **Packaging** into secretory vesicles, lysosomes and membrane-bound granules.
  3. **Secretion** — dispatch to the cell surface (exocytosis).
  4. **Source of lysosomes** and of the **cell plate** during plant cytokinesis.
  5. **Complex sugar synthesis** (mucopolysaccharides, plant cell-wall matrix).

**Conceptual flow to memorise:** RER (make protein) → vesicle → Golgi cis face (modify) → trans face (package) → vesicle → destination (membrane / lysosome / secretion).

## 8. Lysosomes — The Suicide Bags

- Discovered by **Christian de Duve (1949/1955**, Nobel 1974): single-membraned sacs (~0.2–0.8 µm) packed with ~50 **acid hydrolases** (digestive enzymes active at acidic pH ~5).
- **Why they don't digest the cell:** the inner membrane's H⁺-pump keeps the lumen acidic while the cytosol stays near pH 7.2, where the enzymes are inactive — compartmentalisation in action.
- **Forms:** primary lysosome (fresh enzymes) → secondary lysosome (fusing with food vacuole = digestive vacuole) → residual body (undigested waste, expelled by exocytosis).
- **Functions:** intracellular and extracellular digestion; digestion of worn-out organelles (**autophagy**); destruction of engulfed pathogens (in white blood cells); **autolysis** — rupture releases enzymes and digests the cell itself, hence "suicide bags" (e.g. tadpole tail reabsorption during metamorphosis, uterine wall breakdown at menstruation).

**Organelle address book — who does what, where (highly classified)**

| Organelle | Membranes | Core job | Marker enzyme / feature |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mitochondrion | Double (cristae inside) | ATP by aerobic respiration | Own circular DNA + 70S ribosomes |
| Chloroplast | Double (grana inside) | Photosynthesis | Chlorophyll in thylakoids; own DNA |
| Rough ER | Single, ribosome-studded | Protein synthesis + transport | Ribosomes on cytosolic face |
| Smooth ER | Single, no ribosomes | Lipids, detox, Ca2+ store | Abundant in liver and muscle cells |
| Golgi apparatus | Stacked cisternae | Modify, package, dispatch | cis (receiving) vs trans (shipping) faces |
| Lysosome | Single vesicle | Intracellular digestion | Acid hydrolases working at pH ~5 |
| Ribosome | No membrane | Protein synthesis | 80S; free or ER-bound |
| Nucleus | Double envelope with pores | Stores genome; transcription | Nucleolus makes ribosome subunits |

## 9. Ribosomes — The Protein Factories

- Discovered by **Palade (1953**, Nobel 1974) — dense granules ~15–20 nm, made of **rRNA + proteins**, **no membrane**.
- Two subunits: **eukaryotic 80S = 60S + 40S**; prokaryotic/organelle **70S = 50S + 30S**.
- Occur **free in the cytosol** (making proteins used inside the cell) or **attached to RER** (making secretory/membrane proteins). Several ribosomes on one mRNA form a **polyribosome (polysome)**.
- **Function:** site of protein synthesis (translation) — they read mRNA codons and link amino acids by peptide bonds. Because of the 70S/80S difference, antibiotics (streptomycin, tetracycline) can block bacterial ribosomes without stopping ours.

## 10. Nucleus — The Control Centre

### 10.1 Structure

- Discovered by **Robert Brown (1831)**. Usually one per cell (multinucleate cells exist — coenocytes); absent in mature RBCs and sieve tubes.
- **Nuclear envelope:** double membrane with **perinuclear space**; perforated by **nuclear pores** (complex of proteins) that regulate traffic of mRNA out and proteins in.
- **Nucleoplasm:** nucleic acids + proteins + enzymes.
- **Nucleolus:** dense, rounded, membraneless region of rRNA genes — the **ribosome factory**.
- **Chromatin:** DNA + histones in two forms — **euchromatin** (loose, active transcription) and **heterochromatin** (condensed, inactive).

### 10.2 Chromosomes — the packaged genome

- Chromatin condenses into visible **chromosomes** during division. Each chromosome has two **chromatids** joined at the **centromere (primary constriction)**; some carry a secondary constriction with a **satellite**.
- Nucleosome organisation: DNA wound around histone octamers ("beads on a string").
- **Chromosome types by centromere position:** metacentric (middle), submetacentric (off-middle), acrocentric (near end), telocentric (at end).
- **Karyotype** = the ordered photograph of all chromosomes of a species.
- **Functions of the nucleus:** controls all cell activities through gene expression; stores hereditary information; ribosome production; cell division distributes its DNA.

**Deep dive — the endosymbiont clue.** Mitochondria and chloroplasts each carry their own circular DNA, their own 70S ribosomes and a double membrane — the signature of bacteria that moved inside larger cells and stayed. The inner membrane corresponds to the original bacterial membrane; the outer one is the host's engulfing vacuole. NEB loves this as a link between cell structure and evolution: organelle anatomy is fossil evidence you can see in every cell.

## 11. Cilia and Flagella — The Motors

| Basis | Cilia | Flagella |
|---|---|---|
| Size | Short (5–10 µm), numerous | Long (100–200 µm), one or few |
| Movement | Oar-like, coordinated beating | Whip-like, undulating |
| Examples | Paramecium surface, tracheal epithelium | Sperm tail, Euglena |
| Organisation | Both arise from basal bodies and have the **9+2 axoneme**: 9 fused microtubule doublets around a central pair, wrapped in a membrane | Same 9+2 arrangement |

**Function:** locomotion of unicellular organisms; movement of fluid/mucus over tissues; in humans, cilia sweep mucus in the airway — smoking destroys them (real-life link).

## 12. Cell Inclusions — The Non-Living Contents

**Cell inclusions** are non-living, non-membrane-bound deposits in the cytoplasm — stored food or waste:

| Inclusion | Nature | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Starch grains | Stored carbohydrate (plants) | Potato tuber |
| Glycogen granules | Animal storage carbohydrate | Liver, muscle |
| Fat droplets | Stored lipid | Adipose cells, oil seeds |
| Protein crystals (aleuroplasts) | Stored protein | Castor/Aleurites seeds, aleurone layer of grains |
| Pigment granules | Melanin etc. | Skin, hair cells |
| Mineral crystals | Calcium oxalate (raphides), silica | Plant cells |
| Vacuoles (with tonoplast) | Sap, water, dissolved salts/food/wastes | Plant central vacuole — turgor, storage, digestion |

**Vacuole concept:** in plants the central vacuole is a dominant, tonoplast-bound compartment storing water, salts, sugars, pigments and wastes, and maintaining **turgor pressure** that keeps non-woody plants upright.

## 13. Master Comparison Tables

### 13.1 Double-membraned vs single-membraned vs non-membraned organelles

| Membranes | Organelles | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Double | Nucleus (envelope), mitochondria, chloroplasts | Enclose their own DNA/ribosomes; semi-autonomous (endosymbiotic origin) |
| Single | ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vacuoles, microbodies (peroxisomes, glyoxysomes) | Part of the endomembrane system; exchange by vesicles |
| None | Ribosomes, centrioles, nucleolus, cytoskeleton, inclusions | Assembled directly in cytoplasm |

### 13.2 Mitochondria vs chloroplast (guaranteed comparison)

| Basis | Mitochondria | Chloroplast |
|---|---|---|
| Occurrence | All aerobic eukaryotes | Only plants and algae |
| Pigment | None | Chlorophyll a, b, carotenoids |
| Internal folds | Cristae (tubular/sheet infolds of inner membrane) | Thylakoids stacked into grana suspended in stroma |
| Reaction carried out | Respiration — releases energy as ATP | Photosynthesis — traps light to make glucose |
| Gases | Consumes O₂, releases CO₂ | Consumes CO₂, releases O₂ |
| Common features | Double membrane, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, divide by fission | Same — evidence of common endosymbiotic origin |

### 13.3 Rough ER vs smooth ER

| Basis | RER | SER |
|---|---|---|
| Ribosomes | Present on outer surface | Absent |
| Shape | Flattened cisternae | Tubular network |
| Synthesises | Proteins (for secretion/membranes) | Lipids, steroids; detoxifies drugs |
| Continues as | Connected to nuclear envelope; feeds Golgi | Often continuous with RER |
| Special form | — | Sarcoplasmic reticulum in muscle (Ca²⁺ store) |

### 13.4 Organelle discovery quick table

| Organelle | Discoverer | Year |
|---|---|---|
| Cell | Robert Hooke | 1665 |
| Nucleus | Robert Brown | 1831 |
| Golgi apparatus | Camillo Golgi | 1898 |
| Mitochondria (named) | Benda (seen by Kölliker) | 1898 |
| ER | Porter, Claude & Fullam | 1945 |
| Ribosome | Palade | 1953 |
| Lysosome | Christian de Duve | 1949–55 |
| Fluid-mosaic model | Singer & Nicolson | 1972 |

## 14. Conceptual Relationships

- **Topic 1 → here:** every organelle is built from the biomolecules — phospholipid membranes, protein machines, DNA in nucleus/mitochondria/chloroplast.
- **Here → Topic 4:** chromosomes organise for division; the cell plate from Golgi separates plant daughter cells.
- **Here → respiration/photosynthesis (later units):** mitochondria and chloroplasts are the two energy organelles whose chemistry powers the biosphere.
- **Here → health:** lysosome storage diseases, mitochondrial myopathies, cilia damage from smoking, and antibiotic action on 70S ribosomes.
- **Here → ecology:** chloroplasts capture the solar energy that flows through every food chain.

## 15. Exam Orientation

### 15.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

| Year | Unit | Topic | Question | Marks | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2078/2022 | Biomolecules & Cell Biology | Mitochondria | Why is the mitochondrion called the powerhouse of the cell? | 2 | Reasoning |

*(This unit's bank carries one direct question here, but this topic supplies the organelle knowledge behind many unit-1 questions — organelle structure is the most diagram-tested area.)*

### 15.2 Common examination mistakes

1. Drawing chloroplast grana without **stroma lamellae** connecting them, or omitting **stroma**.
2. Writing "lysosomes digest the cell" without the suicide-bag mechanism (**autolysis** after rupture).
3. Confusing **cristae** (mitochondria) with **thylakoids/grana** (chloroplasts).
4. Saying ribosomes have a membrane — they are **non-membranous**.
5. Forgetting that the **cell wall is fully permeable** and the membrane is the selective one.
6. Mixing up **cis** (forming, receives from ER) and **trans** (maturing, ships out) faces of the Golgi.

### Extra depth — mitochondrion and chloroplast as semi-autonomous organelles
Both carry their own circular DNA, 70S ribosomes and double membranes, and both divide by fission — supporting the **endosymbiotic theory**: ancestral eukaryotes engulfed aerobic bacteria (→ mitochondria) and cyanobacteria (→ chloroplasts). The inner mitochondrial membrane folds into cristae carrying the electron-transport chain; the chloroplast stacks thylakoids into grana with the stroma around them. Mitochondria are in every aerobic eukaryote; chloroplasts only in plants and algae — the cleanest single distinction between the two cell types.

### Extra depth — the endomembrane team
The ER, Golgi, lysosomes and vesicles form one functional assembly line: rough ER (studded with ribosomes) synthesises proteins → transport vesicles → Golgi modifies, sorts and packages (glycosylation, phosphate addition) → secretory vesicles ship to the membrane, while lysosomes bud off carrying hydrolytic enzymes at pH ~4.8. Smooth ER makes lipids and detoxifies drugs (abundant in liver cells). Defects show as disease: Zellweger syndrome (peroxisome failure), I-cell disease (Golgi tagging failure) — examiners love one named example.

### Extra depth — cytoskeleton and cell inclusions
Beyond the membrane-bound organelles, the cell has a protein scaffold: microtubules (tubulin; spindle fibres, cilia/flagella 9+2 array), microfilaments (actin; streaming, cleavage furrow) and intermediate filaments (keratin; mechanical strength). Cilia and flagella share the 9+2 microtubule core with dynein arms that slide tubules to bend them. Cell inclusions — starch grains, glycogen, lipid droplets, crystals — are non-living stored material, not organelles.
confusion: **Cell wall vs cell membrane:** the wall is outside, rigid, fully permeable, non-living; the membrane is living, selective, and the true gatekeeper of the cell.
**Cristae vs thylakoids:** cristae are folds of the mitochondrial *inner membrane*; thylakoids are separate flattened discs *inside* the chloroplast stroma, stacked into grana.
**Lysosome vs vacuole:** lysosomes are single-membraned enzyme sacs for digestion; the plant central vacuole is mainly storage/turgor, though it also contains hydrolases.
**RER vs SER:** ribosomes on the surface define RER and protein synthesis; smooth tubules without ribosomes make lipids and detoxify.
**Cilia vs flagella:** same 9+2 axoneme, but cilia are short, numerous and beat like oars; flagella are long, few and undulate.
**Nucleolus vs nucleus:** the nucleolus is a membraneless sub-region of the nucleus that makes rRNA/ribosomes — not a separate organelle.
**Inclusions vs organelles:** inclusions (starch, fat, crystals) are non-living, non-membrane-bound deposits; organelles are living, organised functional structures.

practiceQuestions: **Short answer (2m): Why is the mitochondrion called the powerhouse of the cell?** — Because it performs aerobic respiration: the Krebs cycle in the matrix and the electron transport chain on the cristae convert food energy into most of the cell's ATP, the universal energy currency.

**Short answer (2m): Distinguish RER and SER (two points).** — RER bears ribosomes on flattened cisternae and synthesises proteins for secretion/membranes; SER lacks ribosomes, is tubular, and synthesises lipids/steroids, detoxifies drugs and stores Ca²⁺.

**Short answer (2m): What are cell inclusions? Give two examples.** — Non-living, non-membrane-bound cytoplasmic deposits of food or waste. Examples: starch grains (potato), fat droplets (adipose tissue); also glycogen, protein crystals, pigment granules.

**Short answer (2m): State the fluid-mosaic model in one sentence and name its proposer.** — The membrane is a fluid phospholipid bilayer with a mosaic of embedded integral and peripheral proteins that can move laterally — proposed by Singer and Nicolson (1972).

**Long answer (5m): Describe the structure of a chloroplast with a labelled diagram.** — Double envelope → stroma (Calvin enzymes, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes) → grana of stacked thylakoids carrying chlorophyll (light reaction) → stroma lamellae connecting grana. Functions: light reaction on thylakoids, carbon fixation in stroma, temporary starch storage.

**Long answer (5m): Describe the structure and role of the Golgi apparatus.** — Stacks of curved cisternae; cis (forming) face receives ER vesicles, trans (maturing) face dispatches. Roles: modification (glycosylation), packaging, secretion, lysosome formation, plant cell-plate formation, complex polysaccharide synthesis. Include the RER→Golgi→destination flow diagram.

**Conceptual (3m): Why is the cell membrane called selectively permeable while the cell wall is not?** — The membrane is a lipid bilayer with specific channels, carriers and pumps: small non-polar molecules pass by diffusion, ions and sugars only through controlled proteins — it discriminates. The cellulose wall is an open mesh with large pores: water and solutes pass freely; it provides support, not selection.

**Conceptual (3m): "Lysosomes are suicide bags." Justify.** — Lysosomes hold acid hydrolases that can digest every class of biomolecule. Normally the membrane isolates them and the cytosolic pH keeps the enzymes inactive. When a cell is damaged or programmed to die, lysosomes rupture, the enzymes flood the cytoplasm and digest the cell (autolysis) — e.g. tadpole tail resorption, menstrual endometrium breakdown.

**Application (3m): A patient's ciliated airway epithelium is destroyed by years of smoking. What functional loss follows?** — Cilia normally beat mucus loaded with dust and microbes upward to the pharynx. Without cilia, mucus stagnates, pathogens and particles accumulate, causing chronic cough and repeated chest infections — smokers' "smoker's cough" is the compensatory cough reflex.

enrichedContent.summary: The eukaryotic cell is a city of membrane-bounded departments. The cellulose cell wall (with middle lamella, primary and secondary layers) gives shape but is fully permeable; the fluid-mosaic plasma membrane (Singer & Nicolson, 1972) is the selective gatekeeper. Mitochondria (cristae, matrix, own DNA, 70S ribosomes) run aerobic respiration and supply ATP; plastids — chloroplasts with grana-bearing thylakoids in stroma, chromoplasts and leucoplasts — are the plant's photosynthetic and storage organs. The endoplasmic reticulum (rough = protein synthesis, smooth = lipid/detox), the Golgi apparatus (cis receives, trans dispatches) and lysosomes (acid hydrolases, autolysis) form the endomembrane production line, while non-membranous ribosomes (80S) build proteins. The nucleus — envelope with pores, nucleolus, chromatin condensing into centromere-joined chromosomes — stores and expresses heredity. Cilia and flagella share the 9+2 axoneme for movement, and non-living inclusions (starch, glycogen, fat, crystals, vacuolar sap) fill the cytoplasm's storage needs.
