practiceQuestions: **NEB-style (6m): Prepare benzene in the laboratory from (a) sodium benzoate and (b) phenol, writing balanced equations with conditions.** — **(a) Soda-lime decarboxylation:** heat sodium benzoate strongly with soda lime (NaOH + CaO): C₆H₅COONa + NaOH --(CaO, Δ)--> C₆H₆ + Na₂CO₃. The carboxylate group leaves as carbonate and the ring carbon takes a hydrogen. **(b) Zinc-dust reduction:** distil phenol with zinc dust: C₆H₅OH + Zn --(Δ)--> C₆H₆ + ZnO. Zinc removes the phenolic oxygen as ZnO; the C–O bond is replaced by C–H. **Conditions quoted:** strong heat with the soda-lime mixture for (a); red heat with excess zinc dust for (b). **Deep point:** the two routes are functionally opposite operations on the ring's substituent — one deletes a carboxylate, one deletes an oxygen — and both leave the aromatic sextet untouched; the ring's stability is why such drastic conditions (fusion, red heat) still give clean products.

**NEB-style (5m): Describe the preparation of benzene from ethyne, giving the equation and conditions, and explain the thermodynamic driving force.** — **Reaction:** pass ethyne through a red-hot iron tube at about 873 K: **3C₂H₂ --(red-hot Fe, 873 K)--> C₆H₆** (Berthelot's synthesis). **Driving force:** three C≡C triple bonds (high-energy, each ~835 kJ/mol of bond energy with two π components) are converted into the aromatic ring's delocalised sextet — the product sits far lower in energy because the cyclic conjugation gains the ~150 kJ/mol resonance stabilisation on top of normal bond energies. **Role of the tube:** the red-hot iron supplies the activation energy for cyclisation; the hot surface also favours the six-membered cyclic transition over linear oligomers. **Deep point:** the trimerisation is the one route that *builds* the ring rather than editing it — and the fact that heat alone accomplishes it is evidence of how much energy the aromatic sextet stores back: the reaction is exothermic precisely because the product is aromatic.

**NEB-style (5m): Why is soda lime (a mixture of NaOH and CaO) used for decarboxylation instead of sodium hydroxide alone? Give the equation.** — **NaOH's job:** provides the OH⁻ that converts the acid–carboxylate chemistry and accepts the sodium of the carboxylate into the carbonate by-product. **CaO's jobs:** (1) raises the fusion temperature — pure NaOH melts at 318 °C and the reaction needs a strongly heated, dry, pasty fusion; CaO is refractory and keeps the mass solid at the working temperature; (2) absorbs water — dry conditions suppress side hydrolysis and keep the fusion from frothing. **Equation:** C₆H₅COONa + NaOH --(CaO, Δ)--> C₆H₆ + Na₂CO₃. **Deep point:** "soda lime" is a conditions-and-reagents package — the exam's condition slot (CaO, Δ) encodes two physical reasons; being able to say *why* CaO is there, rather than only *that* it is, converts a recall mark into an understanding mark.

**NEB-style (6m): Sodium p-methylbenzoate is subjected to soda-lime decarboxylation. Predict the product, write the equation, and explain the generalisation.** — **Product:** the carboxylate carbon is replaced by hydrogen; the para-methyl substituent rides through untouched ⟹ **toluene (methylbenzene)**. **Equation:** CH₃–C₆H₄–COONa + NaOH --(CaO, Δ)--> CH₃–C₆H₅ + Na₂CO₃. **Generalisation:** decarboxylation edits only the −COONa group: any ring substituent (methyl, chloro, methoxy) is carried into the product at its original position — the reaction is a universal "carboxyl-out, hydrogen-in" operator on aromatic rings. **Check:** the product's formula C₇H₈ matches toluene; the para relationship is moot after deletion (the ring is monosubstituted). **Deep point:** the generalisation is why decarboxylation appears in synthesis *plans*, not just preparations — it is how a carboxyl group acts as a temporary blocking or directing group that is later removed; the ring's substituent map survives the operation, which is the whole point.

data.title: Physical properties of benzene
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Benzene's Physical Profile

Benzene is a **colourless, mobile liquid** with a characteristic odour: bp 80.5 °C (80.1 °C in some texts), mp 5.5 °C, density 0.879 g/cm³ (lighter than water), immiscible with water, and an excellent solvent for non-polar and moderately polar solutes. Every one of these numbers has a structural reason.

## 2. Theorem Mirror

- **State and appearance:** colourless liquid; characteristic (aromatic) odour; volatile.
- **Boiling point 80.5 °C:** higher than cyclohexane (81 °C is close) but the comparison that matters — vs expected for its molar mass, benzene's planar disk shape gives strong instantaneous dipole dispersion contact.
- **Melting point 5.5 °C:** remarkably high for a small molecule — the flat hexagonal disks pack efficiently into a crystal lattice (symmetry aids packing); the high mp/symmetry link is the physical proof of planarity.
- **Density 0.879 g/cm³:** floats on water; immiscible — the non-polar ring cannot hydrogen-bond into the water network.
- **Solvent behaviour:** dissolves iodine, sulphur, rubber, fats, many organics; the "like dissolves like" non-polar champion.

## 3. Deep Conceptual — Symmetry Packs, Shape Boils

- **Melting point is a packing story:** 5.5 °C is high for a 78 g/mol molecule (cyclohexane, 84 g/mol, melts at 6.5 °C — similar, but n-hexane, 86 g/mol, melts at −95 °C!). The difference is shape: flat, rigid, symmetric disks stack into efficient crystals; floppy chains waste contact area in the solid. Benzene's mp is the macroscopic fingerprint of its planar hexagonal geometry.
- **Boiling point is a surface story:** liquids boil when molecules escape the collective dispersion contact; benzene's disk presents large flat faces for π–π and dispersion contact, giving bp 80.5 °C — comparable to cyclohexane's despite lower molar mass, because contact quality compensates for mass.
- **Water immiscibility is a network story:** inserting benzene into water would break hydrogen-bond bridges without replacing them — the ring offers no donors or acceptors. The two-layer test tube picture is the hydrophobic effect in one glance.

## 4. Deep Conceptual — Reading a Property Table as Evidence

- Each physical constant cross-checks a structural claim: mp 5.5 °C (planarity/packing), bp 80.5 °C (contact area), density < 1 (no strong interaction with water), immiscibility (no H-bonding), sooty combustion (92.3% C). The table is not trivia — it is the same delocalisation story told in five different instruments.
- **Solvent power follows polarity:** benzene dissolves non-polar solutes (I₂, S₈, oils) via dispersion; it will *not* dissolve ionic or strongly H-bonding solutes — the solvent list is the polarity list read backwards.

## 5. Worked Example Types

- **Type A — recite with reasons:** state each property with its structural cause.
- **Type B — compare:** benzene vs cyclohexane vs hexane on mp/bp — the shape argument.
- **Type C — miscibility prediction:** which of two solvents mixes with benzene, why.
- **Type D — density arithmetic:** mass of benzene delivered by a measured volume.

## 6. Common Confusions

**"Benzene is denser than water because it is aromatic":** 0.879 < 1 — it floats; aromaticity does not imply density. **"High mp means strong hydrogen bonding":** benzene has none — its mp is pure packing efficiency.

practiceQuestions: **NEB-style (5m): List the important physical properties of benzene, giving a structural reason for each.** — **Appearance:** colourless, mobile, volatile liquid with a characteristic odour. **Boiling point 80.5 °C:** the flat disk presents large faces for dispersion (and π–π) contact — strong intermolecular attraction for its mass. **Melting point 5.5 °C:** flat, symmetric hexagons pack efficiently into the crystal — packing quality, not hydrogen bonding, sets the high mp. **Density 0.879 g/cm³:** less than water — it floats; the non-polar ring forms no strong interactions to compact it. **Water immiscibility:** the ring offers no H-bond donors or acceptors, so it cannot plug into water's network. **Solvent power:** dissolves non-polar solutes (iodine, sulphur, fats) by dispersion. **Combustion:** burns with a smoky, luminous flame — 92.3% carbon. **Deep point:** each property is a different instrument measuring the same two facts — planarity and non-polarity; answering "property + reason" pairs is the full-mark pattern.

**NEB-style (6m): Benzene (78 g/mol) melts at 5.5 C while n-hexane (86 g/mol) melts at -95 C. Explain the contrast and state what it proves.** — **Mass is not the decider:** hexane is heavier yet melts 100 °C lower. **The decider is crystal packing:** n-hexane is a floppy chain — in the solid it must adopt extended conformations and still leaves poor contact, weak van der Waals registration between chains ⟹ low mp. Benzene is a rigid, flat, sixfold-symmetric disk — disks stack face-to-face with maximal contact per molecule and minimal wasted volume ⟹ efficient lattice, high mp for its size. **What it proves:** the planar, symmetric geometry of the benzene ring — a macroscopic property (melting point) acting as evidence for a molecular-structure claim. **Deep point:** physical-property comparisons are structure determinations in disguise — when two molecules of similar mass differ by 100 °C in mp, the cause is shape and rigidity; the argument generalises to why spherical/planar molecules (neopentane, benzene) melt high and boil relatively low.

**NEB-style (5m): A mixture of benzene and water is shaken and allowed to stand. Describe what is observed and explain at the molecular level.** — **Observation:** two layers form — benzene on top (density 0.879 < 1.00), water below; a sharp meniscus, no mixing even on standing. **Molecular explanation:** water molecules hold each other by an extensive hydrogen-bond network; benzene's ring has no O–H, N–H or lone-pair-exposed sites to donate or accept hydrogen bonds — inserting benzene into water would break water–water H-bonds and replace them with only weak dispersion contact ⟹ energetically unfavourable (the hydrophobic effect). The system minimises free energy by demixing. **Deep point:** immiscibility is usually stated as "non-polar vs polar" — the deeper statement is about *networks*: each liquid keeps its own interaction network intact rather than paying to merge two incompatible ones; that is why even vigorous shaking only emulsifies temporarily.

**NEB-style (6m): Iodine is shaken with (a) water and (b) benzene. Describe and explain the distribution of iodine between the two solvents.** — **Observation:** iodine is barely soluble in water (pale yellow-brown, ~0.3 g/L) but dissolves readily in benzene, giving the characteristic violet solution. **Explanation:** I₂ is non-polar and polarisable — it interacts with benzene's polarisable π cloud by strong dispersion (and weak charge-transfer) forces; water offers only weak dipole-induced contacts and I₂ cannot H-bond ⟹ the non-polar solvent wins decisively. **Distribution:** on shaking with both, iodine partitions overwhelmingly into the benzene layer (the basis of the classic distribution-coefficient demonstration). **Deep point:** "like dissolves like" is the slogan; the mechanism is contact quality — a polarisable solute seeks the most polarisable solvent, and the π cloud of benzene is the best contact available in the pair; the violet colour itself signals I₂ pairs in a non-polar medium (vs the brown complexation seen in polar/donating solvents like KI solution).
keyPoints: Colourless liquid, characteristic odour; bp 80.5 C, mp 5.5 C, density 0.879 g/cm3 (floats on water), immiscible with water, excellent non-polar solvent, burns with sooty flame. mp argument: flat symmetric disks pack efficiently (vs n-hexane mp -95 C at similar mass) - packing is the proof of planarity. bp argument: disk faces give strong dispersion contact. Immiscibility: no H-bond donors/acceptors for the water network.
data.summary: Benzene's physical profile — colourless liquid, bp 80.5 °C, mp 5.5 °C, density 0.879, water-immiscible, non-polar solvent, sooty flame — is one structure read by five instruments: flat symmetric disks pack (high mp), present broad faces (bp), refuse the water network (immiscibility), dissolve the non-polar (solvent list), and burn carbon-rich (flame). The hexane comparison turns the melting point into proof of planarity, and every property question wants the number *with* its structural reason.

data.topicTitle: Chemical properties of benzene: addition reactions (hydrogen, halogen); electrophilic substitution reactions: orientation of benzene derivatives (o, m and p), nitration, sulphonation, halogenation, Friedel-Crafts reaction (alkylation and acylation)
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Benzene's Chemistry: Two Doors, One Preference

Benzene reacts by **addition** (H₂/Ni, X₂/UV, O₃) only under forcing conditions, and by **electrophilic substitution** (nitration, sulphonation, halogenation, Friedel–Crafts) readily — the preference is the resonance energy at work. Orientation in disubstitution follows the director classification: o/p versus meta.

## 2. Theorem Mirror

- **Addition routes:** hydrogenation C₆H₆ + 3H₂ --(Ni, 475 K)--> C₆H₆H₁₂ (cyclohexane); halogen addition C₆H₆ + 3Cl₂ --(UV/sunlight)--> C₆H₆Cl₆ (benzene hexachloride, BHC); ozonolysis → tri-ozonide → hydrolysis gives 3 glyoxal (proving the three-bond skeleton).
- **Nitration:** C₆H₆ + HNO₃ --(conc H₂SO₄, 50–60 °C)--> C₆H₅NO₂ + H₂O; electrophile NO₂⁺ generated: HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ ⇌ NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻.
- **Sulphonation:** C₆H₆ + conc H₂SO₄ (or fuming/oleum) → C₆H₅SO₃H + H₂O; electrophile SO₃.
- **Halogenation:** C₆H₆ + Cl₂ --(FeCl₃, dark)--> C₆H₅Cl + HCl; the Lewis acid polarises X₂.
- **Friedel–Crafts alkylation:** C₆H₆ + R–Cl --(anhyd AlCl₃)--> C₆H₅–R + HCl; limitations — polyalkylation (product more reactive), carbocation rearrangement, fails on strongly deactivated rings.
- **Friedel–Crafts acylation:** C₆H₆ + RCOCl --(AlCl₃)--> C₆H₅COR + HCl; acylium ion R–C≡O⁺ does not rearrange; the acyl group deactivates ⟹ mono-acylation.
- **Orientation:** activating o/p directors (−OH, −NH₂, −OR, −R; halogens deactivating but o/p) vs meta directors (−NO₂, −SO₃H, −CHO, −COOH, −CN); toluene side-chain oxidation (KMnO₄) → benzoic acid.

## 3. Deep Conceptual — The Substitution Mechanism as One Story

- Every electrophilic substitution is the same three acts: **(1)** the electrophile E⁺ attacks the π cloud forming the σ-complex (arenium/Wheland intermediate) — the ring loses aromaticity at one carbon; **(2)** the σ-complex is stabilised by delocalising the positive charge over o/p positions (resonance structures); **(3)** a base removes the proton from the attacked carbon, restoring the aromatic sextet. Step 1 is slow (rate-determining); step 3 is fast and *driven by the regained resonance energy*.
- **Why the σ-complex explains orientation:** a director's effect is read in the σ-complex — an electron-donating group stabilises the positive charge when the electrophile attacks ortho/para to it (the charge sits next door, donation helps); an electron-withdrawing group destabilises those same forms ⟹ meta attack, whose σ-complex keeps the charge away from the deactivator. **Orientation is σ-complex stability bookkeeping.**

## 4. Deep Conceptual — Directors: Two Questions, Two Answers

- **Reactivity** (activating vs deactivating) answers: does the substituent push electrons into the ring (−OH, −NH₂, −CH₃: activate) or pull (−NO₂, −COOH: deactivate)? Halogens pull *inductively* but donate *by resonance* — net deactivating yet o/p-directing: the one famous split verdict.
- **Regiochemistry** (o/p vs meta) answers: where does the σ-complex's positive charge sit relative to the substituent? Donors stabilise charge *near* them ⟹ o/p; withdrawers destabilise it ⟹ meta. The two questions are independent — which is why halogens can be deactivating *and* o/p-directing without contradiction.

## 5. Worked Example Types

- **Type A — write and condition:** each named reaction with reagents/conditions.
- **Type B — mechanism:** nitration's NO₂⁺ generation and the three-act substitution.
- **Type C — orientation prediction:** given substituents, predict the major product.
- **Type D — Friedel–Crafts diagnosis:** limitations and the acylation-vs-alkylation contrast.

## 6. Common Confusions

**"FeCl₃ is consumed":** it is a catalyst — regenerated when the HCl leaves. **"o/p directors always activate":** halogens direct o/p while deactivating — reactivity and regiochemistry are separate axes. **"Friedel–Crafts works on nitrobenzene":** strongly deactivated rings refuse it — the limitation is the deactivation itself.

The sulphuric acid generates the electrophile: HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ ⇌ NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻. **(b) Sulphonation:** C₆H₆ + fuming H₂SO₄ (H₂SO₄ + SO₃) ⇌ **C₆H₅SO₃H (benzene sulphonic acid)** + H₂O; the electrophile is SO₃ (or protonated SO₃), attacking through its sulphur. **Both are electrophilic substitutions** — the ring's hydrogen is replaced, the aromatic sextet restored. **Deep point:** the two reactions share one mechanism but different electrophile-generation chemistry — nitration's acid pair manufactures NO₂⁺ in a measurable equilibrium (the ion is directly observed in spectra), while sulphonation's electrophile comes premade in the fuming acid; quoting the electrophile is the mark-earning step in both.

**NEB 2024 (4m): Describe the mechanism of nitration of benzene.** — **Step 1 — electrophile generation:** HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ ⇌ NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻ — the sulphuric acid protonates nitric acid (H₂NO₃⁺), which loses water to give the nitronium ion NO₂⁺ (linear, O=N=O). **Step 2 — electrophilic attack (slow, rate-determining):** the π electrons of benzene attack N of NO₂⁺, forming the **σ-complex (arenium ion)** — a cyclohexadienyl cation in which the attacked carbon bears both the NO₂ group and the H, sp³-hybridised; the positive charge is delocalised over the ortho and para positions (three resonance forms). **Step 3 — deprotonation (fast):** HSO₄⁻ removes the proton from the sp³ carbon; the C–H bond electrons restore the aromatic π sextet ⟹ nitrobenzene + H₂SO₄ (catalyst regenerated). **Energy profile:** step 2's barrier is the highest — the ring pays temporary aromaticity; step 3 is downhill because aromaticity returns. **Deep point:** the mechanism is the aromaticity story in miniature — lose the sextet in step 2 (slow, costly), regain it in step 3 (fast, repaid); the resonance energy is the thermodynamic motor of the whole substitution class.

**NEB 2020 (3m): Explain why benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution rather than electrophilic addition. Compare with the behaviour of a simple alkene.** — **Benzene:** addition (e.g. of Br₂, HBr) would convert the aromatic ring into a cyclohexadiene — destroying the delocalised π system and forfeiting its ~150 kJ/mol resonance energy; substitution keeps the sextet intact (only one C–H bond trades for C–E) ⟹ substitution is thermodynamically favoured and observed under mild conditions; addition needs forcing conditions (Ni/475 K for H₂; UV for Cl₂). **Alkene:** cyclohexene has *no* aromatic stabilisation to lose — its π bond is localised and electron-rich, so electrophilic addition (decolourising bromine water instantly, no catalyst) is fast and characteristic. **Contrast in one line:** the alkene spends its π bond; benzene invests its π system and only lends it. **Deep point:** the comparison isolates the variable — same six-carbon ring, one with a delocalised sextet and one without; the opposite chemistries (addition vs substitution) are the resonance energy made visible in reactivity.

Write one of its limitations.** — **Definition:** electrophilic substitution of benzene by an alkyl group using an alkyl halide and a Lewis acid catalyst: C₆H₆ + R–Cl --(anhyd AlCl₃)--> C₆H₅–R + HCl. **Electrophile generation:** AlCl₃ coordinates the chlorine (R–Cl···AlCl₃), polarising the C–Cl bond to the point of ionisation ⟹ R⁺ (or a tight R⁺···AlCl₄⁻ pair) attacks the ring; the mechanism follows the standard three acts, with HCl leaving and AlCl₃ regenerated. **Limitation (any one):** (1) **polyalkylation** — the alkyl product (e.g. toluene) is *more* reactive than benzene (the methyl group activates), so it alkylates again ⟹ mixtures; (2) **carbocation rearrangement** — primary halides give rearranged products (n-propyl chloride delivers isopropylbenzene via the more stable secondary cation); (3) **deactivated rings refuse the reaction** — nitrobenzene, benzoic acid and other strongly deactivated aromatics do not undergo Friedel–Crafts. **Deep point:** limitation (1) is the mirror of the director logic — the product's activating substituent invites over-reaction; acylation avoids it because the acyl group *deactivates*, which is why acylation is the cleaner synthetic door.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Benzene's Chemistry: Two Doors, One Preference

Benzene reacts by **addition** (H₂/Ni, X₂/UV, O₃) only under forcing conditions, and by **electrophilic substitution** (nitration, sulphonation, halogenation, Friedel–Crafts) readily — the preference is the resonance energy at work. Orientation in disubstitution follows the director classification: o/p versus meta.

## 2. Theorem Mirror

- **Addition routes:** hydrogenation C₆H₆ + 3H₂ --(Ni, 475 K)--> C₆H₆H₁₂ (cyclohexane); halogen addition C₆H₆ + 3Cl₂ --(UV/sunlight)--> C₆H₆Cl₆ (benzene hexachloride, BHC); ozonolysis → tri-ozonide → hydrolysis gives 3 glyoxal (proving the three-bond skeleton).
- **Nitration:** C₆H₆ + HNO₃ --(conc H₂SO₄, 50–60 °C)--> C₆H₅NO₂ + H₂O; electrophile NO₂⁺ generated: HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ ⇌ NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻.
- **Sulphonation:** C₆H₆ + conc H₂SO₄ (or fuming/oleum) → C₆H₅SO₃H + H₂O; electrophile SO₃.
- **Halogenation:** C₆H₆ + Cl₂ --(FeCl₃, dark)--> C₆H₅Cl + HCl; the Lewis acid polarises X₂.
- **Friedel–Crafts alkylation:** C₆H₆ + R–Cl --(anhyd AlCl₃)--> C₆H₅–R + HCl; limitations — polyalkylation (product more reactive), carbocation rearrangement, fails on strongly deactivated rings.
- **Friedel–Crafts acylation:** C₆H₆ + RCOCl --(AlCl₃)--> C₆H₅COR + HCl; acylium ion R–C≡O⁺ does not rearrange; the acyl group deactivates ⟹ mono-acylation.
- **Orientation:** activating o/p directors (−OH, −NH₂, −OR, −R; halogens deactivating but o/p) vs meta directors (−NO₂, −SO₃H, −CHO, −COOH, −CN); toluene side-chain oxidation (KMnO₄) → benzoic acid.

## 3. Deep Conceptual — The Substitution Mechanism as One Story

- Every electrophilic substitution is the same three acts: **(1)** the electrophile E⁺ attacks the π cloud forming the σ-complex (arenium/Wheland intermediate) — the ring loses aromaticity at one carbon; **(2)** the σ-complex is stabilised by delocalising the positive charge over o/p positions (resonance structures); **(3)** a base removes the proton from the attacked carbon, restoring the aromatic sextet. Step 1 is slow (rate-determining); step 3 is fast and *driven by the regained resonance energy*.
- **Why the σ-complex explains orientation:** a director's effect is read in the σ-complex — an electron-donating group stabilises the positive charge when the electrophile attacks ortho/para to it (the charge sits next door, donation helps); an electron-withdrawing group destabilises those same forms ⟹ meta attack, whose σ-complex keeps the charge away from the deactivator. **Orientation is σ-complex stability bookkeeping.**

## 4. Deep Conceptual — Directors: Two Questions, Two Answers

- **Reactivity** (activating vs deactivating) answers: does the substituent push electrons into the ring (−OH, −NH₂, −CH₃: activate) or pull (−NO₂, −COOH: deactivate)? Halogens pull *inductively* but donate *by resonance* — net deactivating yet o/p-directing: the one famous split verdict.
- **Regiochemistry** (o/p vs meta) answers: where does the σ-complex's positive charge sit relative to the substituent? Donors stabilise charge *near* them ⟹ o/p; withdrawers destabilise it ⟹ meta. The two questions are independent — which is why halogens can be deactivating *and* o/p-directing without contradiction.

## 5. Worked Example Types

- **Type A — write and condition:** each named reaction with reagents/conditions.
- **Type B — mechanism:** nitration's NO₂⁺ generation and the three-act substitution.
- **Type C — orientation prediction:** given substituents, predict the major product.
- **Type D — Friedel–Crafts diagnosis:** limitations and the acylation-vs-alkylation contrast.

## 6. Common Confusions

**"FeCl₃ is consumed":** it is a catalyst — regenerated when the HCl leaves. **"o/p directors always activate":** halogens direct o/p while deactivating — reactivity and regiochemistry are separate axes. **"Friedel–Crafts works on nitrobenzene":** strongly deactivated rings refuse it — the limitation is the deactivation itself.

data.topicTitle: Combustion of benzene (free combustion only) and uses
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Burning Benzene and Using It

Benzene's combustion is the sooty-flame exemplar: **2C₆H₆ + 15O₂ → 12CO₂ + 6H₂O**, highly exothermic but incomplete in ordinary flames because the ring is 92.3% carbon. Its uses follow its properties: solvent, precursor to styrene/phenol/cyclohexane, and — increasingly restricted — fuel additive.

## 2. Theorem Mirror

- **Combustion equation:** 2C₆H₆ + 15O₂ → 12CO₂ + 6H₂O + heat (ΔH ≈ −3268 kJ per 2 mol).
- **Flame character:** luminous, smoky (sooty) — the C : H ratio (1 : 1) leaves carbon unoxidised in the flame's fuel-rich interior; the soot is elemental carbon escaping before full combustion.
- **Generalisation:** aromatic and high-carbon fuels burn smoky; the flame is a composition readout.
- **Principal uses:** (1) solvent for resins, fats, iodine, sulphur; (2) raw material — ethylbenzene → styrene (polystyrene), cumene → phenol + acetone, cyclohexane → nylon precursors (adipic acid), nitrobenzene → aniline (dyes); (3) motor-fuel component (anti-knock value high) — now restricted by benzene's carcinogenicity; (4) laboratory reagent and standard.

## 3. Deep Conceptual — The Sooty Flame as Stoichiometry Made Visible

- The balanced equation demands 15 O₂ per 2 benzene — an oxygen-hungry ratio. In a real flame the fuel-rich zones cannot supply that oxygen locally, so carbon is released as fine particles before reaching CO₂; these particles glow incandescently (luminous yellow) and deposit as soot. **The flame's colour is a local stoichiometry deficit.**
- **Why benzene is *more* sooty than cyclohexane:** C₆H₆ needs 7.5 O₂ per molecule; C₆H₁₂ needs 9 O₂ per molecule but delivers 6 carbons with 12 hydrogens carrying their own combustion oxygen budget — the H : C ratio (2 : 1 vs 1 : 1) is the cleaner predictor: more H per C ⟹ more complete combustion ⟹ cleaner flame.

## 4. Deep Conceptual — Uses Follow Structure, and Safety Follows Toxicity

- **Solvent use** is the non-polarity chapter (dispersion contact with non-polar solutes); **precursor use** is the substitution chemistry chapter (nitration → aniline chain; alkylation → styrene chain; hydrogenation → cyclohexane/nylon chain) — each industrial route is a syllabus reaction scaled up.
- **The safety reversal:** benzene's historical ubiquity (solvent, fuel) met its toxicology — benzene is a proven human carcinogen (bone-marrow suppression, leukaemia via its metabolites). Modern practice substitutes toluene (less volatile, metabolised differently) wherever the *solvent* property, not the ring reactivity, is needed. The uses list is now partly historical by law.

## 5. Worked Example Types

- **Type A — write and balance:** the combustion equation with coefficients.
- **Type B — explain the soot:** C% and H : C ratio reasoning.
- **Type C — list uses by category:** solvent / precursor / fuel with one example each.
- **Type D — energy calculation:** heat released from mass of benzene burnt.

## 6. Common Confusions

**"Sooty flame means incomplete equation":** the equation is complete; the *flame* is locally fuel-rich — the soot is kinetics and mixing, not stoichiometry error. **"Benzene is still a common solvent":** carcinogenicity has largely retired it from open laboratory use — toluene is the modern stand-in.

practiceQuestions: **NEB-style (5m): Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of benzene and explain why it burns with a smoky flame.** — **Equation:** 2C₆H₆ + 15O₂ → 12CO₂ + 6H₂O + heat (check: C 12 = 12; H 12 = 12; O 30 = 24 + 6 ✓). **Sooty flame explanation:** benzene's C : H ratio is 1 : 1 — 92.3% carbon by mass; in the fuel-rich interior of a normal flame the local oxygen supply cannot match the 7.5 O₂-per-molecule demand, so elemental carbon particles form, glow incandescently (the luminous yellow), and escape as soot before full oxidation. **Deep point:** the balanced equation and the smoky flame are not in conflict — the equation describes complete combustion with *sufficient* oxygen; the flame is a mixing and kinetics problem where sufficiency fails locally. Stating both halves is the full answer.

**NEB-style (6m): Compare the flames of burning benzene (C6H6) and cyclohexane (C6H12), and justify the difference using composition.** — **Benzene:** H : C = 6 : 6 = 1 ⟹ oxygen-hungry, fuel-rich zones common ⟹ **luminous, heavily sooty flame**. **Cyclohexane:** H : C = 12 : 6 = 2 ⟹ each carbon arrives with twice the hydrogen, whose combustion supplies water and drives the carbon out as CO₂ ⟹ **cleaner, less sooty flame**. **Generalisation:** down the saturation ladder (benzene → cyclohexene → cyclohexane) the H : C ratio rises 1 → 1.67 → 2 and the flame cleans progressively. **Deep point:** the H : C ratio is a better flame predictor than either C% or molar mass alone — hydrogens are the fuel's internal oxygen-delivery system, and the ratio encodes how much self-help each carbon gets; the soot ladder is a composition ladder.

**NEB-style (6m): List the important uses of benzene, grouped by the property or reaction each use exploits.** — **Solvent uses (exploit non-polarity):** dissolves resins, fats, waxes, iodine, sulphur — the dispersion-contact champion of the early chemical industry. **Precursor uses (exploit substitution and addition chemistry):** nitration → nitrobenzene → aniline (dyes industry); alkylation with ethene → ethylbenzene → styrene (polystyrene); Friedel–Crafts with propene → cumene → phenol + acetone (the cumene process); hydrogenation → cyclohexane → adipic acid (nylon-6,6 chain). **Fuel use (exploits high anti-knock value):** petrol additive — now heavily restricted. **Laboratory standard:** reference solvent and calorimetric standard. **Deep point:** each use is a syllabus reaction scaled to industry — mapping the uses back to the reactions (nitration, alkylation, hydrogenation) converts a memorisation task into a structure-uses argument.

**NEB-style (5m): Calculate the heat released when 78 g of benzene is completely burnt, given that the enthalpy of combustion of benzene is -3268 kJ per mole of reaction as written (2 mol C6H6).** — **Moles:** 78 g / 78 g/mol = 1 mol C₆H₆. **Scaling:** the quoted ΔH corresponds to 2 mol benzene ⟹ per mole: −3268/2 = −1634 kJ/mol. **Answer:** burning 78 g releases **1634 kJ**. **Cross-check via the equation:** 2C₆H₆ + 15O₂ → 12CO₂ + 6H₂O — one mole of benzene is half the reaction entity, so half the quoted enthalpy. **Deep point:** "per mole of reaction as written" is the trap — the coefficient sum (2 + 15) defines the reaction entity; dividing by the benzene coefficient before multiplying by moles is the one algebraic step that separates the correct 1634 kJ from a doubled or halved error.
keyPoints: 2C6H6 + 15O2 -> 12CO2 + 6H2O, highly exothermic; luminous sooty flame from C:H = 1:1 - fuel-rich zones release glowing carbon particles. H:C ratio predicts flame cleanliness (cyclohexane cleaner, benzene smokier). Uses: non-polar solvent; precursor (ethylbenzene->styrene, cumene->phenol+acetone, cyclohexane->nylon chain, nitrobenzene->aniline dyes); fuel anti-knock value - now restricted (carcinogen, bone-marrow/leukaemia); toluene is the modern solvent substitute.
data.summary: Benzene burns as 2C₆H₆ + 15O₂ → 12CO₂ + 6H₂O — exothermic and oxygen-hungry, with a luminous sooty flame that is the 1 : 1 H : C ratio made visible in glowing carbon particles. Its uses split by the property exploited: non-polarity (solvent), substitution and addition chemistry (styrene, phenol, aniline, nylon precursors), anti-knock value (restricted fuel). The carcinogenicity verdict has retired the solvent uses to history — toluene now stands where benzene stood — but the precursor web remains the ring's industrial biography.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Burning Benzene and Using It

Benzene's combustion is the sooty-flame exemplar: **2C₆H₆ + 15O₂ → 12CO₂ + 6H₂O**, highly exothermic but incomplete in ordinary flames because the ring is 92.3% carbon. Its uses follow its properties: solvent, precursor to styrene/phenol/cyclohexane, and — increasingly restricted — fuel additive.

## 2. Theorem Mirror

- **Combustion equation:** 2C₆H₆ + 15O₂ → 12CO₂ + 6H₂O + heat (ΔH ≈ −3268 kJ per 2 mol).
- **Flame character:** luminous, smoky (sooty) — the C : H ratio (1 : 1) leaves carbon unoxidised in the flame's fuel-rich interior; the soot is elemental carbon escaping before full combustion.
- **Generalisation:** aromatic and high-carbon fuels burn smoky; the flame is a composition readout.
- **Principal uses:** (1) solvent for resins, fats, iodine, sulphur; (2) raw material — ethylbenzene → styrene (polystyrene), cumene → phenol + acetone, cyclohexane → nylon precursors (adipic acid), nitrobenzene → aniline (dyes); (3) motor-fuel component (anti-knock value high) — now restricted by benzene's carcinogenicity; (4) laboratory reagent and standard.

## 3. Deep Conceptual — The Sooty Flame as Stoichiometry Made Visible

- The balanced equation demands 15 O₂ per 2 benzene — an oxygen-hungry ratio. In a real flame the fuel-rich zones cannot supply that oxygen locally, so carbon is released as fine particles before reaching CO₂; these particles glow incandescently (luminous yellow) and deposit as soot. **The flame's colour is a local stoichiometry deficit.**
- **Why benzene is *more* sooty than cyclohexane:** C₆H₆ needs 7.5 O₂ per molecule; C₆H₁₂ needs 9 O₂ per molecule but delivers 6 carbons with 12 hydrogens carrying their own combustion oxygen budget — the H : C ratio (2 : 1 vs 1 : 1) is the cleaner predictor: more H per C ⟹ more complete combustion ⟹ cleaner flame.

## 4. Deep Conceptual — Uses Follow Structure, and Safety Follows Toxicity

- **Solvent use** is the non-polarity chapter (dispersion contact with non-polar solutes); **precursor use** is the substitution chemistry chapter (nitration → aniline chain; alkylation → styrene chain; hydrogenation → cyclohexane/nylon chain) — each industrial route is a syllabus reaction scaled up.
- **The safety reversal:** benzene's historical ubiquity (solvent, fuel) met its toxicology — benzene is a proven human carcinogen (bone-marrow suppression, leukaemia via its metabolites). Modern practice substitutes toluene (less volatile, metabolised differently) wherever the *solvent* property, not the ring reactivity, is needed. The uses list is now partly historical by law.

## 5. Worked Example Types

- **Type A — write and balance:** the combustion equation with coefficients.
- **Type B — explain the soot:** C% and H : C ratio reasoning.
- **Type C — list uses by category:** solvent / precursor / fuel with one example each.
- **Type D — energy calculation:** heat released from mass of benzene burnt.

## 6. Common Confusions

**"Sooty flame means incomplete equation":** the equation is complete; the *flame* is locally fuel-rich — the soot is kinetics and mixing, not stoichiometry error. **"Benzene is still a common solvent":** carcinogenicity has largely retired it from open laboratory use — toluene is the modern stand-in.

data.title: α-Particle Scattering — Experimental Detail and Numericals
data.topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: ### Focus of this tab

A close-up of the α-scattering experiment itself: the apparatus, the counting data, and the two quantitative results (distance of closest approach and the scattering law) that NEB numericals are built on. The full model and its limitations are in the main note.
### Apparatus, quantity by quantity
• α-source: radium C (polonium) in a lead block — lead absorbs all radiation except the fine beam escaping the collimator hole; α-particles emerge with KE ≈ 5.5 MeV and speed ≈ 1.6 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹.
• Foil: gold, ≈ 4 × 10⁻⁵ cm (≈ 10⁻⁷ m) thick ≈ 1000 atomic layers; gold is chosen because it is the most malleable metal and Z = 79 gives maximum deflection (∝ Z).
• Detector: circular ZnS screen; every α-hit gives a scintillation counted through a low-power microscope that can rotate about the foil through 0°–180°.
• Enclosure evacuated so α-particles are not absorbed by air (their range in air is only a few cm).
### The counting data (Geiger–Marsden)
• Nearly all α-particles (≈ 99.86%) pass straight through — no deflection.
• About 1 in 8000 is deflected by more than 90°; about 1 in 10⁴–10⁶ comes straight back (θ ≈ 180°).
• The probability of scattering at angle θ falls as sin⁻⁴(θ/2) — from 0° to 180° the count falls by about 10 orders of magnitude.
### Distance of closest approach (numerical pattern)

At the turning point all kinetic energy is stored as electrostatic potential energy: $\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}=\frac{2Ze^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r_{0}}$, giving $r_{0}=\frac{2Ze^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}(KE)}$. For 5.5 MeV α on gold r₀ ≈ 4.1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m — about 40 nuclear radii, so the α-particle never touches the nucleus and the nucleus acts as a point charge. This number is an **upper limit** of the nuclear size, which is why the experiment 'measures' the nucleus without seeing it.
### Impact parameter (the other half of the story)

The scattering angle is fixed by the impact parameter b (the perpendicular distance the α-particle's initial line would pass from the nucleus): $b=\frac{kZe^{2}}{KE}\cot\frac{\theta}{2}$. Head-on approach (b = 0) gives θ = 180° (back-scattering); large b gives tiny θ — the geometric origin of the sin⁻⁴ law.
### What each observation proves
• Undeflected majority → atom mostly empty space.
• Large-angle deflection → a concentrated positive charge much heavier than the α-particle (a light electron cannot turn a 7300-times-heavier projectile).
• Back-scattering → the positive charge and mass are concentrated in a volume 10⁻¹⁵ of the atom.
confusion: ❌ The foil must be thick for good scattering. ✅ It must be extremely thin (≈1000 atoms) so an α-particle meets at most a few nuclei; a thick foil would absorb the particles.
❌ Electrons deflect the α-particles. ✅ Electron mass is ≈1/7300 of the α-mass, so momentum transfer is negligible; only the nucleus can scatter.
❌ r₀ is the nuclear radius. ✅ It is the distance of closest approach — an upper limit; the nuclear radius is ≈10⁻¹⁵ m, ten times smaller.

Calculate r₀ for a 5.5 MeV α-particle against a gold nucleus (Z = 79).
How does the Rutherford scattering law explain the rarity of 180° scattering?
Why is the experiment performed in vacuum?

$$b=\frac{kZe^{2}}{KE}\cot\frac{\theta}{2}$$
universalFacts: ≈1 in 8000 α-particles was deflected by more than 90°; the count falls by ~10 orders of magnitude from 0° to 180°.
For 5.5 MeV α on gold, r₀ ≈ 4.1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m ≈ 40 nuclear radii.
Scattering probability scales as Z² of the foil and as 1/(KE)² of the α-particle.
examples: **Problem:** α-particles of 4 MeV approach silver (Z = 47). Find r₀. **Solution:** r₀ = 2kZe²/KE = (2 × 9×10⁹ × 47 × (1.6×10⁻¹⁹)²)/(4 × 1.6×10⁻¹³) ≈ 3.4 × 10⁻¹⁴ m — the measurement is a nucleus-size upper limit, not the radius itself.

Connect each observation to its conclusion; the marks are for the inference chain, not the apparatus list.

data.title: Rutherford's Atomic Model and its Limitations
data.topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Experiment That Found the Nucleus

Thomson's plum-pudding model (1904) pictured the atom as diffuse positive charge with embedded electrons. Rutherford, Geiger and Marsden (1909–1911) fired α-particles (He²⁺, ~5.5 MeV) at gold foil ~4 × 10⁻⁵ cm thick and got a result the pudding model could not survive: a few α-particles bounced straight back. The atom has a **nucleus**.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 The set-up (state the four parts)

1. **α-source:** radium in a lead block with a collimator → narrow α-beam.
2. **Target:** gold foil ~4 × 10⁻⁵ cm (≈1000 atoms thick) — gold can be beaten very thin and has a heavy nucleus (Z = 79).
3. **Detector:** rotatable ZnS screen viewed through a microscope — each α-hit gives a scintillation.
4. **Enclosure:** evacuated so air does not scatter the beam.

### 2.2 Observations → conclusions (the exam's 3m chain)

| Observation | Conclusion |
|---|---|
| ≈99.86% of α-particles passed straight through | The atom is **mostly empty space** |
| ≈1 in 20,000 deflected by more than 90°; a very few bounced back (≈180°) | A tiny, heavy, **positively charged nucleus** carries nearly all the mass |
| Scattering follows N(θ) ∝ 1/sin⁴(θ/2) | Large-angle scattering is rare but real — Coulomb repulsion off a point-like core |

### 2.3 The nuclear model

- The atom is neutral and largely empty; almost all mass sits in a nucleus of radius ~10⁻¹⁵ m against atomic radius ~10⁻¹⁰ m — a **1 : 100,000** linear ratio, ~10⁻¹⁵ in volume, with nuclear density ~10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.
- Electrons revolve in circular orbits with the Coulomb attraction supplying the centripetal force.
- The nuclear charge is characteristic of the element — the origin of **atomic number**, proved by Moseley (1913).
- Distance of closest approach: r₀ = 2Ze²/(4πε₀·KE) ≈ 4.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ m for 5 MeV α on gold — an experimental upper limit on nuclear size.

### 2.4 Limitations (exam-critical)

1. **Stability not explained:** a revolving, accelerating electron must radiate continuously (Maxwell) and spiral into the nucleus in ~10⁻⁸ s — yet atoms are stable.
2. **Line spectra not explained:** an inward spiral would give a continuous range of frequencies; hydrogen gives sharp discrete lines.
3. **No electronic arrangement:** nothing about shells or energies — periodicity and valency unexplained.
4. **No quantisation:** circular orbits are assumptions; no orbital radii or energies can be calculated.
5. **Ignores the neutron** (isotopes unexplained) and electron–electron repulsion (fails for multi-electron atoms).

### 2.5 Similarities and differences — Thomson's model vs Rutherford's model

**Similarities:** both are pre-quantum classical models; both place electrons inside a positive framework; both try to keep the atom electrically neutral.
**Differences:** Thomson spreads positive charge **throughout the atom** (pudding); Rutherford concentrates it in a **tiny nucleus** (1 : 100,000). Thomson cannot explain large-angle scattering; Rutherford explains it but cannot explain stability or line spectra. Thomson's atom is mostly *filled*; Rutherford's is mostly *empty*.

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Bohr (Topic 14):** Bohr fixes exactly the two failures — stability and line spectra — by adding quantisation.
- **To atomic number (Topic 24):** Moseley's X-ray work turned Rutherford's nuclear charge into Z.
- **To nuclear chemistry:** the nucleus Rutherford found later yields the proton (1919) and neutron (1932).

## 4. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 4.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

No verified PYQ for this exact topic in the bank. Practise observations→conclusions and limitations as **NEB-style practice**.

### 4.2 Likely question forms

1. Describe the α-scattering experiment with observations and conclusions (3–5m).
2. Write four limitations of Rutherford's model (3m).
3. Why was gold foil used? (2m)

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Quoting "1 in 20,000" as "1 in 2000".
2. Saying the atom is "completely empty" — it is *mostly* empty; the nucleus is there.
3. Listing limitations without the stability argument (the one NEB wants).
confusion: **Scattering source:** deflection comes from Coulomb **repulsion** between the positive α-particle and the positive nucleus — not from electron collisions (electrons are too light).
**Atomic radius vs nuclear radius:** 10⁻¹⁰ m vs 10⁻¹⁵ m — the nucleus is 100,000× smaller in linear size but carries ~100% of the mass.
practice: Why were ~99.86% of α-particles undeflected?
formulas:
- N(θ) ∝ 1/sin⁴(θ/2) (scattering law)
- r₀ = 2Ze²/(4πε₀·KE) (distance of closest approach)
- Nuclear radius ~10⁻¹⁵ m; atomic radius ~10⁻¹⁰ m
universalFacts: Rutherford called it "the most incredible event of my life" — as if firing a shell at tissue paper and having it bounce back.
examples: ***1 in 20,000 back-scattered*** — like a shell bouncing off tissue paper: the only explanation is a concentrated positive mass.

notes: **रदरफोर्डको परमाणु मोडेल र यसका सीमाहरू:**

**१. प्रयोगको अर्थ:** थमसनको प्लम-पडिङ मोडेल (१९०४) ले परमाणुलाई फैलिएको धनात्मक आवेश मान्नुभएको थियो जसमा इलेक्ट्रोनहरू समाविष्ट थिए, र यो द्रुत α-कणहरूको (He²⁺, ≈५.५ MeV) ठूला-कोण विक्षेपण व्याख्या गर्न सक्नथ्यो। रदरफोर्डले गाइगर र मार्सडेनसँग (१९०९-१९११) α-विक्षेपणबाट परमाणुको *संरचना* जाँच्नुभएको थियो — यसले **केन्द्रक परमाणु** स्थापित गर्छ।

**२. सेट-अप:** सीसाब्लकमा रेडियम र क्योलिमेटर ले सानो α-बीम दिन्छ; लक्ष्य सोनाको फोइल ≈४ × १०⁻⁵ सेमि मोटो (≈१००० परमाणु) किनभने सोना धेरै पत्लो बन्छ र यसको भारी केन्द्रक छ (Z = ७९); घुम्नसक्ने ZnS स्क्रिन सूक्ष्मदर्शीबाट हेर्ने गरी प्रत्येक स्किनटिलेसन रेकर्ड गर्छ; उपकरण निर्वातमा छ।
**३. अवलोकनहरू:**
• ≈९९.८६% α-कणहरू सीधै पार भए — परमाणु अधिकांश खाली ठाउँ हो।
• ≈२०,००० मा १ कण ९०° भन्दा बढी विक्षेपित भयो, र केही मात्र फिर्ता भए (θ ≈ १८०°)।
• विक्षेपण N(θ) ∝ 1/sin⁴(θ/2) अनुसार हुन्छ; ठूला-कोण विक्षेपण विरल तर वास्तविक छ।
**४. निष्कर्षहरू (केन्द्रक मोडेल):**
• परमाणु उदासीन र प्रायः खाली छ; एक सानो, भारी, धनात्मक **केन्द्रक** प्रायः सबै द्रव्यमान वहन गर्छ।
• केन्द्रकको अर्धव्यास ≈१०⁻¹⁵ मि विरुद्ध परमाणुको अर्धव्यास ≈१०⁻¹⁰ मि (१ : १००,०००); केन्द्रकको आयतन ≈१०⁻¹⁵ परमाणुको आयतनको, केन्द्रकको घनत्व ≈१०¹⁷ किग्रा मि⁻³।
• इलेक्ट्रोनहरू वृत्ताकार कक्षकमा घुम्छन्, केन्द्रकको कुलम्ब आकर्षण केन्द्राभिमुख बल दिन्छ।
• धनात्मक आवेश तत्वको विशेषता हो — परमाणु संख्याको मूल, पहिले मोस्लेले (१९१३) प्रमाणित गरे।
**५. परिमाणात्मक परिणामहरू:**
• नजिकको दूरी (KE → स्थिरविद्युत PE): r₀ = 2Ze²/(4πε₀·KE) ≈ ४.५ × १०⁻¹⁴ मि ५ MeV α सोनामा — केन्द्रकको आकारको प्रयोगात्मक ऊपरी सीमा।
• रदरफोर्ड विक्षेपण नियम N(θ) ∝ 1/sin⁴(θ/2) व्याख्या गर्छ किन भने फिर्ता विक्षेपण विरल घटना हो।
**६. अनुप्रयोगहरू:**
• केन्द्रक भौतिकीको स्थापना: प्रोटोन (१९१९) र न्यूट्रन (१९३२) बाट परमाणु विखण्डन/रिएक्टर प्रविधि; रदरफोर्ड फिर्ता-विक्षेपण स्पेक्ट्रोस्कोपी (RBS) अहिलै पनि पत्लो फिल्महरूको उद्योगी विश्लेषण गर्छ।
• मोस्लेको नियम र आधुनिक आवर्त सारणीको परमाणु-संख्या आधार रचना गर्छ, र संरचनालाई सांख्यिकीय रूपमा (सम्भावनाबाट) निष्कर्ष गर्ने उत्कृष्ट उदाहरण हो, प्रत्यक्ष अवलोकनबाट होइन।
**७. सीमाहरू (परीक्षा-महत्वपूर्ण):**
१. **स्थिरता व्याख्या नगरेको:** घुमिरहने इलेक्ट्रोन निरन्तर त्वरित हुन्छ, त्यसैले मैक्सवेलको सिद्धान्तअनुसार यो ऊर्जा विकिरण गर्छ र ≈१०⁻८ सेकेन्डमा केन्द्रकमा लुन्छ — तर परमाणुहरू स्थिर छन्।
२. **रेखा स्पेक्ट्रम व्याख्या नगरेको:** भित्रको स्पायरलले निरन्तर आवृत्तिको दायरा उत्सर्जन गर्थ्यो, तर हाइड्रोजनले तेज र विविध रेखाहरू दिन्छ।
३. **कोई इलेक्ट्रोन व्यवस्था छैन:** खोलहरू, इलेक्ट्रोन संख्या वा ऊर्जा बारे कुनै कुरा छैन, त्यसैले आवर्तिता र संयोजकता व्याख्या नभएको।
४. **पूर्ण रूपमा शास्त्रीय:** वृत्ताकार कक्षक र बिन्दु केन्द्रक मान्यताहरू हुन्; परिमाणीकरण बिना मोडेलले कक्षक अर्धव्यास वा ऊर्जा दिन सक्दैन।
५. **न्यूट्रन उपेक्षित** (त्यसैले आइसोटोपहरू व्याख्या नभएको) र इलेक्ट्रोन-इलेक्ट्रोन प्रतिकर्षण उपेक्षित, त्यसैले बहु-इलेक्ट्रोन परमाणुहरूको लागि असफल; बन्डिङ वा जिमन/स्टार्क विभाजनको लेखाजोखा छैन।
**८. परीक्षा संकेतहरू:**
अवलोकन + निष्कर्ष र दुई मुख्य दोषहरू (स्थिरता, विविध स्पेक्ट्रम) मानक ४-५ अङ्कका NEB प्रश्नहरू हुन्; संख्यात्मक r₀, केन्द्रक अर्धव्यास/घनत्व र परमाणु : केन्द्रक आयतन अनुपात प्रयोग गर्छन्।

रदरफोर्डले १९०८ मा रेडियोधर्मितामा कामका लागि रसायन विज्ञानको नोबेल पुरस्कार प्राप्त गरे।
केन्द्रकको घनत्व प्रायः सबै केन्द्रकहरूको लागि नै समान हुन्छ किनकि R = R₀A^(1/3), R₀ ≈ १.२ × १०⁻¹⁵ मि।

notes: Nucleus (noun): the dense central core of an atom. Plural: nuclei.
Alpha particle (noun phrase): helium nucleus (He²⁺) emitted in radioactive decay.
Scattering (noun/gerund): deflection of particles from their path. Rutherford scattering is the classic experiment.
Atomic model (noun phrase): a theoretical representation of atom structure.
Limitation (noun): a weakness or shortcoming of a theory/model.
Quantization (noun): restricting values to discrete levels; the key step from Rutherford to Bohr.
importantStatements: In scientific English, 'model' means a simplified representation, not a miniature replica.
The phrase 'mostly empty space' is a relative statement — 99.9% of the volume, not 99.9% of the mass.
Rutherford's experiment 'probed' atomic structure — to probe means to investigate by testing.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Experiment That Found the Nucleus

Thomson's plum-pudding model (1904) pictured the atom as diffuse positive charge with embedded electrons. Rutherford, Geiger and Marsden (1909–1911) fired α-particles (He²⁺, ~5.5 MeV) at gold foil ~4 × 10⁻⁵ cm thick and got a result the pudding model could not survive: a few α-particles bounced straight back. The atom has a **nucleus**.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 The set-up (state the four parts)

1. **α-source:** radium in a lead block with a collimator → narrow α-beam.
2. **Target:** gold foil ~4 × 10⁻⁵ cm (≈1000 atoms thick) — gold can be beaten very thin and has a heavy nucleus (Z = 79).
3. **Detector:** rotatable ZnS screen viewed through a microscope — each α-hit gives a scintillation.
4. **Enclosure:** evacuated so air does not scatter the beam.

### 2.2 Observations → conclusions (the exam's 3m chain)

| Observation | Conclusion |
|---|---|
| ≈99.86% of α-particles passed straight through | The atom is **mostly empty space** |
| ≈1 in 20,000 deflected by more than 90°; a very few bounced back (≈180°) | A tiny, heavy, **positively charged nucleus** carries nearly all the mass |
| Scattering follows N(θ) ∝ 1/sin⁴(θ/2) | Large-angle scattering is rare but real — Coulomb repulsion off a point-like core |

### 2.3 The nuclear model

- The atom is neutral and largely empty; almost all mass sits in a nucleus of radius ~10⁻¹⁵ m against atomic radius ~10⁻¹⁰ m — a **1 : 100,000** linear ratio, ~10⁻¹⁵ in volume, with nuclear density ~10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.
- Electrons revolve in circular orbits with the Coulomb attraction supplying the centripetal force.
- The nuclear charge is characteristic of the element — the origin of **atomic number**, proved by Moseley (1913).
- Distance of closest approach: r₀ = 2Ze²/(4πε₀·KE) ≈ 4.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ m for 5 MeV α on gold — an experimental upper limit on nuclear size.

### 2.4 Limitations (exam-critical)

1. **Stability not explained:** a revolving, accelerating electron must radiate continuously (Maxwell) and spiral into the nucleus in ~10⁻⁸ s — yet atoms are stable.
2. **Line spectra not explained:** an inward spiral would give a continuous range of frequencies; hydrogen gives sharp discrete lines.
3. **No electronic arrangement:** nothing about shells or energies — periodicity and valency unexplained.
4. **No quantisation:** circular orbits are assumptions; no orbital radii or energies can be calculated.
5. **Ignores the neutron** (isotopes unexplained) and electron–electron repulsion (fails for multi-electron atoms).

### 2.5 Similarities and differences — Thomson's model vs Rutherford's model

**Similarities:** both are pre-quantum classical models; both place electrons inside a positive framework; both try to keep the atom electrically neutral.
**Differences:** Thomson spreads positive charge **throughout the atom** (pudding); Rutherford concentrates it in a **tiny nucleus** (1 : 100,000). Thomson cannot explain large-angle scattering; Rutherford explains it but cannot explain stability or line spectra. Thomson's atom is mostly *filled*; Rutherford's is mostly *empty*.

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Bohr (Topic 14):** Bohr fixes exactly the two failures — stability and line spectra — by adding quantisation.
- **To atomic number (Topic 24):** Moseley's X-ray work turned Rutherford's nuclear charge into Z.
- **To nuclear chemistry:** the nucleus Rutherford found later yields the proton (1919) and neutron (1932).

## 4. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 4.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

No verified PYQ for this exact topic in the bank. Practise observations→conclusions and limitations as **NEB-style practice**.

### 4.2 Likely question forms

1. Describe the α-scattering experiment with observations and conclusions (3–5m).
2. Write four limitations of Rutherford's model (3m).
3. Why was gold foil used? (2m)

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Quoting "1 in 20,000" as "1 in 2000".
2. Saying the atom is "completely empty" — it is *mostly* empty; the nucleus is there.
3. Listing limitations without the stability argument (the one NEB wants).

data.summary: Rutherford's α-scattering experiment (1909–1911) on ~4 × 10⁻⁵ cm gold foil destroyed Thomson's pudding model: 99.86% of α-particles passed straight through (the atom is mostly empty space) while ~1 in 20,000 deflected >90° or bounced back — proof of a tiny (10⁻¹⁵ m), heavy, positive **nucleus** carrying nearly all the mass, with electrons revolving around it under Coulomb attraction. Thomson spread charge through the atom; Rutherford concentrated it — and found the nucleus.

data.topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: Alpha-Particle Scattering Experiment: Rutherford (1911) bombarded thin gold foil (~0.00004 cm thick) with fast alpha particles from a radioactive source. A fluorescent zinc sulphide screen detected scattered particles. This experiment fundamentally changed our understanding of atomic structure.

Key Observations: (1) Most alpha particles passed straight through undeflected — atom is mostly empty space. (2) Some were deflected at small angles — positive charge is concentrated. (3) About 1 in 8000 bounced back (>90°) — dense, massive nucleus exists. Rutherford said it was 'as if you fired a 15-inch shell at tissue paper and it came back'.

Rutherford's Nuclear Model: Atom consists of a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus (~10⁻¹⁵ m radius) containing nearly all the mass. Electrons orbit the nucleus at large distances (~10⁻¹⁰ m). The atom is mostly empty space. Nuclear charge = +Ze where Z is atomic number.

Nuclear Size: Nuclear radius R ≈ R₀A^(1/3) where R₀ ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m (1.2 fm) and A is mass number. Nucleus is ~10⁵ times smaller than the atom. If atom were a football stadium, nucleus would be a marble at center.

Distance of Closest Approach: For head-on collision, d = (1/4πε₀)(2Ze²/K) where K is alpha particle kinetic energy. This gives upper limit of nuclear size. For gold (Z=79) with 5.5 MeV alpha: d ≈ 4.1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m.

Limitation 1 — Atomic Stability: According to Maxwell's electromagnetic theory, an accelerating charged particle radiates energy. An orbiting electron should continuously lose energy and spiral into the nucleus in ~10⁻¹¹ s. Rutherford's model cannot explain why atoms are stable.

Limitation 2 — Line Spectra: Rutherford's model predicts continuous emission spectrum (electron spiraling inward emits all frequencies). But hydrogen shows discrete line spectrum (Balmer, Lyman series). The model cannot explain quantized energy levels or spectral lines.

Limitation 3 — Chemical Behavior: The model provides no explanation for chemical bonding, valency, or periodic properties. It says nothing about electron arrangement or energy distribution that determines reactivity.
Impact Parameter: b = perpendicular distance of initial velocity vector from nucleus center. Smaller b → larger scattering angle. Relationship: b ∝ cot(θ/2). Head-on collision has b = 0, θ = 180°.

Transition to Bohr Model: Rutherford's limitations directly motivated Bohr (1913) to propose quantized orbits where electrons do not radiate in stationary states, explaining both stability and line spectra.

specificConditions: Thin Foil Required: Gold foil must be extremely thin (~400 atoms thick) so alpha particles interact with at most one nucleus. Thick foils cause multiple scattering, invalidating single-collision analysis.
Point Charge Approximation: Alpha particle and nucleus treated as point charges. Valid when distance >> nuclear/alpha sizes. Breaks down at very close approach where nuclear forces matter.
Classical Mechanics Applied: Rutherford used Newtonian mechanics and Coulomb's law. Quantum effects ignored — valid for heavy alpha particles but not for electron behavior.
Vacuum Conditions: Experiment performed in vacuum to prevent alpha particles from being absorbed or scattered by air molecules before reaching the foil.

data.title: Postulates of Bohr's Atomic Model and their Applications
data.topicTitle: Postulates of Bohr's atomic model and its application
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Quantisation Saves the Atom

In 1913 Niels Bohr repaired Rutherford's model by adding one idea: the electron's angular momentum is **quantised**. Only certain orbits exist, no radiation is emitted inside them, and light appears only when the electron jumps between orbits. The model works exactly for hydrogen and one-electron ions (He⁺, Li²⁺).

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 The postulates (state in order — NEB 3m)

1. **Stationary orbits:** the electron revolves only in certain permitted circular orbits (stationary states) of fixed energy and does **not** radiate while in one.
2. **Quantisation of angular momentum:** only orbits satisfying mvr = nh/2π (n = 1, 2, 3, …) are allowed.
3. **Frequency condition:** radiation is absorbed or emitted only during a jump: hν = |E₂ − E₁| (emission on falling, absorption on rising).
4. **Force condition:** Coulomb attraction supplies the centripetal force, mv²/r = kZe²/r² — combined with postulate 2 to derive r and E.

### 2.2 The derived results (memorise the three)

| Quantity | Formula | Hydrogen ground state |
|---|---|---|
| Orbit radius | rₙ = 0.529 n²/Z Å | 0.529 Å = 52.9 pm (**Bohr radius**) |
| Orbital speed | vₙ = 2.18 × 10⁶ Z/n m s⁻¹ | c/137 (non-relativistic) |
| Energy | Eₙ = −13.6 Z²/n² eV = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ Z²/n² J | −13.6 eV = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J |

KE = −Eₙ and PE = 2Eₙ; total energy is **negative** because the zero is taken at infinite separation (a bound electron has less energy than a free one).

### 2.3 Worked numericals

**Q (NEB 2022, 3m):** Using Eₙ = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸/n² J, calculate the energy of the electron in the second orbit of hydrogen.
- E₂ = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸/(2)² = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸/4 = **−5.45 × 10⁻¹⁹ J**

**Q (NEB-style):** Calculate the radius of the third Bohr orbit of He⁺ (Z = 2).
- r₃ = 0.529 × 9/2 = **2.38 Å**

**Q (NEB-style):** Find the ionisation energy of He⁺ (Z = 2).
- IE = 13.6 × Z² = 13.6 × 4 = **54.4 eV**

### 2.4 Applications

1. **Hydrogen spectrum:** wavenumber ν̄ = RZ²(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²), R = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ — identifies the Lyman (UV), Balmer (visible), Paschen, Brackett and Pfund (IR) series.
2. **Ionisation energy:** H = 13.6 eV = 1312 kJ mol⁻¹; He⁺ = 54.4 eV; Li²⁺ = 122.4 eV (scales as Z²).
3. **Atomic stability:** stationary orbits do not radiate — the collapse problem is solved.
4. **Energy-level diagrams** still used in spectroscopy, lasers and astrophysics (highly ionised plasmas).

### 2.5 Validity and limits

The model succeeds for hydrogen and hydrogen-like ions but fails for multi-electron atoms (ignores electron–electron repulsion), cannot explain fine structure (doublets), the Zeeman and Stark effects, or the dual wave nature of the electron — de Broglie and Schrödinger take over from here.

### 2.6 Similarities and differences — Rutherford's model vs Bohr's model

**Similarities:** both place a tiny positive nucleus at the centre with electrons revolving around it; both use Coulomb attraction as the centripetal force; both are circular-orbit pictures.
**Differences:** Rutherford allows **any** orbit and continuous radiation (→ collapse predicted); Bohr restricts orbits to mvr = nh/2π with **no radiation inside** an orbit (→ stability). Rutherford explains nothing about spectra; Bohr reproduces the hydrogen line spectrum quantitatively. Rutherford is purely classical; Bohr mixes classical mechanics with Planck's quantum condition.

### 2.7 Similarities and differences — orbit (Bohr) vs orbital (quantum model)

**Similarities:** both describe where the electron may be found around the nucleus; both carry definite energies in their models.
**Differences:** an orbit is a **fixed circular path** (Bohr, definite trajectory); an orbital is a **3-D probability region** (quantum model, ~90% probability cloud). Orbits violate the uncertainty principle; orbitals are its direct consequence.

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Rutherford (Topic 13):** Bohr keeps the nucleus and quantises the orbits.
- **To hydrogen spectrum (Topic 15):** the frequency condition generates every spectral series.
- **To de Broglie (Topic 17):** the wave view explains *why* mvr = nh/2π — n wavelengths must fit the orbit's circumference.

## 4. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 4.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

| Year | Unit | Topic | Question | Marks | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2080/2022 | Atomic structure | Bohr model | Using Eₙ = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸/n² J, calculate the energy of the electron in the second orbit of hydrogen. | 3 | Numerical |

### 4.2 Likely additional forms (NEB-style)

1. State Bohr's postulates (3m).
2. Radius or speed of the n-th orbit (2m).
3. Ionisation energy of He⁺ (2m).

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Writing mvr = nh/2π as mvr = nh/2π² or dropping the π.
2. Forgetting Z² in the energy formula for hydrogen-like ions.
3. Saying energy is "negative so invalid" — negative means bound relative to the free-electron zero.

data.title: The Stability Crisis of Rutherford's Atom
data.topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: ### Focus of this tab
The stability defect worked out quantitatively: how long the classical Rutherford atom would survive, and why that number forces quantisation. The full limitations list is in the main note.
### The classical argument

An electron moving in a circle is in accelerated motion (its velocity vector changes direction continuously). Maxwell's electromagnetic theory requires every accelerated charged body to radiate electromagnetic energy of frequency equal to its revolution frequency. Radiating means losing energy, so the electron must spiral inward.
### The spiral-in time

Using classical electrodynamics for hydrogen (r = 0.529 Å), the energy loss rate gives a collapse time of about $t\approx1.6\times10^{-11}\ \text{s}$ — commonly quoted as ≈10⁻⁸ s or less in textbooks. Either way it is far shorter than any observable lifetime: classical atoms would vanish in a flash.
### Two observable failures follow
• **No stable atoms:** matter could not exist, yet atoms are billions of years old.

• **Continuous spectrum:** as the electron spirals, its revolution frequency (and hence the radiated frequency) changes continuously, so the atom should emit a continuous spectrum. Experiment shows hydrogen emits sharp discrete lines (656.3 nm, 486.1 nm, …).
### Bohr's escape (what had to be assumed)

Bohr (1913) imposed two non-classical rules: (1) electrons move only in certain **stationary orbits** in which they do *not* radiate, and (2) radiation is emitted only during a jump, with $h\nu=E_{2}-E_{1}$. Both rules violate classical electrodynamics — that is precisely the price of saving the atom, and it opened the road to quantum mechanics.
### Why this matters for the exam

The stability crisis is the *reason* Bohr's first postulate exists. A complete answer always links: accelerated charge radiates → energy loss → spiral in → (i) no stability, (ii) continuous spectrum → both contradicted by experiment → quantisation required.
confusion: ❌ An electron radiates because it moves fast. ✅ Uniform motion radiates nothing; it is the *acceleration* (changing direction in a circle) that radiates.
❌ The electron spirals in slowly over years. ✅ Classical theory gives a collapse in ≈10⁻¹¹–10⁻⁸ s — effectively instantaneous.
❌ Bohr removed radiation altogether. ✅ Radiation still occurs during jumps; only radiation *within* a stationary orbit is forbidden.
practice: Use Maxwell's electromagnetic theory to show that Rutherford's atom is unstable.
What two experimental facts does the classical atom fail to explain?
State the two Bohr postulates that resolve the stability crisis and point out where classical physics is violated.
formulas: $$\text{accelerated charge} \Rightarrow \text{radiation},\qquad \nu_{\text{radiated}}=\nu_{\text{revolution}}\ (\text{classical})$$
$$t_{\text{collapse}}\approx10^{-11}-10^{-8}\ \text{s}\ (\text{classical hydrogen})$$
universalFacts: The classical collapse time for the hydrogen ground orbit is about 1.6 × 10⁻¹¹ s.
The discrete 656.3 nm Hα line is the experimental fact the classical atom cannot produce.
Bohr's 1913 postulates were the first successful breach of classical electrodynamics inside the atom.
examples: **Problem:** Why does a spiralling electron give a continuous spectrum? **Solution:** the revolution frequency ν_rev = v/2πr changes continuously as r shrinks; classical radiation copies this frequency, so all frequencies in a range are emitted — contradicting the observed sharp lines.
importantNotes: Always give both consequences (no stability + continuous spectrum); quoting only one loses marks.
State that the postulates are *postulates* — Bohr could not derive them classically.

data.title: Spectrum of the Hydrogen Atom
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Fingerprint That Saved Bohr

Rutherford's model could not explain why atomic hydrogen emits **discrete coloured lines** instead of a continuous glow. Bohr (1913) turned that failure into a triumph: if electrons occupy only **quantised orbits**, an electron dropping from a higher orbit to a lower one emits a photon carrying exactly the energy gap — hν = E₂ − E₁. Each gap is fixed, so each line is fixed. The hydrogen spectrum is therefore the **experimental proof of quantisation**, and the model that predicts its wavelengths to 5 significant figures is the model NEB examines every year.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Energy of the nth orbit

- Eₙ = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J / n² = **−13.6 eV / n²** (n = 1, 2, 3, …).
- The **negative sign** means the electron is bound; E₁ = −13.6 eV is the **ground state**, E∞ = 0 is **ionisation**.
- Energy gaps shrink as n grows — levels crowd together near the ionisation limit.

### 2.2 The transition rule

Photon emitted when the electron falls from n₂ (upper) to n₁ (lower):

**hν = E₂ − E₁ = 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J (1/n₁² − 1/n₂²)**

### 2.3 The Rydberg equation (wavelength form)

**1/λ = R (1/n₁² − 1/n₂²)**, R = **1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹** (Rydberg constant), n₂ > n₁.

### 2.4 The five spectral series (memorise the table — straight 3m)

| Series | n₁ (lower) | n₂ (upper) | Spectral region | Series limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Lyman** | 1 | 2, 3, 4, … | **Ultraviolet** | 91.2 nm |
| **Balmer** | 2 | 3, 4, 5, … | **Visible** | 364.6 nm |
| **Paschen** | 3 | 4, 5, 6, … | Infrared | 1875 nm |
| **Brackett** | 4 | 5, 6, 7, … | Infrared | 4051 nm |
| **Pfund** | 5 | 6, 7, 8, … | Infrared (far) | 7460 nm |

Only **Balmer** lies in the visible region — the four visible lines are called **Hα (656.3 nm, red), Hβ (486.1 nm), Hγ (434.0 nm), Hδ (410.2 nm)**.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| **Line spectrum** | Discrete wavelengths emitted by excited atoms, each from one defined transition | Evidence of quantised energy levels |
| **Ground state** | Lowest orbit n = 1, E = −13.6 eV | Normal state of hydrogen |
| **Excited state** | Any orbit n > 1 | Reached by absorbing energy |
| **Ionisation energy** | Energy to take the electron from n = 1 to n = ∞ = 13.6 eV = 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J | The magnitude of E₁ |
| **Series limit** | The shortest wavelength of a series (n₂ → ∞) | Boundary of the series |
| **Spectral series** | Family of lines sharing one lower level n₁ | Named after their discoverers |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why lines, not a rainbow

Classical physics: an orbiting electron radiates continuously, spirals inward, and the spectrum should be continuous. Bohr: orbits are **stationary** — no radiation while the electron stays put. Radiation happens **only during a jump**, and the jump energy is quantised, so the photon wavelength is one fixed value per jump. Millions of atoms making the same jump produce one bright line; different jumps produce different lines — a **line spectrum**.

### 4.2 Emission vs absorption

- **Emission spectrum:** excited atoms (flame, discharge tube) **release** photons falling down — bright lines on a dark background.
- **Absorption spectrum:** white light passes through cool hydrogen gas; atoms **remove** exactly the photons whose energy matches an upward jump — dark lines on a continuous background at the **same wavelengths**.
- Solar spectrum's Fraunhofer dark lines are absorption lines of elements in the solar atmosphere — the same physics reads the composition of stars.

### 4.3 Worked numerical — NEB 2022 (3m, verified PYQ)

**Q: Using Eₙ = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸/n² J, calculate the energy of the electron in the second orbit of hydrogen and the wavelength of the photon emitted when the electron falls from the third to the second orbit. Express the wavelength in nm.**

**Step 1 — Energy of the second orbit:**
E₂ = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ / 2² = **−5.45 × 10⁻¹⁹ J**

**Step 2 — Energy released (3 → 2):**
ΔE = 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ (1/2² − 1/3²) = 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ × (1/4 − 1/9) = 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 5/36 = **3.03 × 10⁻¹⁹ J**

**Step 3 — Wavelength (λ = hc/ΔE):**
λ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3 × 10⁸) / 3.03 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 6.56 × 10⁻⁷ m ≈ **656 nm** — the red Hα line of the Balmer series.

### 4.4 Worked numerical — series limit

**Q: Find the shortest wavelength of the Lyman series.**
Series limit: n₂ → ∞, so 1/λ = R(1/1² − 0) = R → λ = 1/R = 1/1.097 × 10⁷ = **9.12 × 10⁻⁸ m = 91.2 nm** (extreme UV).

### 4.5 Hydrogen-like species

For He⁺, Li²⁺ (one electron only), the equation becomes Eₙ = −13.6 Z²/n² eV and 1/λ = RZ²(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²) — the spectrum shifts by the factor Z², which is why He⁺ lines appear at λ/4 of the hydrogen positions.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Emission vs absorption spectrum**

| Basis | Emission spectrum | Absorption spectrum |
|---|---|---|
| Source | Excited atoms releasing energy | Cool gas removing energy from white light |
| Appearance | Bright lines on dark background | Dark lines on continuous background |
| Electron jump | Downward (n₂ → n₁) | Upward (n₁ → n₂) |
| Example | Hydrogen discharge tube | Fraunhofer lines of the sun |

**Similarities:** both arise from the same quantised jumps; the line wavelengths are identical in both.

**Continuous vs line vs band spectra**

| Basis | Continuous | Line | Band |
|---|---|---|---|
| Emitter | Hot dense bodies (filament) | Excited **atoms** in gases | Excited **molecules** |
| Distribution | All wavelengths | Discrete wavelengths | Close groups of lines |
| Example | Incandescent bulb, filament | Hydrogen discharge tube | N₂, CN bands |

**Series limit vs first line:** the limit (n₂ → ∞) is the *shortest* wavelength; the first line (smallest gap, e.g. 3 → 2) is the *longest* — students swap them.
**Balmer vs Lyman direction:** Lyman needs jumps **down to n = 1** (from any higher level); Balmer needs jumps **down to n = 2**. A 3 → 2 jump is Balmer even though it starts at n = 3.
**Rydberg sign convention:** 1/λ = R(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²) with n₁ the **lower** level; writing the terms the other way gives a negative 1/λ — physically meaningless.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (2m): Why does hydrogen produce a line spectrum rather than a continuous spectrum?** Because Bohr orbits are quantised and stationary: radiation is emitted only in jumps between fixed levels, so each photon has one definite energy — discrete lines, not a continuum.

data.title: Defects (Limitations) of Bohr's Theory
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Where the Quantum Model Still Breaks

Bohr's model rescued the hydrogen atom from Rutherford's collapse problem and predicted the hydrogen spectrum brilliantly. But it was a **hybrid**: classical circular orbits bolted onto quantum conditions. As soon as the model faced finer spectrographs, multi-electron atoms, or the Zeeman effect, cracks appeared. Knowing **why Bohr fails** is the bridge to the quantum mechanical model — and a standing NEB 3m question.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts — The Defects (state any five for 3m)

1. **Fails for multi-electron atoms.** The model works only for one-electron species (H, He⁺, Li²⁺). With two or more electrons, electron–electron repulsion breaks the simple Coulomb-plus-quantisation picture — the energy depends on more than n.
2. **No explanation of fine structure.** High-resolution spectrographs show each Balmer line (e.g. Hα) is a **close doublet**, not a single line. Bohr's model predicts one line per transition — it has no sub-levels (no l, no spin).
3. **No explanation of the Zeeman effect.** In a magnetic field, spectral lines **split into several components**; Bohr's circular orbits have no mechanism for this (needs magnetic quantum number mₗ).
4. **No explanation of the Stark effect.** Lines also split in an **electric field** — again unexplained.
5. **Orbits are physically unreal.** The model gives precise **position and momentum** of the electron simultaneously — forbidden by Heisenberg's uncertainty principle; the modern picture is a **probability orbital**, not a track.
6. **Cannot explain the dual nature of matter.** de Broglie's wave mechanics shows why only certain orbits are stable (a whole number of wavelengths must fit the circumference) — Bohr quantisation was an arbitrary postulate, not a consequence.
7. **No rule for the intensity (relative brightness) of spectral lines** — the model predicts wavelengths, not how strong each line should be.
8. **Circular orbits only.** Real angular-momentum states include elliptical shapes (Sommerfeld's extension) — Bohr's circles are a special case.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Relevance |
|---|---|---|
| **Fine structure** | Splitting of a single spectral line into closely spaced components | Needs l and s quantum numbers |
| **Zeeman effect** | Splitting of spectral lines in a magnetic field | Needs mₗ |
| **Stark effect** | Splitting of spectral lines in an electric field | Needs mₗ |
| **Uncertainty principle** | Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π — position and momentum cannot both be exact | Kills the fixed-orbit picture |
| **Dual nature** | Every particle is both wave and particle (de Broglie) | Explains why orbits are quantised |
| **One-electron species** | H, He⁺, Li²⁺, Be³⁺ — a single electron around nucleus Z | The model's only success range |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why multi-electron atoms break the model

Bohr's energy Eₙ = −13.6 Z²/n² assumes the electron feels **only the nucleus**. With two electrons, each also feels the **repulsion of the other**, and the electrons **screen** each other from the nuclear charge. The energy then depends on the electron's shape and shielding, not just on n — a single quantum number cannot describe the levels, and the predicted spectrum is wrong.

### 4.2 Why fine structure defeats circular orbits

Bohr's orbit is a circle: one radius, one energy per n. But an electron also has **angular-momentum shape (l)** and **spin (s)**; relativistic and spin effects shift the energy slightly depending on l. Result: one Bohr line is actually several lines a fraction of a nanometre apart — fine structure. Bohr's n alone cannot produce it.

### 4.3 Why the orbit itself is unphysical

The model treats the electron as a particle with an exactly known position (the orbit) and momentum — but Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π forbids knowing both. Sommerfeld tried ellipses; the real cure was Schrödinger's wave mechanics: the electron is a **standing wave of probability** (orbital), and Bohr's quantisation emerges automatically because only waves that fit the orbit constructively survive.

### 4.4 What Bohr got right (keep this — examiners ask the contrast)

- Quantised energy levels (validated by the hydrogen spectrum).
- The energy-gap rule hν = E₂ − E₁.
- Ionisation energy 13.6 eV and the Rydberg constant.
- The concept of stationary states.

## 5. Comparison Table

**Bohr model vs quantum mechanical model**

| Basis | Bohr model | Quantum mechanical model |
|---|---|---|
| Electron path | Fixed circular **orbit** | **Orbital** — probability distribution |
| Certainty | Exact position and momentum | Uncertainty principle obeyed |
| Quantum numbers | One (n) | Four (n, l, mₗ, mₛ) |
| Multi-electron atoms | Fails | Works (with approximation methods) |
| Fine structure, Zeeman, Stark | Cannot explain | Explains naturally |
| Quantisation origin | Postulated arbitrarily | Emerges from wave equation |
| Success range | One-electron species only | All atoms |

**Similarities:** both retain quantised energy levels and the photon rule hν = ΔE; the quantum model contains Bohr's result as its large-n limit.

## 6. Common Confusions

**Zeeman vs Stark:** Zeeman = **magnetic** field splitting; Stark = **electric** field splitting. Both are line splittings, both unexplained by Bohr — but the fields differ.
**Fine structure vs Zeeman:** fine structure appears **without any field** (spin/relativistic splitting); Zeeman needs an external magnetic field.
**"Bohr failed completely" — no.** It succeeded for one-electron species and introduced quantised levels; its defects are specific and each maps to a missing quantum number.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): "Bohr's model could not explain the line spectrum of an atom containing more than one electron." Justify.** — The model's energy formula assumes each electron feels only the nuclear Coulomb pull. In multi-electron atoms, mutual repulsion and shielding make the energy depend on more than n; one quantum number cannot assign the levels, so predicted lines do not match observed spectra.

**NEB-style (2m): What is the Zeeman effect?** — The splitting of a spectral line into several components when the emitting atoms are placed in a magnetic field; Bohr's model cannot explain it because its orbits carry no magnetic quantum number.

**NEB-style (2m): Why is Bohr's orbit incompatible with the uncertainty principle?** — A definite orbit means exact position *and* exact momentum simultaneously; Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π forbids this, so the electron must be described as a probability orbital instead.
