3. **No explanation of the Zeeman effect.** In a magnetic field, spectral lines **split into several components**; Bohr's circular orbits have no mechanism for this (needs magnetic quantum number mₗ).
4. **No explanation of the Stark effect.** Lines also split in an **electric field** — again unexplained.
5. **Orbits are physically unreal.** The model gives precise **position and momentum** of the electron simultaneously — forbidden by Heisenberg's uncertainty principle; the modern picture is a **probability orbital**, not a track.
6. **Cannot explain the dual nature of matter.** de Broglie's wave mechanics shows why only certain orbits are stable (a whole number of wavelengths must fit the circumference) — Bohr quantisation was an arbitrary postulate, not a consequence.
7. **No rule for the intensity (relative brightness) of spectral lines** — the model predicts wavelengths, not how strong each line should be.
8. **Circular orbits only.** Real angular-momentum states include elliptical shapes (Sommerfeld's extension) — Bohr's circles are a special case.

| **Dual nature** | Every particle is both wave and particle (de Broglie) | Explains why orbits are quantised |

data.title: Elementary Idea of the Quantum Mechanical Model — de Broglie's Wave Equation
data.topicTitle: Elementary idea of quantum mechanical model: de Broglie's wave equation
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Matter Learns to Wave

Bohr postulated quantisation; de Broglie (1924) **derived** it. If light — a wave — can behave as particles (photoelectric effect), then particles — electrons — should behave as waves. An electron wave can circle the nucleus only if a **whole number of wavelengths fits the orbit**; that condition *is* Bohr's quantisation, no longer arbitrary. This single idea, developed by Schrödinger into the wave equation, replaced orbits with **orbitals** and opened the quantum mechanical model.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 The de Broglie relation

Every moving particle has a wavelength:

**λ = h / mv = h / p** (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)

- For **macroscopic** objects m is large → λ is absurdly small → wave nature is undetectable.
- For an **electron** (m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) at ordinary speeds λ ≈ 10⁻¹⁰ m — atomic dimensions — so wave behaviour shows.

### 2.2 Deriving Bohr's quantisation (the 3m chain)

1. An electron wave must be a **standing wave** on its orbit — otherwise it destructively interferes with itself and dies.
2. Standing-wave condition: circumference = whole number of wavelengths → **2πr = nλ**.
3. Substitute λ = h/mv: 2πr = nh/mv → **mvr = nh/2π** — exactly Bohr's quantisation of angular momentum.

### 2.3 Experimental proof — Davisson and Germer (1927)

Electrons fired at a **nickel crystal** were **diffracted**, producing a diffraction pattern like X-rays — direct proof that electrons diffract as waves, with the wavelength matching de Broglie's prediction. (Thomson's electron diffraction through thin films confirmed it independently.)

### 2.4 The quantum mechanical model (elementary idea)

- Schrödinger's wave equation treats the electron as a **standing wave in three dimensions**.
- Its solutions, **wave functions ψ**, describe **orbitals** — regions of **high probability** (ψ²) of finding the electron.
- Energy is still quantised; the definite orbit is replaced by a probability cloud obeying the uncertainty principle.
- Four quantum numbers (n, l, mₗ, mₛ) label each solution.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **de Broglie wavelength** | λ = h/mv — the wave length of any moving particle | Inversely proportional to momentum |
| **Standing wave** | A wave whose pattern is fixed because a whole number of wavelengths fits the boundary | The orbit condition 2πr = nλ |
| **Wave function (ψ)** | Solution of the Schrödinger equation for an electron | ψ itself has no physical meaning |
| **Orbital** | Region where the probability of finding the electron (ψ²) is high | Replaces Bohr's orbit |
| **Probability density (ψ²)** | Square of the wave function — likelihood per unit volume | What orbitals display |
| **Heisenberg uncertainty** | Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π | Why orbits must become orbitals |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Worked numerical — wavelength of an electron (NEB-style template)

**Q: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving with a velocity of 10⁶ m s⁻¹.**
λ = h/mv = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / (9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 10⁶) = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / 9.1 × 10⁻²⁵ = **7.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ m ≈ 0.73 nm** — comparable to atomic spacing, which is why crystals diffract electrons.

### 4.2 Worked numerical — the cricket ball contrast

**Q: Find the wavelength of a 150 g cricket ball at 40 m s⁻¹.**
λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / (0.150 × 40) = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / 6 = **1.1 × 10⁻³⁴ m** — smaller than any measurable length by 20 orders of magnitude: macroscopic wave nature is unobservable. This contrast is the favourite NEB application question.

### 4.3 Why only certain orbits survive

An orbit where the circumference is 2.5λ (say) would overlap crests on troughs — the wave cancels itself. Only orbits with 2πr = nλ reinforce; hence discrete radii, discrete energies, discrete spectrum. Quantisation is geometry, not decree.

### 4.4 From ψ to orbitals

The Schrödinger equation ψ solutions depend on three quantum numbers (n, l, mₗ); each allowed combination is one **orbital** with a characteristic shape (s spherical, p dumbbell). ψ² gives the probability picture. Bohr's radius r = 0.529 n² Å survives only as the **most probable distance** of the 1s electron — not a track.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Wave vs particle behaviour**

| Basis | Wave behaviour | Particle behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Evidence | Diffraction, interference | Photoelectric effect, collisions |
| Light shows | Yes (Young's double slit) | Yes (Einstein, photons) |
| Electron shows | Yes (Davisson–Germer diffraction) | Yes (cathode rays, charge/mass) |
| Governing relation | λ = h/mv | E = hν, p = mv |

**Similarity:** the same entity exhibits both — **dual nature**; which face appears depends on the experiment.

**Orbit (Bohr) vs orbital (quantum)**

| Basis | Orbit | Orbital |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | Definite circular path | 3-D probability region |
| Certainty | Exact position claimed | Uncertainty principle obeyed |
| Quantum numbers | n only | n, l, mₗ (labelled by four with spin) |
| Shape | Circle | s spherical, p dumbbell, … |
| Max electrons | 2n² per shell | 2 per orbital |

## 6. Common Confusions

**ψ vs ψ²:** ψ is the wave function (no direct physical meaning); **ψ² is the probability density** — the measurable one. Quoting ψ as "probability" loses the mark.

**Diffraction vs scattering:** diffraction is wave-bending around/through regular arrays (needs wavelength ~ spacing); scattering is any direction change. Davisson–Germer is diffraction — the wave proof.
**de Broglie applies to everything:** the relation is universal; for cricket balls λ is simply too small to matter. Saying "large objects have no wavelength" is wrong — they have unobservable ones.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (2m): State the de Broglie relation and its significance.** — λ = h/mv: every moving particle has a wavelength inversely proportional to its momentum. It explains why microscopic particles show wave behaviour and derives Bohr's quantisation (2πr = nλ → mvr = nh/2π).

**NEB-style (3m): Show that Bohr's quantisation condition follows from de Broglie's hypothesis.** — The electron wave on a stationary orbit must be a standing wave: 2πr = nλ. With λ = h/mv: 2πr = nh/mv → mvr = nh/2π — Bohr's postulate of quantised angular momentum, now derived rather than decreed.

**NEB-style (2m): An electron and a cricket ball move at the same speed. Which has the longer wavelength and why?** — The electron: λ = h/mv, so the smaller mass (9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg vs 0.15 kg) gives the larger λ — electron λ ~ nm scale (observable), ball λ ~ 10⁻³⁴ m (unobservable).
confusion: **ψ vs ψ²:** ψ has no physical interpretation; ψ² is the probability density. Never interchange them.
**Orbit vs orbital:** orbit = Bohr's fixed circular track; orbital = quantum probability region. The words differ by one letter and one revolution of meaning.

The relation asserts that every moving particle has a wave character with λ inversely proportional to its momentum.

**NEB-style (3m): Derive Bohr's quantisation condition from de Broglie's hypothesis.** — (1) For a stable orbit the electron wave must be a standing wave: 2πr = nλ. (2) Substituting λ = h/mv: 2πr = nh/mv. (3) Rearranging: mvr = nh/2π — Bohr's postulate of quantised angular momentum, now a consequence of wave geometry.

data.summary: de Broglie (1924) turned Bohr's postulate into physics: every moving particle has wavelength λ = h/mv, so an orbiting electron is a wave that survives only when a whole number of wavelengths fits its circumference (2πr = nλ) — which rearranges exactly to Bohr's mvr = nh/2π. Davisson and Germer (1927) proved it by diffracting electrons off nickel. Schrödinger's wave equation built the quantum mechanical model on this foundation: wave functions ψ whose squares give probability clouds — **orbitals** — replacing Bohr's exact orbits, which the uncertainty principle had outlawed. An electron at 10⁶ m/s has λ ≈ 0.73 nm (atomic scale, observable); a cricket ball has λ ≈ 10⁻³⁴ m (unobservable) — dual nature is universal, its visibility is not.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Matter Learns to Wave

Bohr postulated quantisation; de Broglie (1924) **derived** it. If light — a wave — can behave as particles (photoelectric effect), then particles — electrons — should behave as waves. An electron wave can circle the nucleus only if a **whole number of wavelengths fits the orbit**; that condition *is* Bohr's quantisation, no longer arbitrary. This single idea, developed by Schrödinger into the wave equation, replaced orbits with **orbitals** and opened the quantum mechanical model.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 The de Broglie relation

Every moving particle has a wavelength:

**λ = h / mv = h / p** (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)

- For **macroscopic** objects m is large → λ is absurdly small → wave nature is undetectable.
- For an **electron** (m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) at ordinary speeds λ ≈ 10⁻¹⁰ m — atomic dimensions — so wave behaviour shows.

### 2.2 Deriving Bohr's quantisation (the 3m chain)

1. An electron wave must be a **standing wave** on its orbit — otherwise it destructively interferes with itself and dies.
2. Standing-wave condition: circumference = whole number of wavelengths → **2πr = nλ**.
3. Substitute λ = h/mv: 2πr = nh/mv → **mvr = nh/2π** — exactly Bohr's quantisation of angular momentum.

### 2.3 Experimental proof — Davisson and Germer (1927)

Electrons fired at a **nickel crystal** were **diffracted**, producing a diffraction pattern like X-rays — direct proof that electrons diffract as waves, with the wavelength matching de Broglie's prediction. (Thomson's electron diffraction through thin films confirmed it independently.)

### 2.4 The quantum mechanical model (elementary idea)

- Schrödinger's wave equation treats the electron as a **standing wave in three dimensions**.
- Its solutions, **wave functions ψ**, describe **orbitals** — regions of **high probability** (ψ²) of finding the electron.
- Energy is still quantised; the definite orbit is replaced by a probability cloud obeying the uncertainty principle.
- Four quantum numbers (n, l, mₗ, mₛ) label each solution.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **de Broglie wavelength** | λ = h/mv — the wave length of any moving particle | Inversely proportional to momentum |
| **Standing wave** | A wave whose pattern is fixed because a whole number of wavelengths fits the boundary | The orbit condition 2πr = nλ |
| **Wave function (ψ)** | Solution of the Schrödinger equation for an electron | ψ itself has no physical meaning |
| **Orbital** | Region where the probability of finding the electron (ψ²) is high | Replaces Bohr's orbit |
| **Probability density (ψ²)** | Square of the wave function — likelihood per unit volume | What orbitals display |
| **Heisenberg uncertainty** | Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π | Why orbits must become orbitals |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Worked numerical — wavelength of an electron (NEB-style template)

**Q: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving with a velocity of 10⁶ m s⁻¹.**
λ = h/mv = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / (9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 10⁶) = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / 9.1 × 10⁻²⁵ = **7.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ m ≈ 0.73 nm** — comparable to atomic spacing, which is why crystals diffract electrons.

### 4.2 Worked numerical — the cricket ball contrast

**Q: Find the wavelength of a 150 g cricket ball at 40 m s⁻¹.**
λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / (0.150 × 40) = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ / 6 = **1.1 × 10⁻³⁴ m** — smaller than any measurable length by 20 orders of magnitude: macroscopic wave nature is unobservable. This contrast is the favourite NEB application question.

### 4.3 Why only certain orbits survive

An orbit where the circumference is 2.5λ (say) would overlap crests on troughs — the wave cancels itself. Only orbits with 2πr = nλ reinforce; hence discrete radii, discrete energies, discrete spectrum. Quantisation is geometry, not decree.

### 4.4 From ψ to orbitals

The Schrödinger equation ψ solutions depend on three quantum numbers (n, l, mₗ); each allowed combination is one **orbital** with a characteristic shape (s spherical, p dumbbell). ψ² gives the probability picture. Bohr's radius r = 0.529 n² Å survives only as the **most probable distance** of the 1s electron — not a track.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Wave vs particle behaviour**

| Basis | Wave behaviour | Particle behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Evidence | Diffraction, interference | Photoelectric effect, collisions |
| Light shows | Yes (Young's double slit) | Yes (Einstein, photons) |
| Electron shows | Yes (Davisson–Germer diffraction) | Yes (cathode rays, charge/mass) |
| Governing relation | λ = h/mv | E = hν, p = mv |

**Similarity:** the same entity exhibits both — **dual nature**; which face appears depends on the experiment.

**Orbit (Bohr) vs orbital (quantum)**

| Basis | Orbit | Orbital |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | Definite circular path | 3-D probability region |
| Certainty | Exact position claimed | Uncertainty principle obeyed |
| Quantum numbers | n only | n, l, mₗ (labelled by four with spin) |
| Shape | Circle | s spherical, p dumbbell, … |
| Max electrons | 2n² per shell | 2 per orbital |

## 6. Common Confusions

**ψ vs ψ²:** ψ is the wave function (no direct physical meaning); **ψ² is the probability density** — the measurable one. Quoting ψ as "probability" loses the mark.

**Diffraction vs scattering:** diffraction is wave-bending around/through regular arrays (needs wavelength ~ spacing); scattering is any direction change. Davisson–Germer is diffraction — the wave proof.
**de Broglie applies to everything:** the relation is universal; for cricket balls λ is simply too small to matter. Saying "large objects have no wavelength" is wrong — they have unobservable ones.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (2m): State the de Broglie relation and its significance.** — λ = h/mv: every moving particle has a wavelength inversely proportional to its momentum. It explains why microscopic particles show wave behaviour and derives Bohr's quantisation (2πr = nλ → mvr = nh/2π).

**NEB-style (3m): Show that Bohr's quantisation condition follows from de Broglie's hypothesis.** — The electron wave on a stationary orbit must be a standing wave: 2πr = nλ. With λ = h/mv: 2πr = nh/mv → mvr = nh/2π — Bohr's postulate of quantised angular momentum, now derived rather than decreed.

**NEB-style (2m): An electron and a cricket ball move at the same speed. Which has the longer wavelength and why?** — The electron: λ = h/mv, so the smaller mass (9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg vs 0.15 kg) gives the larger λ — electron λ ~ nm scale (observable), ball λ ~ 10⁻³⁴ m (unobservable).
confusion: **ψ vs ψ²:** ψ has no physical interpretation; ψ² is the probability density. Never interchange them.
**Orbit vs orbital:** orbit = Bohr's fixed circular track; orbital = quantum probability region. The words differ by one letter and one revolution of meaning.

data.title: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle and the Concept of Probability
data.topicTitle: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle and concept of probability
notes: ### 1. Meaning and statement

Werner Heisenberg (1927) showed that for a microscopic particle it is impossible to determine simultaneously and exactly both its position and its momentum: $\Delta x\cdot\Delta p\ge\frac{h}{4\pi}$, or $\Delta x\cdot\Delta v\ge\frac{h}{4\pi m}$. Other conjugate pairs obey the same pattern: $\Delta E\cdot\Delta t\ge\frac{h}{4\pi}$ and $\Delta L\cdot\Delta\theta\ge\frac{h}{4\pi}$.
### 2. Why it happens

To locate an electron we must 'illuminate' it with radiation of wavelength comparable to its size; such a photon collides with the electron and changes its momentum by an unknown amount, while using longer-wavelength radiation blurs the position. The disturbance is a property of matter, not an experimental defect — the γ-ray microscope is the standard illustration.
### 3. Consequence: the concept of probability

A definite orbit needs exact r and p simultaneously, which the principle forbids. The electron's location can only be described by a wave function ψ, where |ψ|² dV is the **probability** of finding the electron in volume dV — the electron-cloud or **orbital** picture. The radial probability peak for the 1s orbital lies at 0.529 Å: the same number Bohr obtained, now interpreted as a most-probable distance instead of a fixed radius.
### 4. Applications

• **Atomic stability and size:** an electron confined to a nucleus (Δx ≈ 10⁻¹⁵ m) would need Δp ≈ 10⁻¹⁹ kg m s⁻¹, i.e. KE of the order 10¹⁰ eV — impossible; hence electrons cannot sit inside nuclei and atoms are ≈10⁻¹⁰ m across, which also explains why the electron does not fall into the nucleus.
• **Natural line width:** an excited state living Δt ≈ 10⁻⁸ s has ΔE ≥ h/4πΔt, so spectral lines are broadened; the same relation explains tunnelling and virtual-particle processes.

• **Zero-point energy** of confined particles, resolution limits of electron microscopes, quantum-dot behaviour and NMR line widths all follow from the principle, and all quantum-mechanical predictions (average radii, orbital shapes) are probabilistic.
### 5. Limitations and cautions

The relation matters only for microscopic particles — for a 1 g body the product is utterly negligible, so classical mechanics holds. It forbids *simultaneous* exact knowledge, not knowledge of one quantity: perfect momentum knowledge leaves position completely undefined. Interpretations differ (Copenhagen versus measurement-disturbance readings), so it is safest to state it as a property of quantum ensembles; it is not a statement about instrument precision and does not mean measurement is impossible.
**Fact.** P(E) = favourable/total. Additive law: P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B). If mutually exclusive, P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B).
**Fact.** Multiplicative: P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B|A); independence: P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B).
**Fact.** Complement: P(A') = 1 − P(A). For discrete: ΣP = 1; expected value E(X) = Σxᵢpᵢ.
### Focus of this tab
The three standard forms of the principle and the two numerical patterns NEB asks (electron in an atom; electron in the nucleus). The probability interpretation is in the main note.
### The three forms
• Position–momentum: $\Delta x\,\Delta p\ge\frac{h}{4\pi}$, or with velocity $\Delta x\,\Delta v\ge\frac{h}{4\pi m}$.
• Energy–time: $\Delta E\,\Delta t\ge\frac{h}{4\pi}$ — an excited state living Δt has a minimum energy spread ΔE, which broadens spectral lines (natural line width).
• Angular momentum–angle: $\Delta L\,\Delta\theta\ge\frac{h}{4\pi}$.
### Numerical pattern 1 — electron localised to atomic size

Δx = 10⁻¹⁰ m: Δv ≥ h/(4πmΔx) = 6.626×10⁻³⁴/(4π × 9.11×10⁻³¹ × 10⁻¹⁰) ≈ 5.8 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. This is comparable with the electron's own speed (2.2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹), so a definite orbit is impossible — the standard argument against Bohr orbits.
### Numerical pattern 2 — electron inside the nucleus

Δx = 10⁻¹⁴ m (nuclear size): Δp ≈ h/(4πΔx) ≈ 5.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ kg m s⁻¹ → KE ≈ (Δp)²/2m ≈ 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ J ≈ 10⁹ eV. Nuclear binding energies are ~10⁷ eV, so the electron cannot be confined in the nucleus — proof that electrons are not nuclear constituents (β-particles are created at emission).
### Relation to the probability concept

Because r and p cannot both be sharp, the electron's state is described by ψ with |ψ|² = probability density. The 1s radial probability peaks at 0.529 Å — Bohr's radius reappears as the *most probable* distance. 'Electron cloud', boundary surfaces and atomic radii averages all follow from this probabilistic description.
### Limits of the principle
It matters only for microscopic particles: for a 1 g body at Δx = 10⁻¹⁰ m, Δv ≈ 10⁻²⁴ m s⁻¹ — utterly negligible, so classical mechanics remains valid for everyday objects.
confusion: ❌ The principle is due to clumsy instruments. ✅ It is fundamental; better instruments cannot beat h/4π.
❌ It says nothing about the electron can be known. ✅ Either quantity may be exact; only the *product* of uncertainties is bounded below.
❌ It applies equally to a moving cricket ball. ✅ For macroscopic bodies the uncertainty product is negligible, so classical physics applies.
❌ The principle proves electrons do not exist in atoms. ✅ It replaces fixed orbits by probability distributions (orbitals) described by |ψ|².
❌ ΔE·Δt ≥ h/4π is a different law. ✅ It is the energy–time form of the same principle, explaining natural line broadening.
❌ The principle sets a limit on *both* quantities individually. ✅ Only the *product* of the two uncertainties is bounded; either one alone can be exact.
❌ ΔE·Δt means energy conservation is violated. ✅ It permits transient fluctuations within ΔE for times shorter than Δt — the basis of virtual processes and tunnelling.
❌ A better microscope can beat the limit. ✅ The limit is fundamental, not technical.

data.title: Quantum Numbers
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Four-Number Address of Every Electron

The quantum mechanical model replaced orbits with orbitals; **quantum numbers** are the postal address system that labels each electron inside them. Four numbers — **n, l, mₗ, mₛ** — fix an electron's shell, subshell, orientation and spin. NEB examines them two ways every cycle: *define and give values* (3m) and *test which sets are possible* (2m). Master the rules and both are free marks.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts — The Four Quantum Numbers

### 2.1 Principal quantum number (n)

- **Meaning:** main energy shell; size and energy of the orbital.
- **Values:** n = 1, 2, 3, 4, … (K, L, M, N).
- **Consequences:** max electrons in a shell = **2n²**; energy rises with n; distance from nucleus rises with n.

### 2.2 Azimuthal (angular momentum) quantum number (l)

- **Meaning:** shape of the orbital — the **subshell**.
- **Values:** l = 0 to (n − 1).
- **Names:** l = 0 → **s** (sharp, spherical); l = 1 → **p** (principal, dumbbell); l = 2 → **d** (diffuse, cloverleaf); l = 3 → **f** (fundamental).
- **Consequences:** number of subshells in a shell = n; angular momentum = √(l(l+1))·h/2π.

### 2.3 Magnetic quantum number (mₗ)

- **Meaning:** orientation of the orbital in space.
- **Values:** −l to +l including 0 — i.e. **(2l + 1) values**.
- **Consequences:** number of orbitals in a subshell = 2l + 1 → s: 1, p: 3, d: 5, f: 7; max electrons in a subshell = 2(2l + 1) → s: 2, p: 6, d: 10, f: 14.

### 2.4 Spin quantum number (mₛ)

- **Meaning:** intrinsic spin of the electron.
- **Values:** **+1/2 or −1/2** only.
- **Consequences:** Pauli's exclusion principle — no two electrons in one orbital share all four numbers; an orbital holds at most **2** electrons of opposite spin.

### 2.5 The master table (memorise — feeds every question)

| Shell (n) | Subshells (l) | Orbitals | Max electrons (2n²) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (K) | 1s | 1 | 2 |
| 2 (L) | 2s, 2p | 1 + 3 = 4 | 8 |
| 3 (M) | 3s, 3p, 3d | 1 + 3 + 5 = 9 | 18 |
| 4 (N) | 4s, 4p, 4d, 4f | 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 | 32 |

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Shell** | All orbitals with the same n | n = 3 is the M shell |
| **Subshell** | All orbitals with the same n and l | 3p (n = 3, l = 1) |
| **Orbital** | One (n, l, mₗ) state — a probability region | 3p with mₗ = +1 |
| **Electron address** | Full set (n, l, mₗ, mₛ) | 3, 1, +1, +1/2 |
| **Degenerate orbitals** | Orbitals of the same energy (same n, l) | The three 2p orbitals |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Worked example — NEB 2024 (3m, verified PYQ)

**Q: Write the four quantum numbers for the valence electron of sodium (Z = 11).**

Configuration: Na = 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ **3s¹** — the valence electron is in 3s.

| Quantum number | Value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| n | **3** | Third shell |
| l | **0** | s subshell |
| mₗ | **0** | s has only one orientation |
| mₛ | **+1/2** | The single electron takes spin-up by convention |

**Answer: n = 3, l = 0, mₗ = 0, mₛ = +1/2.**

### 4.2 Worked example — NEB 2023 (2m, verified PYQ)

**Q: Which set is not possible: (a) 3, 1, +1, +1/2 (b) 3, 1, +2, −1/2 (c) 3, 1, −1, −1/2 (d) 3, 0, 0, +1/2?**

Rules: l ≤ n − 1; −l ≤ mₗ ≤ +l; mₛ = ±1/2.
- (a) l = 1 allows mₗ = −1, 0, +1 → possible (3p).
- (b) mₗ = +2 **exceeds l = 1** → **not possible** — the answer.
- (c) mₗ = −1 is allowed → possible (3p).
- (d) l = 0 forces mₗ = 0 → possible (3s).

### 4.3 Why the rules exist

- **l ≤ n − 1:** a wave in shell n needs at least one wavelength of curvature; you cannot have a p-shaped (l = 1) wave in a shell too small to hold it.
- **(2l + 1) orientations:** angular momentum has 2l + 1 allowed projections along an axis — the geometric root of the magnetic quantum number.
- **Pauli:** two identical fermions cannot share one quantum state — the deepest reason an orbital holds exactly two opposite-spin electrons.

### 4.4 Electron addresses for common atoms (practice loop)

- H (Z = 1): 1, 0, 0, +1/2.
- C (Z = 6) valence p electron: 2, 1, −1 (or 0, +1), +1/2.
- Na (Z = 11): 3, 0, 0, +1/2.
- Fe (Z = 26) last electron (3d⁶): 3, 2, −2, +1/2 (by convention filling starts at mₗ = −2).

## 5. Comparison Tables

**The four quantum numbers at a glance**

| Symbol | Name | Determines | Allowed values | Number of values |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **n** | Principal | Shell, size, energy | 1, 2, 3, … | Infinite |
| **l** | Azimuthal | Subshell, shape | 0 to n−1 (s, p, d, f) | n per shell |
| **mₗ** | Magnetic | Orientation | −l … 0 … +l | 2l + 1 per subshell |
| **mₛ** | Spin | Electron spin | +1/2, −1/2 | 2 |

**Similarity:** all four together specify exactly one electron state — like country, city, street and house number.

**Shell capacity ladder**

| n | l values | Subshells | Orbitals (n²) | Electrons (2n²) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 1s | 1 | 2 |
| 2 | 0, 1 | 2s 2p | 4 | 8 |
| 3 | 0, 1, 2 | 3s 3p 3d | 9 | 18 |
| 4 | 0, 1, 2, 3 | 4s 4p 4d 4f | 16 | 32 |

**l range vs mₗ range:** l runs **0 to n − 1**; mₗ runs **−l to +l**. For n = 3, l = 2 is legal (3d) but mₗ = 2 with l = 1 is not — the two ranges are different rules.
**"n = 3, l = 3" trap:** l can never equal n; the highest l in shell n is n − 1 (3f does not exist).
**mₛ values:** only ±1/2 — never ±1. Spin "up/down" is shorthand for the two signs, not a literal direction.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Four-Number Address of Every Electron

The quantum mechanical model replaced orbits with orbitals; **quantum numbers** are the postal address system that labels each electron inside them. Four numbers — **n, l, mₗ, mₛ** — fix an electron's shell, subshell, orientation and spin. NEB examines them two ways every cycle: *define and give values* (3m) and *test which sets are possible* (2m). Master the rules and both are free marks.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts — The Four Quantum Numbers

### 2.1 Principal quantum number (n)

- **Meaning:** main energy shell; size and energy of the orbital.
- **Values:** n = 1, 2, 3, 4, … (K, L, M, N).
- **Consequences:** max electrons in a shell = **2n²**; energy rises with n; distance from nucleus rises with n.

### 2.2 Azimuthal (angular momentum) quantum number (l)

- **Meaning:** shape of the orbital — the **subshell**.
- **Values:** l = 0 to (n − 1).
- **Names:** l = 0 → **s** (sharp, spherical); l = 1 → **p** (principal, dumbbell); l = 2 → **d** (diffuse, cloverleaf); l = 3 → **f** (fundamental).
- **Consequences:** number of subshells in a shell = n; angular momentum = √(l(l+1))·h/2π.

### 2.3 Magnetic quantum number (mₗ)

- **Meaning:** orientation of the orbital in space.
- **Values:** −l to +l including 0 — i.e. **(2l + 1) values**.
- **Consequences:** number of orbitals in a subshell = 2l + 1 → s: 1, p: 3, d: 5, f: 7; max electrons in a subshell = 2(2l + 1) → s: 2, p: 6, d: 10, f: 14.

### 2.4 Spin quantum number (mₛ)

- **Meaning:** intrinsic spin of the electron.
- **Values:** **+1/2 or −1/2** only.
- **Consequences:** Pauli's exclusion principle — no two electrons in one orbital share all four numbers; an orbital holds at most **2** electrons of opposite spin.

### 2.5 The master table (memorise — feeds every question)

| Shell (n) | Subshells (l) | Orbitals | Max electrons (2n²) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (K) | 1s | 1 | 2 |
| 2 (L) | 2s, 2p | 1 + 3 = 4 | 8 |
| 3 (M) | 3s, 3p, 3d | 1 + 3 + 5 = 9 | 18 |
| 4 (N) | 4s, 4p, 4d, 4f | 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 | 32 |

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Shell** | All orbitals with the same n | n = 3 is the M shell |
| **Subshell** | All orbitals with the same n and l | 3p (n = 3, l = 1) |
| **Orbital** | One (n, l, mₗ) state — a probability region | 3p with mₗ = +1 |
| **Electron address** | Full set (n, l, mₗ, mₛ) | 3, 1, +1, +1/2 |
| **Degenerate orbitals** | Orbitals of the same energy (same n, l) | The three 2p orbitals |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Worked example — NEB 2024 (3m, verified PYQ)

**Q: Write the four quantum numbers for the valence electron of sodium (Z = 11).**

Configuration: Na = 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ **3s¹** — the valence electron is in 3s.

| Quantum number | Value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| n | **3** | Third shell |
| l | **0** | s subshell |
| mₗ | **0** | s has only one orientation |
| mₛ | **+1/2** | The single electron takes spin-up by convention |

**Answer: n = 3, l = 0, mₗ = 0, mₛ = +1/2.**

### 4.2 Worked example — NEB 2023 (2m, verified PYQ)

**Q: Which set is not possible: (a) 3, 1, +1, +1/2 (b) 3, 1, +2, −1/2 (c) 3, 1, −1, −1/2 (d) 3, 0, 0, +1/2?**

- **(2l + 1) orientations:** angular momentum has 2l + 1 allowed projections along an axis — the geometric root of the magnetic quantum number.
- **Pauli:** two identical fermions cannot share one quantum state — the deepest reason an orbital holds exactly two opposite-spin electrons.

### 4.4 Electron addresses for common atoms (practice loop)

- C (Z = 6) valence p electron: 2, 1, −1 (or 0, +1), +1/2.
- Na (Z = 11): 3, 0, 0, +1/2.
- Fe (Z = 26) last electron (3d⁶): 3, 2, −2, +1/2 (by convention filling starts at mₗ = −2).

## 5. Comparison Tables

**The four quantum numbers at a glance**

data.title: Orbitals and the Shapes of s and p Orbitals
data.topicTitle: Orbitals and shape of s and p orbitals only
notes: ### 1. Meaning of an orbital

An orbital is the three-dimensional region around the nucleus in which the probability of finding the electron is maximum (the ~90–95% boundary-surface region) for a given energy state. It comes from the wave function ψ of the Schrödinger equation, and |ψ|² is the probability density. An orbital has *no sharp boundary* and does not describe a path.
### 2. Orbital vs orbit
• Orbit (Bohr): fixed two-dimensional circular path with definite radius and energy.
• Orbital (quantum mechanics): three-dimensional probability distribution — spherical (s) or directional (p, d) — with no definite path and no sharp edge.
### 3. Shape of s orbitals
• **Spherical** and hence non-directional; present in every shell from n = 1.
• Size and energy increase with n (1s < 2s < 3s); the radial probability distribution shows (n − 1) maxima, the outermost being the most probable distance (0.529 Å for 1s).
• (n − 1) spherical nodes and no nodal plane; 1s has no node.
### 4. Shape of p orbitals
• **Dumbbell (peanut) shaped** — two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus with a nodal plane through the nucleus where probability is zero.
• They appear from n = 2 as three orbitals at 90° to one another: px, py, pz (m = −1, 0, +1).
• The three are **degenerate** in a free atom and split in a magnetic field (Zeeman effect).
• Each p orbital holds 2 electrons, so a p subshell holds 6; the shapes are identical, only the orientation differs.
### 5. Nodes, penetration and degeneracy

Nodes are zero-probability regions: radial = n − l − 1, angular (nodal planes) = l, total = n − 1. Because s orbitals penetrate closer to the nucleus than p orbitals of the same shell, they are less shielded and lower in energy — the reason for the ns < np < nd order in multi-electron atoms.
### 6. Applications
• **Bonding and molecular shape:** the directionality of p orbitals explains the 90° H–S–H angle, the VSEPR shapes, and the σ (end-on) versus π (side-on) classification of bonds.
• **Hybridisation:** mixing s and p orbitals (sp, sp², sp³) explains the linear BeF₂, trigonal-planar BF₃ and tetrahedral CH₄ geometries.
• **Periodic table:** three p orbitals per subshell (capacity 6) explain the six-membered p-block and the period lengths 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32.
• Explains paramagnetism (degenerate orbitals occupied singly per Hund's rule) and the spherical electron cloud of the noble gases.
### 7. Limitations

Orbital pictures are *boundary-surface diagrams* at a chosen probability level — the electron is not confined to the drawn shape and no motion is shown. Exact shapes strictly hold only for one-electron systems; electron correlation and bonding perturb them in real atoms and molecules; d and f orbitals are far more complex (this syllabus limits us to s and p); and orbitals cannot be observed directly — only electron density can.
### Focus of this tab
Spin quantum number and the box-arrow notation, mapped onto the shell structure — the drawing skills needed for configuration and orbital-diagram questions.
### The spin quantum number

mₛ = +½ (↑) or −½ (↓) for every electron, independent of n, l, m. Spin angular momentum is √(3/4)ħ. Consequences: an orbital holds at most 2 electrons (Pauli); a shell holds 2n²; a subshell holds 2(2l + 1).
### Box notation rules
• One box per orbital; label the subshell above (2p: three boxes).
• Aufbau: fill orbitals in increasing (n + l) order.
• Hund: in degenerate boxes, one up-arrow per box before any pairing.
• Pauli: two arrows in one box must be opposite (↑↓).
### Shell mapping (putting orbitals into shells)
### Worked box diagrams
• N (Z = 7): 1s ↑↓ | 2s ↑↓ | 2p ↑ ↑ ↑ → 3 unpaired electrons, paramagnetic.
• O (Z = 8): 2p ↑↓ ↑ ↑ → 2 unpaired.
• Cr (Z = 24): [Ar] 3d ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑ with 4s ↑ — the half-filled exception.
### What the diagrams predict

Unpaired electrons → paramagnetism, μ = √(u(u + 2)) BM; paired → diamagnetic. The diagram also shows why carbon forms two covalent bonds after promotion (two half-filled p orbitals) and why the noble gases are inert (all boxes paired).
The orbit–orbital distinction in tabular form plus the s-orbital details (radial probability distribution) that the main note covers briefly.
### Orbit versus orbital (six-row table)
• Origin: Bohr's model / Schrödinger's equation.
• Nature: fixed 2D circular path / 3D probability region.
• Definiteness: exact radius and momentum / neither is definite (Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π).
• Number: one orbit per n / n² orbitals per shell.
• Direction: non-directional concept / s spherical, p directional.
• Status: contradicted by experiment / the accepted modern picture.
### The s orbital in detail
• Shape: sphere — electron density depends only on distance r, not direction (non-directional, hence s orbitals give no directionality in bonding).

• Radial probability distribution: the chance of finding the electron between r and r + dr peaks at the most probable distance — 0.529 Å for 1s. For 2s the curve has two maxima separated by a radial node where probability is exactly zero.
• Nodes: 1s none; 2s one spherical node at r = 2a₀ ≈ 1.06 Å; 3s two; in general (n − 1) spherical nodes. There are no nodal planes for s.
• Size and energy: both increase with n (1s < 2s < 3s), and higher s orbitals penetrate closer to the nucleus than p of the same shell — the origin of the ns < np energy order.
### Why s orbitals matter chemically

Spherical symmetry makes s orbitals the 'all-direction' bond formers (H uses 1s in every bond), the mixing component of every hybrid (sp, sp², sp³), and the reason the noble-gas electron clouds (filled s and p) are spherically symmetric — the chemical basis of their inertness.
confusion: ❌ Orbit and orbital mean the same thing. ✅ Orbit = fixed 2D path; orbital = 3D probability region.
❌ A p orbital has two lobes, so it holds two electrons in each lobe. ✅ The lobes together form one orbital, which holds a pair of electrons of opposite spin.
❌ s orbitals become dumbbell-shaped in higher shells. ✅ All s orbitals stay spherical; only size and nodes change with n.

data.topicTitle: Aufbau principle, Pauli's exclusion principle, Hund's rule and electronic configurations of atoms and ions (up to atomic no. 30)
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Filling Rules That Build the Periodic Table

Quantum numbers give every electron an address; three rules decide the **order of occupation**: the **Aufbau principle** (fill lowest energy first), **Pauli's exclusion principle** (two electrons maximum per orbital, opposite spins) and **Hund's rule** (degenerate orbitals fill singly with parallel spins first). Apply all three and the electron configurations of every element up to Z = 30 — and the structure of the periodic table — follow mechanically. NEB 2023 asked Aufbau directly (3m); the configurations themselves are permanent exam currency.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Aufbau principle (building-up)

Electrons occupy the **lowest-energy orbital available** before entering higher ones. Energy order (the diagonal rule):

**1s < 2s < 2p < 3s < 3p < 4s < 3d < 4p < 5s < 4d < 5p …**

- The **(n + l) rule** predicts the order: lower (n + l) fills first; on a tie, lower n fills first.
  - 4s: n + l = 4 + 0 = 4 — fills **before** 3d: n + l = 3 + 2 = 5.
- The order is set by **penetration**: s electrons penetrate closer to the nucleus than p, d, f of the same shell, so 4s is stabilised below 3d.

### 2.2 Pauli's exclusion principle

**No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of all four quantum numbers.**

- Consequence: an orbital holds **at most 2 electrons, with opposite spins** (↑↓).
- Capacities: orbital 2, subshell 2(2l + 1), shell 2n².

### 2.3 Hund's rule (of maximum multiplicity)

For **degenerate orbitals** (same energy — the three p, five d, seven f):

1. Electrons **fill singly first**, with **parallel spins** (↑ ↑ ↑).
2. **Pairing starts only after every orbital in the subshell is singly occupied.**

Reason: parallel spins in separate orbitals minimise repulsion and maximise exchange energy — half-filled and fully-filled subshells are extra stable (explains Cr: 3d⁵4s¹ and Cu: 3d¹⁰4s¹).

### 2.4 Worked configurations up to Z = 30

| Z | Element | Configuration | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | H | 1s¹ | |
| 2 | He | 1s² | K shell full |
| 3 | Li | 1s² 2s¹ | |
| 4 | Be | 1s² 2s² | |
| 5 | B | 1s² 2s² 2p¹ | |
| 6 | C | 1s² 2s² 2p² | 2p¹↑ 2p¹↑ (Hund) |
| 7 | N | 1s² 2s² 2p³ | 2p↑ ↑ ↑ — half-filled p |
| 8 | O | 1s² 2s² 2p⁴ | first pairing |
| 9 | F | 1s² 2s² 2p⁵ | |
| 10 | Ne | 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ | noble gas core |
| 11 | Na | [Ne] 3s¹ | NEB 2024's atom |
| 12 | Mg | [Ne] 3s² | |
| 13 | Al | [Ne] 3s² 3p¹ | |
| 16 | S | [Ne] 3s² 3p⁴ | |
| 18 | Ar | [Ne] 3s² 3p⁶ | |
| 19 | K | [Ar] **4s¹** | 4s before 3d |
| 20 | Ca | [Ar] 4s² | |
| 21 | Sc | [Ar] 4s² 3d¹ | 3d begins |
| 24 | Cr | [Ar] 4s¹ **3d⁵** | half-filled d — exception |
| 26 | Fe | [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶ | |
| 29 | Cu | [Ar] 4s¹ **3d¹⁰** | filled d — exception |
| 30 | Zn | [Ar] 4s² 3d¹⁰ | 3d complete |

### 2.5 Ions (remove from the outermost shell first)

- Fe²⁺: [Ar] 3d⁶ (lose 4s² first, **not** 3d).
- Cu⁺: [Ar] 3d¹⁰; Cu²⁺: [Ar] 3d⁹.
- Fe³⁺: [Ar] 3d⁵ — half-filled, extra stable (why Fe³⁺ beats Fe²⁺ in stability).

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Aufbau principle** | Electrons fill the lowest-energy orbitals first | 4s fills before 3d |
| **Pauli exclusion principle** | No two electrons share all four quantum numbers | Orbital capacity = 2 |
| **Hund's rule** | Degenerate orbitals fill singly with parallel spins before pairing | N: 2p ↑ ↑ ↑ |
| **Degenerate orbitals** | Orbitals of equal energy | Three 2p, five 3d |
| **Core notation** | Noble-gas core + valence electrons | Na = [Ne] 3s¹ |
| **Exchange energy** | Stabilisation from parallel-spin electrons in different orbitals | Maximised at half-filled d⁵ |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 NEB 2023 (3m, verified PYQ) — Explain Aufbau's principle with an example

**Statement:** electrons enter the orbital of lowest energy first; higher orbitals are occupied only after all lower ones are filled. The energy order follows the (n + l) rule — lower (n + l) first, and on a tie the lower n first.

**Example:** potassium (Z = 19) — after the argon core [Ar], the next electron enters **4s (n + l = 4)** rather than 3d (n + l = 5): K = [Ar] 4s¹, not [Ar] 3d¹. Similarly Ca = [Ar] 4s², and only from scandium do the 3d orbitals begin to fill.

### 4.2 Why 4s fills before 3d

**Penetration and shielding.** A 4s electron penetrates through the inner shells close to the nucleus, feeling nearly the full nuclear charge; a 3d electron barely penetrates and is heavily shielded. The net energy of 4s is therefore **lower** than 3d despite the larger n — the (n + l) rule is the bookkeeping, penetration is the physics.

### 4.3 The two famous exceptions

- **Cr (Z = 24):** expected [Ar] 4s² 3d⁴, actual [Ar] 4s¹ **3d⁵** — a half-filled d subshell gains extra exchange energy (five parallel-spin electrons) and the s electron supplies it.
- **Cu (Z = 29):** expected [Ar] 4s² 3d⁹, actual [Ar] 4s¹ **3d¹⁰** — a completely filled d subshell is even more stable.
- Symmetry + exchange energy make half-filled and fully-filled subshells special — the same reason N (2p³) is more stable than O (2p⁴).

### 4.4 Hund's rule in action — the p³ → p⁴ step

Nitrogen's three 2p electrons occupy the three separate p orbitals with parallel spins (↑ ↑ ↑). Oxygen's fourth electron **must pair** (↑↓ ↑ ↑), paying pairing repulsion — which is why first-ionisation-energy data show the famous N > O dip in period 2.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**The three rules side by side**

| Rule | Statement | Governs | Visible effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Aufbau** | Lowest energy orbital fills first | Order of subshells | 4s before 3d; K = [Ar] 4s¹ |
| **Pauli** | All four quantum numbers cannot repeat | Capacity | Orbital = 2 electrons, ↑↓ |
| **Hund** | Singly + parallel first, then pair | Degenerate sets | N = 2p ↑ ↑ ↑; Cr, Cu exceptions |

**Similarity:** all three are filling rules for ground-state configurations; each covers a different failure mode (energy order, capacity, pairing timing).

**Ground state vs excited state (the classic 2m)**

| Basis | Ground state | Excited state |
|---|---|---|
| Occupation | Rules obeyed strictly | Electron promoted to higher orbital |
| Example (C) | 1s² 2s² 2p² | 1s² 2s¹ 2p³ |
| Energy | Minimum | Higher; emits light on relaxation |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Ionisation order vs filling order:** electrons are **removed from the outermost shell** — Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶, not [Ar] 4s² 3d⁴. 4s fills first but also empties first.
**Hund's rule scope:** it applies **only within a degenerate set** (p³, d⁵…); it never overrides Aufbau's energy ordering across different subshells.
**Exceptions are ground-state facts:** Cr and Cu configurations apply to the neutral ground-state atoms; their ions follow the normal removal order (Cu⁺ = 3d¹⁰).

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (2m): Write the configuration of Fe (Z = 26) and of Fe³⁺; why is Fe³⁺ more stable than Fe²⁺?** — Fe: [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶; Fe³⁺: [Ar] 3d⁵ (4s² removed first, then one 3d). Fe³⁺ has an exactly **half-filled 3d⁵** — maximum exchange energy and spherical symmetry — so it is extra stable.

**NEB-style (2m): State Hund's rule and illustrate with nitrogen.** — Degenerate orbitals are occupied singly with parallel spins before any pairing. N (Z = 7): 1s² 2s² 2p³ → the three 2p electrons sit in three separate p orbitals as ↑ ↑ ↑.

**NEB-style (2m): Predict the ground-state configuration of Cr (Z = 24) and explain the anomaly.** — [Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵ instead of [Ar] 4s² 3d⁴: the half-filled 3d⁵ gains maximum exchange energy, and promoting one 4s electron to 3d costs little because 4s and 3d are nearly degenerate.
confusion: **4s before 3d — but also 4s out first:** filling order and removal order are different questions. Ions strip the highest-n shell first.

**Pairing needs a partner orbital, not the same orbital:** Hund's rule forbids pairing while a degenerate orbital is still empty — O (2p⁴) pairs only because all three p orbitals already hold one electron.

**NEB-style (2m): Write the configuration of Fe (Z = 26) and of Fe³⁺; why is Fe³⁺ more stable than Fe²⁺?** — Fe: [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶; Fe³⁺: [Ar] 3d⁵ (4s² removed first, then one 3d). Fe³⁺ has an exactly **half-filled 3d⁵** — maximum exchange energy and spherical symmetry — so it is extra stable.

**NEB-style (2m): State Hund's rule and illustrate with nitrogen.** — Degenerate orbitals are occupied singly with parallel spins before any pairing. N (Z = 7): 1s² 2s² 2p³ → the three 2p electrons sit in three separate p orbitals as ↑ ↑ ↑.

**NEB-style (2m): Predict the ground-state configuration of Cr (Z = 24) and explain the anomaly.** — [Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵ instead of [Ar] 4s² 3d⁴: the half-filled 3d⁵ gains maximum exchange energy, and promoting one 4s electron to 3d costs little because 4s and 3d are nearly degenerate.
confusion: **4s before 3d — but also 4s out first:** filling order and removal order are different questions. Ions strip the highest-n shell first.

**Pairing needs a partner orbital, not the same orbital:** Hund's rule forbids pairing while a degenerate orbital is still empty — O (2p⁴) pairs only because all three p orbitals already hold one electron.
keyPoints: Aufbau: fill lowest energy first — order 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s…, predicted by (n + l), tie → lower n. Pauli: no two electrons share all four quantum numbers → orbital max 2, ↑↓. Hund: degenerate orbitals fill singly with parallel spins before pairing. Exceptions: Cr [Ar] 4s¹3d⁵, Cu [Ar] 4s¹3d¹⁰ (half/full-filled stability). Ions: remove 4s before 3d — Fe³⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁵ extra stable.
importantConcepts: **(n + l) rule** — the quick ordering tool: sum n and l; lower sum fills first; equal sums → lower n first. It reproduces the whole diagonal order without memorising it.
examples: ***K (Z = 19) = [Ar] 4s¹*** — the (n + l) rule at work: 4s (4+0 = 4) beats 3d (3+2 = 5), so the 19th electron of potassium enters 4s, not 3d — the single clearest demonstration of Aufbau.
universalFacts: The periodic table's block structure is the Aufbau order made visible: s-block (groups 1–2), p-block (13–18), d-block (3–12), f-block — the filling sequence *is* the table's shape.
importantStatements: "No two electrons in an atom can have identical values of all four quantum numbers." — Pauli; the reason matter occupies space at all.
importantNotes: Verified PYQs: NEB 2023 3m — explain Aufbau with an example (solved above); NEB 2024 3m — quantum numbers of Na's valence electron (topic 19). Configurations up to Z = 30 are standing NEB currency.
examShortTricks: Diagonal chant: "1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s 4d 5p." (n + l) check for any disputed pair. Ions: "last in, first out" — strip the highest shell.
examNotes: Write configurations in full for Z ≤ 18; core notation [Ar] is fine beyond. For ions, show the neutral configuration first, then strike out — the marking scheme follows the steps.

**NEB-style (2m): State Pauli's exclusion principle and one consequence.** — No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of all four quantum numbers. Consequence: an orbital holds at most two electrons with opposite spins (↑↓); shell capacity is 2n².

**NEB-style (3m): Write the ground-state configurations of Cr (Z = 24) and Cu (Z = 29) and account for the anomalies.** — Cr: [Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵; Cu: [Ar] 4s¹ 3d¹⁰. Half-filled (d⁵) and fully-filled (d¹⁰) subshells have maximum exchange energy and symmetrical charge distribution; shifting one 4s electron into 3d (nearly degenerate with 4s) achieves that extra stability.

data.title: From Dalton's Atom to the Nuclear Atom — the Historical Chain
data.topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: ### Focus of this tab

The discovery chain that produced the nuclear atom — Dalton → electron → proton → neutron → Thomson → Rutherford — so that 'Rutherford's model and its limitations' can be answered with its historical context.
### The particles, in order of discovery
• **Electron** (J. J. Thomson, 1897): cathode rays are deflected by E and B fields; e/m = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹, identical for all cathode materials → universal negative particle.

• **Proton** (E. Goldstein's anode/canal rays, 1886, identified as a particle by Thomson 1907; named by Rutherford 1919–20): positive rays bend oppositely in fields; the lightest positive particle (from hydrogen) has charge +e and mass 1836 × electron mass. Rutherford produced it deliberately: ¹⁴N + ⁴He → ¹⁷O + ¹p (first nuclear transmutation).

• **Neutron** (James Chadwick, 1932): beryllium bombarded by α-particles emits a neutral, highly penetrating radiation: ⁹Be + ⁴He → ¹²C + ¹n; mass ≈ 1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, slightly heavier than the proton, charge 0.
### How each discovery reshaped the atom model
• Dalton's indivisible atom (1803) fell once electrons and protons emerged — atoms have internal structure.
• Thomson (1904) embedded electrons in diffuse positive charge — failed on α-scattering.
• Rutherford (1911) put the positive charge and mass in a tiny nucleus with electrons around it — failed on stability and line spectra.
• The neutron completed the nuclear picture: nuclei contain Z protons and A − Z neutrons, explaining isotopes (same Z, different N) that Dalton's 'identical atoms' postulate could not.
### Particle data table (memorise)

Electron: charge −1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mass 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg (0.000549 u, 1/1837 of H atom). Proton: +1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (1.00728 u). Neutron: 0, 1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (1.00867 u). Charge/mass ratio of the electron is the largest, which is why electron beams are easiest to deflect.
### Why the neutron took so long

A neutral particle leaves no track in electric or magnetic fields and is not detected by ionisation chambers — it was first mistaken for γ-radiation. Chadwick's insight was to use the recoiling protons ejected from paraffin wax to measure its mass by momentum conservation.
confusion: ❌ Goldstein discovered the proton in 1886. ✅ Goldstein discovered canal (anode) rays; the proton as the lightest positive particle was characterised later and named by Rutherford.
❌ The neutron is lighter than the proton. ✅ It is slightly heavier (1.675 vs 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg), which is why free neutrons β-decay.
❌ Electrons contribute most of the atomic mass. ✅ They contribute ≈0.05%; nearly all mass is nuclear.

formulas: $$^{14}\text{N}+^{4}\text{He}\rightarrow^{17}\text{O}+^{1}\text{p},\qquad ^{9}\text{Be}+^{4}\text{He}\rightarrow^{12}\text{C}+^{1}\text{n}$$
universalFacts: Chadwick's 1932 neutron discovery completed the particle trio and earned the 1935 Nobel Prize.
The proton is 1836 times heavier than the electron; the neutron is 1839 times heavier.
Cathode-ray e/m is independent of the gas and electrode material — electrons are in all matter.
examples: **Problem:** An atom has Z = 17 and A = 35. Find p, n, e. **Solution:** protons = 17, electrons = 17 (neutral atom), neutrons = A − Z = 18 — the isotope ³⁵Cl.
importantNotes: Keep the discovery order strict: electron (1897) → proton (named 1919–20) → neutron (1932).
Mass number A = protons + neutrons; atomic number Z = protons = electrons in a neutral atom.

data.title: Discovery of the Electron — Cathode Rays
data.topicTitle: Discovery Of Electron And Its Properties
notes: ### Focus of this tab

The discovery of the electron through cathode-ray experiments — the first subatomic particle, and the starting point of every atomic model. (It sits in this unit as the experimental foundation of electronic structure.)
### The cathode-ray tube experiments

• A gas at low pressure (≈10⁻² atm) in a discharge tube with ≈10 000 V across the electrodes emits rays from the cathode that travel in straight lines (shadow of the Maltese cross), carry momentum (paddle-wheel rotation) and heat the target.
• **Electric field:** the rays bend toward the positive plate → negatively charged.
• **Magnetic field:** they bend in the direction expected for negative charges.
• The deflection is independent of the gas and cathode material → the particle is a universal constituent of all matter.
### Thomson's measurements (1897)

Crossed E and B fields (velocity selector): undeflected when Eq = Bqv → v = E/B. Then switching off B gives the deflection, yielding e/m = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹ — about 1837 times larger than the hydrogen ion's e/m. Since the charge is later shown to be the same unit charge, the particle must be ≈1837 times lighter than hydrogen: a new particle, the electron.
### Millikan's oil-drop experiment (1909)

Balancing the electric force against the weight of a charged oil drop gave the charge of a single electron: e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (quantised — all drops carry integer multiples of e). Combined with e/m, the electron mass is m = 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg (0.000549 u).
### Why this matters for the atomic models

Once atoms contain light negative electrons, something positive must balance them — the direct motivation for Thomson's plum-pudding model and then Rutherford's nucleus. The electron also completes the electronic-structure story: its arrangement in orbitals is what this unit's quantum numbers describe.
confusion: ❌ Cathode rays are electromagnetic waves. ✅ They are streams of charged particles — waves are not deflected by E/B fields.
❌ The cathode-ray properties depend on the gas used. ✅ They are independent of gas and electrode material, which is why the particle is universal.
❌ Millikan measured e/m. ✅ He measured e alone; Thomson had already measured e/m.

Thomson received the 1906 Nobel Prize; Millikan the 1923 Nobel Prize.
Cathode rays travel in straight lines but are deflected by fields — the basis of the old CRT television.

data.title: Discovery of the Proton — Anode Rays and Nuclear Transmutation
data.topicTitle: Discovery Of Proton And Its Properties
notes: ### Focus of this tab
How the proton was found: Goldstein's anode (canal) rays, the mass spectrometry evidence, and Rutherford's 1919 transmutation — the second particle needed to build the nuclear atom.
### Anode (canal) rays, 1886

Goldstein used a perforated (perforated-cathode) discharge tube: besides cathode rays, a new radiation passed *through* the holes of the cathode in the direction opposite to cathode rays. Properties: travel in straight lines, deflected by E and B fields in the direction of *positive* charges, and the e/m value **depends on the gas** in the tube — so these are positive ions of the gas, not a universal particle.
### The lightest positive particle

With hydrogen in the tube the e/m is the largest observed (9.58 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹), i.e. the lightest positive particle: the proton, with charge +1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and mass 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 1.00728 u ≈ 1836 electron masses. The proton is the nuclear constituent that carries the atomic number Z.
### Rutherford's transmutation (1919)

Bombarding nitrogen with α-particles produced protons and oxygen: $^{14}\text{N}+\,^{4}\text{He}\rightarrow\,^{17}\text{O}+\,^{1}\text{p}$. This was the first artificial nuclear reaction: it (i) proved protons exist inside nuclei, (ii) changed one element into another (contra Dalton), and (iii) named the particle 'proton' (from protos, first).
### Why the proton matters for structure

The nuclear charge Z counted in protons is the element's identity (Moseley); A = Z + N requires neutrons as well, since protons alone cannot account for the masses and stability of nuclei (electrostatic repulsion of like charges would fly apart — the strong interaction and neutrons are needed).
confusion: ❌ Anode rays are a universal particle like cathode rays. ✅ Their e/m depends on the gas — they are positive ions of that gas; only the hydrogen ion (proton) is universal.
❌ Goldstein named and identified the proton fully. ✅ He discovered the rays; the proton was characterised later and named by Rutherford.
❌ The proton is 1837 times heavier than the electron. ✅ 1836 (the neutron is 1839).

formulas: $$\frac{e}{m}\ (\text{proton})=9.58\times10^{7}\ \text{C kg}^{-1};\quad m_{p}=1.673\times10^{-27}\ \text{kg}=1836\,m_{e}$$
$$^{14}\text{N}+^{4}\text{He}\rightarrow^{17}\text{O}+^{1}\text{p}$$
universalFacts: The proton's mass in u is 1.00728 — the basis of the amu scale (¹²C = 12 exactly).
Canal rays are also called positive rays; Aston's mass spectrograph (1919) developed from them.
Rutherford's transmutation opened nuclear chemistry: element synthesis beyond bismuth became possible.
examples: **Problem:** Why do anode rays bend less than cathode rays in the same field? **Solution:** deflection ∝ q/m; the proton's q/m is ≈1836 times smaller than the electron's, so its curvature is correspondingly tiny.

data.title: The Neutron and the Fundamental Particles Table
data.topicTitle: Discovery Of Neutron And Fundamental Particles
notes: ### Focus of this tab
Chadwick's discovery of the neutron and the complete subatomic-particle data table that the nuclear atom needs (electron, proton, neutron with charge, mass, discoverer and location).
### Why a third particle had to exist

Mass problem: helium (Z = 2) should weigh 2 protons ≈ 2 u, but weighs 4 u. Charge problem: nitrogen (A = 14, Z = 7) would need 7 electrons inside the nucleus under a proton-only model, making the atom's magnetism and the electron's confinement impossible (uncertainty: electrons cannot be confined to 10⁻¹⁵ m). A neutral, massive particle was required.
### Chadwick's experiment (1932)

Polonium's α-particles hit beryllium and released a highly penetrating, neutral radiation: $^{9}\text{Be}+^{4}\text{He}\rightarrow\,^{12}\text{C}+^{1}\text{n}$. The radiation knocked protons out of paraffin wax; by conservation of momentum and energy the unknown particle's mass was calculated as ≈1.15–1.16 u — close to the proton's. Being neutral, it was unaffected by E/B fields and could pass through centimetres of lead.
### The fundamental particles table (memorise)
• Electron (e⁻): charge −1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (−1 unit), mass 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg = 0.000549 u = 1/1837 of H; discovered by J. J. Thomson (1897); location: revolving in orbitals outside the nucleus.
• Proton (p): +1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (+1), 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 1.00728 u; Goldstein's rays/identified by Thomson, named by Rutherford (1919–20); location: nucleus.

• Neutron (n): 0, 1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 1.00867 u (heaviest of the three); Chadwick (1932); location: nucleus. Free neutrons β-decay (half-life ≈ 11 min) because they are slightly heavier than a proton plus an electron.
### What the trio explains

Isotopes (same Z, different N), radioactivity (nuclear instability), nuclear stability (N/Z ratio ≈ 1 for light nuclei, rising to ≈1.5 for heavy), fission/fusion energy, and the notation ᴬZX that summarises every nuclide.
Mass number A, the isotope concept it makes possible, and the average-atomic-mass calculation — the accounting that sits on top of the fundamental particles.
### Mass number

A = number of protons + number of neutrons = Z + N. It is always a whole number because it counts particles; the *atomic mass* measured for an element is usually not a whole number because it is a weighted average over isotopes (e.g. Cl = 35.45 u). Notation ᴬZX places A upper-left, Z lower-left.
### Isotopes (same Z, different A)
• Hydrogen: ¹H protium, ²H deuterium (D, in heavy water D₂O), ³H tritium (radioactive) — the only element whose isotopes have separate names.
• Carbon: ¹²C (98.9%, the amu standard), ¹³C (NMR), ¹⁴C (dating). Chlorine: ³⁵Cl (75%), ³⁷Cl (25%). Uranium: ²³⁵U (fissile, 0.7%), ²³⁸U (99.3%).
• Chemical properties are almost identical (same electron configuration); physical properties differ with mass (density, diffusion rate, spectra — the D line shift identified deuterium).
### Average atomic mass (the numerical pattern)

Average = Σ(abundance × isotopic mass). Cl: 0.75 × 35 + 0.25 × 37 = 35.5 u. Ne: 0.905 × 20 + 0.0027 × 21 + 0.0923 × 22 ≈ 20.18 u. Working backwards: given the average and one abundance, the second isotopic mass can be found.
### Separation and uses

Because isotopes differ only in mass, separation uses mass-dependent processes: gaseous diffusion (UF₆) or centrifugation for ²³⁵U, electrolysis/distillation for D₂O. Uses: ¹⁴C dating, ¹³¹I thyroid therapy, ⁶⁰Co radiotherapy, D₂O as a neutron moderator, tracer studies in metabolism.
### Relation to Dalton's theory
Isotopes violate Dalton's postulate that all atoms of an element are identical in mass; the nuclear model plus the neutron explains them — same proton count, different neutron count.
confusion: ❌ The neutron is lighter than the proton. ✅ It is heavier (1.675 vs 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) — hence free-neutron β-decay.
❌ The neutron was discovered before the proton was named. ✅ Proton named 1919–20; neutron 1932.
❌ Neutrons carry a small charge. ✅ Exactly zero charge; that is why they penetrate deeply and leave no ion tracks.
❌ Mass number is the atomic mass. ✅ A is a whole-number particle count; atomic mass is the weighted average in u.
❌ Isotopes have different chemical properties. ✅ Nearly identical chemically; they differ in mass and nuclear stability.
❌ ²³⁵U and ²³⁸U are isobars. ✅ They are isotopes (same Z = 92); isobars need equal A.

formulas: $$^{9}\text{Be}+^{4}\text{He}\rightarrow^{12}\text{C}+^{1}\text{n};\qquad A=Z+N$$
$$m_{n}=1.675\times10^{-27}\ \text{kg}>m_{p}+m_{e}\ \Rightarrow\ \text{free neutron decays}$$
$$A=Z+N;\qquad \text{average mass}=\sum(\text{abundance}\times\text{isotopic mass})$$
universalFacts: Chadwick received the 1935 Nobel Prize for the neutron; it made the fission chain reaction conceivable.
Neutron half-life outside the nucleus ≈ 10.7 min.
The neutron's magnetic moment is not zero (−1.91 nuclear magnetons) despite zero charge — evidence of internal quark structure.
¹²C defines the unified mass unit: 1 u = 1/12 mass of a ¹²C atom = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.
Heavy water (D₂O) is used as moderator-cum-coolant in CANDU reactors.
Uranium enrichment to ≈3–5% ²³⁵U is what reactor fuel requires (weapons need ≈90%).
examples: **Problem:** An atom has Z = 6 and A = 14. Give p, n, e and its isotope name. **Solution:** 6 protons, 8 neutrons, 6 electrons — carbon-14 (¹⁴C), the dating isotope.
**Problem:** An element of average mass 10.8 consists of isotopes 10 and 11. Find abundances. **Solution:** let x be the 10-isotope fraction: 10x + 11(1 − x) = 10.8 → x = 0.2 → 20% mass-10 (boron).

data.title: Atomic Number — Meaning, Moseley's Evidence and Uses
data.topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: ### Focus of this tab

The atomic number Z: its definition, the X-ray evidence that made it the true identity of an element, and its uses. It belongs logically with Rutherford's model because Z is the nuclear charge his experiment revealed.
### Definition and meaning

The atomic number Z is the number of protons in the nucleus — equivalently the nuclear charge in units of +e, or the number of electrons in the neutral atom. It is written as a left subscript (₁₁Na). In 1920 Rutherford named the nuclear charge 'atomic number'; it is now the defining property of an element.
### Moseley's X-ray evidence (1913)

Henry Moseley bombarded metal targets with fast cathode rays and measured the characteristic X-ray frequencies: $\sqrt{\nu}=a(Z-b)$. Plotting √ν against Z gives a straight line, but √ν against atomic mass does not — proving that Z, not atomic mass, is the fundamental quantity. This (i) corrected the anomalous pairs (Ar/K, Co/Ni, Te/I), (ii) gave isotopes one place in the table, (iii) fixed hydrogen's position, and (iv) predicted missing elements by gaps in the line.
### Uses of Z
• Identifies the element and fixes its position in the modern periodic table (periods by shell filling, groups by valence configuration).
• Gives the electron count of a neutral atom (e⁻ = Z) and the neutron count (n = A − Z).
• Enters Bohr-type formulas: rₙ ∝ n²/Z, Eₙ ∝ −Z²/n², ν of spectral lines ∝ Z² (used for He⁺, Li²⁺).
• In medicine/engineering Z governs X-ray absorption (bone vs tissue imaging) and shielding choices (lead, Z = 82).
### Relation to the other identifiers

Mass number A = Z + N (whole number); atomic mass is the weighted average over isotopes (e.g. Cl = 35.5 u from 75% ³⁵Cl + 25% ³⁷Cl). Only Z is unique to a chemical element — that is why the modern periodic law is stated in terms of Z.
confusion: ❌ Atomic number is the number of neutrons. ✅ It is the number of protons (nuclear charge); neutrons = A − Z.
❌ Elements are defined by atomic mass. ✅ Moseley showed the identity is Z; mass varies with isotopic composition.
❌ An ion has a different atomic number from its atom. ✅ Z never changes in chemistry — only the electron count does (Na and Na⁺ both Z = 11).
practice: Define atomic number and describe Moseley's experiment that established it.
Write Moseley's law and explain how it corrected Mendeleev's anomalous pairs.
An atom has Z = 20 and A = 40; find p, n, e and write its mass number.
Why does the plot of √ν versus atomic mass fail to be a straight line?
formulas: $$\sqrt{\nu}=a(Z-b),\qquad Z=p=e^{-}(\text{neutral atom}),\qquad n=A-Z$$
universalFacts: Moseley died at Gallipoli in 1915 at 27, shortly after establishing atomic number.
The 'missing' Z = 43 (technetium) and 61 (promethium) were later found — their X-ray lines had been predicted by gaps.
Beryllium's low Z = 4 makes it the window material of X-ray tubes (low absorption).
examples: **Problem:** An element has A = 23 and 12 neutrons. Identify it. **Solution:** Z = 23 − 12 = 11 → sodium (Na); in the neutral atom it has 11 electrons.
importantNotes: Always connect Z to the nuclear charge Rutherford measured — the two ideas belong together.
Quote Moseley's law with the square root of frequency, not frequency itself.

data.title: Isotopes, Isobars, Isotones and Isodiaphers
data.topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: ### Focus of this tab
The family of 'same/different' atom pairs that the nuclear model makes possible — definitions, examples and exam traps. These follow directly from the concepts of Z and A.
### Definitions with examples
• **Isotopes** (same Z, different A): ¹H, ²H, ³H; ³⁵Cl/³⁷Cl; ¹²C/¹³C/¹⁴C; ²³⁵U/²³⁸U. Same chemical properties (same electronic configuration), different physical properties and different mass.
• **Isobars** (same A, different Z): ⁴⁰Ar (18 p) and ⁴⁰Ca (20 p); ¹⁴C and ¹⁴N. Different elements, same mass number — different chemical properties.
• **Isotones** (same neutron number N = A − Z): ³⁶S, ³⁷Cl, ³⁸Ar, ³⁹K, ⁴⁰Ca (all N = 20); ³H and ⁴Li (N = 2).
• **Isodiaphers** (same difference N − Z): ²³⁹U and ²³⁵Th (N − Z = 51); ²³⁵U and ²³¹Th.
• (Bonus) **Isoelectronic species** (same electron count): N³⁻, O²⁻, F⁻, Ne, Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺ — all 10 electrons.
### Why they exist

Rutherford's nucleus separates identity (Z) from mass (A = Z + N). Once the neutron was found (1932), atoms of one element could differ in mass (isotopes) and atoms of different elements could share a mass number (isobars) — resolving the contradictions that Dalton's 'identical atoms' postulate created.
### Chemical versus nuclear behaviour

Isotopes are chemically almost identical (the electrons decide chemistry) but differ in nuclear stability (¹⁴C decays, ¹²C does not) — the basis of carbon dating, radioisotope tracers (¹³¹I in thyroid studies, ⁶⁰Co in radiotherapy) and isotope separation by mass (gaseous diffusion of UF₆). Isobars, being different elements, are chemically completely different.
### Average atomic mass (numerical pattern)

Average mass = Σ(fractional abundance × isotopic mass). Chlorine: 0.75 × 35 + 0.25 × 37 = 35.5 u; neon: 0.905 × 20 + 0.0027 × 21 + 0.0923 × 22 ≈ 20.18 u. The fractional pattern explains why most atomic masses are not whole numbers — Dalton's 'identical atoms in whole-number ratios' fails here.
confusion: ❌ Isotopes have different chemical properties. ✅ Nearly identical chemically; they differ in mass and nuclear stability.
❌ Isobars are atoms of the same element. ✅ Same A but different Z — different elements entirely.
❌ Isotones are defined by equal protons. ✅ Equal neutron number (N = A − Z).
❌ ¹²C and ¹⁴C belong to different elements. ✅ Both are carbon (Z = 6); ¹⁴C is simply radioactive.
practice: Define isotopes, isobars, isotones and isodiaphers with one example each.
Which postulate of Dalton's atomic theory is contradicted by isotopes?
Chlorine has 75% ³⁵Cl and 25% ³⁷Cl; calculate its average atomic mass.

formulas: $$\text{average atomic mass}=\sum(\text{abundance}\times\text{isotopic mass}),\qquad N=A-Z$$
$$\text{isotopes: }Z_{1}=Z_{2};\quad \text{isobars: }A_{1}=A_{2};\quad \text{isotones: }N_{1}=N_{2};\quad \text{isodiaphers: }(N-Z)_{1}=(N-Z)_{2}$$
universalFacts: Carbon dating uses the ¹⁴C/¹²C ratio (half-life 5730 years).
³⁵Cl/³⁷Cl in a 3 : 1 ratio gives the familiar 35.5 u average mass.
Radio-iodine ¹³¹I concentrates in the thyroid because it is chemically indistinguishable from ordinary iodine.
examples: **Problem:** Boron is 20% ¹⁰B and 80% ¹¹B. Find its atomic mass. **Solution:** 0.20 × 10 + 0.80 × 11 = 10.8 u — matching the tabulated 10.81 u.
**Problem:** Show that ¹⁴C and ¹⁴N are isobars. **Solution:** ¹⁴C: Z = 6, N = 8, A = 14; ¹⁴N: Z = 7, N = 7, A = 14 — same A, different Z.
importantNotes: State the defining quantity first (Z, A, N, N − Z) — the four names are easy to mix up.
Connect isotopes back to Dalton's limitation: identical atoms of an element is the false postulate.

data.title: Thomson's Plum-Pudding Model and its Failure
data.topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: ### Focus of this tab
The model Rutherford disproved. Knowing exactly what Thomson's atom predicted — and which prediction failed — shows why the α-scattering result was so decisive.
### Background: the electron came first

J. J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897 from cathode-ray studies: cathode rays are deflected by electric and magnetic fields, so they are negatively charged particles, and their charge-to-mass ratio e/m = 1.76 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹ is the same for every cathode material — electrons are universal constituents of all atoms. Since atoms are neutral, positive charge had to exist somewhere.
### The plum-pudding (watermelon) model, 1904
• The atom is a sphere of positive charge with radius ≈10⁻¹⁰ m — the size of the whole atom.
• Electrons are embedded in it like plums in a pudding (or seeds in a watermelon), arranged to minimise their mutual repulsion.
• Total positive charge = total negative charge → the atom is neutral.
• Mass is spread uniformly through the sphere; electrons are held by electrostatic forces and can oscillate about their positions — which is how Thomson tried to explain light emission.
### Predictions versus the α-scattering result

• Prediction: positive charge is diffuse, so an α-particle (mass 4 u, charge +2e) passing through should experience many small, cumulative deflections — large-angle scattering should be vanishingly rare.
• Observation: ≈1 in 8000 α-particles is deflected by more than 90°, and some bounce straight back.

• Conclusion: the model is untenable — the positive charge must be concentrated in a tiny, massive nucleus. Rutherford said it was 'as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you'.
### Why the model still mattered
• It was the first model built on measured particles (e/m, charge of the electron from Millikan's oil-drop experiment, 1909).
• It correctly demanded neutrality and electron arrangement, and it could explain single small-angle scattering.
• Its failure set the two requirements every later model must meet: explain atomic stability and discrete line spectra.
### The chain of models (exam framing)

Dalton (indivisible atom) → Thomson (electrons in diffuse positive sphere) → Rutherford (nuclear atom) → Bohr (quantised orbits) → quantum-mechanical model (orbitals). Each model keeps the successes of the previous one and repairs one specific failure.
confusion: ❌ Thomson discovered the proton along with the electron. ✅ Only the electron (1897); the proton was identified by Rutherford in 1919.
❌ The plum-pudding model explained the line spectrum of hydrogen. ✅ It could not; oscillating electrons would give a continuous spectrum.
❌ Thomson's model placed the nucleus at the centre. ✅ It had no nucleus at all — positive charge was spread over the whole atom.
practice: Describe Thomson's model of the atom and state its main postulates.
Which observation of the α-scattering experiment contradicts Thomson's model, and why?
How did the discovery of the electron lead to the need for a positive constituent in the atom?
Compare Dalton's, Thomson's and Rutherford's models in a table (charge distribution, mass distribution, success, failure).
formulas: $$\frac{e}{m}=1.76\times10^{11}\ \text{C kg}^{-1}\ (\text{electron}),\qquad e=1.602\times10^{-19}\ \text{C}$$
universalFacts: Thomson's e/m value is identical for every cathode material — the evidence that electrons are universal building blocks.
Rutherford's '15-inch shell' remark refers to the improbability of back-scattering in a diffuse-charge atom.
The oil-drop experiment (Millikan, 1909) fixed the electron's charge, completing Thomson's picture.
examples: **Problem:** Why could small-angle scattering be explained by Thomson's model? **Solution:** a uniform positive charge density gives each passing α-particle a small, smoothly varying electrostatic impulse; summed over ≈1000 atoms the net deflection stays small — consistent with most α-particles passing nearly straight through.
importantNotes: Frame Thomson's model as the *hypothesis under test* in the α-scattering experiment.
Do not confuse the plum-pudding model with Dalton's indivisible atom — Dalton had no substructure at all.

data.title: Rutherford's Nuclear Model — Features, Successes and Drawbacks (Summary Tab)
data.topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: ### Focus of this tab

A compact revision summary of the nuclear atom — the six features, three successes and five drawbacks in tabular form, ideal for last-minute revision. The detailed experiment and limitations are in the main and companion tabs.
### Features (six points)
1. Atom is electrically neutral and mostly empty space.
2. A tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus (r ≈ 10⁻¹⁵ m) sits at the centre and holds ≈99.9% of the mass.
3. Nuclear volume ≈ 10⁻¹⁵ of atomic volume (r_atom ≈ 10⁻¹⁰ m).
4. Electrons revolve in circular orbits; Coulomb attraction supplies the centripetal force.
5. Number of electrons = number of protons → neutrality.
6. Nuclear charge is characteristic of the element — the seed of the atomic-number concept.
### Successes (three points)
• Explained the α-scattering observations quantitatively (including the sin⁻⁴ law).
• Established the nucleus and the division of the atom into nucleus + electron shell — the birth of nuclear physics.
• Led to Moseley's atomic number, the discovery of the proton (1919) and neutron (1932), and the modern periodic law.
### Drawbacks (five points)
1. Instability: an orbiting (accelerated) electron must radiate and spiral into the nucleus in ≈10⁻⁸ s.
2. No explanation of line spectra — a spiralling electron would radiate continuously.
3. No arrangement of electrons: shells, energies and electron numbers are unspecified, so periodicity and valency are unexplained.
4. Purely classical: circular orbits and a point nucleus are assumptions; no quantisation means no orbital radii or energies.
5. Ignores the neutron, electron–electron interaction and bonding — fails for multi-electron atoms.
confusion: ❌ Rutherford's model places electrons in fixed energy levels. ✅ That is Bohr's addition; Rutherford allowed any circular orbit.
❌ The model was rejected as useless. ✅ It explained scattering perfectly; it failed only beyond that scope (stability, spectra).
practice: State any six features of Rutherford's nuclear model.
Give two successes and four limitations of the model with reasons.
Which single feature of the model leads directly to the idea of atomic number?
formulas: $$\frac{r_{\text{nucleus}}}{r_{\text{atom}}}\approx10^{-5};\qquad \rho_{\text{nucleus}}\approx10^{17}\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$$
universalFacts: 99.9% of the atomic mass sits in a volume 10⁻¹⁵ of the atom's — the densest matter known outside neutron stars.
Rutherford announced the nuclear model in 1911 and explained it fully in his 1911 Philosophical Magazine paper.
examples: **Problem:** Give the one-sentence essence of the model. **Solution:** 'The atom consists of a tiny massive positive nucleus around which electrons revolve, the whole being mostly empty space and held together electrostatically.'
importantNotes: Use this tab for quick revision; quote the limitations with reasons in full-length answers.
Feature 6 (characteristic nuclear charge) is the bridge to Moseley's atomic number.
