data.title: Ion pumps (sodium-potassium and sodium-glucose pump)
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Body's Electricity Bill

Ion pumps are the molecular machines that move ions **against** their concentration gradients, spending ATP to do it. The syllabus names two: the **sodium–potassium pump** (Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase), which keeps nerves liveable, and the **sodium–glucose pump**, which uses the sodium gradient as a battery to absorb glucose. Understanding them means understanding **active versus passive transport** — one of the cleanest contrasts in the unit.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Passive versus active transport

- **Passive transport (diffusion):** particles move **down** their concentration gradient; no energy spent. Ions need a channel/protein, but the gradient does the work.
- **Active transport:** particles are pushed **against** their gradient; this costs energy, supplied directly by ATP (**primary active transport**) or indirectly by another ion's gradient (**secondary active transport**).

### 2.2 The sodium–potassium pump (Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase)

- A membrane enzyme (Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase) that, **per ATP hydrolysed, expels 3 Na⁺ and imports 2 K⁺** — both against their gradients.
- Consequences it maintains:
  - high K⁺ inside, high Na⁺ outside → the **resting membrane potential** (inside ≈ −70 mV) that nerves and muscles fire on;
  - cell **volume** control (osmotic balance);
  - the Na⁺ gradient itself, which powers secondary transport.
- The ratio 3:2 is the exam's favourite number.

### 2.3 The sodium–glucose pump (Na⁺–glucose symport)

- In the **intestine** and **kidney tubules**, glucose must be absorbed **against** its concentration gradient.
- A carrier protein (SGLT) binds **Na⁺ and glucose on the same side** and moves them **together in the same direction** (symport): Na⁺ rushes in **down** its gradient (maintained by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump) and drags glucose **up** its gradient with it.
- This is **secondary active transport**: the direct energy is the Na⁺ electrochemical gradient; the ultimate energy is the ATP the pump spent building that gradient.
- The same principle underlies **oral rehydration therapy (ORS)**: sugar plus salt in the drink lets the gut co-absorb water and glucose even in diarrhoea.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Active transport** | Movement against the gradient, requiring energy | Na⁺/K⁺ pump |
| **Primary active transport** | Energy taken directly from ATP | Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase |
| **Secondary active transport** | Energy taken from another ion's gradient | Na⁺–glucose symport |
| **Symport** | Carrier moving two species in the same direction | Na⁺ + glucose |
| **Resting potential** | Voltage across a resting nerve membrane (≈ −70 mV) | maintained by the pump |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why the pump must run constantly

- Na⁺ and K⁺ leak slowly through membrane channels down their gradients all the time; without continuous pumping the gradients would collapse within minutes and every nerve would fall silent. The pump is estimated to consume a large fraction of the body's resting ATP (up to ~⅓ in some tissues, more in brain) — the body's single biggest energy customer.

### 4.2 How the sodium–glucose pump chains two gradients

- The Na⁺/K⁺ pump builds a steep Na⁺ gradient (high outside). The symporter opens a door for Na⁺ to flow back in down that gradient — but the door only opens when glucose is aboard. Na⁺'s downhill trip pays for glucose's uphill one. One gradient spends, one gradient earns; the ATP bill was paid in advance by the pump.

### 4.3 Clinical hooks

- **ORS (oral rehydration solution):** glucose actively co-transports Na⁺ (and water follows osmotically) — the reason ORS contains both sugar and salt and saves lives in cholera/diarrhoea.
- **Digitalis/digoxin** (heart drug) works by inhibiting the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, indirectly raising Ca²⁺ inside heart cells and strengthening contraction.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Primary vs secondary active transport**

| Basis | Primary | Secondary |
|---|---|---|
| direct energy source | ATP hydrolysis | another ion's gradient (usually Na⁺) |
| example | Na⁺/K⁺ pump (3 Na⁺ out : 2 K⁺ in) | Na⁺–glucose symport (intestine, kidney) |
| direction of ions | both against gradient | Na⁺ down, glucose up |
| who pays | the pump itself | the Na⁺ gradient (built by the pump) |

**The two syllabus pumps**

| Feature | Na⁺/K⁺ pump | Na⁺–glucose pump |
|---|---|---|
| type | primary active (ATPase) | secondary active (symport) |
| stoichiometry | 3 Na⁺ out : 2 K⁺ in per ATP | 1 Na⁺ : 1 glucose (typical) |
| location | all animal cell membranes | intestine, kidney tubules |
| maintains | resting potential, cell volume, Na⁺ gradient | glucose absorption against gradient |

## 6. Common Confusions

**The sodium–glucose pump does not split ATP:** its direct energy is the Na⁺ gradient; the ATP was spent upstream by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump. Calling it "ATP-driven" without the intermediate loses the mechanism mark.
**3 Na⁺ out : 2 K⁺ in — not the reverse:** the pump exports more than it imports (which is why it is electrogenic), but the counts are 3 out, 2 in.
**Diffusion never needs ATP; active transport always needs an energy source** — but the source may be indirect (a gradient), which is why "no ATP here" does not mean "passive".

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): Describe the sodium–potassium pump. What is its stoichiometry and why is it important?** — The **Na⁺/K⁺ pump (Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase)** is a membrane protein that hydrolyses ATP and uses the energy to transport ions **against** their gradients: **for every ATP hydrolysed, 3 Na⁺ are pumped out of the cell and 2 K⁺ are pumped in**. **Importance:** (i) it maintains high K⁺ inside and high Na⁺ outside, establishing the **resting membrane potential** (≈ −70 mV) on which nerve impulses and muscle contraction depend; (ii) it controls cell volume (osmotic balance); (iii) it maintains the Na⁺ gradient that powers secondary active transport, including the sodium–glucose pump. Because ions constantly leak back down their gradients, the pump must run continuously — it is one of the body's largest consumers of ATP.

**NEB-style (3m): How is glucose absorbed in the intestine against its concentration gradient? Explain the sodium–glucose pump.** — Glucose is absorbed by **secondary active transport**. A carrier protein in the intestinal lining (**SGLT, the sodium–glucose symporter**) binds **Na⁺ and glucose together on the luminal side** and changes shape to release both **inside the cell**. The Na⁺ moves **down** the steep Na⁺ electrochemical gradient maintained by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump; glucose hitches a ride and is carried **up** — against — its own gradient. The energy for glucose transport is therefore the Na⁺ gradient, which the Na⁺/K⁺ pump built with ATP — hence "secondary" active transport. The same mechanism in the kidney reclaims glucose from the filtrate, and it is the basis of **oral rehydration solution (ORS)**: supplying glucose and sodium together lets the gut absorb water and salts even during diarrhoea.

**NEB-style (2m): Distinguish active transport from diffusion with one example of each.** — **Diffusion (passive transport)** moves particles **down** their concentration gradient with no energy input (e.g. O₂ crossing the alveolar membrane into blood). **Active transport** moves particles **against** their gradient and requires energy (e.g. the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, which expels 3 Na⁺ and imports 2 K⁺ per ATP hydrolysed). The direction of movement relative to the gradient, and the need for energy, are the two discriminating features.

examples: ***ORS in a cholera ward*** — sugar and salt in the right proportions keep the SGLT symporter loaded, so the gut keeps absorbing water precisely when its passive absorption has failed; the pump mechanism saves millions of lives a year.
practiceQuestions: **NEB-style (3m): Describe the sodium–potassium pump, its stoichiometry and its importance.** — The **Na⁺/K⁺ pump (Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase)** is a membrane enzyme that hydrolyses ATP and uses the energy to move ions **against** their gradients: **3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ into the cell per ATP hydrolysed**. **Importance:** (i) it keeps K⁺ high inside and Na⁺ high outside, creating the **resting membrane potential** (≈ −70 mV) that nerve impulses and muscle contraction require; (ii) it regulates **cell volume** by controlling osmotic balance; (iii) it maintains the **Na⁺ gradient** that drives secondary transport such as the sodium–glucose pump. Since Na⁺ and K⁺ leak back continuously, the pump runs all the time and is one of the body's biggest ATP consumers.

**NEB-style (3m): Explain the sodium–glucose pump in the intestine. Why is it called secondary active transport?** — In the intestinal lining, a symporter protein (**SGLT**) binds **Na⁺ and glucose on the same side** of the membrane and carries both **in the same direction** into the cell. The Na⁺ travels **down** the steep electrochemical gradient maintained by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, while the glucose is carried **up** — against — its own gradient. It is called **secondary** active transport because the direct energy source is not ATP but the **Na⁺ gradient**; the ATP was consumed earlier by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump that built the gradient. The same transporter reclaims glucose in the kidney tubule, and the mechanism is the scientific basis of **oral rehydration solution (ORS)**, which supplies glucose and sodium together so the gut keeps absorbing water during diarrhoea.

**NEB-style (2m): Why must the Na⁺/K⁺ pump run continuously, and what happens if it stops?** — Na⁺ and K⁺ leak through membrane channels **down** their gradients at all times; only the pump pushes them back. If the pump stops (e.g. oxygen starvation halts ATP production), the gradients dissipate within minutes, the **resting membrane potential collapses**, nerves and muscles fail, and cells swell osmotically — which is why disruption of blood supply to the brain is so rapidly fatal.
keyPoints: Passive transport = down gradient, no energy; active transport = against gradient, needs energy. Na+/K+ pump (Na+/K+ ATPase, primary active): 3 Na+ out : 2 K+ in per ATP; maintains resting potential (~ -70 mV), cell volume, and the Na+ gradient; runs constantly because ions leak. Na+-glucose pump (SGLT symport, secondary active): Na+ flows in down its gradient, glucose carried up against its gradient, in intestine and kidney tubules; energy = Na+ gradient built by the Na+/K+ pump with ATP. ORS works by this co-transport (glucose + Na+ + water absorbed even in diarrhoea).
data.summary: Ion pumps move ions **uphill**, and the syllabus names two machines. The **Na⁺/K⁺ pump (Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase)** is **primary** active transport: one ATP buys **3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in**, maintaining the ≈ −70 mV resting potential, cell volume, and the Na⁺ gradient everything else feeds on. The **sodium–glucose pump** is **secondary** active transport: in the intestine and kidney tubules a symporter lets Na⁺ rush in **down** its gradient and drags glucose **up** its gradient in the same step — one gradient spends, one earns. Because the Na⁺/K⁺ pump built the sodium gradient with ATP, every glucose molecule absorbed carries a hidden ATP price — and oral rehydration solution exploits exactly this co-transport to keep patients absorbing water in cholera.

practiceQuestions: **NEB-style (3m): Describe the sodium–potassium pump, its stoichiometry and its importance.** — The **Na⁺/K⁺ pump (Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase)** is a membrane enzyme that hydrolyses ATP and uses the energy to move ions **against** their gradients: **3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ into the cell per ATP hydrolysed**. **Importance:** (i) it keeps K⁺ high inside and Na⁺ high outside, creating the **resting membrane potential** (≈ −70 mV) that nerve impulses and muscle contraction require; (ii) it regulates **cell volume** by controlling osmotic balance; (iii) it maintains the **Na⁺ gradient** that drives secondary transport such as the sodium–glucose pump. Since Na⁺ and K⁺ leak back continuously, the pump runs all the time and is one of the body's biggest ATP consumers.

**NEB-style (3m): Explain the sodium–glucose pump in the intestine. Why is it called secondary active transport?** — In the intestinal lining, a symporter protein (**SGLT**) binds **Na⁺ and glucose on the same side** of the membrane and carries both **in the same direction** into the cell. The Na⁺ travels **down** the steep electrochemical gradient maintained by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, while the glucose is carried **up** — against — its own gradient. It is called **secondary** active transport because the direct energy source is not ATP but the **Na⁺ gradient**; the ATP was consumed earlier by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump that built the gradient. **NEB-style (2m): Why must the Na⁺/K⁺ pump run continuously, and what happens if it stops?** — Na⁺ and K⁺ leak through membrane channels **down** their gradients at all times; only the pump pushes them back. If the pump stops (e.g. oxygen starvation halts ATP production), the gradients dissipate within minutes, the **resting membrane potential collapses**, nerves and muscles fail, and cells swell osmotically — which is why disruption of blood supply to the brain is so rapidly fatal.

data.topicTitle: Metal toxicity (toxicity due to iron, arsenic, mercury, lead and cadmium)
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — When the Metal Is the Poison

The same d-block chemistry that makes Fe, Cu and Zn essential makes Pb, Hg, Cd and As dangerous: they bind sulphur and other biological ligands where they do not belong, or imitate essential ions and hijack their machinery. The syllabus names five toxic metals — **Fe (in excess), As, Hg, Pb, Cd** — each with a classic disease story and a chemistry explanation.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Iron — essential metal, toxic in excess

- **Overdose** (especially iron tonic tablets in children) causes gastrointestinal corrosion, liver damage and death; free Fe²⁺ catalyses formation of damaging radicals (Fenton chemistry) and overwhelms transport proteins.
- **Haemochromatosis** — chronic iron overload: iron deposits in liver, pancreas and heart; treated by repeated blood removal or chelation (desferrioxamine).
- The lesson: even the most essential metal poisons above its window.

### 2.2 Arsenic — the enzyme poison

- Arsenic (especially As(III), arsenite) **binds –SH (thiol) groups of enzymes**, blocking them; it also interferes with ATP production.
- Chronic exposure → **arsenicosis**: skin lesions (keratosis), skin/lung cancer, peripheral nerve damage.
- **Groundwater contamination** — the classic NEB-relevant case: arsenic in tube-well water (WHO limit 10 ppb); Nepal's Terai and neighbouring Gangetic plains are affected regions.

### 2.3 Mercury — the nerve poison

- Elemental Hg vapour and organic **methylmercury** are the dangerous forms; methylmercury **bioaccumulates** up the aquatic food chain.
- Attacks the **central nervous system**: tremors, memory loss, numbness, mood changes.
- **Minamata disease** (Japan, 1950s): a factory discharged mercury compounds into a bay; methylmercury concentrated in fish; thousands poisoned — the textbook case study.

### 2.4 Lead — the childhood poison

- **Pb²⁺ imitates Ca²⁺** (deposits in bone) and **inhibits the enzymes of haem synthesis** (ALA dehydratase, ferrochelatase) → **anaemia**.
- In children: **neurological damage** — lowered IQ, learning and behaviour problems, even at low exposure; also abdominal colic ("lead colic").
- Sources: old lead paints, leaded petrol (now phased out), lead pipes, battery recycling.

### 2.5 Cadmium — the kidney poison

- **Cd²⁺ imitates Zn²⁺** (same group) and slips into zinc enzymes, but cannot do their chemistry; accumulates in **kidneys** (protein in urine) and bones.
- **Itai-itai disease** (Japan): cadmium-polluted irrigation water → kidney damage plus painful bone decalcification ("ouch-ouch").
- Sources: Ni–Cd batteries, galvanised/plated metal, **tobacco smoke** (smokers carry significantly more cadmium).

### 2.6 Chelation therapy — the chemistry antidote

- Toxic metals are removed by **chelating agents** — ligands that grip the metal in soluble complexes excreted in urine:
  - **EDTA** (lead); **dimercaprol/BAL** (arsenic, mercury); **penicillamine** (copper, Wilson's disease); **desferrioxamine** (iron).

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Haemochromatosis** | Chronic iron-overload disease | iron deposits in liver/pancreas |
| **Arsenicosis** | Chronic arsenic poisoning via water/food | skin lesions, cancer |
| **Minamata disease** | Methylmercury poisoning from contaminated fish | Japan, 1950s |
| **Itai-itai disease** | Cadmium poisoning: kidney + bone damage | Japan, Cd-polluted water |
| **Chelation therapy** | Removing a toxic metal with a chelating ligand | EDTA for lead |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why soft metals attack sulphur

- Hg²⁺, Pb²⁺, Cd²⁺ and As(III) are **soft/borderline Lewis acids** with high affinity for the **soft –SH sulphur** of cysteine residues. Binding an enzyme's essential cysteine disables it. This one preference explains why these metals hit so many different enzymes at once — and why the antidotes (BAL, penicillamine) are dithiols/thiols: they out-compete the enzyme for the metal.

### 4.2 Mimicry as a poisoning strategy

- **Pb²⁺ ≈ Ca²⁺** (same charge, not too different radius) → enters bone, disrupts signalling and haem synthesis enzymes.
- **Cd²⁺ ≈ Zn²⁺** (same group) → occupies zinc's enzyme seats but is catalytically useless.
- This is why the toxic metals are dangerous in trace amounts: they do not need to be abundant, only similar.

### 4.3 Bioaccumulation and the food chain

- Mercury enters water as inorganic Hg, is converted by bacteria to **lipid-soluble methylmercury**, and concentrates at each step of the food chain — top predators (tuna, swordfish) carry the highest loads. Cadmium and lead behave similarly in soils. Human exposure is therefore often via **food and water**, not direct contact.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**The five toxic metals**

| Metal | Worst form | Main target | Classic disease | Key source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fe (excess) | Fe²⁺ overdose | liver, gut | haemochromatosis | tonics, overload |
| As | As(III) arsenite | enzymes (–SH) | arsenicosis | groundwater (10 ppb limit) |
| Hg | methylmercury | CNS | Minamata disease | contaminated fish |
| Pb | Pb²⁺ | haem synthesis, CNS (children) | lead poisoning/plumbism | paints, petrol, batteries |
| Cd | Cd²⁺ | kidneys, bone | itai-itai disease | batteries, smoke |

**Mimicry table**

| Toxic ion | Mimics | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Pb²⁺ | Ca²⁺ | bone deposition; blocks haem enzymes |
| Cd²⁺ | Zn²⁺ | occupies Zn enzyme sites, inert |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Mercury's danger is the organic form and vapour, not liquid contact:** liquid metallic mercury swallowed in small amount passes through the gut largely unabsorbed; the vapour and methylmercury are the killers.
**Iron toxicity is about dose, not identity:** iron is essential; its toxicity (overdose, haemochromatosis) is the dose rule of row 91 seen from the other side.
**Minamata = mercury, itai-itai = cadmium:** the two Japanese disease names are the most-swapped pair in the exam — mercury ate the nerves, cadmium ate the kidneys and bones.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB 2024 (verified PYQ): Write the harmful effects of lead and mercury on human health.** — **Lead:** Pb²⁺ enters via contaminated water, paint dust, batteries and formerly leaded petrol. It **inhibits the enzymes of haem synthesis**, causing **anaemia**; it deposits in bone like calcium; and it is a potent **neurotoxin in children**, causing reduced IQ, learning and behavioural problems even at low exposure, plus abdominal pain (lead colic) and kidney damage in chronic cases. **Mercury:** the dangerous forms are **mercury vapour and methylmercury**; methylmercury bioaccumulates in fish and attacks the **central nervous system**, causing tremors, numbness of the limbs, memory loss, mood disturbance and, in severe cases (Minamata disease, Japan), paralysis and death; it also damages the kidneys and harms the developing fetus.

**NEB-style (2m): Why does arsenic in groundwater pose a health hazard? Name its chronic disease.** — Arsenic (mainly As(III), arsenite) leached into tube-well groundwater binds the **–SH groups of enzymes**, disabling them, and impairs energy metabolism. Chronic drinking of arsenic-contaminated water (above the WHO limit of **10 ppb**) causes **arsenicosis**: skin keratosis and pigmentation, skin and other cancers, and peripheral nerve damage. The Terai belt of Nepal and the Gangetic plains are affected regions; the remedy is switching to tested deep wells or arsenic-removal filters.

**NEB-style (2m): What is chelation therapy? Give one chelating agent and the metal it removes.** — **Chelation therapy** treats metal poisoning by administering a **chelating ligand** that binds the toxic metal ion into a stable, water-soluble complex which the body excretes in urine. Examples: **EDTA** for **lead**; **dimercaprol (BAL)** for **arsenic and mercury**; **penicillamine** for **copper** (Wilson's disease); **desferrioxamine** for **iron** overload. The ligand must grip the metal more tightly than the biological target does — antidote chemistry is coordination chemistry.

It **inhibits the enzymes that synthesise haem** (ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase), producing **anaemia**; being Ca²⁺-like it **deposits in bone**; it is a powerful **neurotoxin in children**, lowering IQ and causing learning and behavioural disorders even at low exposure; chronic adult exposure gives abdominal "lead colic", kidney damage and raised blood pressure. **Mercury:** the harmful forms are **mercury vapour** (inhaled) and **methylmercury** (from contaminated fish, where it bioaccumulates up the food chain). Both attack the **central nervous system**: tremors, numbness of limbs, memory loss, mood changes, and in severe poisoning (the classic **Minamata disease**, Japan) paralysis and death; mercury also damages the kidneys and the developing fetus.

**NEB-style (2m): Why is arsenic-contaminated groundwater dangerous, and what disease does chronic exposure cause?** — Arsenic in groundwater occurs mainly as **arsenite, As(III)**, a soft Lewis acid that binds the **–SH (thiol) groups of enzymes** and blocks them, besides disrupting energy metabolism. Drinking water above the **WHO limit of 10 ppb** over years causes **arsenicosis**: thickened skin patches (keratosis), pigmentation changes, skin and internal cancers, and peripheral nerve damage. Tube-well water in the Terai of Nepal and the Gangetic plains is the classic affected source; the remedies are tested alternative wells and arsenic-removal filters.

**NEB-style (2m): Name the disease caused by cadmium poisoning and explain why cadmium is toxic.** — Chronic cadmium poisoning causes **itai-itai disease** ("ouch-ouch", Japan) — severe kidney damage together with painful **bone decalcification** and fractures. **Why toxic:** Cd²⁺ sits directly below Zn²⁺ in Group IIB and **mimics zinc**, occupying the zinc sites of enzymes; but cadmium cannot perform zinc's catalytic chemistry, so the enzymes are silenced. Cadmium also accumulates in the kidneys over decades (biological half-life ~10–30 years) and reaches humans through Ni–Cd batteries, contaminated rice/irrigation water and **tobacco smoke**.

Arsenic: As(III) binds -SH groups of enzymes; arsenicosis = skin lesions + cancer + neuropathy; groundwater hazard, WHO limit 10 ppb (Nepal Terai affected). Mercury: vapour + methylmercury (bioaccumulates in fish) attack CNS; Minamata disease (Japan 1950s). Lead: Pb2+ mimics Ca2+ (bone), inhibits haem-synthesis enzymes (ALA dehydratase, ferrochelatase) -> anaemia; children's IQ loss; lead colic. data.summary: Toxicity has two mechanisms and five names. **Mechanism one — soft-metal sulphur binding:** As(III), Hg²⁺, Pb²⁺ and Cd²⁺ all latch onto the –SH groups of enzymes (arsenicosis from >10 ppb groundwater; **Minamata disease** from methylmercury that bioaccumulates in fish and destroys the CNS). **Mechanism two — mimicry:** **Pb²⁺** poses as Ca²⁺ (bone deposits) while blocking haem-synthesis enzymes → anaemia and permanent IQ loss in children; **Cd²⁺** poses as Zn²⁺, wrecking kidneys and bones (**itai-itai disease**; batteries and tobacco smoke are the sources). Even essential iron poisons in excess — overdose and **haemochromatosis**. The chemical antidote is **chelation therapy**: EDTA for lead, BAL for arsenic and mercury, penicillamine for copper, desferrioxamine for iron — ligands that grip the poison more tightly than the body does.

It **inhibits the enzymes that synthesise haem** (ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase), producing **anaemia**; being Ca²⁺-like it **deposits in bone**; it is a powerful **neurotoxin in children**, lowering IQ and causing learning and behavioural disorders even at low exposure; chronic adult exposure gives abdominal "lead colic", kidney damage and raised blood pressure. **Mercury:** the harmful forms are **mercury vapour** (inhaled) and **methylmercury** (from contaminated fish, where it bioaccumulates up the food chain). Both attack the **central nervous system**: tremors, numbness of limbs, memory loss, mood changes, and in severe poisoning (the classic **Minamata disease**, Japan) paralysis and death; mercury also damages the kidneys and the developing fetus.

**NEB-style (2m): Why is arsenic-contaminated groundwater dangerous, and what disease does chronic exposure cause?** — Arsenic in groundwater occurs mainly as **arsenite, As(III)**, a soft Lewis acid that binds the **–SH (thiol) groups of enzymes** and blocks them, besides disrupting energy metabolism. Drinking water above the **WHO limit of 10 ppb** over years causes **arsenicosis**: thickened skin patches (keratosis), pigmentation changes, skin and internal cancers, and peripheral nerve damage. data.topicTitle: Valence shell, valence electron and octet theory
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Why Atoms Bother to Bond

Every bond answers one question: how does an atom reach the **stability of a noble gas**? Noble gases (He, Ne, Ar…) are chemically inert because their valence shells are complete — ns²np⁶, an **octet** (or the duet of helium). All other atoms borrow, give, or share electrons to copy that arrangement. Kossel's **electron-transfer** picture explains ionic bonds; Lewis's **electron-sharing** picture explains covalent bonds. Both are bookkeeping devices built on the same observation: complete valence shells mean low energy.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Valence shell and valence electrons

- **Valence shell:** the outermost occupied shell of an atom (highest n). **Valence electrons:** the electrons in it — the only electrons that participate in bonding.
- Examples: Na (2,8,1) has 1 valence electron; Cl (2,8,7) has 7; C (2,4) has 4. Core electrons stay spectators.
- The **valency** of an element = electrons it must lose, gain or share to complete its octet (Na: 1; O: 2; N: 3; C: 4; noble gases: 0).

### 2.2 Octet rule (Kossel–Lewis, 1916)

- **Statement:** atoms tend to acquire an eight-electron outer shell (ns²np⁶) by transferring or sharing electrons.
- **Driving force:** a complete octet has the extra stability of the noble-gas configuration — lowest energy, no tendency to react.
- **Success:** explains formulae NaCl, MgO, CaCl₂, CCl₄, H₂O, NH₃ and the inertness of He, Ne, Ar.

### 2.3 Limitations of the octet rule

- **Incomplete octet:** BeCl₂ (4 e⁻ around Be), BF₃ (6 e⁻ around B) — stable despite shortage.
- **Expanded octet:** PCl₅ (10 e⁻), SF₆ (12 e⁻), H₂SO₄ (12 e⁻ around S) — possible from the third shell onward.
- **Odd-electron molecules:** NO (11 valence e⁻), NO₂ (17), ClO₂ — octet impossible for all atoms.
- **Noble-gas compounds:** XeF₂, XeF₄, XeO₃ exist — octet rule cannot explain them.
- **Shape-blind:** the octet rule says nothing about molecular geometry — VSEPR and hybridisation are needed for shapes.

### 2.4 Duet rule

- Hydrogen and lithium reach the **helium configuration (2 e⁻)** — the duet. H₂, LiH, and the two electrons around H in all covalent compounds follow it.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Value to quote |
|---|---|---|
| **Valence shell** | Outermost occupied electron shell (highest n) | Na: n = 3 |
| **Valence electrons** | Electrons in the valence shell available for bonding | Cl: 7 |
| **Octet rule** | Tendency to acquire eight electrons in the outer shell by transfer or sharing | ns²np⁶ |
| **Duet rule** | Tendency of H and Li to hold two electrons (He configuration) | H₂: 2 e⁻ shared |
| **Expanded octet** | More than eight electrons around a central atom (n ≥ 3) | SF₆: 12 e⁻ |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 How the rule generates formulae

- Na (2,8,1) transfers one electron to Cl (2,8,7): both reach (2,8) and (2,8,8) — **Na⁺Cl⁻**, formula NaCl.
- Mg (2,8,2) gives one electron each to two Cl atoms → **MgCl₂**; Mg gives two to O → **MgO**.
- Two Cl atoms each need one electron; they **share** a pair → Cl₂. C shares four pairs with four Cl → **CCl₄**.
- Water: O shares one pair with each of two H atoms → H₂O with **two lone pairs left over** — which later explain its bent shape.

### 4.2 Electron counting in practice

- Total valence electrons = sum over atoms (adjust for charge: add electrons for anions, subtract for cations).
- Example CO₂: 4 + 2(6) = 16 electrons → two C=O double bonds, two lone pairs on each O — every atom reaches an octet.
- Example NH₄⁺: 5 + 4(1) − 1 = 8 electrons → four N–H bonds; N formally has no lone pair.

### 4.3 Where the rule fails — and why that is still useful

- BeCl₂ and BF₃ are **electron-deficient** and therefore strong Lewis acids — the "failure" predicts reactivity.
- PCl₅ and SF₆ exist only because the 3d subshell is energetically reachable for third-period atoms; second-period atoms (C, N, O, F) can never expand.
- The rule's shape-blindness is the opening act for VSEPR theory (topic 32) — octet decides *how many* pairs, VSEPR decides *where they point*.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Octet success vs failure**

| Case | Example | Electrons around central atom | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Normal octet | CH₄, H₂O, CO₂ | 8 | Rule holds |
| Incomplete octet | BeCl₂, BF₃ | 4, 6 | Rule fails; Lewis acids |
| Expanded octet | PCl₅, SF₆ | 10, 12 | Rule fails; n ≥ 3 only |
| Odd electron | NO, NO₂ | 9, 13 total | Rule cannot apply |

**Transfer vs sharing (preview of topics 28–29)**

| Basis | Kossel (transfer) | Lewis (sharing) |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | Electrons given/taken | Pairs shared |
| Result | Ions held electrostatically | Molecules held by shared pairs |
| Best for | NaCl, MgO (metal + non-metal) | Cl₂, H₂O, CH₄ (non-metals) |
| Rule satisfied by | Full shells on both ions | Shared + own electrons = octet |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Octet ≠ eight bonds:** the octet counts electrons *around* an atom (bonding pairs counted twice, once per atom), not bonds. In CO₂ carbon owns 8 electrons via two double bonds — but forms only two bonds.
**Valence electrons vs valency:** Cl has 7 valence electrons but valency 1 — valency is 8 − valence electrons (for non-metals), not the count itself.
**Expanded octets are third-row-only:** C, N, O, F (period 2) have no accessible d orbitals; P, S, Cl and beyond can exceed 8. Never write five bonds on carbon.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (2m): State the octet rule and give one limitation with an example.** — Atoms tend to acquire eight electrons in their valence shell by transfer or sharing of electrons. Limitation: **expanded octet** — in SF₆, sulphur is surrounded by 12 electrons (six S–F bonds), which the octet rule cannot accommodate; similarly PCl₅ holds 10 electrons around P.

**NEB-style (2m): Why are noble gases chemically inert?** — Their valence shells are already complete (ns²np⁶; He 1s²). They have no tendency to lose, gain or share electrons — no bond formation lowers their energy — so they exist as monatomic molecules and resist reaction.

**NEB-style (3m): Explain the formation of MgCl₂ using the octet rule.** — Mg (2,8,2) has two excess valence electrons; Cl (2,8,7) is one short of an octet. Mg transfers one electron to each of two Cl atoms → Mg²⁺ (2,8) and two Cl⁻ (2,8,8). Both ions attain neon/argon configurations, and electrostatic attraction between Mg²⁺ and 2Cl⁻ builds the ionic lattice.
confusion: **Octet counts electrons, not bonds:** CO₂'s carbon has 8 electrons but only 2 bonds (double bonds count four electrons each).
**Valency vs valence electrons:** for non-metals valency = 8 − valence electrons (Cl: 7 valence e⁻, valency 1).

Explain its application in the formation of NaCl and Cl₂.** — The octet rule states that atoms acquire eight electrons in the valence shell by transfer or sharing. **NaCl:** Na (2,8,1) transfers one electron to Cl (2,8,7) → Na⁺ (2,8) and Cl⁻ (2,8,8), both noble-gas configurations, bound electrostatically. **Cl₂:** each Cl needs one electron; the two atoms share one pair, giving each Cl seven own + one shared = 8 electrons.

**NEB-style (3m): What is the expanded octet? Illustrate with PCl₅ and SF₆.** — An expanded octet has more than eight electrons around the central atom, possible only for period-3 elements and beyond where empty d orbitals can accept electron density. **PCl₅:** five P–Cl bonds = 10 electrons around P (trigonal bipyramidal). **SF₆:** six S–F bonds = 12 electrons around S (octahedral). - Valency (non-metals) = 8 − valence electrons
- Total valence e⁻ = Σ valence e⁻ (atoms) ± charge (anion +, cation −)

Limitations: incomplete octet (BeCl₂, BF₃), expanded octet (PCl₅, SF₆ — third period onward), odd-electron molecules (NO, NO₂), noble-gas compounds (XeF₂), and no shape prediction.
data.summary: Bonding exists to copy noble-gas stability. The **valence shell** (outermost shell) supplies the electrons; the **octet rule** of Kossel and Lewis says atoms reach ns²np⁶ either by transferring electrons (Kossel — ionic bonds, NaCl, MgO) or sharing pairs (Lewis — covalent bonds, Cl₂, CH₄), while hydrogen and lithium settle for the helium duet. The rule explains formulae brilliantly but fails five ways: incomplete octets (BeCl₂ with 4, BF₃ with 6 — which make them Lewis acids), expanded octets (PCl₅ 10, SF₆ 12 — period 3 onward only), odd-electron molecules (NO, NO₂), noble-gas compounds (XeF₂), and total silence on molecular shape. Octet decides how many electrons gather; VSEPR decides where they point.

points: Transfer of electrons — ionic bonding (metal loses, non-metal gains)
Sharing of electrons — covalent bonding (both contribute)
Coordination — one atom donates a lone pair to another

subtopics.name: Lewis structures
points: Dots represent valence electrons; a shared pair is a bond
Total valence electrons must be conserved when drawing
Formal charge helps decide between competing structures

branches.topic: Level 3 — Upgraded: where the octet rule fails

subtopics.name: Exceptions
points: Incomplete octet: BeCl2 (4 electrons), BF3 (6 electrons), LiCl
Expanded octet: PCl5 (10), SF6 (12) — possible only for period 3 and below with accessible d orbitals
Odd-electron species: NO and NO2 have unpaired electrons and cannot satisfy an octet

subtopics.name: Why it still matters
points: The octet rule is a useful first approximation, not a law
Molecular orbital theory is needed for O2 paramagnetism, which the octet picture cannot explain
Hydrogen obeys a duet rule, not an octet

data.title: Ionic Bond and Its Properties
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Bond of Full Transfer

When the electronegativity gap is a canyon — metal meets non-metal — electrons are not shared but **surrendered**. Sodium hands its 3s electron to chlorine; the resulting Na⁺ and Cl⁻ lock into a three-dimensional lattice by sheer electrostatic attraction. That attraction **is** the ionic (electrovalent) bond. Its consequences cascade through chemistry: high melting points, molten-state conductivity, water solubility — and, through Fajan's rules, the admission that no ionic bond is perfectly ionic.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Formation mechanism

- **Electron transfer:** metal atoms (low IE) lose electrons → cations; non-metal atoms (high EA) gain them → anions.
- Na (2,8,1) → Na⁺ (2,8) + e⁻; Cl (2,8,7) + e⁻ → Cl⁻ (2,8,8). Both reach noble-gas configurations.
- **Coulombic attraction** between oppositely charged ions, in all directions, builds the **crystal lattice** — NaCl is a cubic array of alternating ions, not discrete NaCl molecules.

### 2.2 Conditions favouring ionic bond formation

- **Low ionisation energy** of the metal (Cs, K, Na — IE₁ 376, 419, 496 kJ mol⁻¹).
- **High negative electron affinity** of the non-metal (Cl −349 kJ mol⁻¹).
- **High lattice energy** — the larger the energy released packing ions into the lattice, the more stable the compound.
- Consequence: ionic compounds are typical of Group 1/2 metals with Group 17/16 non-metals (NaCl, MgO, CaF₂).

### 2.3 Properties rooted in the lattice

- **Hard, brittle crystalline solids:** displacement of a layer brings like charges face-to-face → repulsion cracks the crystal.
- **High melting/boiling points:** strong, non-directional electrostatic forces must be broken throughout the lattice (NaCl mp 801 °C; MgO mp 2852 °C).
- **Conduct in molten/aqueous state only:** ions are fixed in the solid but mobile once freed; solid ionic crystals do not conduct.
- **Soluble in polar solvents (water):** dipole–ion attractions prise ions from the lattice; insoluble in non-polar solvents (benzene).
- **No isomerism, fast ionic reactions:** no directional bonds; reactions are simply ion encounters in solution.

### 2.4 Fajan's rules — covalent character in ionic bonds

- A cation's positive charge **polarises** the anion's electron cloud; the distorted, shared-looking cloud is covalent character.
- Covalent character increases with: **small cation, large anion, high charge on either ion**, and cations with **pseudo-noble-gas (18-electron) configurations** (Cu⁺ vs Na⁺).
- Classic ordering: LiCl more covalent than NaCl (Li⁺ smaller, polarises Cl⁻ more); LiI most covalent of the lithium halides (I⁻ largest).

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Value to quote |
|---|---|---|
| **Ionic (electrovalent) bond** | Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by electron transfer | Na⁺Cl⁻ |
| **Lattice energy** | Energy released when gaseous ions pack into one mole of crystal | NaCl ≈ −788 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| **Polarisation** | Distortion of an anion's electron cloud by an adjacent cation | Fajan's basis |
| **Polarising power** | Ability of a cation to distort an anion (∝ charge/size) | Li⁺ > Na⁺ > K⁺ |
| **Polarizability** | Ease with which an anion's cloud is distorted (∝ size) | I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻ |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Verified PYQ (NEB 2024): ionic vs covalent — the distinction

| Basis | Ionic bond | Covalent bond |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | Complete electron transfer | Sharing of electron pairs |
| Particles formed | Ions (Na⁺, Cl⁻) | Molecules (H₂O, CH₄) |
| Directionality | Non-directional electrostatic pull | Directional, between specific atoms |
| Melting point | High (NaCl 801 °C) | Low to moderate (H₂O 0 °C solid, CH₄ −182 °C) |
| Conductivity | Molten/aqueous only | Non-conducting (except graphite/electrovalent exceptions) |
| Solubility | Polar solvents | Non-polar solvents (generally) |
| Example | NaCl, MgO | Cl₂, H₂O, CO₂ |

**One example each:** NaCl (transfer: Na loses 3s¹ to Cl) and H₂O (sharing: one pair per O–H bond).

### 4.2 Verified PYQ (NEB 2024): Fajan's rules and LiCl vs NaCl

- **Rules:** covalent character rises with (i) smaller cation, (ii) larger anion, (iii) higher charges, (iv) 18-electron cation configuration.
- **LiCl vs NaCl:** Li⁺ (76 pm) is much smaller than Na⁺ (102 pm), so Li⁺ has greater polarising power — it distorts Cl⁻'s cloud more, giving LiCl **higher covalent character** (evidenced by LiCl's solubility in organic solvents such as ethanol and acetone, and its lower melting point than NaCl).

### 4.3 Why brittleness and conductivity follow from geometry

- The lattice is a 3D checkerboard; slide it one ion across and Cl⁻ meets Cl⁻ — repulsion shatters the crystal. Hardness (resists scratching) and brittleness (cleaves under shear) come from the same force.
- In the solid, ions vibrate about fixed lattice points — no charge carrier movement, no conduction. Melt or dissolve: ions migrate to electrodes — conduction, and electrolysis becomes possible.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Polarising power and polarizability (Fajan's levers)**

| Lever | Increases covalent character | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Cation size ↓ | Li⁺ > Na⁺ > K⁺ > Rb⁺ | LiCl > NaCl in covalency |
| Anion size ↑ | I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻ | LiI most covalent LiX |
| Charge ↑ | Al³⁺ ≫ Na⁺ | AlCl₃ largely covalent |
| 18-e⁻ cation | Cu⁺ > Na⁺ (same size) | CuCl more covalent than NaCl |

**Property fingerprint of ionic compounds**

| Property | Origin | Observation |
|---|---|---|
| High mp/bp | Strong non-directional lattice forces | MgO 2852 °C |
| Brittleness | Layer slip → like-charge repulsion | Crystal cleaves |
| Molten/aqueous conduction | Mobile ions | Electrolysis of molten NaCl |
| Polar-solvent solubility | Ion–dipole attraction | NaCl in water, not hexane |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Ionic bond is not directional:** an Na⁺ attracts every neighbouring Cl⁻ equally — the "bond" is the whole lattice's attraction, not a pair-specific link. That is why formula units (NaCl) are not molecules.
**Covalent character in ionic bonds is normal, not anomalous:** Fajan's rules mean every "ionic" compound has some electron distortion; 100% ionic exists only as an idealisation.
**Solid ionic compounds do not conduct:** conduction requires mobile charge carriers; in the solid the ions are locked in place — the common exam trap.

## 7. Exam Application

**Verified PYQ (NEB 2024, 2m): Distinguish between ionic and covalent bonds with one example of each.** — Ionic bond: complete transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal, giving oppositely charged ions held by electrostatic attraction (NaCl). Covalent bond: mutual sharing of one or more electron pairs between non-metal atoms (H₂O). Key consequences: ionic compounds have high melting points and conduct when molten; covalent compounds have low melting points and are non-conducting.

**Verified PYQ (NEB 2024, 3m): State Fajan's rules. How do they explain the covalent character of LiCl vs NaCl?** — Covalent character increases with small cation size, large anion size, high ionic charges and cations of 18-electron configuration. Li⁺ (76 pm) is smaller than Na⁺ (102 pm) — greater charge density, stronger polarising power — so Li⁺ distorts the chloride cloud more than Na⁺ does, making LiCl more covalent: it dissolves in organic solvents and melts lower than NaCl.

**NEB-style (2m): Why is MgO's melting point (2852 °C) far higher than NaCl's (801 °C)?** — Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ carry double the charge of Na⁺/Cl⁻ and are smaller, so the electrostatic attraction (and lattice energy, ≈ −3795 kJ mol⁻¹) is far greater — more energy is needed to disrupt the lattice.

data.summary: When a low-ionisation-energy metal meets a high-electron-affinity non-metal, electrons transfer completely: Na gives its 3s electron to Cl, and the Na⁺/Cl⁻ pair assembles into a **three-dimensional lattice** whose electrostatic attraction is the ionic bond. That geometry explains everything: hardness yet brittleness (layer slip brings like charges together), high melting points (NaCl 801 °C, MgO 2852 °C — charge and size set the lattice energy), conduction only when molten or dissolved (mobile ions needed), and solubility in polar solvents (ion–dipole prize ions out). Fajan's rules then admit reality: small, highly charged cations distort anion clouds — **LiCl is measurably more covalent than NaCl** (smaller Li⁺, organic-solvent solubility). No bond is perfectly ionic; the ionic–covalent contrast is a continuum, and the exam's favourite probes are the NEB 2024 pair — the distinction table and Fajan's LiCl comparison.

subtopics.name: Electron transfer
points: A metal with low ionisation energy loses electrons to form a cation
A non-metal with high electron affinity gains them to form an anion
The ions are held by electrostatic attraction in a giant lattice

subtopics.name: Energetics
points: Lattice enthalpy is the energy released when gaseous ions form the solid
Born-Haber cycle accounts for the full energy balance
High lattice enthalpy means a high melting point

subtopics.name: Physical properties
points: High melting and boiling points — strong electrostatic forces must be broken
Hard and brittle — a shift brings like charges together and the crystal cleaves
Usually soluble in polar solvents such as water, insoluble in non-polar solvents

subtopics.name: Electrical behaviour
points: Solid does not conduct — ions are locked in the lattice
Molten or aqueous state conducts — ions become mobile
This is the classic test distinguishing ionic from covalent compounds

subtopics.name: Fajans' rules
points: Small, highly charged cations polarise anions strongly, adding covalent character
LiCl and BeCl2 are more covalent than NaCl and MgCl2 for this reason
No bond is purely ionic — all have some covalent character

subtopics.name: Real examples
points: NaCl: melting point 801 degrees Celsius, conducts when molten
MgO: very high lattice enthalpy, melting point ~2852 degrees Celsius
Ionic liquids are salts molten near room temperature — a modern exception

notes: VSEPR theory predicts molecular geometry from electron pairs.
sp³: 4 pairs → tetrahedral (109.5°).
sp²: 3 pairs → trigonal planar (120°).
sp: 2 pairs → linear (180°).
Lone pairs compress bond angles.
confusion: ❌ All atoms are identical in an element. ✅ Isotopes have same protons but different neutrons.
❌ Atoms are indivisible. ✅ Atoms consist of protons, neutrons, and electrons.
❌ Electrons orbit in fixed paths like planets. ✅ Electrons exist in probability clouds (orbitals).
❌ Heisenberg uncertainty means we cannot measure position and momentum precisely simultaneously — not that we lack good instruments.
❌ de Broglie wavelength applies only to light. ✅ All matter has wave nature; detectable mainly for small masses like electrons.
❌ Quantum number l can be any integer. ✅ l ranges from 0 to n−1.
❌ Magnetic quantum number ml determines energy. ✅ ml determines orbital orientation, not energy (in absence of magnetic field).
❌ Spin quantum number ms can be ±½ or any value. ✅ ms is always +½ or −½.
❌ Aufbau principle means filling from bottom to top of the diagram. ✅ Fill lowest-energy orbitals first: 1s→2s→2p→3s→3p→4s→3d→4p→...
❌ Pauli exclusion allows two electrons per orbital with any spin. ✅ Two electrons in same orbital must have opposite spins.
❌ Hund's rule means pair electrons before spreading. ✅ Electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly first with parallel spins.
❌ The mole is just a number like dozen. ✅ 1 mole = 6.022×10²³ particles (Avogadro constant) — a bridge between atomic and macroscopic scales.
❌ Molar mass and molecular mass are the same thing. ✅ Molecular mass is in amu; molar mass is in g/mol — numerically equal but different units.
❌ Limiting reagent is the reactant with smallest mass. ✅ Limiting reagent is the one that produces the least product (determined by moles, not mass).
❌ % yield can exceed 100%. ✅ % yield >100% indicates impure product or incomplete drying.
❌ Molarity and molality are the same. ✅ Molarity = mol/L solution (changes with T); Molality = mol/kg solvent (temperature-independent).
❌ A strong acid completely ionizes in water. ✅ Strong acids (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄) are ~100% ionized; weak acids partially ionize.
❌ pH can be negative. ✅ pH < 0 is possible for concentrations >1M (e.g., 2M HCl has pH ≈ −0.3).
❌ Kc changes when concentration changes. ✅ Kc is constant at constant temperature; only temperature changes K.
❌ Adding catalyst shifts equilibrium position. ✅ Catalyst speeds both forward and backward reactions equally; no shift in equilibrium.
❌ High pressure always favors products. ✅ High pressure favors side with fewer gas moles (Le Chatelier).
❌ Exothermic reactions are spontaneous. ✅ Spontaneity depends on ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, not just ΔH.
❌ Endothermic reactions cannot be spontaneous. ✅ Endothermic reactions can be spontaneous if TΔS > ΔH (e.g., ice melting above 0°C).
❌ ΔH and ΔU are always the same. ✅ ΔH = ΔU + PΔV; they differ when gas moles change.
❌ Heat (q) and work (w) are state functions. ✅ q and w are path functions; only ΔU, ΔH, ΔS, ΔG are state functions.
❌ Oxidation and reduction happen separately. ✅ Oxidation and reduction always occur together (redox).
❌ Oxidizing agent gets oxidized. ✅ Oxidizing agent accepts electrons and gets reduced.
❌ Reducing agent gets reduced. ✅ Reducing agent donates electrons and gets oxidized.
❌ Faraday's laws apply only to metals. ✅ Faraday's laws apply to any substance deposited/dissolved at electrodes.
❌ Real gases obey PV=nRT at all conditions. ✅ Real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature.
❌ van der Waals constants a and b are same for all gases. ✅ a (attraction) and b (volume) are gas-specific.
❌ Surface tension increases with temperature. ✅ Surface tension decreases as temperature increases.
❌ Viscosity decreases with temperature for liquids. ✅ Viscosity of liquids decreases with T; gases increase with T.
❌ Colligative properties depend on nature of solute. ✅ Colligative properties depend only on number of particles, not identity.
❌ Raoult's law applies to all solutions. ✅ Raoult's law is exact for ideal solutions; approximate for dilute real solutions.
❌ Osmotic pressure is a colligative property. ✅ Yes — π = CRT depends on solute particle concentration.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Bond of Shared Ownership

Between two identical non-metal atoms there is no transfer — only **sharing**. Two chlorine atoms each bring one electron; the pair sits between both nuclei and pulls on each equally: the covalent bond. When one atom supplies **both** electrons, the link is a coordinate (dative) bond — chemically identical once formed, but with a revealing origin story. This topic builds the bond, its multiple varieties, and the property profile of covalent compounds.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Covalent bond — definition and formation

- **Definition:** the bond formed by the mutual sharing of one or more electron pairs between atoms, each contributing one electron per pair.
- **H₂:** two H atoms share one pair; each nucleus attracts the pair — energy minimum at 74 pm, bond energy 436 kJ mol⁻¹.
- **Cl₂:** each Cl (2,8,7) contributes one electron → shared pair completes both octets.
- Forces: attraction (nucleus–opposite electron cloud) versus repulsion (nucleus–nucleus, electron–electron) balance at the bond length.

### 2.2 Multiple bonds

- **Single bond (–):** one shared pair — H₂, Cl₂, CH₄ (C–H).
- **Double bond (=):** two shared pairs — O₂, CO₂ (O=C=O), ethene C₂H₄.
- **Triple bond (≡):** three shared pairs — N₂, ethyne C₂H₂. Triple > double > single in bond energy, and shorter in length.

### 2.3 Coordinate (dative) bond

- **Definition:** a bond in which the shared pair is supplied by **one atom only** (the donor); the acceptor contributes none.
- **Conditions:** donor has a lone pair; acceptor has an empty orbital.
- **Examples:** **NH₄⁺** (N donates its lone pair to H⁺), **H₃O⁺** (H₂O donates to H⁺), **NH₃·BF₃** (N→B), **O₃** (one O→O link), **SO₂/SO₃** (drawn with S→O links), metal complexes (Ni(CO)₄).
- **Key point:** once formed, a coordinate bond is indistinguishable from an ordinary covalent bond — same strength, same length. It is conventionally drawn as an arrow (→) from donor to acceptor.

### 2.4 Properties of covalent compounds

- **Low melting/boiling points:** forces between molecules are weak van der Waals/dipole forces (I₂ sublimes; CH₄ bp −161 °C) — the covalent bonds themselves are strong, but they are *intra*molecular.
- **Non-conductors:** no free ions or electrons (exceptions: graphite, HCl(aq) which ionises in water).
- **Solubility:** dissolve in non-polar (organic) solvents; generally insoluble in water — "like dissolves like".
- **Molecular, not lattices of ions:** exist as discrete molecules with definite shapes; show **isomerism** (directional bonds permit structural variety).
- **Reactions are slow:** covalent bonds must be broken and rearranged via molecular collisions — unlike the lightning-fast ion recombinations.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Value to quote |
|---|---|---|
| **Covalent bond** | Mutual sharing of one or more electron pairs between atoms | H₂: 436 kJ mol⁻¹, 74 pm |
| **Coordinate bond** | Shared pair supplied entirely by one atom (donor → acceptor) | NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺ |
| **Double bond** | Two shared pairs | O=C=O |
| **Triple bond** | Three shared pairs | N≡N, 945 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| **Isomerism** | Same formula, different arrangement — possible due to directional bonds | C₂H₅OH vs CH₃OCH₃ |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Energy profile of H₂ formation

- As two H atoms approach: attraction lowers potential energy; below ~74 pm, nucleus–nucleus repulsion dominates and energy climbs steeply.
- The minimum (−436 kJ mol⁻¹ relative to separated atoms) is the bond energy; the internuclear distance there is the bond length. The same logic underlies every covalent bond.

### 4.2 Coordinate bond anatomy — NH₄⁺

- N in NH₃ has one lone pair; H⁺ offers an empty 1s orbital.
- N donates the pair: N→H⁺ creates the fourth N–H link; all four N–H bonds in NH₄⁺ become **equivalent** (identical length/strength) — the origin is invisible in the final ion.
- Same recipe: H₂O + H⁺ → H₃O⁺ (hydronium — the species that carries "H⁺" in water); NH₃ + BF₃ → NH₃·BF₃ adduct (N donates, B accepts — filling boron's deficient octet).

### 4.3 Why "low melting point" does not mean "weak bond"

- Diamond (covalent, network solid) melts above 3500 °C; iodine (covalent, molecular solid) sublimes at 184 °C. The difference is what holds **between** molecules: diamond is one giant covalent network; I₂ molecules cling by weak dispersion forces. Quote both to show the distinction between intramolecular and intermolecular forces.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Covalent vs coordinate bond**

| Basis | Covalent | Coordinate |
|---|---|---|
| Pair supplied by | Both atoms (one each) | One atom (donor) |
| Before formation | Both need an electron | Donor has lone pair; acceptor empty orbital |
| After formation | Identical | Identical — no detectable difference |
| Representation | A–B | A→B |
| Example | H₂, CH₄ | NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺, NH₃·BF₃ |

**Covalent vs ionic compounds (full property contrast)**

| Basis | Covalent compounds | Ionic compounds |
|---|---|---|
| Particles | Molecules | Ions in a lattice |
| mp/bp | Low (weak intermolecular forces) | High (strong lattice forces) |
| Conductivity | Non-conducting | Molten/aqueous conduction |
| Solubility | Organic (non-polar) solvents | Water (polar) |
| Isomerism | Shown | Not shown |
| Reaction speed | Slow (bond breaking needed) | Fast (ion recombination) |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Coordinate bond ≠ weaker bond:** after formation it is electronically identical to any covalent bond; only the bookkeeping of origin differs.
**Intermolecular vs intramolecular:** low boiling points reflect weak forces *between* molecules; the covalent bonds *within* each molecule remain strong.
**H⁺ never travels free in water:** it immediately coordinate-bonds to H₂O forming H₃O⁺ — writing bare H⁺(aq) is a shorthand, not a structure.

## 7. Exam Application

**Verified PYQ (NEB 2024, 2m): Distinguish between ionic and covalent bonds with one example of each.** — Ionic: complete transfer (NaCl); covalent: mutual sharing (H₂O). Property contrast: mp/bp, conductivity, solubility as tabulated in section 5.

**NEB-style (3m): What is a coordinate covalent bond? Explain the formation of NH₄⁺ and H₃O⁺.** — A coordinate bond is a shared pair donated by a single atom. In NH₄⁺, nitrogen's lone pair is donated to H⁺ (empty 1s), creating a fourth N–H link; all four bonds become equivalent. In H₃O⁺, the water oxygen donates its lone pair to H⁺, giving a dative O→H bond on top of the two ordinary O–H bonds.

**NEB-style (2m): Why are covalent compounds generally non-conductors of electricity?** — They contain no free ions and no free electrons; the shared pairs are locked between specific nuclei. (Exceptions to mention: aqueous HCl ionises; graphite conducts via delocalised electrons.)
confusion: **Origin vs identity:** a coordinate bond looks identical to a covalent bond after formation — the arrow is history, not a property.
**Diamond vs iodine:** both covalent, yet diamond melts above 3500 °C and iodine at 184 °C — network vs molecular solid; intermolecular forces set the difference.

practiceQuestions: **NEB 2024 (2m): Distinguish between ionic and covalent bonds with one example of each.** — **Ionic bond:** complete electron transfer from metal to non-metal; oppositely charged ions attract electrostatically in a lattice — **NaCl**. **Covalent bond:** mutual sharing of electron pairs between non-metal atoms — **H₂O**. Consequences: ionic compounds are high-melting, molten/aqueous conductors, water-soluble; covalent compounds are low-melting, non-conducting molecular species, generally organic-soluble.

**NEB-style (3m): Define coordinate covalent bond. Describe the formation of the ammonium ion and the hydronium ion.** — A coordinate (dative) bond forms when **one atom supplies both electrons** of the shared pair: the donor must own a lone pair, the acceptor an empty orbital. **NH₄⁺:** ammonia's nitrogen has a lone pair; it donates it to H⁺ (bare proton, empty 1s orbital) → N→H⁺; the ion carries four equivalent N–H bonds and one positive charge. **H₃O⁺:** water's oxygen donates a lone pair to H⁺ → O→H⁺; the hydronium ion carries two ordinary O–H bonds, one dative O→H bond, and one positive charge — it is the actual form of "H⁺" in aqueous acid.

**NEB-style (3m): Explain three properties of covalent compounds, each with its cause.** — **(a) Low melting and boiling points:** the forces between molecules are weak van der Waals/dipole attractions; melting separates molecules without touching the strong C–H or O–H bonds inside them. **(b) Non-conduction:** no free ions and no delocalised electrons — shared pairs are fixed between particular nuclei (graphite and ionising acids like HCl are the standard exceptions). **(c) Solubility in organic, not aqueous, solvents:** "like dissolves like" — non-polar molecular solutes interact well with non-polar solvents; water's hydrogen-bond network does not accommodate them (sugar and ethanol are the polar-covalent exceptions that do dissolve).
keyPoints: Covalent bond = mutual sharing of electron pairs (single/double/triple; energy rises, length falls with multiplicity). Coordinate bond = shared pair from one atom (donor→acceptor): NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺, NH₃·BF₃; identical to covalent once formed. Properties of covalent compounds: low mp/bp (weak intermolecular forces), non-conducting, organic-solvent soluble, molecular, isomerism shown, slow reactions.
data.summary: Where transfer is impossible, sharing takes over. Two chlorine atoms each contribute one electron to a pair both nuclei pull on — the **covalent bond**, with its single (H₂), double (CO₂) and triple (N₂) grades trading length for strength. A variant where one atom donates the whole pair — the **coordinate bond** — builds NH₄⁺ from NH₃ + H⁺ and H₃O⁺ from H₂O + H⁺, yet becomes electronically identical to any covalent bond once formed. Covalent compounds are molecular: low melting points (weak intermolecular forces, not weak bonds — diamond proves the point at 3500 °C), non-conducting (no free carriers), organic-soluble ("like dissolves like"), capable of isomerism (directional bonds), and slow to react (bonds must be broken, not just recombined). Ionic vs covalent is the NEB 2024 distinction question; the coordinate-bond trio NH₄⁺/H₃O⁺/NH₃·BF₃ is the stock 3m answer.

| Example | H₂, CH₄ | NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺, NH₃·BF₃ |

**Covalent vs ionic compounds (full property contrast)**

| Basis | Covalent compounds | Ionic compounds |
|---|---|---|
| Particles | Molecules | Ions in a lattice |
| mp/bp | Low (weak intermolecular forces) | High (strong lattice forces) |
| Conductivity | Non-conducting | Molten/aqueous conduction |
| Solubility | Organic (non-polar) solvents | Water (polar) |
| Isomerism | Shown | Not shown |
| Reaction speed | Slow (bond breaking needed) | Fast (ion recombination) |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Coordinate bond ≠ weaker bond:** after formation it is electronically identical to any covalent bond; only the bookkeeping of origin differs.
**Intermolecular vs intramolecular:** low boiling points reflect weak forces *between* molecules; the covalent bonds *within* each molecule remain strong.
**H⁺ never travels free in water:** it immediately coordinate-bonds to H₂O forming H₃O⁺ — writing bare H⁺(aq) is a shorthand, not a structure.

## 7. Exam Application

**Verified PYQ (NEB 2024, 2m): Distinguish between ionic and covalent bonds with one example of each.** — Ionic: complete transfer (NaCl); covalent: mutual sharing (H₂O). Property contrast: mp/bp, conductivity, solubility as tabulated in section 5.

**NEB-style (3m): What is a coordinate covalent bond? Explain the formation of NH₄⁺ and H₃O⁺.** — A coordinate bond is a shared pair donated by a single atom. In NH₄⁺, nitrogen's lone pair is donated to H⁺ (empty 1s), creating a fourth N–H link; all four bonds become equivalent. In H₃O⁺, the water oxygen donates its lone pair to H⁺, giving a dative O→H bond on top of the two ordinary O–H bonds.

**NEB-style (2m): Why are covalent compounds generally non-conductors of electricity?** — They contain no free ions and no free electrons; the shared pairs are locked between specific nuclei. (Exceptions to mention: aqueous HCl ionises; graphite conducts via delocalised electrons.)

**Diamond vs iodine:** both covalent, yet diamond melts above 3500 °C and iodine at 184 °C — network vs molecular solid; intermolecular forces set the difference.

Coordinate bond = shared pair from one atom (donor→acceptor): NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺, NH₃·BF₃; identical to covalent once formed. notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Chemistry in Dots and Lines

A Lewis dot structure is a molecule's electron budget made visible: every valence electron accounted for, either as a bonding pair (a line) or a lone pair (dots). Draw it correctly and the shape, polarity and reactivity of the molecule follow almost mechanically. NEB has asked the CO₂ dot structure directly (2022, 2024) and the H₂O/NH₃ structures with their shapes (2024) — this topic is the drawing manual.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 The drawing procedure

1. **Count** total valence electrons (adjust for charge: add for anions, subtract for cations).
2. **Choose the skeleton** — least electronegative atom central (H is always terminal).
3. **Place one bond pair** between every connected pair; complete the octets (duets for H) of outer atoms with lone pairs.
4. **Park leftovers on the central atom**; if its octet is short, convert outer lone pairs into double/triple bonds.
5. **Verify:** electrons used = electrons counted; every atom at its octet (or a known exception: Be, B, expanded P/S).

### 2.2 The standard gallery (s and p block)

- **H₂O:** 8 e⁻ → two O–H bonds + **two lone pairs** on O (bent, 104.5°).
- **NH₃:** 8 e⁻ → three N–H bonds + **one lone pair** (pyramidal, 107°).
- **CH₄:** 8 e⁻ → four C–H bonds, no lone pairs (tetrahedral, 109.5°).
- **CO₂:** 16 e⁻ → two C=O double bonds, two lone pairs per O (linear, 180°).
- **BF₃:** 24 e⁻ → three B–F bonds, no lone pair on B — **incomplete octet (6 e⁻)** (trigonal planar, 120°).
- **PCl₅:** 40 e⁻ → five P–Cl bonds — **expanded octet (10 e⁻)** (trigonal bipyramidal).
- **SF₆:** 48 e⁻ → six S–F bonds — **expanded octet (12 e⁻)** (octahedral).
- **H₂S:** 8 e⁻ → two S–H bonds + two lone pairs (bent, 92°).

### 2.3 Formal charge — choosing between rival structures

- **FC = valence e⁻ − (non-bonding e⁻ + ½ bonding e⁻).**
- The best structure minimises formal charges and puts negative FC on the more electronegative atom.
- Example O₃: the two resonance forms each carry FC +1 on central O and −1 on one terminal O — formal charge bookkeeping justifies resonance (topic 31).

### 2.4 Polyatomic ions

- **NH₄⁺:** 5 + 4 − 1 = 8 e⁻ → four N–H bonds; formal charge +1 on N.
- **OH⁻:** 6 + 1 + 1 = 8 e⁻ → one O–H bond, three lone pairs, FC −1 on O.
- **CO₃²⁻:** 4 + 18 + 2 = 24 e⁻ → one C=O, two C–O⁻, one lone pair on C — and resonance spreads the double bond (topic 31).

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Value to quote |
|---|---|---|
| **Lewis structure** | Diagram of valence electrons as dots/lines showing bonding and lone pairs | CO₂: O=C=O |
| **Lone pair** | Valence pair not shared between atoms | H₂O: 2 LP |
| **Bonding pair** | Electron pair shared between two atoms | CH₄: 4 BP |
| **Formal charge** | FC = valence e⁻ − (non-bonding e⁻ + ½ bonding e⁻) | O₃: +1/−1/0 |
| **Expanded octet** | More than 8 e⁻ around central atom (period ≥ 3) | SF₆: 12 e⁻ |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Verified PYQ (NEB 2022 & 2024): Lewis dot structure of CO₂ and its shape

- Count: 4 + 2(6) = **16 electrons**.
- Skeleton O–C–O; place one pair in each C–O bond (4 e⁻), complete O octets with lone pairs (12 e⁻) — carbon has only 4 e⁻.
- Convert one lone pair from each O into a bonding pair → **O=C=O**, two double bonds.
- Each atom reaches an octet; all 16 electrons placed. **Shape: linear, 180°** (two electron domains around C).

### 4.2 Verified PYQ (NEB 2024): Lewis structures of H₂O and NH₃ with VSEPR shapes

- **H₂O:** 6 + 2(1) = 8 e⁻ → two O–H bonds + two lone pairs on O. Four electron domains → tetrahedral electron geometry, but **molecular shape bent (V-shaped), ≈104.5°** — lone pairs compress the angle.
- **NH₃:** 5 + 3(1) = 8 e⁻ → three N–H bonds + one lone pair. Four domains → **pyramidal shape, ≈107°** — one lone pair compresses 109.5° to 107°.

### 4.3 Reading the exceptions straight off the dots

- BF₃'s drawing forces 6 electrons onto B — the structure itself announces the incomplete octet and the Lewis-acid character.
- PCl₅/SF₆ demand 10/12 electrons on the central atom — only legal for period ≥ 3.
- The dot count is also the raw material for VSEPR: **bonding pairs + lone pairs = electron domains**, and domains set the shape (topic 32).

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Molecule-by-molecule dot audit**

| Molecule | Total e⁻ | Bonds | Lone pairs (central) | Shape |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| H₂O | 8 | 2 O–H | 2 | Bent 104.5° |
| NH₃ | 8 | 3 N–H | 1 | Pyramidal 107° |
| CH₄ | 8 | 4 C–H | 0 | Tetrahedral 109.5° |
| CO₂ | 16 | 2 C=O | 0 | Linear 180° |
| BF₃ | 24 | 3 B–F | 0 | Trigonal planar 120° |
| PCl₅ | 40 | 5 P–Cl | 0 | Trigonal bipyramidal |
| SF₆ | 48 | 6 S–F | 0 | Octahedral |
| H₂S | 8 | 2 S–H | 2 | Bent ≈92° |

**Formal charge worked: O₃**

| Atom | valence e⁻ | non-bonding | ½ bonding | FC |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Central O | 6 | 2 | 3 | +1 |
| Double-bond O | 6 | 4 | 2 | 0 |
| Single-bond O | 6 | 6 | 1 | −1 |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Lone pairs are not optional decoration:** omitting them changes the VSEPR count and hence the predicted shape — H₂O without its lone pairs would be drawn "linear" and lose all the marks.
**Total electrons ≠ electrons shown as dots around one atom:** in CO₂ the 16 electrons distribute over three atoms; the audit line "used = counted" is the safety check.
**Formal charge ≠ real charge:** it is a bookkeeping index for choosing among structures; the molecule's real charge distribution comes from electronegativity (partial charges), not FC.

## 7. Exam Application

**Verified PYQ (NEB 2022/2024): Write the Lewis dot structure of CO₂. What is its molecular shape?** — 16 valence electrons; O=C=O with two lone pairs on each oxygen; carbon's octet completed by two double bonds. Two electron domains, no lone pairs on C → **linear, 180°**, and the two C=O bond dipoles cancel, making the molecule non-polar.

**Verified PYQ (NEB 2024): Draw the Lewis structures of H₂O and NH₃ and predict their shapes using VSEPR theory.** — H₂O: two bonds + two lone pairs → bent, ≈104.5°. NH₃: three bonds + one lone pair → pyramidal, ≈107°. Both angles sit below 109.5° because lone pair–bond pair repulsion exceeds bond pair–bond pair repulsion.

**NEB-style (2m): Draw the Lewis structure of BF₃ and comment on boron's octet.** — 24 valence electrons; three B–F single bonds, three lone pairs on each F; boron holds only 6 electrons — an incomplete octet, making BF₃ a strong Lewis acid that completes its octet by accepting a pair (e.g. from NH₃).
confusion: **Draw lone pairs first, shapes later:** every VSEPR answer begins with the completed Lewis structure — lone pairs included — or the domain count collapses.

**Formal charge vs oxidation state:** FC assigns bonding electrons equally; oxidation state assigns them to the more electronegative atom — the two bookkeeping systems give different numbers on purpose.

Why must hydrogen always occupy a terminal position in a Lewis structure?
Draw SO₂ and explain why sulphur carries a lone pair despite two S=O-style links.
examples: ***CO₂'s 16 electrons: 8 in two double bonds, 8 in four lone pairs*** — the full audit, quoted in NEB 2022 and 2024.
practiceQuestions: **NEB 2022 & 2024 (2m): Write the Lewis dot structure of CO₂. What is its molecular shape?** — Carbon dioxide has 4 + 2(6) = **16 valence electrons**. Skeleton O–C–O: one pair in each C–O link, six electrons (three lone pairs) on each oxygen complete their octets but leave carbon with only four. Moving one lone pair from each oxygen into bonding gives **O=C=O** — two double bonds, two lone pairs per oxygen, every atom at an octet. Carbon carries two electron domains and no lone pairs, so VSEPR gives a **linear molecule, 180°**; the equal, opposite C=O dipoles cancel and CO₂ is non-polar.

**NEB 2024 (3m): Draw the Lewis structures of H₂O and NH₃ and predict their shapes using VSEPR theory.** — **H₂O:** 8 valence electrons → two O–H bonding pairs plus **two lone pairs** on oxygen. Four electron domains give tetrahedral electron geometry; the two lone pairs push the bonds together, so the molecular shape is **bent (V-shaped) with H–O–H ≈ 104.5°**. **NH₃:** 8 valence electrons → three N–H bonds plus **one lone pair** on nitrogen. Four domains again, but one lone pair compresses the angle less: **pyramidal shape, H–N–H ≈ 107°**. Both angles fall below the ideal 109.5° because lone pair–bond pair repulsion exceeds bond pair–bond pair repulsion.

**NEB-style (2m): Compute the formal charges in the ozone molecule and state what they imply.** — For O₃ (central O double-bonded to one O, single-bonded to the other): central O = 6 − (2 + 3) = **+1**; double-bond terminal O = 6 − (4 + 2) = **0**; single-bond terminal O = 6 − (6 + 1) = **−1**. The mirror-image structure carries the −1 on the other terminal oxygen. Neither structure alone is real — the charges and the two different O–O lengths (128 and 136 pm) show the true molecule is a **resonance hybrid** of the two forms.
formulas:
- Total valence e⁻ = Σ(valence e⁻) ± charge
- FC = V − (N + ½B)
- Domains = bonding pairs + lone pairs (central atom)
keyPoints: Procedure: count valence e⁻ (± charge) → skeleton (least EN central) → bonds → outer octets → leftovers on central atom → double/triple bonds if short → verify. Gallery: H₂O (2 LP, bent), NH₃ (1 LP, pyramidal), CH₄ (tetrahedral), CO₂ (2 C=O, linear), BF₃ (6 e⁻, trigonal planar), PCl₅ (10 e⁻, TBP), SF₆ (12 e⁻, octahedral), H₂S (bent ≈92°). Formal charge = valence − (non-bonding + ½ bonding); minimise FC, negative on the more EN atom.
data.summary: A Lewis structure is an electron audit made visible. Count the valence electrons (adjusting for charge), pick the least electronegative central atom, spend electrons on bonds first and outer octets second, park the remainder on the centre, and promote lone pairs to double or triple bonds when the central octet falls short. The gallery every exam draws from: **H₂O** (2 bonds + 2 lone pairs, bent 104.5°), **NH₃** (3 + 1, pyramidal 107°), **CH₄** (4 + 0, tetrahedral 109.5°), **CO₂** (two C=O, linear 180° — NEB 2022 and 2024), **BF₃** (incomplete octet, 6 e⁻), **PCl₅** (10 e⁻) and **SF₆** (12 e⁻) as expanded-octet legal cases, **H₂S** (bent ≈92°). Formal charge (V − N − ½B) referees rival structures and sets up resonance. Lone pairs are never optional: they are the hinge between the dot picture and the VSEPR shape.

| Atom | valence e⁻ | non-bonding | ½ bonding | FC |

**Formal charge ≠ real charge:** it is a bookkeeping index for choosing among structures; the molecule's real charge distribution comes from electronegativity (partial charges), not FC.

## 7. Exam Application

**Verified PYQ (NEB 2022/2024): Write the Lewis dot structure of CO₂. **Verified PYQ (NEB 2024): Draw the Lewis structures of H₂O and NH₃ and predict their shapes using VSEPR theory.** — H₂O: two bonds + two lone pairs → bent, ≈104.5°.
