confusion: ❌ All atoms are identical in an element. ✅ Isotopes have same protons but different neutrons.
❌ Atoms are indivisible. ✅ Atoms consist of protons, neutrons, and electrons.
❌ Electrons orbit in fixed paths like planets. ✅ Electrons exist in probability clouds (orbitals).
❌ Heisenberg uncertainty means we cannot measure position and momentum precisely simultaneously — not that we lack good instruments.
❌ de Broglie wavelength applies only to light. ✅ All matter has wave nature; detectable mainly for small masses like electrons.
❌ Quantum number l can be any integer. ✅ l ranges from 0 to n−1.
❌ Magnetic quantum number ml determines energy. ✅ ml determines orbital orientation, not energy (in absence of magnetic field).
❌ Spin quantum number ms can be ±½ or any value. ✅ ms is always +½ or −½.
❌ Aufbau principle means filling from bottom to top of the diagram. ✅ Fill lowest-energy orbitals first: 1s→2s→2p→3s→3p→4s→3d→4p→...
❌ Pauli exclusion allows two electrons per orbital with any spin. ✅ Two electrons in same orbital must have opposite spins.
❌ Hund's rule means pair electrons before spreading. ✅ Electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly first with parallel spins.
❌ The mole is just a number like dozen. ✅ 1 mole = 6.022×10²³ particles (Avogadro constant) — a bridge between atomic and macroscopic scales.
❌ Molar mass and molecular mass are the same thing. ✅ Molecular mass is in amu; molar mass is in g/mol — numerically equal but different units.
❌ Limiting reagent is the reactant with smallest mass. ✅ Limiting reagent is the one that produces the least product (determined by moles, not mass).
❌ % yield can exceed 100%. ✅ % yield >100% indicates impure product or incomplete drying.
❌ Molarity and molality are the same. ✅ Molarity = mol/L solution (changes with T); Molality = mol/kg solvent (temperature-independent).
❌ A strong acid completely ionizes in water. ✅ Strong acids (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄) are ~100% ionized; weak acids partially ionize.
❌ pH can be negative. ✅ pH < 0 is possible for concentrations >1M (e.g., 2M HCl has pH ≈ −0.3).
❌ Kc changes when concentration changes. ✅ Kc is constant at constant temperature; only temperature changes K.
❌ Adding catalyst shifts equilibrium position. ✅ Catalyst speeds both forward and backward reactions equally; no shift in equilibrium.
❌ High pressure always favors products. ✅ High pressure favors side with fewer gas moles (Le Chatelier).
❌ Exothermic reactions are spontaneous. ✅ Spontaneity depends on ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, not just ΔH.
❌ Endothermic reactions cannot be spontaneous. ✅ Endothermic reactions can be spontaneous if TΔS > ΔH (e.g., ice melting above 0°C).
❌ ΔH and ΔU are always the same. ✅ ΔH = ΔU + PΔV; they differ when gas moles change.
❌ Heat (q) and work (w) are state functions. ✅ q and w are path functions; only ΔU, ΔH, ΔS, ΔG are state functions.
❌ Oxidation and reduction happen separately. ✅ Oxidation and reduction always occur together (redox).
❌ Oxidizing agent gets oxidized. ✅ Oxidizing agent accepts electrons and gets reduced.
❌ Reducing agent gets reduced. ✅ Reducing agent donates electrons and gets oxidized.
❌ Faraday's laws apply only to metals. ✅ Faraday's laws apply to any substance deposited/dissolved at electrodes.
❌ Real gases obey PV=nRT at all conditions. ✅ Real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature.
❌ van der Waals constants a and b are same for all gases. ✅ a (attraction) and b (volume) are gas-specific.
❌ Surface tension increases with temperature. ✅ Surface tension decreases as temperature increases.
❌ Viscosity decreases with temperature for liquids. ✅ Viscosity of liquids decreases with T; gases increase with T.
❌ Colligative properties depend on nature of solute. ✅ Colligative properties depend only on number of particles, not identity.
❌ Raoult's law applies to all solutions. ✅ Raoult's law is exact for ideal solutions; approximate for dilute real solutions.
❌ Osmotic pressure is a colligative property. ✅ Yes — π = CRT depends on solute particle concentration.

Atomic structure: From Rutherford's nuclear model through Bohr's quantized orbits to the modern quantum mechanical model, understanding electron configuration using four quantum numbers is fundamental.

Stoichiometry: The mole concept bridges atomic and macroscopic scales; limiting reagent determines theoretical yield; concentration expressed as molarity or molality.

Solutions: Molarity and molality express concentration; colligative properties depend on particle number; Raoult's law describes vapor pressure of ideal solutions.

Chemical bonding: Ionic bonds form from electron transfer; covalent bonds from sharing; VSEPR predicts molecular geometry; hybridization explains bonding orbitals.

Hydrocarbons: Alkanes (CnH2n+2) are saturated; alkenes (CnH2n) have C=C; alkynes (CnH2n-2) have C≡C; aromatic compounds based on benzene ring.

Periodic table: Elements arranged by atomic number; periodic trends in radius, ionization energy, electronegativity; s, p, d, f blocks based on orbital type.

Applied chemistry: Petrochemical industry, polymer science, green chemistry principles; importance of sustainable chemical manufacturing for environmental protection.

data.topicTitle: Introduction of ores; gangue or matrix, flux and slag, alloy and amalgam
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Vocabulary of Extraction

Before any metal flows, the ore must be described: what mineral it is, what worthless rock travels with it (**gangue**), what is added to make the impurities flow (**flux**), what the flux turns them into (**slag**), and what metals are blended into alloys. These five words — ore, gangue, flux, slag, alloy — are the working vocabulary of every extraction plant, and NEB asks them as short questions almost every year.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Ore, mineral, gangue

- A **mineral** is any natural compound of a metal; a **mineral becomes an ore** when the metal can be extracted profitably.
- **Gangue (matrix)** is the worthless sandy/rocky material mixed with the ore — silica, clay, limestone. Concentration removes most of it; the flux deals with the rest.

### 2.2 Flux and slag

- A **flux** is a substance added to the charge to combine with the gangue and form a fusible **slag**.
- **Acidic flux** removes basic gangue: silica (SiO₂) for iron oxides/lime. **Basic flux** removes acidic gangue: limestone (CaCO₃) for silica in the iron blast furnace — CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, then CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃ (slag).
- A good slag: low melting, immiscible with the metal, lighter — it floats and is drawn off, protecting the metal from oxidation.

### 2.3 Alloys and amalgam

- An **alloy** is a homogeneous mixture of a metal with other metals (or non-metals) made to improve hardness, resistance to corrosion, or casting quality: brass (Cu + Zn), bronze (Cu + Sn), stainless steel (Fe + Cr + Ni + C).
- An **amalgam** is an alloy in which one component is **mercury**: sodium amalgam (a safe handling form of reactive sodium, used as a reducing agent), dental amalgam (Ag–Sn–Hg). Iron does not form an amalgam — which is why iron vessels can hold mercury.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Ore** | Mineral from which metal is extracted profitably | Haematite Fe₂O₃ |
| **Gangue (matrix)** | Worthless rocky impurity in the ore | Silica, clay |
| **Flux** | Substance added to fuse with gangue | CaCO₃ (basic), SiO₂ (acidic) |
| **Slag** | Fusible product of flux + gangue | CaSiO₃ |
| **Alloy** | Homogeneous mixture of metals (or metal + non-metal) | Brass Cu–Zn |
| **Amalgam** | Alloy containing mercury | Na–Hg, dental Ag–Sn–Hg |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 How flux chooses its gangue

- Chemistry of pairing: an acidic oxide neutralises a basic one. Iron ore carries silica (acidic) → basic flux CaO (from limestone) snares it into calcium silicate slag. If the gangue were basic (lime), the flux would be acidic sand. Picking the wrong flux thickens the slag, slows the furnace and loses metal into it.

### 4.2 Why alloys beat pure metals

- Pure gold is too soft for rings — copper (and silver) harden it. Pure iron is soft and rusts — chromium and nickel make stainless steel. Bronze (Cu–Sn ~88/12) is harder than either component and cast the ancient world's tools. Alloying lowers grain-boundary slip and can passivate the surface (Cr₂O₃ film on stainless).

### 4.3 Sodium amalgam in practice

- Sodium metal reacts violently with water; sodium **amalgam** reacts calmly — the mercury dilutes the reactivity — so it is used as a portable reducing agent and was the cathode product of older chlor-alkali cells, water later decomposing it to NaOH + H₂ + Hg (mercury returned).

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Flux families**

| Basis | Acidic flux | Basic flux |
|---|---|---|
| Substance | SiO₂ (silica) | CaCO₃ / CaO, MgCO₃ |
| Removes gangue | basic (metal oxides, lime) | acidic (silica, alumina) |
| Slag formed | silicates of Fe/Mn | CaSiO₃ |
| Used in | extraction of Cu, Fe (basic gangue) | iron blast furnace, steelmaking |

**Common alloys**

| Alloy | Composition | Key property | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Brass | Cu + Zn | machinable, gold-like | fittings, instruments |
| Bronze | Cu + Sn | hard, corrosion-proof | statues, bearings |
| Stainless steel | Fe + Cr (≥10.5%) + Ni, C | passive Cr₂O₃ film | cutlery, chemical plant |
| Solder | Pb + Sn | low melting | joining wires |
| Na amalgam | Na + Hg | moderated reactivity | reducing agent |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Flux is not fuel:** the flux does not burn or reduce anything — it only chemically binds the gangue into a fusible slag. The coke both heats and reduces; the limestone only cleans.
**Slag is not dross:** dross is oxide scum floating on a melt; slag is the deliberate flux+gangue product with a controlled composition (CaSiO₃).
**Amalgam ≠ alloy with any liquid:** an amalgam is specifically with mercury; brass in mercury is not an amalgam.

## 7. Exam Application

**Verified PYQ NEB 2024 (2m): Write the composition of brass, bronze, and stainless steel, with one use of each.** — **Brass:** copper + zinc (roughly 60–90 % Cu, the rest Zn); use — musical instruments and fittings (machinable, gold-like lustre). **Bronze:** copper + tin (about 88 % Cu, 12 % Sn); use — statues, bearings and bells (hard, corrosion-resistant). **Stainless steel:** iron + at least ~10.5 % chromium (often with nickel and some carbon); use — cutlery and chemical-plant equipment, because the chromium forms a passive Cr₂O₃ film that stops rust.

**NEB-style (2m): What is a flux? notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Vocabulary of Extraction

Before any metal flows, the ore must be described: what mineral it is, what worthless rock travels with it (**gangue**), what is added to make the impurities flow (**flux**), what the flux turns them into (**slag**), and what metals are blended into alloys. These five words — ore, gangue, flux, slag, alloy — are the working vocabulary of every extraction plant, and NEB asks them as short questions almost every year.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Ore, mineral, gangue

- A **mineral** is any natural compound of a metal; a **mineral becomes an ore** when the metal can be extracted profitably.
- **Gangue (matrix)** is the worthless sandy/rocky material mixed with the ore — silica, clay, limestone. Concentration removes most of it; the flux deals with the rest.

### 2.2 Flux and slag

- A **flux** is a substance added to the charge to combine with the gangue and form a fusible **slag**.
- **Acidic flux** removes basic gangue: silica (SiO₂) for iron oxides/lime. **Basic flux** removes acidic gangue: limestone (CaCO₃) for silica in the iron blast furnace — CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, then CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃ (slag).
- A good slag: low melting, immiscible with the metal, lighter — it floats and is drawn off, protecting the metal from oxidation.

### 2.3 Alloys and amalgam

- An **alloy** is a homogeneous mixture of a metal with other metals (or non-metals) made to improve hardness, resistance to corrosion, or casting quality: brass (Cu + Zn), bronze (Cu + Sn), stainless steel (Fe + Cr + Ni + C).
- An **amalgam** is an alloy in which one component is **mercury**: sodium amalgam (a safe handling form of reactive sodium, used as a reducing agent), dental amalgam (Ag–Sn–Hg). Iron does not form an amalgam — which is why iron vessels can hold mercury.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Ore** | Mineral from which metal is extracted profitably | Haematite Fe₂O₃ |
| **Gangue (matrix)** | Worthless rocky impurity in the ore | Silica, clay |
| **Flux** | Substance added to fuse with gangue | CaCO₃ (basic), SiO₂ (acidic) |
| **Slag** | Fusible product of flux + gangue | CaSiO₃ |
| **Alloy** | Homogeneous mixture of metals (or metal + non-metal) | Brass Cu–Zn |
| **Amalgam** | Alloy containing mercury | Na–Hg, dental Ag–Sn–Hg |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 How flux chooses its gangue

- Chemistry of pairing: an acidic oxide neutralises a basic one. Iron ore carries silica (acidic) → basic flux CaO (from limestone) snares it into calcium silicate slag. If the gangue were basic (lime), the flux would be acidic sand. Picking the wrong flux thickens the slag, slows the furnace and loses metal into it.

### 4.2 Why alloys beat pure metals

- Pure gold is too soft for rings — copper (and silver) harden it. Pure iron is soft and rusts — chromium and nickel make stainless steel. Bronze (Cu–Sn ~88/12) is harder than either component and cast the ancient world's tools. Alloying lowers grain-boundary slip and can passivate the surface (Cr₂O₃ film on stainless).

### 4.3 Sodium amalgam in practice

- Sodium metal reacts violently with water; sodium **amalgam** reacts calmly — the mercury dilutes the reactivity — so it is used as a portable reducing agent and was the cathode product of older chlor-alkali cells, water later decomposing it to NaOH + H₂ + Hg (mercury returned).

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Flux families**

| Basis | Acidic flux | Basic flux |
|---|---|---|
| Substance | SiO₂ (silica) | CaCO₃ / CaO, MgCO₃ |
| Removes gangue | basic (metal oxides, lime) | acidic (silica, alumina) |
| Slag formed | silicates of Fe/Mn | CaSiO₃ |
| Used in | extraction of Cu, Fe (basic gangue) | iron blast furnace, steelmaking |

**Common alloys**

| Alloy | Composition | Key property | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Brass | Cu + Zn | machinable, gold-like | fittings, instruments |
| Bronze | Cu + Sn | hard, corrosion-proof | statues, bearings |
| Stainless steel | Fe + Cr (≥10.5%) + Ni, C | passive Cr₂O₃ film | cutlery, chemical plant |
| Solder | Pb + Sn | low melting | joining wires |
| Na amalgam | Na + Hg | moderated reactivity | reducing agent |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Flux is not fuel:** the flux does not burn or reduce anything — it only chemically binds the gangue into a fusible slag. The coke both heats and reduces; the limestone only cleans.
**Slag is not dross:** dross is oxide scum floating on a melt; slag is the deliberate flux+gangue product with a controlled composition (CaSiO₃).
**Amalgam ≠ alloy with any liquid:** an amalgam is specifically with mercury; brass in mercury is not an amalgam.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (2m): What is an amalgam? Why does iron not form one, and what practical use follows?** — An **amalgam** is an alloy in which one component is mercury; sodium amalgam and dental amalgam (Ag–Sn–Hg) are examples. Iron is the common metal that does **not** dissolve in or wet mercury — no iron amalgam forms. Practical consequence: mercury is shipped and stored in iron/steel flasks, and the old mercury-cell chlor-alkali plant used an iron trough holding the mercury cathode.

confusion: ❌ All cells look the same under a microscope. ✅ Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells have them.
❌ DNA and RNA are identical in structure. ✅ DNA is double-stranded with deoxyribose and thymine; RNA is single-stranded with ribose and uracil.
❌ Mitosis produces genetically different cells. ✅ Mitosis produces genetically identical diploid daughter cells.
❌ Meiosis produces identical cells. ✅ Meiosis produces 4 genetically diverse haploid gametes.
❌ Crossing over occurs in mitosis. ✅ Crossing over occurs in Prophase I of meiosis only.
❌ All enzymes are proteins. ✅ Most enzymes are proteins; some RNA molecules (ribozymes) also have catalytic activity.
❌ ATP is the only energy currency. ✅ GTP, UTP, and CTP also serve as energy carriers in specific pathways.
❌ Photosynthesis occurs in all plant cells. ✅ Photosynthesis occurs only in cells containing chloroplasts (mainly mesophyll).
❌ Respiration and photosynthesis are opposite processes with same equation. ✅ They are complementary but occur in different organelles and under different conditions.
❌ Oxygen is produced during respiration. ✅ Oxygen is consumed in aerobic respiration; produced during photosynthesis.
❌ Food chain shows all feeding relationships. ✅ Food chain is linear; food web shows interconnected feeding relationships.
❌ 90% of energy is transferred to next trophic level. ✅ Only ~10% energy transfers; ~90% lost as heat.
❌ Biomagnification decreases toxin concentration up the food chain. ✅ Biomagnification increases toxin concentration at higher trophic levels.
❌ Carbon cycle only involves plants and animals. ✅ Carbon cycle involves atmosphere, oceans, fossils, rocks, and decomposers.
❌ Nitrogen fixation only occurs in bacteria. ✅ Some lightning and industrial processes (Haber) also fix nitrogen.
❌ All fungi are harmful. ✅ Many fungi are beneficial (decomposers, mycorrhizae, food, antibiotics like penicillin).
❌ Viruses are living organisms. ✅ Viruses are acellular — they cannot reproduce without a host and lack metabolism.
❌ Bacteria are always harmful. ✅ Most bacteria are harmless or beneficial (gut flora, nitrogen fixation, decomposition).
❌ Gram-positive and Gram-negative differ only in color. ✅ Gram-positive has thick peptidoglycan layer; Gram-negative has thin layer + outer membrane.
❌ Natural selection creates perfect organisms. ✅ Natural selection favors traits suited to current environment; environments change.
❌ Evolution is goal-oriented. ✅ Evolution has no goal; it acts on random variation filtered by selection.
❌ Homologous and analogous structures mean the same thing. ✅ Homologous = common ancestry (divergent); Analogous = similar function, different origin (convergent).
❌ Fossils are preserved bones only. ✅ Fossils include impressions, trace fossils, amber-preserved organisms, and molecular fossils.
❌ Lamarckism is completely wrong. ✅ Lamarck's inheritance of acquired characteristics is largely rejected, but epigenetics shows some environmental effects can be inherited.
❌ Five-kingdom classification is outdated. ✅ Six-kingdom (adding Archaea) and phylogenetic systems are more current, but five-kingdom remains useful for education.
❌ Binomial nomenclature names change frequently. ✅ Names are stable once formally published; changes require formal revision by taxonomic authorities.
❌ All algae are aquatic. ✅ Some algae live in soil, on tree bark, or in symbiotic relationships (lichens).
❌ Bryophytes have vascular tissue. ✅ Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts, hornworts) lack true vascular tissue (xylem/phloem).
❌ Gymnosperms produce flowers. ✅ Gymnosperms have naked seeds in cones; angiosperms produce flowers and enclosed seeds.
❌ Double fertilization occurs in gymnosperms. ✅ Double fertilization (zygote + endosperm) is unique to angiosperms.
❌ Earthworms have an open circulatory system. ✅ Earthworms have a closed circulatory system with dorsal and ventral vessels.
❌ Frogs breathe only through lungs. ✅ Frogs use cutaneous respiration (skin), buccal cavity, and lungs.
❌ Conservation only means protecting animals. ✅ Conservation includes genetic, species, and ecosystem diversity; in-situ and ex-situ strategies.
❌ In-situ and ex-situ conservation are the same. ✅ In-situ = conservation in natural habitat (national parks); Ex-situ = conservation outside habitat (zoos, seed banks).

data.summary:
Biomolecules and cell biology: Living organisms built from four macromolecule classes; cell theory unifies all life; membrane structure enables compartmentalization.

Cell division: Mitosis maintains chromosome number for growth/repair; meiosis halves it for gamete formation; crossing over creates genetic diversity.

Ecology: Ecosystems integrate biotic and abiotic components; energy flows unidirectionally with 10% transfer efficiency; nutrients cycle through biogeochemical pathways.

Evolutionary biology: Darwin's natural selection explains adaptation; fossil, morphological, and molecular evidence support common ancestry; human evolution from hominid ancestors.

Floral diversity: Plant evolution from simple algae to complex angiosperms; five-kingdom classification; double fertilization unique to flowering plants.

Faunal diversity: Animal kingdom spans from unicellular protists to complex chordates; segmentation and body cavities key evolutionary innovations; earthworm and frog as model organisms.

Biota and environment: Aquatic, terrestrial, and aerial adaptations reflect evolutionary pressures; pollution from human activities threatens ecosystem stability.

Conservation biology: Biodiversity exists at genetic, species, and ecosystem levels; Nepal's protected areas and community forestry demonstrate effective conservation strategies.

Introduction to biology: Biology studies life from molecules to ecosystems; scientific method drives discovery; interdisciplinary connections with physics, chemistry, and earth science.

Introductory microbiology: Bacteria (prokaryotes) and viruses (acellular) are foundational to life sciences; Gram stain differentiates bacteria; biotechnology applications transform medicine and industry.

Vegetation: Nepal's altitude-dependent vegetation zones reflect climate gradients; in-situ (protected areas) and ex-situ (seed banks) conservation preserve plant diversity.

data.topicTitle: General principles of extraction of metals: concentration, calcination and roasting, smelting, carbon reduction, thermite and electrochemical reduction
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — From Rock to Metal

This topic is the engine room of the unit: how a concentrated ore becomes a metal. Four verbs carry it — **calcination** (heat the carbonate), **roasting** (heat the sulphide in air), **smelting with carbon reduction** (coke does the chemistry), and **electrochemical reduction** (electrons do what coke cannot). NEB 2024 asked three of these directly; the thermite reaction and Hall–Héroult complete the picture.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Concentration (dressing) of the ore

- **Gravity/washing** — lighter gangue washes away (oxide ores, gold).
- **Magnetic separation** — magnetite (Fe₃O₄) pulled from silica by a magnet belt.
- **Froth flotation** — for sulphides: powdered ore + water + pine oil + air; sulphide particles are wetted by oil and ride the froth, silicate gangue is wetted by water and sinks. (Verified PYQ NEB 2024.)

### 2.2 Calcination vs roasting

| Basis | Calcination | Roasting |
|---|---|---|
| Ore type | carbonates, hydrated oxides | sulphides |
| Air | absent/limited | in excess air |
| Chemistry | thermal decomposition | oxidation to oxide + SO₂ |
| Example | ZnCO₃ → ZnO + CO₂; Al₂O₃·2H₂O → Al₂O₃ | 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂ |
| Purpose | porous oxide, drive off H₂O/CO₂ | oxide form + volatile As/Sb removal |

### 2.3 Reduction of the oxide

- **Carbon reduction (smelting):** coke at 1000–1500 °C — ZnO + C → Zn + CO; Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ (CO made in situ: C + O₂ → CO₂, CO₂ + C → 2CO).
- **Thermite:** Al reduces less active oxides, 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe (ΔH ≈ −850 kJ) — molten iron for track welding; also the proof that Al is a stronger oxygen-lover than Fe.
- **Electrochemical reduction:** for Na, K, Mg, Ca, Al — molten salt electrolysis (Downs cell, Hall–Héroult). Aluminium cannot be won by carbon reduction (NEB 2022): needs ~2000 °C, forms Al₄C₃ — so Al₂O₃ is dissolved in molten cryolite Na₃AlF₆ (~950 °C) and electrolysed: cathode 2Al³⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Al, anode 3O²⁻ → 1½O₂ + 6e⁻ (carbon anodes burn away).

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Calcination** | Heating the ore without/with little air to decompose carbonates | CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ |
| **Roasting** | Heating the sulphide ore in excess air below the melting point | 2PbS + 3O₂ → 2PbO + 2SO₂ |
| **Smelting** | Melting the roasted ore with flux and reductant to yield metal + slag | blast furnace |
| **Thermite process** | Reduction of metal oxides by aluminium powder | Fe₂O₃ + 2Al |
| **Froth flotation** | Concentration of sulphide ores by oil-wetted air bubbles | ZnS, PbS, CuFeS₂ |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Froth flotation — surface chemistry doing the sorting

- Sulphide surfaces are hydrophobic once pine oil adsorbs; blown air attaches bubbles to the sulphide grains and floats them as a mineralised froth, while water-wetted silica sinks. Collectors (xanthates) and depressants fine-tune which sulphide floats — one plant can separate ZnS from PbS from FeS₂.

### 4.2 Why roast below the melting point

- Roasting must leave the charge porous and solid so the furnace gas (O₂) reaches every grain; melting would glaze the charge and trap unroasted cores. "Roasting in excess air below the melting point" is the definitional phrase NEB wants.

### 4.3 The thermite temperature

- The reaction Al + Fe₂O₃ releases ~850 kJ per mole of Fe₂O₃ with no external heat once started — the iron produced is white-hot molten (mp 1538 °C exceeded), which is why field railway welders pour it straight into the joint mould.

### 4.4 Hall–Héroult in numbers

- Electrolyte: Al₂O₃ ~2–5 % in molten cryolite + CaF₂, ~950–980 °C; steel cell with carbon lining = cathode; consumable carbon anodes; cell voltage ~4–5 V, current ~100–400 kA. Oxygen formed oxidises the anode (CO₂), so anodes are replaced continuously.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Reduction methods by metal**

| Metal | Oxide | Reductant | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fe, Zn, Pb, Cu | Fe₂O₃, ZnO, PbO | C / CO | oxide reducible at furnace T |
| Cr, Mn | Cr₂O₃, MnO₂ | Al (thermite) | C gives carbides; Al stronger |
| Na, Mg, Ca | NaCl, MgCl₂, CaCl₂ | electrolysis | ΔG too negative for C |
| Al | Al₂O₃ | electrolysis (cryolite) | 2000 °C + Al₄C₃ problem |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Calcination is not "heating in air":** the defining difference from roasting is the **absence of excess air** — calcination decomposes, roasting oxidises.

**Thermite does not extract aluminium:** it *consumes* aluminium to make iron; aluminium itself must be electrolysed first. The exam question "why is Al not extracted by carbon reduction" is answered with temperature + carbide, not with thermite.
**Smelting vs roasting:** roasting is a solid-gas oxidation below melting point; smelting melts the charge and separates metal from slag.

## 7. Exam Application

**Verified PYQ NEB 2024 (2m): Distinguish between calcination and roasting with one example of each.** — **Calcination** is heating the ore in the absence or limited supply of air below its melting point, used for carbonate and hydrated ores: zinc carbonate decomposes to the oxide, ZnCO₃ → ZnO + CO₂↑, and hydrated alumina loses water. **Roasting** is heating the sulphide ore in **excess air** below its melting point, oxidising the sulphide to the oxide and driving off sulphur dioxide: 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂↑. Both leave the oxide needed for reduction, but calcination is decomposition without air and roasting is oxidation with air.

**Verified PYQ NEB 2024 (2m): What is froth flotation? For which ores is it used?** — **Froth flotation** is a concentration process for finely powdered **sulphide** ores: the ore is agitated with water, pine oil and a collector; air is blown through, and sulphide particles, preferentially wetted by the oil, attach to the air bubbles and rise as a mineralised froth that is skimmed off, while the siliceous gangue, wetted by water, sinks to the bottom. It is used for zinc blende (ZnS), galena (PbS) and copper pyrites (CuFeS₂).

**Verified PYQ NEB 2024 (3m): Describe the Hall-Heroult process for the extraction of aluminium.** — Purified bauxite (Al₂O₃) is dissolved at ~2–5 % in **molten cryolite** (Na₃AlF₆) with some CaF₂, which lowers the working temperature to about 950–980 °C (pure Al₂O₃ would melt at 2050 °C). The electrolytic cell is a steel tank lined with carbon that serves as the **cathode**; thick carbon blocks dipped into the melt are the **anodes**. On passing a large direct current, aluminium is deposited at the cathode: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al (tapped from the bottom), and at the anode oxygen is liberated which burns the carbon away: 2O²⁻ − 4e⁻ → O₂, C + O₂ → CO₂ — hence the anodes are continuously replaced. Overall: 2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂.

**Verified PYQ NEB 2022 (2m): Explain why aluminium cannot be extracted by carbon reduction of its oxide but is obtained by the electrolysis of a solution of alumina in molten cryolite.** — Aluminium has a very large affinity for oxygen: Al₂O₃ has an extremely negative free energy of formation, so carbon reduction would require a temperature of about 2000 °C, and at such temperatures the aluminium produced reacts with the coke forming aluminium carbide (Al₄C₃) — the yield is poor and the process impractical. Instead, Al₂O₃ is dissolved in molten cryolite (Na₃AlF₆), which lowers the melting point to ~950 °C and increases conductivity, and the melt is electrolysed: Al³⁺ is discharged at the carbon-lined cathode as molten metal, so the electrical work does what carbon cannot.

Calcination: no/limited air, carbonates/hydrates -> oxide (ZnCO3 -> ZnO + CO2; Al2O3.2H2O -> Al2O3). Roasting: excess air, sulphides -> oxide + SO2 (2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2), below melting point. data.summary: The extraction chain runs: **concentrate** (gravity, magnets, or froth flotation for sulphides — oil-wetted grains ride air bubbles while wetted gangue sinks), then **calcination** (carbonates → oxide, no air: ZnCO₃ → ZnO + CO₂) or **roasting** (sulphides → oxide, excess air: 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂), then **reduction**: carbon reduction in the smelter where CO made in situ (CO₂ + C → 2CO) strips the oxygen (Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂); thermite (2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe) for Cr/Mn and rail welding; and **electrolysis of molten salts** where carbon fails — Hall–Héroult dissolves Al₂O₃ in molten cryolite at ~950 °C, deposits aluminium at the carbon-lined cathode and burns carbon anodes at the anode surface, because direct carbon reduction of Al₂O₃ would need 2000 °C and yield carbide.

Stoichiometry: The mole concept bridges atomic and macroscopic scales; limiting reagent determines theoretical yield; concentration expressed as molarity or molality.

Oxidation-reduction: Redox involves electron transfer; oxidation numbers track electron flow; electrochemical cells convert chemical to electrical energy; Faraday's laws quantify electrolysis.

States of matter: Gas laws relate P, V, T, n; kinetic theory explains gas behavior; real gases deviate due to intermolecular forces and molecular volume.

Solutions: Molarity and molality express concentration; colligative properties depend on particle number; Raoult's law describes vapor pressure of ideal solutions.

Chemical bonding: Ionic bonds form from electron transfer; covalent bonds from sharing; VSEPR predicts molecular geometry; hybridization explains bonding orbitals.

Organic chemistry basics: Carbon's tetravalency and catenation enable millions of compounds; functional groups determine reactivity; IUPAC nomenclature provides systematic naming.

Hydrocarbons: Alkanes (CnH2n+2) are saturated; alkenes (CnH2n) have C=C; alkynes (CnH2n-2) have C≡C; aromatic compounds based on benzene ring.

Periodic table: Elements arranged by atomic number; periodic trends in radius, ionization energy, electronegativity; s, p, d, f blocks based on orbital type.

data.title: Refining of metals (poling and electro-refinement)
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Last 0.1 %

Extraction gets the metal; **refining** makes it usable — copper must reach 99.99 % for wiring, otherwise its resistance and machinability collapse. This topic covers the purification toolkit: liquation, distillation, oxidation (poling), and the workhorse — **electrolytic refinement** (verified PYQ NEB 2024 on copper).

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Why crude metal is impure

- Blast-furnace/reduction metal carries dissolved C, S, P, Si (from coke and flux), other reduced metals (Pb in Ag, Fe in Cu), and mechanically trapped slag. Each impurity dictates its own removal method.

### 2.2 Refining methods

- **Distillation** — for volatile metals: Zn (bp 907 °C), Hg, Cd are distilled off from less volatile impurities.
- **Liquation** — for low-melting metals: impure Sn or Pb is run down an inclined hearth at a temperature just above the metal's melting point; the pure metal flows out, high-melting impurities (Fe, Cu, C) stay on the hearth.
- **Poling** — for oxidised molten metal (especially crude copper with Cu₂O): green wood poles are stirred into the melt; the wood releases hydrocarbons and steam, the hydrocarbons reduce Cu₂O back to Cu, and the stirring collects dross. ("Poling" — from the pole.)
- **Electrolytic refinement** — impure metal = anode, thin pure metal = cathode, salt solution = electrolyte; the metal dissolves from the anode and deposits pure on the cathode, while nobler impurities fall as **anode mud** and baser ones stay in solution.

### 2.3 Electrorefining of copper (the exam classic)

- Anode: impure Cu (99 %, with Ag, Au, Pt, Ni, Fe, Zn). Cathode: thin pure Cu sheet. Electrolyte: acidified CuSO₄.
- Anode: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ (also Zn, Fe, Ni dissolve as ions).
- Cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (only copper deposits; Zn²⁺/Fe²⁺/Ni²⁺ stay in solution because they are harder to reduce).
- **Anode mud:** Ag, Au, Pt are nobler — they do not ionise and fall to the bottom; the mud pays for the refining (gold and silver recovery).

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Refining** | Purification of extracted metal | Cu to 99.99 % |
| **Liquation** | Purifying a low-melting metal by letting it flow from impurities | Sn, Pb |
| **Poling** | Stirring molten metal with green wood poles to reduce oxide impurities | crude Cu |
| **Electrorefinement** | Electrolytic purification: impure anode → pure cathode | Cu in CuSO₄ |
| **Anode mud** | Noble impurities settling below the anode | Ag, Au, Pt from Cu |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 The selectivity logic of electrorefining

- Electrolysis separates by electrode potential: baser metals (Zn, Fe) ionise at the anode but their ions stay dissolved (their reduction potentials are below Cu²⁺/Cu); copper shuttles anode→cathode; nobler metals (Ag, Au, Pt) refuse to ionise and drop as mud. One tank, three-way separation.

### 4.2 Why poling uses *green* wood

- Dry wood would only stir. Green wood releases water vapour (stirs, prevents air oxidation) and hydrocarbon gases (CH₄, etc.) that chemically reduce Cu₂O: 2Cu₂O + C(H₄) → 4Cu + CO₂ + 2H₂O-ish reduction chemistry. The pole chars at the surface — the process is visible and self-limiting.

### 4.3 Choosing the method

- Volatile metal → distillation (Zn, Hg). Low melting → liquation (Sn, Pb). Oxide contamination → poling (Cu, Sn). Everything else, and any metal needed at high purity → electrorefining (Cu, Ag, Au, Al three-layer, Ni).

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Refining methods**

| Basis | Distillation | Liquation | Poling | Electrorefining |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Uses | volatility | low melting point | reducing hydrocarbons | electrode potentials |
| Metal | Zn, Hg, Cd | Sn, Pb | crude Cu, Sn | Cu, Ag, Au, Ni |
| Purity | good | moderate | moderate | 99.99 % |
| By-product | — | — | — | anode mud (Ag, Au) |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Poling refines, it does not extract:** poling happens on molten metal already won; it removes dissolved oxide (Cu₂O), not ore.
**Anode mud is not slag:** it is the *noblest* impurities — they are valuable (Ag, Au, Pt), not waste; their sale often pays the refining bill.
**Baser impurities do not deposit:** Zn²⁺/Fe²⁺/Ni²⁺ from the anode remain in the electrolyte because Cu²⁺ reduces at a higher potential; the electrolyte is periodically bled and refreshed.

## 7. Exam Application

**Verified PYQ NEB 2024 (3m): Describe the electrolytic refining of copper.** — The electrolytic tank contains **acidified copper sulphate solution** as electrolyte. The **anode is a thick block of impure copper** (about 99 %, containing Ag, Au, Pt, Ni, Fe, Zn) and the **cathode is a thin sheet of pure copper**. On passing direct current, copper (and the baser metals) dissolve at the anode: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻; at the cathode only copper is deposited: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, because the baser ions (Zn²⁺, Fe²⁺, Ni²⁺) need a lower reduction potential and remain in solution. The **noble impurities — silver, gold and platinum — do not ionise** and settle below the anode as valuable **anode mud**. The cathode copper reaches ~99.99 % purity, and the gold and silver recovered from the mud repay the cost of refining.

**NEB-style (2m): What is poling? Why is green wood used?** — **Poling** is the refining of molten crude metal (chiefly copper containing cuprous oxide) by stirring it with poles of **green wood**. The hydrocarbon gases released by the charring wood reduce the dissolved oxide back to metal (Cu₂O → Cu), while the steam released stirs the bath and shields it from air oxidation; the stirring also collects the dross on the pole. Green (not dry) wood is used because dry wood would give neither the reducing gases nor the steam.

**NEB-style (2m): Name the refining method suited to (i) zinc, (ii) tin, (iii) crude copper with Cu₂O, with one reason each.** — **(i) Zinc — distillation:** zinc boils at 907 °C, far below its main impurities, so it distils over and condenses pure. **(ii) Tin — liquation:** tin melts at 232 °C; on an inclined hearth just above this temperature the tin flows away from the high-melting impurities (Fe, C) which remain. **(iii) Crude copper — poling:** the green-wood gases reduce the dissolved Cu₂O back to copper.

When direct current flows, copper dissolves from the anode: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻, together with the baser impurities (Zn, Fe, Ni) which also pass into solution as ions. At the cathode **only copper is deposited**, Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, because the baser metal ions require a lower (more negative) reduction potential than Cu²⁺ and therefore stay dissolved in the electrolyte. The **noble impurities — silver, gold and platinum — do not dissolve at all**; they fall to the bottom beneath the anode as **anode mud**, from which they are later recovered (and they pay for the refining). The cathode copper is 99.99 % pure — the "electrolytic copper" used for electrical wiring.

**NEB-style (2m): What is poling? Why must the poles be of green wood?** — **Poling** is a refining step for molten crude metal — chiefly copper — in which the melt is stirred with poles of green wood while it is covered with an inert material. The purpose is to remove dissolved cuprous oxide: the hydrocarbon gases given off by the charring wood **reduce Cu₂O back to metallic copper**, and the water vapour released stirs the bath and blankets its surface against further oxidation, while the stirring collects dross. **Green wood** is essential because dry wood supplies neither the reducing hydrocarbons nor the steam — it would only stir.

**NEB-style (2m): By which method are (i) zinc, (ii) tin and (iii) crude copper containing Cu₂O refined, and why?** — **(i) Zinc — distillation:** zinc is volatile (bp 907 °C), far below the boiling points of its impurities (iron, lead), so retort distillation leaves them behind and the vapour condenses as pure zinc. **(ii) Tin — liquation:** tin melts at only 232 °C; the impure block is heated on the sloping hearth of a liquation furnace just above this temperature, the pure tin flows down and away, and the high-melting impurities (iron, carbon) remain on the hearth. **(iii) Crude copper — poling:** the molten metal is stirred with green wood poles whose hydrocarbon gases reduce the dissolved Cu₂O to copper while the steam stirs and shields the melt.

## 1. Topic Introduction — The Last 0.1 %

Extraction gets the metal; **refining** makes it usable — copper must reach 99.99 % for wiring, otherwise its resistance and machinability collapse. This topic covers the purification toolkit: liquation, distillation, oxidation (poling), and the workhorse — **electrolytic refinement** (verified PYQ NEB 2024 on copper).

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Why crude metal is impure

- Blast-furnace/reduction metal carries dissolved C, S, P, Si (from coke and flux), other reduced metals (Pb in Ag, Fe in Cu), and mechanically trapped slag. Each impurity dictates its own removal method.

### 2.2 Refining methods

- **Distillation** — for volatile metals: Zn (bp 907 °C), Hg, Cd are distilled off from less volatile impurities.
- **Liquation** — for low-melting metals: impure Sn or Pb is run down an inclined hearth at a temperature just above the metal's melting point; the pure metal flows out, high-melting impurities (Fe, Cu, C) stay on the hearth.
- **Poling** — for oxidised molten metal (especially crude copper with Cu₂O): green wood poles are stirred into the melt; the wood releases hydrocarbons and steam, the hydrocarbons reduce Cu₂O back to Cu, and the stirring collects dross. ("Poling" — from the pole.)
- **Electrolytic refinement** — impure metal = anode, thin pure metal = cathode, salt solution = electrolyte; the metal dissolves from the anode and deposits pure on the cathode, while nobler impurities fall as **anode mud** and baser ones stay in solution.

### 2.3 Electrorefining of copper (the exam classic)

- Anode: impure Cu (99 %, with Ag, Au, Pt, Ni, Fe, Zn). Cathode: thin pure Cu sheet. Electrolyte: acidified CuSO₄.
- Anode: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ (also Zn, Fe, Ni dissolve as ions).
- Cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (only copper deposits; Zn²⁺/Fe²⁺/Ni²⁺ stay in solution because they are harder to reduce).
- **Anode mud:** Ag, Au, Pt are nobler — they do not ionise and fall to the bottom; the mud pays for the refining (gold and silver recovery).

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Refining** | Purification of extracted metal | Cu to 99.99 % |
| **Liquation** | Purifying a low-melting metal by letting it flow from impurities | Sn, Pb |
| **Poling** | Stirring molten metal with green wood poles to reduce oxide impurities | crude Cu |
| **Electrorefinement** | Electrolytic purification: impure anode → pure cathode | Cu in CuSO₄ |
| **Anode mud** | Noble impurities settling below the anode | Ag, Au, Pt from Cu |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 The selectivity logic of electrorefining

- Electrolysis separates by electrode potential: baser metals (Zn, Fe) ionise at the anode but their ions stay dissolved (their reduction potentials are below Cu²⁺/Cu); copper shuttles anode→cathode; nobler metals (Ag, Au, Pt) refuse to ionise and drop as mud. One tank, three-way separation.

### 4.2 Why poling uses *green* wood

- Dry wood would only stir. Green wood releases water vapour (stirs, prevents air oxidation) and hydrocarbon gases (CH₄, etc.) that chemically reduce Cu₂O: 2Cu₂O + C(H₄) → 4Cu + CO₂ + 2H₂O-ish reduction chemistry. The pole chars at the surface — the process is visible and self-limiting.

### 4.3 Choosing the method

- Volatile metal → distillation (Zn, Hg). Low melting → liquation (Sn, Pb). Oxide contamination → poling (Cu, Sn). Everything else, and any metal needed at high purity → electrorefining (Cu, Ag, Au, Al three-layer, Ni).

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Refining methods**

| Basis | Distillation | Liquation | Poling | Electrorefining |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Uses | volatility | low melting point | reducing hydrocarbons | electrode potentials |
| Metal | Zn, Hg, Cd | Sn, Pb | crude Cu, Sn | Cu, Ag, Au, Ni |
| Purity | good | moderate | moderate | 99.99 % |
| By-product | — | — | — | anode mud (Ag, Au) |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Poling refines, it does not extract:** poling happens on molten metal already won; it removes dissolved oxide (Cu₂O), not ore.
**Anode mud is not slag:** it is the *noblest* impurities — they are valuable (Ag, Au, Pt), not waste; their sale often pays the refining bill.
**Baser impurities do not deposit:** Zn²⁺/Fe²⁺/Ni²⁺ from the anode remain in the electrolyte because Cu²⁺ reduces at a higher potential; the electrolyte is periodically bled and refreshed.

## 7. Exam Application

**Verified PYQ NEB 2024 (3m): Describe the electrolytic refining of copper.** — The electrolytic tank contains **acidified copper sulphate solution** as electrolyte. The **anode is a thick block of impure copper** (about 99 %, containing Ag, Au, Pt, Ni, Fe, Zn) and the **cathode is a thin sheet of pure copper**. On passing direct current, copper (and the baser metals) dissolve at the anode: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻; at the cathode only copper is deposited: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, because the baser ions (Zn²⁺, Fe²⁺, Ni²⁺) need a lower reduction potential and remain in solution. The **noble impurities — silver, gold and platinum — do not ionise** and settle below the anode as valuable **anode mud**. The cathode copper reaches ~99.99 % purity, and the gold and silver recovered from the mud repay the cost of refining.

**NEB-style (2m): What is poling? Why is green wood used?** — **Poling** is the refining of molten crude metal (chiefly copper containing cuprous oxide) by stirring it with poles of **green wood**. The hydrocarbon gases released by the charring wood reduce the dissolved oxide back to metal (Cu₂O → Cu), while the steam released stirs the bath and shields it from air oxidation; the stirring also collects the dross on the pole. Green (not dry) wood is used because dry wood would give neither the reducing gases nor the steam.

**NEB-style (2m): Name the refining method suited to (i) zinc, (ii) tin, (iii) crude copper with Cu₂O, with one reason each.** — **(i) Zinc — distillation:** zinc boils at 907 °C, far below its main impurities, so it distils over and condenses pure. **(ii) Tin — liquation:** tin melts at 232 °C; on an inclined hearth just above this temperature the tin flows away from the high-melting impurities (Fe, C) which remain. **(iii) Crude copper — poling:** the green-wood gases reduce the dissolved Cu₂O back to copper.

data.topicTitle: Alkali metals: general characteristics of alkali metals
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Softest Family

The alkali metals — Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr — are Group IA: one valence electron, desperate to lose it. Everything characteristic follows from that single fact: extreme reactivity, low densities, low melting points, flame colours, ionic chemistry only. This topic collects the group trends NEB asks every year.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Electronic structure and the losing electron

- General configuration [NG]ns¹. The single s-electron is shielded by the noble-gas core and easily lost → +1 oxidation state, no other common state (unlike neighbouring groups).
- Ionisation energy **decreases down the group** (Li 520 → Cs 376 kJ/mol): the valence shell grows farther from the nucleus with more shielding — so reactivity **increases** Li → Cs.

### 2.2 Physical trends

| Property | Trend down the group | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Atomic/ionic radius | increases | new shell each period |
| Density | increases (but Na, K < 1 g/mL) | mass grows faster than volume |
| Melting point | decreases | metallic bond weakens as radius grows |
| Ionisation energy | decreases | shielding + distance |
| Electropositivity/reactivity | increases | easier electron loss |
| Flame colour | Li crimson, Na golden-yellow, K lilac, Rb red-violet, Cs blue | emission lines |

### 2.3 Chemical behaviour

- **Soft, low-melting metals** — cut with a knife; mp Li 181 °C → Cs 28 °C (Cs melts in the hand, nearly).
- **Vigorous reaction with water:** 2M + 2H₂O → 2MOH + H₂↑; Li fizzes, Na skates and burns, K ignites instantly, Rb/Cs explode — the hydroxides are the strongest bases known (KOH, NaOH).
- **Reaction with oxygen:** Li → normal oxide Li₂O; Na → peroxide Na₂O₂; K → superoxide KO₂. (The famous exception to "form normal oxides".)
- **With hydrogen:** 2M + H₂ → 2MH — ionic hydrides with H⁻.
- All compounds are **ionic, colourless (unless anion coloured), water-soluble**; ions are hydrated heavily — Li⁺ most hydrated (smallest), which makes Li salts often the least soluble despite the smallest lattice.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Alkali metal** | Group IA element, [NG]ns¹ | Na: [Ne]3s¹ |
| **Flame test** | Emission colour of excited metal vapour in a flame | Na golden-yellow |
| **Superoxide** | Compound with O₂⁻ ion | KO₂ |
| **Hydride (ionic)** | Salt-like compound with H⁻ | NaH |
| **Electropositivity** | Tendency to lose electrons and form cations | Cs the most electropositive stable metal |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why sodium glows yellow in every flame test

- The 3s electron, excited in the flame, falls back through the intense sodium D-lines (589.0/589.6 nm) — a transition with enormous oscillator strength. A pinprick of Na salt colours a whole Bunsen flame, which is why the sodium test must be looked *through cobalt glass* when testing potassium (the yellow masks the lilac).

### 4.2 Why Li is the odd one out

- Li⁺ is tiny and heavily hydrated; its salts (Li₂CO₃, LiF, Li₃PO₄) are **less soluble** than the Na/K analogues (opposite of the group trend). Li burns to the **normal oxide** Li₂O (not peroxide), forms the nitride Li₃N directly in air (no other alkali metal does), and its compounds show covalent character (Fajans: high charge density polarises anions).

### 4.3 Why K is more reactive than Na despite similar size

- Each step down adds a shell: the electron is farther out and better shielded, so the ionisation energy drops by ~70–80 kJ/mol per step. The water reaction's activation energy is paid by easier electron transfer — hence the escalation fizz → fire → explosion.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Group IA at a glance**

| Metal | mp (°C) | Density (g/mL) | Flame | Water reaction | Oxide formed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Li | 181 | 0.53 | crimson | steady fizz | Li₂O (+ Li₃N in air) |
| Na | 98 | 0.97 | golden-yellow | melts, burns | Na₂O₂ |
| K | 63 | 0.86 | lilac | ignites | KO₂ |
| Rb | 39 | 1.53 | red-violet | explodes | mixture |
| Cs | 28 | 1.93 | blue | explodes violently | mixture |

## 6. Common Confusions

**"Low density" does not mean light across the group:** Li, Na, K float on water (ρ < 1); Rb and Cs sink (1.53, 1.93). The trend is "increases", with the famous dip at Na/K.
**Flame colour vs radioactivity:** the colours are emission lines of the neutral atoms, not heat colour; the test identifies the element, not the temperature.
**Li's exceptions are not errors:** Li₂O (normal oxide), Li₃N (direct nitride), low solubility of Li salts — all follow from the tiny, heavily hydrated Li⁺ and its polarising power.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): Describe the general characteristics of alkali metals: electronic configuration, trends in ionisation energy and reactivity, and their reaction with water.** — Alkali metals (Group IA: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr) have the general outer configuration **ns¹** — one valence electron over a noble-gas core. The **ionisation energy decreases down the group** (Li 520 → Na 496 → K 419 → Cs 376 kJ/mol) because each element adds a shell, so the valence electron is farther from the nucleus and better shielded. Consequently **reactivity increases down the group**: with water, Li reacts steadily with effervescence, sodium melts and races about burning with a yellow flame, potassium ignites instantly with a lilac flame, and rubidium and caesium explode — all according to 2M + 2H₂O → 2MOH + H₂, forming the strongest known bases, the hydroxides MOH.

**NEB-style (2m): Give the flame colours of Li, Na, K and Cs, and explain the origin of the colour.** — **Lithium: crimson; sodium: golden-yellow; potassium: lilac; caesium: blue.** In the flame the s-electron of the vapourised metal atoms is excited to higher levels and, falling back, emits photons of characteristic wavelength — for sodium the intense 589 nm D-lines, which is why even traces of sodium colour the flame golden-yellow and why the potassium (lilac) test is viewed through cobalt glass to filter the sodium yellow.

**NEB-style (2m): What oxide does each of Li, Na and K form on burning in air, and what ion is present in the potassium product?** — **Lithium burns to the normal oxide Li₂O** (4Li + O₂ → 2Li₂O), **sodium to the peroxide Na₂O₂** (2Na + O₂ → Na₂O₂), and **potassium to the superoxide KO₂** (K + O₂ → KO₂). The potassium product contains the **superoxide ion O₂⁻**, with one unpaired electron — paramagnetic — and it is the basis of oxygen masks (KO₂ releases O₂ on absorbing CO₂/H₂O).

The **ionisation energy falls steadily down the group** (Li 520 → Na 496 → K 419 → Rb 403 → Cs 376 kJ/mol): each element adds a filled shell, so the valence electron is farther from the nucleus and more strongly shielded. As a direct consequence **reactivity rises down the group**. With water the reaction 2M + 2H₂O → 2MOH + H₂ escalates: lithium fizzes steadily, sodium melts into a ball and burns with a golden-yellow flame, potassium ignites instantly with a lilac flame, and rubidium and caesium react explosively; the products MOH are the strongest bases in common chemistry.

**NEB-style (2m): Give the flame colours of lithium, sodium, potassium and caesium, and explain why the colours appear.** — **Lithium — crimson; sodium — golden-yellow; potassium — lilac; caesium — blue.** When a salt of the metal is placed in a flame, a small amount of metal vapourises; the valence electron absorbs flame energy and is excited to higher orbitals, and as it falls back it emits photons of fixed wavelength characteristic of the element. Sodium's 3p→3s transition gives the intense 589 nm D-lines — so intense that a trace of sodium contamination colours a flame yellow and masks potassium's lilac, which must therefore be viewed through cobalt glass.

**NEB-style (2m): What products are formed when lithium, sodium and potassium burn in excess air? Name the anion present in the potassium compound.** — **Lithium** forms the normal oxide, 4Li + O₂ → 2Li₂O. **Sodium** forms the peroxide, 2Na + O₂ → Na₂O₂. **Potassium** forms the superoxide, K + O₂ → KO₂. The anion in KO₂ is the **superoxide ion O₂⁻** — a paramagnetic species with one unpaired electron, which is why KO₂ is used in breathing apparatus: it releases oxygen while absorbing CO₂ and moisture from exhaled air.
keyPoints: Group IA, [NG]ns1, one valence electron, +1 only. Down the group: radius up, IE down (Li 520 -> Cs 376 kJ/mol), reactivity up, mp down (Li 181 -> Cs 28 C), density up with dip (Li 0.53, Na 0.97, K 0.86, Rb 1.53, Cs 1.93 - Na/K float). Flame colours: Li crimson, Na golden-yellow (589 nm D lines), K lilac, Rb red-violet, Cs blue. Water: 2M + 2H2O -> 2MOH + H2, strongest bases, escalation fizz->burn->explode. Oxides: Li2O normal, Na2O2 peroxide, KO2 superoxide (O2- ion). Hydrides MH ionic (H-). All ionic, colourless, soluble; Li+ most hydrated -> Li salts less soluble (Li2CO3, LiF, Li3PO4); Li odd: normal oxide, direct Li3N, covalent character.
data.summary: The alkali metals — Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr — carry a single ns¹ electron that defines everything: it is easily lost (+1 only), so the metals are soft, low-melting (181 °C → 28 °C down the group), light (Li 0.53 g/mL; Na and K float), and violently reactive. Ionisation energy falls from 520 to 376 kJ/mol as shells are added, so reactivity climbs — water gives 2M + 2H₂O → 2MOH + H₂ from a fizz (Li) to an explosion (Cs), and the MOH products are the strongest bases known. Burning in air steps through the oxide ladder Li₂O → Na₂O₂ → KO₂ (the superoxide O₂⁻ anion), flames step crimson → golden-yellow (Na 589 nm) → lilac → blue, and lithium plays its exceptions — normal oxide, direct Li₃N, poorly soluble salts — because the tiny, heavily hydrated Li⁺ polarises anions and hogs the water.

### 2.3 Chemical behaviour

- **Soft, low-melting metals** — cut with a knife; mp Li 181 °C → Cs 28 °C (Cs melts in the hand, nearly).
- **Vigorous reaction with water:** 2M + 2H₂O → 2MOH + H₂↑; Li fizzes, Na skates and burns, K ignites instantly, Rb/Cs explode — the hydroxides are the strongest bases known (KOH, NaOH).
- **Reaction with oxygen:** Li → normal oxide Li₂O; Na → peroxide Na₂O₂; K → superoxide KO₂. (The famous exception to "form normal oxides".)
- **With hydrogen:** 2M + H₂ → 2MH — ionic hydrides with H⁻.
- All compounds are **ionic, colourless (unless anion coloured), water-soluble**; ions are hydrated heavily — Li⁺ most hydrated (smallest), which makes Li salts often the least soluble despite the smallest lattice.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Alkali metal** | Group IA element, [NG]ns¹ | Na: [Ne]3s¹ |
| **Flame test** | Emission colour of excited metal vapour in a flame | Na golden-yellow |
| **Superoxide** | Compound with O₂⁻ ion | KO₂ |
| **Hydride (ionic)** | Salt-like compound with H⁻ | NaH |
| **Electropositivity** | Tendency to lose electrons and form cations | Cs the most electropositive stable metal |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why sodium glows yellow in every flame test

- The 3s electron, excited in the flame, falls back through the intense sodium D-lines (589.0/589.6 nm) — a transition with enormous oscillator strength. A pinprick of Na salt colours a whole Bunsen flame, which is why the sodium test must be looked *through cobalt glass* when testing potassium (the yellow masks the lilac).

### 4.2 Why Li is the odd one out

- Li⁺ is tiny and heavily hydrated; its salts (Li₂CO₃, LiF, Li₃PO₄) are **less soluble** than the Na/K analogues (opposite of the group trend). Li burns to the **normal oxide** Li₂O (not peroxide), forms the nitride Li₃N directly in air (no other alkali metal does), and its compounds show covalent character (Fajans: high charge density polarises anions).

### 4.3 Why K is more reactive than Na despite similar size

- Each step down adds a shell: the electron is farther out and better shielded, so the ionisation energy drops by ~70–80 kJ/mol per step. The water reaction's activation energy is paid by easier electron transfer — hence the escalation fizz → fire → explosion.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Group IA at a glance**

| Metal | mp (°C) | Density (g/mL) | Flame | Water reaction | Oxide formed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Li | 181 | 0.53 | crimson | steady fizz | Li₂O (+ Li₃N in air) |
| Na | 98 | 0.97 | golden-yellow | melts, burns | Na₂O₂ |
| K | 63 | 0.86 | lilac | ignites | KO₂ |
| Rb | 39 | 1.53 | red-violet | explodes | mixture |
| Cs | 28 | 1.93 | blue | explodes violently | mixture |

## 6. Common Confusions

**"Low density" does not mean light across the group:** Li, Na, K float on water (ρ < 1); Rb and Cs sink (1.53, 1.93). The trend is "increases", with the famous dip at Na/K.
**Flame colour vs radioactivity:** the colours are emission lines of the neutral atoms, not heat colour; the test identifies the element, not the temperature.
**Li's exceptions are not errors:** Li₂O (normal oxide), Li₃N (direct nitride), low solubility of Li salts — all follow from the tiny, heavily hydrated Li⁺ and its polarising power.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): Describe the general characteristics of alkali metals: electronic configuration, trends in ionisation energy and reactivity, and their reaction with water.** — Alkali metals (Group IA: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr) have the general outer configuration **ns¹** — one valence electron over a noble-gas core. The **ionisation energy decreases down the group** (Li 520 → Na 496 → K 419 → Cs 376 kJ/mol) because each element adds a shell, so the valence electron is farther from the nucleus and better shielded. Consequently **reactivity increases down the group**: with water, Li reacts steadily with effervescence, sodium melts and races about burning with a yellow flame, potassium ignites instantly with a lilac flame, and rubidium and caesium explode — all according to 2M + 2H₂O → 2MOH + H₂, forming the strongest known bases, the hydroxides MOH.

**NEB-style (2m): Give the flame colours of Li, Na, K and Cs, and explain the origin of the colour.** — **Lithium: crimson; sodium: golden-yellow; potassium: lilac; caesium: blue.** In the flame the s-electron of the vapourised metal atoms is excited to higher levels and, falling back, emits photons of characteristic wavelength — for sodium the intense 589 nm D-lines, which is why even traces of sodium colour the flame golden-yellow and why the potassium (lilac) test is viewed through cobalt glass to filter the sodium yellow.

**NEB-style (2m): What oxide does each of Li, Na and K form on burning in air, and what ion is present in the potassium product?** — **Lithium burns to the normal oxide Li₂O** (4Li + O₂ → 2Li₂O), **sodium to the peroxide Na₂O₂** (2Na + O₂ → Na₂O₂), and **potassium to the superoxide KO₂** (K + O₂ → KO₂). The potassium product contains the **superoxide ion O₂⁻**, with one unpaired electron — paramagnetic — and it is the basis of oxygen masks (KO₂ releases O₂ on absorbing CO₂/H₂O).

confusion: ❌ All atoms are identical in an element. ✅ Isotopes have same protons but different neutrons.
❌ Atoms are indivisible. ✅ Atoms consist of protons, neutrons, and electrons.
❌ Electrons orbit in fixed paths like planets. ✅ Electrons exist in probability clouds (orbitals).
❌ Heisenberg uncertainty means we cannot measure position and momentum precisely simultaneously — not that we lack good instruments.
❌ de Broglie wavelength applies only to light. ✅ All matter has wave nature; detectable mainly for small masses like electrons.
❌ Quantum number l can be any integer. ✅ l ranges from 0 to n−1.
❌ Magnetic quantum number ml determines energy. ✅ ml determines orbital orientation, not energy (in absence of magnetic field).
❌ Spin quantum number ms can be ±½ or any value. ✅ ms is always +½ or −½.
❌ Aufbau principle means filling from bottom to top of the diagram. ✅ Fill lowest-energy orbitals first: 1s→2s→2p→3s→3p→4s→3d→4p→...
❌ Pauli exclusion allows two electrons per orbital with any spin. ✅ Two electrons in same orbital must have opposite spins.
❌ Hund's rule means pair electrons before spreading. ✅ Electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly first with parallel spins.
❌ The mole is just a number like dozen. ✅ 1 mole = 6.022×10²³ particles (Avogadro constant) — a bridge between atomic and macroscopic scales.
❌ Molar mass and molecular mass are the same thing. ✅ Molecular mass is in amu; molar mass is in g/mol — numerically equal but different units.
❌ Limiting reagent is the reactant with smallest mass. ✅ Limiting reagent is the one that produces the least product (determined by moles, not mass).
❌ % yield can exceed 100%. ✅ % yield >100% indicates impure product or incomplete drying.
❌ Molarity and molality are the same. ✅ Molarity = mol/L solution (changes with T); Molality = mol/kg solvent (temperature-independent).
❌ A strong acid completely ionizes in water. ✅ Strong acids (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄) are ~100% ionized; weak acids partially ionize.
❌ pH can be negative. ✅ pH < 0 is possible for concentrations >1M (e.g., 2M HCl has pH ≈ −0.3).
❌ Kc changes when concentration changes. ✅ Kc is constant at constant temperature; only temperature changes K.
❌ Adding catalyst shifts equilibrium position. ✅ Catalyst speeds both forward and backward reactions equally; no shift in equilibrium.
❌ High pressure always favors products. ✅ High pressure favors side with fewer gas moles (Le Chatelier).
❌ Exothermic reactions are spontaneous. ✅ Spontaneity depends on ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, not just ΔH.
❌ Endothermic reactions cannot be spontaneous. ✅ Endothermic reactions can be spontaneous if TΔS > ΔH (e.g., ice melting above 0°C).
❌ ΔH and ΔU are always the same. ✅ ΔH = ΔU + PΔV; they differ when gas moles change.
❌ Heat (q) and work (w) are state functions. ✅ q and w are path functions; only ΔU, ΔH, ΔS, ΔG are state functions.
❌ Oxidation and reduction happen separately. ✅ Oxidation and reduction always occur together (redox).
❌ Oxidizing agent gets oxidized. ✅ Oxidizing agent accepts electrons and gets reduced.
❌ Reducing agent gets reduced. ✅ Reducing agent donates electrons and gets oxidized.
❌ Faraday's laws apply only to metals. ✅ Faraday's laws apply to any substance deposited/dissolved at electrodes.
❌ Real gases obey PV=nRT at all conditions. ✅ Real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature.
❌ van der Waals constants a and b are same for all gases. ✅ a (attraction) and b (volume) are gas-specific.
❌ Surface tension increases with temperature. ✅ Surface tension decreases as temperature increases.
❌ Viscosity decreases with temperature for liquids. ✅ Viscosity of liquids decreases with T; gases increase with T.
❌ Colligative properties depend on nature of solute. ✅ Colligative properties depend only on number of particles, not identity.
❌ Raoult's law applies to all solutions. ✅ Raoult's law is exact for ideal solutions; approximate for dilute real solutions.
❌ Osmotic pressure is a colligative property. ✅ Yes — π = CRT depends on solute particle concentration.

data.summary:
Atomic structure: From Rutherford's nuclear model through Bohr's quantized orbits to the modern quantum mechanical model, understanding electron configuration using four quantum numbers is fundamental.

Stoichiometry: The mole concept bridges atomic and macroscopic scales; limiting reagent determines theoretical yield; concentration expressed as molarity or molality.

Chemical equilibrium: Dynamic equilibrium has equal forward and backward rates; Kc/Kp are temperature-dependent; Le Chatelier's principle predicts response to stress.

Thermodynamics: First law (energy conservation); enthalpy changes in reactions; Gibbs free energy determines spontaneity; entropy of universe always increases.

Oxidation-reduction: Redox involves electron transfer; oxidation numbers track electron flow; electrochemical cells convert chemical to electrical energy; Faraday's laws quantify electrolysis.

States of matter: Gas laws relate P, V, T, n; kinetic theory explains gas behavior; real gases deviate due to intermolecular forces and molecular volume.

Solutions: Molarity and molality express concentration; colligative properties depend on particle number; Raoult's law describes vapor pressure of ideal solutions.

Chemical bonding: Ionic bonds form from electron transfer; covalent bonds from sharing; VSEPR predicts molecular geometry; hybridization explains bonding orbitals.

Organic chemistry basics: Carbon's tetravalency and catenation enable millions of compounds; functional groups determine reactivity; IUPAC nomenclature provides systematic naming.

Hydrocarbons: Alkanes (CnH2n+2) are saturated; alkenes (CnH2n) have C=C; alkynes (CnH2n-2) have C≡C; aromatic compounds based on benzene ring.

Periodic table: Elements arranged by atomic number; periodic trends in radius, ionization energy, electronegativity; s, p, d, f blocks based on orbital type.

Applied chemistry: Petrochemical industry, polymer science, green chemistry principles; importance of sustainable chemical manufacturing for environmental protection.

confusion: ❌ All cells look the same under a microscope. ✅ Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells have them.
❌ DNA and RNA are identical in structure. ✅ DNA is double-stranded with deoxyribose and thymine; RNA is single-stranded with ribose and uracil.
❌ Mitosis produces genetically different cells. ✅ Mitosis produces genetically identical diploid daughter cells.
❌ Meiosis produces identical cells. ✅ Meiosis produces 4 genetically diverse haploid gametes.
❌ Crossing over occurs in mitosis. ✅ Crossing over occurs in Prophase I of meiosis only.
❌ All enzymes are proteins. ✅ Most enzymes are proteins; some RNA molecules (ribozymes) also have catalytic activity.
❌ ATP is the only energy currency. ✅ GTP, UTP, and CTP also serve as energy carriers in specific pathways.
❌ Photosynthesis occurs in all plant cells. ✅ Photosynthesis occurs only in cells containing chloroplasts (mainly mesophyll).
❌ Respiration and photosynthesis are opposite processes with same equation. ✅ They are complementary but occur in different organelles and under different conditions.
❌ Oxygen is produced during respiration. ✅ Oxygen is consumed in aerobic respiration; produced during photosynthesis.
❌ Food chain shows all feeding relationships. ✅ Food chain is linear; food web shows interconnected feeding relationships.
❌ 90% of energy is transferred to next trophic level. ✅ Only ~10% energy transfers; ~90% lost as heat.
❌ Biomagnification decreases toxin concentration up the food chain. ✅ Biomagnification increases toxin concentration at higher trophic levels.
❌ Carbon cycle only involves plants and animals. ✅ Carbon cycle involves atmosphere, oceans, fossils, rocks, and decomposers.
❌ Nitrogen fixation only occurs in bacteria. ✅ Some lightning and industrial processes (Haber) also fix nitrogen.
❌ All fungi are harmful. ✅ Many fungi are beneficial (decomposers, mycorrhizae, food, antibiotics like penicillin).
❌ Viruses are living organisms. ✅ Viruses are acellular — they cannot reproduce without a host and lack metabolism.
❌ Bacteria are always harmful. ✅ Most bacteria are harmless or beneficial (gut flora, nitrogen fixation, decomposition).
❌ Gram-positive and Gram-negative differ only in color. ✅ Gram-positive has thick peptidoglycan layer; Gram-negative has thin layer + outer membrane.
❌ Natural selection creates perfect organisms. ✅ Natural selection favors traits suited to current environment; environments change.
❌ Evolution is goal-oriented. ✅ Evolution has no goal; it acts on random variation filtered by selection.
❌ Homologous and analogous structures mean the same thing. ✅ Homologous = common ancestry (divergent); Analogous = similar function, different origin (convergent).
❌ Fossils are preserved bones only. ✅ Fossils include impressions, trace fossils, amber-preserved organisms, and molecular fossils.
❌ Lamarckism is completely wrong. ✅ Lamarck's inheritance of acquired characteristics is largely rejected, but epigenetics shows some environmental effects can be inherited.
❌ Five-kingdom classification is outdated. ✅ Six-kingdom (adding Archaea) and phylogenetic systems are more current, but five-kingdom remains useful for education.
❌ Binomial nomenclature names change frequently. ✅ Names are stable once formally published; changes require formal revision by taxonomic authorities.
❌ All algae are aquatic. ✅ Some algae live in soil, on tree bark, or in symbiotic relationships (lichens).
❌ Bryophytes have vascular tissue. ✅ Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts, hornworts) lack true vascular tissue (xylem/phloem).
❌ Gymnosperms produce flowers. ✅ Gymnosperms have naked seeds in cones; angiosperms produce flowers and enclosed seeds.
❌ Double fertilization occurs in gymnosperms. ✅ Double fertilization (zygote + endosperm) is unique to angiosperms.
❌ Earthworms have an open circulatory system. ✅ Earthworms have a closed circulatory system with dorsal and ventral vessels.
❌ Frogs breathe only through lungs. ✅ Frogs use cutaneous respiration (skin), buccal cavity, and lungs.
❌ Conservation only means protecting animals. ✅ Conservation includes genetic, species, and ecosystem diversity; in-situ and ex-situ strategies.
❌ In-situ and ex-situ conservation are the same. ✅ In-situ = conservation in natural habitat (national parks); Ex-situ = conservation outside habitat (zoos, seed banks).

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Sodium, the Industry Metal

Sodium is the cheapest strong reducer and the cheapest strong base source, and it cannot be won from its compounds by chemistry — only by electricity. The **Downs cell** (verified PYQs NEB 2023 and NEB 2024) is the classic answer, and its product feeds the reactions with oxygen, water, acids, non-metals and ammonia that fill this topic.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 The Downs cell

- Electrolyte: **molten NaCl + CaCl₂ (≈ 42 : 58)** — the CaCl₂ lowers the melting point from 801 °C to about **600 °C** and raises conductivity.
- **Cathode (steel):** Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na; molten sodium floats (ρ 0.97 < melt) and is collected in a bell and siphoned.
- **Anode (graphite):** 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻; a **steel gauze diaphragm** between the electrodes keeps the products apart — without it Na + Cl₂ would recombine, and Na would form the unsafe NaCl·Ca mixture.
- Ca²⁺ is not reduced at the cathode despite being present: at 600 °C only Na⁺ discharges practically (overpotential/electrode kinetics); any calcium formed dissolves back into the melt.
- Overall: 2NaCl(l) → 2Na + Cl₂.

### 2.2 Reactions of sodium

| Partner | Equation | Note |
|---|---|---|
| O₂ (limited) | 4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O | normal oxide |
| O₂ (excess) | 2Na + O₂ → Na₂O₂ | peroxide — bleaching |
| H₂O | 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂↑ | violent, melts, skates |
| Acids | 2Na + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂↑ | even more violent |
| Cl₂ | 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl | burns yellow |
| H₂ | 2Na + H₂ → 2NaH | ionic hydride |
| NH₃ (liq) | Na + NH₃ → NaNH₂ + ½H₂ (with Fe catalyst) | sodamide |
| NH₃ (gas, hot) | no reaction at room T; with hot Na: NaNH₂ forms slowly | |

### 2.3 Uses

- Na₂O₂ bleaching, NaOH manufacture (with Hg or via amalgam), sodium vapour lamps (589 nm), coolant in fast nuclear reactors (liquid metal, huge heat capacity, low mp), reducing agent (Ti from TiCl₄, zirconium), NaPb alloy for anti-knock lead additive precursor, laboratory desiccant (in ether).

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Downs cell** | Electrolytic cell for molten NaCl–CaCl₂ producing Na and Cl₂ | 2NaCl → 2Na + Cl₂ |
| **Diaphragm** | Steel gauze separating anode and cathode products | keeps Na and Cl₂ apart |
| **Peroxide** | Compound with O₂²⁻ | Na₂O₂ |
| **Sodamide** | Sodium amide NaNH₂ | from Na + NH₃ |
| **Sodium amalgam** | Na dissolved in Hg | moderated reactivity |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why the Downs cell adds CaCl₂

- Pure NaCl melts at 801 °C — sodium boils at 883 °C, so a pure-salt cell runs within 80 degrees of the metal's boiling point: the sodium vapourises, contaminates the chlorine, and the cell corrodes. The 42:58 NaCl:CaCl₂ eutectic melts at ~600 °C, comfortably below both, and the mixture conducts better. Ca²⁺ stays in the melt because its discharge needs a higher voltage than Na⁺ at the working conditions.

### 4.2 Why sodium reacts so violently with water

- Thermodynamics is enormous (2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂, strongly exothermic) and kinetics help: the reaction heat melts sodium (mp 98 °C), the melt spreads, the H₂ film ignites in air, and the NaOH formed locally accelerates attack. The classic school demonstration — a pea of sodium skating on water — is the same equation.

### 4.3 Sodium and ammonia — the subtle one

- In **liquid ammonia** sodium dissolves to a deep blue conducting solution of solvated electrons (Na⁺ + e⁻(NH₃)⁻); with an iron catalyst (or on warming) the electron reduces NH₃ to amide: Na + NH₃ → NaNH₂ + ½H₂. In **gaseous** ammonia at room temperature sodium does not react — the reaction needs heat or the solution route.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Downs cell vs fused MgCl₂ electrolysis (NEB 2023 comparison)**

| Basis | Downs cell (Na) | Mg cell |
|---|---|---|
| Electrolyte | NaCl + CaCl₂ (600 °C) | fused MgCl₂ (+ NaCl, CaCl₂) ~700 °C |
| Cathode product | Na, floats on melt | Mg, floats |
| Anode | graphite, Cl₂ | graphite, Cl₂ |
| Separator | steel gauze diaphragm | steel diaphragm |
| Cell type | central cathode arrangement | iron pot cathode |

## 6. Common Confusions

**The diaphragm is essential, not decorative:** without it the cell would short-circuit chemically — sodium would reduce chlorine back to NaCl, and heat + mixing could cause a violent local reaction.
**CaCl₂ is not reduced:** its job is melting point and conductivity; Ca²⁺ remains in the melt — quoting "Ca is also deposited" is a classic wrong answer.
**Na₂O₂ is the excess-oxygen product:** limited air gives Na₂O; excess gives Na₂O₂ — the exam expects both equations.

## 7. Exam Application

**Verified PYQ NEB 2024 / NEB 2023 (3m): Explain Down's process for the extraction of sodium.** — Sodium is extracted by the electrolysis of **fused sodium chloride** in the **Downs cell**. Pure NaCl melts at 801 °C — too hot (sodium boils at 883 °C) — so it is mixed with **calcium chloride (≈42 : 58)**, which lowers the melting point to about **600 °C** and improves conductivity. The cell has a **graphite anode** and a **steel cathode** separated by a **steel-gauze diaphragm**. On electrolysis: cathode — Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na; the molten sodium floats up inside a bell-shaped collector and is drawn off. Anode — 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻; chlorine leaves through a hood. The **diaphragm prevents the sodium from meeting the chlorine** (they would recombine to NaCl) and keeps the calcium, which is not discharged at this temperature, in the melt. Overall: 2NaCl(l) → 2Na + Cl₂.

**Verified PYQ NEB 2023 (3m): Compare the extraction of sodium by the Downs cell with the extraction of magnesium by the electrolysis of fused magnesium chloride. Give the electrode reactions.** — Both are molten-salt electrolyses with graphite anodes liberating chlorine and steel cathodes, and both need CaCl₂/NaCl mixtures to lower the melting point. **Downs cell:** electrolyte NaCl + CaCl₂ at ~600 °C; cathode reaction Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na (sodium floats and is collected in a bell); anode 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻; a steel gauze diaphragm separates the products. **Magnesium cell:** electrolyte fused MgCl₂ (dried, mixed with NaCl and CaCl₂) at ~700 °C; cathode Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mg (molten magnesium floats to the surface and is skimmed); anode 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻; chlorine is prevented from recombining with magnesium by a diaphragm and by withdrawing the metal. The differences: sodium's cell runs cooler (600 vs ~700 °C), uses a central ring cathode arrangement, and calcium stays unreduced, while magnesium is won from its own chloride with iron-pot cathodes.

**NEB-style (2m): What happens when sodium is heated (i) in limited air, (ii) in excess air/oxygen?** — **(i) Limited air:** sodium forms the normal oxide, 4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O (white solid). **(ii) Excess air/oxygen:** sodium burns with a golden-yellow flame to the **peroxide**, 2Na + O₂ → Na₂O₂, which contains the peroxide ion O₂²⁻ and is used for bleaching and for oxygen generation (Na₂O₂ + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃ + ½O₂).
