practiceQuestions: **Verified PYQ NEB 2024 (3m): Explain Down's process for the extraction of sodium.** — Sodium is obtained by the **electrolysis of fused sodium chloride mixed with calcium chloride** in the Downs cell. Pure NaCl melts at 801 °C — dangerously close to sodium's boiling point (883 °C) — so CaCl₂ is added in roughly **42 : 58** proportion, lowering the melting point to about **600 °C** and improving the melt's conductivity. The cell carries a central **graphite anode** and **steel cathodes**, separated by a **steel-gauze diaphragm**. Reactions: cathode, Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na — the molten sodium (density 0.97, lighter than the melt) rises inside a bell-shaped collector and is siphoned off; anode, 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ — chlorine is led away through a hood. The **diaphragm keeps sodium and chlorine apart**, preventing their recombination into NaCl, and the Ca²⁺ ions, not being discharged at 600 °C, remain in the melt. Overall: 2NaCl(l) → 2Na + Cl₂.

**Verified PYQ NEB 2023 (3m): Compare the extraction of sodium by the Downs cell with the extraction of magnesium by the electrolysis of fused magnesium chloride, giving the electrode reactions.** — **Similarities:** both electrolyse a **molten chloride** (water would hydrogen-evolve first), both use **graphite anodes** where 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻, both collect a light molten metal that floats, and both add other chlorides (CaCl₂/NaCl) to lower the melting point. **Downs cell:** electrolyte NaCl + CaCl₂ (42:58) at ~600 °C; cathode Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na; sodium is collected in a bell under the melt; a steel-gauze **diaphragm** separates Na from Cl₂; Ca²⁺ is not discharged. **Magnesium cell:** electrolyte fused MgCl₂ with NaCl/CaCl₂ at ~700 °C; cathode Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mg; molten magnesium rises to the surface of the iron-pot cathode and is skimmed off; a diaphragm and prompt withdrawal keep Mg from the chlorine. **Differences:** temperature (600 vs ~700 °C), cathode arrangement (ring vs iron pot), and the inert behaviour of Ca²⁺ versus the straightforward Mg²⁺ discharge.

**NEB-style (2m): How does sodium react with (i) water, (ii) liquid ammonia, (iii) hydrogen? Write the equations.** — **(i) Water — violently:** sodium melts from the reaction heat and skates on the surface, igniting the hydrogen: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂↑; the product is the strong base sodium hydroxide. **(ii) Liquid ammonia:** sodium dissolves giving an intense **blue solution of solvated electrons** (Na⁺ + e⁻(solvated)); with an iron catalyst (or on standing/warming) the solution decomposes ammonia to **sodamide**: Na + NH₃ → NaNH₂ + ½H₂↑. With gaseous ammonia at room temperature sodium does not react. **(iii) Hydrogen:** on heating in hydrogen sodium forms the ionic hydride, 2Na + H₂ → 2NaH, containing the hydride ion H⁻, which reacts with water to give hydrogen again.

importantConcepts: The Downs cell is a temperature problem solved with a composition trick: the eutectic drops the melt 200 degrees below sodium's boiling point, buying the 200-degree safety margin the pure salt never had.
importantStatements: "In the Downs cell, calcium chloride is added to lower the melting point of sodium chloride and a steel gauze diaphragm separates the sodium from the chlorine."

confusion: ❌ All atoms are identical in an element. ✅ Isotopes have same protons but different neutrons.
❌ Atoms are indivisible. ✅ Atoms consist of protons, neutrons, and electrons.
❌ Electrons orbit in fixed paths like planets. ✅ Electrons exist in probability clouds (orbitals).
❌ Heisenberg uncertainty means we cannot measure position and momentum precisely simultaneously — not that we lack good instruments.
❌ de Broglie wavelength applies only to light. ✅ All matter has wave nature; detectable mainly for small masses like electrons.
❌ Quantum number l can be any integer. ✅ l ranges from 0 to n−1.
❌ Magnetic quantum number ml determines energy. ✅ ml determines orbital orientation, not energy (in absence of magnetic field).
❌ Spin quantum number ms can be ±½ or any value. ✅ ms is always +½ or −½.
❌ Aufbau principle means filling from bottom to top of the diagram. ✅ Fill lowest-energy orbitals first: 1s→2s→2p→3s→3p→4s→3d→4p→...
❌ Pauli exclusion allows two electrons per orbital with any spin. ✅ Two electrons in same orbital must have opposite spins.
❌ Hund's rule means pair electrons before spreading. ✅ Electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly first with parallel spins.
❌ The mole is just a number like dozen. ✅ 1 mole = 6.022×10²³ particles (Avogadro constant) — a bridge between atomic and macroscopic scales.
❌ Molar mass and molecular mass are the same thing. ✅ Molecular mass is in amu; molar mass is in g/mol — numerically equal but different units.
❌ Limiting reagent is the reactant with smallest mass. ✅ Limiting reagent is the one that produces the least product (determined by moles, not mass).
❌ % yield can exceed 100%. ✅ % yield >100% indicates impure product or incomplete drying.
❌ Molarity and molality are the same. ✅ Molarity = mol/L solution (changes with T); Molality = mol/kg solvent (temperature-independent).
❌ A strong acid completely ionizes in water. ✅ Strong acids (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄) are ~100% ionized; weak acids partially ionize.
❌ pH can be negative. ✅ pH < 0 is possible for concentrations >1M (e.g., 2M HCl has pH ≈ −0.3).
❌ Kc changes when concentration changes. ✅ Kc is constant at constant temperature; only temperature changes K.
❌ Adding catalyst shifts equilibrium position. ✅ Catalyst speeds both forward and backward reactions equally; no shift in equilibrium.
❌ High pressure always favors products. ✅ High pressure favors side with fewer gas moles (Le Chatelier).
❌ Exothermic reactions are spontaneous. ✅ Spontaneity depends on ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, not just ΔH.
❌ Endothermic reactions cannot be spontaneous. ✅ Endothermic reactions can be spontaneous if TΔS > ΔH (e.g., ice melting above 0°C).
❌ ΔH and ΔU are always the same. ✅ ΔH = ΔU + PΔV; they differ when gas moles change.
❌ Heat (q) and work (w) are state functions. ✅ q and w are path functions; only ΔU, ΔH, ΔS, ΔG are state functions.
❌ Oxidation and reduction happen separately. ✅ Oxidation and reduction always occur together (redox).
❌ Oxidizing agent gets oxidized. ✅ Oxidizing agent accepts electrons and gets reduced.
❌ Reducing agent gets reduced. ✅ Reducing agent donates electrons and gets oxidized.
❌ Faraday's laws apply only to metals. ✅ Faraday's laws apply to any substance deposited/dissolved at electrodes.
❌ Real gases obey PV=nRT at all conditions. ✅ Real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature.
❌ van der Waals constants a and b are same for all gases. ✅ a (attraction) and b (volume) are gas-specific.
❌ Surface tension increases with temperature. ✅ Surface tension decreases as temperature increases.
❌ Viscosity decreases with temperature for liquids. ✅ Viscosity of liquids decreases with T; gases increase with T.
❌ Colligative properties depend on nature of solute. ✅ Colligative properties depend only on number of particles, not identity.
❌ Raoult's law applies to all solutions. ✅ Raoult's law is exact for ideal solutions; approximate for dilute real solutions.
❌ Osmotic pressure is a colligative property. ✅ Yes — π = CRT depends on solute particle concentration.

Atomic structure: From Rutherford's nuclear model through Bohr's quantized orbits to the modern quantum mechanical model, understanding electron configuration using four quantum numbers is fundamental.

Stoichiometry: The mole concept bridges atomic and macroscopic scales; limiting reagent determines theoretical yield; concentration expressed as molarity or molality.

Chemical equilibrium: Dynamic equilibrium has equal forward and backward rates; Kc/Kp are temperature-dependent; Le Chatelier's principle predicts response to stress.

Thermodynamics: First law (energy conservation); enthalpy changes in reactions; Gibbs free energy determines spontaneity; entropy of universe always increases.

Oxidation-reduction: Redox involves electron transfer; oxidation numbers track electron flow; electrochemical cells convert chemical to electrical energy; Faraday's laws quantify electrolysis.

States of matter: Gas laws relate P, V, T, n; kinetic theory explains gas behavior; real gases deviate due to intermolecular forces and molecular volume.

Solutions: Molarity and molality express concentration; colligative properties depend on particle number; Raoult's law describes vapor pressure of ideal solutions.

Chemical bonding: Ionic bonds form from electron transfer; covalent bonds from sharing; VSEPR predicts molecular geometry; hybridization explains bonding orbitals.

Organic chemistry basics: Carbon's tetravalency and catenation enable millions of compounds; functional groups determine reactivity; IUPAC nomenclature provides systematic naming.

Hydrocarbons: Alkanes (CnH2n+2) are saturated; alkenes (CnH2n) have C=C; alkynes (CnH2n-2) have C≡C; aromatic compounds based on benzene ring.

Periodic table: Elements arranged by atomic number; periodic trends in radius, ionization energy, electronegativity; s, p, d, f blocks based on orbital type.

Applied chemistry: Petrochemical industry, polymer science, green chemistry principles; importance of sustainable chemical manufacturing for environmental protection.

data.topicTitle: Sodium hydroxide: properties (precipitation reaction and action with carbon monoxide) and uses
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Base of the Chemical World

Sodium hydroxide (caustic soda) is produced on a scale matched only by sulphuric acid. Its two faces — a **strong base** that neutralises and precipitates, and a **strong alkali** that absorbs acidic gases like CO₂ and SO₂ — plus its manufacture route make this topic a guaranteed short-question source.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Properties

- White deliquescent solid, mp 318 °C; extremely soluble in water with strong heat evolution; fully dissociated: NaOH → Na⁺ + OH⁻ — a **strong monobasic base**.
- Soapy touch, corrosive to skin (saponifies fats) — hence "caustic".
- Absorbs CO₂ and moisture from air (must be stoppered): 2NaOH + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O.

### 2.2 Precipitation reactions (the exam list)

| Cation | Observation | Equation |
|---|---|---|
| Cu²⁺ | pale blue ppt, insoluble in excess | CuSO₄ + 2NaOH → Cu(OH)₂↓ + Na₂SO₄ |
| Fe²⁺ | dirty green ppt | FeSO₄ + 2NaOH → Fe(OH)₂↓ + Na₂SO₄ |
| Fe³⁺ | reddish-brown ppt | FeCl₃ + 3NaOH → Fe(OH)₃↓ + 3NaCl |
| Zn²⁺, Al³⁺, Pb²⁺ | white ppt, **soluble in excess** (amphoteric) | ZnSO₄ + 2NaOH → Zn(OH)₂↓ + Na₂SO₄; Zn(OH)₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂ZnO₂ + 2H₂O |
| NH₄⁺ | no ppt — pungent NH₃ on warming | NH₄Cl + NaOH → NaCl + NH₃↑ + H₂O |

### 2.3 Action with CO₂ and SO₂ (acidic oxides)

- Limited CO₂: 2NaOH + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O; excess CO₂: Na₂CO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → 2NaHCO₃.
- SO₂: 2NaOH + SO₂ → Na₂SO₃ + H₂O (then NaHSO₃ with excess) — the chemistry of scrubbing acidic gases, and the reason NaOH pellets must be kept sealed.

### 2.4 Action with carbon monoxide (the topic's namesake)

- Under pressure (~6–8 atm, ~200 °C) sodium hydroxide absorbs CO to give **sodium formate (sodium methanoate)**: CO + NaOH → HCOONa — the historical basis of formic acid manufacture. No reaction at ordinary pressure/temperature; the pressure forces the weakly acidic CO into addition.

### 2.5 Manufacture and uses

- **Chlor-alkali electrolysis** of brine: cathode 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻; anode 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂; products NaOH + Cl₂ + H₂ (diaphragm or membrane cell keeps Cl₂ away from the OH⁻).
- Uses: soap and detergents (saponification), paper pulping, rayon, petroleum refining, bauxite purification (Bayer), laboratory reagent, drain cleaner.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Caustic soda** | Sodium hydroxide NaOH | strong monobasic base |
| **Amphoteric hydroxide** | Hydroxide reacting with both acids and bases | Zn(OH)₂, Al(OH)₃ |
| **Saponification** | Hydrolysis of ester (fat) by alkali to soap + glycerol | fat + NaOH |
| **Chlor-alkali process** | Electrolysis of brine giving NaOH, Cl₂, H₂ | membrane cell |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why Zn(OH)₂ dissolves in excess NaOH but Cu(OH)₂ does not

- Zinc and aluminium hydroxides are **amphoteric**: their oxides/hydroxides react with strong alkali to form zincate/aluminate, Zn(OH)₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂ZnO₂ + 2H₂O. Copper(II) hydroxide is purely basic — no acid character — so excess NaOH leaves the pale blue precipitate untouched. This single contrast is the standard qualitative-analysis question.

### 4.2 Why NaOH grabs CO₂ from the air

- OH⁻ is a stronger base than CO₃²⁻'s conjugate position requires: the acid anhydride CO₂ + OH⁻ → HCO₃⁻ → CO₃²⁻ + H₂O is fast and irreversible on drying. A pellet left on the bench becomes a crust of soda ash overnight — the reason "standard" NaOH solutions are standardised against a primary standard, not weighed as pellets.

### 4.3 Saponification — the oldest use

- Fat (glyceryl ester) + 3NaOH → 3RCOONa (soap) + glycerol. The OH⁻ attacks the ester bonds; the sodium salts of long-chain acids are the soap molecules. This is why NaOH is "caustic" to skin — skin fat is being saponified.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**NaOH vs Na₂CO₃ as bases**

| Basis | NaOH | Na₂CO₃ |
|---|---|---|
| Strength | strong base (OH⁻) | mild base (hydrolysis of CO₃²⁻) |
| With NH₄⁺ salt | liberates NH₃ on warming | no NH₃ |
| With phenolphthalein | pink immediately | pink (slow) |
| Air uptake | CO₂ + H₂O → Na₂CO₃ crust | already carbonate |

## 6. Common Confusions

**"Soluble in excess" means the hydroxide is amphoteric:** Zn(OH)₂, Al(OH)₃, Pb(OH)₂ dissolve in excess NaOH; Cu(OH)₂, Fe(OH)₂/₃ do not — memorise which side of the line each cation sits on.
**NaOH does not precipitate NH₃:** ammonium salts give no precipitate with NaOH — only ammonia gas on warming; writing "NH₄OH ppt" is wrong.
**Caustic soda vs washing soda:** NaOH is caustic soda; Na₂CO₃·10H₂O is washing soda — different compounds, different strengths.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): Describe the precipitation reactions of sodium hydroxide with solutions of copper sulphate, ferric chloride and zinc sulphate.** — **Copper sulphate:** NaOH gives a **pale blue precipitate** of copper(II) hydroxide, CuSO₄ + 2NaOH → Cu(OH)₂↓ + Na₂SO₄; the precipitate is **insoluble in excess** NaOH (Cu(OH)₂ is not amphoteric). **Ferric chloride:** a **reddish-brown precipitate** of ferric hydroxide, FeCl₃ + 3NaOH → Fe(OH)₃↓ + 3NaCl, also insoluble in excess. **Zinc sulphate:** a **white precipitate** of zinc hydroxide, ZnSO₄ + 2NaOH → Zn(OH)₂↓ + Na₂SO₄, which **dissolves in excess NaOH** because zinc hydroxide is amphoteric: Zn(OH)₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂ZnO₂ (sodium zincate) + 2H₂O.

**NEB-style (2m): What happens when excess CO₂ is passed into sodium hydroxide solution? Write both stages.** — **Stage 1 (limited CO₂):** the hydroxide takes up the acid anhydride to form the carbonate, 2NaOH + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O. **Stage 2 (excess CO₂):** the carbonate is converted to the soluble bicarbonate, Na₂CO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → 2NaHCO₃. The same chemistry explains why NaOH pellets left open to air gain mass and turn into a crust of sodium carbonate.

**NEB-style (2m): How is sodium hydroxide manufactured? Give the electrode reactions of the brine electrolysis.** — Sodium hydroxide is made by the **chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine** (concentrated NaCl solution) in a diaphragm or membrane cell that keeps the chlorine away from the hydroxide. **Cathode:** 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂↑ + 2OH⁻ (Na⁺ stays spectator; NaOH accumulates in the cathode compartment). **Anode:** 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂↑ + 2e⁻. Overall: 2NaCl + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ + Cl₂ — three products at once.

practiceQuestions: **NEB-style (3m): Describe the action of sodium hydroxide on solutions of copper sulphate, ferric chloride and zinc sulphate, noting the behaviour in excess NaOH.** — **Copper sulphate:** addition of NaOH gives a **pale blue precipitate** of copper(II) hydroxide, CuSO₄ + 2NaOH → Cu(OH)₂↓ + Na₂SO₄; the precipitate does **not** dissolve in excess NaOH, since Cu(OH)₂ is purely basic. **Ferric chloride:** a **reddish-brown precipitate** of ferric hydroxide forms, FeCl₃ + 3NaOH → Fe(OH)₃↓ + 3NaCl; again insoluble in excess. **Zinc sulphate:** a **white gelatinous precipitate** of zinc hydroxide, ZnSO₄ + 2NaOH → Zn(OH)₂↓ + Na₂SO₄, which **dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide** because zinc hydroxide is amphoteric, forming sodium zincate: Zn(OH)₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂ZnO₂ + 2H₂O.

**NEB-style (2m): What is observed when carbon dioxide is passed through sodium hydroxide solution (i) in limited amount, (ii) in excess?** — **(i) Limited CO₂:** the hydroxide is converted to the carbonate — 2NaOH + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O — no visible change beyond possible slight cloudiness. **(ii) Excess CO₂:** the carbonate takes up more CO₂ and water to form the soluble **bicarbonate** — Na₂CO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → 2NaHCO₃. The reverse of stage (i) explains why an open bottle of NaOH solution slowly loses its strength: the OH⁻ has been converted to CO₃²⁻ by atmospheric CO₂.

**NEB-style (2m): What happens when carbon monoxide is heated with sodium hydroxide under pressure?** — Sodium hydroxide absorbs the weakly acidic CO under pressure (~6–8 atm, ~200 °C) to form **sodium formate (sodium methanoate)**: CO + NaOH → HCOONa. At ordinary pressure and temperature there is no reaction — the pressure is what drives the addition; acidification of the formate regenerates formic acid, which was the historical route to it.

**NEB-style (2m): How is sodium hydroxide manufactured by the electrolysis of brine? Give the electrode reactions and the overall equation.** — Concentrated brine is electrolysed in a cell with a **diaphragm/membrane** that prevents the chlorine liberated at the anode from mixing with the hydroxide formed at the cathode. **Cathode (steel):** 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂↑ + 2OH⁻ — hydrogen gas evolves and OH⁻ accumulates with the spectator Na⁺, giving NaOH solution. **Anode (graphite/Ti):** 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂↑ + 2e⁻. **Overall:** 2NaCl + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂↑ + Cl₂↑ — one process, three saleable products.
keyPoints: NaOH: white deliquescent solid, mp 318 C, very soluble (exothermic), strong monobasic base, soapy touch, absorbs CO2+H2O from air -> Na2CO3 crust. Precipitations: Cu2+ pale blue Cu(OH)2 (insoluble in excess), Fe2+ dirty green, Fe3+ reddish-brown Fe(OH)3, Zn2+/Al3+/Pb2+ white ppt soluble in excess (amphoteric -> Na2ZnO2/NaAlO2), NH4+ no ppt but NH3 on warming. Acidic oxides: 2NaOH + CO2 -> Na2CO3 + H2O, excess CO2 -> NaHCO3; 2NaOH + SO2 -> Na2SO3 + H2O. Manufacture: chlor-alkali brine electrolysis, cathode 2H2O + 2e -> H2 + 2OH-, anode 2Cl- -> Cl2; overall 2NaCl + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2 + Cl2. Uses: soap/saponification, paper, rayon, Bayer alumina, drain cleaner.
data.summary: **Sodium hydroxide** — white, deliquescent, mp 318 °C, strongly exothermic in water — is the strongest cheap base in the lab: NaOH → Na⁺ + OH⁻ completely. It **precipitates** metal hydroxides with exam-signature colours: pale blue Cu(OH)₂ (insoluble in excess), dirty green Fe(OH)₂, reddish-brown Fe(OH)₃, and white Zn(OH)₂/Al(OH)₃ that **dissolve in excess** as zincate/aluminate because they are amphoteric; ammonium salts yield no precipitate, only NH₃ on warming. As a base it drinks **acidic oxides**: 2NaOH + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃ (then NaHCO₃ with excess CO₂) and 2NaOH + SO₂ → Na₂SO₃ — the chemistry of scrubbing and of the crust on an unstoppered pellet. Industrially it comes from the **chlor-alkali** electrolysis of brine (2NaCl + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ + Cl₂) and is consumed saponifying fats into soap, pulping wood, and digesting bauxite.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Base of the Chemical World

Sodium hydroxide (caustic soda) is produced on a scale matched only by sulphuric acid. Its two faces — a **strong base** that neutralises and precipitates, and a **strong alkali** that absorbs acidic gases like CO₂ and SO₂ — plus its manufacture route make this topic a guaranteed short-question source.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Properties

- White deliquescent solid, mp 318 °C; extremely soluble in water with strong heat evolution; fully dissociated: NaOH → Na⁺ + OH⁻ — a **strong monobasic base**.
- Soapy touch, corrosive to skin (saponifies fats) — hence "caustic".
- Absorbs CO₂ and moisture from air (must be stoppered): 2NaOH + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O.

### 2.2 Precipitation reactions (the exam list)

| Cation | Observation | Equation |
|---|---|---|
| Cu²⁺ | pale blue ppt, insoluble in excess | CuSO₄ + 2NaOH → Cu(OH)₂↓ + Na₂SO₄ |
| Fe²⁺ | dirty green ppt | FeSO₄ + 2NaOH → Fe(OH)₂↓ + Na₂SO₄ |
| Fe³⁺ | reddish-brown ppt | FeCl₃ + 3NaOH → Fe(OH)₃↓ + 3NaCl |
| Zn²⁺, Al³⁺, Pb²⁺ | white ppt, **soluble in excess** (amphoteric) | ZnSO₄ + 2NaOH → Zn(OH)₂↓ + Na₂SO₄; Zn(OH)₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂ZnO₂ + 2H₂O |
| NH₄⁺ | no ppt — pungent NH₃ on warming | NH₄Cl + NaOH → NaCl + NH₃↑ + H₂O |

### 2.3 Action with CO₂ and SO₂ (acidic oxides)

- Limited CO₂: 2NaOH + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O; excess CO₂: Na₂CO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → 2NaHCO₃.
- SO₂: 2NaOH + SO₂ → Na₂SO₃ + H₂O (then NaHSO₃ with excess) — the chemistry of scrubbing acidic gases, and the reason NaOH pellets must be kept sealed.

### 2.4 Action with carbon monoxide (the topic's namesake)

- Under pressure (~6–8 atm, ~200 °C) sodium hydroxide absorbs CO to give **sodium formate (sodium methanoate)**: CO + NaOH → HCOONa — the historical basis of formic acid manufacture. No reaction at ordinary pressure/temperature; the pressure forces the weakly acidic CO into addition.

### 2.5 Manufacture and uses

- **Chlor-alkali electrolysis** of brine: cathode 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻; anode 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂; products NaOH + Cl₂ + H₂ (diaphragm or membrane cell keeps Cl₂ away from the OH⁻).
- Uses: soap and detergents (saponification), paper pulping, rayon, petroleum refining, bauxite purification (Bayer), laboratory reagent, drain cleaner.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Caustic soda** | Sodium hydroxide NaOH | strong monobasic base |
| **Amphoteric hydroxide** | Hydroxide reacting with both acids and bases | Zn(OH)₂, Al(OH)₃ |
| **Saponification** | Hydrolysis of ester (fat) by alkali to soap + glycerol | fat + NaOH |
| **Chlor-alkali process** | Electrolysis of brine giving NaOH, Cl₂, H₂ | membrane cell |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why Zn(OH)₂ dissolves in excess NaOH but Cu(OH)₂ does not

- Zinc and aluminium hydroxides are **amphoteric**: their oxides/hydroxides react with strong alkali to form zincate/aluminate, Zn(OH)₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂ZnO₂ + 2H₂O. Copper(II) hydroxide is purely basic — no acid character — so excess NaOH leaves the pale blue precipitate untouched. This single contrast is the standard qualitative-analysis question.

### 4.2 Why NaOH grabs CO₂ from the air

- OH⁻ is a stronger base than CO₃²⁻'s conjugate position requires: the acid anhydride CO₂ + OH⁻ → HCO₃⁻ → CO₃²⁻ + H₂O is fast and irreversible on drying. A pellet left on the bench becomes a crust of soda ash overnight — the reason "standard" NaOH solutions are standardised against a primary standard, not weighed as pellets.

### 4.3 Saponification — the oldest use

- Fat (glyceryl ester) + 3NaOH → 3RCOONa (soap) + glycerol. The OH⁻ attacks the ester bonds; the sodium salts of long-chain acids are the soap molecules. This is why NaOH is "caustic" to skin — skin fat is being saponified.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**NaOH vs Na₂CO₃ as bases**

| Basis | NaOH | Na₂CO₃ |
|---|---|---|
| Strength | strong base (OH⁻) | mild base (hydrolysis of CO₃²⁻) |
| With NH₄⁺ salt | liberates NH₃ on warming | no NH₃ |
| With phenolphthalein | pink immediately | pink (slow) |
| Air uptake | CO₂ + H₂O → Na₂CO₃ crust | already carbonate |

## 6. Common Confusions

**"Soluble in excess" means the hydroxide is amphoteric:** Zn(OH)₂, Al(OH)₃, Pb(OH)₂ dissolve in excess NaOH; Cu(OH)₂, Fe(OH)₂/₃ do not — memorise which side of the line each cation sits on.
**NaOH does not precipitate NH₃:** ammonium salts give no precipitate with NaOH — only ammonia gas on warming; writing "NH₄OH ppt" is wrong.
**Caustic soda vs washing soda:** NaOH is caustic soda; Na₂CO₃·10H₂O is washing soda — different compounds, different strengths.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): Describe the precipitation reactions of sodium hydroxide with solutions of copper sulphate, ferric chloride and zinc sulphate.** — **Copper sulphate:** NaOH gives a **pale blue precipitate** of copper(II) hydroxide, CuSO₄ + 2NaOH → Cu(OH)₂↓ + Na₂SO₄; the precipitate is **insoluble in excess** NaOH (Cu(OH)₂ is not amphoteric). **Ferric chloride:** a **reddish-brown precipitate** of ferric hydroxide, FeCl₃ + 3NaOH → Fe(OH)₃↓ + 3NaCl, also insoluble in excess. **Zinc sulphate:** a **white precipitate** of zinc hydroxide, ZnSO₄ + 2NaOH → Zn(OH)₂↓ + Na₂SO₄, which **dissolves in excess NaOH** because zinc hydroxide is amphoteric: Zn(OH)₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂ZnO₂ (sodium zincate) + 2H₂O.

**NEB-style (2m): What happens when excess CO₂ is passed into sodium hydroxide solution? Write both stages.** — **Stage 1 (limited CO₂):** the hydroxide takes up the acid anhydride to form the carbonate, 2NaOH + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O. **Stage 2 (excess CO₂):** the carbonate is converted to the soluble bicarbonate, Na₂CO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → 2NaHCO₃. The same chemistry explains why NaOH pellets left open to air gain mass and turn into a crust of sodium carbonate.

**NEB-style (2m): How is sodium hydroxide manufactured? Give the electrode reactions of the brine electrolysis.** — Sodium hydroxide is made by the **chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine** (concentrated NaCl solution) in a diaphragm or membrane cell that keeps the chlorine away from the hydroxide. **Cathode:** 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂↑ + 2OH⁻ (Na⁺ stays spectator; NaOH accumulates in the cathode compartment). **Anode:** 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂↑ + 2e⁻. Overall: 2NaCl + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ + Cl₂ — three products at once.

Acidic oxides: 2NaOH + CO2 -> Na2CO3 + H2O, excess CO2 -> NaHCO3; 2NaOH + SO2 -> Na2SO3 + H2O. confusion: ❌ All atoms are identical in an element. ✅ Isotopes have same protons but different neutrons.
❌ Atoms are indivisible. ✅ Atoms consist of protons, neutrons, and electrons.
❌ Electrons orbit in fixed paths like planets. ✅ Electrons exist in probability clouds (orbitals).
❌ Heisenberg uncertainty means we cannot measure position and momentum precisely simultaneously — not that we lack good instruments.
❌ de Broglie wavelength applies only to light. ✅ All matter has wave nature; detectable mainly for small masses like electrons.
❌ Quantum number l can be any integer. ✅ l ranges from 0 to n−1.
❌ Magnetic quantum number ml determines energy. ✅ ml determines orbital orientation, not energy (in absence of magnetic field).
❌ Spin quantum number ms can be ±½ or any value. ✅ ms is always +½ or −½.
❌ Aufbau principle means filling from bottom to top of the diagram. ✅ Fill lowest-energy orbitals first: 1s→2s→2p→3s→3p→4s→3d→4p→...
❌ Pauli exclusion allows two electrons per orbital with any spin. ✅ Two electrons in same orbital must have opposite spins.
❌ Hund's rule means pair electrons before spreading. ✅ Electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly first with parallel spins.
❌ The mole is just a number like dozen. ✅ 1 mole = 6.022×10²³ particles (Avogadro constant) — a bridge between atomic and macroscopic scales.
❌ Molar mass and molecular mass are the same thing. ✅ Molecular mass is in amu; molar mass is in g/mol — numerically equal but different units.
❌ Limiting reagent is the reactant with smallest mass. ✅ Limiting reagent is the one that produces the least product (determined by moles, not mass).
❌ % yield can exceed 100%. ✅ % yield >100% indicates impure product or incomplete drying.
❌ Molarity and molality are the same. ✅ Molarity = mol/L solution (changes with T); Molality = mol/kg solvent (temperature-independent).
❌ A strong acid completely ionizes in water. ✅ Strong acids (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄) are ~100% ionized; weak acids partially ionize.
❌ pH can be negative. ✅ pH < 0 is possible for concentrations >1M (e.g., 2M HCl has pH ≈ −0.3).
❌ Kc changes when concentration changes. ✅ Kc is constant at constant temperature; only temperature changes K.
❌ Adding catalyst shifts equilibrium position. ✅ Catalyst speeds both forward and backward reactions equally; no shift in equilibrium.
❌ High pressure always favors products. ✅ High pressure favors side with fewer gas moles (Le Chatelier).
❌ Exothermic reactions are spontaneous. ✅ Spontaneity depends on ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, not just ΔH.
❌ Endothermic reactions cannot be spontaneous. ✅ Endothermic reactions can be spontaneous if TΔS > ΔH (e.g., ice melting above 0°C).
❌ ΔH and ΔU are always the same. ✅ ΔH = ΔU + PΔV; they differ when gas moles change.
❌ Heat (q) and work (w) are state functions. ✅ q and w are path functions; only ΔU, ΔH, ΔS, ΔG are state functions.
❌ Oxidation and reduction happen separately. ✅ Oxidation and reduction always occur together (redox).
❌ Oxidizing agent gets oxidized. ✅ Oxidizing agent accepts electrons and gets reduced.
❌ Reducing agent gets reduced. ✅ Reducing agent donates electrons and gets oxidized.
❌ Faraday's laws apply only to metals. ✅ Faraday's laws apply to any substance deposited/dissolved at electrodes.
❌ Real gases obey PV=nRT at all conditions. ✅ Real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature.
❌ van der Waals constants a and b are same for all gases. ✅ a (attraction) and b (volume) are gas-specific.
❌ Surface tension increases with temperature. ✅ Surface tension decreases as temperature increases.
❌ Viscosity decreases with temperature for liquids. ✅ Viscosity of liquids decreases with T; gases increase with T.
❌ Colligative properties depend on nature of solute. ✅ Colligative properties depend only on number of particles, not identity.
❌ Raoult's law applies to all solutions. ✅ Raoult's law is exact for ideal solutions; approximate for dilute real solutions.
❌ Osmotic pressure is a colligative property. ✅ Yes — π = CRT depends on solute particle concentration.

data.summary:
Atomic structure: From Rutherford's nuclear model through Bohr's quantized orbits to the modern quantum mechanical model, understanding electron configuration using four quantum numbers is fundamental.

Stoichiometry: The mole concept bridges atomic and macroscopic scales; limiting reagent determines theoretical yield; concentration expressed as molarity or molality.

Chemical equilibrium: Dynamic equilibrium has equal forward and backward rates; Kc/Kp are temperature-dependent; Le Chatelier's principle predicts response to stress.

Thermodynamics: First law (energy conservation); enthalpy changes in reactions; Gibbs free energy determines spontaneity; entropy of universe always increases.

Oxidation-reduction: Redox involves electron transfer; oxidation numbers track electron flow; electrochemical cells convert chemical to electrical energy; Faraday's laws quantify electrolysis.

States of matter: Gas laws relate P, V, T, n; kinetic theory explains gas behavior; real gases deviate due to intermolecular forces and molecular volume.

Solutions: Molarity and molality express concentration; colligative properties depend on particle number; Raoult's law describes vapor pressure of ideal solutions.

Chemical bonding: Ionic bonds form from electron transfer; covalent bonds from sharing; VSEPR predicts molecular geometry; hybridization explains bonding orbitals.

Organic chemistry basics: Carbon's tetravalency and catenation enable millions of compounds; functional groups determine reactivity; IUPAC nomenclature provides systematic naming.

Hydrocarbons: Alkanes (CnH2n+2) are saturated; alkenes (CnH2n) have C=C; alkynes (CnH2n-2) have C≡C; aromatic compounds based on benzene ring.

Periodic table: Elements arranged by atomic number; periodic trends in radius, ionization energy, electronegativity; s, p, d, f blocks based on orbital type.

Applied chemistry: Petrochemical industry, polymer science, green chemistry principles; importance of sustainable chemical manufacturing for environmental protection.

## 1. Topic Introduction — Washing Soda and Its Reactions

Sodium carbonate exists anhydrous (soda ash) and as the decahydrate Na₂CO₃·10H₂O (**washing soda**). It is a **mild base** — too weak to liberate NH₃ from ammonium salts but strong enough to neutralise acids and precipitate metal carbonates. Its reactions with CO₂, SO₂, water and metal salts are the topic's checklist.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Properties

- White crystalline decahydrate (washing soda); effloresces on exposure — loses 9 H₂O to become the monohydrate powder. Anhydrous Na₂CO₃ mp 851 °C.
- Hydrolysis makes its solutions **mildly basic**: CO₃²⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻ (pH ~11 for 0.1 M).
- **Solubility anomaly:** Na₂CO₃ is less soluble in cold water than NaHCO₃'s family trend suggests, and its solubility *decreases* on heating near the decahydrate's decomposition — the classic exception quoted in solubility questions.

### 2.2 Reaction checklist

| Reagent | Equation | Observation |
|---|---|---|
| acids | Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂↑ | brisk effervescence |
| CO₂ + H₂O | Na₂CO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → 2NaHCO₃ | dissolves to bicarbonate |
| SO₂ | Na₂CO₃ + SO₂ → Na₂SO₃ + CO₂↑ | pungent gas |
| water (hard) | Na₂CO₃ + CaSO₄ → CaCO₃↓ + Na₂SO₄ | precipitates hardness |
| CaCl₂ | Na₂CO₃ + CaCl₂ → CaCO₃↓ + 2NaCl | white ppt |
| CuSO₄ | Na₂CO₃ + CuSO₄ → CuCO₃↓(basic) + Na₂SO₄ | green-blue ppt |
| ZnSO₄ | white ppt of ZnCO₃/Zn(OH)₂ mix | white ppt |
| NH₄Cl (on heating) | no NH₃ — too weak a base | distinguishes from NaOH |

### 2.3 Manufacture (Solvay, for context) and uses

- Solvay: NH₃ + CO₂ + brine → NaHCO₃ (precipitates) → heated to Na₂CO₃; NH₃ recovered.
- Uses: glass (largest), washing soda (cleaning, softening hard water), paper, NaHCO₃ (baking soda), standard base for acidimetry (primary standard when anhydrous).

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Washing soda** | Na₂CO₃·10H₂O | efflorescent crystals |
| **Efflorescence** | Loss of water of crystallisation to air | decahydrate → monohydrate |
| **Hydrolysis (salt)** | Ion reaction with water shifting pH | CO₃²⁻ + H₂O → HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻ |
| **Water softening** | Precipitation/removal of Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ | Na₂CO₃ + CaSO₄ → CaCO₃↓ |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why Na₂CO₃ is basic but NaHCO₃ is weaker

- The carbonate ion is the conjugate base of a very weak acid (HCO₃⁻, pKa₂ ≈ 10.3), so it grabs a proton from water: CO₃²⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻. The bicarbonate ion is the conjugate base of a *stronger* acid (H₂CO₃, pKa₁ ≈ 6.4), so its hydrolysis is weaker — pH ~8.3. Two ions, two pH values — the essence of "mild base".

### 4.2 Why washing soda softens hard water

- Permanent hardness (CaSO₄) is removed by exchange of anions: Na₂CO₃ + CaSO₄ → CaCO₃↓ + Na₂SO₄ — the calcium leaves the solution as insoluble carbonate, so soap no longer scums. Magnesium behaves the same (MgCO₃↓).

### 4.3 Why copper gives a *basic* carbonate

- Cu²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ in water precipitates not pure CuCO₃ but a basic carbonate (CuCO₃·Cu(OH)₂-ish, green-blue) because the carbonate solution is basic enough to co-precipitate OH⁻. The colour — green-blue — is the exam observation.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**NaOH vs Na₂CO₃ vs NaHCO₃**

| Basis | NaOH | Na₂CO₃ | NaHCO₃ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Basic strength | strong | mild | weak |
| With NH₄⁺ (warm) | NH₃↑ | no NH₃ | no NH₃ |
| With acid | salt + water | salt + water + CO₂ | salt + water + CO₂ |
| Thermal decomposition | no | no (decahydrate loses H₂O) | → Na₂CO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O |
| Common name | caustic soda | washing soda | baking soda |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Na₂CO₃ + SO₂ gives Na₂SO₃, not sulphate:** sulphur dioxide is the +4 anhydride — no oxygen is added; oxidation to sulphate would need O₂/oxidant.
**Efflorescence is not deliquescence:** the decahydrate *loses* water to air (efflorescent); NaOH *gains* water (deliquescent). Opposite directions, both about vapour pressure.
**No ammonia from ammonium salts with carbonate:** NaOH does, Na₂CO₃ does not — the standard distinguishing test between the two bases.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): Describe the action of sodium carbonate on (i) CO₂, (ii) SO₂, (iii) calcium chloride solution, with equations.** — **(i) CO₂:** in water, sodium carbonate absorbs carbon dioxide to form the bicarbonate, Na₂CO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → 2NaHCO₃ — the reverse of the baking-soda decomposition. **(ii) SO₂:** the acidic oxide displaces the weaker anhydride: Na₂CO₃ + SO₂ → Na₂SO₃ + CO₂↑ (sodium sulphite, the basis of SO₂ absorption scrubbers). **(iii) CaCl₂:** double decomposition precipitates calcium carbonate, Na₂CO₃ + CaCl₂ → CaCO₃↓ + 2NaCl — a white precipitate; the same reaction removes permanent hardness from water (with CaSO₄: Na₂CO₃ + CaSO₄ → CaCO₃↓ + Na₂SO₄).

**NEB-style (2m): Why is an aqueous solution of sodium carbonate alkaline, although the salt contains no OH⁻?** — Sodium carbonate is a salt of a **strong base and a very weak acid**, so its anion hydrolyses: CO₃²⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻. The equilibrium releases hydroxide ions into solution, making it alkaline (pH ≈ 11 for 0.1 M) — the alkalinity belongs to the hydrolysis of CO₃²⁻, not to any OH⁻ in the formula. Bicarbonate hydrolyses less strongly (HCO₃⁻ is the conjugate base of the stronger acid H₂CO₃), so NaHCO₃ solutions are only mildly alkaline (pH ≈ 8.3).

**NEB-style (2m): How does washing soda remove permanent hardness of water?** — Permanent hardness is due to dissolved calcium (and magnesium) salts such as CaSO₄ that soap cannot precipitate. Washing soda supplies carbonate ions which precipitate them: Na₂CO₃ + CaSO₄ → CaCO₃↓ + Na₂SO₄ (and MgSO₄ + Na₂CO₃ → MgCO₃↓ + Na₂SO₄). The calcium and magnesium leave the solution as insoluble carbonates, the sodium salts left behind do not scum with soap, and the water lathers freely.

data.summary: **Sodium carbonate** — anhydrous soda ash (mp 851 °C) or efflorescent decahydrate washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O → Na₂CO₃·H₂O in air) — is a **mild base by hydrolysis**: CO₃²⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻ gives pH ≈ 11, while bicarbonate sits at 8.3. It neutralises acids with brisk effervescence (Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂), absorbs **CO₂** to bicarbonate and **SO₂** to sulphite (Na₂SO₃ + CO₂ — never sulphate), and **precipitates** Ca²⁺/Ba²⁺ as white carbonate (Na₂CO₃ + CaCl₂ → CaCO₃↓ + 2NaCl) — the reaction that softens permanent hardness (CaSO₄ → CaCO₃↓) and gives copper its green-blue basic carbonate. Unlike NaOH it cannot liberate ammonia from ammonium salts — the standard distinguishing test. Manufactured by Solvay, consumed by the glass industry, and kept in every lab as the primary standard for acidimetry.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Other Alkaline Earths

Group IIA — Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra — carries two valence electrons and a different personality from Group IA: harder, denser, higher-melting, less reactive, and famous for **flame colours** and **sulphate solubility**. This topic is the trend table NEB asks as a 2–3 marker.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Electronic structure

- General configuration [NG]ns²; oxidation state **+2 only** (Be²⁺ exceptional covalency). Removing the second s-electron costs more (second IE ~1800 kJ/mol) but the +2 lattice energies repay it — hence no +1 chemistry in solution.

### 2.2 Trends down the group

| Property | Trend | Reason/numbers |
|---|---|---|
| Radius | increases | new shell (Be 111 pm covalent → Ba 198) |
| IE₁ | decreases | Be 899 → Ba 503 kJ/mol |
| Density | generally increases | Be 1.85 → Ba 3.62 g/mL (Mg 1.74 dip) |
| Melting point | no regular trend | Ca 842, Sr 777, Ba 727 °C — irregular |
| Reactivity with water | increases | Be none; Mg slow (hot); Ca brisk; Sr/Ba vigorous |
| Flame colour | Ca brick-red, Sr crimson, Ba apple-green | Be/Mg none (small atoms, high IE) |
| Electropositivity | increases | Be least, Ba most |

### 2.3 Signature chemistry

- With water: M + 2H₂O → M(OH)₂ + H₂ (Ca briskly cold, Mg slowly hot).
- With oxygen: burn to MO; Ba also forms BaO₂ (peroxide).
- With nitrogen: 3M + N₂ → M₃N₂ (all form nitrides — unlike alkali metals except Li).
- With hydrogen: M + H₂ → MH₂ (ionic hydrides; CaH₂ = "hydrolith" for H₂ generation).
- Hydroxides: solubility **increases** down (Be(OH)₂ insoluble → Ba(OH)₂ quite soluble); basicity increases (Be(OH)₂ amphoteric).
- Carbonates/sulphates: carbonate solubility **decreases** down; **sulphate solubility decreases sharply** down (MgSO₄ soluble → BaSO₄ insoluble) — the basis of the SO₄²⁻ test with BaCl₂.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Alkaline earth metal** | Group IIA element, [NG]ns² | Ca: [Ar]4s² |
| **Flame test (IIA)** | Emission colour of excited vapour | Sr crimson |
| **Hydrolith** | Calcium hydride CaH₂ | H₂ generator |
| **Amphoteric hydroxide** | Reacts with acids and bases | Be(OH)₂ |
| **Hardness (water)** | Dissolved Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ preventing lather | Ca(HCO₃)₂ |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why Be and Mg show no flame colour

- Flame colour requires easy excitation of valence electrons. Be and Mg have high ionisation energies (899, 738 kJ/mol) and small atoms whose excited states lie too high for Bunsen-flame energy — the electrons are not excited, so no emission. Ca, Sr, Ba excite readily and glow brick-red, crimson, apple-green.

### 4.2 The sulphate solubility ladder

- MgSO₄, CaSO₄ (sparingly), SrSO₄ (very low), BaSO₄ (insoluble, 2.4 mg/L). Lattice energy falls slowly down the group while hydration energy falls fast — the balance tips against dissolution. Result: BaCl₂ is the standard reagent for sulphate, and BaSO₄'s insolubility + non-absorption makes it the barium meal for X-rays (Ba²⁺ is toxic when absorbed — BaSO₄ is not).

### 4.3 Why Ca reacts briskly with cold water but Mg barely

- Reactivity tracks ionisation energy and oxide/hydroxide solubility: Ca²⁺'s hydroxide is moderately soluble, so the surface stays clean and reaction continues; Mg(OH)₂ is insoluble and coats the metal, quenching the reaction — until hot water or steam strips it (Mg + H₂O(steam) → MgO + H₂).

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Group IIA vs IA (the classic comparison)**

| Basis | Alkali metals (IA) | Alkaline earths (IIA) |
|---|---|---|
| Valence electrons | 1 (ns¹) | 2 (ns²) |
| Hardness/mp | soft, low mp | harder, higher mp |
| Density | very low (float) | higher (mostly sink) |
| Water reaction | violent even for K | gentler; Be/Mg need heat |
| Oxides | M₂O/M₂O₂/KO₂ | MO (basic; BeO amphoteric) |
| Carbonate solubility | all soluble | decreasing down; MgCO₃ sparingly |
| Flame | all coloured | Be/Mg none; Ca/Sr/Ba coloured |
| Nitrides | only Li₃N | all M₃N₂ |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Melting point has no monotonic trend here:** unlike IA (falling), IIA mp values zig-zag (Be 1287, Mg 650, Ca 842, Sr 777, Ba 727 °C) — quoting "decreases down" is wrong.
**Be is the odd one:** amphoteric BeO/Be(OH)₂, covalent compounds, no flame colour — its tiny polarising ion makes it more like aluminium.
**BaSO₄ in the stomach is safe; BaCl₂ is not:** insolubility is the safety — Ba²⁺ absorbed is toxic (blocks K⁺ channels); the insoluble sulphate passes through unabsorbed.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): Describe the general characteristics of alkaline earth metals: configuration, trends in ionisation energy and reactivity, and their reaction with water.** — Alkaline earth metals (Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra) have the outer configuration **ns²** and show only the **+2 oxidation state**. The **ionisation energy decreases down the group** (Be 899 → Ba 503 kJ/mol) as shells are added, so **reactivity increases**: with water, beryllium does not react even with steam, magnesium reacts only slowly with cold water ( briskly with steam, Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂), calcium reacts briskly with cold water (Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂↑), and strontium and barium react vigorously. The hydroxides MOH formed grow more soluble and more basic down the group.

**NEB-style (2m): Give the flame colours of calcium, strontium and barium, and explain why beryllium and magnesium give none.** — **Calcium: brick-red; strontium: crimson; barium: apple-green.** In the flame the outer electrons of the vapourised atoms are excited and emit their characteristic wavelengths on falling back. **Beryllium and magnesium give no flame colour** because their valence electrons are held too tightly (high ionisation energies, 899 and 738 kJ/mol) for Bunsen-flame energy to excite them — no excitation, no emission.

**NEB-style (2m): Arrange the sulphates of Group IIA in order of solubility and explain the trend.** — **MgSO₄ (soluble) > CaSO₄ (sparingly) > SrSO₄ (very sparingly) > BaSO₄ (practically insoluble).** Down the group the sulphate lattice energy decreases only slightly (the large SO₄²⁻ dominates), while the hydration energy of the shrinking… rather, growing M²⁺ ion decreases rapidly; the free-energy balance shifts against dissolution, so solubility falls. The near-insolubility of BaSO₄ makes BaCl₂ the test reagent for sulphate ions and BaSO₄ safe as the X-ray "barium meal".

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Quick Lime, Bleaching Powder, Plaster of Paris, Magnesia, Epsom Salt

Three calcium compounds and two magnesium ones carry most of the unit's industrial chemistry: **CaO** (quick lime) — made by calcining limestone and slaked to Ca(OH)₂; **bleaching powder** Ca(OCl)Cl — chlorine absorbed in slaked lime; **plaster of Paris** CaSO₄·½H₂O — gypsum dehydrated at ~120 °C; **magnesia** MgO — from magnesite or magnesium chloride; **Epsom salt** MgSO₄·7H₂O — the heptahydrate laxative. Each has a preparation equation, a set of reactions and a use list that NEB asks in rotation.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Calcium oxide (quick lime)

- **Preparation:** calcination of limestone in a lime kiln ~1000 °C: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂↑ (reversible; CO₂ swept out).
- White amorphous solid, mp ~2600 °C; reacts violently with water (**slaking**): CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + heat — the slaked lime.
- With acids: CaO + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O. With CO₂ (slowly) back to carbonate. With SiO₂ at high T: CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃ (flux chemistry).
- **Uses:** cement/lime mortar, steelmaking flux, CaC₂ (carbide), paper, water treatment, drying agent (does not dry ammonia — reacts; use for alcohol), self-heating food cans.

### 2.2 Bleaching powder (calcium oxychloride)

- **Preparation:** pass dry Cl₂ over **slaked lime**: Ca(OH)₂ + Cl₂ → Ca(OCl)Cl + H₂O (Hasenclever plant, rotating drums).
- Formula written CaOCl₂ or Ca(OCl)Cl — "available chlorine" ~35–38 %.
- **Reactions:** with dilute acid liberates Cl₂: Ca(OCl)Cl + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂O + Cl₂↑ (the "available chlorine" test); with CO₂ from air slowly decomposes (must be stored dry/sealed); with excess CO₂ + H₂O: Ca(OCl)Cl + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + Cl₂.
- **Uses:** bleaching cotton/linen (never wool/silk — protein fibres damaged by Cl₂/HOCl), disinfecting water and drains, making chloroform and CHCl₃ precursor chemistry, laboratory Cl₂ source.

### 2.3 Plaster of Paris

- **Preparation:** heat gypsum **CaSO₄·2H₂O at ~120 °C (393 K)**, not above (over-heating gives anhydrite, dead-burnt, which will not set): CaSO₄·2H₂O → CaSO₄·½H₂O + 1½H₂O.
- White powder; **setting**: mixed with water it re-hydrates and interlocks needle crystals, expanding slightly: CaSO₄·½H₂O + 1½H₂O → CaSO₄·2H₂O; sets in ~10–15 min, slight expansion → sharp moulds.
- **Uses:** plaster casts (fractured bones), moulds/statues, chalk boards, surgical plaster bandages, dentistry.

### 2.4 Magnesia (MgO) and Epsom salt (MgSO₄·7H₂O)

- **Magnesia:** white refractory powder, mp ~2850 °C; made by heating magnesite (MgCO₃ → MgO + CO₂) or by boiling MgCl₂·6H₂O with lime: MgCl₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → Mg(OH)₂↓ + CaCl₂, then Mg(OH)₂ → MgO + H₂O. Refractory furnace linings (basic refractory for steel), milk of magnesia (suspended Mg(OH)₂ antacid), Sorel cement (MgO + MgCl₂ paste), source of magnesium.
- **Epsom salt:** MgSO₄·7H₂O — colourless efflorescent needles, very soluble, bitter; used as a purgative/laxative in medicine, bath soaks for sore muscles, fertiliser (Mg + S nutrient), and as a flocculant in dyeing/soap. Heating loses water stepwise to the anhydrous sulphate.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Quick lime** | Calcium oxide CaO | from calcined limestone |
| **Slaking** | Exothermic hydration of CaO to Ca(OH)₂ | CaO + H₂O |
| **Bleaching powder** | Calcium oxychloride Ca(OCl)Cl | Cl₂ + slaked lime |
| **Available chlorine** | % Cl₂ equivalent liberated by acid | 35–38 % |
| **Plaster of Paris** | CaSO₄·½H₂O (calcium sulphate hemihydrate) | from gypsum at 120 °C |
| **Magnesia** | Magnesium oxide MgO | from magnesite MgCO₃ |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why gypsum must not be overheated

- At ~120 °C exactly half the water leaves, leaving hemihydrate with channels that re-accept water rapidly — the setting property. ### 4.2 Why bleaching powder bleaches

- In the presence of moisture/acid it releases **hypochlorous acid** and chlorine: Ca(OCl)Cl + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + Cl₂; Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HOCl; HOCl → HCl + [O] — the **nascent oxygen** oxidises the colouring matter of the fibre. This is also why wool and silk (protein fibres) are ruined: HOCl attacks the amide bonds.

### 4.3 Why quick lime heats water so fiercely

- Slaking, CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂, is strongly exothermic (ΔH ≈ −65 kJ/mol): enough heat to boil the local water and crack a lump of lime with steam. The same heat makes lime useful in self-heating ration cans.

## 1. Topic Introduction — Quick Lime, Bleaching Powder, Plaster of Paris, Magnesia, Epsom Salt

Three calcium compounds and two magnesium ones carry most of the unit's industrial chemistry: **CaO** (quick lime) — made by calcining limestone and slaked to Ca(OH)₂; **bleaching powder** Ca(OCl)Cl — chlorine absorbed in slaked lime; **plaster of Paris** CaSO₄·½H₂O — gypsum dehydrated at ~120 °C; **magnesia** MgO — from magnesite or magnesium chloride; **Epsom salt** MgSO₄·7H₂O — the heptahydrate laxative. Each has a preparation equation, a set of reactions and a use list that NEB asks in rotation.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Calcium oxide (quick lime)

- **Preparation:** calcination of limestone in a lime kiln ~1000 °C: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂↑ (reversible; CO₂ swept out).
- White amorphous solid, mp ~2600 °C; reacts violently with water (**slaking**): CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + heat — the slaked lime.
- With acids: CaO + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O. With CO₂ (slowly) back to carbonate. With SiO₂ at high T: CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃ (flux chemistry).
- **Uses:** cement/lime mortar, steelmaking flux, CaC₂ (carbide), paper, water treatment, drying agent (does not dry ammonia — reacts; use for alcohol), self-heating food cans.

### 2.2 Bleaching powder (calcium oxychloride)

- **Preparation:** pass dry Cl₂ over **slaked lime**: Ca(OH)₂ + Cl₂ → Ca(OCl)Cl + H₂O (Hasenclever plant, rotating drums).
- Formula written CaOCl₂ or Ca(OCl)Cl — "available chlorine" ~35–38 %.
- **Reactions:** with dilute acid liberates Cl₂: Ca(OCl)Cl + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂O + Cl₂↑ (the "available chlorine" test); with CO₂ from air slowly decomposes (must be stored dry/sealed); with excess CO₂ + H₂O: Ca(OCl)Cl + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + Cl₂.
- **Uses:** bleaching cotton/linen (never wool/silk — protein fibres damaged by Cl₂/HOCl), disinfecting water and drains, making chloroform and CHCl₃ precursor chemistry, laboratory Cl₂ source.

### 2.3 Plaster of Paris

- **Preparation:** heat gypsum **CaSO₄·2H₂O at ~120 °C (393 K)**, not above (over-heating gives anhydrite, dead-burnt, which will not set): CaSO₄·2H₂O → CaSO₄·½H₂O + 1½H₂O.
- White powder; **setting**: mixed with water it re-hydrates and interlocks needle crystals, expanding slightly: CaSO₄·½H₂O + 1½H₂O → CaSO₄·2H₂O; sets in ~10–15 min, slight expansion → sharp moulds.
- **Uses:** plaster casts (fractured bones), moulds/statues, chalk boards, surgical plaster bandages, dentistry.

### 2.4 Magnesia (MgO) and Epsom salt (MgSO₄·7H₂O)

- **Magnesia:** white refractory powder, mp ~2850 °C; made by heating magnesite (MgCO₃ → MgO + CO₂) or by boiling MgCl₂·6H₂O with lime: MgCl₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → Mg(OH)₂↓ + CaCl₂, then Mg(OH)₂ → MgO + H₂O. Refractory furnace linings (basic refractory for steel), milk of magnesia (suspended Mg(OH)₂ antacid), Sorel cement (MgO + MgCl₂ paste), source of magnesium.
- **Epsom salt:** MgSO₄·7H₂O — colourless efflorescent needles, very soluble, bitter; used as a purgative/laxative in medicine, bath soaks for sore muscles, fertiliser (Mg + S nutrient), and as a flocculant in dyeing/soap. Heating loses water stepwise to the anhydrous sulphate.

With **dilute sulphuric acid** it liberates its "available chlorine" (about 35–38 % of its mass): Ca(OCl)Cl + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂O + Cl₂↑. **Uses:** (i) bleaching cotton and linen — with water it releases hypochlorous acid, Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HOCl, and HOCl → HCl + [O], the nascent oxygen destroying the colouring matter (it must never be used on wool or silk, whose protein fibres it destroys); (ii) disinfecting drinking water, drains and floors — the same chlorine kills bacteria; it also serves as a convenient laboratory source of chlorine.

**NEB-style (2m): How is plaster of Paris prepared? Why should gypsum not be heated above about 200 °C?** — Plaster of Paris (calcium sulphate hemihydrate, CaSO₄·½H₂O) is prepared by **heating gypsum, CaSO₄·2H₂O, at about 120 °C**: CaSO₄·2H₂O → CaSO₄·½H₂O + 1½H₂O. If heating continues above about 200 °C, the remaining half-molecule of water is also expelled, giving **anhydrite (CaSO₄)** — "dead-burnt" plaster. Anhydrite lacks the open channels that let the hemihydrate re-absorb water rapidly, so it hydrates too slowly to set and loses all plastering value; the setting property lives only in the hemihydrate, which takes up 1½H₂O to reform gypsum in interlocking needle crystals (CaSO₄·½H₂O + 1½H₂O → CaSO₄·2H₂O), expanding slightly so it fills moulds sharply.

**NEB-style (2m): What happens when quick lime (i) is treated with water, (ii) is heated with coke in an electric furnace? Write equations.** — **(i) Slaking:** quick lime reacts with water with the evolution of much heat — the lump hisses, steams and crumbles — forming slaked lime: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂; the product is used in lime mortar, whitewash and water treatment. **(ii) With coke at ~2000 °C in the electric furnace:** calcium oxide is reduced to **calcium carbide**: CaO + 3C → CaC₂ + CO↑; the carbide, in turn, gives acetylene with water (CaC₂ + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + C₂H₂), which is the industrial route to oxy-acetylene welding gas.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Three Ladders, One Explanation

The alkaline earth metals carry three solubility ladders that all point different ways: **hydroxides** get *more* soluble down the group, **carbonates** get *less* soluble, and **sulphates** collapse to near-insoluble barium sulphate. One thermodynamic argument — lattice energy vs hydration energy — explains all three, and NEB asks for it nearly every year.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 The two competing energies

- Dissolution pays two bills: breaking the crystal lattice (**lattice energy, ΔL**, always endothermic) and rewarding the ions with water (**hydration energy, ΔH, always exothermic**). Solubility follows the balance: hydration wins → soluble; lattice wins → insoluble.
- Down the group the M²⁺ ion grows (Be²⁺ 31 pm → Ba²⁺ 135 pm): its **hydration energy falls steeply** (Be²⁺ ≈ −2494 → Ba²⁺ ≈ −1305 kJ/mol), while **lattice energy falls only modestly** and at a rate that depends on the size of the anion.

### 2.2 The anion decides the direction

- **Small anion (OH⁻):** lattice energy falls *fast* as M²⁺ grows (the small anion was what made the lattice tight) — faster than hydration falls → **solubility increases** down: Be(OH)₂ (insoluble) → Ba(OH)₂ (quite soluble, ~56 g/L).
- **Large anion (SO₄²⁻, CO₃²⁻):** the big anion dominates the lattice, so lattice energy falls only slightly as M²⁺ grows — hydration falls faster → **solubility decreases** down: MgSO₄ soluble → BaSO₄ insoluble (2.4 mg/L); MgCO₃ sparingly → BaCO₃ almost insoluble.

### 2.3 The ladders in numbers

| Salt | Trend down IIA | Endpoints |
|---|---|---|
| M(OH)₂ | increases | Be(OH)₂ insoluble → Ba(OH)₂ soluble |
| MCO₃ | decreases | MgCO₃ ~0.1 g/L → BaCO₃ ~0.002 g/L |
| MSO₄ | decreases sharply | MgSO₄ soluble → BaSO₄ 2.4 mg/L |

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Lattice energy** | Energy to separate 1 mol of ionic solid to gaseous ions | ΔL of BaSO₄ large |
| **Hydration energy** | Energy released when gaseous ions are hydrated | Be²⁺ ≈ −2494 kJ/mol |
| **Solubility product (Ksp)** | Equilibrium constant of dissolution | Ksp(BaSO₄) ≈ 1×10⁻¹⁰ |
| **Basicity trend** | Basic character of hydroxides down the group | Be(OH)₂ amphoteric → Ba(OH)₂ strongly basic |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why the hydroxide ladder rises

- OH⁻ is small (radius ~140 pm effective). In Be(OH)₂ the tiny Be²⁺ packs against the small OH⁻ → very high lattice energy. As M²⁺ grows, the lattice loosens rapidly (big cation, small anion = weak packing), while the cation's hydration loss is more gradual in relative terms — net: dissolution becomes easier. Consequence: lime water exists (Ca(OH)₂ sparingly), barium water is a usable reagent, and Be(OH)₂ is amphoteric and insoluble.

### 4.2 Why the carbonate and sulphate ladders fall

- CO₃²⁻ and SO₄²⁻ are large, so the lattice is already "loose" with respect to cation size: growing M²⁺ barely lowers lattice energy. But hydration energy keeps falling fast — the growing cation holds water less tightly. Net: dissolution becomes harder. Consequences: the BaCl₂ test for sulphate (BaSO₄ precipitates completely), and hard-water carbonate scale (CaCO₃ precipitates on heating bicarbonate).

### 4.3 The flip side — thermal stability (preview of the next topic)

- The same size logic explains stability: small cations polarise CO₃²⁻ more (Fajans), so BeCO₃/MgCO₃ decompose easily while BaCO₃ needs ~1300 °C. Solubility and stability are two views of the same polarisation argument.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Ladder summary**

| Group | Anion size | Lattice energy fall vs hydration fall | Solubility trend |
|---|---|---|---|
| M(OH)₂ | small | lattice falls faster | increases down |
| MCO₃ | large | hydration falls faster | decreases down |
| MSO₄ | large | hydration falls faster | decreases (sharply) down |

## 6. Common Confusions

**"Small anion → increasing solubility" is the rule, not "hydroxides are soluble":** Be(OH)₂ and Mg(OH)₂ are insoluble; only Ca(OH)₂ onward are usable in water — the ladder matters, not the label.
**BaSO₄ insolubility is not "covalency":** it is the lattice/hydration balance; quoting "covalent character" misses the thermodynamic argument NEB wants.
**Carbonates vs hydroxides directions are opposite:** memorise by anion size — small OH⁻ rises, big CO₃²⁻/SO₄²⁻ fall.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): State and explain the general trend in the solubility of the hydroxides, carbonates and sulphates of the alkaline earth metals.** — **Hydroxides:** solubility **increases** down the group — Be(OH)₂ is insoluble, Mg(OH)₂ sparingly, Ca(OH)₂ sparingly (lime water), Sr(OH)₂ more, Ba(OH)₂ quite soluble. **Carbonates:** solubility **decreases** down — MgCO₃ is the most soluble of the four, BaCO₃ nearly insoluble. **Sulphates:** solubility **decreases sharply** down — MgSO₄ soluble, CaSO₄ sparingly, SrSO₄ very sparingly, BaSO₄ practically insoluble. **Explanation:** dissolution balances lattice energy (endothermic) against hydration energy (exothermic). Descending the group the M²⁺ ion grows, so its hydration energy falls rapidly. With the **small OH⁻ anion**, lattice energy also falls fast as the cation grows — faster than hydration — so solubility rises. With the **large CO₃²⁻ and SO₄²⁻ anions**, the lattice energy falls only slightly (the big anion dominates the lattice), while hydration keeps falling — so solubility drops, most catastrophically for BaSO₄.

**NEB-style (2m): Why is barium chloride solution used to test for sulphate ions, and why is MgSO₄ soluble while BaSO₄ is not?** — Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄↓ gives a dense white precipitate insoluble in acids — the definitive sulphate test. The solubility contrast follows the lattice/hydration balance: in MgSO₄ the small Mg²⁺ is strongly hydrated (≈ −1922 kJ/mol for Mg²⁺), paying the lattice bill, so the salt dissolves; in BaSO₄ the large Ba²⁺ is weakly hydrated (≈ −1305 kJ/mol) while the large SO₄²⁻ anion keeps the lattice energy high, so hydration cannot pay for the lattice — Ksp ≈ 10⁻¹⁰ and the salt precipitates almost completely.

**NEB-style (2m): Arrange the hydroxides of Be, Mg, Ca, Ba in order of increasing solubility and basicity.** — **Solubility:** Be(OH)₂ < Mg(OH)₂ < Ca(OH)₂ < Ba(OH)₂. **Basicity:** the same order — Be(OH)₂ is amphoteric (dissolves in acids *and* NaOH), Mg(OH)₂ is a weak base, Ca(OH)₂ a strong base (sparingly soluble), Ba(OH)₂ a strong base and appreciably soluble. Both trends follow the growing M²⁺: less polarising of O–H (more ionic, more basic hydroxide) and a looser lattice (more soluble).

With the **small OH⁻ anion**, the lattice energy also falls rapidly as the cation grows — faster than hydration energy — so dissolution gets easier and solubility rises. **NEB-style (2m): Why is MgSO₄ soluble in water but BaSO₄ practically insoluble?** — Dissolution must be paid for by the lattice energy and funded by hydration energy. **MgSO₄:** the small Mg²⁺ ion is very strongly hydrated (hydration enthalpy ≈ −1922 kJ/mol); this large exothermic hydration more than compensates the lattice energy, so the salt dissolves freely. **BaSO₄:** the large Ba²⁺ ion is only weakly hydrated (≈ −1305 kJ/mol), while the large SO₄²⁻ anion keeps the lattice energy high — the hydration "income" cannot cover the lattice "cost", the free energy of dissolution is positive, and the salt precipitates (Ksp ≈ 1×10⁻¹⁰, solubility 2.4 mg/L). This contrast is exactly why BaCl₂ is the standard reagent for testing sulphate ions: Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄↓, a dense white precipitate insoluble in acids.

**NEB-style (2m): Arrange the hydroxides of Be, Mg, Ca and Ba in order of increasing solubility and increasing basic character, and account for both orders.** — **Solubility:** Be(OH)₂ < Mg(OH)₂ < Ca(OH)₂ < Ba(OH)₂. **Basic character:** the same order — Be(OH)₂ is **amphoteric** (reacts with acids and with NaOH, Be(OH)₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂BeO₂ + 2H₂O), Mg(OH)₂ is a weak base, Ca(OH)₂ strong, Ba(OH)₂ strong and appreciably soluble. **Reason:** as the M²⁺ ion grows down the group it polarises the O–H bond less, so the hydroxide becomes more ionic and more strongly basic; simultaneously the lattice of the small-anion hydroxide loosens faster than hydration energy falls, so solubility rises — both trends are the same ionic-size story.

Hydroxides (small OH-): lattice falls faster -> solubility increases: Be(OH)2 insoluble < Mg(OH)2 < Ca(OH)2 (lime water) < Ba(OH)2 soluble; basicity same order, Be(OH)2 amphoteric. Carbonates (large anion): hydration falls faster -> solubility decreases: MgCO3 > CaCO3 > SrCO3 > BaCO3. Sulphates: same, sharply: MgSO4 soluble > CaSO4 sparingly > SrSO4 > BaSO4 2.4 mg/L (Ksp ~1e-10) -> BaCl2 test for SO4^2-, barium meal. data.summary: Three solubility ladders, one thermodynamic engine. Dissolution spends **lattice energy** and earns **hydration energy**; down Group IIA the growing M²⁺ loses hydration enthalpy fast (Be²⁺ −2494 → Ba²⁺ −1305 kJ/mol). **NEB-style (2m): Why is MgSO₄ soluble in water but BaSO₄ practically insoluble?** — Dissolution must be paid for by the lattice energy and funded by hydration energy. **MgSO₄:** the small Mg²⁺ ion is very strongly hydrated (hydration enthalpy ≈ −1922 kJ/mol); this large exothermic hydration more than compensates the lattice energy, so the salt dissolves freely. **BaSO₄:** the large Ba²⁺ ion is only weakly hydrated (≈ −1305 kJ/mol), while the large SO₄²⁻ anion keeps the lattice energy high — the hydration "income" cannot cover the lattice "cost", the free energy of dissolution is positive, and the salt precipitates (Ksp ≈ 1×10⁻¹⁰, solubility 2.4 mg/L). This contrast is exactly why BaCl₂ is the standard reagent for testing sulphate ions: Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄↓, a dense white precipitate insoluble in acids.

**NEB-style (2m): Arrange the hydroxides of Be, Mg, Ca and Ba in order of increasing solubility and increasing basic character, and account for both orders.** — **Solubility:** Be(OH)₂ < Mg(OH)₂ < Ca(OH)₂ < Ba(OH)₂. **Basic character:** the same order — Be(OH)₂ is **amphoteric** (reacts with acids and with NaOH, Be(OH)₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂BeO₂ + 2H₂O), Mg(OH)₂ is a weak base, Ca(OH)₂ strong, Ba(OH)₂ strong and appreciably soluble. **Reason:** as the M²⁺ ion grows down the group it polarises the O–H bond less, so the hydroxide becomes more ionic and more strongly basic; simultaneously the lattice of the small-anion hydroxide loosens faster than hydration energy falls, so solubility rises — both trends are the same ionic-size story.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Why Small Cations Burn Their Carbonates

Thermal stability of the Group IIA carbonates and nitrates is the Fajans polarisation story: the smaller the M²⁺ ion, the harder it distorts the big anion's electron cloud, weakening a C–O or N–O bond until CO₂ or NO₂+O₂ escapes. The result is a clean ladder — BeCO₃ decomposes on a warm bench, BaCO₃ needs a blast furnace — and a clean set of facts NEB asks every year.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 The decomposition reactions

- Carbonates: MCO₃ → MO + CO₂↑ (all except BeCO₃ need heating; BeCO₃ decomposes below 100 °C, MgCO₃ ~350 °C, CaCO₃ ~900 °C, SrCO₃ ~1290 °C, BaCO₃ ~1360 °C).
- Nitrates: all decompose on heating, but in two stages of product:
  - **Be and Mg:** 2M(NO₃)₂ → 2MO + 4NO₂↑ + O₂↑ (nitrate → oxide).
  - **Ca, Sr, Ba:** M(NO₃)₂ → M(NO₂)₂ (nitrite) + O₂↑ (nitrate → nitrite + oxygen).
- The nitrate split is the exam's favourite contrast.

### 2.2 The polarisation (Fajans) explanation

- CO₃²⁻ (and NO₃⁻) is a large, polarisable anion. A small, doubly-charged M²⁺ (Be²⁺, Mg²⁺) has high charge density and **polarises the anion**: it drags electron density toward one O, weakening that C–O bond, so the anion breaks into oxide + CO₂ with little heat. A large M²⁺ (Ba²⁺) polarises weakly — the anion stays intact until very high temperature.
- The same polarisation explains BeO/Be(OH)₂ amphoterism and Be's covalency — one idea, many consequences.

### 2.3 Hydrates and stability in context

- MgCO₃ and CaCO₃ occur as magnesite and limestone/chalk/marble; the thermal lability of MgCO₃ is why magnesite calcines easily to magnesia, while limestone needs a proper kiln (~1000 °C) for quick lime.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Thermal stability** | Resistance to decomposition on heating | BaCO₃ stable to ~1360 °C |
| **Polarisation (Fajans)** | Distortion of anion electron cloud by cation | Be²⁺ on CO₃²⁻ |
| **Polarising power** | Charge/size ratio of the cation | Be²⁺ highest in group |
| **Nitrite** | Salt of NO₂⁻ | Ba(NO₂)₂ from Ba(NO₃)₂ |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why the carbonate ladder runs Be → Ba

- Decomposition temperature climbs steadily: BeCO₃ <100, MgCO₃ 350, CaCO₃ 900, SrCO₃ 1290, BaCO₃ 1360 °C. The cation's polarising power falls as its radius grows (charge constant), so the anion distortion weakens and the C–O bond survives longer. The intermediate "basic carbonate" stage (MO·CO₂ character) shrinks as stability grows.

### 4.2 Why nitrates split into two product families

- For Be and Mg, even the nitrite stage is too polarised to survive: heating drives the decomposition all the way to the **oxide + NO₂ + O₂**. For Ca, Sr, Ba, the nitrate anion survives the first step and only loses oxygen: **nitrite + O₂**. The dividing line sits between Mg and Ca — exactly where polarising power drops below the threshold that destroys NO₂⁻.

### 4.3 Connecting to the alkali metals

- Group IA nitrates (except Li) also give nitrites + O₂ on heating — NaNO₃ → NaNO₂ + ½O₂; LiNO₃, like Mg(NO₃)₂, gives the oxide + NO₂ + O₂ (the diagonal Li–Mg similarity). Carbonates of IA (except Li₂CO₃) never decompose on heating — the +1 cation is too weak a polariser; only Li₂CO₃ → Li₂O + CO₂.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Stability ladders**

| Compound class | Trend down IIA | Products on heating |
|---|---|---|
| MCO₃ | stability increases | MO + CO₂ (all members) |
| M(NO₃)₂ (Be, Mg) | least stable | MO + NO₂ + O₂ |
| M(NO₃)₂ (Ca, Sr, Ba) | more stable | M(NO₂)₂ + O₂ |

**IA vs IIA carbonates**

| Basis | Group IA | Group IIA |
|---|---|---|
| Cation charge | +1, weak polariser | +2, strong polariser |
| Thermal stability | high (Li₂CO₃ the exception) | low, rising down |
| On heating | mostly unchanged | MCO₃ → MO + CO₂ |

## 6. Common Confusions

**"More stable down the group" applies to carbonates AND to the nitrate decomposition *temperature*, but the nitrate *products* change family:** Be/Mg give oxide, Ca/Sr/Ba give nitrite — stability and product identity are different statements.
**NO₂ is brown, O₂ is not:** the decomposition of Mg(NO₃)₂ gives brown fumes (NO₂) plus a colourless gas that relights a glowing splint (O₂) — quote both observations.
**BaCO₃ does not decompose in a Bunsen flame:** ~1360 °C is beyond ordinary lab heat; writing "carbonates decompose on heating" without the temperature ladder loses the discrimination mark.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): Describe the trend in the thermal stability of the carbonates of the alkaline earth metals and explain it using the polarisation concept.** — The carbonates become **more thermally stable down the group**: BeCO₃ decomposes below 100 °C, MgCO₃ at about 350 °C, CaCO₃ at about 900 °C (lime kiln), SrCO₃ at about 1290 °C, and BaCO₃ only at about 1360 °C — all giving MO + CO₂. **Explanation (Fajans polarisation):** the M²⁺ cation distorts the electron cloud of the large CO₃²⁻ anion; the distortion pulls electron density onto one oxygen and weakens its C–O bond, so the anion splits into oxide + CO₂. **Polarising power = charge/size**; down the group the charge stays +2 while the radius grows, so polarising power falls from Be²⁺ (extreme) to Ba²⁺ (weak). The smaller the cation, the more the carbonate is destabilised and the lower its decomposition temperature — hence the ladder Be → Ba.

**NEB-style (3m): What happens when the nitrates of beryllium, magnesium and barium are heated? Write equations and explain the difference.** — **Beryllium and magnesium nitrates** decompose all the way to the oxide, with brown nitrogen dioxide and oxygen: 2Be(NO₃)₂ → 2BeO + 4NO₂↑ + O₂↑ and 2Mg(NO₃)₂ → 2MgO + 4NO₂↑ + O₂↑. **Barium nitrate** decomposes only to the **nitrite** with oxygen: Ba(NO₃)₂ → Ba(NO₂)₂ + O₂↑ (similarly Ca and Sr). **Explanation:** Be²⁺ and Mg²⁺ are small, doubly charged ions with high polarising power; they distort NO₃⁻ so strongly that even the nitrite product cannot survive — the decomposition proceeds to the oxide. The larger Ca²⁺, Sr²⁺, Ba²⁺ polarise weakly, the anion framework survives the first stage, and only oxygen is lost. The same split appears in Group IA: LiNO₃ gives the oxide, NaNO₃ and KNO₃ give nitrite + O₂.

**NEB-style (2m): Why is Li₂CO₃, alone among the alkali metal carbonates, decomposed on heating while Na₂CO₃ and K₂CO₃ are not?** — Li⁺ is the smallest alkali cation and, although singly charged, its high charge density polarises CO₃²⁻ enough to weaken a C–O bond, so lithium carbonate decomposes on heating: Li₂CO₃ → Li₂O + CO₂↑. Na⁺ and K⁺ are much larger with far lower polarising power — the carbonate anion remains intact and the salts are stable to strong heating (Na₂CO₃ melts at 851 °C without decomposing). This is one face of the **Li–Mg diagonal similarity**: Li₂CO₃ behaves like MgCO₃, not like Na₂CO₃.

data.summary: Thermal stability in Group IIA is the **polarisation ladder**. practiceQuestions: **NEB-style (3m): Describe the trend in thermal stability of the carbonates of the alkaline earth metals and explain it with the polarisation concept.** — The carbonates grow **steadily more stable down the group**: BeCO₃ decomposes below 100 °C (it is stable only under a CO₂ atmosphere), MgCO₃ at about 350 °C, CaCO₃ at about 900 °C, SrCO₃ at about 1290 °C, and BaCO₃ only at about 1360 °C — each giving the oxide and carbon dioxide, MCO₃ → MO + CO₂↑. **Explanation:** the carbonate ion is large and easily polarised. The doubly charged M²⁺ cation attracts and distorts the anion's electron cloud; the distortion concentrates electron density toward one oxygen and **weakens that C–O bond**, so the anion breaks into oxide plus CO₂. Polarising power is proportional to **charge/size** — down the group the charge stays +2 while the radius grows from Be²⁺ to Ba²⁺, so the distortion, and hence the destabilisation, falls continuously: Be²⁺ wrecks its carbonate on a warm bench, Ba²⁺ needs a blast furnace.

**NEB-style (3m): What products are obtained on heating the nitrates of beryllium, magnesium and barium? Write the equations and explain the difference in behaviour.** — **Beryllium nitrate and magnesium nitrate** decompose completely to the **oxide**, evolving brown nitrogen dioxide and oxygen: 2Be(NO₃)₂ → 2BeO + 4NO₂↑ + O₂↑; 2Mg(NO₃)₂ → 2MgO + 4NO₂↑ + O₂↑. **Barium nitrate** (like calcium and strontium nitrates) decomposes only to the **nitrite**, losing oxygen: Ba(NO₃)₂ → Ba(NO₂)₂ + O₂↑. **Explanation:** Be²⁺ and Mg²⁺ are small, doubly charged cations of high polarising power; they distort the nitrate ion so strongly that even the intermediate nitrite (NO₂⁻) cannot survive the heating — the decomposition goes all the way to the oxide. The larger Ca²⁺, Sr²⁺ and Ba²⁺ polarise weakly, the anion framework survives the first step, and only the extra oxygen is expelled. The same dividing behaviour appears in Group IA: LiNO₃ gives the oxide (like Mg), while NaNO₃ and KNO₃ give the nitrite.

**NEB-style (2m): Why does lithium carbonate, unlike the other alkali metal carbonates, decompose on heating?** — **Li⁺ is the smallest alkali cation**, so despite its single charge it has an unusually high charge density and **polarises the carbonate ion** appreciably; the distortion weakens a C–O bond and the salt decomposes on heating: Li₂CO₃ → Li₂O + CO₂↑. The larger Na⁺ and K⁺ polarise CO₃²⁻ far too weakly to break it, so sodium and potassium carbonates are thermally stable (Na₂CO₃ melts at 851 °C without decomposition). This is the **lithium–magnesium diagonal similarity** at work: in thermal behaviour Li₂CO₃ resembles MgCO₃ (which decomposes at ~350 °C), not Na₂CO₃.

importantConcepts: Polarising power is charge over size, and it is the single dial that tunes the whole group: the smaller the cation, the more it bends the big anion's cloud, and the lower the temperature at which CO2 or NO2+O2 escapes.
importantStatements: "The thermal stability of the carbonates of the alkaline earth metals increases with increasing atomic number, because the polarising power of the doubly charged cation decreases as its size increases."
importantNotes: No verified PYQ on carbonate/nitrate stability exists in the bank; all items here are NEB-style practice.
examNotes: The nitrate question needs both equations AND the polarisation explanation of the split — products alone score half.
