confusion: ❌ All cells look the same under a microscope. ✅ Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells have them.
❌ DNA and RNA are identical in structure. ✅ DNA is double-stranded with deoxyribose and thymine; RNA is single-stranded with ribose and uracil.
❌ Mitosis produces genetically different cells. ✅ Mitosis produces genetically identical diploid daughter cells.
❌ Meiosis produces identical cells. ✅ Meiosis produces 4 genetically diverse haploid gametes.
❌ Crossing over occurs in mitosis. ✅ Crossing over occurs in Prophase I of meiosis only.
❌ All enzymes are proteins. ✅ Most enzymes are proteins; some RNA molecules (ribozymes) also have catalytic activity.
❌ ATP is the only energy currency. ✅ GTP, UTP, and CTP also serve as energy carriers in specific pathways.
❌ Photosynthesis occurs in all plant cells. ✅ Photosynthesis occurs only in cells containing chloroplasts (mainly mesophyll).
❌ Respiration and photosynthesis are opposite processes with same equation. ✅ They are complementary but occur in different organelles and under different conditions.
❌ Oxygen is produced during respiration. ✅ Oxygen is consumed in aerobic respiration; produced during photosynthesis.
❌ Food chain shows all feeding relationships. ✅ Food chain is linear; food web shows interconnected feeding relationships.
❌ 90% of energy is transferred to next trophic level. ✅ Only ~10% energy transfers; ~90% lost as heat.
❌ Biomagnification decreases toxin concentration up the food chain. ✅ Biomagnification increases toxin concentration at higher trophic levels.
❌ Carbon cycle only involves plants and animals. ✅ Carbon cycle involves atmosphere, oceans, fossils, rocks, and decomposers.
❌ Nitrogen fixation only occurs in bacteria. ✅ Some lightning and industrial processes (Haber) also fix nitrogen.
❌ All fungi are harmful. ✅ Many fungi are beneficial (decomposers, mycorrhizae, food, antibiotics like penicillin).
❌ Viruses are living organisms. ✅ Viruses are acellular — they cannot reproduce without a host and lack metabolism.
❌ Bacteria are always harmful. ✅ Most bacteria are harmless or beneficial (gut flora, nitrogen fixation, decomposition).
❌ Gram-positive and Gram-negative differ only in color. ✅ Gram-positive has thick peptidoglycan layer; Gram-negative has thin layer + outer membrane.
❌ Natural selection creates perfect organisms. ✅ Natural selection favors traits suited to current environment; environments change.
❌ Evolution is goal-oriented. ✅ Evolution has no goal; it acts on random variation filtered by selection.
❌ Homologous and analogous structures mean the same thing. ✅ Homologous = common ancestry (divergent); Analogous = similar function, different origin (convergent).
❌ Fossils are preserved bones only. ✅ Fossils include impressions, trace fossils, amber-preserved organisms, and molecular fossils.
❌ Lamarckism is completely wrong. ✅ Lamarck's inheritance of acquired characteristics is largely rejected, but epigenetics shows some environmental effects can be inherited.
❌ Five-kingdom classification is outdated. ✅ Six-kingdom (adding Archaea) and phylogenetic systems are more current, but five-kingdom remains useful for education.
❌ Binomial nomenclature names change frequently. ✅ Names are stable once formally published; changes require formal revision by taxonomic authorities.
❌ All algae are aquatic. ✅ Some algae live in soil, on tree bark, or in symbiotic relationships (lichens).
❌ Bryophytes have vascular tissue. ✅ Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts, hornworts) lack true vascular tissue (xylem/phloem).
❌ Gymnosperms produce flowers. ✅ Gymnosperms have naked seeds in cones; angiosperms produce flowers and enclosed seeds.
❌ Double fertilization occurs in gymnosperms. ✅ Double fertilization (zygote + endosperm) is unique to angiosperms.
❌ Earthworms have an open circulatory system. ✅ Earthworms have a closed circulatory system with dorsal and ventral vessels.
❌ Frogs breathe only through lungs. ✅ Frogs use cutaneous respiration (skin), buccal cavity, and lungs.
❌ Conservation only means protecting animals. ✅ Conservation includes genetic, species, and ecosystem diversity; in-situ and ex-situ strategies.
❌ In-situ and ex-situ conservation are the same. ✅ In-situ = conservation in natural habitat (national parks); Ex-situ = conservation outside habitat (zoos, seed banks).

notes: Non-metals: electronegative, form anions.
Halogen reactivity decreases down group.
Nitrogen: N₂ triple bond, very stable.
Oxygen: O₂ paramagnetic, supports combustion.
confusion: ❌ All cells look the same under a microscope. ✅ Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells have them.
❌ DNA and RNA are identical in structure. ✅ DNA is double-stranded with deoxyribose and thymine; RNA is single-stranded with ribose and uracil.
❌ Mitosis produces genetically different cells. ✅ Mitosis produces genetically identical diploid daughter cells.
❌ Meiosis produces identical cells. ✅ Meiosis produces 4 genetically diverse haploid gametes.
❌ Crossing over occurs in mitosis. ✅ Crossing over occurs in Prophase I of meiosis only.
❌ All enzymes are proteins. ✅ Most enzymes are proteins; some RNA molecules (ribozymes) also have catalytic activity.
❌ ATP is the only energy currency. ✅ GTP, UTP, and CTP also serve as energy carriers in specific pathways.
❌ Photosynthesis occurs in all plant cells. ✅ Photosynthesis occurs only in cells containing chloroplasts (mainly mesophyll).
❌ Respiration and photosynthesis are opposite processes with same equation. ✅ They are complementary but occur in different organelles and under different conditions.
❌ Oxygen is produced during respiration. ✅ Oxygen is consumed in aerobic respiration; produced during photosynthesis.
❌ Food chain shows all feeding relationships. ✅ Food chain is linear; food web shows interconnected feeding relationships.
❌ 90% of energy is transferred to next trophic level. ✅ Only ~10% energy transfers; ~90% lost as heat.
❌ Biomagnification decreases toxin concentration up the food chain. ✅ Biomagnification increases toxin concentration at higher trophic levels.
❌ Carbon cycle only involves plants and animals. ✅ Carbon cycle involves atmosphere, oceans, fossils, rocks, and decomposers.
❌ Nitrogen fixation only occurs in bacteria. ✅ Some lightning and industrial processes (Haber) also fix nitrogen.
❌ All fungi are harmful. ✅ Many fungi are beneficial (decomposers, mycorrhizae, food, antibiotics like penicillin).
❌ Viruses are living organisms. ✅ Viruses are acellular — they cannot reproduce without a host and lack metabolism.
❌ Bacteria are always harmful. ✅ Most bacteria are harmless or beneficial (gut flora, nitrogen fixation, decomposition).
❌ Gram-positive and Gram-negative differ only in color. ✅ Gram-positive has thick peptidoglycan layer; Gram-negative has thin layer + outer membrane.
❌ Natural selection creates perfect organisms. ✅ Natural selection favors traits suited to current environment; environments change.
❌ Evolution is goal-oriented. ✅ Evolution has no goal; it acts on random variation filtered by selection.
❌ Homologous and analogous structures mean the same thing. ✅ Homologous = common ancestry (divergent); Analogous = similar function, different origin (convergent).
❌ Fossils are preserved bones only. ✅ Fossils include impressions, trace fossils, amber-preserved organisms, and molecular fossils.
❌ Lamarckism is completely wrong. ✅ Lamarck's inheritance of acquired characteristics is largely rejected, but epigenetics shows some environmental effects can be inherited.
❌ Five-kingdom classification is outdated. ✅ Six-kingdom (adding Archaea) and phylogenetic systems are more current, but five-kingdom remains useful for education.
❌ Binomial nomenclature names change frequently. ✅ Names are stable once formally published; changes require formal revision by taxonomic authorities.
❌ All algae are aquatic. ✅ Some algae live in soil, on tree bark, or in symbiotic relationships (lichens).
❌ Bryophytes have vascular tissue. ✅ Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts, hornworts) lack true vascular tissue (xylem/phloem).
❌ Gymnosperms produce flowers. ✅ Gymnosperms have naked seeds in cones; angiosperms produce flowers and enclosed seeds.
❌ Double fertilization occurs in gymnosperms. ✅ Double fertilization (zygote + endosperm) is unique to angiosperms.
❌ Earthworms have an open circulatory system. ✅ Earthworms have a closed circulatory system with dorsal and ventral vessels.
❌ Frogs breathe only through lungs. ✅ Frogs use cutaneous respiration (skin), buccal cavity, and lungs.
❌ Conservation only means protecting animals. ✅ Conservation includes genetic, species, and ecosystem diversity; in-situ and ex-situ strategies.
❌ In-situ and ex-situ conservation are the same. ✅ In-situ = conservation in natural habitat (national parks); Ex-situ = conservation outside habitat (zoos, seed banks).

data.topicTitle: Ozone: occurrence, preparation of ozone from oxygen, structure of ozone, test for ozone, uses of ozone
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Sharp-Smelling Shield

Ozone (O₃) is oxygen's aggressive allotrope: made by lightning and ozonisers, decomposing back to O₂ with nascent oxygen in hand. This topic covers its occurrence, preparation, bent resonance structure, the starch-iodide test, and its uses — from sterilising water to the stratospheric shield whose depletion is topic 62.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Occurrence

- **Stratosphere:** the ozone layer (~15–35 km altitude) absorbs most solar UV-B/UV-C — life's sunscreen.
- **Trace ground-level:** after thunderstorms (lightning discharge), around electric motors and copiers, in smog (a pollutant there).

### 2.2 Preparation

- **Silent electric discharge ozoniser:** 3O₂ ⇌ 2O₃, ΔH = +142 kJ. Dry, pure O₂ streams through an annular gap between electrodes cooled in dilute H₂SO₄; ~10 % ozone at steady state (higher conversion blocked by O₃'s own decomposition under the discharge).
- Conditions matter: **silent** discharge (no sparking — sparks heat the gas and destroy ozone); dry oxygen (moisture aids decomposition); low temperature favours yield (exothermic product side is disfavoured... actually the forward reaction is endothermic, but O₃ decomposes faster when hot — cooling protects the product).

### 2.3 Structure

- **Bent molecule**, bond angle ≈ 117°, O–O bond length 128 pm (between single 148 and double 121 pm).
- **Resonance:** two equivalent structures with one single and one double bond; the real molecule has both bonds equivalent, bond order 1.5; central O carries +, terminal O's carry − formally.
- **Diamagnetic** — all electrons paired (contrast O₂'s paramagnetism).

### 2.4 Test for ozone

- **Starch–iodide paper:** O₃ oxidises iodide to iodine, which turns starch blue-black: 2KI + H₂O + O₃ → 2KOH + I₂ + O₂. (H₂O₂ does the same, so moist litmus/peroxide interference is checked by the turpentine test: ozone decolourises turpentine's violet colour.)
- Ozone also turns **turpentine blue** and liberates iodine from iodides — the classic pair of confirmatory tests.

### 2.5 Uses

- **Water sterilisation** (no chlorinated taste or residue); **bleaching** delicate fabrics, oils, waxes, ivory, flour; **air purification** in closed spaces; **oxidant** in organic synthesis (ozonolysis locating C=C positions); **medical** disinfection of operating rooms; stratospheric UV shield.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|

### 4.1 Why the ozoniser yields only ~10 % O₃

### 4.2 The bond-angle story

- Central oxygen is sp²-hybridised: two sigma bonds plus one lone pair → bent, ~117° (slightly compressed from 120° by the lone pair). The delocalised π system across three atoms gives the 1.5 bond order and the 128 pm compromise bond length.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Occurrence

- **Stratosphere:** the ozone layer (~15–35 km altitude) absorbs most solar UV-B/UV-C — life's sunscreen.

### 2.2 Preparation

- **Silent electric discharge ozoniser:** 3O₂ ⇌ 2O₃, ΔH = +142 kJ. Dry, pure O₂ streams through an annular gap between electrodes cooled in dilute H₂SO₄; ~10 % ozone at steady state (higher conversion blocked by O₃'s own decomposition under the discharge).
- Conditions matter: **silent** discharge (no sparking — sparks heat the gas and destroy ozone); dry oxygen (moisture aids decomposition); low temperature favours yield (exothermic product side is disfavoured... actually the forward reaction is endothermic, but O₃ decomposes faster when hot — cooling protects the product).

### 2.3 Structure

- **Bent molecule**, bond angle ≈ 117°, O–O bond length 128 pm (between single 148 and double 121 pm).

confusion: ❌ All cells look the same under a microscope. ✅ Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells have them.
❌ DNA and RNA are identical in structure. ✅ DNA is double-stranded with deoxyribose and thymine; RNA is single-stranded with ribose and uracil.
❌ Mitosis produces genetically different cells. ✅ Mitosis produces genetically identical diploid daughter cells.
❌ Meiosis produces identical cells. ✅ Meiosis produces 4 genetically diverse haploid gametes.
❌ Crossing over occurs in mitosis. ✅ Crossing over occurs in Prophase I of meiosis only.
❌ All enzymes are proteins. ✅ Most enzymes are proteins; some RNA molecules (ribozymes) also have catalytic activity.
❌ ATP is the only energy currency. ✅ GTP, UTP, and CTP also serve as energy carriers in specific pathways.
❌ Photosynthesis occurs in all plant cells. ✅ Photosynthesis occurs only in cells containing chloroplasts (mainly mesophyll).
❌ Respiration and photosynthesis are opposite processes with same equation. ✅ They are complementary but occur in different organelles and under different conditions.
❌ Oxygen is produced during respiration. ✅ Oxygen is consumed in aerobic respiration; produced during photosynthesis.
❌ Food chain shows all feeding relationships. ✅ Food chain is linear; food web shows interconnected feeding relationships.
❌ 90% of energy is transferred to next trophic level. ✅ Only ~10% energy transfers; ~90% lost as heat.
❌ Biomagnification decreases toxin concentration up the food chain. ✅ Biomagnification increases toxin concentration at higher trophic levels.
❌ Carbon cycle only involves plants and animals. ✅ Carbon cycle involves atmosphere, oceans, fossils, rocks, and decomposers.
❌ Nitrogen fixation only occurs in bacteria. ✅ Some lightning and industrial processes (Haber) also fix nitrogen.
❌ All fungi are harmful. ✅ Many fungi are beneficial (decomposers, mycorrhizae, food, antibiotics like penicillin).
❌ Viruses are living organisms. ✅ Viruses are acellular — they cannot reproduce without a host and lack metabolism.
❌ Bacteria are always harmful. ✅ Most bacteria are harmless or beneficial (gut flora, nitrogen fixation, decomposition).
❌ Gram-positive and Gram-negative differ only in color. ✅ Gram-positive has thick peptidoglycan layer; Gram-negative has thin layer + outer membrane.
❌ Natural selection creates perfect organisms. ✅ Natural selection favors traits suited to current environment; environments change.
❌ Evolution is goal-oriented. ✅ Evolution has no goal; it acts on random variation filtered by selection.
❌ Homologous and analogous structures mean the same thing. ✅ Homologous = common ancestry (divergent); Analogous = similar function, different origin (convergent).
❌ Fossils are preserved bones only. ✅ Fossils include impressions, trace fossils, amber-preserved organisms, and molecular fossils.
❌ Lamarckism is completely wrong. ✅ Lamarck's inheritance of acquired characteristics is largely rejected, but epigenetics shows some environmental effects can be inherited.
❌ Five-kingdom classification is outdated. ✅ Six-kingdom (adding Archaea) and phylogenetic systems are more current, but five-kingdom remains useful for education.
❌ Binomial nomenclature names change frequently. ✅ Names are stable once formally published; changes require formal revision by taxonomic authorities.
❌ All algae are aquatic. ✅ Some algae live in soil, on tree bark, or in symbiotic relationships (lichens).
❌ Bryophytes have vascular tissue. ✅ Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts, hornworts) lack true vascular tissue (xylem/phloem).
❌ Gymnosperms produce flowers. ✅ Gymnosperms have naked seeds in cones; angiosperms produce flowers and enclosed seeds.
❌ Double fertilization occurs in gymnosperms. ✅ Double fertilization (zygote + endosperm) is unique to angiosperms.
❌ Earthworms have an open circulatory system. ✅ Earthworms have a closed circulatory system with dorsal and ventral vessels.
❌ Frogs breathe only through lungs. ✅ Frogs use cutaneous respiration (skin), buccal cavity, and lungs.
❌ Conservation only means protecting animals. ✅ Conservation includes genetic, species, and ecosystem diversity; in-situ and ex-situ strategies.
❌ In-situ and ex-situ conservation are the same. ✅ In-situ = conservation in natural habitat (national parks); Ex-situ = conservation outside habitat (zoos, seed banks).

confusion: ❌ All atoms are identical in an element. ✅ Isotopes have same protons but different neutrons.
❌ Atoms are indivisible. ✅ Atoms consist of protons, neutrons, and electrons.
❌ Electrons orbit in fixed paths like planets. ✅ Electrons exist in probability clouds (orbitals).
❌ Heisenberg uncertainty means we cannot measure position and momentum precisely simultaneously — not that we lack good instruments.
❌ de Broglie wavelength applies only to light. ✅ All matter has wave nature; detectable mainly for small masses like electrons.
❌ Quantum number l can be any integer. ✅ l ranges from 0 to n−1.
❌ Magnetic quantum number ml determines energy. ✅ ml determines orbital orientation, not energy (in absence of magnetic field).
❌ Spin quantum number ms can be ±½ or any value. ✅ ms is always +½ or −½.
❌ Aufbau principle means filling from bottom to top of the diagram. ✅ Fill lowest-energy orbitals first: 1s→2s→2p→3s→3p→4s→3d→4p→...
❌ Pauli exclusion allows two electrons per orbital with any spin. ✅ Two electrons in same orbital must have opposite spins.
❌ Hund's rule means pair electrons before spreading. ✅ Electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly first with parallel spins.
❌ The mole is just a number like dozen. ✅ 1 mole = 6.022×10²³ particles (Avogadro constant) — a bridge between atomic and macroscopic scales.
❌ Molar mass and molecular mass are the same thing. ✅ Molecular mass is in amu; molar mass is in g/mol — numerically equal but different units.
❌ Limiting reagent is the reactant with smallest mass. ✅ Limiting reagent is the one that produces the least product (determined by moles, not mass).
❌ % yield can exceed 100%. ✅ % yield >100% indicates impure product or incomplete drying.
❌ Molarity and molality are the same. ✅ Molarity = mol/L solution (changes with T); Molality = mol/kg solvent (temperature-independent).
❌ A strong acid completely ionizes in water. ✅ Strong acids (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄) are ~100% ionized; weak acids partially ionize.
❌ pH can be negative. ✅ pH < 0 is possible for concentrations >1M (e.g., 2M HCl has pH ≈ −0.3).
❌ Kc changes when concentration changes. ✅ Kc is constant at constant temperature; only temperature changes K.
❌ Adding catalyst shifts equilibrium position. ✅ Catalyst speeds both forward and backward reactions equally; no shift in equilibrium.
❌ High pressure always favors products. ✅ High pressure favors side with fewer gas moles (Le Chatelier).
❌ Exothermic reactions are spontaneous. ✅ Spontaneity depends on ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, not just ΔH.
❌ Endothermic reactions cannot be spontaneous. ✅ Endothermic reactions can be spontaneous if TΔS > ΔH (e.g., ice melting above 0°C).
❌ ΔH and ΔU are always the same. ✅ ΔH = ΔU + PΔV; they differ when gas moles change.
❌ Heat (q) and work (w) are state functions. ✅ q and w are path functions; only ΔU, ΔH, ΔS, ΔG are state functions.
❌ Oxidation and reduction happen separately. ✅ Oxidation and reduction always occur together (redox).
❌ Oxidizing agent gets oxidized. ✅ Oxidizing agent accepts electrons and gets reduced.
❌ Reducing agent gets reduced. ✅ Reducing agent donates electrons and gets oxidized.
❌ Faraday's laws apply only to metals. ✅ Faraday's laws apply to any substance deposited/dissolved at electrodes.
❌ Real gases obey PV=nRT at all conditions. ✅ Real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature.
❌ van der Waals constants a and b are same for all gases. ✅ a (attraction) and b (volume) are gas-specific.
❌ Surface tension increases with temperature. ✅ Surface tension decreases as temperature increases.
❌ Viscosity decreases with temperature for liquids. ✅ Viscosity of liquids decreases with T; gases increase with T.
❌ Colligative properties depend on nature of solute. ✅ Colligative properties depend only on number of particles, not identity.
❌ Raoult's law applies to all solutions. ✅ Raoult's law is exact for ideal solutions; approximate for dilute real solutions.
❌ Osmotic pressure is a colligative property. ✅ Yes — π = CRT depends on solute particle concentration.

data.title: Ozone layer depletion: causes, effects and control measures
data.topicTitle: Ozone layer depletion: causes, effects and control measures
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Hole We Made and Are Closing

The ozone layer's depletion is chemistry's best-known environmental lesson: CFCs — once celebrated as miracle refrigerants — drift to the stratosphere, surrender chlorine atoms to UV, and each chlorine atom destroys tens of thousands of ozone molecules. This topic covers the causes, the Antarctic hole's mechanism, the effects, and the Montreal Protocol's control measures.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 The natural ozone balance

- Formation: O₂ + UV (< 242 nm) → 2O; O + O₂ → O₃.
- Destruction: O₃ + UV → O₂ + O; O₃ + O → 2O₂.
- In the unpolluted stratosphere formation and destruction balance — a steady ~300 DU (Dobson units) column.

### 2.2 Causes of depletion

- **CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons, freons: CFCl₃, CF₂Cl₂):** inert in the troposphere (that was their selling point), but UV in the stratosphere breaks the C–Cl bond: CFCl₃ + UV → CFCl₂• + Cl•.
- **The catalytic cycle:** Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂; ClO• + O → Cl• + O₂. Net: O₃ + O → 2O₂ — the chlorine atom is **regenerated**, so one Cl destroys ~100,000 O₃ molecules before it is sequestered (as ClONO₂ reservoirs).
- **Other culprits:** halons (bromine — even more efficient per atom), methyl bromide (pesticides), N₂O (nitrous oxide from fertilisers → NO catalytic cycle), carbon tetrachloride, methyl chloroform.

### 2.3 The Antarctic ozone hole

- **Polar stratospheric clouds (PSCs)** form in the Antarctic winter's −80 °C vortex; they convert inactive reservoirs (ClONO₂, HCl) into active Cl₂; spring sunlight (September–October) photolyses Cl₂ → 2Cl• — the hole opens.
- Discovered by Farman et al. (1985, British Antarctic Survey); column ozone fell below 100 DU at the minimum.

### 2.4 Effects

- **Human health:** more UV-B → skin cancers (melanoma), cataracts, immune suppression.
- **Ecosystems:** phytoplankton damage (marine food web base), crop yield losses, polymer degradation.
- **Climate interaction:** CFCs are also potent greenhouse gases (thousands of times CO₂'s warming power per kg).

### 2.5 Control measures

- **Montreal Protocol (1987):** phase-out schedule for CFCs and halons — universally ratified; amended (London, Copenhagen, Kigali) to cover HCFCs and HFCs.
- **Replacements:** HCFCs (transitional, lower ozone depletion potential), HFCs (zero ODP but greenhouse — Kigali 2016 phases them down), and newer options (HFO-1234yf, hydrocarbons, CO₂ systems, ammonia in industry).
- **Individual/national measures:** recover and recycle CFC refrigerants, ban CFC production, monitor with satellites (TOMS/OMI), halon banking.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **CFC** | Chlorofluorocarbon, fully halogenated alkane | CF₂Cl₂ (freon-12) |
| **ODP** | Ozone depletion potential relative to CFC-11 | CFC-11 = 1.0 |
| **Dobson unit** | Column ozone measure; 300 DU ≈ 3 mm pure O₃ at STP | Hole < 100 DU |
| **Polar stratospheric cloud** | Ice/nitric-acid clouds at −80 °C activating chlorine | Antarctic winter |
| **Reservoir species** | Inactive chlorine stores | ClONO₂, HCl |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why the catalytic cycle is so lethal

- The Cl• + O₃ and ClO• + O steps are both fast and both regenerate the chlorine radical — a true catalyst of ozone destruction. Compare: natural cycles destroy ozone slowly; each chlorine atom multiplies the destruction by ~100,000× over its stratospheric lifetime (1–2 years before conversion to HCl reservoirs).

### 4.2 Why the hole is Antarctic

- Only the Antarctic gets the cold isolated vortex + PSCs + spring sunlight sequence. The Arctic's vortex is weaker and warmer, so depletion there is milder (though 2011 and 2020 saw Arctic "mini-holes").

### 4.3 The recovery scoreboard

- CFC atmospheric concentrations peaked ~1994 and are declining; the hole's September minimum shows slow healing (projected full recovery ~2066 for Antarctica); the 2023-published confirmation of declining CFC-11 attributed a bump to illegal East Asian production (now curbed).

## 5. Comparison Tables

**CFC vs HFC vs HCFC**

| Property | CFC | HCFC | HFC |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chlorine | Yes | Yes (weaker C–Cl) | None |
| ODP | 1.0 | ~0.05 | 0 |
| GWP | High | High | High (Kigali target) |
| Status | Banned | Phasing out | Phasing down |

**Causes ranked**

| Source | Active agent | Note |
|---|---|---|
| CFCs (refrigerants, aerosols, foam) | Cl• | Dominant cause |
| Halons (fire extinguishers) | Br• | ~45× more potent per atom |
| Methyl bromide (fumigant) | Br• | Agricultural |
| N₂O (fertilisers) | NO• cycle | Also greenhouse gas |

## 6. Common Confusions

**The chlorine atom is recycled, not consumed:** the classic error is writing Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂ as the end — the second step regenerating Cl• is what makes the cycle catalytic.
**The hole is thinning, not a literal hole:** "hole" means column ozone below ~220 DU — the layer thins dramatically; it does not vanish to zero.
**Ozone depletion ≠ global warming:** different mechanisms, though CFCs contribute to both; HFCs warm without depleting — conflating them loses analytical marks.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): What are CFCs? Explain with equations how they deplete the ozone layer.** — **CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons, freons)** such as CFCl₃ and CF₂Cl₂ are fully halogenated organic compounds once used as refrigerants, aerosol propellants and foam-blowing agents; they are chemically inert in the lower atmosphere and therefore survive to reach the stratosphere. **Depletion:** intense UV there breaks the C–Cl bond: CFCl₃ + UV → CFCl₂• + Cl•. The chlorine radical then destroys ozone catalytically: Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂, and ClO• + O → Cl• + O₂. Summing: O₃ + O → 2O₂ — ozone is destroyed while the chlorine atom is **regenerated**, so a single Cl atom can destroy tens of thousands of ozone molecules before being locked away in reservoirs such as ClONO₂.

**NEB-style (2m): State three harmful effects of ozone depletion and two control measures.** — **Effects:** (1) increased UV-B reaching the ground raises skin cancers (including melanoma) and eye cataracts; (2) damage to phytoplankton disturbs marine food chains and lowers crop yields; (3) faster degradation of plastics, paints and polymers outdoors. **Control measures:** (1) the **Montreal Protocol (1987)** and its amendments — international phase-out of CFC and halon production; (2) substitution by safe alternatives — HCFCs/HFCs transitionally and now HFOs, hydrocarbons, CO₂ or ammonia systems — plus recovery and recycling of old refrigerants rather than venting.

**NEB-style (2m): Why is the ozone hole found over Antarctica?** — The Antarctic winter creates an isolated, extremely cold (−80 °C) circumpolar vortex in which **polar stratospheric clouds** form; their ice surfaces convert the inactive chlorine reservoirs (ClONO₂, HCl) into molecular chlorine (Cl₂). When spring sunlight returns (September–October), Cl₂ is rapidly photolysed into chlorine radicals, which destroy ozone in the catalytic cycle — hence the deep, seasonal hole appears over Antarctica and not elsewhere.
confusion: ❌ All cells look the same under a microscope. ✅ Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells have them.
❌ DNA and RNA are identical in structure. ✅ DNA is double-stranded with deoxyribose and thymine; RNA is single-stranded with ribose and uracil.
❌ Mitosis produces genetically different cells. ✅ Mitosis produces genetically identical diploid daughter cells.
❌ Meiosis produces identical cells. ✅ Meiosis produces 4 genetically diverse haploid gametes.
❌ Crossing over occurs in mitosis. ✅ Crossing over occurs in Prophase I of meiosis only.
❌ All enzymes are proteins. ✅ Most enzymes are proteins; some RNA molecules (ribozymes) also have catalytic activity.
❌ ATP is the only energy currency. ✅ GTP, UTP, and CTP also serve as energy carriers in specific pathways.
❌ Photosynthesis occurs in all plant cells. ✅ Photosynthesis occurs only in cells containing chloroplasts (mainly mesophyll).
❌ Respiration and photosynthesis are opposite processes with same equation. ✅ They are complementary but occur in different organelles and under different conditions.
❌ Oxygen is produced during respiration. ✅ Oxygen is consumed in aerobic respiration; produced during photosynthesis.
❌ Food chain shows all feeding relationships. ✅ Food chain is linear; food web shows interconnected feeding relationships.
❌ 90% of energy is transferred to next trophic level. ✅ Only ~10% energy transfers; ~90% lost as heat.
❌ Biomagnification decreases toxin concentration up the food chain. ✅ Biomagnification increases toxin concentration at higher trophic levels.
❌ Carbon cycle only involves plants and animals. ✅ Carbon cycle involves atmosphere, oceans, fossils, rocks, and decomposers.
❌ Nitrogen fixation only occurs in bacteria. ✅ Some lightning and industrial processes (Haber) also fix nitrogen.
❌ All fungi are harmful. ✅ Many fungi are beneficial (decomposers, mycorrhizae, food, antibiotics like penicillin).
❌ Viruses are living organisms. ✅ Viruses are acellular — they cannot reproduce without a host and lack metabolism.
❌ Bacteria are always harmful. ✅ Most bacteria are harmless or beneficial (gut flora, nitrogen fixation, decomposition).
❌ Gram-positive and Gram-negative differ only in color. ✅ Gram-positive has thick peptidoglycan layer; Gram-negative has thin layer + outer membrane.
❌ Natural selection creates perfect organisms. ✅ Natural selection favors traits suited to current environment; environments change.
❌ Evolution is goal-oriented. ✅ Evolution has no goal; it acts on random variation filtered by selection.
❌ Homologous and analogous structures mean the same thing. ✅ Homologous = common ancestry (divergent); Analogous = similar function, different origin (convergent).
❌ Fossils are preserved bones only. ✅ Fossils include impressions, trace fossils, amber-preserved organisms, and molecular fossils.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Hole We Made and Are Closing

The ozone layer's depletion is chemistry's best-known environmental lesson: CFCs — once celebrated as miracle refrigerants — drift to the stratosphere, surrender chlorine atoms to UV, and each chlorine atom destroys tens of thousands of ozone molecules. This topic covers the causes, the Antarctic hole's mechanism, the effects, and the Montreal Protocol's control measures.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 The natural ozone balance

- Formation: O₂ + UV (< 242 nm) → 2O; O + O₂ → O₃.
- Destruction: O₃ + UV → O₂ + O; O₃ + O → 2O₂.
- In the unpolluted stratosphere formation and destruction balance — a steady ~300 DU (Dobson units) column.

### 2.2 Causes of depletion

- **CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons, freons: CFCl₃, CF₂Cl₂):** inert in the troposphere (that was their selling point), but UV in the stratosphere breaks the C–Cl bond: CFCl₃ + UV → CFCl₂• + Cl•.
- **The catalytic cycle:** Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂; ClO• + O → Cl• + O₂. Net: O₃ + O → 2O₂ — the chlorine atom is **regenerated**, so one Cl destroys ~100,000 O₃ molecules before it is sequestered (as ClONO₂ reservoirs).
- **Other culprits:** halons (bromine — even more efficient per atom), methyl bromide (pesticides), N₂O (nitrous oxide from fertilisers → NO catalytic cycle), carbon tetrachloride, methyl chloroform.

### 2.3 The Antarctic ozone hole

- **Polar stratospheric clouds (PSCs)** form in the Antarctic winter's −80 °C vortex; they convert inactive reservoirs (ClONO₂, HCl) into active Cl₂; spring sunlight (September–October) photolyses Cl₂ → 2Cl• — the hole opens.
- Discovered by Farman et al. (1985, British Antarctic Survey); column ozone fell below 100 DU at the minimum.

### 2.4 Effects

- **Human health:** more UV-B → skin cancers (melanoma), cataracts, immune suppression.
- **Ecosystems:** phytoplankton damage (marine food web base), crop yield losses, polymer degradation.
- **Climate interaction:** CFCs are also potent greenhouse gases (thousands of times CO₂'s warming power per kg).

### 2.5 Control measures

- **Montreal Protocol (1987):** phase-out schedule for CFCs and halons — universally ratified; amended (London, Copenhagen, Kigali) to cover HCFCs and HFCs.
- **Replacements:** HCFCs (transitional, lower ozone depletion potential), HFCs (zero ODP but greenhouse — Kigali 2016 phases them down), and newer options (HFO-1234yf, hydrocarbons, CO₂ systems, ammonia in industry).
- **Individual/national measures:** recover and recycle CFC refrigerants, ban CFC production, monitor with satellites (TOMS/OMI), halon banking.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **CFC** | Chlorofluorocarbon, fully halogenated alkane | CF₂Cl₂ (freon-12) |
| **ODP** | Ozone depletion potential relative to CFC-11 | CFC-11 = 1.0 |
| **Dobson unit** | Column ozone measure; 300 DU ≈ 3 mm pure O₃ at STP | Hole < 100 DU |
| **Polar stratospheric cloud** | Ice/nitric-acid clouds at −80 °C activating chlorine | Antarctic winter |
| **Reservoir species** | Inactive chlorine stores | ClONO₂, HCl |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why the catalytic cycle is so lethal

- The Cl• + O₃ and ClO• + O steps are both fast and both regenerate the chlorine radical — a true catalyst of ozone destruction. Compare: natural cycles destroy ozone slowly; each chlorine atom multiplies the destruction by ~100,000× over its stratospheric lifetime (1–2 years before conversion to HCl reservoirs).

### 4.2 Why the hole is Antarctic

- Only the Antarctic gets the cold isolated vortex + PSCs + spring sunlight sequence. The Arctic's vortex is weaker and warmer, so depletion there is milder (though 2011 and 2020 saw Arctic "mini-holes").

### 4.3 The recovery scoreboard

- CFC atmospheric concentrations peaked ~1994 and are declining; the hole's September minimum shows slow healing (projected full recovery ~2066 for Antarctica); the 2023-published confirmation of declining CFC-11 attributed a bump to illegal East Asian production (now curbed).

## 5. Comparison Tables

**CFC vs HFC vs HCFC**

| Property | CFC | HCFC | HFC |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chlorine | Yes | Yes (weaker C–Cl) | None |
| ODP | 1.0 | ~0.05 | 0 |
| GWP | High | High | High (Kigali target) |
| Status | Banned | Phasing out | Phasing down |

**Causes ranked**

| Source | Active agent | Note |
|---|---|---|
| CFCs (refrigerants, aerosols, foam) | Cl• | Dominant cause |
| Halons (fire extinguishers) | Br• | ~45× more potent per atom |
| Methyl bromide (fumigant) | Br• | Agricultural |
| N₂O (fertilisers) | NO• cycle | Also greenhouse gas |

## 6. Common Confusions

**The chlorine atom is recycled, not consumed:** the classic error is writing Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂ as the end — the second step regenerating Cl• is what makes the cycle catalytic.
**The hole is thinning, not a literal hole:** "hole" means column ozone below ~220 DU — the layer thins dramatically; it does not vanish to zero.
**Ozone depletion ≠ global warming:** different mechanisms, though CFCs contribute to both; HFCs warm without depleting — conflating them loses analytical marks.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): What are CFCs? Explain with equations how they deplete the ozone layer.** — **CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons, freons)** such as CFCl₃ and CF₂Cl₂ are fully halogenated organic compounds once used as refrigerants, aerosol propellants and foam-blowing agents; they are chemically inert in the lower atmosphere and therefore survive to reach the stratosphere. **Depletion:** intense UV there breaks the C–Cl bond: CFCl₃ + UV → CFCl₂• + Cl•. The chlorine radical then destroys ozone catalytically: Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂, and ClO• + O → Cl• + O₂. Summing: O₃ + O → 2O₂ — ozone is destroyed while the chlorine atom is **regenerated**, so a single Cl atom can destroy tens of thousands of ozone molecules before being locked away in reservoirs such as ClONO₂.

**NEB-style (2m): State three harmful effects of ozone depletion and two control measures.** — **Effects:** (1) increased UV-B reaching the ground raises skin cancers (including melanoma) and eye cataracts; (2) damage to phytoplankton disturbs marine food chains and lowers crop yields; (3) faster degradation of plastics, paints and polymers outdoors. **Control measures:** (1) the **Montreal Protocol (1987)** and its amendments — international phase-out of CFC and halon production; (2) substitution by safe alternatives — HCFCs/HFCs transitionally and now HFOs, hydrocarbons, CO₂ or ammonia systems — plus recovery and recycling of old refrigerants rather than venting.

**NEB-style (2m): Why is the ozone hole found over Antarctica?** — The Antarctic winter creates an isolated, extremely cold (−80 °C) circumpolar vortex in which **polar stratospheric clouds** form; their ice surfaces convert the inactive chlorine reservoirs (ClONO₂, HCl) into molecular chlorine (Cl₂). When spring sunlight returns (September–October), Cl₂ is rapidly photolysed into chlorine radicals, which destroy ozone in the catalytic cycle — hence the deep, seasonal hole appears over Antarctica and not elsewhere.

CFCs — prized precisely for their inertness — ride to the stratosphere where UV cracks their C–Cl bonds; the freed **Cl•** strips ozone (Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂) and is **regenerated** by ClO• + O → Cl• + O₂, so each atom destroys ~100,000 ozone molecules — net O₃ + O → 2O₂. confusion: ❌ All cells look the same under a microscope. ✅ Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells have them.
❌ DNA and RNA are identical in structure. ✅ DNA is double-stranded with deoxyribose and thymine; RNA is single-stranded with ribose and uracil.
❌ Mitosis produces genetically different cells. ✅ Mitosis produces genetically identical diploid daughter cells.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Triple Bond That Refuses to Break

Nitrogen is 78 % of every breath yet almost inert: its N≡N triple bond (941 kJ/mol) is among chemistry's strongest. This topic explains that inertness quantitatively, then shows the two ways chemistry defeats it — the violent "active nitrogen" of the electric discharge and the enzymatic miracle of nitrogen fixation.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Occurrence and preparation

- **Air:** 78.1 % by volume (N₂); combined: nitrates (Chile saltpetre NaNO₃), ammonium salts, proteins.
- **Laboratory:** heating ammonium dichromate (green-route volcano): (NH₄)₂Cr₂O₇ → N₂ + Cr₂O₃ + 4H₂O; or NH₄Cl + NaNO₂ solution warmed: NH₄Cl + NaNO₂ → N₂ + NaCl + 2H₂O.
- **Industrial:** fractional distillation of liquid air (N₂ bp −196 °C vs O₂ −183 °C).

### 2.2 Reason for inertness — the NEB core answer

1. **Triple bond energy:** N≡N bond dissociation energy = 941 kJ/mol — one of the strongest bonds known; breaking it costs enormous energy.
2. **Short bond length:** 110 pm; the small atoms overlap strongly.
3. **Non-polarity:** the symmetrical N₂ molecule has no dipole, so it is barely solvated or polarised — weak interactions with reagents.
4. **High ionisation energy** and stable electronic configuration (each N has a lone pair + 3 shared pairs — full octet per atom within the molecule).
- Consequence: N₂ reacts only with the most aggressive partners — Li (6 Li + N₂ → 2Li₃N at room temperature, the only alkali metal to do so), Mg burning in air (Mg₃N₂), O₂ under lightning/Haber conditions, H₂ at high T/P with catalyst.

### 2.3 Active nitrogen

- Passing N₂ through an **electric discharge** at low pressure excites the molecule into energetic atomic/molecular states; the glowing yellow "active nitrogen" recombines, emitting light, and reacts with metals, H₂S, and even water vapour — chemistry the ground-state molecule refuses.
- Active nitrogen's reactivity comes from stored electronic excitation energy (metastable states) that substitutes for the bond-breaking cost.

### 2.4 Nitrogen fixation — beating the bond biologically

- **Nitrogen-fixing bacteria** (Rhizobium in legume root nodules, free-living Azotobacter, cyanobacteria) use the enzyme **nitrogenase** to convert N₂ → NH₃ at ambient temperature and pressure — chemistry the Haber process needs 450 °C/200 atm to force.
- Lightning's discharge also fixes nitrogen naturally (N₂ + O₂ → 2NO, then to nitrates delivered by rain).

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Triple bond** | Three shared electron pairs, σ + 2π | N≡N, 941 kJ/mol |
| **Active nitrogen** | Excited-state nitrogen from electric discharge | Glowing yellow glow in discharge tube |
| **Nitrogen fixation** | Conversion of N₂ to combined nitrogen | Rhizobium → NH₃ |
| **Nitrogenase** | Enzyme complex reducing N₂ at ambient conditions | Fe-Mo cofactor |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 The bond-energy ledger

- To react N₂ with H₂ (Haber), the 941 kJ/mol bond must be broken before N–H bonds (386 kJ/mol each, ×3) can form — the balance only tips with high temperature, high pressure and an iron catalyst; and even then the equilibrium is unfavourable, which is why the process is a masterpiece of compromise.

### 4.2 Why lithium is special

- Li⁺ is tiny and Li₃N is extremely stable (lattice energy compensates the bond-breaking cost); the reaction runs even at room temperature — a favourite exam contrast with Na, K, Rb, Cs which need heating.

### 4.3 Active nitrogen in the discharge tube

- Low-pressure N₂ + discharge → pink-yellow afterglow persisting seconds after the discharge stops — metastable N atoms recombining. This "active nitrogen" attacks H₂S (giving NH₃ + S), metals (nitrides), and hydrocarbons — demonstrating that inertness is kinetic, not absolute.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Inert vs active nitrogen**

| Basis | Ordinary N₂ | Active nitrogen |
|---|---|---|
| State | Ground-state molecule | Excited atoms/molecules |
| Source | Air | Electric discharge, low pressure |
| Reaction with H₂S | None | NH₃ + S |
| Glow | None | Yellow afterglow |

**Natural vs industrial fixation**

| Basis | Biological (nitrogenase) | Haber process |
|---|---|---|
| Conditions | 25 °C, 1 atm | 450 °C, 200 atm, Fe catalyst |
| Energy | ATP from respiration | Fossil fuel |
| Product | NH₃ into amino acids | NH₃ for fertiliser |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Inertness is kinetic, not thermodynamic:** N₂ → NH₃ is thermodynamically favourable (ΔG negative) but kinetically blocked by the triple bond — that distinction is the analytical heart of the answer.
**Active nitrogen is not ionised nitrogen:** it is electronically excited N atoms/molecules from the discharge — no net charge involved.
**Nitrogen's non-polarity matters:** quoting only the bond energy misses the second reason (no dipole → weak intermolecular attraction with reagents); full answers cite both.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): Why is molecular nitrogen inert at ordinary conditions?** — **(1) The triple bond:** N₂ contains an N≡N triple bond with a very high dissociation energy of about 941 kJ/mol — among the strongest bonds in chemistry — so breaking it requires enormous energy that ordinary conditions cannot supply. **(2) Short bond length:** the bond is only 110 pm long, the small nitrogen atoms overlapping very strongly. **(3) Non-polar symmetry:** the molecule has zero dipole moment, so it interacts only weakly with other reactants (poor solvation, poor polarisation). **(4) Complete octets:** each nitrogen atom already has an octet (one lone pair plus three shared pairs) within the molecule, so there is no driving force to react. Hence N₂ reacts only under forcing conditions (Haber process: 450 °C, 200 atm, Fe catalyst) or with very electropositive partners (Li at room temperature: 6Li + N₂ → 2Li₃N).

**NEB-style (2m): What is active nitrogen? How is it prepared and how does it differ from ordinary nitrogen?** — **Active nitrogen** is nitrogen in an electronically excited, highly reactive state, produced by passing nitrogen gas at **low pressure through an electric discharge**; it glows with a characteristic yellow afterglow that persists briefly after the discharge stops. **Differences:** ordinary N₂ is inert — it does not react with H₂S, metals or water vapour at ordinary conditions — whereas active nitrogen reacts readily: it converts H₂S to NH₃ and sulphur, forms nitrides with metals, and attacks many substances at room temperature, because the excitation energy it carries substitutes for the enormous energy otherwise needed to break the N≡N triple bond.

**NEB-style (2m): How do nitrogen-fixing bacteria manage to fix nitrogen at ordinary conditions while industry needs 450 °C and 200 atm?** — Nitrogen-fixing bacteria (e.g. *Rhizobium* in legume root nodules) possess the enzyme complex **nitrogenase**, which binds N₂ at an iron–molybdenum cofactor and reduces it stepwise to ammonia using electrons and ATP from the plant's respiration — all at ambient temperature and pressure. The enzyme's active site weakens and progressively hydrogenates the triple bond without ever requiring its full 941 kJ/mol to be supplied at once. Industry, lacking such catalysis, must force the same overall reaction (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃) with high temperature, high pressure and an iron catalyst — and even then the equilibrium is only moderately favourable.

How is it prepared and how does it differ in reactivity from ordinary nitrogen?** — **Active nitrogen** is nitrogen in an electronically excited, unusually reactive state. The enzyme's active site holds and progressively hydrogenates the triple bond, so the full 941 kJ/mol never has to be supplied at once, and the ATP from the plant's respiration drives the process at **ambient temperature and pressure**. The industrial Haber process, lacking such sophisticated catalysis, must compensate with high temperature (~450 °C), high pressure (~200 atm) and an iron catalyst — and even then the equilibrium conversion per pass remains modest.

data.summary: Nitrogen dominates the atmosphere and refuses to join it. Its inertness is a four-reason argument: the **N≡N triple bond at 941 kJ/mol** (bond length 110 pm), the molecule's **zero dipole moment** (weak grip on reagents), the **complete octets** inside N₂, and hence a purely **kinetic block** — N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ is thermodynamically downhill yet needs the Haber process's 450 °C, 200 atm and iron to run at all. The exceptions prove the accounting: **lithium** nitridises cold (6Li + N₂ → 2Li₃N) because its nitride's lattice energy repays the bond cost, and burning magnesium sneaks in Mg₃N₂. **Active nitrogen** shows the block is surmountable by energy storage: a low-pressure electric discharge excites N₂ into a yellow-glowing state that attacks H₂S, metals and hydrocarbons the ground-state molecule ignores. And biology runs the ultimate workaround: **nitrogenase** (Fe–Mo cofactor) in *Rhizobium* and *Azotobacter* reduces N₂ to NH₃ at ambient conditions using ATP — fixing 100+ kg/ha/year in legume fields where industry must burn fuel to match. Preparation routes — ammonium dichromate's volcano, NH₄Cl/NaNO₂, and liquid-air distillation (N₂ bp −196 °C) — supply the gas for all of it.

practiceQuestions: **NEB-style (3m): Why is molecular nitrogen inert at ordinary conditions? Support your answer with one reaction showing an exception.** — **(1) Very high bond energy:** the N≡N triple bond has a dissociation energy of about **941 kJ/mol**, one of the strongest bonds known, so breaking it demands energy unavailable under ordinary conditions. **(2) Short bond length:** at 110 pm the two small nitrogen atoms overlap very strongly, reinforcing the bond. **(3) Non-polar molecule:** N₂ has zero dipole moment due to its symmetry, so it is poorly solvated and only weakly attracted to (or polarised by) reagents. **(4) Stable octets:** each nitrogen atom already possesses an octet — one lone pair plus three shared pairs — within the molecule, leaving no electronic drive to react. The inertness is therefore **kinetic**: reactions like N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ are thermodynamically favoured but kinetically blocked, and proceed only under forcing conditions (Haber: ~450 °C, 200 atm, iron catalyst). **Exception:** lithium, the most electropositive alkali metal with a very small cation, reacts at **room temperature**: 6Li + N₂ → 2Li₃N — the extreme lattice energy of Li₃N repays the bond-breaking cost; magnesium burning in air also forms Mg₃N₂.

**NEB-style (2m): What is active nitrogen? How is it prepared and how does it differ in reactivity from ordinary nitrogen?** — **Active nitrogen** is nitrogen in an electronically excited, unusually reactive state. It is prepared by passing nitrogen gas at **low pressure through an electric discharge** (or a hot filament); the gas then glows with a characteristic **yellow afterglow** that persists for several seconds after the discharge ceases, caused by metastable excited nitrogen atoms and molecules recombining. **Difference in reactivity:** ordinary N₂ is almost completely inert — it does not react with hydrogen sulphide, most metals, or water vapour at ordinary temperatures. Active nitrogen, carrying stored excitation energy that substitutes for the ~941 kJ/mol needed to break the triple bond, reacts readily at room temperature: it converts H₂S into NH₃ and sulphur, forms nitrides with many metals, and attacks hydrocarbons — demonstrating that nitrogen's inertness is kinetic rather than absolute.

**NEB-style (2m): How does biological nitrogen fixation achieve at ordinary conditions what the Haber process needs 450 °C and 200 atm to do?** — Nitrogen-fixing microorganisms — *Rhizobium* bacteria in the root nodules of legumes, free-living *Azotobacter*, and cyanobacteria — contain the enzyme complex **nitrogenase**, whose iron–molybdenum cofactor binds the N₂ molecule and reduces it stepwise to ammonia: N₂ + 8H⁺ + 8e⁻ + 16ATP → 2NH₃ + H₂ + 16ADP. The enzyme's active site holds and progressively hydrogenates the triple bond, so the full 941 kJ/mol never has to be supplied at once, and the ATP from the plant's respiration drives the process at **ambient temperature and pressure**. The industrial Haber process, lacking such sophisticated catalysis, must compensate with high temperature (~450 °C), high pressure (~200 atm) and an iron catalyst — and even then the equilibrium conversion per pass remains modest.

importantConcepts: Inertness is a rate problem, not a stability problem: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ is downhill in free energy yet blocked for centuries by 941 kJ/mol of bond energy — catalysts and enzymes are the only ways through.
importantStatements: "The inertness of nitrogen is due to the very high bond dissociation energy of its triple bond and its non-polar character."

confusion: ❌ All cells look the same under a microscope. ✅ Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells have them.
❌ DNA and RNA are identical in structure. ✅ DNA is double-stranded with deoxyribose and thymine; RNA is single-stranded with ribose and uracil.
❌ Mitosis produces genetically different cells. ✅ Mitosis produces genetically identical diploid daughter cells.
❌ Meiosis produces identical cells. ✅ Meiosis produces 4 genetically diverse haploid gametes.
❌ Crossing over occurs in mitosis. ✅ Crossing over occurs in Prophase I of meiosis only.
❌ All enzymes are proteins. ✅ Most enzymes are proteins; some RNA molecules (ribozymes) also have catalytic activity.
❌ ATP is the only energy currency. ✅ GTP, UTP, and CTP also serve as energy carriers in specific pathways.
❌ Photosynthesis occurs in all plant cells. ✅ Photosynthesis occurs only in cells containing chloroplasts (mainly mesophyll).
❌ Respiration and photosynthesis are opposite processes with same equation. ✅ They are complementary but occur in different organelles and under different conditions.
❌ Oxygen is produced during respiration. ✅ Oxygen is consumed in aerobic respiration; produced during photosynthesis.
❌ Food chain shows all feeding relationships. ✅ Food chain is linear; food web shows interconnected feeding relationships.
❌ 90% of energy is transferred to next trophic level. ✅ Only ~10% energy transfers; ~90% lost as heat.
❌ Biomagnification decreases toxin concentration up the food chain. ✅ Biomagnification increases toxin concentration at higher trophic levels.
❌ Carbon cycle only involves plants and animals. ✅ Carbon cycle involves atmosphere, oceans, fossils, rocks, and decomposers.
❌ Nitrogen fixation only occurs in bacteria. ✅ Some lightning and industrial processes (Haber) also fix nitrogen.
❌ All fungi are harmful. ✅ Many fungi are beneficial (decomposers, mycorrhizae, food, antibiotics like penicillin).
❌ Viruses are living organisms. ✅ Viruses are acellular — they cannot reproduce without a host and lack metabolism.
❌ Bacteria are always harmful. ✅ Most bacteria are harmless or beneficial (gut flora, nitrogen fixation, decomposition).
❌ Gram-positive and Gram-negative differ only in color. ✅ Gram-positive has thick peptidoglycan layer; Gram-negative has thin layer + outer membrane.
❌ Natural selection creates perfect organisms. ✅ Natural selection favors traits suited to current environment; environments change.
❌ Evolution is goal-oriented. ✅ Evolution has no goal; it acts on random variation filtered by selection.
❌ Homologous and analogous structures mean the same thing. ✅ Homologous = common ancestry (divergent); Analogous = similar function, different origin (convergent).
❌ Fossils are preserved bones only. ✅ Fossils include impressions, trace fossils, amber-preserved organisms, and molecular fossils.
❌ Lamarckism is completely wrong. ✅ Lamarck's inheritance of acquired characteristics is largely rejected, but epigenetics shows some environmental effects can be inherited.
❌ Five-kingdom classification is outdated. ✅ Six-kingdom (adding Archaea) and phylogenetic systems are more current, but five-kingdom remains useful for education.
❌ Binomial nomenclature names change frequently. ✅ Names are stable once formally published; changes require formal revision by taxonomic authorities.
❌ All algae are aquatic. ✅ Some algae live in soil, on tree bark, or in symbiotic relationships (lichens).
❌ Bryophytes have vascular tissue. ✅ Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts, hornworts) lack true vascular tissue (xylem/phloem).
❌ Gymnosperms produce flowers. ✅ Gymnosperms have naked seeds in cones; angiosperms produce flowers and enclosed seeds.
❌ Double fertilization occurs in gymnosperms. ✅ Double fertilization (zygote + endosperm) is unique to angiosperms.
❌ Earthworms have an open circulatory system. ✅ Earthworms have a closed circulatory system with dorsal and ventral vessels.
❌ Frogs breathe only through lungs. ✅ Frogs use cutaneous respiration (skin), buccal cavity, and lungs.
❌ Conservation only means protecting animals. ✅ Conservation includes genetic, species, and ecosystem diversity; in-situ and ex-situ strategies.
❌ In-situ and ex-situ conservation are the same. ✅ In-situ = conservation in natural habitat (national parks); Ex-situ = conservation outside habitat (zoos, seed banks).

data.topicTitle: Chemical properties of ammonia (action with CuSO4 solution, water, FeCl3 solution, conc. HCl, mercurous nitrate paper, O2); applications and harmful effects of ammonia
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Gas That Feeds and Chokes

Ammonia is nitrogen's most useful compound — fertiliser feedstock, refrigerant, laboratory base — and its chemistry with CuSO₄, water, FeCl₃, concentrated HCl, mercurous nitrate paper and oxygen is a standard NEB checklist. This topic runs the reaction list, then weighs its applications against its hazards.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Preparation and structure

- **Laboratory:** heating an ammonium salt with an alkali: 2NH₄Cl + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O + 2NH₃ (dried over quicklime CaO — never conc. H₂SO₄, which absorbs it).
- **Industrial (Haber):** N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, 450 °C, 200 atm, Fe catalyst.
- **Structure:** pyramidal, sp³ nitrogen with one lone pair, bond angle 107°; the lone pair drives every reaction — basicity, complexation, hydrogen bonding (bp −33 °C, unusually high for its mass).

### 2.2 The NEB reaction checklist

| Reagent | Equation | Observation |
|---|---|---|
| **CuSO₄ solution (excess NH₃)** | CuSO₄ + 2NH₄OH → Cu(OH)₂↓ + (NH₄)₂SO₄; Cu(OH)₂ + 4NH₃ → [Cu(NH₃)₄]SO₄ (dissolves) | pale blue ppt dissolving to deep blue solution |
| **Water** | NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄OH ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ | alkaline solution, turns red litmus blue; fountain experiment |
| **FeCl₃ solution** | FeCl₃ + 3NH₄OH → Fe(OH)₃↓ + 3NH₄Cl | reddish-brown ppt, insoluble in excess |
| **Conc. HCl** | NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl | white fumes/ring (glass rod dipped in NH₄OH) |
| **Mercurous nitrate paper** | 2Hg₂(NO₃)₂ + 4NH₃ + H₂O → [NHg₂]₂O? — practical form: blackening due to Millon's base formation | paper turns black — test for NH₃ |
| **O₂ (burning)** | 4NH₃ + 3O₂ → 2N₂ + 6H₂O (without catalyst); 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O (Pt, 800 °C — Ostwald) | yellow-green flame; catalytic oxidation to NO |

### 2.3 Applications

- **Fertilisers:** urea, ammonium sulphate, ammonium nitrate, ammonium phosphate — the largest use (~80 % of production).
- **Refrigerant:** large latent heat of vaporisation (1370 kJ/kg at bp), non-CFC — cold-storage plants and ice plants.
- **Chemical feedstock:** nitric acid (Ostwald), ammonium nitrate (explosives), sodium carbonate (Solvay), nylon via caprolactam.
- **Laboratory reagent:** NH₄OH in qualitative analysis (precipitating and complexing hydroxides).

### 2.4 Harmful effects

- **Toxicity:** irritates eyes and respiratory tract; 2500+ ppm life-threatening; suffocating in enclosed spaces.
- **Environmental:** ammonia run-off from fertilisers causes eutrophication of water bodies; volatilised NH₃ contributes to acid deposition (NH₄⁺ → NOₓ chemistry) and PM2.5.
- **Explosion risk:** NH₃–air mixtures (15–28 % NH₃) are flammable; refrigeration leaks dangerous.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Lewis base** | Lone-pair donor | NH₃ → H⁺; NH₃ → Cu²⁺ |
| **Complex ion** | Central ion + ligands | [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ deep blue |
| **Fountain experiment** | NH₃'s extreme water solubility demonstrated | Water jet rises into flask |
| **Ostwald oxidation** | Catalytic NH₃ → NO step of HNO₃ | Pt gauze, 800 °C |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 The CuSO₄ two-step

- NH₄OH first precipitates pale-blue Cu(OH)₂; **excess** ammonia then dissolves it as the deep-blue tetraammine complex [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ — the solubility-in-excess is the distinguishing observation (contrast Fe(OH)₃, insoluble in excess).

### 4.2 Why the HCl white ring works

- NH₃ and HCl gases meet and form fine NH₄Cl particles — a solid aerosol, seen as white smoke. Glass rod dipped in concentrated NH₄OH near open HCl bottle: instant white fumes — the classic ammonia test.

### 4.3 The two oxygen reactions

- Without catalyst NH₃ burns in O₂ with a yellowish-green flame to **N₂**: 4NH₃ + 3O₂ → 2N₂ + 6H₂O.
- Over heated platinum (Ostwald step), oxidation goes to **NO**: 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O — the gateway to nitric acid (topic 65).

### 4.4 The mercurous nitrate test

- Ammonia blackens mercurous nitrate paper: Hg₂²⁺ is reduced/aminated to finely divided black nitrogen-containing mercury compounds (Millon's base chemistry, Hg₂N•H₂O related species) — a sensitive confirmatory test.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Fe(OH)₃ vs Cu(OH)₂ with excess NH₄OH**

| Basis | Fe(OH)₃ | Cu(OH)₂ |
|---|---|---|
| Colour | Reddish-brown | Pale blue |
| In excess NH₄OH | Insoluble | Dissolves → deep blue [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ |
| Complexation | No ammine complex | Strong ammine complex |

**NH₃ as refrigerant vs CFCs**

| Basis | NH₃ | CFCs |
|---|---|---|
| Latent heat | Very high (1370 kJ/kg) | Moderate |
| Ozone impact | None | Depleting (now banned) |
| Toxicity | Toxic, flammable | Safe but ozone-killer |
| Use today | Industrial plants | Phased out |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Excess reagent matters:** with CuSO₄, "blue precipitate" is only half the story — the deep-blue *solution* in excess NH₄OH is the observation that earns the complex-ion mark.
**Drying agent choice:** drying NH₃ over conc. H₂SO₄ or CaCl₂ destroys it (both absorb it); only **quicklime CaO** works — a permanent NEB trap.
**The two O₂ products:** uncatalysed burning gives N₂; catalytic (Pt) oxidation gives NO — quoting the wrong one for the wrong condition costs the equation.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): What happens when ammonia is passed into copper sulphate solution — first in limited and then in excess amount? Give equations.** — **Limited ammonia (as NH₄OH):** the hydroxide it generates precipitates pale-blue copper(II) hydroxide: CuSO₄ + 2NH₄OH → Cu(OH)₂↓ + (NH₄)₂SO₄. **Excess ammonia:** the precipitate dissolves because ammonia ligands replace water around Cu²⁺, forming the deep-blue soluble complex tetraamminecopper(II) sulphate: Cu(OH)₂ + 4NH₃ → [Cu(NH₃)₄]SO₄. The final deep-blue clear solution is the diagnostic observation distinguishing copper from iron(III), whose brown hydroxide stays insoluble in excess.

**NEB-style (2m): A glass rod dipped in concentrated ammonium hydroxide brought near the mouth of a bottle of concentrated hydrochloric acid produces white fumes. Explain with equation.** — Ammonia vapour from the rod meets hydrogen chloride vapour from the bottle; they combine directly to form minute solid particles of ammonium chloride, seen as dense white fumes (and as the "white ring" in the gas-jar demonstration): **NH₃(g) + HCl(g) → NH₄Cl(s)**. This is a standard confirmatory test for ammonia gas.

**NEB-style (2m): Why is ammonia used as a refrigerant? State two of its harmful effects.** — **Refrigerant:** ammonia has a very **high latent heat of vaporisation** (about 1370 kJ/kg at its boiling point, −33 °C), so it absorbs large amounts of heat when it evaporates — ideal for the compression–expansion refrigeration cycle; it is also cheap and free of ozone-depleting chlorine, which is why cold-storage and ice plants still use it. **Harmful effects:** (1) it is **toxic and irritating** — even moderate concentrations attack the eyes and respiratory tract, and 15–28 % mixtures with air are flammable; (2) **environmentally**, ammonia run-off and volatilisation from fertilisers cause eutrophication of lakes and contribute to acidification and secondary particulate (PM2.5) formation.

practiceQuestions: **NEB-style (3m): What happens when ammonia is passed into copper sulphate solution, first in limited amount and then in excess? Give equations and observations.** — **Limited ammonia (added as ammonium hydroxide):** the OH⁻ ions generated by NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄OH ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ precipitate pale-blue copper(II) hydroxide: **CuSO₄ + 2NH₄OH → Cu(OH)₂↓ + (NH₄)₂SO₄** — a pale blue precipitate forms. **Excess ammonia:** ammonia molecules act as ligands, coordinating to Cu²⁺ and dissolving the hydroxide as the deep-blue complex **tetraamminecopper(II) sulphate: Cu(OH)₂ + 4NH₃ → [Cu(NH₃)₄]SO₄** — the precipitate disappears and the solution turns an intense royal blue. This "dissolves in excess to deep blue" behaviour is diagnostic for copper(II) ions; by contrast, the reddish-brown Fe(OH)₃ obtained from FeCl₃ + 3NH₄OH → Fe(OH)₃↓ + 3NH₄Cl remains insoluble in excess ammonia.

**NEB-style (2m): A glass rod dipped in concentrated ammonium hydroxide and brought near the mouth of a bottle of concentrated hydrochloric acid produces dense white fumes. Explain with an equation.** — The rod releases **ammonia vapour** and the bottle releases **hydrogen chloride vapour**; where the two gases meet they combine directly to form extremely fine solid particles of **ammonium chloride**, which scatter light and appear as dense white fumes (in a gas jar the same chemistry draws the famous "white ring"): **NH₃(g) + HCl(g) → NH₄Cl(s)**. Because no other common gas gives this instant white smoke with HCl vapour, it serves as a confirmatory test for ammonia.

**NEB-style (2m): Why is ammonia used as a refrigerant in cold-storage plants? Mention two harmful effects of ammonia.** — **Refrigerant use:** ammonia has an exceptionally **high latent heat of vaporisation** — about 1370 kJ/kg at its normal boiling point of −33 °C — so each kilogram evaporating absorbs a large quantity of heat, making the compression–expansion cycle highly effective; it is also cheap, chemically stable in the cycle, and contains **no chlorine**, so unlike CFCs it does not deplete the ozone layer — reasons it remains the working fluid of industrial ice plants and cold storages. **Harmful effects:** (1) **Toxicity and flammability:** ammonia strongly irritates the eyes, skin and respiratory tract (concentrations above ~2500 ppm are life-threatening), and mixtures with air containing 15–28 % ammonia are flammable, so leaks are dangerous. (2) **Environmental damage:** ammonia lost from over-applied fertilisers runs into water bodies causing **eutrophication** (algal blooms, oxygen depletion), and volatilised NH₃ contributes to soil acidification and to secondary fine particulate (PM2.5) formation in the atmosphere.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Gas That Feeds and Chokes

Ammonia is nitrogen's most useful compound — fertiliser feedstock, refrigerant, laboratory base — and its chemistry with CuSO₄, water, FeCl₃, concentrated HCl, mercurous nitrate paper and oxygen is a standard NEB checklist. This topic runs the reaction list, then weighs its applications against its hazards.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Preparation and structure

- **Laboratory:** heating an ammonium salt with an alkali: 2NH₄Cl + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O + 2NH₃ (dried over quicklime CaO — never conc. H₂SO₄, which absorbs it).
- **Industrial (Haber):** N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, 450 °C, 200 atm, Fe catalyst.
- **Structure:** pyramidal, sp³ nitrogen with one lone pair, bond angle 107°; the lone pair drives every reaction — basicity, complexation, hydrogen bonding (bp −33 °C, unusually high for its mass).

### 2.2 The NEB reaction checklist

| Reagent | Equation | Observation |
|---|---|---|
| **CuSO₄ solution (excess NH₃)** | CuSO₄ + 2NH₄OH → Cu(OH)₂↓ + (NH₄)₂SO₄; Cu(OH)₂ + 4NH₃ → [Cu(NH₃)₄]SO₄ (dissolves) | pale blue ppt dissolving to deep blue solution |
| **Water** | NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄OH ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ | alkaline solution, turns red litmus blue; fountain experiment |
| **FeCl₃ solution** | FeCl₃ + 3NH₄OH → Fe(OH)₃↓ + 3NH₄Cl | reddish-brown ppt, insoluble in excess |
| **Conc. HCl** | NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl | white fumes/ring (glass rod dipped in NH₄OH) |
| **Mercurous nitrate paper** | 2Hg₂(NO₃)₂ + 4NH₃ + H₂O → [NHg₂]₂O? — practical form: blackening due to Millon's base formation | paper turns black — test for NH₃ |
| **O₂ (burning)** | 4NH₃ + 3O₂ → 2N₂ + 6H₂O (without catalyst); 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O (Pt, 800 °C — Ostwald) | yellow-green flame; catalytic oxidation to NO |

### 2.3 Applications

- **Fertilisers:** urea, ammonium sulphate, ammonium nitrate, ammonium phosphate — the largest use (~80 % of production).
- **Refrigerant:** large latent heat of vaporisation (1370 kJ/kg at bp), non-CFC — cold-storage plants and ice plants.
- **Chemical feedstock:** nitric acid (Ostwald), ammonium nitrate (explosives), sodium carbonate (Solvay), nylon via caprolactam.
- **Laboratory reagent:** NH₄OH in qualitative analysis (precipitating and complexing hydroxides).

### 2.4 Harmful effects

- **Toxicity:** irritates eyes and respiratory tract; 2500+ ppm life-threatening; suffocating in enclosed spaces.
- **Environmental:** ammonia run-off from fertilisers causes eutrophication of water bodies; volatilised NH₃ contributes to acid deposition (NH₄⁺ → NOₓ chemistry) and PM2.5.
- **Explosion risk:** NH₃–air mixtures (15–28 % NH₃) are flammable; refrigeration leaks dangerous.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Lewis base** | Lone-pair donor | NH₃ → H⁺; NH₃ → Cu²⁺ |
| **Complex ion** | Central ion + ligands | [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ deep blue |
| **Fountain experiment** | NH₃'s extreme water solubility demonstrated | Water jet rises into flask |
| **Ostwald oxidation** | Catalytic NH₃ → NO step of HNO₃ | Pt gauze, 800 °C |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 The CuSO₄ two-step

- NH₄OH first precipitates pale-blue Cu(OH)₂; **excess** ammonia then dissolves it as the deep-blue tetraammine complex [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ — the solubility-in-excess is the distinguishing observation (contrast Fe(OH)₃, insoluble in excess).

### 4.2 Why the HCl white ring works

- NH₃ and HCl gases meet and form fine NH₄Cl particles — a solid aerosol, seen as white smoke. Glass rod dipped in concentrated NH₄OH near open HCl bottle: instant white fumes — the classic ammonia test.

### 4.3 The two oxygen reactions

- Without catalyst NH₃ burns in O₂ with a yellowish-green flame to **N₂**: 4NH₃ + 3O₂ → 2N₂ + 6H₂O.
- Over heated platinum (Ostwald step), oxidation goes to **NO**: 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O — the gateway to nitric acid (topic 65).

### 4.4 The mercurous nitrate test

- Ammonia blackens mercurous nitrate paper: Hg₂²⁺ is reduced/aminated to finely divided black nitrogen-containing mercury compounds (Millon's base chemistry, Hg₂N•H₂O related species) — a sensitive confirmatory test.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Fe(OH)₃ vs Cu(OH)₂ with excess NH₄OH**

| Basis | Fe(OH)₃ | Cu(OH)₂ |
|---|---|---|
| Colour | Reddish-brown | Pale blue |
| In excess NH₄OH | Insoluble | Dissolves → deep blue [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ |
| Complexation | No ammine complex | Strong ammine complex |

**NH₃ as refrigerant vs CFCs**

| Basis | NH₃ | CFCs |
|---|---|---|
| Latent heat | Very high (1370 kJ/kg) | Moderate |
| Ozone impact | None | Depleting (now banned) |
| Toxicity | Toxic, flammable | Safe but ozone-killer |
| Use today | Industrial plants | Phased out |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Excess reagent matters:** with CuSO₄, "blue precipitate" is only half the story — the deep-blue *solution* in excess NH₄OH is the observation that earns the complex-ion mark.
**Drying agent choice:** drying NH₃ over conc. H₂SO₄ or CaCl₂ destroys it (both absorb it); only **quicklime CaO** works — a permanent NEB trap.
**The two O₂ products:** uncatalysed burning gives N₂; catalytic (Pt) oxidation gives NO — quoting the wrong one for the wrong condition costs the equation.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): What happens when ammonia is passed into copper sulphate solution — first in limited and then in excess amount? Give equations.** — **Limited ammonia (as NH₄OH):** the hydroxide it generates precipitates pale-blue copper(II) hydroxide: CuSO₄ + 2NH₄OH → Cu(OH)₂↓ + (NH₄)₂SO₄. **Excess ammonia:** the precipitate dissolves because ammonia ligands replace water around Cu²⁺, forming the deep-blue soluble complex tetraamminecopper(II) sulphate: Cu(OH)₂ + 4NH₃ → [Cu(NH₃)₄]SO₄. The final deep-blue clear solution is the diagnostic observation distinguishing copper from iron(III), whose brown hydroxide stays insoluble in excess.

**NEB-style (2m): A glass rod dipped in concentrated ammonium hydroxide brought near the mouth of a bottle of concentrated hydrochloric acid produces white fumes. Explain with equation.** — Ammonia vapour from the rod meets hydrogen chloride vapour from the bottle; they combine directly to form minute solid particles of ammonium chloride, seen as dense white fumes (and as the "white ring" in the gas-jar demonstration): **NH₃(g) + HCl(g) → NH₄Cl(s)**. This is a standard confirmatory test for ammonia gas.

**NEB-style (2m): Why is ammonia used as a refrigerant? State two of its harmful effects.** — **Refrigerant:** ammonia has a very **high latent heat of vaporisation** (about 1370 kJ/kg at its boiling point, −33 °C), so it absorbs large amounts of heat when it evaporates — ideal for the compression–expansion refrigeration cycle; it is also cheap and free of ozone-depleting chlorine, which is why cold-storage and ice plants still use it. **Harmful effects:** (1) it is **toxic and irritating** — even moderate concentrations attack the eyes and respiratory tract, and 15–28 % mixtures with air are flammable; (2) **environmentally**, ammonia run-off and volatilisation from fertilisers cause eutrophication of lakes and contribute to acidification and secondary particulate (PM2.5) formation.

Mention two harmful effects of ammonia.** — **Refrigerant use:** ammonia has an exceptionally **high latent heat of vaporisation** — about 1370 kJ/kg at its normal boiling point of −33 °C — so each kilogram evaporating absorbs a large quantity of heat, making the compression–expansion cycle highly effective; it is also cheap, chemically stable in the cycle, and contains **no chlorine**, so unlike CFCs it does not deplete the ozone layer — reasons it remains the working fluid of industrial ice plants and cold storages. **Harmful effects:** (1) **Toxicity and flammability:** ammonia strongly irritates the eyes, skin and respiratory tract (concentrations above ~2500 ppm are life-threatening), and mixtures with air containing 15–28 % ammonia are flammable, so leaks are dangerous. confusion: ❌ All atoms are identical in an element. ✅ Isotopes have same protons but different neutrons.
❌ Atoms are indivisible. ✅ Atoms consist of protons, neutrons, and electrons.
❌ Electrons orbit in fixed paths like planets. ✅ Electrons exist in probability clouds (orbitals).
❌ Heisenberg uncertainty means we cannot measure position and momentum precisely simultaneously — not that we lack good instruments.
❌ de Broglie wavelength applies only to light. ✅ All matter has wave nature; detectable mainly for small masses like electrons.
❌ Quantum number l can be any integer. ✅ l ranges from 0 to n−1.
❌ Magnetic quantum number ml determines energy. ✅ ml determines orbital orientation, not energy (in absence of magnetic field).
❌ Spin quantum number ms can be ±½ or any value. ✅ ms is always +½ or −½.
❌ Aufbau principle means filling from bottom to top of the diagram. ✅ Fill lowest-energy orbitals first: 1s→2s→2p→3s→3p→4s→3d→4p→...
❌ Pauli exclusion allows two electrons per orbital with any spin. ✅ Two electrons in same orbital must have opposite spins.
❌ Hund's rule means pair electrons before spreading. ✅ Electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly first with parallel spins.
❌ The mole is just a number like dozen. ✅ 1 mole = 6.022×10²³ particles (Avogadro constant) — a bridge between atomic and macroscopic scales.
❌ Molar mass and molecular mass are the same thing. ✅ Molecular mass is in amu; molar mass is in g/mol — numerically equal but different units.
❌ Limiting reagent is the reactant with smallest mass. ✅ Limiting reagent is the one that produces the least product (determined by moles, not mass).
❌ % yield can exceed 100%. ✅ % yield >100% indicates impure product or incomplete drying.
❌ Molarity and molality are the same. ✅ Molarity = mol/L solution (changes with T); Molality = mol/kg solvent (temperature-independent).
❌ A strong acid completely ionizes in water. ✅ Strong acids (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄) are ~100% ionized; weak acids partially ionize.
❌ pH can be negative. ✅ pH < 0 is possible for concentrations >1M (e.g., 2M HCl has pH ≈ −0.3).
❌ Kc changes when concentration changes. ✅ Kc is constant at constant temperature; only temperature changes K.
❌ Adding catalyst shifts equilibrium position. ✅ Catalyst speeds both forward and backward reactions equally; no shift in equilibrium.
❌ High pressure always favors products. ✅ High pressure favors side with fewer gas moles (Le Chatelier).
❌ Exothermic reactions are spontaneous. ✅ Spontaneity depends on ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, not just ΔH.
❌ Endothermic reactions cannot be spontaneous. ✅ Endothermic reactions can be spontaneous if TΔS > ΔH (e.g., ice melting above 0°C).
❌ ΔH and ΔU are always the same. ✅ ΔH = ΔU + PΔV; they differ when gas moles change.
❌ Heat (q) and work (w) are state functions. ✅ q and w are path functions; only ΔU, ΔH, ΔS, ΔG are state functions.
❌ Oxidation and reduction happen separately. ✅ Oxidation and reduction always occur together (redox).
❌ Oxidizing agent gets oxidized. ✅ Oxidizing agent accepts electrons and gets reduced.
❌ Reducing agent gets reduced. ✅ Reducing agent donates electrons and gets oxidized.
❌ Faraday's laws apply only to metals. ✅ Faraday's laws apply to any substance deposited/dissolved at electrodes.
❌ Real gases obey PV=nRT at all conditions. ✅ Real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature.
❌ van der Waals constants a and b are same for all gases. ✅ a (attraction) and b (volume) are gas-specific.
❌ Surface tension increases with temperature. ✅ Surface tension decreases as temperature increases.
❌ Viscosity decreases with temperature for liquids. ✅ Viscosity of liquids decreases with T; gases increase with T.
❌ Colligative properties depend on nature of solute. ✅ Colligative properties depend only on number of particles, not identity.
❌ Raoult's law applies to all solutions. ✅ Raoult's law is exact for ideal solutions; approximate for dilute real solutions.
❌ Osmotic pressure is a colligative property. ✅ Yes — π = CRT depends on solute particle concentration.

data.summary:
Atomic structure: From Rutherford's nuclear model through Bohr's quantized orbits to the modern quantum mechanical model, understanding electron configuration using four quantum numbers is fundamental.

Stoichiometry: The mole concept bridges atomic and macroscopic scales; limiting reagent determines theoretical yield; concentration expressed as molarity or molality.

Chemical equilibrium: Dynamic equilibrium has equal forward and backward rates; Kc/Kp are temperature-dependent; Le Chatelier's principle predicts response to stress.

Thermodynamics: First law (energy conservation); enthalpy changes in reactions; Gibbs free energy determines spontaneity; entropy of universe always increases.

Oxidation-reduction: Redox involves electron transfer; oxidation numbers track electron flow; electrochemical cells convert chemical to electrical energy; Faraday's laws quantify electrolysis.

States of matter: Gas laws relate P, V, T, n; kinetic theory explains gas behavior; real gases deviate due to intermolecular forces and molecular volume.

Solutions: Molarity and molality express concentration; colligative properties depend on particle number; Raoult's law describes vapor pressure of ideal solutions.
