data.title: Nuclear charge and effective nuclear charge
data.topicTitle: Nuclear charge and effective nuclear charge
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Tug-of-War Inside Every Atom

Every periodic trend — radius, ionisation energy, electron affinity, metallic character — is one contest: the **nuclear charge pulling electrons in** versus **inner-electron shielding pushing the outer experience out**. The score of that contest is the **effective nuclear charge (Z_eff)**. Define it, compute it, and the whole of Unit 4's trend section becomes derivation instead of memorisation.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Nuclear charge (Z)

- **Z = number of protons** in the nucleus = the element's atomic number.
- It is the true pull available: +Z on every electron (Coulomb attraction).

### 2.2 Shielding (screening) effect

Inner-shell electrons sit **between** the nucleus and the valence electrons, repelling the outer electrons and **cancelling part of the nuclear pull**. The outer electron feels less than +Z — it is *shielded*.

### 2.3 Effective nuclear charge (Z_eff)

**Z_eff = Z − σ** (σ = screening constant, the shielding contribution of the intervening electrons).

- Example, Na (Z = 11): the single 3s valence electron is shielded by 10 inner electrons → Z_eff ≈ 11 − 10 = **+1** (simple estimate) — Na's valence electron is held loosely, hence low ionisation energy and high reactivity.
- Example, Cl (Z = 17): 7 valence electrons shield each other poorly (same shell) → Z_eff ≈ 17 − 10 − (small same-shell contribution) ≈ **+7** — the outer electron is gripped tightly; Cl is a strong electron acceptor.

### 2.4 Slater's rules (elementary estimate)

Approximate σ for a valence electron:
1. **Same-shell** (n) other electrons: contribute **0.35** each (0.30 for 1s).
2. **(n − 1) shell** electrons: contribute **0.85** each.
3. **Deeper shells** (n − 2 and in): contribute **1.00** each.

Then Z_eff = Z − σ. (NEB needs only the concept and the simple Z − σ form; Slater's numbers are the bonus that shows *how* the estimate is made.)

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Nuclear charge (Z)** | Number of protons; the total positive pull | Na: Z = 11 |
| **Shielding effect** | Reduction of nuclear pull by inner electrons | 10 inner e⁻ shield Na's 3s electron |
| **Screening constant (σ)** | Total shielding contribution | Na: σ ≈ 10 (simple) |
| **Effective nuclear charge** | Net pull felt by an electron: Z − σ | Na valence: ≈ +1 |
| **Penetration** | Ability of an orbital's electron to approach the nucleus | s > p > d > f |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Worked estimates (the 2m template)

**Q: Estimate Z_eff for the valence electron of Li (Z = 3) and F (Z = 9).**
- Li: 1s² shields the 2s¹ electron → Z_eff = 3 − 2 = **+1**.
- F: 1s² shields; the other six 2p electrons add small same-shell shielding → Z_eff = 9 − 2 − 6(0.35) ≈ **+5.2**.
Result: F's valence electron is pulled ~5× harder than Li's — one line that explains F's tiny radius, huge ionisation energy and electronegativity, and Li's readiness to lose its electron.

### 4.2 Z_eff across a period (left → right)

Electrons enter the **same shell**; same-shell electrons shield each other poorly (0.35 each) while Z grows by +1 per step → **Z_eff rises steadily** (Na +1 → Cl +7 roughly). Consequences: radius shrinks, ionisation energy climbs, electronegativity climbs, metallic character falls.

### 4.3 Z_eff down a group (top → bottom)

Each step adds a **whole new inner shell** (σ jumps by ~8–10) while Z's increase is fully cancelled → **Z_eff on the valence shell stays nearly constant**. But n grows, so the valence electrons sit farther out: radius grows, ionisation energy falls, metallic character rises.

### 4.4 Penetration and the s < p < d < f energy order

Within the same shell, an **s** electron penetrates closest to the nucleus (feels the largest Z_eff), then p, then d, then f. That is why 4s fills before 3d (Aufbau) and why subshell energies split — Z_eff is the physical content of the (n + l) rule.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Nuclear charge vs effective nuclear charge**

| Basis | Nuclear charge (Z) | Effective nuclear charge (Z_eff) |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | Total proton count | Net pull after shielding: Z − σ |
| Value | Fixed by the element | Less than Z; depends on the electron watched |
| Changes across a period | +1 per element | Rises (poor same-shell shielding) |
| Changes down a group | Rises | Nearly constant on the valence shell |
| Role | Identity of the element | Predicts trends (radius, IE, EA) |

**Similarity:** both measure pull on electrons; Z_eff is simply Z corrected for the shield.

**Z_eff behaviour — period vs group**

| Direction | Z | σ | Z_eff (valence) | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Across a period | ↑ +1/step | ↑ slightly (same shell) | **↑** | Radius ↓, IE ↑, EN ↑ |
| Down a group | ↑ | ↑↑ (new shell) | **≈ constant** | Radius ↑, IE ↓, EN ↓ |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Z_eff is electron-specific:** the inner 1s electrons of Na feel Z_eff ≈ +10.9, not +1 — always say *which electron* you are computing for.
**Down a group Z grows but Z_eff does not:** the new shell's shielding cancels the extra protons; students who quote "Z increases so pull increases down a group" get the trend backwards.
**Shielding vs penetration:** shielding is what *other electrons do to you*; penetration is how *close you get* despite them. s penetrates best and is least shielded.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (2m): Why is the first ionisation energy of Na much lower than that of Mg?** — Both valence electrons sit in n = 3, but Mg's extra proton raises Z_eff on 3s (Mg ≈ +2 vs Na ≈ +1) while shielding is nearly equal; the stronger net pull holds Mg's 3s² pair more tightly → higher IE.

**NEB-style (2m): The atomic radius of Na is greater than that of Mg although Mg has more protons. Explain.** — Across period 3, Z_eff rises (Na ≈ +1 → Mg ≈ +2); the same shell is pulled inward more strongly in Mg → smaller radius. (The other half of NEB 2022's irregularity pair — see topic 26.)

**NEB-style (3m): Define effective nuclear charge and explain its variation across a period and down a group.** — Z_eff = Z − σ, the net nuclear pull an electron feels after shielding by intervening electrons. **Across a period:** electrons enter the same shell, same-shell shielding is poor, so Z_eff rises → radius falls, IE rises. **Down a group:** each element adds an inner shell whose strong shielding cancels the added protons, so valence Z_eff stays nearly constant while n grows → radius grows, IE falls.
confusion: **Z vs Z_eff:** Z is the total proton count and never changes with position; Z_eff is what a *particular* electron actually feels — quoting one where the other is asked loses the mark.
**Same-shell shielding is weak (0.35):** that is the entire reason Z_eff rises across a period; treating all shielding as equal makes the trend disappear.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Tug-of-War Inside Every Atom

Every periodic trend — radius, ionisation energy, electron affinity, metallic character — is one contest: the **nuclear charge pulling electrons in** versus **inner-electron shielding pushing the outer experience out**. The score of that contest is the **effective nuclear charge (Z_eff)**. Define it, compute it, and the whole of Unit 4's trend section becomes derivation instead of memorisation.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Nuclear charge (Z)

- **Z = number of protons** in the nucleus = the element's atomic number.
- It is the true pull available: +Z on every electron (Coulomb attraction).

### 2.2 Shielding (screening) effect

Inner-shell electrons sit **between** the nucleus and the valence electrons, repelling the outer electrons and **cancelling part of the nuclear pull**. The outer electron feels less than +Z — it is *shielded*.

### 2.3 Effective nuclear charge (Z_eff)

**Z_eff = Z − σ** (σ = screening constant, the shielding contribution of the intervening electrons).

- Example, Na (Z = 11): the single 3s valence electron is shielded by 10 inner electrons → Z_eff ≈ 11 − 10 = **+1** (simple estimate) — Na's valence electron is held loosely, hence low ionisation energy and high reactivity.
- Example, Cl (Z = 17): 7 valence electrons shield each other poorly (same shell) → Z_eff ≈ 17 − 10 − (small same-shell contribution) ≈ **+7** — the outer electron is gripped tightly; Cl is a strong electron acceptor.

### 2.4 Slater's rules (elementary estimate)

Approximate σ for a valence electron:
1. **Same-shell** (n) other electrons: contribute **0.35** each (0.30 for 1s).
2. **(n − 1) shell** electrons: contribute **0.85** each.
3. **Deeper shells** (n − 2 and in): contribute **1.00** each.

Then Z_eff = Z − σ. (NEB needs only the concept and the simple Z − σ form; Slater's numbers are the bonus that shows *how* the estimate is made.)

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Nuclear charge (Z)** | Number of protons; the total positive pull | Na: Z = 11 |
| **Shielding effect** | Reduction of nuclear pull by inner electrons | 10 inner e⁻ shield Na's 3s electron |
| **Screening constant (σ)** | Total shielding contribution | Na: σ ≈ 10 (simple) |
| **Effective nuclear charge** | Net pull felt by an electron: Z − σ | Na valence: ≈ +1 |
| **Penetration** | Ability of an orbital's electron to approach the nucleus | s > p > d > f |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Worked estimates (the 2m template)

**Q: Estimate Z_eff for the valence electron of Li (Z = 3) and F (Z = 9).**
- Li: 1s² shields the 2s¹ electron → Z_eff = 3 − 2 = **+1**.
- F: 1s² shields; the other six 2p electrons add small same-shell shielding → Z_eff = 9 − 2 − 6(0.35) ≈ **+5.2**.
Result: F's valence electron is pulled ~5× harder than Li's — one line that explains F's tiny radius, huge ionisation energy and electronegativity, and Li's readiness to lose its electron.

### 4.2 Z_eff across a period (left → right)

Electrons enter the **same shell**; same-shell electrons shield each other poorly (0.35 each) while Z grows by +1 per step → **Z_eff rises steadily** (Na +1 → Cl +7 roughly). Consequences: radius shrinks, ionisation energy climbs, electronegativity climbs, metallic character falls.

### 4.3 Z_eff down a group (top → bottom)

Each step adds a **whole new inner shell** (σ jumps by ~8–10) while Z's increase is fully cancelled → **Z_eff on the valence shell stays nearly constant**. But n grows, so the valence electrons sit farther out: radius grows, ionisation energy falls, metallic character rises.

### 4.4 Penetration and the s < p < d < f energy order

Within the same shell, an **s** electron penetrates closest to the nucleus (feels the largest Z_eff), then p, then d, then f. That is why 4s fills before 3d (Aufbau) and why subshell energies split — Z_eff is the physical content of the (n + l) rule.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Nuclear charge vs effective nuclear charge**

| Basis | Nuclear charge (Z) | Effective nuclear charge (Z_eff) |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | Total proton count | Net pull after shielding: Z − σ |
| Value | Fixed by the element | Less than Z; depends on the electron watched |
| Changes across a period | +1 per element | Rises (poor same-shell shielding) |
| Changes down a group | Rises | Nearly constant on the valence shell |
| Role | Identity of the element | Predicts trends (radius, IE, EA) |

**Similarity:** both measure pull on electrons; Z_eff is simply Z corrected for the shield.

**Z_eff behaviour — period vs group**

| Direction | Z | σ | Z_eff (valence) | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Across a period | ↑ +1/step | ↑ slightly (same shell) | **↑** | Radius ↓, IE ↑, EN ↑ |
| Down a group | ↑ | ↑↑ (new shell) | **≈ constant** | Radius ↑, IE ↓, EN ↓ |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Z_eff is electron-specific:** the inner 1s electrons of Na feel Z_eff ≈ +10.9, not +1 — always say *which electron* you are computing for.
**Down a group Z grows but Z_eff does not:** the new shell's shielding cancels the extra protons; students who quote "Z increases so pull increases down a group" get the trend backwards.
**Shielding vs penetration:** shielding is what *other electrons do to you*; penetration is how *close you get* despite them. s penetrates best and is least shielded.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (2m): Why is the first ionisation energy of Na much lower than that of Mg?** — Both valence electrons sit in n = 3, but Mg's extra proton raises Z_eff on 3s (Mg ≈ +2 vs Na ≈ +1) while shielding is nearly equal; the stronger net pull holds Mg's 3s² pair more tightly → higher IE.

**NEB-style (2m): The atomic radius of Na is greater than that of Mg although Mg has more protons. Explain.** — Across period 3, Z_eff rises (Na ≈ +1 → Mg ≈ +2); the same shell is pulled inward more strongly in Mg → smaller radius. (The other half of NEB 2022's irregularity pair — see topic 26.)

**NEB-style (3m): Define effective nuclear charge and explain its variation across a period and down a group.** — Z_eff = Z − σ, the net nuclear pull an electron feels after shielding by intervening electrons. **Across a period:** electrons enter the same shell, same-shell shielding is poor, so Z_eff rises → radius falls, IE rises. **Down a group:** each element adds an inner shell whose strong shielding cancels the added protons, so valence Z_eff stays nearly constant while n grows → radius grows, IE falls.
confusion: **Z vs Z_eff:** Z is the total proton count and never changes with position; Z_eff is what a *particular* electron actually feels — quoting one where the other is asked loses the mark.
**Same-shell shielding is weak (0.35):** that is the entire reason Z_eff rises across a period; treating all shielding as equal makes the trend disappear.

confusion: ❌ All atoms are identical in an element. ✅ Isotopes have same protons but different neutrons.
❌ Atoms are indivisible. ✅ Atoms consist of protons, neutrons, and electrons.
❌ Electrons orbit in fixed paths like planets. ✅ Electrons exist in probability clouds (orbitals).
❌ Heisenberg uncertainty means we cannot measure position and momentum precisely simultaneously — not that we lack good instruments.
❌ de Broglie wavelength applies only to light. ✅ All matter has wave nature; detectable mainly for small masses like electrons.
❌ Quantum number l can be any integer. ✅ l ranges from 0 to n−1.
❌ Magnetic quantum number ml determines energy. ✅ ml determines orbital orientation, not energy (in absence of magnetic field).
❌ Spin quantum number ms can be ±½ or any value. ✅ ms is always +½ or −½.
❌ Aufbau principle means filling from bottom to top of the diagram. ✅ Fill lowest-energy orbitals first: 1s→2s→2p→3s→3p→4s→3d→4p→...
❌ Pauli exclusion allows two electrons per orbital with any spin. ✅ Two electrons in same orbital must have opposite spins.
❌ Hund's rule means pair electrons before spreading. ✅ Electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly first with parallel spins.
❌ The mole is just a number like dozen. ✅ 1 mole = 6.022×10²³ particles (Avogadro constant) — a bridge between atomic and macroscopic scales.
❌ Molar mass and molecular mass are the same thing. ✅ Molecular mass is in amu; molar mass is in g/mol — numerically equal but different units.
❌ Limiting reagent is the reactant with smallest mass. ✅ Limiting reagent is the one that produces the least product (determined by moles, not mass).
❌ % yield can exceed 100%. ✅ % yield >100% indicates impure product or incomplete drying.
❌ Molarity and molality are the same. ✅ Molarity = mol/L solution (changes with T); Molality = mol/kg solvent (temperature-independent).
❌ A strong acid completely ionizes in water. ✅ Strong acids (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄) are ~100% ionized; weak acids partially ionize.
❌ pH can be negative. ✅ pH < 0 is possible for concentrations >1M (e.g., 2M HCl has pH ≈ −0.3).
❌ Kc changes when concentration changes. ✅ Kc is constant at constant temperature; only temperature changes K.
❌ Adding catalyst shifts equilibrium position. ✅ Catalyst speeds both forward and backward reactions equally; no shift in equilibrium.
❌ High pressure always favors products. ✅ High pressure favors side with fewer gas moles (Le Chatelier).
❌ Exothermic reactions are spontaneous. ✅ Spontaneity depends on ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, not just ΔH.
❌ Endothermic reactions cannot be spontaneous. ✅ Endothermic reactions can be spontaneous if TΔS > ΔH (e.g., ice melting above 0°C).
❌ ΔH and ΔU are always the same. ✅ ΔH = ΔU + PΔV; they differ when gas moles change.
❌ Heat (q) and work (w) are state functions. ✅ q and w are path functions; only ΔU, ΔH, ΔS, ΔG are state functions.
❌ Oxidation and reduction happen separately. ✅ Oxidation and reduction always occur together (redox).
❌ Oxidizing agent gets oxidized. ✅ Oxidizing agent accepts electrons and gets reduced.
❌ Reducing agent gets reduced. ✅ Reducing agent donates electrons and gets oxidized.
❌ Faraday's laws apply only to metals. ✅ Faraday's laws apply to any substance deposited/dissolved at electrodes.
❌ Real gases obey PV=nRT at all conditions. ✅ Real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature.
❌ van der Waals constants a and b are same for all gases. ✅ a (attraction) and b (volume) are gas-specific.
❌ Surface tension increases with temperature. ✅ Surface tension decreases as temperature increases.
❌ Viscosity decreases with temperature for liquids. ✅ Viscosity of liquids decreases with T; gases increase with T.
❌ Colligative properties depend on nature of solute. ✅ Colligative properties depend only on number of particles, not identity.
❌ Raoult's law applies to all solutions. ✅ Raoult's law is exact for ideal solutions; approximate for dilute real solutions.
❌ Osmotic pressure is a colligative property. ✅ Yes — π = CRT depends on solute particle concentration.

data.summary:
Atomic structure: From Rutherford's nuclear model through Bohr's quantized orbits to the modern quantum mechanical model, understanding electron configuration using four quantum numbers is fundamental.

Stoichiometry: The mole concept bridges atomic and macroscopic scales; limiting reagent determines theoretical yield; concentration expressed as molarity or molality.

Chemical equilibrium: Dynamic equilibrium has equal forward and backward rates; Kc/Kp are temperature-dependent; Le Chatelier's principle predicts response to stress.

Thermodynamics: First law (energy conservation); enthalpy changes in reactions; Gibbs free energy determines spontaneity; entropy of universe always increases.

Oxidation-reduction: Redox involves electron transfer; oxidation numbers track electron flow; electrochemical cells convert chemical to electrical energy; Faraday's laws quantify electrolysis.

States of matter: Gas laws relate P, V, T, n; kinetic theory explains gas behavior; real gases deviate due to intermolecular forces and molecular volume.

Solutions: Molarity and molality express concentration; colligative properties depend on particle number; Raoult's law describes vapor pressure of ideal solutions.

Chemical bonding: Ionic bonds form from electron transfer; covalent bonds from sharing; VSEPR predicts molecular geometry; hybridization explains bonding orbitals.

Organic chemistry basics: Carbon's tetravalency and catenation enable millions of compounds; functional groups determine reactivity; IUPAC nomenclature provides systematic naming.

Hydrocarbons: Alkanes (CnH2n+2) are saturated; alkenes (CnH2n) have C=C; alkynes (CnH2n-2) have C≡C; aromatic compounds based on benzene ring.

Periodic table: Elements arranged by atomic number; periodic trends in radius, ionization energy, electronegativity; s, p, d, f blocks based on orbital type.

Applied chemistry: Petrochemical industry, polymer science, green chemistry principles; importance of sustainable chemical manufacturing for environmental protection.

notes: Periodic table: 7 periods, 18 groups.
Groups: similar valence electron configuration.
Periods: increasing atomic number.
Metals left, non-metals right, metalloids diagonal.
confusion: ❌ All atoms are identical in an element. ✅ Isotopes have same protons but different neutrons.
❌ Atoms are indivisible. ✅ Atoms consist of protons, neutrons, and electrons.
❌ Electrons orbit in fixed paths like planets. ✅ Electrons exist in probability clouds (orbitals).
❌ Heisenberg uncertainty means we cannot measure position and momentum precisely simultaneously — not that we lack good instruments.
❌ de Broglie wavelength applies only to light. ✅ All matter has wave nature; detectable mainly for small masses like electrons.
❌ Quantum number l can be any integer. ✅ l ranges from 0 to n−1.
❌ Magnetic quantum number ml determines energy. ✅ ml determines orbital orientation, not energy (in absence of magnetic field).
❌ Spin quantum number ms can be ±½ or any value. ✅ ms is always +½ or −½.
❌ Aufbau principle means filling from bottom to top of the diagram. ✅ Fill lowest-energy orbitals first: 1s→2s→2p→3s→3p→4s→3d→4p→...
❌ Pauli exclusion allows two electrons per orbital with any spin. ✅ Two electrons in same orbital must have opposite spins.
❌ Hund's rule means pair electrons before spreading. ✅ Electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly first with parallel spins.
❌ The mole is just a number like dozen. ✅ 1 mole = 6.022×10²³ particles (Avogadro constant) — a bridge between atomic and macroscopic scales.
❌ Molar mass and molecular mass are the same thing. ✅ Molecular mass is in amu; molar mass is in g/mol — numerically equal but different units.
❌ Limiting reagent is the reactant with smallest mass. ✅ Limiting reagent is the one that produces the least product (determined by moles, not mass).
❌ % yield can exceed 100%. ✅ % yield >100% indicates impure product or incomplete drying.
❌ Molarity and molality are the same. ✅ Molarity = mol/L solution (changes with T); Molality = mol/kg solvent (temperature-independent).
❌ A strong acid completely ionizes in water. ✅ Strong acids (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄) are ~100% ionized; weak acids partially ionize.
❌ pH can be negative. ✅ pH < 0 is possible for concentrations >1M (e.g., 2M HCl has pH ≈ −0.3).
❌ Kc changes when concentration changes. ✅ Kc is constant at constant temperature; only temperature changes K.
❌ Adding catalyst shifts equilibrium position. ✅ Catalyst speeds both forward and backward reactions equally; no shift in equilibrium.
❌ High pressure always favors products. ✅ High pressure favors side with fewer gas moles (Le Chatelier).
❌ Exothermic reactions are spontaneous. ✅ Spontaneity depends on ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, not just ΔH.
❌ Endothermic reactions cannot be spontaneous. ✅ Endothermic reactions can be spontaneous if TΔS > ΔH (e.g., ice melting above 0°C).
❌ ΔH and ΔU are always the same. ✅ ΔH = ΔU + PΔV; they differ when gas moles change.
❌ Heat (q) and work (w) are state functions. ✅ q and w are path functions; only ΔU, ΔH, ΔS, ΔG are state functions.
❌ Oxidation and reduction happen separately. ✅ Oxidation and reduction always occur together (redox).
❌ Oxidizing agent gets oxidized. ✅ Oxidizing agent accepts electrons and gets reduced.
❌ Reducing agent gets reduced. ✅ Reducing agent donates electrons and gets oxidized.
❌ Faraday's laws apply only to metals. ✅ Faraday's laws apply to any substance deposited/dissolved at electrodes.
❌ Real gases obey PV=nRT at all conditions. ✅ Real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature.
❌ van der Waals constants a and b are same for all gases. ✅ a (attraction) and b (volume) are gas-specific.
❌ Surface tension increases with temperature. ✅ Surface tension decreases as temperature increases.
❌ Viscosity decreases with temperature for liquids. ✅ Viscosity of liquids decreases with T; gases increase with T.
❌ Colligative properties depend on nature of solute. ✅ Colligative properties depend only on number of particles, not identity.
❌ Raoult's law applies to all solutions. ✅ Raoult's law is exact for ideal solutions; approximate for dilute real solutions.
❌ Osmotic pressure is a colligative property. ✅ Yes — π = CRT depends on solute particle concentration.

subtopics.name: Across a period
points: Nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same shell
Effective nuclear charge rises, so the atom contracts
Atomic radius decreases left to right

subtopics.name: Down a group
points: A new shell is added each period
Shielding increases faster than nuclear charge
Atomic radius increases down the group

subtopics.name: Ionisation energy and electron affinity
points: Ionisation energy increases across a period, decreases down a group
Electron affinity becomes more negative across a period
Exceptions: Be > B and N > O in ionisation energy, due to filled or half-filled subshells

subtopics.name: Electronegativity and metallic character
points: Electronegativity increases across a period, decreases down a group
Fluorine is the most electronegative element at 3.98
Metallic character decreases across a period, increases down a group

subtopics.name: Why anomalies occur
points: Half-filled and fully-filled subshells are extra stable, raising ionisation energy
N has 2p3 half-filled, so its ionisation energy exceeds O's
Be has 2s2 filled, so it exceeds B's

subtopics.name: Ionic versus atomic radius
points: Cations are smaller than their parent atoms; anions are larger
Isoelectronic species: more protons means smaller radius (Na+ < F- < O2-)
Across an isoelectronic series, radius falls as nuclear charge rises

notes: Matter: anything with mass and volume.
Atoms: basic unit of elements.
Molecules: combinations of atoms.
Mixtures: physical combinations, separable.
Pure substances: elements and compounds.
confusion: ❌ All cells look the same under a microscope. ✅ Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells have them.
❌ DNA and RNA are identical in structure. ✅ DNA is double-stranded with deoxyribose and thymine; RNA is single-stranded with ribose and uracil.
❌ Mitosis produces genetically different cells. ✅ Mitosis produces genetically identical diploid daughter cells.
❌ Meiosis produces identical cells. ✅ Meiosis produces 4 genetically diverse haploid gametes.
❌ Crossing over occurs in mitosis. ✅ Crossing over occurs in Prophase I of meiosis only.
❌ All enzymes are proteins. ✅ Most enzymes are proteins; some RNA molecules (ribozymes) also have catalytic activity.
❌ ATP is the only energy currency. ✅ GTP, UTP, and CTP also serve as energy carriers in specific pathways.
❌ Photosynthesis occurs in all plant cells. ✅ Photosynthesis occurs only in cells containing chloroplasts (mainly mesophyll).
❌ Respiration and photosynthesis are opposite processes with same equation. ✅ They are complementary but occur in different organelles and under different conditions.
❌ Oxygen is produced during respiration. ✅ Oxygen is consumed in aerobic respiration; produced during photosynthesis.
❌ Food chain shows all feeding relationships. ✅ Food chain is linear; food web shows interconnected feeding relationships.
❌ 90% of energy is transferred to next trophic level. ✅ Only ~10% energy transfers; ~90% lost as heat.
❌ Biomagnification decreases toxin concentration up the food chain. ✅ Biomagnification increases toxin concentration at higher trophic levels.
❌ Carbon cycle only involves plants and animals. ✅ Carbon cycle involves atmosphere, oceans, fossils, rocks, and decomposers.
❌ Nitrogen fixation only occurs in bacteria. ✅ Some lightning and industrial processes (Haber) also fix nitrogen.
❌ All fungi are harmful. ✅ Many fungi are beneficial (decomposers, mycorrhizae, food, antibiotics like penicillin).
❌ Viruses are living organisms. ✅ Viruses are acellular — they cannot reproduce without a host and lack metabolism.
❌ Bacteria are always harmful. ✅ Most bacteria are harmless or beneficial (gut flora, nitrogen fixation, decomposition).
❌ Gram-positive and Gram-negative differ only in color. ✅ Gram-positive has thick peptidoglycan layer; Gram-negative has thin layer + outer membrane.
❌ Natural selection creates perfect organisms. ✅ Natural selection favors traits suited to current environment; environments change.
❌ Evolution is goal-oriented. ✅ Evolution has no goal; it acts on random variation filtered by selection.
❌ Homologous and analogous structures mean the same thing. ✅ Homologous = common ancestry (divergent); Analogous = similar function, different origin (convergent).
❌ Fossils are preserved bones only. ✅ Fossils include impressions, trace fossils, amber-preserved organisms, and molecular fossils.
❌ Lamarckism is completely wrong. ✅ Lamarck's inheritance of acquired characteristics is largely rejected, but epigenetics shows some environmental effects can be inherited.
❌ Five-kingdom classification is outdated. ✅ Six-kingdom (adding Archaea) and phylogenetic systems are more current, but five-kingdom remains useful for education.
❌ Binomial nomenclature names change frequently. ✅ Names are stable once formally published; changes require formal revision by taxonomic authorities.
❌ All algae are aquatic. ✅ Some algae live in soil, on tree bark, or in symbiotic relationships (lichens).
❌ Bryophytes have vascular tissue. ✅ Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts, hornworts) lack true vascular tissue (xylem/phloem).
❌ Gymnosperms produce flowers. ✅ Gymnosperms have naked seeds in cones; angiosperms produce flowers and enclosed seeds.
❌ Double fertilization occurs in gymnosperms. ✅ Double fertilization (zygote + endosperm) is unique to angiosperms.
❌ Earthworms have an open circulatory system. ✅ Earthworms have a closed circulatory system with dorsal and ventral vessels.
❌ Frogs breathe only through lungs. ✅ Frogs use cutaneous respiration (skin), buccal cavity, and lungs.
❌ Conservation only means protecting animals. ✅ Conservation includes genetic, species, and ecosystem diversity; in-situ and ex-situ strategies.
❌ In-situ and ex-situ conservation are the same. ✅ In-situ = conservation in natural habitat (national parks); Ex-situ = conservation outside habitat (zoos, seed banks).

Biomolecules and cell biology: Living organisms built from four macromolecule classes; cell theory unifies all life; membrane structure enables compartmentalization.

Cell division: Mitosis maintains chromosome number for growth/repair; meiosis halves it for gamete formation; crossing over creates genetic diversity.

Ecology: Ecosystems integrate biotic and abiotic components; energy flows unidirectionally with 10% transfer efficiency; nutrients cycle through biogeochemical pathways.

Evolutionary biology: Darwin's natural selection explains adaptation; fossil, morphological, and molecular evidence support common ancestry; human evolution from hominid ancestors.

Floral diversity: Plant evolution from simple algae to complex angiosperms; five-kingdom classification; double fertilization unique to flowering plants.

Faunal diversity: Animal kingdom spans from unicellular protists to complex chordates; segmentation and body cavities key evolutionary innovations; earthworm and frog as model organisms.

Biota and environment: Aquatic, terrestrial, and aerial adaptations reflect evolutionary pressures; pollution from human activities threatens ecosystem stability.

Conservation biology: Biodiversity exists at genetic, species, and ecosystem levels; Nepal's protected areas and community forestry demonstrate effective conservation strategies.

Introduction to biology: Biology studies life from molecules to ecosystems; scientific method drives discovery; interdisciplinary connections with physics, chemistry, and earth science.

Introductory microbiology: Bacteria (prokaryotes) and viruses (acellular) are foundational to life sciences; Gram stain differentiates bacteria; biotechnology applications transform medicine and industry.

Vegetation: Nepal's altitude-dependent vegetation zones reflect climate gradients; in-situ (protected areas) and ex-situ (seed banks) conservation preserve plant diversity.

data.title: General introduction of chemistry
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Central Science

Chemistry studies matter — its composition, structure, properties and the changes it undergoes. Sitting between physics and biology, it is called the **central science**: it explains materials, medicines, fuels, fertilisers and life's own molecules in one framework.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Definition and scope

**Chemistry** is the branch of science that deals with the composition, structure, properties of matter and the changes (reactions) it undergoes, together with the energy changes accompanying them.

### 2.2 Branches of chemistry — classification table

| Branch | Studies | Example topic |
|---|---|---|
| **Physical chemistry** | Laws and principles governing chemical change; energy, rates, equilibrium | Gas laws, thermodynamics |
| **Inorganic chemistry** | All elements and their compounds except most carbon compounds | Acids, salts, metals |
| **Organic chemistry** | Carbon compounds (hydrocarbons and derivatives) | Alkanes, benzene |
| **Analytical chemistry** | Identification and measurement of composition | Titration, tests |
| **Biochemistry** | Chemistry of living systems | Enzymes, DNA |
| **Industrial/Applied chemistry** | Large-scale manufacture | Fertilisers, acids |

### 2.3 Matter and its classification

- **Matter:** anything that has mass and occupies space.
- Classification by state: solid, liquid, gas (and plasma).
- Classification by composition: **pure substances** (elements, compounds) vs **mixtures** (homogeneous solutions, heterogeneous suspensions).

| | Element | Compound | Mixture |
|---|---|---|---|
| Composition | One kind of atom | Two+ elements, fixed ratio | Variable ratio |
| Separation | Cannot be broken chemically | By chemical means | By physical means |
| Example | Fe, O₂ | H₂O, CO₂ | Air, salt water |

### 2.4 Similarities and differences — element vs compound

**Similarities:** both are pure substances; both have fixed, definite composition; both cannot be separated by physical methods.
**Differences:** an element contains one kind of atom and cannot be decomposed chemically; a compound contains two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio and can be decomposed into its elements.

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 2:** scope answers "why study this?" — chemistry's reach into daily life.
- **To stoichiometry (Unit 2):** composition and formula flow directly from matter's particulate nature.
- **To states of matter (Unit 7):** the three states are chemistry's first classification.

## 4. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 4.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

No verified PYQ for this exact topic in the bank. Practise the definition, branches and classification of matter as **NEB-style practice** (2–3m).

### 4.2 Likely question forms

1. Define chemistry and name its branches (2–3m).
2. Differentiate element, compound and mixture with examples (3m).
3. Why is chemistry called the central science? (2m)

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Calling air an element or compound — it is a mixture.
2. Listing branches without examples.
3. Saying mixtures have fixed composition — only compounds do.
confusion: **Mixture vs compound:** air is a mixture (variable composition); water is a compound (fixed H:O = 1:8 by mass).
**Chemistry is "central"** — it links physics (laws) with biology (life processes).

Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Chemistry — don't mix them.
State the limit / condition where a formula or rule stops being valid before applying it.
practice: Why is chemistry called the central science?
universalFacts: Everything you can touch, see or breathe is matter — chemistry's subject matter is literally the material world.
examples: ***Water (H₂O)*** — a compound: fixed 2:1 atom ratio, decomposable by electrolysis into H₂ and O₂.
practiceQuestions: **NEB-style (3m): Differentiate element, compound and mixture with one example each.** — Element: one kind of atom, cannot be decomposed (Fe). Compound: two+ elements in fixed ratio, chemically combined, separable only chemically (H₂O). Mixture: variable composition, separable physically (air).

keyPoints: Chemistry = composition + structure + properties + changes of matter. Branches: physical, inorganic, organic, analytical, biochemical, applied.
data.summary: **Chemistry** studies matter's composition, structure, properties and changes — the central science linking physics and biology. Its branches — physical, inorganic, organic, analytical, biochemical and applied — divide the field by what is studied and how. Matter itself classifies by state (solid, liquid, gas) and by composition: **elements** (one atom type), **compounds** (fixed ratio, chemical bonds, chemical separation only) and **mixtures** (variable composition, physical separation). Similarities between elements and compounds (pure, definite composition) hide their key difference: decomposability. Air vs water is the classic contrast pair.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Central Science

Chemistry studies matter — its composition, structure, properties and the changes it undergoes. Sitting between physics and biology, it is called the **central science**: it explains materials, medicines, fuels, fertilisers and life's own molecules in one framework.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Definition and scope

**Chemistry** is the branch of science that deals with the composition, structure, properties of matter and the changes (reactions) it undergoes, together with the energy changes accompanying them.

### 2.2 Branches of chemistry — classification table

| Branch | Studies | Example topic |
|---|---|---|
| **Physical chemistry** | Laws and principles governing chemical change; energy, rates, equilibrium | Gas laws, thermodynamics |
| **Inorganic chemistry** | All elements and their compounds except most carbon compounds | Acids, salts, metals |
| **Organic chemistry** | Carbon compounds (hydrocarbons and derivatives) | Alkanes, benzene |
| **Analytical chemistry** | Identification and measurement of composition | Titration, tests |
| **Biochemistry** | Chemistry of living systems | Enzymes, DNA |
| **Industrial/Applied chemistry** | Large-scale manufacture | Fertilisers, acids |

### 2.3 Matter and its classification

- **Matter:** anything that has mass and occupies space.
- Classification by state: solid, liquid, gas (and plasma).
- Classification by composition: **pure substances** (elements, compounds) vs **mixtures** (homogeneous solutions, heterogeneous suspensions).

| | Element | Compound | Mixture |
|---|---|---|---|
| Composition | One kind of atom | Two+ elements, fixed ratio | Variable ratio |
| Separation | Cannot be broken chemically | By chemical means | By physical means |
| Example | Fe, O₂ | H₂O, CO₂ | Air, salt water |

### 2.4 Similarities and differences — element vs compound

**Similarities:** both are pure substances; both have fixed, definite composition; both cannot be separated by physical methods.
**Differences:** an element contains one kind of atom and cannot be decomposed chemically; a compound contains two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio and can be decomposed into its elements.

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 2:** scope answers "why study this?" — chemistry's reach into daily life.
- **To stoichiometry (Unit 2):** composition and formula flow directly from matter's particulate nature.
- **To states of matter (Unit 7):** the three states are chemistry's first classification.

## 4. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 4.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

No verified PYQ for this exact topic in the bank. Practise the definition, branches and classification of matter as **NEB-style practice** (2–3m).

### 4.2 Likely question forms

1. Define chemistry and name its branches (2–3m).
2. Differentiate element, compound and mixture with examples (3m).
3. Why is chemistry called the central science? (2m)

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Calling air an element or compound — it is a mixture.
2. Listing branches without examples.
3. Saying mixtures have fixed composition — only compounds do.

data.title: Introduction and Importance of Chemistry
notes: Matter: anything with mass and volume.
Atoms: basic unit of elements.
Molecules: combinations of atoms.
Mixtures: physical combinations, separable.
Pure substances: elements and compounds.
confusion: ❌ All cells look the same under a microscope. ✅ Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells have them.
❌ DNA and RNA are identical in structure. ✅ DNA is double-stranded with deoxyribose and thymine; RNA is single-stranded with ribose and uracil.
❌ Mitosis produces genetically different cells. ✅ Mitosis produces genetically identical diploid daughter cells.
❌ Meiosis produces identical cells. ✅ Meiosis produces 4 genetically diverse haploid gametes.
❌ Crossing over occurs in mitosis. ✅ Crossing over occurs in Prophase I of meiosis only.
❌ All enzymes are proteins. ✅ Most enzymes are proteins; some RNA molecules (ribozymes) also have catalytic activity.
❌ ATP is the only energy currency. ✅ GTP, UTP, and CTP also serve as energy carriers in specific pathways.
❌ Photosynthesis occurs in all plant cells. ✅ Photosynthesis occurs only in cells containing chloroplasts (mainly mesophyll).
❌ Respiration and photosynthesis are opposite processes with same equation. ✅ They are complementary but occur in different organelles and under different conditions.
❌ Oxygen is produced during respiration. ✅ Oxygen is consumed in aerobic respiration; produced during photosynthesis.
❌ Food chain shows all feeding relationships. ✅ Food chain is linear; food web shows interconnected feeding relationships.
❌ 90% of energy is transferred to next trophic level. ✅ Only ~10% energy transfers; ~90% lost as heat.
❌ Biomagnification decreases toxin concentration up the food chain. ✅ Biomagnification increases toxin concentration at higher trophic levels.
❌ Carbon cycle only involves plants and animals. ✅ Carbon cycle involves atmosphere, oceans, fossils, rocks, and decomposers.
❌ Nitrogen fixation only occurs in bacteria. ✅ Some lightning and industrial processes (Haber) also fix nitrogen.
❌ All fungi are harmful. ✅ Many fungi are beneficial (decomposers, mycorrhizae, food, antibiotics like penicillin).
❌ Viruses are living organisms. ✅ Viruses are acellular — they cannot reproduce without a host and lack metabolism.
❌ Bacteria are always harmful. ✅ Most bacteria are harmless or beneficial (gut flora, nitrogen fixation, decomposition).
❌ Gram-positive and Gram-negative differ only in color. ✅ Gram-positive has thick peptidoglycan layer; Gram-negative has thin layer + outer membrane.
❌ Natural selection creates perfect organisms. ✅ Natural selection favors traits suited to current environment; environments change.
❌ Evolution is goal-oriented. ✅ Evolution has no goal; it acts on random variation filtered by selection.
❌ Homologous and analogous structures mean the same thing. ✅ Homologous = common ancestry (divergent); Analogous = similar function, different origin (convergent).
❌ Fossils are preserved bones only. ✅ Fossils include impressions, trace fossils, amber-preserved organisms, and molecular fossils.
❌ Lamarckism is completely wrong. ✅ Lamarck's inheritance of acquired characteristics is largely rejected, but epigenetics shows some environmental effects can be inherited.
❌ Five-kingdom classification is outdated. ✅ Six-kingdom (adding Archaea) and phylogenetic systems are more current, but five-kingdom remains useful for education.
❌ Binomial nomenclature names change frequently. ✅ Names are stable once formally published; changes require formal revision by taxonomic authorities.
❌ All algae are aquatic. ✅ Some algae live in soil, on tree bark, or in symbiotic relationships (lichens).
❌ Bryophytes have vascular tissue. ✅ Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts, hornworts) lack true vascular tissue (xylem/phloem).
❌ Gymnosperms produce flowers. ✅ Gymnosperms have naked seeds in cones; angiosperms produce flowers and enclosed seeds.
❌ Double fertilization occurs in gymnosperms. ✅ Double fertilization (zygote + endosperm) is unique to angiosperms.
❌ Earthworms have an open circulatory system. ✅ Earthworms have a closed circulatory system with dorsal and ventral vessels.
❌ Frogs breathe only through lungs. ✅ Frogs use cutaneous respiration (skin), buccal cavity, and lungs.
❌ Conservation only means protecting animals. ✅ Conservation includes genetic, species, and ecosystem diversity; in-situ and ex-situ strategies.
❌ In-situ and ex-situ conservation are the same. ✅ In-situ = conservation in natural habitat (national parks); Ex-situ = conservation outside habitat (zoos, seed banks).

data.summary:
Biomolecules and cell biology: Living organisms built from four macromolecule classes; cell theory unifies all life; membrane structure enables compartmentalization.

Cell division: Mitosis maintains chromosome number for growth/repair; meiosis halves it for gamete formation; crossing over creates genetic diversity.

Ecology: Ecosystems integrate biotic and abiotic components; energy flows unidirectionally with 10% transfer efficiency; nutrients cycle through biogeochemical pathways.

Evolutionary biology: Darwin's natural selection explains adaptation; fossil, morphological, and molecular evidence support common ancestry; human evolution from hominid ancestors.

Floral diversity: Plant evolution from simple algae to complex angiosperms; five-kingdom classification; double fertilization unique to flowering plants.

Faunal diversity: Animal kingdom spans from unicellular protists to complex chordates; segmentation and body cavities key evolutionary innovations; earthworm and frog as model organisms.

Biota and environment: Aquatic, terrestrial, and aerial adaptations reflect evolutionary pressures; pollution from human activities threatens ecosystem stability.

Conservation biology: Biodiversity exists at genetic, species, and ecosystem levels; Nepal's protected areas and community forestry demonstrate effective conservation strategies.

Introduction to biology: Biology studies life from molecules to ecosystems; scientific method drives discovery; interdisciplinary connections with physics, chemistry, and earth science.

Introductory microbiology: Bacteria (prokaryotes) and viruses (acellular) are foundational to life sciences; Gram stain differentiates bacteria; biotechnology applications transform medicine and industry.

Vegetation: Nepal's altitude-dependent vegetation zones reflect climate gradients; in-situ (protected areas) and ex-situ (seed banks) conservation preserve plant diversity.

notes: Matter: anything with mass and volume.

confusion: ❌ All atoms are identical in an element. ✅ Isotopes have same protons but different neutrons.
❌ Atoms are indivisible. ✅ Atoms consist of protons, neutrons, and electrons.
❌ Electrons orbit in fixed paths like planets. ✅ Electrons exist in probability clouds (orbitals).
❌ Heisenberg uncertainty means we cannot measure position and momentum precisely simultaneously — not that we lack good instruments.
❌ de Broglie wavelength applies only to light. ✅ All matter has wave nature; detectable mainly for small masses like electrons.
❌ Quantum number l can be any integer. ✅ l ranges from 0 to n−1.
❌ Magnetic quantum number ml determines energy. ✅ ml determines orbital orientation, not energy (in absence of magnetic field).
❌ Spin quantum number ms can be ±½ or any value. ✅ ms is always +½ or −½.
❌ Aufbau principle means filling from bottom to top of the diagram. ✅ Fill lowest-energy orbitals first: 1s→2s→2p→3s→3p→4s→3d→4p→...
❌ Pauli exclusion allows two electrons per orbital with any spin. ✅ Two electrons in same orbital must have opposite spins.
❌ Hund's rule means pair electrons before spreading. ✅ Electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly first with parallel spins.
❌ The mole is just a number like dozen. ✅ 1 mole = 6.022×10²³ particles (Avogadro constant) — a bridge between atomic and macroscopic scales.
❌ Molar mass and molecular mass are the same thing. ✅ Molecular mass is in amu; molar mass is in g/mol — numerically equal but different units.
❌ Limiting reagent is the reactant with smallest mass. ✅ Limiting reagent is the one that produces the least product (determined by moles, not mass).
❌ % yield can exceed 100%. ✅ % yield >100% indicates impure product or incomplete drying.
❌ Molarity and molality are the same. ✅ Molarity = mol/L solution (changes with T); Molality = mol/kg solvent (temperature-independent).
❌ A strong acid completely ionizes in water. ✅ Strong acids (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄) are ~100% ionized; weak acids partially ionize.
❌ pH can be negative. ✅ pH < 0 is possible for concentrations >1M (e.g., 2M HCl has pH ≈ −0.3).
❌ Kc changes when concentration changes. ✅ Kc is constant at constant temperature; only temperature changes K.
❌ Adding catalyst shifts equilibrium position. ✅ Catalyst speeds both forward and backward reactions equally; no shift in equilibrium.
❌ High pressure always favors products. ✅ High pressure favors side with fewer gas moles (Le Chatelier).
❌ Exothermic reactions are spontaneous. ✅ Spontaneity depends on ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, not just ΔH.
❌ Endothermic reactions cannot be spontaneous. ✅ Endothermic reactions can be spontaneous if TΔS > ΔH (e.g., ice melting above 0°C).
❌ ΔH and ΔU are always the same. ✅ ΔH = ΔU + PΔV; they differ when gas moles change.
❌ Heat (q) and work (w) are state functions. ✅ q and w are path functions; only ΔU, ΔH, ΔS, ΔG are state functions.
❌ Oxidation and reduction happen separately. ✅ Oxidation and reduction always occur together (redox).
❌ Oxidizing agent gets oxidized. ✅ Oxidizing agent accepts electrons and gets reduced.
❌ Reducing agent gets reduced. ✅ Reducing agent donates electrons and gets oxidized.
❌ Faraday's laws apply only to metals. ✅ Faraday's laws apply to any substance deposited/dissolved at electrodes.
❌ Real gases obey PV=nRT at all conditions. ✅ Real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature.
❌ van der Waals constants a and b are same for all gases. ✅ a (attraction) and b (volume) are gas-specific.
❌ Surface tension increases with temperature. ✅ Surface tension decreases as temperature increases.
❌ Viscosity decreases with temperature for liquids. ✅ Viscosity of liquids decreases with T; gases increase with T.
❌ Colligative properties depend on nature of solute. ✅ Colligative properties depend only on number of particles, not identity.
❌ Raoult's law applies to all solutions. ✅ Raoult's law is exact for ideal solutions; approximate for dilute real solutions.
❌ Osmotic pressure is a colligative property. ✅ Yes — π = CRT depends on solute particle concentration.
❌ Atomic number equals mass number. ✅ Atomic number = protons; mass number = protons + neutrons.
❌ Bohr model explains all atoms. ✅ Bohr model works only for hydrogen-like (one-electron) systems.

Atomic structure: From Rutherford's nuclear model through Bohr's quantized orbits to the modern quantum mechanical model, understanding electron configuration using four quantum numbers is fundamental.

Stoichiometry: The mole concept bridges atomic and macroscopic scales; limiting reagent determines theoretical yield; concentration expressed as molarity or molality.

Chemical equilibrium: Dynamic equilibrium has equal forward and backward rates; Kc/Kp are temperature-dependent; Le Chatelier's principle predicts response to stress.

Thermodynamics: First law (energy conservation); enthalpy changes in reactions; Gibbs free energy determines spontaneity; entropy of universe always increases.

Oxidation-reduction: Redox involves electron transfer; oxidation numbers track electron flow; electrochemical cells convert chemical to electrical energy; Faraday's laws quantify electrolysis.

States of matter: Gas laws relate P, V, T, n; kinetic theory explains gas behavior; real gases deviate due to intermolecular forces and molecular volume.

Solutions: Molarity and molality express concentration; colligative properties depend on particle number; Raoult's law describes vapor pressure of ideal solutions.

Chemical bonding: Ionic bonds form from electron transfer; covalent bonds from sharing; VSEPR predicts molecular geometry; hybridization explains bonding orbitals.

Organic chemistry basics: Carbon's tetravalency and catenation enable millions of compounds; functional groups determine reactivity; IUPAC nomenclature provides systematic naming.

Hydrocarbons: Alkanes (CnH2n+2) are saturated; alkenes (CnH2n) have C=C; alkynes (CnH2n-2) have C≡C; aromatic compounds based on benzene ring.

Periodic table: Elements arranged by atomic number; periodic trends in radius, ionization energy, electronegativity; s, p, d, f blocks based on orbital type.

Applied chemistry: Petrochemical industry, polymer science, green chemistry principles; importance of sustainable chemical manufacturing for environmental protection.

Quantum numbers fully describe electron state; Aufbau, Pauli, and Hund guide electron configuration.

Heisenberg uncertainty is a fundamental limit, not measurement error.

data.title: Importance and scope of chemistry
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Chemistry Everywhere You Look

Fertilisers that feed billions, medicines that cure, polymers that clothe, fuels that move — and the pollution that threatens. Chemistry's importance is double-edged: it creates solutions and creates problems, and understanding it is how we maximise the first and manage the second.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Importance of chemistry — classification table

| Area | Contribution | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Agriculture** | Fertilisers, pesticides | Urea, NPK, ammonium sulphate |
| **Medicine** | Drugs, anaesthetics, antiseptics | Aspirin, chloroform, Dettol |
| **Industry** | Acids, alkalis, dyes, alloys | H₂SO₄, NaOH, steel |
| **Energy** | Fuels, batteries, solar materials | Petrol, LPG, Li-ion cells |
| **Daily life** | Soaps, detergents, paints, cosmetics | Detergents, toothpaste |
| **Food** | Preservatives, additives, packaging | Salt, preservatives |
| **Environment** | Pollution control, green chemistry | Catalytic converters, CFC ban |
| **Research/defence** | New materials, explosives, semiconductors | Nanomaterials, silicon chips |

### 2.2 Scope of chemistry

The **scope** spans:
- **Pure research:** discovering structures, reactions, new compounds.
- **Applied fields:** engineering processes, quality control, forensic analysis.
- **Interdisciplinary frontiers:** medicinal chemistry, environmental chemistry, materials science, computational chemistry, biochemistry.

### 2.3 Harmful effects — the responsibility side

Chemistry also brings: **pollution** (industrial effluents, smog), **ozone depletion** (CFCs), **greenhouse gases** (CO₂ from fossil-fuel combustion), **toxic waste** (heavy metals), and **drug/narcotic misuse**. Modern chemistry responds with **green chemistry** — designing processes that reduce or eliminate hazardous substances.

### 2.4 Similarities and differences — benefits vs hazards of chemistry

**Similarities:** both arise from the same chemical knowledge and reactions; both scale with industrial use; both are manageable through informed control.
**Differences:** benefits are intended products (fertiliser, medicine) improving life; hazards are unintended by-products (effluents, emissions) harming life. Benefits are maximised by design; hazards are minimised by regulation, treatment and green chemistry.

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 1:** importance and scope follow directly from what chemistry studies.
- **To modern chemical manufactures (Unit 17):** the industrial applications made concrete.
- **To bio-inorganic chemistry (Unit 11):** chemistry's role in living systems.

## 4. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 4.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

No verified PYQ for this exact topic in the bank. Practise importance/scope lists and the benefits-vs-hazards discussion as **NEB-style practice** (2–3m).

### 4.2 Likely question forms

1. Describe the importance of chemistry in daily life with four examples (3m).
2. What are the harmful effects of chemistry? How can they be minimised? (3m)
3. Define the scope of chemistry (2m).

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Giving only benefits — NEB expects the harm side too.
2. Vague examples without naming actual chemicals.
3. Missing green chemistry as the modern response.

**The same chemistry that feeds also pollutes** — the difference is design and control.

Its **scope** runs from pure research to applied fields and interdisciplinary frontiers — medicinal, environmental, materials and computational chemistry. data.topicTitle: Basic concepts of chemistry: atoms, molecules, relative masses of atoms and molecules, atomic mass unit (amu), radicals, molecular formula, empirical formula
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Vocabulary of Matter

Atoms, molecules, ions, radicals, amu, empirical and molecular formula — this topic builds the precise vocabulary every later calculation uses. Master it here and stoichiometry becomes arithmetic; fumble it and every chapter after leaks marks.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2023, 2022, 2021, 2024)

### 2.1 Atoms, molecules, ions and radicals

- **Atom:** the smallest particle of an element that takes part in a chemical reaction (e.g. Fe, He).
- **Molecule:** the smallest particle of an element or compound that exists independently (H₂, O₂, CO₂, H₂O).
- **Ion:** an atom or group carrying charge — cation (+, e.g. Na⁺) or anion (−, e.g. Cl⁻).
- **Radical:** an atom or group of atoms behaving as a single unit in reactions, carrying charge (inorganic radicals: SO₄²⁻, NO₃⁻, NH₄⁺) or an unpaired electron (free radicals: Cl·).

### 2.2 Relative atomic mass and the amu

- **Relative atomic mass (A_r):** mass of an atom compared with 1/12 the mass of one carbon-12 atom — dimensionless (H = 1, C = 12, O = 16).
- **Atomic mass unit (amu):** 1 amu = 1/12 mass of one C-12 atom = **1.66×10⁻²⁷ kg**.
- **Relative molecular mass (M_r):** sum of the A_r of all atoms in the molecule (H₂O = 18, CO₂ = 44, H₂SO₄ = 98).

### 2.3 Measurement basics (NEB 2023, 2022, 2021)

- **SI base units** (NEB 2022, 1m): metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, **mole** (amount of substance), candela.
- **Significant figures** (NEB 2023, 3m): in a product, the number of significant figures equals the least precise factor.
- **Mean and absolute error** (NEB 2021, 2m): mean = (x₁+x₂)/2; absolute error = (x_max − x_min)/2; relative error = Δx/mean × 100%.

### 2.4 Molecular formula vs empirical formula — similarities and differences

**Similarities:** both express which elements are present and in what whole-number ratio; both are derived from percentage composition; both obey valency rules.
**Differences:**

| | Empirical formula | Molecular formula |
|---|---|---|
| Shows | Simplest whole-number ratio | Actual number of atoms per molecule |
| Value | One per compound (ratio) | n × empirical formula |
| Example (glucose) | CH₂O | C₆H₁₂O₆ |
| Determined from | % composition | % composition + molar mass |

### 2.5 Worked numericals

**Q (2m, 2024):** Calculate the number of atoms in 5.6 g of iron (Fe = 56).
Moles = 5.6/56 = 0.1 mol → atoms = 0.1 × 6.022×10²³ = **6.022×10²² atoms**.

**Q (3m, 2023):** The density of a liquid is 0.8792 g/cm³. Calculate the mass of 45.6 cm³, to three significant figures.
m = ρV = 0.8792 × 45.6 = 40.09152 g → **40.1 g** (3 s.f., limited by the 45.6).

**Q (2m, 2021):** Two readings of a wire's length are 10.4 cm and 10.6 cm. Find the mean and absolute error.
Mean = 10.5 cm; absolute error = (10.6 − 10.4)/2 = **0.1 cm** (relative error ≈ 0.95%).

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 4:** % composition → empirical formula → molecular formula chain.
- **To Unit 2 (stoichiometry):** moles, formulas and ratios power every calculation.
- **To Unit 3 (atomic structure):** the atom's internal structure explains its chemical behaviour.

## 4. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 4.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

| Year | Unit | Topic | Question | Marks | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2080/2024 | Foundation | Basic concepts | Calculate the number of atoms in 5.6 g of iron (Fe = 56). | 2 | Numerical |
| 2079/2023 | Foundation | Measurement | The density of a liquid is 0.8792 g/cm³. Calculate the mass of 45.6 cm³ to three significant figures. | 3 | Numerical |
| 2078/2022 | Foundation | Measurement | Which of the following is the SI base unit of amount of substance? (a) gram (b) mole (c) millimole (d) kilogram | 1 | MCQ |
| 2077/2021 | Foundation | Measurement | Two readings for the length of a wire are 10.4 cm and 10.6 cm. Calculate the mean value and absolute error. | 2 | Numerical |

### 4.2 Likely additional forms (NEB-style)

1. Define radical; give ionic and free-radical examples (2m).
2. Differentiate empirical and molecular formula (2m).
3. amu definition and value (2m).

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Treating "amu" and "relative atomic mass" as identical — one is a unit, the other a ratio.
2. Rounding before the final step in sig-fig numericals.
3. Confusing radicals (charged groups) with free radicals (unpaired electrons).
confusion: **Atom vs molecule:** Fe is an atom (and also its molecule); O₂ is a molecule of two atoms — oxygen's atom is O.
**Empirical = ratio; molecular = reality** — CH₂O is the ratio, C₆H₁₂O₆ the molecule.

data.summary: The **atom** is the smallest reacting particle; the **molecule** the smallest independently existing one; **ions** carry charge; **radicals** act as units (SO₄²⁻) or carry unpaired electrons (Cl·). The **amu** = 1/12 of carbon-12 = 1.66×10⁻²⁷ kg, and **relative atomic mass** compares atoms to that standard. SI's base unit of amount of substance is the **mole** (NEB 2022, 1m). Measurement demands **significant figures** (product keeps the least precise count — NEB 2023: 0.8792 × 45.6 → 40.1 g) and **error analysis** (mean 10.5 cm, absolute error 0.1 cm — NEB 2021). The **empirical formula** (simplest ratio, CH₂O) differs from the **molecular formula** (actual atoms, C₆H₁₂O₆ = 6 × CH₂O) in scale, not in kind.

- **Mean and absolute error** (NEB 2021, 2m): mean = (x₁+x₂)/2; absolute error = (x_max − x_min)/2; relative error = Δx/mean × 100%.

### 2.4 Molecular formula vs empirical formula — similarities and differences

**Similarities:** both express which elements are present and in what whole-number ratio; both are derived from percentage composition; both obey valency rules.
**Differences:**

| | Empirical formula | Molecular formula |
|---|---|---|
| Shows | Simplest whole-number ratio | Actual number of atoms per molecule |
| Value | One per compound (ratio) | n × empirical formula |
| Example (glucose) | CH₂O | C₆H₁₂O₆ |
| Determined from | % composition | % composition + molar mass |

### 2.5 Worked numericals

**Q (2m, 2024):** Calculate the number of atoms in 5.6 g of iron (Fe = 56).
Moles = 5.6/56 = 0.1 mol → atoms = 0.1 × 6.022×10²³ = **6.022×10²² atoms**.

**Q (3m, 2023):** The density of a liquid is 0.8792 g/cm³. Calculate the mass of 45.6 cm³, to three significant figures.
m = ρV = 0.8792 × 45.6 = 40.09152 g → **40.1 g** (3 s.f., limited by the 45.6).

**Q (2m, 2021):** Two readings of a wire's length are 10.4 cm and 10.6 cm. Find the mean and absolute error.
Mean = 10.5 cm; absolute error = (10.6 − 10.4)/2 = **0.1 cm** (relative error ≈ 0.95%).

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 4:** % composition → empirical formula → molecular formula chain.
- **To Unit 2 (stoichiometry):** moles, formulas and ratios power every calculation.
- **To Unit 3 (atomic structure):** the atom's internal structure explains its chemical behaviour.

## 4. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

| 2080/2024 | Foundation | Basic concepts | Calculate the number of atoms in 5.6 g of iron (Fe = 56). | 2 | Numerical |
| 2079/2023 | Foundation | Measurement | The density of a liquid is 0.8792 g/cm³. Calculate the mass of 45.6 cm³ to three significant figures. | 3 | Numerical |
| 2078/2022 | Foundation | Measurement | Which of the following is the SI base unit of amount of substance? (a) gram (b) mole (c) millimole (d) kilogram | 1 | MCQ |
| 2077/2021 | Foundation | Measurement | Two readings for the length of a wire are 10.4 cm and 10.6 cm. Calculate the mean value and absolute error. | 2 | Numerical |

### 4.2 Likely additional forms (NEB-style)

1. Define radical; give ionic and free-radical examples (2m).
2. Differentiate empirical and molecular formula (2m).
3. amu definition and value (2m).

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Treating "amu" and "relative atomic mass" as identical — one is a unit, the other a ratio.
2. Rounding before the final step in sig-fig numericals.
3. Confusing radicals (charged groups) with free radicals (unpaired electrons).

confusion: ❌ All cells look the same under a microscope. ✅ Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells have them.
❌ DNA and RNA are identical in structure. ✅ DNA is double-stranded with deoxyribose and thymine; RNA is single-stranded with ribose and uracil.
❌ Mitosis produces genetically different cells. ✅ Mitosis produces genetically identical diploid daughter cells.
❌ Meiosis produces identical cells. ✅ Meiosis produces 4 genetically diverse haploid gametes.
❌ Crossing over occurs in mitosis. ✅ Crossing over occurs in Prophase I of meiosis only.
❌ All enzymes are proteins. ✅ Most enzymes are proteins; some RNA molecules (ribozymes) also have catalytic activity.
❌ ATP is the only energy currency. ✅ GTP, UTP, and CTP also serve as energy carriers in specific pathways.
❌ Photosynthesis occurs in all plant cells. ✅ Photosynthesis occurs only in cells containing chloroplasts (mainly mesophyll).
❌ Respiration and photosynthesis are opposite processes with same equation. ✅ They are complementary but occur in different organelles and under different conditions.
❌ Oxygen is produced during respiration. ✅ Oxygen is consumed in aerobic respiration; produced during photosynthesis.
❌ Food chain shows all feeding relationships. ✅ Food chain is linear; food web shows interconnected feeding relationships.
❌ 90% of energy is transferred to next trophic level. ✅ Only ~10% energy transfers; ~90% lost as heat.
❌ Biomagnification decreases toxin concentration up the food chain. ✅ Biomagnification increases toxin concentration at higher trophic levels.
❌ Carbon cycle only involves plants and animals. ✅ Carbon cycle involves atmosphere, oceans, fossils, rocks, and decomposers.
❌ Nitrogen fixation only occurs in bacteria. ✅ Some lightning and industrial processes (Haber) also fix nitrogen.
❌ All fungi are harmful. ✅ Many fungi are beneficial (decomposers, mycorrhizae, food, antibiotics like penicillin).
❌ Viruses are living organisms. ✅ Viruses are acellular — they cannot reproduce without a host and lack metabolism.
❌ Bacteria are always harmful. ✅ Most bacteria are harmless or beneficial (gut flora, nitrogen fixation, decomposition).
❌ Gram-positive and Gram-negative differ only in color. ✅ Gram-positive has thick peptidoglycan layer; Gram-negative has thin layer + outer membrane.
❌ Natural selection creates perfect organisms. ✅ Natural selection favors traits suited to current environment; environments change.
❌ Evolution is goal-oriented. ✅ Evolution has no goal; it acts on random variation filtered by selection.
❌ Homologous and analogous structures mean the same thing. ✅ Homologous = common ancestry (divergent); Analogous = similar function, different origin (convergent).
❌ Fossils are preserved bones only. ✅ Fossils include impressions, trace fossils, amber-preserved organisms, and molecular fossils.
❌ Lamarckism is completely wrong. ✅ Lamarck's inheritance of acquired characteristics is largely rejected, but epigenetics shows some environmental effects can be inherited.
❌ Five-kingdom classification is outdated. ✅ Six-kingdom (adding Archaea) and phylogenetic systems are more current, but five-kingdom remains useful for education.
❌ Binomial nomenclature names change frequently. ✅ Names are stable once formally published; changes require formal revision by taxonomic authorities.
❌ All algae are aquatic. ✅ Some algae live in soil, on tree bark, or in symbiotic relationships (lichens).
❌ Bryophytes have vascular tissue. ✅ Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts, hornworts) lack true vascular tissue (xylem/phloem).
❌ Gymnosperms produce flowers. ✅ Gymnosperms have naked seeds in cones; angiosperms produce flowers and enclosed seeds.
❌ Double fertilization occurs in gymnosperms. ✅ Double fertilization (zygote + endosperm) is unique to angiosperms.
❌ Earthworms have an open circulatory system. ✅ Earthworms have a closed circulatory system with dorsal and ventral vessels.
❌ Frogs breathe only through lungs. ✅ Frogs use cutaneous respiration (skin), buccal cavity, and lungs.
❌ Conservation only means protecting animals. ✅ Conservation includes genetic, species, and ecosystem diversity; in-situ and ex-situ strategies.
❌ In-situ and ex-situ conservation are the same. ✅ In-situ = conservation in natural habitat (national parks); Ex-situ = conservation outside habitat (zoos, seed banks).

data.title: Percentage composition from molecular formula
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Weighing a Molecule on Paper

Given a formula, you can compute exactly what fraction of its mass each element contributes — the **percentage composition**. It is the bridge between formulas and laboratory analysis, and the first step of every empirical-formula problem.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2024)

### 2.1 The percentage composition formula

$$\%\text{ of element} = \frac{\text{mass of element in 1 mol of compound}}{\text{molar mass of compound}} \times 100$$

The percentages of all elements sum to 100% — a built-in check.

### 2.2 Worked numericals

**Q (2m, 2024):** Calculate the percentage of nitrogen in urea, CO(NH₂)₂ (C = 12, O = 16, N = 14, H = 1).
- Molar mass = 12 + 16 + 2(14 + 2×1) = 12 + 16 + 32 = 60 g/mol
- Mass of N = 2 × 14 = 28 g
$$\%N = \frac{28}{60} \times 100 ≈ \boxed{46.7\%}$$
— the highest nitrogen content of common fertilisers, which is why urea dominates the market.

**Q (NEB-style):** Find the percentage composition of CaCO₃ (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16).
- M = 40 + 12 + 48 = 100 g/mol
- %Ca = 40%, %C = 12%, %O = 48% (sums to 100 ✓)

**Q (NEB-style):** Which is the richer iron ore by mass — Fe₂O₃ or Fe₃O₄? (Fe = 56, O = 16)
- Fe₂O₃: M = 160, %Fe = 112/160 = 70%
- Fe₃O₄: M = 232, %Fe = 168/232 ≈ 72.4% → **Fe₃O₄** is richer.

### 2.3 Reverse direction — % composition to formula

The same arithmetic runs backwards: assume 100 g of compound → convert each percentage to moles → divide by the smallest → simplest ratio = **empirical formula** → multiply by n = M/empirical-mass for the **molecular formula** (full treatment in Unit 2, Topic 12).

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 3:** molecular formula is the input; empirical/molecular distinction matters.
- **To stoichiometry (Unit 2):** every mole calculation begins with molar mass from the formula.
- **To chemistry of metals (Unit 10):** ore richness comparisons use exactly this arithmetic.

## 4. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 4.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

| Year | Unit | Topic | Question | Marks | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2080/2024 | Foundation | Percentage composition | Calculate the percentage of nitrogen in urea, CO(NH₂)₂. (C = 12, O = 16, N = 14, H = 1) | 2 | Numerical |

### 4.2 Likely additional forms (NEB-style)

1. % composition of a named compound (2m).
2. Compare two ores/compounds by % of a target element (3m).
3. Check that percentages sum to 100 (1m).

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Miscounting atoms in parentheses — CO(NH₂)₂ has TWO NH₂ groups.
2. Forgetting × 100.
3. Not checking the total sums to 100%.

data.topicTitle: IUPAC Nomenclature of Organic Compounds (up to chain having 6-carbon atoms)
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — A Name That Encodes the Structure

Before IUPAC, one compound wore many names (wood spirit, grain alcohol…). The **IUPAC system** builds every name from the structure itself: a **word root** for chain length, a **suffix** for the bond type/functional group, and **prefixes** for substituents. Master the rules for chains up to six carbons and you can name — or draw — any simple organic compound from its formula alone.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 The three parts of an IUPAC name

- **Word root:** chain length — meth (1), eth (2), prop (3), but (4), pent (5), hex (6).
- **Primary suffix:** saturation — **ane** (single bonds), **ene** (C=C), **yne** (C≡C).
- **Prefix:** substituents (methyl, ethyl, chloro…) written before the root in **alphabetical order**, each with a **locant** (position number). Functional-group suffixes (–ol, –al, –one, –oic acid) replace or follow the primary suffix with their own locant.

### 2.2 The rules

1. Select the **longest continuous carbon chain** as parent (must include the functional group or multiple bond if present).
2. **Number from the end** that gives the **lowest locants** — to the functional group first, then multiple bonds, then substituents.
3. Name substituents with locants; use **di-, tri-** for repeats; list prefixes **alphabetically** (di/tri ignored in alphabetising).
4. Assemble: prefixes (alphabetical) + root + suffix (+ functional locant): e.g. **butan-2-ol**, **2-methylpropanoic acid**.

### 2.3 Worked examples

- CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ → **butane**. CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ → **2-methylbutane**.
- **NEB 2024:** CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃ → 4-carbon chain, OH on C-2 → **butan-2-ol**.

- **NEB 2023 (harder):** CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH(CH₂CH₃)CH₂OH → longest chain with OH = 6 carbons; number from the OH end → OH at C-1, ethyl at C-2, methyl at C-5 → **2-ethyl-5-methylhexan-1-ol** (ethyl before methyl alphabetically).

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Word root** | Name part giving the parent chain length | pent- = 5 carbons |
| **Primary suffix** | Saturation class of the chain | -ane, -ene, -yne |
| **Locant** | Number fixing a substituent or group position | butan-**2**-ol |
| **Prefix** | Substituent name before the root | 2-methyl… |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why "longest chain" and "lowest locant" exist

- One structure must yield one name — every chemist in the world must draw the same molecule from the same words. The longest-chain rule fixes the parent; the lowest-locant rule fixes the numbering; alphabetical order fixes the listing. Any other choice would give two names for one compound.

### 4.2 Functional groups outrank substituents

- When a functional group (OH, CHO, COOH) is present, numbering serves **it first** — butan-2-ol is numbered from the OH end even if a methyl then gets a higher number. Priority: COOH > CHO > C=O > OH > C=C/C≡C > alkyl.

### 4.3 Common vs systematic names

- Acetone = propanone; acetic acid = ethanoic acid; ethylene = ethene. Common names persist in industry and labs, but NEB answers should use IUPAC.

## 5. Comparison Tables

|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | meth- | methane | — | — |
| 2 | eth- | ethane | ethene | ethyne |
| 3 | prop- | propane | propene | propyne |
| 4 | but- | butane | but-1-ene | but-1-yne |
| 5 | pent- | pentane | pent-1-ene | pent-1-yne |
| 6 | hex- | hexane | hex-1-ene | hex-1-yne |

| Group | Suffix | Example |
|---|---|---|

| –CHO | -al | ethanal |

confusion: ❌ All atoms are identical in an element. ✅ Isotopes have same protons but different neutrons.
❌ Atoms are indivisible. ✅ Atoms consist of protons, neutrons, and electrons.
❌ Electrons orbit in fixed paths like planets. ✅ Electrons exist in probability clouds (orbitals).
❌ Heisenberg uncertainty means we cannot measure position and momentum precisely simultaneously — not that we lack good instruments.
❌ de Broglie wavelength applies only to light. ✅ All matter has wave nature; detectable mainly for small masses like electrons.
❌ Quantum number l can be any integer. ✅ l ranges from 0 to n−1.
❌ Magnetic quantum number ml determines energy. ✅ ml determines orbital orientation, not energy (in absence of magnetic field).
❌ Spin quantum number ms can be ±½ or any value. ✅ ms is always +½ or −½.
❌ Aufbau principle means filling from bottom to top of the diagram. ✅ Fill lowest-energy orbitals first: 1s→2s→2p→3s→3p→4s→3d→4p→...
❌ Pauli exclusion allows two electrons per orbital with any spin. ✅ Two electrons in same orbital must have opposite spins.
❌ Hund's rule means pair electrons before spreading. ✅ Electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly first with parallel spins.
❌ The mole is just a number like dozen. ✅ 1 mole = 6.022×10²³ particles (Avogadro constant) — a bridge between atomic and macroscopic scales.
❌ Molar mass and molecular mass are the same thing. ✅ Molecular mass is in amu; molar mass is in g/mol — numerically equal but different units.
❌ Limiting reagent is the reactant with smallest mass. ✅ Limiting reagent is the one that produces the least product (determined by moles, not mass).
❌ % yield can exceed 100%. ✅ % yield >100% indicates impure product or incomplete drying.
❌ Molarity and molality are the same. ✅ Molarity = mol/L solution (changes with T); Molality = mol/kg solvent (temperature-independent).
❌ A strong acid completely ionizes in water. ✅ Strong acids (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄) are ~100% ionized; weak acids partially ionize.
❌ pH can be negative. ✅ pH < 0 is possible for concentrations >1M (e.g., 2M HCl has pH ≈ −0.3).
❌ Kc changes when concentration changes. ✅ Kc is constant at constant temperature; only temperature changes K.
❌ Adding catalyst shifts equilibrium position. ✅ Catalyst speeds both forward and backward reactions equally; no shift in equilibrium.
❌ High pressure always favors products. ✅ High pressure favors side with fewer gas moles (Le Chatelier).
❌ Exothermic reactions are spontaneous. ✅ Spontaneity depends on ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, not just ΔH.
❌ Endothermic reactions cannot be spontaneous. ✅ Endothermic reactions can be spontaneous if TΔS > ΔH (e.g., ice melting above 0°C).
❌ ΔH and ΔU are always the same. ✅ ΔH = ΔU + PΔV; they differ when gas moles change.
❌ Heat (q) and work (w) are state functions. ✅ q and w are path functions; only ΔU, ΔH, ΔS, ΔG are state functions.
❌ Oxidation and reduction happen separately. ✅ Oxidation and reduction always occur together (redox).
❌ Oxidizing agent gets oxidized. ✅ Oxidizing agent accepts electrons and gets reduced.
❌ Reducing agent gets reduced. ✅ Reducing agent donates electrons and gets oxidized.
❌ Faraday's laws apply only to metals. ✅ Faraday's laws apply to any substance deposited/dissolved at electrodes.
❌ Real gases obey PV=nRT at all conditions. ✅ Real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature.
❌ van der Waals constants a and b are same for all gases. ✅ a (attraction) and b (volume) are gas-specific.
❌ Surface tension increases with temperature. ✅ Surface tension decreases as temperature increases.
❌ Viscosity decreases with temperature for liquids. ✅ Viscosity of liquids decreases with T; gases increase with T.
❌ Colligative properties depend on nature of solute. ✅ Colligative properties depend only on number of particles, not identity.
❌ Raoult's law applies to all solutions. ✅ Raoult's law is exact for ideal solutions; approximate for dilute real solutions.
❌ Osmotic pressure is a colligative property. ✅ Yes — π = CRT depends on solute particle concentration.
❌ All carbon compounds are organic. ✅ CO, CO₂, carbonates, and carbides are inorganic despite containing carbon.

Before IUPAC, one compound wore many names (wood spirit, grain alcohol…).
