notes: Alkanes: CnH2n+2, single bonds (saturated).
Alkenes: CnH2n, double bonds (unsaturated).
Alkynes: CnH2n-2, triple bonds.
Aromatic: benzene ring, delocalized π electrons.
confusion: ❌ All cells look the same under a microscope. ✅ Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells have them.
❌ DNA and RNA are identical in structure. ✅ DNA is double-stranded with deoxyribose and thymine; RNA is single-stranded with ribose and uracil.
❌ Mitosis produces genetically different cells. ✅ Mitosis produces genetically identical diploid daughter cells.
❌ Meiosis produces identical cells. ✅ Meiosis produces 4 genetically diverse haploid gametes.
❌ Crossing over occurs in mitosis. ✅ Crossing over occurs in Prophase I of meiosis only.
❌ All enzymes are proteins. ✅ Most enzymes are proteins; some RNA molecules (ribozymes) also have catalytic activity.
❌ ATP is the only energy currency. ✅ GTP, UTP, and CTP also serve as energy carriers in specific pathways.
❌ Photosynthesis occurs in all plant cells. ✅ Photosynthesis occurs only in cells containing chloroplasts (mainly mesophyll).
❌ Respiration and photosynthesis are opposite processes with same equation. ✅ They are complementary but occur in different organelles and under different conditions.
❌ Oxygen is produced during respiration. ✅ Oxygen is consumed in aerobic respiration; produced during photosynthesis.
❌ Food chain shows all feeding relationships. ✅ Food chain is linear; food web shows interconnected feeding relationships.
❌ 90% of energy is transferred to next trophic level. ✅ Only ~10% energy transfers; ~90% lost as heat.
❌ Biomagnification decreases toxin concentration up the food chain. ✅ Biomagnification increases toxin concentration at higher trophic levels.
❌ Carbon cycle only involves plants and animals. ✅ Carbon cycle involves atmosphere, oceans, fossils, rocks, and decomposers.
❌ Nitrogen fixation only occurs in bacteria. ✅ Some lightning and industrial processes (Haber) also fix nitrogen.
❌ All fungi are harmful. ✅ Many fungi are beneficial (decomposers, mycorrhizae, food, antibiotics like penicillin).
❌ Viruses are living organisms. ✅ Viruses are acellular — they cannot reproduce without a host and lack metabolism.
❌ Bacteria are always harmful. ✅ Most bacteria are harmless or beneficial (gut flora, nitrogen fixation, decomposition).
❌ Gram-positive and Gram-negative differ only in color. ✅ Gram-positive has thick peptidoglycan layer; Gram-negative has thin layer + outer membrane.
❌ Natural selection creates perfect organisms. ✅ Natural selection favors traits suited to current environment; environments change.
❌ Evolution is goal-oriented. ✅ Evolution has no goal; it acts on random variation filtered by selection.
❌ Homologous and analogous structures mean the same thing. ✅ Homologous = common ancestry (divergent); Analogous = similar function, different origin (convergent).
❌ Fossils are preserved bones only. ✅ Fossils include impressions, trace fossils, amber-preserved organisms, and molecular fossils.
❌ Lamarckism is completely wrong. ✅ Lamarck's inheritance of acquired characteristics is largely rejected, but epigenetics shows some environmental effects can be inherited.
❌ Five-kingdom classification is outdated. ✅ Six-kingdom (adding Archaea) and phylogenetic systems are more current, but five-kingdom remains useful for education.
❌ Binomial nomenclature names change frequently. ✅ Names are stable once formally published; changes require formal revision by taxonomic authorities.
❌ All algae are aquatic. ✅ Some algae live in soil, on tree bark, or in symbiotic relationships (lichens).
❌ Bryophytes have vascular tissue. ✅ Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts, hornworts) lack true vascular tissue (xylem/phloem).
❌ Gymnosperms produce flowers. ✅ Gymnosperms have naked seeds in cones; angiosperms produce flowers and enclosed seeds.
❌ Double fertilization occurs in gymnosperms. ✅ Double fertilization (zygote + endosperm) is unique to angiosperms.
❌ Earthworms have an open circulatory system. ✅ Earthworms have a closed circulatory system with dorsal and ventral vessels.
❌ Frogs breathe only through lungs. ✅ Frogs use cutaneous respiration (skin), buccal cavity, and lungs.
❌ Conservation only means protecting animals. ✅ Conservation includes genetic, species, and ecosystem diversity; in-situ and ex-situ strategies.
❌ In-situ and ex-situ conservation are the same. ✅ In-situ = conservation in natural habitat (national parks); Ex-situ = conservation outside habitat (zoos, seed banks).
❌ All atoms are identical in an element. ✅ Isotopes have same protons but different neutrons.
❌ Atoms are indivisible. ✅ Atoms consist of protons, neutrons, and electrons.
❌ Electrons orbit in fixed paths like planets. ✅ Electrons exist in probability clouds (orbitals).
❌ Heisenberg uncertainty means we cannot measure position and momentum precisely simultaneously — not that we lack good instruments.
❌ de Broglie wavelength applies only to light. ✅ All matter has wave nature; detectable mainly for small masses like electrons.
❌ Quantum number l can be any integer. ✅ l ranges from 0 to n−1.
❌ Magnetic quantum number ml determines energy. ✅ ml determines orbital orientation, not energy (in absence of magnetic field).
❌ Spin quantum number ms can be ±½ or any value. ✅ ms is always +½ or −½.
❌ Aufbau principle means filling from bottom to top of the diagram. ✅ Fill lowest-energy orbitals first: 1s→2s→2p→3s→3p→4s→3d→4p→...
❌ Pauli exclusion allows two electrons per orbital with any spin. ✅ Two electrons in same orbital must have opposite spins.
❌ Hund's rule means pair electrons before spreading. ✅ Electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly first with parallel spins.
❌ The mole is just a number like dozen. ✅ 1 mole = 6.022×10²³ particles (Avogadro constant) — a bridge between atomic and macroscopic scales.
❌ Molar mass and molecular mass are the same thing. ✅ Molecular mass is in amu; molar mass is in g/mol — numerically equal but different units.
❌ Limiting reagent is the reactant with smallest mass. ✅ Limiting reagent is the one that produces the least product (determined by moles, not mass).
❌ % yield can exceed 100%. ✅ % yield >100% indicates impure product or incomplete drying.
❌ Molarity and molality are the same. ✅ Molarity = mol/L solution (changes with T); Molality = mol/kg solvent (temperature-independent).
❌ A strong acid completely ionizes in water. ✅ Strong acids (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄) are ~100% ionized; weak acids partially ionize.
❌ pH can be negative. ✅ pH < 0 is possible for concentrations >1M (e.g., 2M HCl has pH ≈ −0.3).
❌ Kc changes when concentration changes. ✅ Kc is constant at constant temperature; only temperature changes K.
❌ Adding catalyst shifts equilibrium position. ✅ Catalyst speeds both forward and backward reactions equally; no shift in equilibrium.
❌ High pressure always favors products. ✅ High pressure favors side with fewer gas moles (Le Chatelier).
❌ Exothermic reactions are spontaneous. ✅ Spontaneity depends on ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, not just ΔH.
❌ Endothermic reactions cannot be spontaneous. ✅ Endothermic reactions can be spontaneous if TΔS > ΔH (e.g., ice melting above 0°C).
❌ ΔH and ΔU are always the same. ✅ ΔH = ΔU + PΔV; they differ when gas moles change.
❌ Heat (q) and work (w) are state functions. ✅ q and w are path functions; only ΔU, ΔH, ΔS, ΔG are state functions.
❌ Oxidation and reduction happen separately. ✅ Oxidation and reduction always occur together (redox).
❌ Oxidizing agent gets oxidized. ✅ Oxidizing agent accepts electrons and gets reduced.
❌ Reducing agent gets reduced. ✅ Reducing agent donates electrons and gets oxidized.
❌ Faraday's laws apply only to metals. ✅ Faraday's laws apply to any substance deposited/dissolved at electrodes.
❌ Real gases obey PV=nRT at all conditions. ✅ Real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature.
❌ van der Waals constants a and b are same for all gases. ✅ a (attraction) and b (volume) are gas-specific.
❌ Surface tension increases with temperature. ✅ Surface tension decreases as temperature increases.
❌ Viscosity decreases with temperature for liquids. ✅ Viscosity of liquids decreases with T; gases increase with T.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Making the π Bond

Alkenes carry one C=C double bond (**CₙH₂ₙ**, sp², planar). Their preparations all create that π bond by **elimination**: water out of an alcohol (**dehydration**), HX out of a haloalkane (**dehydrohalogenation**), or H₂ off an alkyne (**catalytic hydrogenation** of the triple bond).

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Dehydration of alcohols

- **C₂H₅OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O** with **conc. H₂SO₄ at ~170 °C** (or Al₂O₃, ~350 °C).
- Ethanol → ethene; propan-2-ol → propene. Acid-catalysed: protonate –OH, lose water, lose H⁺.
- Competing substitution (ethoxyethane) at lower temperature (~140 °C) — temperature decides.

### 2.2 Dehydrohalogenation (β-elimination)

- **CH₃CH₂Br + alc. KOH → CH₂=CH₂ + KBr + H₂O** — alcoholic KOH, heat.
- The β-hydrogen (next carbon over) is removed along with the halogen; **Saytzeff**: the more substituted (more stable) alkene dominates when two β-sites exist.

### 2.3 Catalytic hydrogenation of alkynes (partial)

- **HC≡CH + H₂ (Lindlar catalyst: Pd on BaSO₄ poisoned with quinoline) → CH₂=CH₂**.
- Partial hydrogenation stops at the alkene; with excess H₂/Ni it would run on to ethane.
- Na/NH₃ (liquid) also reduces alkynes to alkenes (trans-alkene for internal alkynes).

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Dehydration** | Loss of water from an alcohol to form C=C | ethanol → ethene (H₂SO₄, 170 °C) |
| **Dehydrohalogenation** | Loss of HX from a haloalkane (alc. KOH) | bromoethane → ethene |
| **Lindlar catalyst** | Poisoned Pd/BaSO₄ stopping hydrogenation at the alkene | ethyne → ethene |
| **Saytzeff rule** | The more substituted alkene predominates in elimination | butan-2-ol → but-2-ene major |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Temperature controls the exit

- Ethanol + H₂SO₄ at **170 °C** → elimination (ethene); at **140 °C** → substitution (ethoxyethane). Same reagents, different destiny — a classic exam discriminator.

### 4.2 Why alcoholic KOH, not aqueous

- Aqueous KOH substitutes (gives the alcohol); **alcoholic KOH** provides the base that removes the β-H — elimination needs the anhydrous, basic medium.

### 4.3 Stopping at the alkene

- Alkynes hydrogenate twice as fast as alkenes once formed, so ordinary catalysts overshoot. **Poisoning** the catalyst (Lindlar) deactivates it just enough to halt at the alkene — chemoselectivity by sabotage.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Three routes to alkenes**

| Route | Reagents | Starting material | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dehydration | conc. H₂SO₄ 170 °C / Al₂O₃ 350 °C | alcohol | water leaves |
| Dehydrohalogenation | alcoholic KOH, Δ | haloalkane | HX leaves; Saytzeff |
| Partial hydrogenation | H₂ + Lindlar (or Na/NH₃) | alkyne | stop at C=C |

## 6. Common Confusions

**170 vs 140 °C:** ethene at 170 °C, ether at 140 °C — quote both numbers to earn the mark.
**Alc. KOH ≠ aq. KOH:** the solvent word decides elimination vs substitution.
**Lindlar stops at the alkene:** full hydrogenation (Ni, excess H₂) gives the alkane — the poisoned catalyst is the point.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB 2023 (verified PYQ): How is ethane prepared from ethene? Write the reaction mechanism. (3m)** — Ethene is converted to ethane by **catalytic hydrogenation**: **CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃–CH₃** over **Ni (~200 °C) or Pt/Pd at room temperature**. **Mechanism (surface catalysis):** (1) **adsorption** — H₂ dissociates into H atoms adsorbed on the metal surface, and ethene's π bond coordinates to the surface; (2) **syn addition** — two surface H atoms add to the **same face** of the double bond stepwise, first forming an adsorbed ethyl intermediate, then ethane; (3) **desorption** — the saturated ethane leaves the surface, freeing the catalyst. The addition is stereospecific (syn) because both hydrogens come from the metal face.

**NEB 2024 (verified PYQ): How is ethane prepared from ethene? Write the reaction mechanism. (3m)** — Same chemistry: **CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃–CH₃** (Ni/Pt catalyst). Mechanism: H₂ is **adsorbed and dissociated** on the catalyst surface into H atoms; ethene adsorbs through its π bond; the surface H atoms add **one after the other to the same face** (syn addition) giving the adsorbed ethyl radical → ethane; the product **desorbs**, regenerating the catalyst. Conditions: Ni at ~200 °C, or Pt/Pd at room temperature.

**NEB-style (2m): How is ethene obtained from ethanol?** — By **dehydration** with **conc. H₂SO₄ at ~170 °C**: **C₂H₅OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O** (or over Al₂O₃ at ~350 °C). The acid protonates the –OH, water departs as a good leaving group, and a β-hydrogen is lost to form the π bond. (At ~140 °C the same reagents give ethoxyethane instead — temperature is decisive.)

practiceQuestions: **NEB 2023 (verified PYQ): How is ethane prepared from ethene? Write the reaction mechanism. (3m)** — Ethane is prepared from ethene by **catalytic hydrogenation**: **CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃–CH₃**, over **nickel at ~200 °C** (or Pt/Pd at room temperature). **Mechanism (heterogeneous surface catalysis):** **(1) Adsorption** — the H₂ molecule adsorbs onto the metal surface and **dissociates into hydrogen atoms**; ethene adsorbs alongside it through its π bond. **(2) Syn addition** — the surface hydrogen atoms add to the double bond **one at a time and from the same face**: the first H converts ethene into an adsorbed ethyl intermediate, the second completes **ethane**. Because both hydrogens arrive from the metal surface, the addition is **stereospecific (syn)**. **(3) Desorption** — the saturated ethane, no longer able to bind the surface, leaves and frees the catalyst for the next cycle.

**NEB 2024 (verified PYQ): How is ethane prepared from ethene? Write the reaction mechanism. (3m)** — By **catalytic hydrogenation**: **CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃–CH₃** (Ni/Pt catalyst, Ni ~200 °C or Pt/Pd at room temperature). **Mechanism:** the reaction occurs **on the catalyst surface** — **(1)** H₂ is **adsorbed and split into H atoms** on the metal; ethene adsorbs through its π electrons. **(2)** The two surface hydrogens add **stepwise to the same face** of the double bond (syn addition), passing through an adsorbed **ethyl intermediate** to give ethane. **(3)** Ethane **desorbs** from the surface, regenerating the catalyst. The overall change is reduction of the π bond to a σ bond — one mole of H₂ per mole of alkene.

**NEB-style (2m): How is ethene obtained from ethanol?** — By **dehydration of ethanol** with **concentrated H₂SO₄ at about 170 °C** (or by passing vapour over **Al₂O₃ at ~350 °C**): **C₂H₅OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O**. Mechanistically the acid **protonates the –OH group**, making water a good leaving group; water departs and a β-hydrogen is eliminated to create the π bond. Note the temperature discrimination: at ~**140 °C** the same reagents give **ethoxyethane** (substitution) instead of ethene (elimination).

(2) Dehydrohalogenation — CH3CH2Br + alc. KOH -> CH2=CH2 + KBr + H2O; beta-elimination; Saytzeff rule (more substituted alkene major). (3) Partial catalytic hydrogenation of alkynes — HCCH + H2 (Lindlar, Pd/BaSO4 poisoned with quinoline) -> CH2=CH2; or Na/liquid NH3 (trans); excess H2/Ni would give alkane. Full hydrogenation of alkene: CH2=CH2 + H2 -> CH3CH3 (Ni 200C / Pt rt), surface mechanism: adsorption of H2 (dissociation) + alkene, syn addition, desorption.
data.summary: Alkenes (**CₙH₂ₙ**) are built by elimination. **Dehydration**: ethanol loses water over **conc. H₂SO₄ at 170 °C** (Al₂O₃ at 350 °C) → **CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O** — but at 140 °C the same mix gives the ether, so the temperature is the discriminator. **Dehydrohalogenation**: **alc. KOH** pulls the β-hydrogen while the halide leaves — **CH₃CH₂Br → CH₂=CH₂ + KBr + H₂O** — with **Saytzeff's rule** favouring the more substituted alkene. **Partial hydrogenation**: an alkyne plus **H₂ over the Lindlar catalyst** (Pd/BaSO₄ poisoned with quinoline) stops exactly at the alkene, since ordinary Ni with excess H₂ would run through to the alkane. Conversely, ethene → ethane is **catalytic hydrogenation** — **CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃–CH₃** — via the surface mechanism the NEB 2023 and 2024 papers ask for: **adsorption** (H₂ dissociates on the metal), **syn addition** (both H from the same face, via an adsorbed ethyl), **desorption**.

practiceQuestions: **NEB 2023 (verified PYQ): How is ethane prepared from ethene? Write the reaction mechanism. (3m)** — Ethane is prepared from ethene by **catalytic hydrogenation**: **CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃–CH₃**, over **nickel at ~200 °C** (or Pt/Pd at room temperature). **Mechanism (heterogeneous surface catalysis):** **(1) Adsorption** — the H₂ molecule adsorbs onto the metal surface and **dissociates into hydrogen atoms**; ethene adsorbs alongside it through its π bond. **(2) Syn addition** — the surface hydrogen atoms add to the double bond **one at a time and from the same face**: the first H converts ethene into an adsorbed ethyl intermediate, the second completes **ethane**. Because both hydrogens arrive from the metal surface, the addition is **stereospecific (syn)**. **(3) Desorption** — the saturated ethane, no longer able to bind the surface, leaves and frees the catalyst for the next cycle.

**NEB 2024 (verified PYQ): How is ethane prepared from ethene? Write the reaction mechanism. (3m)** — By **catalytic hydrogenation**: **CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃–CH₃** (Ni/Pt catalyst, Ni ~200 °C or Pt/Pd at room temperature). **Mechanism:** the reaction occurs **on the catalyst surface** — **(1)** H₂ is **adsorbed and split into H atoms** on the metal; ethene adsorbs through its π electrons. **(2)** The two surface hydrogens add **stepwise to the same face** of the double bond (syn addition), passing through an adsorbed **ethyl intermediate** to give ethane. **(3)** Ethane **desorbs** from the surface, regenerating the catalyst. The overall change is reduction of the π bond to a σ bond — one mole of H₂ per mole of alkene.

**NEB-style (2m): How is ethene obtained from ethanol?** — By **dehydration of ethanol** with **concentrated H₂SO₄ at about 170 °C** (or by passing vapour over **Al₂O₃ at ~350 °C**): **C₂H₅OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O**. Mechanistically the acid **protonates the –OH group**, making water a good leaving group; water departs and a β-hydrogen is eliminated to create the π bond. Note the temperature discrimination: at ~**140 °C** the same reagents give **ethoxyethane** (substitution) instead of ethene (elimination).

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The π Bond Under Attack

A π bond is an exposed electron cloud — every electrophile wants it. Alkene chemistry is **electrophilic addition**: HX, H₂O, H₂SO₄ and O₃ all add across the double bond, with **Markovnikov's rule** and the **peroxide effect** deciding which carbon gets which fragment.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Addition of HX and Markovnikov's rule

- **CH₃–CH=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃–CHBr–CH₃** (2-bromopropane, major).
- **Markovnikov's rule:** the **negative part** of the addendum attaches to the carbon with **fewer hydrogens**; equivalently H⁺ goes to the carbon already holding more H.
- Reason: the more stable **carbocation** (3° > 2° > 1°) forms on the more substituted carbon.

### 2.2 The peroxide effect (anti-Markovnikov)

- With **peroxides present, HBr alone** adds the **reverse** way: **CH₃–CH=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃–CH₂–CH₂Br** (1-bromopropane).
- Mechanism is **free-radical**: Br· adds first to give the more stable radical; only **HBr** shows this (HF/HCl/HI bonds are energetically wrong).

### 2.3 Addition of H₂O and H₂SO₄

- **Hydration:** CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O (conc. H₂SO₄ catalyst) → **CH₃CH₂OH** — industrial ethanol.
- **CH₃–CH=CH₂ + H₂O →** isopropanol (Markovnikov).
- **CH₂=CH₂ + H₂SO₄ → CH₃CH₂OSO₃H** (ethyl hydrogen sulphate) → hydrolysis gives ethanol.

### 2.4 Ozonolysis

- **O₃ at ~195 K** adds to C=C forming an **ozonide**; **Zn/H₂O** cleaves it to **carbonyl compounds**.
- **CH₂=CH₂ → 2HCHO** (formaldehyde); **CH₃–CH=CH–CH₃ → 2CH₃CHO**; terminal carbons give HCHO.
- Locates the double bond — a structure-detection tool.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Markovnikov's rule** | Negative addendum goes to the C with fewer H (via the stabler carbocation) | propene + HBr → 2-bromopropane |
| **Peroxide effect** | Radical anti-Markovnikov addition, HBr only | propene + HBr/ROOR → 1-bromopropane |
| **Ozonolysis** | O₃ addition then Zn/H₂O cleavage to carbonyls | but-2-ene → 2 CH₃CHO |
| **Ozonide** | The cyclic peroxide intermediate of ozonolysis | cleaved by Zn/H₂O |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 The carbocation is the hinge

- H⁺ adds first (electrophilic), creating a carbocation; the more substituted cation forms preferentially, and the anion then attacks it. Every Markovnikov question is a carbocation-stability question.

### 4.2 Why only HBr misbehaves

- The radical chain needs both steps exothermic: Br· adding to the alkene is, but Cl· is too reactive (unselective) and I· too weak (reversible). Hence the peroxide effect is **HBr's private quirk**.

### 4.3 Ozonolysis as structure detection

- Count the carbonyl fragments back together and the original double-bond position reappears — ozonolysis is how unknown alkene structures are read.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Markovnikov vs peroxide (Kharasch) addition**

| Basis | Markovnikov | Peroxide effect |
|---|---|---|
| mechanism | ionic (carbocation) | free-radical |
| condition | normal | peroxides, HBr only |
| H goes to | C with more H | C with fewer H |
| Br goes to | C with fewer H | C with more H |
| propene + HBr | 2-bromopropane | 1-bromopropane |

## 6. Common Confusions

**The rule speaks of the negative part:** it is Br⁻ that goes to the H-poor carbon — students misplace the H instead.
**Peroxide effect is HBr-only:** writing it for HCl or HI is a classic error — bond energetics forbid the chain.
**Ozonolysis reductive workup:** Zn/H₂O stops at aldehydes/ketones; oxidative workup would push to acids — quote Zn.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB 2024 (verified PYQ): State Markovnikov's rule and apply it to the addition of HBr to propene. (3m)** — **Markovnikov's rule:** when an unsymmetrical reagent (HX) adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the **negative part of the reagent (X⁻) attaches to the carbon of the double bond bearing fewer hydrogen atoms**, while H⁺ goes to the carbon bearing more hydrogens — because addition proceeds through the **more stable carbocation**. **Application to propene:** CH₃–CH=CH₂ has H on C2 (one H) and C1 (two H). H⁺ adds to C1, generating the **secondary carbocation at C2** (rather than a primary one at C1); Br⁻ then attacks C2: **CH₃–CH=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃–CHBr–CH₃ (2-bromopropane, major product)**.

**NEB 2024 (verified PYQ): What happens when ethene undergoes ozonolysis? Write the products. (3m)** — Ethene adds ozone at low temperature (~195 K) to form an **ozonide**, which on **reductive cleavage with Zn/H₂O** splits the C=C completely: **CH₂=CH₂ + O₃ → ozonide → 2 HCHO**. Both carbons of the double bond carry hydrogens, so both fragments are **formaldehyde (methanal)**. Ozonolysis of an alkene always gives carbonyl compounds; terminal =CH₂ carbons give HCHO, which is how the position of a double bond is located.

**NEB 2022 (verified PYQ): What happens when but-2-ene is treated with ozone followed by zinc and water? Give the equations involved and identify the products. (3m)** — **Step 1 — ozonide formation (at ~195 K):** CH₃–CH=CH–CH₃ + O₃ → **but-2-ene ozonide** (a cyclic peroxide across the double bond). **Step 2 — reductive cleavage (Zn/H₂O):** the ozonide decomposes to carbonyl fragments: **CH₃–CH=CH–CH₃ → 2 CH₃CHO** — **two molecules of ethanal (acetaldehyde)**. Because but-2-ene is symmetrical, both fragments are identical; an unsymmetrical alkene would give two different carbonyls, letting the original C=C position be reconstructed.

confusion: ❌ All cells look the same under a microscope. ✅ Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells have them.
❌ DNA and RNA are identical in structure. ✅ DNA is double-stranded with deoxyribose and thymine; RNA is single-stranded with ribose and uracil.
❌ Mitosis produces genetically different cells. ✅ Mitosis produces genetically identical diploid daughter cells.
❌ Meiosis produces identical cells. ✅ Meiosis produces 4 genetically diverse haploid gametes.
❌ Crossing over occurs in mitosis. ✅ Crossing over occurs in Prophase I of meiosis only.
❌ All enzymes are proteins. ✅ Most enzymes are proteins; some RNA molecules (ribozymes) also have catalytic activity.
❌ ATP is the only energy currency. ✅ GTP, UTP, and CTP also serve as energy carriers in specific pathways.
❌ Photosynthesis occurs in all plant cells. ✅ Photosynthesis occurs only in cells containing chloroplasts (mainly mesophyll).
❌ Respiration and photosynthesis are opposite processes with same equation. ✅ They are complementary but occur in different organelles and under different conditions.
❌ Oxygen is produced during respiration. ✅ Oxygen is consumed in aerobic respiration; produced during photosynthesis.
❌ Food chain shows all feeding relationships. ✅ Food chain is linear; food web shows interconnected feeding relationships.
❌ 90% of energy is transferred to next trophic level. ✅ Only ~10% energy transfers; ~90% lost as heat.
❌ Biomagnification decreases toxin concentration up the food chain. ✅ Biomagnification increases toxin concentration at higher trophic levels.
❌ Carbon cycle only involves plants and animals. ✅ Carbon cycle involves atmosphere, oceans, fossils, rocks, and decomposers.
❌ Nitrogen fixation only occurs in bacteria. ✅ Some lightning and industrial processes (Haber) also fix nitrogen.
❌ All fungi are harmful. ✅ Many fungi are beneficial (decomposers, mycorrhizae, food, antibiotics like penicillin).
❌ Viruses are living organisms. ✅ Viruses are acellular — they cannot reproduce without a host and lack metabolism.
❌ Bacteria are always harmful. ✅ Most bacteria are harmless or beneficial (gut flora, nitrogen fixation, decomposition).
❌ Gram-positive and Gram-negative differ only in color. ✅ Gram-positive has thick peptidoglycan layer; Gram-negative has thin layer + outer membrane.
❌ Natural selection creates perfect organisms. ✅ Natural selection favors traits suited to current environment; environments change.
❌ Evolution is goal-oriented. ✅ Evolution has no goal; it acts on random variation filtered by selection.
❌ Homologous and analogous structures mean the same thing. ✅ Homologous = common ancestry (divergent); Analogous = similar function, different origin (convergent).
❌ Fossils are preserved bones only. ✅ Fossils include impressions, trace fossils, amber-preserved organisms, and molecular fossils.
❌ Lamarckism is completely wrong. ✅ Lamarck's inheritance of acquired characteristics is largely rejected, but epigenetics shows some environmental effects can be inherited.
❌ Five-kingdom classification is outdated. ✅ Six-kingdom (adding Archaea) and phylogenetic systems are more current, but five-kingdom remains useful for education.
❌ Binomial nomenclature names change frequently. ✅ Names are stable once formally published; changes require formal revision by taxonomic authorities.
❌ All algae are aquatic. ✅ Some algae live in soil, on tree bark, or in symbiotic relationships (lichens).
❌ Bryophytes have vascular tissue. ✅ Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts, hornworts) lack true vascular tissue (xylem/phloem).
❌ Gymnosperms produce flowers. ✅ Gymnosperms have naked seeds in cones; angiosperms produce flowers and enclosed seeds.
❌ Double fertilization occurs in gymnosperms. ✅ Double fertilization (zygote + endosperm) is unique to angiosperms.
❌ Earthworms have an open circulatory system. ✅ Earthworms have a closed circulatory system with dorsal and ventral vessels.
❌ Frogs breathe only through lungs. ✅ Frogs use cutaneous respiration (skin), buccal cavity, and lungs.
❌ Conservation only means protecting animals. ✅ Conservation includes genetic, species, and ecosystem diversity; in-situ and ex-situ strategies.
❌ In-situ and ex-situ conservation are the same. ✅ In-situ = conservation in natural habitat (national parks); Ex-situ = conservation outside habitat (zoos, seed banks).

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Two π Bonds, One Carbon Rod

Alkynes (**CₙH₂ₙ₋₂**) carry a C≡C triple bond. The syllabus routes to them start from the **elements themselves** (carbon + hydrogen → ethyne via calcium carbide) and from **vicinal dihalides** (1,2-dibromoethane) and **haloform-derived** substrates (chloroform/iodoform routes).

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 From carbon and hydrogen — industrial ethyne

- **CaO + 3C → CaC₂ + CO** (electric furnace, ~2000 °C) — calcium carbide.
- **CaC₂ + 2H₂O → HC≡CH + Ca(OH)₂** — ethyne (acetylene) on contact with water.
- Impure carbide gives PH₃/H₂S contamination — purified through acid or CuCl/NH₃ washes.

### 2.2 From 1,2-dibromoethane (vicinal dihalide)

- **BrCH₂CH₂Br + 2 alc. KOH → HC≡CH + 2KBr + 2H₂O** — double dehydrohalogenation.
- First equivalent gives the **vinyl halide** (CH₂=CHBr); the second (stronger base, NaNH₂ often needed) removes the second HX.

### 2.3 From chloroform/iodoform routes

- **CHCl₃ + 2Ag (or Ag powder, Δ) → HC≡CH + 2AgCl** — dehalogenation of a dihalomethane.
- **CHI₃ + 2Ag → HC≡CH + 2AgI** — the silver-salt route (2×2 dehalogenation).
- General: **dihalomethanes + heated silver → alkyne + 2AgX**.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Calcium carbide route** | C + CaO → CaC₂, then hydrolysis to ethyne | CaC₂ + 2H₂O → C₂H₂ |
| **Vicinal dihalide** | Two halogens on adjacent carbons; double elimination gives the alkyne | 1,2-dibromoethane → ethyne |
| **Vinyl halide** | Haloalkene intermediate of the first elimination | CH₂=CHBr |
| **Dehalogenation** | Removal of halogens (by hot Ag) to build C≡C | CHCl₃ + 2Ag → C₂H₂ |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why two eliminations are needed

- A triple bond needs two π bonds; the first elimination makes the alkene (vinyl halide), the second must remove HX from an **sp² carbon** — harder, hence the stronger base (NaNH₂) for the second step in modern practice.

### 4.2 The carbide chemistry

- CaC₂ is an **acetylide salt**: C₂²⁻ + 2H₂O → C₂H₂ + 2OH⁻. The water attacks the carbide carbon; the reaction is violently exothermic — the old miners' lamp chemistry.

### 4.3 Silver's role

- Hot silver scavenges halogens as stable AgX, pulling two halides off the small carbon framework and leaving the C≡C behind.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Three routes to alkynes**

| Route | Starting material | Reagents | Product |
|---|---|---|---|
| carbide | CaO + C (electric furnace) | then H₂O | HC≡CH |
| vicinal dihalide | BrCH₂CH₂Br | 2 alc. KOH (or NaNH₂) | HC≡CH |
| haloform/Ag | CHCl₃ or CHI₃ | hot Ag powder | HC≡CH + 2AgX |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Calcium carbide is not carbon:** the furnace step (CaO + 3C → CaC₂ + CO) precedes the hydrolysis — write both equations.
**Vinyl halide intermediate:** the first elimination stops at CH₂=CHBr; the second needs stronger conditions.
**Ag route stoichiometry:** two Ag per halomethane — 2AgCl or 2AgI by-products belong in the equation.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): How is ethyne prepared from calcium carbide? Give both equations.** — **Step 1:** limestone-derived **quicklime (CaO)** is heated with **coke** in an **electric furnace at ~2000 °C**: **CaO + 3C → CaC₂ + CO↑** — calcium carbide forms. **Step 2:** carbide is treated with **water**: **CaC₂ + 2H₂O → HC≡CH + Ca(OH)₂** — **ethyne (acetylene)** evolves as a gas (the carbide's C₂²⁻ anion is protonated by water). Technical carbide carries phosphide/sulphide impurities, so the gas is washed to remove PH₃ and H₂S before use.

**NEB-style (2m): Prepare ethyne from 1,2-dibromoethane.** — **1,2-Dibromoethane (a vicinal dihalide)** undergoes **double dehydrohalogenation** with two equivalents of **alcoholic KOH** (strong base, heat): **BrCH₂CH₂Br + 2KOH → HC≡CH + 2KBr + 2H₂O**. The first elimination gives the **vinyl halide CH₂=CHBr**; the second removes HBr from that sp² carbon to complete the **triple bond**.

**NEB-style (2m): How does chloroform give ethyne?** — **Chloroform is dehalogenated by heated silver powder**: **CHCl₃ + 2Ag → HC≡CH + 2AgCl**. Silver abstracts the three chlorines' partners stepwise — formally removing two equivalents of HCl equivalents — leaving the **C≡C triple bond**; the same chemistry works for **iodoform (CHI₃ + 2Ag → HC≡CH + 2AgI)**.

practiceQuestions: **NEB-style (3m): How is ethyne prepared from calcium carbide? Give both equations.** — **Step 1 — carbide manufacture:** **quicklime (CaO)** and **coke (C)** are heated in an **electric furnace at about 2000 °C**: **CaO + 3C → CaC₂ + CO↑**. Calcium carbide is effectively the salt of the **acetylide anion (C₂²⁻)**. **Step 2 — hydrolysis:** carbide is treated with **water**: **CaC₂ + 2H₂O → HC≡CH + Ca(OH)₂**. Water protonates the carbide dianion, releasing **ethyne (acetylene)** gas and slaked lime. The reaction is strongly exothermic. Technical carbide contains **calcium phosphide and sulphide** impurities, so the crude gas carries **PH₃ and H₂S** and is washed (through acid or ammoniacal CuCl) before use — pure ethyne has the characteristic garlic-like odour of the impurities removed.

**NEB-style (2m): Prepare ethyne from 1,2-dibromoethane.** — **1,2-Dibromoethane** is a **vicinal dihalide** (halogens on adjacent carbons). Heating it with **two equivalents of alcoholic KOH** effects **double dehydrohalogenation**: **BrCH₂CH₂Br + 2KOH(alc.) → HC≡CH + 2KBr + 2H₂O**. The **first** elimination removes HBr to give the **vinyl halide, bromoethene (CH₂=CHBr)**; the **second** must remove HBr from that sp² carbon, which is harder and needs the stronger basic medium (in modern practice **NaNH₂** in liquid NH₃). Completion of the second elimination creates the **C≡C triple bond** of ethyne.

**NEB-style (2m): How does chloroform give ethyne?** — **Chloroform is heated with silver powder**, which scavenges halogen as insoluble silver chloride: **CHCl₃ + 2Ag → HC≡CH + 2AgCl**. Formally two equivalents of HCl are stripped from the single carbon framework, and the carbons couple into the **triple bond**. The identical chemistry applies to **iodoform**: **CHI₃ + 2Ag → HC≡CH + 2AgI**. In both cases the driving force is the stability of the **AgX lattice** — silver's love of halide pays for the dehalogenation.
keyPoints: Alkynes CnH2n-2, sp, C≡C. Preparation: (1) from elements: CaO + 3C -> CaC2 + CO (electric furnace ~2000C); CaC2 + 2H2O -> HCCH + Ca(OH)2 (industrial ethyne; impure gas washed of PH3/H2S). (2) From 1,2-dibromoethane (vicinal dihalide): BrCH2CH2Br + 2 alc. KOH -> HCCH + 2KBr + 2H2O; first elimination gives vinyl halide CH2=CHBr, second needs stronger base (NaNH2). (3) From chloroform/iodoform: CHCl3 + 2Ag (hot) -> HCCH + 2AgCl; CHI3 + 2Ag -> HCCH + 2AgI (dehalogenation by silver).
data.summary: Alkynes (**CₙH₂ₙ₋₂**) come from three doors. **From the elements:** electric-furnace fusion of lime and coke — **CaO + 3C → CaC₂ + CO** — followed by hydrolysis — **CaC₂ + 2H₂O → HC≡CH + Ca(OH)₂** — the industrial acetylene route (gas washed free of PH₃/H₂S). **From vicinal dihalides:** **1,2-dibromoethane + 2 alc. KOH → HC≡CH + 2KBr + 2H₂O**, a double dehydrohalogenation that pauses at the **vinyl halide** before the tougher second elimination (NaNH₂ territory). **From haloforms:** hot **silver** strips the halogens — **CHCl₃ + 2Ag → HC≡CH + 2AgCl** (and CHI₃ → 2AgI) — driven by the stability of the silver halide lattice. Two eliminations or a carbide's dianion: either way, the triple bond is assembled.

Give both equations.** — **Step 1 — carbide manufacture:** **quicklime (CaO)** and **coke (C)** are heated in an **electric furnace at about 2000 °C**: **CaO + 3C → CaC₂ + CO↑**. data.topicTitle: Chemical properties of alkynes: addition reaction with H2, HX, H2O; acidic nature (action with sodium, ammoniacal AgNO3 and ammoniacal Cu2Cl2)
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Add Like an Alkene, Acid Like No Other

The C≡C bond adds H₂, HX and H₂O just as C=C does (twice over), but the sp carbons hold their electrons so tightly that a **terminal alkyne hydrogen becomes acidic** — the only hydrocarbon H that metals can replace. That acidity powers the **ammoniacal AgNO₃ and Cu₂Cl₂ tests**.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Addition of H₂

- **HC≡CH + H₂ (Lindlar) → CH₂=CH₂**; **+ H₂ (Ni, excess) → CH₃–CH₃**.
- Two π bonds → up to two equivalents of H₂; catalyst choice sets the stop point.

### 2.2 Addition of HX

- **HC≡CH + HCl (HgCl₂ catalyst) → CH₂=CHCl** (vinyl chloride — PVC feedstock).
- **HC≡CH + HBr → CH₂=CHBr → CH₃CHBr₂** (Markovnikov, twice for internal alkynes).

### 2.3 Addition of H₂O (hydration)

- **HC≡CH + H₂O (H₂SO₄, HgSO₄) → CH₃CHO** — Markovnikov water addition gives the **enol**, which tautomerises to **acetaldehyde**.
- Internal alkynes give **ketones**; only ethyne gives an aldehyde.

### 2.4 Acidic nature and metal tests

- Terminal ≡C–H (sp, 50% s-character) is weakly acidic (pKa ≈ 25): **HC≡CH + Na → HC≡CNa + ½H₂**; + NaNH₂ → sodium acetylide.
- **Ammoniacal AgNO₃:** HC≡CH → **white precipitate Ag₂C₂** (silver acetylide).
- **Ammoniacal Cu₂Cl₂:** → **red precipitate Cu₂C₂** (copper acetylide).
- Only **terminal** alkynes respond — internal ones (no ≡C–H) do not.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Acetylide** | Salt of a deprotonated terminal alkyne | NaC≡CH, Ag₂C₂ |
| **Enol tautomerisation** | Vinyl alcohol rearranging to the carbonyl | vinyl alcohol → acetaldehyde |
| **Lindlar reduction** | Poisoned-catalyst hydrogenation stopping at the alkene | ethyne → ethene |
| **Terminal alkyne** | Alkyne with ≡C–H at the chain end | ethyne, propyne |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why sp hydrogens are acidic

- An sp orbital is 50% s-character: the carbanion's lone pair sits closer to the nucleus, stabilising it. pKa ladder: alkane ≈ 50, alkene ≈ 44, **alkyne ≈ 25** — weak acids, but acids.

### 4.2 Hydration's tautomer detour

- Water adds Markovnikov-wise to give **vinyl alcohol (enol)** — unstable; the H migrates from O to C and the product is the **carbonyl**. Ethyne's enol is the special one that lands on an **aldehyde**; all other alkynes land on **ketones**.

### 4.3 The tests as structure probes

- Ag₂C₂ (white) and Cu₂C₂ (red) form only when a **≡C–H** exists — so these precipitates distinguish **terminal from internal alkynes**. Dry acetylides of heavy metals are explosive — handle wet, dispose fresh.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Alkyne vs alkene chemistry**

| Basis | Alkyne | Alkene |
|---|---|---|
| π bonds | two | one |
| H₂ uptake | up to 2 eq | 1 eq |
| hydration product | enol → aldehyde/ketone | alcohol |
| acidic H | terminal ≡C–H yes | no |
| metal tests | Ag₂C₂ white / Cu₂C₂ red | none |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Ethyne hydration gives an aldehyde, not an alcohol or ketone:** the enol tautomerises all the way to CH₃CHO — the one aldehyde in the family.
**Only terminal alkynes give precipitates:** internal alkynes have no ≡C–H — a negative AgNO₃ test is informative, not a failure.
**Acidity is relative:** pKa 25 is "acidic" only next to 44 and 50 — water and alcohols are far stronger acids.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB 2024 (verified PYQ): Acetylene is acidic in nature. Explain with a chemical test. (3m)** — In **ethyne (HC≡CH)** the C–H bond uses an **sp hybrid orbital (50% s-character)**, which holds the bonding electrons closer to the carbon nucleus; when the proton is removed, the resulting **acetylide carbanion** is correspondingly stabilised (pKa ≈ 25 — far more acidic than alkenes, pKa ≈ 44, or alkanes, pKa ≈ 50). Hence terminal alkynes react with strong bases and active metals: **HC≡CH + 2Na → 2HC≡CNa + H₂↑** (sodium acetylide + hydrogen). **Chemical test:** with **ammoniacal silver nitrate**, ethyne gives a **white precipitate of silver acetylide, Ag₂C₂**: **HC≡CH + 2[Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ → Ag₂C₂↓ + 2NH₄⁺ + 2NH₃**; with **ammoniacal Cu₂Cl₂** it gives a **red precipitate of Cu₂C₂**. These precipitations prove the acidic ≡C–H — and only terminal alkynes give them.

**NEB-style (2m): What is the product of hydration of ethyne and how is it formed?** — **Ethyne + H₂O (dilute H₂SO₄, HgSO₄ catalyst) → acetaldehyde (CH₃CHO).** Water adds **Markovnikov-style** across the triple bond to give **vinyl alcohol (CH₂=CHOH), an enol**, which is unstable and **tautomerises** — the O–H hydrogen migrates to carbon and the π bond shifts — giving the **carbonyl compound acetaldehyde**. Ethyne is the only alkyne whose hydration yields an aldehyde; all other alkynes give ketones.

**NEB-style (2m): Distinguish between but-1-yne and but-2-yne.** — **But-1-yne is terminal** (has ≡C–H): with **ammoniacal AgNO₃ it gives a white Ag₂C₂ precipitate**, and with **ammoniacal Cu₂Cl₂ a red Cu₂C₂ precipitate**. **But-2-yne is internal** (no ≡C–H): **no precipitate with either reagent**. The acidic terminal hydrogen is the entire difference — sp-carbon acidity is absent in the internal isomer.

(Only **terminal** alkynes respond; dry heavy-metal acetylides are explosive, so the precipitates are kept wet and destroyed after testing.)

**NEB-style (2m): What is the product of hydration of ethyne and how is it formed?** — Ethyne adds water in the presence of **dilute H₂SO₄ and HgSO₄ catalyst**: the water adds **Markovnikov-fashion** across the triple bond to give **vinyl alcohol, CH₂=CHOH — an enol**. Enols are unstable: the hydrogen on oxygen migrates to the adjacent carbon while the π bond shifts, a process called **tautomerisation**, yielding the carbonyl compound **acetaldehyde, CH₃CHO**: **HC≡CH + H₂O —(H₂SO₄/HgSO₄)→ CH₃CHO**. Ethyne is the **only alkyne that gives an aldehyde** on hydration; any other alkyne (unsymmetrical) gives a **ketone**, because the enol's OH lands on an internal carbon.

**NEB-style (2m): Distinguish between but-1-yne and but-2-yne.** — **But-1-yne (CH₃CH₂C≡CH)** is a **terminal alkyne**: its ≡C–H hydrogen is acidic (sp, 50% s-character), so with **ammoniacal AgNO₃** it forms a **white precipitate of silver acetylide**, and with **ammoniacal Cu₂Cl₂** a **red precipitate of copper acetylide**. **But-2-yne (CH₃–C≡C–CH₃)** is **internal**: it has **no ≡C–H hydrogen**, so **no precipitate forms with either reagent**. The pair of ammoniacal tests cleanly separates terminal from internal alkynes — a negative result is itself structural information.

importantConcepts: s-character is acidity: the sp orbital holds the carbanion's pair close to the nucleus — the only acidic hydrocarbon hydrogens, and the only ones metals can pull off.

data.topicTitle: Test of unsaturation (ethene and ethyne): bromine water test and Baeyer's test
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Two Drops That Tell the Truth

Unsaturation announces itself in colour: **bromine water** decolourises (addition across π), and **Baeyer's reagent** — cold, dilute, alkaline KMnO₄ — loses its purple and deposits a brown solid (**Baeyer's test**). Ethene and ethyne pass both; ethane fails both.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Bromine water test

- **CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ (aq) → BrCH₂CH₂Br** (1,2-dibromoethane) — the **red-brown/orange colour of Br₂ disappears instantly** at room temperature, without catalyst.
- Ethyne: **HC≡CH + 2Br₂ → CHBr₂CHBr₂** (1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane) — colour goes, twice over.
- Alkanes: no decolourisation in the dark/cold (substitution needs UV) — the negative control.

### 2.2 Baeyer's test

- **Cold, dilute, alkaline KMnO₄** (Baeyer's reagent) adds **two OH groups** across C=C: **3CH₂=CH₂ + 2KMnO₄ + 4H₂O → 3CH₂(OH)CH₂(OH) + 2MnO₂↓ + 2KOH**.
- **Purple → brown MnO₂ precipitate** = unsaturation; the product of ethene is **ethane-1,2-diol (glycol)**.
- Ethyne oxidises further (to oxalic acid ultimately) but still kills the purple.

### 2.3 The decision logic

- Decolourised Br₂ water (no UV) OR discharged KMnO₄ (cold) → π bond present. Both negative → saturated.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Bromine water test** | Instant decolourisation of Br₂(aq) by addition across π bonds | ethene → 1,2-dibromoethane |
| **Baeyer's reagent** | Cold, dilute, alkaline KMnO₄ oxidising π bonds to diols | ethene → glycol + MnO₂ |
| **Syn dihydroxylation** | Cis addition of two OH groups across the double bond | ethene → ethane-1,2-diol |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why the tests work

- π electrons are exposed and nucleophilic; Br₂ polarises and adds; KMnO₄ (Mn⁷⁺) is reduced to Mn⁴⁺ (brown MnO₂) while the alkene is oxidised. Saturated σ-frameworks can neither add nor reduce under these mild conditions.

### 4.2 Conditions are the message

- **Cold and dilute** keeps KMnO₄ from over-oxidising and cleaving the bond (hot/concentrated would cut the C=C to acids/CO₂). **No UV** for the bromine test keeps alkanes honest (they'd substitute in sunlight).

### 4.3 Reading the results

- Both tests are **decolourisation tests**: the eye is the instrument. Ethene and ethyne: instant discharge. Ethane: colour persists. Terminal vs internal alkynes: both positive — these tests detect unsaturation, not acidity.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**The two unsaturation tests**

| Basis | Bromine water | Baeyer's test |
|---|---|---|
| reagent | Br₂(aq) | cold dilute alk. KMnO₄ |
| type | addition | oxidation (dihydroxylation) |
| visible change | red-brown → colourless | purple → brown MnO₂↓ |
| ethene product | 1,2-dibromoethane | ethane-1,2-diol |
| ethane result | no change (dark) | no change |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Dark condition matters for Br₂:** alkanes substitute in UV light — the test is only valid without light.
**Brown ≠ purple:** MnO₂ (brown solid) is the positive sign; faded purple without precipitate is ambiguous — look for the MnO₂.
**Both tests say "unsaturated":** neither distinguishes C=C from C≡C alone — pair them with the ammoniacal tests for the full picture.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB 2024 (verified PYQ): How will you distinguish ethane, ethene and ethyne using bromine water? (2m)** — Add each gas to **bromine water** (red-brown). **Ethene**: the colour is **instantly discharged** — addition gives **1,2-dibromoethane**: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → BrCH₂–CH₂Br. **Ethyne**: the colour is also **discharged** (addition of **two** Br₂): HC≡CH + 2Br₂ → CHBr₂–CHBr₂ (1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane). **Ethane**: **no decolourisation** in the dark — saturated alkanes do not add to bromine water (they would substitute only in UV light). Ethene and ethyne both decolourise; to separate those two, use the **ammoniacal AgNO₃ test** (ethyne gives white Ag₂C₂, ethene nothing).

**NEB-style (2m): Describe Baeyer's test for ethene with equation.** — Shake ethene with **cold, dilute, alkaline KMnO₄ (Baeyer's reagent)**: the **purple colour disappears and a brown precipitate of MnO₂ forms**, while the alkene is converted to a **diol**: **3CH₂=CH₂ + 2KMnO₄ + 4H₂O → 3CH₂(OH)–CH₂(OH) + 2MnO₂↓ + 2KOH** — ethene becomes **ethane-1,2-diol (glycol)**. A saturated hydrocarbon leaves the reagent unchanged.

**NEB-style (2m): Why must the bromine water test be done away with sunlight?** — In **UV light, alkanes undergo free-radical substitution** with bromine (slowly decolourising it), which would give a **false positive** for ethane. The test's discriminating power rests on **addition (instant, dark, cold)** versus **substitution (UV only)** — so the bromine water test is performed **in the dark and in the cold**, where only π bonds can consume the bromine.

So ethene and ethyne both decolourise bromine water while ethane does not; to separate ethene from ethyne, follow with the **ammoniacal silver nitrate test** — ethyne alone gives the **white Ag₂C₂ precipitate**.

**NEB-style (2m): Describe Baeyer's test for ethene with equation.** — Shake ethene with **cold, dilute, alkaline potassium permanganate** — **Baeyer's reagent**. The **purple permanganate is decolourised** and a **brown precipitate of MnO₂** appears, while the double bond is converted into two hydroxyl groups (**syn dihydroxylation**): **3CH₂=CH₂ + 2KMnO₄ + 4H₂O → 3CH₂(OH)–CH₂(OH) + 2MnO₂↓ + 2KOH**. The organic product is **ethane-1,2-diol (glycol)**. Any unsaturated hydrocarbon gives this purple-to-brown change; saturated hydrocarbons leave the reagent untouched. The conditions matter — **hot or concentrated** KMnO₄ would cleave the double bond to acids instead of stopping at the diol.

**NEB-style (2m): Why must the bromine water test be performed away from sunlight?** — Because **ultraviolet light initiates free-radical substitution** of bromine onto **alkanes**: ethane in sunlight would slowly consume Br₂ and fade the colour, producing a **false positive** for unsaturation. The test distinguishes π bonds from σ bonds only through the contrast between **instant addition** (alkenes/alkynes, dark, cold) and **UV-dependent substitution** (alkanes). Performed **in the dark**, bromine water responds exclusively to unsaturation, and the negative control — ethane keeping its colour — becomes trustworthy.

Baeyer's test: cold dilute alkaline KMnO4; 3CH2=CH2 + 2KMnO4 + 4H2O -> 3CH2OH-CH2OH (ethane-1,2-diol, glycol) + 2MnO2 brown ppt + 2KOH; purple -> brown = unsaturated; hot/conc KMnO4 would cleave to acids - keep it cold and dilute. data.summary: Two colour tests expose unsaturation. **Bromine water**: ethene discharges the red-brown instantly — **CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → BrCH₂CH₂Br**; ethyne consumes **two** Br₂ — **CHBr₂CHBr₂**; ethane does nothing **in the dark** (UV would substitute, so darkness keeps the test honest). **Baeyer's test**: cold, dilute, alkaline **KMnO₄** is decolourised with **brown MnO₂** depositing while the π bond gains two OH groups — **ethene → ethane-1,2-diol**; keep it cold and dilute or the bond cleaves instead. Both tests certify "unsaturated" but cannot by themselves split ethene from ethyne — that final call belongs to the **ammoniacal AgNO₃** test, where only ethyne's acidic ≡C–H gives the white precipitate.

data.topicTitle: Comparative studies of physical properties of alkane, alkene and alkyne
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Three Families, One Table

Alkanes, alkenes and alkynes differ by π-bond count — and every physical property follows: **boiling points, melting points, densities, solubilities** rise with molar mass and with unsaturation's extra intermolecular contact, while all three stay **non-polar and water-insoluble**.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 State and odour

- **C₁–C₄** gases (all three families), **C₅–C₁₇** liquids, **C₁₈+** waxy solids.
- Pure alkanes/alkenes/alkynes are odourless; commercial fuels smell from additives/impurities (ethyne's garlic smell is phosphine impurity).

### 2.2 Boiling and melting points

- Rise with carbon number (more surface → stronger van der Waals).
- At equal carbons: **alkyne ≥ alkene > alkane** — the π electrons are more polarisable, tightening intermolecular attraction. (B.p.: ethane −89 °C < ethene −104 °C... small-member anomalies exist; the general ladder holds from C₃ up.)
- Branching **lowers** b.p. (less contact surface): n-butane −0.5 °C > isobutane −11.7 °C.

### 2.3 Density and solubility

- All **less dense than water** (float); density rises slowly with carbon number (≈0.6–0.8 g/cm³).
- **Insoluble in water** (non-polar vs polar); **soluble in non-polar organic solvents** (benzene, ether, CCl₄) — like dissolves like.

### 2.4 Combustion and stability

- All burn to CO₂ + H₂O; **alkynes burn with a smoky, luminous flame** (higher carbon percentage).
- Stability: more substituted π systems are more stable; alkynes are less reactive toward electrophilic addition than alkenes (vinyl cation instability) despite "two π bonds".

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **van der Waals forces** | Intermolecular attraction scaling with surface area and polarisability | b.p. rises C₁→C₁₇ |
| **Branching effect** | Branched isomers pack worse → lower b.p. | n-butane > isobutane |
| **Like dissolves like** | Non-polar solutes dissolve in non-polar solvents | hexane in benzene, not water |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Reading the periodic trend across the table

- Within a family, properties change **gradually with n** — gases to liquids to solids. Across families at fixed n, unsaturation nudges b.p./density **up** because π clouds are more polarisable than σ frameworks.

### 4.2 Why water says no

- Water's hydrogen-bonded network gains nothing by hosting a non-polar hydrocarbon; dissolving would cost order without repaying energy. Organic solvents offer van der Waals company instead.

### 4.3 The smoky flame

- Alkynes carry the **highest carbon-to-hydrogen ratio**; combustion is carbon-rich and oxygen-starved at the flame front — free carbon glows (luminous, smoky). A diagnostic flame test in itself.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Physical properties at a glance (same carbon number n)**

| Property | Alkane | Alkene | Alkyne |
|---|---|---|---|
| general formula | CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ | CₙH₂ₙ | CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ |
| polarity | non-polar | weak (π) | weak (π) |
| b.p. trend | lowest | middle | highest (C₃+) |
| water solubility | insoluble | insoluble | insoluble |
| flame | clean blue (small n) | luminous | smoky, luminous |
| density | < 1 g/cm³ | < 1 | < 1 |

## 6. Common Confusions

**The C₂ anomaly:** ethene boils below ethane (−104 vs −89 °C) despite more unsaturation — small-molecule packing quirks; the alkyne ≥ alkene > alkane ladder is reliable from C₃ upward.
**Branching beats unsaturation:** a branched alkane can boil lower than a straight alkene of the same formula — surface area matters as much as π.

Alkanes, alkenes and alkynes differ by π-bond count — and every physical property follows: **boiling points, melting points, densities, solubilities** rise with molar mass and with unsaturation's extra intermolecular contact, while all three stay **non-polar and water-insoluble**.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 State and odour

- **C₁–C₄** gases (all three families), **C₅–C₁₇** liquids, **C₁₈+** waxy solids.
- Pure alkanes/alkenes/alkynes are odourless; commercial fuels smell from additives/impurities (ethyne's garlic smell is phosphine impurity).

### 2.2 Boiling and melting points

- Rise with carbon number (more surface → stronger van der Waals).
- At equal carbons: **alkyne ≥ alkene > alkane** — the π electrons are more polarisable, tightening intermolecular attraction. (B.p.: ethane −89 °C < ethene −104 °C... small-member anomalies exist; the general ladder holds from C₃ up.)
- Branching **lowers** b.p. (less contact surface): n-butane −0.5 °C > isobutane −11.7 °C.

### 2.3 Density and solubility

- All **less dense than water** (float); density rises slowly with carbon number (≈0.6–0.8 g/cm³).
- **Insoluble in water** (non-polar vs polar); **soluble in non-polar organic solvents** (benzene, ether, CCl₄) — like dissolves like.

### 2.4 Combustion and stability

- All burn to CO₂ + H₂O; **alkynes burn with a smoky, luminous flame** (higher carbon percentage).
- Stability: more substituted π systems are more stable; alkynes are less reactive toward electrophilic addition than alkenes (vinyl cation instability) despite "two π bonds".

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **van der Waals forces** | Intermolecular attraction scaling with surface area and polarisability | b.p. rises C₁→C₁₇ |
| **Branching effect** | Branched isomers pack worse → lower b.p. | n-butane > isobutane |
| **Like dissolves like** | Non-polar solutes dissolve in non-polar solvents | hexane in benzene, not water |

### 4.1 Reading the periodic trend across the table

- Within a family, properties change **gradually with n** — gases to liquids to solids. Across families at fixed n, unsaturation nudges b.p./density **up** because π clouds are more polarisable than σ frameworks.

### 4.2 Why water says no

- Water's hydrogen-bonded network gains nothing by hosting a non-polar hydrocarbon; dissolving would cost order without repaying energy. Organic solvents offer van der Waals company instead.

### 4.3 The smoky flame

- Alkynes carry the **highest carbon-to-hydrogen ratio**; combustion is carbon-rich and oxygen-starved at the flame front — free carbon glows (luminous, smoky). A diagnostic flame test in itself.

data.topicTitle: Kolbe's electrolysis methods for the preparation of alkanes, alkenes and alkynes
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Electricity Builds Hydrocarbons

Kolbe's electrolysis passes current through a **carboxylate solution**: at the anode, carboxylate ions surrender electrons, lose CO₂, and **couple into hydrocarbons**. Sodium acetate gives **ethane**; succinic acid gives **ethyne**; a suitable salt can even deliver **ethene** — electrolysis as a C–C bond factory.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Kolbe electrolysis of sodium acetate → alkane

- Electrolyte: **concentrated sodium acetate solution**; electrodes: platinum; product at **anode**.
- **CH₃COO⁻ → CH₃· + CO₂ + e⁻** (anodic oxidation); **2CH₃· → CH₃–CH₃** (ethane).
- Cathode: **2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻** (hydrogen evolves); solution turns alkaline.
- Overall: **2CH₃COONa + 2H₂O → C₂H₆ + 2CO₂ + H₂ + 2NaOH**.

### 2.2 Kolbe route to alkynes (potassium succinate)

- **Potassium succinate** — KOOC–CH₂–CH₂–COOK — loses both carboxyls at the anode; the two CH₂· radicals couple with **two fewer H**: product **HC≡CH (ethyne)**.
- Overall: **KOOC–CH₂–CH₂–COOK + 2KOH → HC≡CH + 2K₂CO₃ + 2H₂** (electrolysis).
- Geometry does the work: the two radicals are born joined — they combine and shed the extra hydrogens.

### 2.3 Kolbe route to alkenes

- Electrolysing salts that leave radicals with a β-H and the right geometry gives alkenes — e.g. electrolysis of **potassium succinate under modified conditions/adipate-type salts** yields **ethene** from the coupled intermediate by further loss of H₂; textbook-level: **succinate → ethyne; modified/adjacent-dicarboxylate electrolysis → ethene**.
- Simpler framing for the syllabus: **Kolbe of sodium propionate gives butane; the alkene/alkyne variants come from dicarboxylates** — succinic (alkyne), and electrolysis of **potassium maleate/succinate variants** for ethene.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Kolbe electrolysis** | Anodic decarboxylative coupling of carboxylates to hydrocarbons | acetate → ethane |
| **Anodic oxidation** | Loss of electron(s) at the anode: RCOO⁻ → R· + CO₂ | the coupling engine |
| **Dicarboxylate electrolysis** | Both ends decarboxylate; intramolecular coupling builds π bonds | succinate → ethyne |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 The anode is the workshop

- Every carbon–carbon bond of the product is forged **at the anode**: RCOO⁻ surrenders its electron, CO₂ departs, the naked R· radicals meet and couple. The cathode merely makes hydrogen and base.

### 4.2 Counting carbons

- Two acetates (C₂ each) − two carboxyl carbons → **C₂ ethane**. The rule: **product carbons = (carbons of R) × 2** where R is the group remaining after –COO⁻.

### 4.3 The succinate surprise

- Succinate's two carboxylates sit at the two ends of –CH₂–CH₂–; decarboxylating both leaves two joined CH₂· units that shed H₂ to become **C≡C** — the only syllabus route where a **triple bond appears from electrolysis**.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Kolbe products by electrolyte**

| Electrolyte | Product | Family |
|---|---|---|
| sodium acetate | ethane | alkane |
| sodium propionate | butane (n-) | alkane |
| potassium succinate | ethyne | alkyne |
| suitable dicarboxylate (modified) | ethene | alkene |

## 6. Common Confusions

**The product appears at the anode:** oxidation happens there; students who put ethane at the cathode lose the logic (and the marks).
**Carboxyl carbons vanish as CO₂:** acetate (C₂) gives ethane (C₂) because both carboxyl carbons leave — count R groups, not the whole salt.
**Cathode chemistry still happens:** H₂ evolves and NaOH forms — the full equation includes them.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): Describe the Kolbe electrolysis of sodium acetate with the overall equation.** — Concentrated **sodium acetate solution** is electrolysed with **platinum electrodes**. **At the anode:** acetate ions are oxidised — **CH₃COO⁻ → CH₃· + CO₂ + e⁻** — and the methyl radicals **dimerise**: **2CH₃· → CH₃–CH₃ (ethane)**. **At the cathode:** water is reduced — **2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂↑ + 2OH⁻** — so hydrogen evolves and the solution becomes **alkaline (NaOH)**. **Overall:** **2CH₃COONa + 2H₂O → C₂H₆ + 2CO₂ + H₂ + 2NaOH**. The two carboxyl carbons leave as CO₂; the two methyl groups couple into the alkane.

**NEB-style (2m): How does the electrolysis of potassium succinate give ethyne?** — **Potassium succinate, KOOC–CH₂–CH₂–COOK**, is electrolysed: **both carboxylate groups are oxidised at the anode**, each losing CO₂ and an electron, leaving the two central carbons as joined radicals — **·CH₂–CH₂·** — which shed **two hydrogens** to form the triple bond: **HC≡CH (ethyne)**. Overall: **KOOC–CH₂–CH₂–COOK + 2KOH(electrolysis) → HC≡CH + 2K₂CO₃ + 2H₂**. The dicarboxylate's own skeleton becomes the alkyne.

**NEB-style (2m): Predict the Kolbe product of sodium propionate.** — Sodium propionate, **CH₃CH₂COONa**: anodic oxidation gives **ethyl radicals (C₂H₅·)** which couple: **2C₂H₅· → C₄H₁₀ (n-butane)**. Overall **2CH₃CH₂COONa + 2H₂O → C₄H₁₀ + 2CO₂ + H₂ + 2NaOH**. The rule: **product carbons = 2 × (carbons in R)** — propionate's R has 2 carbons, so the alkane has 4.

Overall: **2CH₃CH₂COONa + 2H₂O → C₄H₁₀ + 2CO₂ + H₂ + 2NaOH**. data.summary: Kolbe's electrolysis forges C–C bonds with electricity. In **sodium acetate solution (Pt electrodes)** the **anode** oxidises acetate — **CH₃COO⁻ → CH₃· + CO₂ + e⁻** — and methyl radicals couple to **ethane**, while the **cathode** makes H₂ and NaOH: **2CH₃COONa + 2H₂O → C₂H₆ + 2CO₂ + H₂ + 2NaOH**. notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Electricity Builds Hydrocarbons

Kolbe's electrolysis passes current through a **carboxylate solution**: at the anode, carboxylate ions surrender electrons, lose CO₂, and **couple into hydrocarbons**. Sodium acetate gives **ethane**; succinic acid gives **ethyne**; a suitable salt can even deliver **ethene** — electrolysis as a C–C bond factory.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Kolbe electrolysis of sodium acetate → alkane

- Electrolyte: **concentrated sodium acetate solution**; electrodes: platinum; product at **anode**.
- **CH₃COO⁻ → CH₃· + CO₂ + e⁻** (anodic oxidation); **2CH₃· → CH₃–CH₃** (ethane).
- Cathode: **2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻** (hydrogen evolves); solution turns alkaline.
- Overall: **2CH₃COONa + 2H₂O → C₂H₆ + 2CO₂ + H₂ + 2NaOH**.

### 2.2 Kolbe route to alkynes (potassium succinate)

- **Potassium succinate** — KOOC–CH₂–CH₂–COOK — loses both carboxyls at the anode; the two CH₂· radicals couple with **two fewer H**: product **HC≡CH (ethyne)**.
- Overall: **KOOC–CH₂–CH₂–COOK + 2KOH → HC≡CH + 2K₂CO₃ + 2H₂** (electrolysis).
- Geometry does the work: the two radicals are born joined — they combine and shed the extra hydrogens.

### 2.3 Kolbe route to alkenes

- Electrolysing salts that leave radicals with a β-H and the right geometry gives alkenes — e.g. electrolysis of **potassium succinate under modified conditions/adipate-type salts** yields **ethene** from the coupled intermediate by further loss of H₂; textbook-level: **succinate → ethyne; modified/adjacent-dicarboxylate electrolysis → ethene**.
- Simpler framing for the syllabus: **Kolbe of sodium propionate gives butane; the alkene/alkyne variants come from dicarboxylates** — succinic (alkyne), and electrolysis of **potassium maleate/succinate variants** for ethene.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Kolbe electrolysis** | Anodic decarboxylative coupling of carboxylates to hydrocarbons | acetate → ethane |
| **Anodic oxidation** | Loss of electron(s) at the anode: RCOO⁻ → R· + CO₂ | the coupling engine |
| **Dicarboxylate electrolysis** | Both ends decarboxylate; intramolecular coupling builds π bonds | succinate → ethyne |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 The anode is the workshop

- Every carbon–carbon bond of the product is forged **at the anode**: RCOO⁻ surrenders its electron, CO₂ departs, the naked R· radicals meet and couple. The cathode merely makes hydrogen and base.

### 4.2 Counting carbons

- Two acetates (C₂ each) − two carboxyl carbons → **C₂ ethane**. The rule: **product carbons = (carbons of R) × 2** where R is the group remaining after –COO⁻.

### 4.3 The succinate surprise

- Succinate's two carboxylates sit at the two ends of –CH₂–CH₂–; decarboxylating both leaves two joined CH₂· units that shed H₂ to become **C≡C** — the only syllabus route where a **triple bond appears from electrolysis**.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Kolbe products by electrolyte**

| Electrolyte | Product | Family |
|---|---|---|
| sodium acetate | ethane | alkane |
| sodium propionate | butane (n-) | alkane |
| potassium succinate | ethyne | alkyne |
| suitable dicarboxylate (modified) | ethene | alkene |

## 6. Common Confusions

**The product appears at the anode:** oxidation happens there; students who put ethane at the cathode lose the logic (and the marks).
**Carboxyl carbons vanish as CO₂:** acetate (C₂) gives ethane (C₂) because both carboxyl carbons leave — count R groups, not the whole salt.
**Cathode chemistry still happens:** H₂ evolves and NaOH forms — the full equation includes them.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): Describe the Kolbe electrolysis of sodium acetate with the overall equation.** — Concentrated **sodium acetate solution** is electrolysed with **platinum electrodes**. **At the anode:** acetate ions are oxidised — **CH₃COO⁻ → CH₃· + CO₂ + e⁻** — and the methyl radicals **dimerise**: **2CH₃· → CH₃–CH₃ (ethane)**. **At the cathode:** water is reduced — **2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂↑ + 2OH⁻** — so hydrogen evolves and the solution becomes **alkaline (NaOH)**. **Overall:** **2CH₃COONa + 2H₂O → C₂H₆ + 2CO₂ + H₂ + 2NaOH**. The two carboxyl carbons leave as CO₂; the two methyl groups couple into the alkane.

**NEB-style (2m): How does the electrolysis of potassium succinate give ethyne?** — **Potassium succinate, KOOC–CH₂–CH₂–COOK**, is electrolysed: **both carboxylate groups are oxidised at the anode**, each losing CO₂ and an electron, leaving the two central carbons as joined radicals — **·CH₂–CH₂·** — which shed **two hydrogens** to form the triple bond: **HC≡CH (ethyne)**. Overall: **KOOC–CH₂–CH₂–COOK + 2KOH(electrolysis) → HC≡CH + 2K₂CO₃ + 2H₂**. The dicarboxylate's own skeleton becomes the alkyne.

**NEB-style (2m): Predict the Kolbe product of sodium propionate.** — Sodium propionate, **CH₃CH₂COONa**: anodic oxidation gives **ethyl radicals (C₂H₅·)** which couple: **2C₂H₅· → C₄H₁₀ (n-butane)**. Overall **2CH₃CH₂COONa + 2H₂O → C₄H₁₀ + 2CO₂ + H₂ + 2NaOH**. The rule: **product carbons = 2 × (carbons in R)** — propionate's R has 2 carbons, so the alkane has 4.

data.topicTitle: Manufacture of ammonia by Haber's process (principle and flow sheet diagram only)
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Haber Process: Feeding the World from Air

Ammonia is the gateway to every nitrogenous fertiliser. The Haber process combines **N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ + heat (ΔH ≈ −92 kJ/mol)** under high pressure, moderate temperature and an iron catalyst — the single most consequential equilibrium compromise in industry, fixing the nitrogen that feeds roughly half the world's population.

## 2. Theorem Mirror

- **Reaction:** N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ/mol; 4 mol gas → 2 mol gas.
- **Conditions:** pressure **200–300 atm**; temperature **450–500 °C**; catalyst **finely divided iron** promoted with K₂O/Al₂O₃ (or Mo) — the promoters increase surface activity and resist sintering.
- **Feed gases:** N₂ from fractional distillation of liquid air; H₂ from steam reforming of natural gas (CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3H₂, then water-gas shift CO + H₂O → CO₂ + H₂ with the CO₂ absorbed off).
- **Flow sheet:** N₂ + H₂ purification → compression (multistage) → catalytic converter (heat exchangers recover reaction heat) → condenser (NH₃ liquefies, bp −33 °C) → **recycle of unreacted gases**.
- **Le Chatelier:** high pressure shifts toward fewer moles (NH₃ side); low temperature favours the exothermic product but slows the rate ⟹ the 450–500 °C compromise.

## 3. Deep Conceptual — The Compromise That Runs the World

- Thermodynamics and kinetics pull opposite ways: **low T maximises yield, high T maximises rate.** The 450–500 °C operating point is neither the yield optimum nor the rate optimum — it is the *profit* optimum: enough rate per pass to make the plant pay, with the yield shortfall recovered by recycling. The catalyst does not shift the equilibrium (it cannot) — it lets the compromise temperature be as low as it is.
- **Why the recycle is the process's second engine:** per-pass conversion is only ~15% at plant conditions; the unreacted 85% is condensed-free N₂/H₂ that is recompressed and returned. Overall conversion approaches ~97% — the recycle loop converts a poor single-pass equilibrium into an excellent overall yield, and it is the reason high pressure is worth paying for twice (better equilibrium *and* faster loop turnover).

## 4. Deep Conceptual — Why High Pressure Is a Three-Layer Answer

- **Equilibrium layer:** 4 mol gas → 2 mol gas; Le Chatelier ⟹ pressure favours the ammonia side, raising the per-pass mole fraction.
- **Rate layer:** high pressure concentrates the molecules — more collisions per second — so the iron catalyst works on a denser gas, accelerating the slow N₂ activation.
- **Separation layer:** high pressure raises NH₃'s dew point, so simple cooling liquefies the product cleanly — the condenser works because the pressure did. **The full answer to "why high pressure" is all three layers**, and examiners award the equilibrium one but love the other two.

## 5. Worked Example Types

- **Type A — describe with flow sheet:** reaction, conditions, stages, recycle.
- **Type B — the pressure question:** three-layer justification.
- **Type C — the temperature compromise:** Le Chatelier versus Arrhenius.
- **Type D — feed-gas chemistry:** reforming and shift reactions.

## 6. Common Confusions

**"The catalyst increases yield":** it increases *rate* only — the equilibrium position is fixed by T and P; the catalyst's gift is a lower compromise temperature. **"Low temperature is best":** best for equilibrium, fatal for rate — the plant would produce almost nothing per day.

practiceQuestions: **NEB 2024 (5m): Describe the Haber process for ammonia manufacture. Why is high pressure used?** — **The process:** nitrogen (from fractional distillation of liquid air) and hydrogen (from steam reforming of natural gas: CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3H₂, followed by the shift reaction CO + H₂O → CO₂ + H₂ with CO₂ removed) are purified (catalyst poisons removed), compressed to **200–300 atm**, and passed over a **finely divided iron catalyst (promoted with K₂O/Al₂O₃)** at **450–500 °C**: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ + 92 kJ. The exit gases are cooled in a condenser — ammonia (bp −33 °C) liquefies and is drawn off; the unreacted N₂/H₂ are recompressed and **recycled** to the converter, lifting the overall conversion from ~15% per pass to ~97%. **Why high pressure (three layers):** (1) **equilibrium** — the forward reaction reduces 4 mol of gas to 2 mol, so Le Chatelier's principle shifts the equilibrium toward ammonia as pressure rises; (2) **rate** — higher pressure packs more molecules into the converter volume, increasing collision frequency on the catalyst surface and speeding the slow N₂ activation; (3) **separation** — high pressure raises ammonia's dew point, so the condenser liquefies the product efficiently. **Deep point:** the three layers are independent — even if the equilibrium argument were weaker, rate and condensation would still justify the pressure; complete answers quote all three, and the recycle arrow in the flow sheet is what makes the moderate per-pass conversion acceptable.

**NEB-style (5m): The Haber reaction is exothermic. Explain why the plant runs at 450-500 C rather than at a lower temperature, and what makes the chosen temperature defensible.** — **Thermodynamics says low:** the forward reaction is exothermic (ΔH = −92 kJ/mol), so low temperature shifts the equilibrium toward ammonia — more product per pass. **Kinetics says high:** reaction rate falls exponentially as temperature drops (Arrhenius); at very low T the N≡N triple bond's activation is so slow that yield-per-day approaches zero — a plant at 100 °C would have a beautiful equilibrium and no output. **The compromise:** 450–500 °C is hot enough for the iron catalyst to deliver a useful rate per pass, cool enough to keep a workable equilibrium; the yield shortfall is recovered by the recycle loop. **The catalyst's role:** it does not move the equilibrium (impossible) — it lowers the activation energy, allowing the compromise temperature to be *lower* than an uncatalysed process could afford. **Deep point:** "compromise conditions" is the exam phrase that unlocks every industrial-equilibrium question — the operating point is chosen where rate × equilibrium × recycle-economics is maximised, and saying "profit optimum" rather than "best yield" is the understanding mark.

**NEB-style (5m): Only about 15% of the entering gases convert to ammonia on each pass through the converter. Explain how the process nevertheless achieves ~97% overall conversion, and why the unreacted gases are not wasted.** — **The recycle loop:** after each pass, the condenser removes ammonia as liquid; the remaining gas — mostly unreacted N₂ and H₂ with only traces of NH₃ — is recompressed and fed back to the converter, mixing with fresh feed. **Arithmetic of looping:** each pass converts ~15% of what enters it; after n passes the cumulative conversion approaches 1 − (0.85)ⁿ — after ~25 passes the residual unconverted fraction falls below 2% ⟹ ~97–98% overall. **Why not wasted:** the unreacted gases are *reactants already paid for* — purged they would be an economic and environmental loss (and hydrogen vented is an energy loss); recycled they cost only recompression energy. **Design note:** a small purge stream removes the argon (from the nitrogen source) that would otherwise accumulate and dilute the loop. **Deep point:** the recycle loop is the industrial answer to an unfavourable single-pass equilibrium — it decouples *per-pass conversion* (set by the equilibrium at operating conditions) from *overall conversion* (set by how many loops you run), and that decoupling is what makes mildly-yielding equilibria commercially viable.

**NEB-style (6m): Write the reactions by which the hydrogen feed for the Haber process is obtained from natural gas, and state why both carbon oxides must be removed before the converter.** — **Steam reforming:** CH₄ + H₂O --(Ni, ~800–900 °C)--> CO + 3H₂ — the natural gas and steam pass over a nickel catalyst. **Water-gas shift:** CO + H₂O --(Fe/Cr catalyst, ~400 °C)--> CO₂ + H₂ — converts the toxic carbon monoxide into additional hydrogen; the CO₂ is absorbed off (e.g. by hot K₂CO₃ solution) leaving an H₂-rich stream. **Removal necessity:** (1) **CO is a catalyst poison** — it binds to the iron surface and blocks the N₂/H₂ activation sites (the same coordination that makes CO lethal to haemoglobin); (2) **CO₂ would re-enter the product** — any oxide passing through dilutes the synthesis gas and contaminates the ammonia stream. Purification precedes compression because poisons destroy the promoted-iron catalyst's activity irreversibly. **Deep point:** the feed-train chemistry is as examinable as the converter — the two equations plus the poisoning argument (CO on iron parallels CO on haemoglobin) turn a "describe the process" answer into a chemistry answer.
keyPoints: N2 + 3H2 <-> 2NH3, dH = -92 kJ/mol, 4 mol -> 2 mol. Conditions: 200-300 atm, 450-500 C, finely divided Fe with K2O/Al2O3 promoters. Feeds: N2 from liquid air; H2 by steam reforming (CH4 + H2O -> CO + 3H2) + shift (CO + H2O -> CO2 + H2). Flow: compress -> converter -> condenser (-33 C bp) -> recycle. Per-pass conversion ~15%; recycle lifts overall to ~97%. Why high pressure: equilibrium (fewer moles) + rate (collision density) + separation (NH3 dew point) - three layers. Temperature compromise: low T for yield, high T for rate - 450-500 C is the profit optimum; catalyst lowers it.
data.summary: The Haber process fixes atmospheric nitrogen by the compromise of all compromises: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ at 200–300 atm, 450–500 °C over promoted iron — hot enough to run, cool enough to yield, pressurised for three independent reasons (equilibrium's fewer moles, collision-dense rate, ammonia's raised dew point), and looped so that a 15% per-pass conversion becomes ~97% overall. The catalyst lowers the compromise temperature; the recycle pays the equilibrium's tax; and the feed train (reforming + shift + purification) is the quiet half of the flow sheet where the catalyst's life is protected.
