practiceQuestions: **NEB 2024 (verified PYQ): Solve x² − 5x + 6 = 0. (2m)** — **Factoring:** two numbers with product 6 and sum −5 are −2 and −3: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0 ⟹ **x = 2 or x = 3**. **Viète verification:** the roots' sum is 2 + 3 = 5, matching −b/a = −(−5)/1 = 5 ✓; their product is 6, matching c/a = 6/1 ✓ — the root–coefficient relations independently confirm the factorisation. **Discriminant reading:** D = 25 − 24 = 1 > 0 (a perfect square ⟹ rational roots, exactly what factoring found).

**NEB-style (3m): If α and β are the roots of 2x² − 5x + 3 = 0, find α² + β² and 1/α + 1/β without solving the equation.** — **Viète relations:** α + β = −b/a = 5/2 and αβ = c/a = 3/2. **Sum of squares:** α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ = (5/2)² − 2(3/2) = 25/4 − 3 = **13/4**. **Sum of reciprocals:** 1/α + 1/β = (α + β)/(αβ) = (5/2)/(3/2) = **5/3**. **Method note:** both target expressions are **symmetric** in α, β — expressible through the sum and product alone — so the roots themselves never need to be found; Viète's relations are exactly the translation dictionary from root-symmetric language to coefficient language.

**NEB-style (3m): For what values of k does the equation x² + kx + 9 = 0 have (i) equal roots, (ii) real roots?** — **(i) Equal roots ⟺ D = 0:** D = k² − 4(1)(9) = k² − 36 = 0 ⟹ **k = ±6**. For k = 6 the repeated root is −b/2a = −3; for k = −6 it is +3 — the parabola is tangent to the x-axis in either case. **(ii) Real roots ⟺ D ≥ 0:** k² − 36 ≥ 0 ⟹ **k ≤ −6 or k ≥ 6**, i.e. |k| ≥ 6 — outside the open interval (−6, 6) the parabola meets the axis (twice for |k| > 6, once at |k| = 6), and inside it the roots retreat into a conjugate complex pair.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Quadratics Fully Decoded

The discriminant b² − 4ac governs everything: **nature of roots**, and the **Viète relations** sum = −b/a, product = c/a — the pair that converts root information into coefficient equations and back.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 The quadratic formula and discriminant

- **x = (−b ± √D)/2a**, D = b² − 4ac.
- **Nature theorem:** D > 0 ⟹ two distinct real roots; **D = 0** ⟹ one repeated real root (−b/2a); **D < 0** ⟹ two conjugate complex roots (−b ± i√|D|)/2a.
- **Perfect-square sub-case:** D > 0 and a perfect square ⟹ rational roots (factorable over ℚ).

### 2.2 Viète's relations (root–coefficient theorems)

- For roots α, β of ax² + bx + c = 0: **α + β = −b/a** and **αβ = c/a**.
- Proof: ax² + bx + c = a(x − α)(x − β) = a[x² − (α+β)x + αβ]; comparing coefficients gives both relations.
- Consequences: α² + β² = (α+β)² − 2αβ = b²/a² − 2c/a; 1/α + 1/β = (α+β)/αβ = −b/c; |α − β| = √D/|a|.

### 2.3 Building equations from roots

- **Theorem:** the monic quadratic with roots α, β is **x² − (α+β)x + αβ = 0** — sum with a minus, product as is.
- Symmetric transformations: roots kα, kβ or α+k, β+k or 1/α, 1/β — recompute the new sum and product, then rebuild.

### 2.4 Graph connections

- Real roots ⟺ the parabola cuts the x-axis; repeated root ⟺ tangency (vertex on the axis); complex roots ⟺ no intersection. Sign of a and position of c refine the picture.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Discriminant** | D = b² − 4ac — root classifier | D = 0: double root |
| **Viète relations** | α+β = −b/a, αβ = c/a | sum/product from coefficients |
| **Conjugate roots** | D < 0 gives z and z̄ | 1 ± i√3 |
| **Repeated root** | D = 0: both roots −b/2a | (x−3)² = 0 |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why the discriminant decides

- √D must be real (D ≥ 0) or imaginary (D < 0); the formula's structure makes D the complete classifier — one number, three regimes.

### 4.2 Viète as a translation device

- Many questions never ask for the roots — only for symmetric combinations (sums of squares, reciprocals). Viète converts such expressions into coefficients without solving anything.

### 4.3 The reconstruction template

- Any "new roots are f(α), f(β)" question: compute the new sum S′ and product P′ via Viète, then write x² − S′x + P′ = 0. Four lines, every time.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Discriminant regimes**

| D | Roots | Graph |
|---|---|---|
| > 0 | two distinct real | cuts x-axis twice |
| = 0 | repeated real | tangent to x-axis |
| < 0 | conjugate complex | misses x-axis |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Sum carries the minus:** α + β = −b/a — dropping the sign is the most common Viète error.
**Complex roots come in conjugate pairs** only when coefficients are real — state the hypothesis.
**|α − β| = √D/|a|:** the |a| in the denominator is forgotten when a is negative.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB 2024 (verified PYQ): Solve x² − 5x + 6 = 0. (2m)** — Factor: (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0 ⟹ **x = 2, 3**. Viète check: sum 5 = −(−5)/1 ✓, product 6 = 6/1 ✓ — the root–coefficient relations confirm the factorisation.

**NEB-style (3m): If α and β are the roots of 2x² − 5x + 3 = 0, find α² + β² and 1/α + 1/β.** — Viète: α+β = 5/2, αβ = 3/2. **α² + β²** = (α+β)² − 2αβ = 25/4 − 3 = **13/4**. **1/α + 1/β** = (α+β)/αβ = (5/2)/(3/2) = **5/3**. No root was ever computed — Viète did all the work.

**NEB-style (3m): For what value of k does x² + kx + 9 = 0 have equal roots?** — Equal roots ⟺ **D = 0**: k² − 36 = 0 ⟹ **k = ±6**. For k = 6 the double root is −3; for k = −6 it is +3 — the sign of k only moves the root's position, not the tangency.

**NEB-style (2m): Form the quadratic equation whose roots are 2 + √3 and 2 − √3.** — Sum = 4; product = 4 − 3 = 1. **Equation: x² − 4x + 1 = 0.** (The roots are conjugate surds, so the coefficients are rational — as guaranteed for quadratics with rational coefficients.)

data.topicTitle: Complex number: imaginary unit, algebra of complex numbers, geometric representation, absolute (modulus) value and conjugate of complex numbers and their properties, square root of a complex number
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — √(−1) Becomes Legitimate

The **imaginary unit i** with i² = −1 extends ℝ to ℂ, making every quadratic solvable. The theorems: algebra of complex numbers, **conjugate properties**, **modulus** |z| = √(x² + y²), and the geometric (Argand) representation where multiplication becomes rotation-and-scaling.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 The imaginary unit and standard form

- **i² = −1**; every complex number is **z = x + iy** (x = real part Re z, y = imaginary part Im z).
- Equality: x + iy = u + vi ⟺ x = u and y = v — real and imaginary parts match separately.
- **Theorem (quadratic solvability):** ax² + bx + c = 0 with negative discriminant has roots (−b ± i√|D|)/2a — ℂ is algebraically closed for quadratics.

### 2.2 Algebra of complex numbers

- Addition/subtraction componentwise; **multiplication:** (x + iy)(u + iv) = (xu − yv) + i(xv + yu) — expand and replace i² by −1.
- **Division:** multiply by the conjugate of the denominator: z₁/z₂ = z₁z̄₂/|z₂|².
- Powers of i cycle with period 4: i, −1, −i, 1 — iⁿ = i^(n mod 4).

### 2.3 Conjugate theorems

- **z̄ = x − iy**; z + z̄ = 2x (real), z − z̄ = 2iy (imaginary), **z·z̄ = |z|² = x² + y²**.
- **Theorems:** conjugation distributes: (z̄₁+z̄₂) = z̄₁ + z̄₂, (z₁z₂)‾ = z̄₁z̄₂, (z₁/z₂)‾ = z̄₁/z̄₂; z real ⟺ z = z̄.

### 2.4 Modulus and the Argand plane

- **|z| = √(x² + y²)** — distance from the origin; satisfies the **triangle inequality |z₁ + z₂| ≤ |z₁| + |z₂|** and |z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂|.
- Argand diagram: z = x + iy is the point (x, y); |z − z₀| = r is a **circle** of radius r about z₀; conjugation reflects in the real axis.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Imaginary unit** | i² = −1 | √(−9) = 3i |
| **Conjugate** | z̄ = x − iy — mirror in real axis | (2 + 3i)‾ = 2 − 3i |
| **Modulus** | |z| = √(x² + y²) — distance from 0 | |3 + 4i| = 5 |
| **Argand diagram** | Complex plane: (x, y) ↔ x + iy | geometry of ℂ |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why ℂ is closed

- ℝ failed √(−1); ℂ fixes it, and the price is small: order is lost (no "z₁ < z₂" for complex numbers). Gain: every quadratic equation now has two roots.

### 4.2 Conjugates as the division tool

- Dividing by z multiplies by z̄/|z|²: the conjugate realises the denominator, and the modulus² normalises it. Conjugation is the workhorse of complex arithmetic.

### 4.3 Multiplication is rotation

- In polar form z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), multiplying multiplies moduli and **adds angles** — multiplication by i is a 90° rotation. The Argand plane turns algebra into geometry.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Real vs complex arithmetic**

| Operation | ℝ | ℂ |
|---|---|---|
| √ of negative | undefined | defined via i |
| order | yes | **no** |
| conjugate | trivial (x̄ = x) | non-trivial, essential |
| algebraically closed | no | yes |

## 6. Common Confusions

**√(−a) = i√a, not ±:** the principal root carries the i; the ± appears when solving equations, not when evaluating the radical.
**|z| is not z's "absolute value" algebraically:** it is √(z·z̄) — the distance — and obeys |z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂| but not |z₁ + z₂| = |z₁| + |z₂|.
**iⁿ cycles mod 4:** i⁴⁰⁰ = 1, i⁴⁰¹ = i — reduce the exponent modulo 4 before anything else.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): Express (2 + 3i)(1 − 2i) + (3 − i)/(1 + i) in the form x + iy.** — **Product:** (2 + 3i)(1 − 2i) = 2 − 4i + 3i − 6i² = 2 − i + 6 = **8 − i**. **Quotient:** multiply by the conjugate: (3 − i)(1 − i)/(1 + i)(1 − i) = (3 − 3i − i + i²)/2 = (2 − 4i)/2 = **1 − 2i**. **Sum:** (8 − i) + (1 − 2i) = **9 − 3i**.

**NEB-style (2m): If z = 2 + i, express z² + z̄² in the form x + iy and deduce that it is real.** — z² = (2 + i)² = 4 + 4i + i² = **3 + 4i**; z̄² = (2 − i)² = 3 − 4i. Sum: **6 + 0i — purely real**. Deduction: z² + z̄² = 2Re(z²) = 2(3) = 6 — the general theorem z² + z̄² = 2Re(z²) ∈ ℝ at work.

**NEB-style (2m): Solve x² + x + 1 = 0 over ℂ.** — D = 1 − 4 = −3 < 0 ⟹ complex roots: x = (−1 ± i√3)/2 — the **cube roots of unity** (excluding 1). The quadratic formula extends verbatim to negative discriminants once i is admitted.

practiceQuestions: **NEB-style (3m): Express (2 + 3i)(1 − 2i) + (3 − i)/(1 + i) in the form x + iy.** — **Product:** (2 + 3i)(1 − 2i) = 2·1 + 2·(−2i) + 3i·1 + 3i·(−2i) = 2 − 4i + 3i − 6i² = 2 − i + 6 = **8 − i** (i² = −1 flips the sign of the last term). **Quotient:** multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate (1 − i): (3 − i)(1 − i)/[(1 + i)(1 − i)] = (3 − 3i − i + i²)/(1 − i²) = (3 − 4i − 1)/2 = (2 − 4i)/2 = **1 − 2i**. **Sum:** (8 − i) + (1 − 2i) = **9 − 3i** — real part 9, imaginary part −3. Every complex computation reduces to: expand with i² = −1, and divide via the conjugate.

**NEB-style (2m): Find the modulus and the conjugate of z = (1 + 2i)/(3 − 4i).** — **Rationalise:** z = (1 + 2i)(3 + 4i)/[(3 − 4i)(3 + 4i)] = (3 + 4i + 6i + 8i²)/(9 + 16) = (3 − 8 + 10i)/25 = (−5 + 10i)/25 = **(−1 + 2i)/5**. **Modulus:** |z| = √((−1/5)² + (2/5)²) = √5/5 = **1/√5**. **Cross-check by the modulus theorem:** |z| = |1 + 2i|/|3 − 4i| = √5/√25 = √5/5 ✓ — moduli of quotients divide, exactly as |z₁/z₂| = |z₁|/|z₂| demands. **Conjugate:** conjugating termwise, **z̄ = (−1 − 2i)/5** — equivalently conjugate before rationalising; both routes agree since conjugation respects division.

**NEB-style (2m): Solve the equation x² + x + 1 = 0 over the complex numbers.** — **Discriminant:** D = b² − 4ac = 1 − 4 = **−3 < 0** — no real roots, but ℂ supplies them. **Quadratic formula with i:** x = (−1 ± √(−3))/2 = (−1 ± i√3)/2. **Roots: x = (−1 + i√3)/2 and x = (−1 − i√3)/2** — a conjugate pair (real quadratics always have conjugate-pair roots). **Identification:** these are the primitive **cube roots of unity** ω and ω², satisfying 1 + ω + ω² = 0 and ω³ = 1 — the same pair that powers the factorisation x³ − 1 = (x − 1)(x² + x + 1).

| **Modulus** | |z| = √(x² + y²) — distance from 0 | |3 + 4i| = 5 |
| **Argand diagram** | Complex plane: (x, y) ↔ x + iy | geometry of ℂ |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why ℂ is closed

- ℝ failed √(−1); ℂ fixes it, and the price is small: order is lost (no "z₁ < z₂" for complex numbers). Gain: every quadratic equation now has two roots.

### 4.2 Conjugates as the division tool

- Dividing by z multiplies by z̄/|z|²: the conjugate realises the denominator, and the modulus² normalises it. Conjugation is the workhorse of complex arithmetic.

### 4.3 Multiplication is rotation

- In polar form z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), multiplying multiplies moduli and **adds angles** — multiplication by i is a 90° rotation. The Argand plane turns algebra into geometry.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Real vs complex arithmetic**

| Operation | ℝ | ℂ |
|---|---|---|
| √ of negative | undefined | defined via i |
| order | yes | **no** |
| conjugate | trivial (x̄ = x) | non-trivial, essential |
| algebraically closed | no | yes |

## 6. Common Confusions

**√(−a) = i√a, not ±:** the principal root carries the i; the ± appears when solving equations, not when evaluating the radical.
**|z| is not z's "absolute value" algebraically:** it is √(z·z̄) — the distance — and obeys |z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂| but not |z₁ + z₂| = |z₁| + |z₂|.
**iⁿ cycles mod 4:** i⁴⁰⁰ = 1, i⁴⁰¹ = i — reduce the exponent modulo 4 before anything else.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): Express (2 + 3i)(1 − 2i) + (3 − i)/(1 + i) in the form x + iy.** — **Product:** (2 + 3i)(1 − 2i) = 2 − 4i + 3i − 6i² = 2 − i + 6 = **8 − i**. **Quotient:** multiply by the conjugate: (3 − i)(1 − i)/(1 + i)(1 − i) = (3 − 3i − i + i²)/2 = (2 − 4i)/2 = **1 − 2i**. **Sum:** (8 − i) + (1 − 2i) = **9 − 3i**.

**NEB-style (2m): If z = 2 + i, express z² + z̄² in the form x + iy and deduce that it is real.** — z² = (2 + i)² = 4 + 4i + i² = **3 + 4i**; z̄² = (2 − i)² = 3 − 4i. Sum: **6 + 0i — purely real**. Deduction: z² + z̄² = 2Re(z²) = 2(3) = 6 — the general theorem z² + z̄² = 2Re(z²) ∈ ℝ at work.

**NEB-style (2m): Solve x² + x + 1 = 0 over ℂ.** — D = 1 − 4 = −3 < 0 ⟹ complex roots: x = (−1 ± i√3)/2 — the **cube roots of unity** (excluding 1). The quadratic formula extends verbatim to negative discriminants once i is admitted.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Three Extra Canonicals

Rows 25–26 and 22 are the **duplicate-slug canonicals**: shorter companion notes (`function-domain-range`, `sequence-series`, `minors-cofactors-determinants`) that mirror the main topics. This session upgrades them with the same theorem-grade fields so no canonical file stays thin.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Function: domain and range (companion)

- **Domain bans:** denominator ≠ 0, even-root radicand ≥ 0, log argument > 0; combinations intersect.
- **Range by inversion:** solve y = f(x) for x; the feasible y's are the range.
- **Inverse theorem:** f⁻¹ exists ⟺ one-to-one; construct y = f(x) → solve → swap; graph reflects in y = x.

### 2.2 Sequence and series (companion)

- **AP:** aₙ = a + (n−1)d, Sₙ = n/2(a + l). **GP:** aₙ = arⁿ⁻¹, Sₙ = a(rⁿ−1)/(r−1), S∞ = a/(1−r) iff |r| < 1.
- **Means:** AM ≥ GM ≥ HM, equality iff a = b. **Special sums:** Σi = n(n+1)/2, Σi² = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6, Σi³ = [n(n+1)/2]².

### 2.3 Minors, cofactors, determinants (companion)

- **Cᵢⱼ = (−1)^(i+j)Mᵢⱼ**; Laplace expansion along any row/column.
- **Adjoint identity:** A·adj A = |A|I ⟹ A⁻¹ = adj A/|A| for |A| ≠ 0; |AB| = |A||B|.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Domain** | Legal inputs under the bans | [2, 3) ∪ (3, ∞) example |
| **S∞** | GP limit, |r| < 1 | a/(1−r) |
| **Cofactor** | Signed minor | checkerboard signs |
| **Adjoint identity** | A·adj A = \|A\|·I | keystone of inversion |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why companions exist

- The manifest carries both a long canonical note and a short companion per duplicate slug; learners meet different entry pages. Consistent enrichment prevents a thin back door.

### 4.2 The three-in-one drill set

- Each companion gets worked example types mirroring its parent: domain/interleaved inverse drills, AP–GP numericals, and a cofactor–adjoint–inverse chain.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Companion vs parent coverage**

| Companion | Parent topic | Shared theorems |
|---|---|---|
| function-domain-range | row 15/16 | domain bans, inverse theorem |
| sequence-series | rows 18/19 | AP/GP sums, means |
| minors-cofactors-determinants | rows 21/22 | cofactors, adjoint, inverse |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Same slug, two files:** the first manifest entry is canonical; companions must not contradict the parent's formulas.
**S∞ needs its licence:** every companion GP numerical must show |r| < 1 before a/(1−r).
**adj A transposes:** the companion repeats the rule because it is the single most-failed step.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (2m): Find the domain of f(x) = 1/√(4 − x²).** — Two bans: radicand 4 − x² ≥ 0 ⟹ −2 ≤ x ≤ 2; **denominator ≠ 0** ⟹ √(4 − x²) ≠ 0 ⟹ x ≠ ±2. Intersection: **−2 < x < 2**, the open interval (−2, 2) — the endpoints die not by the root rule but by the denominator rule.
keyPoints: Companion canonicals mirror their parents. Function: domain bans (denominator, even root, log) intersected; range by inversion; inverse iff one-to-one, reflection in y = x. Sequence/series: AP a_n = a + (n-1)d, S_n = n/2(a + l); GP a_n = ar^(n-1), S_n = a(r^n - 1)/(r-1), S_inf = a/(1-r) iff |r| < 1; AM >= GM >= HM; sum i = n(n+1)/2, sum i^2 = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6, sum i^3 = [n(n+1)/2]^2. Determinants: C_ij = (-1)^(i+j) M_ij; Laplace expansion any row/column; A adj A = |A| I; A^-1 = adj A/|A|; |AB| = |A||B|.

Companions must agree with parents: one theorem set, several doors.
importantStatements: "A adj A = |A| I; S_inf = a/(1 - r) iff |r| < 1; the inverse exists iff the function is one-to-one."
importantNotes: No verified PYQ on these rows exists in the bank; all items here are NEB-style practice.
examShortTricks: Domain: intersect the bans. GP count: set S_n and solve for 2^n. Inverse 2x2: swap, negate, divide by |A|.
importantConcepts: Companion notes are the same theorems through a narrower door: consistent enrichment keeps every entry page exam-ready.
formulas:
- domain bans: denominator ≠ 0, radicand ≥ 0, log > 0 (intersected)
- AP/GP sums as in rows 18–19; Σi³ = [n(n+1)/2]²
- Cᵢⱼ = (−1)^(i+j)Mᵢⱼ; A·adj A = |A|I; A⁻¹ = adj A/|A|
examples: ***The denominator ban inside a root*** - 1/sqrt(4 - x^2) loses its endpoints twice: the root wants them, the denominator forbids them - intersection wins.
practiceQuestions: **NEB-style (2m): Find the domain of f(x) = 1/√(4 − x²).** — **Ban 1 (even root):** the radicand must be non-negative: 4 − x² ≥ 0 ⟹ x² ≤ 4 ⟹ −2 ≤ x ≤ 2. **Ban 2 (denominator):** 1/√(4 − x²) requires √(4 − x²) ≠ 0 ⟹ x ≠ ±2 — the endpoints are **forbidden**, not merely allowed. **Intersection of the bans:** **−2 < x < 2**, i.e. the open interval **(−2, 2)**. The lesson: when a root sits in a denominator, the root's ≥ becomes a strict > — the two rules interact, and the intersection is the whole answer.

**NEB-style (2m): How many terms of the geometric progression 3 + 6 + 12 + ⋯ must be added to give a sum of 765?** — **Setup:** a = 3, r = 6/3 = 2, Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) = 3(2ⁿ − 1). **Equation:** 3(2ⁿ − 1) = 765 ⟹ 2ⁿ − 1 = 255 ⟹ 2ⁿ = 256 = 2⁸ ⟹ **n = 8 terms**. **Verification:** the terms are 3, 6, 12, 24, 48, 96, 192, 384; their sum = 3(2⁸ − 1) = 3 × 255 = 765 ✓. (No S∞ licence is needed here — r = 2 ≥ 1, so the series diverges and only finite sums exist, which is exactly why the question asks for a partial sum.)
confusion: Forgetting that adj A is the transpose of the cofactor matrix; using the cofactor matrix directly gives the wrong inverse.
Believing a row swap leaves the determinant unchanged; it actually reverses the sign.
practice: Find the domain of 1/√(4 − x²).
How many terms of 3 + 6 + 12 + ⋯ sum to 765?
Find adj A and A⁻¹ for A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]].
universalFacts: Summing a GP to 765 terms is the compound-interest question in school clothes: n = 8 doublings from 3.
specialNotes: Cramer's rule needs det A ≠ 0; when det A = 0 switch to rank comparison instead.
For a 2 × 2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]], adj A = [[d, −b], [−c, a]] — swap the diagonal and negate the off-diagonal.
examNotes: Companion answers must match the parent's formulas exactly - a mismatched S_inf licence or adjoint transpose is an internal inconsistency.
importantTasks: Build a cofactor matrix for a 3 × 3 case
Solve a 3-variable system by Cramer's rule

mcs.question: For a 3 × 3 matrix, the cofactor C_23 equals
mcs.explanation: (−1)^(2+3) = −1, and a cofactor uses the same indices' minor, not the transposed one.

mcs.question: If det A = 0 for a square matrix A, then
mcs.explanation: A zero determinant means A is singular and no inverse exists.

notes: Question 3: Without expanding the determinants, show that the value of each of the following determinants is zero

General approach pattern: Look for a row/column that is a linear combination of others (common factor, sum of two other rows, etc.) using Row/Column Operations (Râ†’R+kR or Câ†’C+kC). If you can reduce any row or column entirely to zeros, the determinant is instantly 0 by Property that says a zero row/column gives zero determinant.
Solution:
$$\begin{vmatrix}6&1&9\\2&4&7\\18&3&27\end{vmatrix}$$
Notice Row 3 = 3 Ã— Row 1 (18=3Ã—6, 3=3Ã—1, 27=3Ã—9). Take 3 common from Row 3:
$$= 3\begin{vmatrix}6&1&9\\2&4&7\\6&1&9\end{vmatrix}$$
Now Row 1 = Row 3, so by Property (iii):
Proved.
Pattern to recognize: whenever one row/column is a multiple of another, factor out the multiple first â€” this immediately reveals identical rows.
(ii) Show |1 a b+c; 1 b c+a; 1 c a+b| = 0
Solution: Adding Column 2 into Column 3 (Câ‚ƒ â†’ Câ‚ƒ + Câ‚‚):
$$= \begin{vmatrix}1&a&a+b+c\\1&b&a+b+c\\1&c&a+b+c\end{vmatrix}$$
Taking (a+b+c) common from Column 3:
$$= (a+b+c)\begin{vmatrix}1&a&1\\1&b&1\\1&c&1\end{vmatrix}$$
Since Column 1 = Column 3 (both all 1's):
Proved.

Pattern to recognize: whenever you see 'x, y, x+y' type entries, try adding the other column/row to combine them into a constant sum like (a+b+c) â€” this is the single most common trick in this whole exercise.
(iii) Show |(aâˆ’b) (bâˆ’c) (câˆ’a); (bâˆ’c) (câˆ’a) (aâˆ’b); (câˆ’a) (aâˆ’b) (bâˆ’c)| = 0
Solution: Using Câ‚ƒ â†’ Câ‚‚ + Câ‚ƒ:
$$= \begin{vmatrix}(a-b)&(b-c)&(b-c+c-a)\\(b-c)&(c-a)&(c-a+a-b)\\(c-a)&(a-b)&(a-b+b-c)\end{vmatrix}$$
$$= \begin{vmatrix}(a-b)&(b-c)&(b-a)\\(b-c)&(c-a)&(c-b)\\(c-a)&(a-b)&(a-c)\end{vmatrix}$$
Taking (âˆ’1) common from Column 3 (since bâˆ’a = âˆ’(aâˆ’b), etc.):
$$= -\begin{vmatrix}(a-b)&(b-c)&(a-b)\\(b-c)&(c-a)&(b-c)\\(c-a)&(a-b)&(c-a)\end{vmatrix}$$
Since Column 1 = Column 3:
Proved.
(iv) Show |1 bc a(b+c); 1 ca b(c+a); 1 ab c(a+b)| = 0
Solution: Expanding a(b+c) = ab+ac, b(c+a) = bc+ab, c(a+b) = ac+bc, so Column 3 becomes:
$$= \begin{vmatrix}1&bc&bc+ab+ca\\1&ca&ca+bc+ab\\1&ab&ab+ca+bc\end{vmatrix}$$
Each entry in Column 3 equals (ab+bc+ca):
$$= (ab+bc+ca)\begin{vmatrix}1&bc&1\\1&ca&1\\1&ab&1\end{vmatrix}$$
Since Column 1 = Column 3:
$$= (ab+bc+ca) \times 0 = 0$$
Proved.
(v) Show |1 bc bc(b+c); 1 ca ac(c+a); 1 ab ab(a+b)| = 0
Solution: Multiply Row 1 by a, Row 2 by b, Row 3 by c (and divide the whole determinant by abc to compensate):
$$= \frac{1}{abc}\begin{vmatrix}a&abc&abc(b+c)\\b&abc&abc(c+a)\\c&abc&abc(a+b)\end{vmatrix}$$
Taking abc common from Column 2 and Column 3:
$$= \frac{1(abc) \cdot abc}{abc}\begin{vmatrix}a&1&a+b+c\\b&1&a+b+c\\c&1&a+b+c\end{vmatrix}$$
$$= abc\begin{vmatrix}a&1&a+b+c\\b&1&a+b+c\\c&1&a+b+c\end{vmatrix}$$
Using Câ‚ƒ â†’ Câ‚ƒ + aÃ—Câ‚, and then noting Câ‚‚ = Câ‚ƒ after simplification:
$$= abc(a+b+c)\begin{vmatrix}a&1&1\\b&1&1\\c&1&1\end{vmatrix}$$
Since Column 2 = Column 3:
$$= abc(a+b+c) \times 0 = 0$$
Proved.
(vi) Show |1 Ï‰ Ï‰Â²; Ï‰ Ï‰Â² 1; Ï‰Â² 1 Ï‰| = 0 (where Ï‰ is a cube root of unity)
Solution: Using Câ‚ â†’ Câ‚ + Câ‚‚ + Câ‚ƒ:
$$= \begin{vmatrix}1+\omega+\omega^2&\omega&\omega^2\\\omega+\omega^2+1&\omega^2&1\\\omega^2+1+\omega&1&\omega\end{vmatrix}$$
Key identity: 1 + Ï‰ + Ï‰Â² = 0 (a fundamental property of cube roots of unity). So Column 1 becomes all zeros:
$$= \begin{vmatrix}0&\omega&\omega^2\\0&\omega^2&1\\0&1&\omega\end{vmatrix} = 0$$
(Since Column 1 is entirely zero, the determinant is zero.)
Proved.
Pattern to recognize: whenever you see Ï‰ or Ï‰Â² in a determinant question, the identity 1+Ï‰+Ï‰Â²=0 is almost always the key to unlocking it.
Question 6: Show That (Determinant Identity Proofs)
(i) Show |1 1 1; a b c; bc ca ab| = (aâˆ’b)(bâˆ’c)(câˆ’a)
Solution: Using Câ‚ â†’ Câ‚ âˆ’ Câ‚‚, Câ‚‚ â†’ Câ‚‚ âˆ’ Câ‚ƒ:
$$= \begin{vmatrix}0&0&1\\a-b&b-c&c\\bc-ca&ca-ab&ab\end{vmatrix}$$
$$= \begin{vmatrix}0&0&1\\(a-b)&(b-c)&c\\-(a-b)c&-c(c-b)&ab\end{vmatrix}$$
Taking (aâˆ’b) common from Column 1 and (bâˆ’c) common from Column 2:
$$= (a-b)(b-c)\begin{vmatrix}0&0&1\\1&1&c\\-c&-a&ab\end{vmatrix}$$
Expanding along Row 1:
$$= (a-b)(b-c) \times 1 \times \begin{vmatrix}1&1\\-c&-a\end{vmatrix}$$
Proved.
(ii) Show |a b c; aÂ² bÂ² cÂ²; b+c c+a a+b| = (bâˆ’c)(câˆ’a)(aâˆ’b)(a+b+c)
Solution: Using Câ‚ â†’ Câ‚ âˆ’ Câ‚‚, Câ‚‚ â†’ Câ‚‚ âˆ’ Câ‚ƒ:
$$= \begin{vmatrix}a-b&b-c&c\\a^2-b^2&b^2-c^2&c^2\\b+c-c-a&c+a-a-b&a+b\end{vmatrix}$$
$$= \begin{vmatrix}(a-b)&(b-c)&c\\(a+b)(a-b)&(b+c)(b-c)&c^2\\-(a-b)&-(b-c)&a+b\end{vmatrix}$$
Taking (aâˆ’b) common from Column 1 and (bâˆ’c) common from Column 2:
$$= (a-b)(b-c)\begin{vmatrix}1&1&c\\a+b&b+c&c^2\\-1&-1&a+b\end{vmatrix}$$
Using Râ‚ â†’ Râ‚ + Râ‚ƒ:
$$= (a-b)(b-c)\begin{vmatrix}0&0&c+a+b\\a+b&b+c&c^2\\-1&-1&a+b\end{vmatrix}$$
Expanding along Row 1:
$$= (a-b)(b-c)(a+b+c)\begin{vmatrix}a+b&b+c\\-1&-1\end{vmatrix}$$
Proved.
(iii) Show |1 1 1; a b c; aÂ³ bÂ³ cÂ³| = (bâˆ’c)(câˆ’a)(aâˆ’b)(a+b+c)
Solution: Using Câ‚ â†’ Câ‚ âˆ’ Câ‚‚, Câ‚‚ â†’ Câ‚‚ âˆ’ Câ‚ƒ:
$$= \begin{vmatrix}0&0&1\\a-b&b-c&c\\a^3-b^3&b^3-c^3&c^3\end{vmatrix}$$
Taking (aâˆ’b) common from Column 1 and (bâˆ’c) common from Column 2, using aÂ³âˆ’bÂ³=(aâˆ’b)(aÂ²+ab+bÂ²):
$$= (a-b)(b-c)\begin{vmatrix}0&0&1\\1&1&c\\a^2+ab+b^2&b^2+cb+c^2&c^3\end{vmatrix}$$
Expanding along Row 1:
Proved.

Meta-pattern across (i), (ii), (iii): these three prove increasingly complex versions of the same identity family. Once you master the Câ‚â†’Câ‚âˆ’Câ‚‚, Câ‚‚â†’Câ‚‚âˆ’Câ‚ƒ trick + factoring (aâˆ’b), (bâˆ’c) from resulting columns, you can solve all of them the same way.
(iv) Show |x y z; xÂ² yÂ² zÂ²; yz zx xy| = (yâˆ’z)(zâˆ’x)(xâˆ’y)(yz+zx+xy)
Solution: Using Câ‚ â†’ Câ‚ âˆ’ Câ‚‚, Câ‚‚ â†’ Câ‚‚ âˆ’ Câ‚ƒ:
$$= \begin{vmatrix}x-y&y-z&z\\x^2-y^2&y^2-z^2&z^2\\yz-zx&zx-xy&xy\end{vmatrix}$$
Taking (xâˆ’y) common from Column 1, (yâˆ’z) common from Column 2:
$$= (x-y)(y-z)\begin{vmatrix}1&1&z\\x+y&y+z&z^2\\-z&-x&xy\end{vmatrix}$$
Using Râ‚ â†’ Râ‚ (adjustment via elimination and expansion along Row 1 after Câ‚ â†’ Câ‚ âˆ’ Câ‚‚ applied again):
$$= (x-y)(y-z)(x-z)\begin{vmatrix}0&1&z\\1&y+z&z^2\\1&-x&xy\end{vmatrix}$$
$$= (x-y)(y-z)(z-x)(xy+xz+yz)$$

(v) Show |b+c a b; c+a c a; a+b b c| = (a+b+c)(aâˆ’c)Â²
Solution: Using Câ‚ â†’ Câ‚ + Câ‚‚ + Câ‚ƒ:
$$= \begin{vmatrix}2(a+b+c)&a&b\\c+a&c&a\\a+b&b&c\end{vmatrix}$$
Taking (a+b+c) common from Column 1:
$$= (a+b+c)\begin{vmatrix}2&1&1\\c+a&c&a\\a+b&b&c\end{vmatrix}$$
Using Râ‚‚ â†’ Râ‚‚ (row simplification), then expanding after producing zeros:
$$= (a+b+c)(a-c)\begin{vmatrix}1&1\\c&a\end{vmatrix} = (a+b+c)(a-c)(a-c) = (a+b+c)(a-c)^2$$

(vi) Show |aâˆ’bâˆ’c 2a 2a; 2b bâˆ’câˆ’a 2b; 2c 2c câˆ’aâˆ’b| = (a+b+c)Â³
Solution: Using Râ‚ â†’ Râ‚ + Râ‚‚ + Râ‚ƒ:
$$= \begin{vmatrix}a+b+c&a+b+c&a+b+c\\2b&b-c-a&2b\\2c&2c&c-a-b\end{vmatrix}$$

$$= (a+b+c)\begin{vmatrix}1&1&1\\2b&b-c-a&2b\\2c&2c&c-a-b\end{vmatrix}$$
Using Câ‚‚ â†’ Câ‚‚ âˆ’ Câ‚, Câ‚ƒ â†’ Câ‚ƒ âˆ’ Câ‚:
$$= (a+b+c)\begin{vmatrix}1&0&0\\2b&-(a+b+c)&0\\2c&0&-(a+b+c)\end{vmatrix}$$
Expanding along Row 1:
$$= (a+b+c)\left[-(a+b+c)\cdot-(a+b+c)-0\right] = (a+b+c)^3$$
Proved.

practiceQuestions: Q1. **NEB-style (5m):** Find the perpendicular distance from the point (3, 4) to the line 3x + 4y - 5 = 0. **Solution.** $d=\frac{|3(3)+4(4)-5|}{\sqrt{3^2+4^2}}=\frac{|9+16-5|}{5}=\frac{20}{5}=4$ units. Deep point: the denominator is the normaliser that converts the raw expression into signed distance - the numerator is the signed distance times exactly that normaliser, which is why the formula has the shape it has.

Q2. **NEB-style (6m):** Find the equations of the bisectors of the angles between x + 2y - 5 = 0 and 4x + 2y + 9 = 0, labelling the acute one. **Solution.** Standardise: L$_1$ as $-x-2y+5=0$; L$_2$ has $c=9>0$. Normalisers $\sqrt5$ and $2\sqrt5$; multiply by $2\sqrt5$: $2(-x-2y+5)=\pm(4x+2y+9)$. (+): $6x+6y-1=0$; (-): $2x-2y+19=0$. Rule: $a_1a_2+b_1b_2=(-1)(4)+(-2)(2)=-8<0$ ⟹ (+) is acute. Check: slopes $-1$ and $1$ ⟹ perpendicular. Deep point: the lcm multiplication by $2\sqrt5$ is where the factor 2 enters - dropping it produces lines that are not bisectors.

Q3. **NEB-style (5m):** Find all values of k for which the point (2, k) lies at distance 3 from the line 4x - 3y + 1 = 0. **Solution.** $\frac{|8-3k+1|}{5}=3$ ⟹ $|9-3k|=15$ ⟹ $9-3k=\pm15$ ⟹ $k=-2$ or $k=8$. Deep point: the absolute value splits into two linear equations - distance-3 points form a pair of lines parallel to the given one, one on each side; both solutions live one on each side.

Q4. **NEB-style (6m):** Find the direction cosines of the line joining P(1, 2, 3) and Q(4, 6, 15), and verify the fundamental identity. **Solution.** Direction ratios (3, 4, 12); magnitude $\sqrt{9+16+144}=13$. Cosines: $l=\pm\frac{3}{13}$, $m=\pm\frac{4}{13}$, $n=\pm\frac{12}{13}$ (signs together). Identity: $\frac{9+16+144}{169}=1$ ✓. Deep point: the cosines are the unit vector's components - the identity is $|\hat{u}|=1$ restated, and the $\pm$ pair is the line's two directions.

Q5. **NEB-style (6m):** Find the foot of the perpendicular from P(2, 3) to the line x + 2y - 4 = 0. **Solution.** Signed distance numerator: $D=2+6-4=4$; $a^2+b^2=5$. Foot: $\left(2-\frac{1\cdot4}{5},\ 3-\frac{2\cdot4}{5}\right)=\left(\frac65,\frac75\right)$. Verify on the line: $\frac65+\frac{14}5-4=0$ ✓. Deep point: the foot formula subtracts the signed-distance vector $\frac{D}{a^2+b^2}(a,b)$ - the normal direction scaled to reach the line; the on-line check certifies it.

Q6. **NEB-style (5m):** Find the distance between the parallel lines 3x + 4y + 5 = 0 and 3x + 4y - 10 = 0. **Solution.** Shortcut: $\frac{|c_1-c_2|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}=\frac{|5-(-10)|}{5}=\frac{15}{5}=3$ units - valid because the two equations share identical (a, b), hence the same normaliser and orientation. Direct check: take $(-\frac53, 0)$ on the first line; distance to the second: $\frac{|3(-\frac53)+0+10|}{5}=\frac{|-5+10|}{5}=3$ ✓. Deep point: the parallel-lines shortcut is the point-substitution route compressed - identical (a, b) is its licence, and without it the general point-on-line-1 method is the honest fallback.

Q7. **NEB-style (6m):** Find the bisector of the angle between x - 2y + 1 = 0 and 2x + y - 3 = 0 that bisects the angle containing the origin. **Solution.** Standardise: L$_1$ has $c=1>0$; L$_2$ has $c=-3<0$ ⟹ rewrite as $-2x-y+3=0$. Normalisers both $\sqrt5$. (+) bisector: $x-2y+1=-2x-y+3$ ⟹ $3x-y-2=0$. Origin's wedge: plugging (0,0) into both standardised forms gives $+\frac{1}{\sqrt5}$ and $+\frac{3}{\sqrt5}$ - both positive, the same-signed region ⟹ the (+) bisector $3x-y-2=0$ bisects the origin's angle. Deep point: with constants positive, the origin sits on the positive side of both lines, so the same-signed (+) equation is automatically the origin's bisector - the convention does the selection.

## 1. Topic Introduction — Angle Bisector Worked Example (the a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ Method at Full Speed)

This canonical runs the **complete bisector computation on one concrete pair**: the lines x + 2y − 5 = 0 and 4x + 2y + 9 = 0, from normalisation through the acute/obtuse verdict to the finished equations. It is the worked-example face of the rule canonical.

## 2. Theorem Mirror (as used in the example)

- **Standardise:** both constants made positive — L₁: −x − 2y + 5 = 0 (a₁ = −1, b₁ = −2), L₂: 4x + 2y + 9 = 0 (a₂ = 4, b₂ = 2).
- **Normalisers:** √5 and √20 = 2√5.
- **Rule:** a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ = (−1)(4) + (−2)(2) = **−8 < 0** ⟹ the (+) bisector is **acute**, the (−) bisector obtuse.
- **Bisectors:** (+) 6x + 6y − 1 = 0 (acute); (−) 2x − 2y + 19 = 0 (obtuse); slopes −1 and +1 ⟹ perpendicular ✓.

## 3. Deep Conceptual — Reading the Example as a Chain of Licences

- Each step consumes a theorem: the standardisation licenses the rule, the normalisers convert equations into distances, the dot-product verdict assigns the labels, and the perpendicularity closes the audit. The example is not "arithmetic that happens to work" — it is four named theorems in sequence.
- **The unequal normalisers are the interesting part:** √5 vs 2√5 means the bisector equations carry a factor 2 — 2(−x−2y+5) = ±(4x+2y+9). Forgetting the factor is the classic error; the fix is to multiply through by the lcm of the normalisers before expanding.
- **Verification layers:** slopes multiply to −1 (perpendicularity), and substituting a point of one bisector into both normalised forms gives equal absolute distances (the definition itself). Two independent checks, one computation.

## 4. Deep Conceptual — Why the Verdict (−8 < 0) Was Predictable

- The normals (−1, −2) and (4, 2) point in *opposing* half-plane directions (dot product negative) — the same-side wedge (the (+) equation) is the narrow one. Geometrically: two normals pointing away from each other sandwich the acute wedge between the lines.
- **The constant-sign convention's role:** with c₁ = 5, c₂ = 9 both positive, the origin side is the (+) side of both lines; the (+) bisector therefore passes through the origin's wedge — and here that wedge is acute. Every label in the final answer is traceable to one dot product computed under one convention.

## 5. Worked Example Types

- **Type A — full pipeline:** standardise → normalise → rule → both bisectors → checks.
- **Type B — factor discipline:** unequal normalisers, lcm multiplication.
- **Type C — definition check:** equidistance verified at a bisector point.
- **Type D — classification narration:** the −8 verdict explained as normal geometry.

## 6. Common Confusions

**"Drop the factor 2":** unequal normalisers must be cleared before expanding. **"The labels are arbitrary":** they follow from the dot product under the convention — traceable, not chosen.

practiceQuestions: **NEB-style (6m): Find the equations of the bisectors of the angles between x + 2y − 5 = 0 and 4x + 2y + 9 = 0, and label the acute one.** — **Standardise:** L₁ ⟹ −x − 2y + 5 = 0 (c = 5 > 0); L₂ already has c = 9 > 0. **Normalisers:** √5 and √(16+4) = √20 = 2√5. **Bisector skeleton:** (−x−2y+5)/√5 = ±(4x+2y+9)/(2√5) ⟹ multiply by 2√5: **2(−x−2y+5) = ±(4x+2y+9)**. **(+):** −2x−4y+10 = 4x+2y+9 ⟹ 6x+6y−1 = 0. **(−):** −2x−4y+10 = −4x−2y−9 ⟹ 2x−2y+19 = 0. **Rule:** a₁a₂+b₁b₂ = −8 < 0 ⟹ (+) = 6x+6y−1 = 0 is **acute**. **Check:** slopes −1 and +1 ⟹ perpendicular ✓. **Deep point:** the lcm multiplication (by 2√5) is where the example's difficulty lives — every coefficient in the final answers is integer precisely because it was done; expanding with the raw fractions invites both arithmetic errors and dropped factors.

**NEB-style (5m): Verify that the point (1/6, 0) lies on the acute bisector 6x + 6y − 1 = 0 and is equidistant from the two lines.** — **On the bisector:** 6(1/6) + 0 − 1 = 0 ✓. **Distance to L₁ (x+2y−5=0):** |1/6 + 0 − 5|/√5 = |−29/6|/√5 = 29/(6√5). **Distance to L₂ (4x+2y+9=0):** |4/6 + 0 + 9|/√20 = |29/3 + 9|... compute: 4(1/6) = 2/3; 2/3 + 9 = 29/3 ⟹ (29/3)/(2√5) = 29/(6√5) ✓ — **equal distances**, as the bisector definition demands. **Deep point:** the definition check is the strongest verification — perpendicularity could hold for other perpendicular pairs, but equidistance is the *defining* property; a point on the line with equal distances certifies the bisector from first principles.

**NEB-style (5m): Without computing the bisectors, determine which of the (+)/(−) bisectors of x + 2y − 5 = 0 and 4x + 2y + 9 = 0 is acute, and justify.** — **Standardise:** L₁ ⟹ −x−2y+5 = 0 (a₁ = −1, b₁ = −2); L₂: a₂ = 4, b₂ = 2. **Dot product:** a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ = −4 − 4 = **−8 < 0**. **Verdict:** under the constants-positive convention, the (+) bisector — the same-signed-distance equation — is the **acute** one. **Geometric reading:** the normals (−1, −2) and (4, 2) have opposing senses (negative dot product), so the wedge where a point lies on the same side of both lines is the narrow one. **Deep point:** the classification is one multiplication and one comparison — the full bisector equations are not needed for the verdict; the rule exists precisely to make this label cheap.

**NEB-style (6m): The bisectors of two lines are 6x + 6y − 1 = 0 and 2x − 2y + 19 = 0. Find the angle between the bisectors and comment on what it verifies.** — **Slopes:** m₁ = −1, m₂ = 1. **Angle:** tan θ = |(m₂ − m₁)/(1 + m₁m₂)| = |2/(1 − 1)| = 2/0 ⟹ θ = **90°**. **Comment:** the bisectors of any pair of intersecting lines are perpendicular — this is not a special property of these lines but an identity (the normalised coefficients' cross terms cancel in the dot product). **Consistency:** the original lines' angle is bisected into two equal halves by each bisector, and the bisectors' own right angle is the envelope of that bisection. **Deep point:** when a problem *gives* you the bisectors, the perpendicularity check is the fastest sanity test — a non-right-angle pair cannot be the bisectors of any two lines, so the check can falsify an answer in one line of arithmetic.

practiceQuestions: Q1. **NEB-style (5m):** Show that 2x$^2$ + 5xy + 3y$^2$ = 0 represents a pair of real straight lines and find them. **Solution.** Condition: $h^2-ab=\frac{25}{4}-6=\frac14>0$ ✓ real pair. Factor: $2x^2+5xy+3y^2=(2x+3y)(x+y)$ ⟹ lines $2x+3y=0$ and $x+y=0$, both through the origin. Check by expansion: $2x^2+2xy+3xy+3y^2$ ✓. Deep point: a homogeneous second-degree equation always passes through the origin - the pair's vertex is fixed there; the discriminant condition $h^2\ge ab$ decides real versus imaginary lines.

Q2. **NEB-style (5m):** For which values of k does x$^2$ - kxy + 9y$^2$ = 0 represent a pair of real lines? **Solution.** Here $a=1$, $h=-\frac{k}{2}$, $b=9$; condition $h^2\ge ab$: $\frac{k^2}{4}\ge9$ ⟹ $|k|\ge6$, i.e. $k\le-6$ or $k\ge6$. Boundary: $k=\pm6$ gives $h^2=ab$ - coincident lines (a perfect square: $(x\mp3y)^2$). Deep point: the inequality's boundary is the coincidence case - the pair degenerates to a double line exactly when the discriminant vanishes, the quadratic-form analogue of a repeated root.

Q3. **NEB-style (6m):** Find the angle between the pair of lines 3x$^2$ - 8xy - 3y$^2$ = 0. **Solution.** $a=3$, $h=-4$, $b=-3$: $h^2-ab=16+9=25$, $\sqrt{h^2-ab}=5$. $\tan\theta=\frac{2\sqrt{h^2-ab}}{|a+b|}=\frac{10}{|0|}$ ⟹ denominator zero ⟹ $\theta=90°$ - the lines are perpendicular. Confirm by factoring: $3x^2-8xy-3y^2=(3x+y)(x-3y)$ ⟹ slopes $-3$ and $\frac13$ ⟹ product $-1$ ✓. Deep point: perpendicularity of a pair is $a+b=0$ - the tangent formula's infinite value is the vertical-angle case read through the formula's failure mode.

Q4. **NEB-style (5m):** Factor 6x$^2$ - xy - y$^2$ = 0 into its pair of lines and state their slopes. **Solution.** $6x^2-xy-y^2=(3x+y)(2x-y)$ ⟹ lines $3x+y=0$ (slope $-3$) and $2x-y=0$ (slope 2). Slope check via $m_1+m_2=-\frac{2h}{b}=\frac{1}{-1}=-1$ and $m_1m_2=\frac{a}{b}=\frac{6}{-1}=-6$: $-3+2=-1$ ✓, $(-3)(2)=-6$ ✓. Deep point: the slope relations $\sum m=-2h/b$, $\prod m=a/b$ (from substituting $y=mx$) verify a factoring without re-expanding - two one-line checks against two expansion-prone multiplications.

Q5. **NEB-style (6m):** Find the equations of the bisectors of the angles between the pair 2x$^2$ + 5xy + 3y$^2$ = 0. **Solution.** The pair's lines: $2x+3y=0$, $x+y=0$; standardise: $-2x-3y=0$ and $-x-y=0$ (constants 0 - homogeneous lines need no constant fix). Normalisers $\sqrt{13}$ and $\sqrt2$. Bisectors: $\frac{-2x-3y}{\sqrt{13}}=\pm\frac{-x-y}{\sqrt2}$; rationalise: $\sqrt2(-2x-3y)=\pm\sqrt{13}(x+y)$ ⟹ $(-2\sqrt2\mp\sqrt{13})x+(-3\sqrt2\mp\sqrt{13})y=0$ - two bisectors through the origin, perpendicular as required. Deep point: homogeneous pairs have bisectors through the origin (the pair's vertex); irrational coefficients are normal here - the bisector formula does not promise integers.

Q6. **NEB-style (5m):** Determine whether the point (2, 2) lies on either line of the pair x$^2$ - 3xy + 2y$^2$ = 0. **Solution.** Factor: $(x-y)(x-2y)=0$ ⟹ lines $x-y=0$ and $x-2y=0$. At (2, 2): $x-y=0$ ✓ - the point lies on the first line (and on the second? $2-4=-2\ne0$, no). Deep point: a point lies on the pair iff it lies on at least one member line - substituting into the combined quadratic gives 0 for points on either line, but locating *which* line needs the factorisation.

Q7. **NEB-style (6m):** The equation 6x$^2$ + 5xy + y$^2$ + 7x + ... represents a pair of lines. Explain the role of the condition $h^2-ab$ versus the full determinant condition abc + 2fgh - af$^2$ - bg$^2$ - ch$^2$ = 0. **Solution.** For the homogeneous part $6x^2+5xy+y^2$: $h^2-ab=\frac{25}{4}-6=\frac14>0$ - the quadratic part *factors*, but a general second-degree equation (with $x$ and $y$ terms and constant) represents a real pair only if the full determinant condition holds AND $h^2>ab$ (non-parallel) or $h^2=ab$ with further conditions (parallel). The homogeneous condition alone governs only the direction pair; the linear terms shift the pair's vertex away from the origin. Deep point: two conditions, two jobs - $h^2\ge ab$ reads the *directions* (real or imaginary), the determinant reads the *whole conic* (pair, point, or nothing); confusing them misclassifies every non-homogeneous equation.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The tan θ Verification of a Bisector

This canonical carries the **cross-check that certifies a bisector's label**: measure the angle θ between one original line and the claimed bisector; θ < 45° certifies the acute bisector, θ > 45° the obtuse one. It is the geometric audit that closes the algebraic pipeline.

## 2. Theorem Mirror

- **Angle between two lines:** tan θ = |(m₂ − m₁)/(1 + m₁m₂)| for slopes m₁, m₂ (1 + m₁m₂ ≠ 0).
- **The bisection fact:** each bisector makes equal angles with the two original lines; the acute bisector's half-angle is θ/2 < 45°, the obtuse bisector's is > 45° (when the lines' angle ≠ 90°).
- **The test:** compute tan θ between an original line and the candidate bisector; **tan θ < 1 ⟹ acute bisector; tan θ > 1 ⟹ obtuse bisector.**
- **Perpendicularity audit:** the two claimed bisectors must have slopes multiplying to −1.

## 3. Deep Conceptual — The Verification Reads the Angle's Own Geometry

- The acute bisector splits the *small* angle: any ray inside the acute wedge makes an angle < 45° with each arm (when the wedge is narrower than 90°). The test exploits exactly this: measure one arm-to-bisector angle and compare with 45° — the threshold is the right angle, the wedge's boundary case.
- **Why tan θ = 1 is the threshold:** θ = 45° ⟺ tan θ = 1; the comparison with 1 avoids ever computing the angle itself. One tangent, one comparison, one verdict — the arithmetic stays in fractions.
- **The 1 + m₁m₂ = 0 escape:** when the denominator vanishes the lines are perpendicular and the angle is 90° — the formula's failure mode is itself the answer, read as "vertical relative angle".

## 4. Deep Conceptual — Verification as an Independent Channel

- The tan θ test verifies the *label* (acute vs obtuse) through geometry, while the a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ rule derived it through algebra — two independent channels agreeing is far stronger evidence than one computation repeated. The habit of dual-channel verification (algebra says, geometry confirms) is the transferable skill.
- **Slope-based limits:** the test needs slopes, so vertical lines require the reciprocal-angle trick (use the angle with the x-axis directly) — a small reminder that every slope-based tool has a domain, and the angle-with-axis reading is the universal fallback.

## 5. Worked Example Types

- **Type A — certify the acute label:** tan θ < 1 with full fraction working.
- **Type B — certify the obtuse label:** tan θ > 1.
- **Type C — both bisectors audited:** the pair tested against each other's arms.
- **Type D — perpendicularity re-check:** slopes product −1 as the companion audit.

## 6. Common Confusions

**"tan θ < 1 means the lines are acute":** it means the *bisector* splits an angle below 45° — the statement is about the half-angle. **"The test replaces the rule":** it verifies it — the two channels agree, which is the point.
keyPoints: tan theta = |(m2-m1)/(1+m1 m2)|. The acute bisector's half-angle is below 45 degrees, so tan theta < 1 certifies acute, > 1 certifies obtuse - the threshold is the right angle. One tangent comparison replaces angle computation. Dual-channel verification: algebra (the rule) derives, geometry (tan theta) confirms. 1 + m1 m2 = 0 means perpendicular - the formula's failure mode is the answer.

practiceQuestions: **NEB-style (6m): Using the tangent formula, verify that 6x + 6y − 1 = 0 is the acute angle bisector of the lines x + 2y − 5 = 0 and 4x + 2y + 9 = 0.** — **Slopes:** bisector m_b = −6/6 = **−1**; L₁: y = (5−x)/2 ⟹ m₁ = **−1/2**. **Tangent:** tan θ = |(−1 − (−1/2))/(1 + (−1)(−1/2))| = |−1/2|/(1 + 1/2) = (1/2)/(3/2) = **1/3**. **Verdict:** tan θ = 1/3 < 1 ⟹ θ ≈ 18.4° < 45° ⟹ the bisector splits the **acute** angle ✓ — the label is certified geometrically. **Consistency:** the lines' full acute angle is 2θ ≈ 36.9°, plausible for slopes −1/2 and −2 (tan = |(−2+1/2)/(1+1)| = 3/4 ⟹ 36.9° ✓ — the doubling checks). **Deep point:** the verification's last line (the doubled angle matching the two lines' computed angle) is the complete audit: half-angle, threshold comparison, and doubling all agree — three independent confirmations in three fractions.

**NEB-style (6m): Verify that 2x − 2y + 19 = 0 is the obtuse bisector of x + 2y − 5 = 0 and 4x + 2y + 9 = 0.** — **Slopes:** bisector m_b = 1; L₁ slope m₁ = −1/2. **Tangent:** tan θ = |(1 + 1/2)/(1 + (1)(−1/2))| = (3/2)/(1/2) = **3**. **Verdict:** tan θ = 3 > 1 ⟹ θ ≈ 71.6° > 45° ⟹ this bisector splits the **obtuse** angle ✓. **Consistency:** the obtuse angle is 180° − 36.9° = 143.1°, half is 71.55° ✓ — the half-angle lands exactly where the tangent predicted. **Deep point:** the two verifications (1/3 and 3) are tangent reciprocals — the acute and obtuse half-angles are complementary (18.4° + 71.6° = 90°), which is the perpendicularity of the bisectors showing up inside the tangent arithmetic itself.

**NEB-style (5m): Show that the bisectors 6x + 6y − 1 = 0 and 2x − 2y + 19 = 0 are perpendicular, and explain why this had to happen.** — **Slopes:** m₁ = −6/6 = −1; m₂ = 2/2 = 1 ⟹ m₁m₂ = **−1** ⟹ perpendicular ✓. **Why necessary:** each bisector makes equal angles with the two arms; the two bisectors' directions differ by (half-angle + half-angle) measured around the intersection — one from the acute side, one from the obtuse — summing to half the full 180° sweep ⟹ 90°. Algebraically the normalised coefficients' cross terms cancel in the dot product (an identity). **Deep point:** the perpendicularity is the bisector system's invariant — it holds for *every* pair of intersecting lines, which is why it works as a falsification test: a non-right pair of "bisectors" is proof of an arithmetic slip somewhere.

**NEB-style (6m): The line y = 2x is claimed to be a bisector of the angle between x = 0 and y = x. Verify or refute using the tangent test.** — **Slopes:** candidate m_b = 2; arms m₁ = ∞ (the y-axis, vertical) and m₂ = 1. **Angle with the vertical arm (via axis angles):** y = 2x makes atan(2) ≈ 63.43° with the x-axis; the y-axis is at 90° ⟹ angle between = **26.57°**. **Angle with y = x (45°):** 63.43° − 45° = **18.43°**. **Verdict:** 26.57° ≠ 18.43° ⟹ the angles are **unequal** ⟹ y = 2x is **not** a bisector — refuted. **What the true bisector is:** the wedge between 90° and 45° has its bisector at 67.5° ⟹ slope tan(67.5°) = 1 + √2 ≈ 2.414, not 2. **Deep point:** the definition (equal angles) is the ultimate court — the tangent test compares against 45° for *labelled* bisectors, but the equal-angle check works even for vertical arms where slopes fail; when a claim is refuted, the definition shows what the true answer must be.

**NEB-style (6m): The line y = 2x is claimed to be a bisector of the angle between x = 0 and y = x. Verify or refute using the tangent test.** — **Slopes:** candidate m_b = 2; arms m₁ = ∞ (the y-axis, vertical) and m₂ = 1. **Angle with the vertical arm (via axis angles):** y = 2x makes atan(2) ≈ 63.43° with the x-axis; the y-axis is at 90° ⟹ angle between = **26.57°**. **Angle with y = x (45°):** 63.43° − 45° = **18.43°**. **Verdict:** 26.57° ≠ 18.43° ⟹ the angles are **unequal** ⟹ y = 2x is **not** a bisector — refuted. **What the true bisector is:** the wedge between 90° and 45° has its bisector at 67.5° ⟹ slope tan(67.5°) = 1 + √2 ≈ 2.414, not 2. **Deep point:** the definition (equal angles) is the ultimate court — the tangent test compares against 45° for *labelled* bisectors, but the equal-angle check works even for vertical arms where slopes fail; when a claim is refuted, the definition shows what the true answer must be.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Coordinates in Space, Distance and Direction Cosines

This canonical carries the **three-dimensional foundation**: points in space, the distance formula, direction cosines and direction ratios. Everything in space geometry — lines, planes, angles — is built from these three tools, and each is a direct descendant of its two-dimensional ancestor.

## 2. Theorem Mirror

- **Coordinates in space:** a point P is an ordered triple (x, y, z) — perpendicular distances from the three coordinate planes; eight octants partition space.
- **Distance formula:** d = √[(x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)² + (z₂−z₁)²] — Pythagoras applied twice (the diagonal of the box, then the space diagonal).
- **Direction cosines:** l = cos α, m = cos β, n = cos γ for a directed line's angles with the axes; **l² + m² + n² = 1** always.
- **Direction ratios:** any triple (a, b, c) proportional to (l, m, n); l = ±a/√(a²+b²+c²), and so on — the sign tracks direction, the magnitude only the line.
- **Section formula / midpoint:** ((mx₂+nx₁)/(m+n), …) — the 2D formula with a third passenger.

## 3. Deep Conceptual — Direction Cosines Are a Unit Vector Read Componentwise

- The triple (l, m, n) is **exactly the unit vector** along the line: cosines of the axis angles are the components of û = (cos α, cos β, cos γ), and l² + m² + n² = 1 is the statement |û| = 1. The identity is not a formula to memorise but the Pythagorean theorem on the unit vector.
- **Ratios vs cosines:** direction ratios (a, b, c) are any vector along the line — unnormalised; dividing by the magnitude produces the cosines. The ± ambiguity in l = ±a/√(…) is real: a line (undirected) has two cosine triples, opposite in sign; a *directed* line has one.
- **The angle between two lines:** cos θ = |l₁l₂ + m₁m₂ + n₂n₁| — the dot product of unit vectors; perpendicularity is the vanishing of the dot product, parallelism the proportionality of the triples.

## 4. Deep Conceptual — Distance in Space Is Pythagoras Iterated

- The space diagonal formula is **two applications of Pythagoras**: first in the base plane (√[(x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²]), then in the vertical plane containing that diagonal and the z-difference. Three squared differences, one square root — the pattern extends to any dimension, which is why the formula "looks the same" in n dimensions.
- **The box picture:** every distance computation is the space diagonal of a rectangular box with edges Δx, Δy, Δz — drawing the box converts the formula into a visible diagonal and makes the two-step Pythagoras derivation instant.

## 5. Worked Example Types

- **Type A — distance and midpoint:** three-coordinate arithmetic, box picture as a check.
- **Type B — cosines from ratios:** normalise (a, b, c), attach ±, verify l²+m²+n² = 1.
- **Type C — angles between lines:** dot product of normalised triples.
- **Type D — section formula:** internal/external division in space.

## 6. Common Confusions

**"Direction cosines are unique":** a line has two triples (±); only a directed ray has one. **"Ratios must satisfy l²+m²+n² = 1":** that identity belongs to cosines; ratios satisfy it only after normalisation.

notes: Question 5 (a)

Problem: Find the equations of the bisectors of the angles between the lines containing the origin in each of the following cases:
i) $4x - 3y + 1 = 0$ and $12x - 5y + 7 = 0$
ii) $7x - y + 11 = 0$ and $x + y - 15 = 0$
Prove that the bisectors of the angles are at right angles to each other.
Formula: The equations of the bisectors of the angles between two lines $a_1x+b_1y+c_1=0$ and $a_2x+b_2y+c_2=0$ are given by:
To find the bisector containing the origin, first make the constant terms $c_1$ and $c_2$ positive. The bisector containing the origin takes the positive (+) sign.
Solution for i):
Both constant terms ($+1$ and $+7$) are already positive.
Taking the positive sign (bisector containing the origin):
The other bisector (not containing the origin) uses the negative sign:
Perpendicularity Proof:
Slope of first bisector $(m_1) = -\frac{4}{7}$
Slope of second bisector $(m_2) = -\frac{7}{-4} = \frac{7}{4}$
$$m_1 \times m_2 = \left(-\frac{4}{7}\right) \times \left(\frac{7}{4}\right) = -1 \text{ (Hence, they are at right angles).}$$
Solution for ii):
First, rewrite the second equation to make the constant positive: $-x - y + 15 = 0$.
Since $\sqrt{50}=5\sqrt{2}$:
The other bisector (using the negative sign):
Perpendicularity Proof: Slope of $3x+y-16=0$ is $-3$. Slope of $x-3y+43=0$ is $\frac{1}{3}$.
$$(-3) \times \frac{1}{3} = -1 \text{ (Hence, they are at right angles).}$$
Question 5 (b)

Problem: Find the equations of the bisectors of the acute angle between each of the following pairs of lines:
i) $y = x$ and $y = 7x + 4$
ii) $x + 2y - 5 = 0$ and $4x + 2y + 9 = 0$
Solution for i):
Rearrange equations to $x - y = 0$ and $7x - y + 4 = 0$. Make constants positive (already positive or zero).
examples: Application of Geometry 9-1
practiceQuestions: Q1. **NEB-style (5m):** Find the equations of the bisectors of the angles between the coordinate axes x = 0 and y = 0. **Solution.** Standardised forms: $x=0$ (i.e. $1\cdot x+0\cdot y+0=0$) and $y=0$; normalisers both 1. Bisectors: $x=\pm y$ ⟹ $y=x$ and $y=-x$ - the two 45-degree lines through the origin, perpendicular as required. Deep point: the coordinate axes are the bisector machinery's simplest input - equal normalisers, zero constants, and the answer's symmetry is visible before any algebra.

Q2. **NEB-style (6m):** Find the bisector of the angle between 4x + 3y - 12 = 0 and 3x + 4y - 6 = 0 that contains the origin. **Solution.** Standardise: L$_1$ as $-4x-3y+12=0$, L$_2$ as $-3x-4y+6=0$ (both constants positive). Normalisers both 5. (+) bisector: $-4x-3y+12=-3x-4y+6$ ⟹ $-x+y+6=0$, i.e. $y=x-6$. Origin's wedge: (0,0) gives $+\frac{12}5$ and $+\frac65$ - both positive, the same-signed region ⟹ the (+) bisector $y=x-6$ bisects the origin's angle. Deep point: with constants positive the origin is automatically on the (+) side of both lines - the selection is the convention's corollary, not a new computation.

Q3. **NEB-style (6m):** Verify that the point (3, -3) on the bisector y = -x is equidistant from the axes x = 0 and y = 0. **Solution.** Distance to x = 0 (the y-axis): $|3|=3$. Distance to y = 0 (the x-axis): $|-3|=3$ ✓ equal. The point lies on $y=-x$: $-3=-3$ ✓. Deep point: equidistance from the axes is exactly $|x|=|y|$ - the bisector equations $y=\pm x$ are that condition written as lines; the definition and the equations are the same statement.

Q4. **NEB-style (5m):** Show that the bisectors y = x and y = -x of the coordinate axes are perpendicular. **Solution.** Slopes 1 and $-1$ ⟹ product $-1$ ⟹ perpendicular ✓. In general: the two bisectors of any pair of intersecting lines are perpendicular - algebraically the normalised coefficients' cross terms cancel in the dot product; geometrically the two half-angles (acute and obtuse sides) are complementary. Deep point: the perpendicularity is the bisector system's invariant - it holds for every pair, which is what makes it a falsification test for computed bisectors.

Q5. **NEB-style (6m):** For the lines x + 2y - 5 = 0 and 4x + 2y + 9 = 0, determine which bisector is acute without computing the bisectors, then verify with the tangent test on 6x + 6y - 1 = 0. **Solution.** Standardise L$_1$ as $-x-2y+5=0$; rule: $a_1a_2+b_1b_2=(-1)(4)+(-2)(2)=-8<0$ ⟹ the (+) bisector is acute. Compute (+): $\frac{-x-2y+5}{\sqrt5}=\frac{4x+2y+9}{2\sqrt5}$ ⟹ $2(-x-2y+5)=4x+2y+9$ ⟹ $6x+6y-1=0$. Tangent test: bisector slope $-1$, L$_1$ slope $-\frac12$: $\tan\theta=\frac{|-1+\frac12|}{1+\frac12}=\frac13<1$ ⟹ acute ✓ - algebra and geometry agree. Deep point: the rule classifies cheaply, the tangent test certifies independently - dual-channel agreement is the standard of proof.

Q6. **NEB-style (6m):** Find the bisectors of the lines 3x + y = 7 and x - 3y = 1, and explain the shape of the answer. **Solution.** Standardise: L$_1$: $-3x-y+7=0$; L$_2$: $-x+3y-1=0$ has $c=-1<0$ ⟹ rewrite $x-3y+1=0$. Normalisers $\sqrt{10}$ and $\sqrt{10}$ - equal. Skeleton: $-3x-y+7=\pm(x-3y+1)$. (+): $-3x-y+7=x-3y+1$ ⟹ $-4x+2y+6=0$ ⟹ $2x-y-3=0$. (-): $-3x-y+7=-x+3y-1$ ⟹ $-2x-4y+8=0$ ⟹ $x+2y-4=0$. Shape: slopes 2 and $-\frac12$ ⟹ product $-1$ ✓ perpendicular; the lines' slopes $-3$ and $\frac13$ are negative reciprocals - the original pair is perpendicular, so its bisectors sit at 45 degrees to each line. Deep point: when the original lines are perpendicular ($a_1a_2+b_1b_2=0$), the acute/obtuse distinction dissolves and both bisectors bisect right angles - the classification step retires.

Q7. **NEB-style (6m):** A circle is inscribed in the angle formed by 3x + 4y - 5 = 0 and 4x - 3y + 10 = 0 with centre on the internal bisector through the origin's side. Find the bisector line the centre lies on. **Solution.** Standardise: L$_1$: $-3x-4y+5=0$; L$_2$: $4x-3y+10=0$ ($c=10>0$). Normalisers 5 and 5. (+) bisector: $-3x-4y+5=4x-3y+10$ ⟹ $-7x-y+5=0$ ⟹ $7x+y-5=0$. Origin check: (0,0) gives $+\frac55$ and $+\frac{10}5$ - both positive ⟹ the (+) bisector $7x+y-5=0$ is the origin-side (internal, for this wedge) bisector; an inscribed circle's centre lies on it. Deep point: the in-centre application is the bisector's purpose - equal distances to both arms is exactly the circle's tangency condition, which is why bisector loci and incircles are the same geometry.

data.topicTitle: Limits and continuity: limits of a function, indeterminate forms, algebraic properties of limits (without proof), basic theorems on limits of algebraic, trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Limits as a System

This canonical consolidates the **limit of a function**, the **indeterminate forms**, and the **algebraic properties of limits** — the operating system every later technique runs on.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 The definition, restated

- **lim_{x→a} f(x) = L** ⟺ f(x) can be made arbitrarily close to L by taking x sufficiently close to a (x ≠ a). The limit is about the **neighbourhood**, not the point.

### 2.2 The indeterminate forms

- **0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞, ∞ − ∞, 1^∞, 0⁰, ∞⁰** — seven forms where substitution fails and transformation is mandatory. Each is a *shape*, not a value: 0/0 candidates can converge to anything (x/x → 1; x²/x² → 1; x·0 forms vary).
- **Determinate outcomes:** c/0⁺ → +∞, c/0⁻ → −∞ (c ≠ 0), 0/∞ → 0, ∞/c → ∞ — these need no transformation.

### 2.3 The algebraic properties (theorems)

- If lim f = L and lim g = M (both finite): **sum:** lim (f+g) = L + M; **product:** lim fg = LM; **quotient:** lim f/g = L/M (M ≠ 0); **constant multiple:** lim cf = cL; **power:** lim fⁿ = Lⁿ.
- **Root property:** lim ⁿ√f = ⁿ√L (L ≥ 0 for even n).
- **Sandwich (squeeze) theorem:** g ≤ f ≤ h with lim g = lim h = L ⟹ lim f = L.
- **Composition:** lim_{x→a} f(g(x)) = f(lim_{x→a} g(x)) when f is continuous at the inner limit.

### 2.4 The method ladder

- Substitution → factor/conjugate (0/0) → degree comparison (∞/∞) → standard limits → squeeze. Properties justify every step: splitting a fraction into factors is the product theorem; steering through u is the composition theorem.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Limit** | Neighbourhood approach value | x → 2 behaviour |
| **Indeterminate form** | Shape needing transformation | 0/0 |
| **Limit theorems** | Sum/product/quotient rules | split and multiply |
| **Squeeze theorem** | Bounded between convergent pair | sin x/x proof |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why indeterminate ≠ undefined

- 0/0 is *undetermined*, not *nonexistent*: the neighbourhood values may conspire toward any number, ∞, or nothing. The form is a flag to investigate, not a verdict.

### 4.2 The theorems as a licence system

- Splitting (x²−4)/(x−2) into (x+2)·(x−2)/(x−2) uses the product theorem — but only after each factor's limit exists. The theorems have hypotheses; the licence metaphor keeps them visible.

### 4.3 Squeeze as the endgame

- When algebra cannot isolate the value (oscillating factors), bounding does. The squeeze theorem is the only property that works without an explicit formula for f.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Forms triage**

| Form | Meaning | First tool |
|---|---|---|
| 0/0 | shared zero | factor/conjugate |
| ∞/∞ | race of growths | degree comparison |
| ∞ − ∞ | difference of giants | conjugate/combine |
| 1^∞ | power tug | bridge e^{lim uv} |
| c/0 | determinate | ±∞ by sign |

## 6. Common Confusions

**lim f = L does not need f(a) = L:** the point is excluded — that is why 0/0 limits exist at all.
**Splitting without existence:** the product theorem fails if a factor's limit DNE — regroup before splitting.
**c/0 is not indeterminate:** it is determinately infinite (with sign from the side); only 0/0 needs work.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB 2023 (verified PYQ): Find lim_{x→2} (x² − 4)/(x − 2). (2m)** — **Substitute:** (4 − 4)/0 = **0/0** ⟹ transform. **Factor:** x² − 4 = (x − 2)(x + 2); cancel (x ≠ 2 licensed): x + 2. **Substitute:** 2 + 2 = **4**. (Cross-check via the star (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) → naⁿ⁻¹: 2·2 = 4 ✓.)

**NEB-style (2m): State the seven indeterminate forms and show that 0/0 has no fixed value.** — The forms: **0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞, ∞ − ∞, 1^∞, 0⁰, ∞⁰**. **No fixed value:** (x² − 4)/(x − 2) → 4; (x³ − 8)/(x − 2) → 12; (x − 2)²/(x − 2) → 0; (x − 2)/(x − 2)² → ∞ — all are 0/0 at x = 2 yet converge differently ⟹ the form alone determines nothing; the specific functions decide.

**NEB-style (3m): Prove the product rule for limits: if lim_{x→a} f = L and lim_{x→a} g = M (finite), then lim_{x→a} f·g = LM.** — Write f = L + α, g = M + β where α, β → 0 (this is what the limits mean). Then fg = LM + Lβ + Mα + αβ, so |fg − LM| ≤ |L||β| + |M||α| + |α||β|. Given ε > 0, choose δ so that |α|, |β| < min(1, ε/(3(|L|+1)), ε/(3(|M|+1))); then |fg − LM| < ε. Hence lim fg = LM ∎ — the decomposition f = L + (f − L) is the standard trick that turns limit theorems into algebra.

## 8. Deep Conceptual — The Theorems Do Not Reverse

- **The converses fail:** lim (f + g) can exist while lim f and lim g do not — take f = |x|/x (sides ±1) and g = −|x|/x: the sum is 0 everywhere, yet neither piece has a limit at 0. Similarly lim fg can exist with neither factor converging (f = g = the Dirichlet-style oscillator: product of two wild functions can be tame).
- **Why this matters:** the limit theorems are **one-way licences** — they certify the limit of a combination from the limits of the parts, never the reverse. Diagnosing "why can't I split this limit?" is precisely the skill of citing hypotheses.
- **Squeeze is the only non-algebraic property:** it needs no formula for f, only bounds — which is why it is the tool of last resort for oscillating integrands.

## 9. Deep Conceptual — Epsilon–Delta for the Working Student

- **Proving lim_{x→a} f(x) = L by ε–δ** is a recipe: (1) simplify |f(x) − L| algebraically; (2) factor out |x − a|; (3) bound the leftover factor on a preliminary window (say |x − a| < 1); (4) choose δ = min(1, ε/bound).
- **The preliminary window is the whole trick:** it converts an unknown factor into a constant, making δ computable. This is the same "restrict then divide" move used in every first-principles derivative proof.
- **Disproving a limit:** exhibit one ε > 0 for which **no** δ works — typically by finding two sequences approaching a whose images converge to different values (the sequential test in ε-clothing).

## 10. Deep Conceptual — Indeterminate Forms as Dimensional Analysis

- Each form encodes a **race between two rates**: 0/0 is "which vanishes faster", ∞/∞ is "which grows faster", 0·∞ is "collapse versus explosion", 1^∞ is "approach to 1 versus unbounded exponent". The answer is always decided by the **relative rates**, never the individual behaviours.
- This is why the same algebraic trick (factoring out the dominant term) resolves both 0/0 and ∞/∞: in both cases you isolate the race's deciding factor and let the rest collapse to 1 or 0.
- **Exam instinct:** name the race, identify the two contestants, compare their orders (degree, exponent, logarithm) — the form's species tells you which comparison to run.

practiceQuestions: **NEB 2023 (verified PYQ): Find lim_{x→2} (x² − 4)/(x − 2). (2m)** — **Substitute:** (2² − 4)/(2 − 2) = 0/0 — **indeterminate** ⟹ transform. **Factor:** x² − 4 = (x − 2)(x + 2) (difference of squares), so (x² − 4)/(x − 2) = **x + 2 for x ≠ 2** — the cancellation is licensed on the punctured neighbourhood. **Substitute:** 2 + 2 = **4**. **Cross-check:** the algebraic star lim_{x→a} (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = naⁿ⁻¹ with n = 2, a = 2 gives 2·2¹ = 4 ✓. The two routes agree — the star *is* the factoring method compressed.

**NEB-style (2m): State the seven indeterminate forms and demonstrate that the 0/0 form has no fixed value.** — **The seven forms:** 0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞, ∞ − ∞, 1^∞, 0⁰, ∞⁰ — each names a *shape* of failure, not a value. **Demonstration:** at x = 2, all four of these are 0/0: (x² − 4)/(x − 2) → **4**; (x³ − 8)/(x − 2) → **12**; (x − 2)²/(x − 2) → **0**; (x − 2)/(x − 2)² → **∞**. Same form, four different outcomes ⟹ the form is a *flag to transform*, never an answer. **Contrast:** c/0 (c ≠ 0) is **determinate** — the quotient grows without bound, sign depending on the side — and needs no transformation, only a sign analysis.

**NEB-style (3m): Prove the product rule: if lim_{x→a} f(x) = L and lim_{x→a} g(x) = M (both finite), then lim_{x→a} f(x)g(x) = LM.** — **Decomposition:** write f = L + α and g = M + β, where α = f − L → 0 and β = g − M → 0 as x → a — this is precisely what the two limits assert. **Expand:** fg = (L + α)(M + β) = **LM + Lβ + Mα + αβ**, so |fg − LM| ≤ |L|·|β| + |M|·|α| + |α|·|β|. **Epsilon bookkeeping:** given ε > 0, choose δ so that for |x − a| < δ: |α| < 1 and |α| < ε/(3(|M|+1)), and |β| < ε/(3(|L|+1)). Then |fg − LM| ≤ |L|·ε/(3(|L|+1)) + |M|·ε/(3(|M|+1)) + 1·ε/3 < ε/3 + ε/3 + ε/3 = ε. **Conclusion:** lim fg = LM ∎. The decomposition f = L + (f − L) — "the limit plus a vanishing error" — is the master trick behind every limit theorem.

**NEB-style (5m): Using the ε–δ definition, prove that lim_{x→3} (2x − 5) = 1.** — **Setup:** given ε > 0, we must find δ > 0 such that 0 < |x − 3| < δ ⟹ |(2x − 5) − 1| < ε. **Simplify the target:** |(2x − 5) − 1| = |2x − 6| = **2|x − 3|** — the error is exactly twice the input distance. **Choose δ:** take **δ = ε/2**. Then |x − 3| < δ ⟹ |2x − 6| = 2|x − 3| < 2·(ε/2) = ε ✓. **Conclusion:** lim_{x→3} (2x − 5) = 1 ∎. **Conceptual reading:** for linear functions the error is a *constant multiple* of the input distance, so δ = ε/slope works exactly — no preliminary window needed. The slope 2 is, of course, the derivative — ε–δ for linear functions is the derivative wearing a formal costume.

**NEB-style (5m): Using the ε–δ definition, prove that lim_{x→2} x² = 4.** — **Setup:** given ε > 0, find δ > 0 with |x − 2| < δ ⟹ |x² − 4| < ε. **Factor:** |x² − 4| = |x + 2|·|x − 2| — the unwanted factor |x + 2| must be tamed. **Preliminary window:** restrict |x − 2| < 1, i.e. 1 < x < 3, so |x + 2| < 5. Then |x² − 4| < 5|x − 2|. **Choose δ = min(1, ε/5):** then |x − 2| < δ forces both the window and |x² − 4| < 5·(ε/5) = ε ✓. **Conclusion:** lim_{x→2} x² = 4 ∎. **Deep point:** the preliminary window converts the *unknown* factor |x + 2| into the *constant* 5 — the universal trick for every nonlinear ε–δ proof, and the reason δ is a min(), never a bare formula.

**NEB-style (6m): For f(x) = x + 1 (x < 2), f(2) = 5, f(x) = 8 − x (x > 2): find LHL, RHL, decide whether lim_{x→2} f(x) exists, and discuss continuity.** — **Left-hand limit** (left branch): lim_{x→2⁻} (x + 1) = **3**. **Right-hand limit** (right branch): lim_{x→2⁺} (8 − x) = **6**. **Existence verdict:** the two sides are finite but **3 ≠ 6** ⟹ the two-sided limit **does not exist** — f has a **jump discontinuity** at x = 2 with jump size 6 − 3 = 3. **Continuity analysis:** f(2) = 5 equals neither side ⟹ f is continuous at 2 from neither side; changing f(2) cannot help (it can match at most one branch). **Deep conceptual point:** the assigned value f(2) = 5 is a *third independent claim* — here it disagrees with both sides, producing a graph with a **floating dot** at (2, 5) suspended between the two rays. The existence of a limit is a property of the **neighbourhoods**; the value of f(a) is a property of the **point** — continuity demands all three agree, and this example breaks all three pairwise agreements at once.

**NEB-style (5m): Use the squeeze theorem to evaluate lim_{x→0} x² cos(1/x²), and explain why no algebraic method can resolve it.** — **The obstacle:** cos(1/x²) oscillates infinitely fast near 0 (its argument → ∞), so it has no limit and no standard-limit steering applies — algebra is powerless. **The bounds:** −1 ≤ cos(1/x²) ≤ 1 for every x ≠ 0; multiplying by the non-negative x²: **−x² ≤ x² cos(1/x²) ≤ x²**. **The squeeze:** both bounds → 0 as x → 0, so by the squeeze theorem the limit is **0**. **Deep conceptual point:** the squeeze theorem is the *only* property that works without an explicit formula for the limit — it replaces computation with **bounding**. The factor x² is a *damping coefficient*: wild oscillation squeezed between vanishing walls must itself vanish. The same pattern certifies continuity of x² sin(1/x) at 0 and underlies every "bounded times vanishing" argument in analysis.

| 0/0 | shared zero | factor/conjugate |
| ∞/∞ | race of growths | degree comparison |
| ∞ − ∞ | difference of giants | conjugate/combine |
| 1^∞ | power tug | bridge e^{lim uv} |
| c/0 | determinate | ±∞ by sign |

## 6. Common Confusions

**lim f = L does not need f(a) = L:** the point is excluded — that is why 0/0 limits exist at all.
**Splitting without existence:** the product theorem fails if a factor's limit DNE — regroup before splitting.
**c/0 is not indeterminate:** it is determinately infinite (with sign from the side); only 0/0 needs work.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB 2023 (verified PYQ): Find lim_{x→2} (x² − 4)/(x − 2). (2m)** — **Substitute:** (4 − 4)/0 = **0/0** ⟹ transform. **Factor:** x² − 4 = (x − 2)(x + 2); cancel (x ≠ 2 licensed): x + 2. **Substitute:** 2 + 2 = **4**. (Cross-check via the star (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) → naⁿ⁻¹: 2·2 = 4 ✓.)

**NEB-style (2m): State the seven indeterminate forms and show that 0/0 has no fixed value.** — The forms: **0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞, ∞ − ∞, 1^∞, 0⁰, ∞⁰**. **No fixed value:** (x² − 4)/(x − 2) → 4; (x³ − 8)/(x − 2) → 12; (x − 2)²/(x − 2) → 0; (x − 2)/(x − 2)² → ∞ — all are 0/0 at x = 2 yet converge differently ⟹ the form alone determines nothing; the specific functions decide.

**NEB-style (3m): Prove the product rule for limits: if lim_{x→a} f = L and lim_{x→a} g = M (finite), then lim_{x→a} f·g = LM.** — Write f = L + α, g = M + β where α, β → 0 (this is what the limits mean). Then fg = LM + Lβ + Mα + αβ, so |fg − LM| ≤ |L||β| + |M||α| + |α||β|. Given ε > 0, choose δ so that |α|, |β| < min(1, ε/(3(|L|+1)), ε/(3(|M|+1))); then |fg − LM| < ε. Hence lim fg = LM ∎ — the decomposition f = L + (f − L) is the standard trick that turns limit theorems into algebra.

## 8. Deep Conceptual — The Theorems Do Not Reverse

- **The converses fail:** lim (f + g) can exist while lim f and lim g do not — take f = |x|/x (sides ±1) and g = −|x|/x: the sum is 0 everywhere, yet neither piece has a limit at 0. Similarly lim fg can exist with neither factor converging (f = g = the Dirichlet-style oscillator: product of two wild functions can be tame).
- **Why this matters:** the limit theorems are **one-way licences** — they certify the limit of a combination from the limits of the parts, never the reverse. Diagnosing "why can't I split this limit?" is precisely the skill of citing hypotheses.
- **Squeeze is the only non-algebraic property:** it needs no formula for f, only bounds — which is why it is the tool of last resort for oscillating integrands.

## 9. Deep Conceptual — Epsilon–Delta for the Working Student

- **Proving lim_{x→a} f(x) = L by ε–δ** is a recipe: (1) simplify |f(x) − L| algebraically; (2) factor out |x − a|; (3) bound the leftover factor on a preliminary window (say |x − a| < 1); (4) choose δ = min(1, ε/bound).
- **The preliminary window is the whole trick:** it converts an unknown factor into a constant, making δ computable. This is the same "restrict then divide" move used in every first-principles derivative proof.
- **Disproving a limit:** exhibit one ε > 0 for which **no** δ works — typically by finding two sequences approaching a whose images converge to different values (the sequential test in ε-clothing).

## 10. Deep Conceptual — Indeterminate Forms as Dimensional Analysis

- Each form encodes a **race between two rates**: 0/0 is "which vanishes faster", ∞/∞ is "which grows faster", 0·∞ is "collapse versus explosion", 1^∞ is "approach to 1 versus unbounded exponent". The answer is always decided by the **relative rates**, never the individual behaviours.
- This is why the same algebraic trick (factoring out the dominant term) resolves both 0/0 and ∞/∞: in both cases you isolate the race's deciding factor and let the rest collapse to 1 or 0.
- **Exam instinct:** name the race, identify the two contestants, compare their orders (degree, exponent, logarithm) — the form's species tells you which comparison to run.

Squeeze theorem: g <= f <= h with common limit L => lim f = L. Composition theorem: f continuous at inner limit => lim f(g(x)) = f(lim g(x)). Method ladder: substitute -> factor/conjugate -> degree comparison -> standard limits -> squeeze.
