data.title: Right Hand Limit
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Approaching From the Right

The **right-hand limit** lim_{x→a⁺} f(x) reads the function's behaviour as x slides toward a from values **greater** than a. Piecewise functions, domain edges and blow-ups make one-sided thinking unavoidable.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Definition

- **lim_{x→a⁺} f(x) = L** ⟺ f(x) → L as x takes values **a < x < a + δ** with δ → 0 — from the right side of a on the number line.
- Graphically: follow the curve toward x = a moving **leftward** (from larger x); the y-height approached is L.

### 2.2 When the right-hand limit is the whole story

- **Domain edge:** √x at 0 exists only from the right (x ≥ 0) — lim_{x→0⁺} √x = 0 and no left approach is even defined.
- **Piecewise boundary:** on [a, ∞) pieces, a⁺ reads the branch that owns the right neighbourhood.

### 2.3 Computation

- Substitute a value slightly greater than a into the **branch/rule governing the right side**; for blow-ups, track the sign of the denominator for x > a.

### 2.4 The existence theorem (preview)

- lim_{x→a} f(x) = L ⟺ **both** one-sided limits exist and equal L. One-sided limits are the atoms; two-sided limits are molecules.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Right-hand limit** | Approach from x > a | lim_{x→0⁺} √x = 0 |
| **Domain edge** | a at the boundary of the domain | √x at 0 |
| **Blow-up side** | Sign of denominator for x > a | 1/(x−2)⁺ → +∞ |
| **Existence theorem** | Both sides must agree | fails for 1/x |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why one side at a time

- Functions may behave differently on either side of a — different branch formulas, different signs, different rates. One-sided limits isolate each story before the existence test merges them.

### 4.2 Reading the graph right-to-left

- The finger traces the curve from the right toward a: the height it settles toward is lim_{x→a⁺}. Open dots, jumps and asymptotes all become readable.

### 4.3 Blow-up signs

- For 1/(x − 2): x > 2 ⟹ denominator positive ⟹ +∞; the right-hand limit is +∞ while the left is −∞ — sign bookkeeping done side by side.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Right-hand limit scenarios**

| Case at a | Right-hand behaviour |
|---|---|
| continuous | equals f(a) |
| piecewise branch | that branch's value approached |
| domain edge | only side that exists |
| c/0 with positive side | +∞ |

## 6. Common Confusions

**a⁺ means x > a:** the plus is about *where x comes from*, not the sign of the limit.
**Domain edges are one-sided by nature:** √x at 0 has no left-hand limit because the left side isn't in the domain — not because it disagrees.
**∞ on one side still kills the two-sided limit:** the existence theorem needs finite agreement.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (2m): Evaluate lim_{x→2⁺} 1/(x − 2).** — For x slightly greater than 2, x − 2 is **positive and small** ⟹ 1/(x−2) is large positive: **lim = +∞**. (The left-hand limit would be −∞ — the sides disagree, so the two-sided limit does not exist.)

**NEB-style (2m): For f(x) = { x + 1 if x < 2; x² if x ≥ 2 }, evaluate lim_{x→2⁺} f(x).** — The right neighbourhood x > 2 belongs to the **second branch**: lim_{x→2⁺} x² = **4**. (The left-hand limit via the first branch is 3 — the mismatch at 2 is a jump discontinuity of size 1.)

**NEB-style (2m): Evaluate lim_{x→0⁺} √x and explain why no left-hand limit exists.** — √x is defined for x ≥ 0; approaching 0 from the right: √x → **0**. notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Approaching From the Left

The mirror of the right-hand limit: **lim_{x→a⁻} f(x)** reads behaviour as x approaches a through values **less** than a. Together with a⁺ it completes the one-sided pair whose agreement (or disagreement) decides every two-sided question.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Definition

- **lim_{x→a⁻} f(x) = L** ⟺ f(x) → L as x runs through **a − δ < x < a** — from the left of a.
- Graphically: trace the curve toward a moving **rightward** (from smaller x).

### 2.2 Computation

- Use the **branch governing the left neighbourhood** (piecewise); for blow-ups, the **sign of the denominator for x < a** decides ±∞.
- Example: 1/(x−2) as x → 2⁻: denominator negative-small ⟹ **−∞**.

### 2.3 The pair in action

- **Existence theorem:** lim_{x→a} f(x) = L ⟺ LHL = RHL = L. Disagreement ⟹ DNE (jump or blow-up).
- **Jump size:** RHL − LHL measures the step at a jump discontinuity.

### 2.4 Left-side-only cases

- Functions like √(−x) or log(x) at domain edges may have only a left-hand limit; the missing side is a domain fact, not a value disagreement.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Left-hand limit** | Approach from x < a | lim_{x→2⁻} 1/(x−2) = −∞ |
| **Jump size** | RHL − LHL at a jump | 4 − 3 = 1 |
| **Existence test** | LHL = RHL required | fails at jumps |
| **Domain edge (left)** | Only the left approach exists | log x at 0⁺... at 0 |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 The left branch rule

- Piecewise definitions assign each side its formula; the left-hand limit always consults the branch whose interval **ends at a from below**. Boundary ownership (≤ vs <) matters for f(a), not for the limit — limits ignore the point.

### 4.2 Blow-up bookkeeping from the left

- For x < a, x − a < 0: odd-power denominators give −∞, even powers +∞. The multiplicity of the zero (odd/even) is the whole sign story.

### 4.3 Disagreement taxonomy

- LHL ≠ RHL (both finite) ⟹ **jump**; one side infinite ⟹ **infinite discontinuity**; both infinite, opposite signs ⟹ the two-sided limit DNE with a "split asymptote".

## 5. Comparison Tables

**The one-sided pair at work**

| LHL | RHL | Verdict at a |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 3 | continuous (if f(a) = 3) |
| 3 | 4 | jump, DNE two-sided |
| −∞ | +∞ | split asymptote, DNE |
| 0 | — | domain edge (left only) |

## 6. Common Confusions

**a⁻ means x < a:** the minus locates the approach side, not the limit's sign.

data.title: Existence of Limit (LHL = RHL)
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — When Both Sides Must Agree

**Existence of a limit** is the theorem that merges the one-sided atoms: lim_{x→a} f(x) = L ⟺ LHL = RHL = L. This topic works the theorem in both directions — building limits from agreement and detecting DNE from disagreement.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 The existence theorem

- **Theorem:** lim_{x→a} f(x) = L **if and only if** lim_{x→a⁻} f(x) = lim_{x→a⁺} f(x) = L (finite).
- Both directions matter: agreement ⟹ existence; existence ⟹ agreement. One infinite side, or unequal finite sides, ⟹ **DNE**.

### 2.2 Modes of non-existence

- **Jump:** LHL ≠ RHL, both finite (piecewise mismatch).
- **Split asymptote:** sides infinite with opposite signs (1/x at 0).
- **Unified blow-up:** both sides +∞ (1/x²) — still **no (finite) limit**; ∞ is behaviour, not a value.
- **Oscillation:** sin(1/x) near 0 never settles — sides exist in no sense; a genuinely wild DNE.

### 2.3 Working the theorem

- Protocol: compute LHL, compute RHL, compare. Equal (finite) ⟹ write the two-sided limit; unequal or infinite ⟹ DNE **with classification**.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): Discuss the existence of lim_{x→0} f(x) for f(x) = { x + 2 if x < 0; x² if x > 0 }.** — **LHL:** first branch: 0 + 2 = **2**. **RHL:** second branch: 0² = **0**. **Comparison:** 2 ≠ 0 ⟹ **the two-sided limit does not exist** — a jump discontinuity at 0 (f is not defined at 0 at all, but the limit question is independent of that). ## 1. Topic Introduction — The Limit Hall of Fame

**Standard limits** are the pre-computed results every other limit reduces to: lim sin x/x = 1, lim (1+x)^{1/x} = e, lim (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = naⁿ⁻¹, and their kin. Memorise the statements; understand the reductions.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 The trigonometric star

- **lim_{x→0} sin x/x = 1** (x in radians — the radian is what makes it true).
- **Companion:** lim_{x→0} tan x/x = 1; lim_{x→0} (1 − cos x)/x² = 1/2.

### 2.2 The exponential star

- **lim_{x→0} (1 + x)^{1/x} = e** and the twin **lim_{x→∞} (1 + 1/x)^x = e**.
- **lim_{x→0} (eˣ − 1)/x = 1** — the exponential's rate at 0, the seed of its derivative.
- **lim_{x→0} (aˣ − 1)/x = ln a** (general base).
- **lim_{x→0} ln(1 + x)/x = 1.**

### 2.3 The algebraic star

- **lim_{x→a} (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = n·aⁿ⁻¹** — valid for all rational n; the factorisation theorem wearing a limit.
- **lim_{x→0} (1 + x)ᵏ... ((1+x)ⁿ − 1)/x = n** — the binomial baby case.

### 2.4 Reduction discipline

- Any 0/0 candidate: try to rewrite into a standard form via substitution (u = g(x) → 0), algebraic identity, or multiplication by 1. The standard limits are the *targets* of every transformation.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Standard limit** | Pre-proved fundamental limit | sin x/x → 1 |
| **Reduction** | Rewriting to a standard form | substitute, factor, ×1 |
| **Radian requirement** | sin x/x = 1 holds in radians | degrees break it |
| **e** | lim (1+x)^{1/x} | the natural base |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why radians

- sin x/x → 1 is a *geometry* statement: arc length ≈ chord length for tiny angles — true only when x measures arc in radius units. Degrees smuggle in a factor π/180.

### 4.2 The (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) theorem as a bridge

- For integer n it is factoring; for general rational n it is the derivative of xⁿ at a in disguise — the standard limit that calculus will generalise.

### 4.3 e's double definition

- (1 + x)^{1/x} at 0 and (1 + 1/x)^x at ∞ are the same limit seen from the two ends of u = 1/x — compound interest's continuous limit.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**The standard limit shelf**

| Limit | Value | Domain of use |
|---|---|---|
| sin x/x (x→0) | 1 | radians |
| tan x/x (x→0) | 1 | via sin/cos |
| (1 − cos x)/x² | 1/2 | half-angle route |
| (eˣ − 1)/x | 1 | exponential rate |
| (aˣ − 1)/x | ln a | general base |
| ln(1+x)/x | 1 | log rate |
| (xⁿ−aⁿ)/(x−a) (x→a) | naⁿ⁻¹ | algebraic |
| (1+x)^{1/x} (x→0) | e | compound limit |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Degrees break sin x/x:** always check the angle unit; convert degrees to radians first.
**(1 − cos x)/x² = 1/2, not 1:** the half-angle identity sin²(x/2) = (1 − cos x)/2 supplies the factor.
**(aˣ − 1)/x → ln a:** specialising a = e gives 1; the general base keeps the ln a factor.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB 2022 (verified PYQ): lim_{x→0} (eˣ − 1)/x equals: (a) 0 (b) 1 (c) e (d) ∞ (1m)** — This is the **standard limit**: lim_{x→0} (eˣ − 1)/x = **1 → option (b)**. It is the definition of eˣ's instantaneous rate at 0 — the fact that makes (eˣ)′ = eˣ true.

**NEB 2024 (verified PYQ): Evaluate (i) lim_{x→0} (sin x − x cos x)/x³, (ii) lim_{x→0} (x − sin x)/x³. (4m)** — **(i)** Write (sin x − x cos x)/x³ = [sin x/x − cos x]/x². Now sin x/x → 1 and cos x → 1, giving 0/0 again — refine: sin x − x cos x = x[sin x/x − cos x]; using the standard-limit toolkit (sin x = x − x³/6 + ⋯, cos x = 1 − x²/2 + ⋯): sin x − x cos x = (x − x³/6) − x(1 − x²/2) = x − x³/6 − x + x³/2 = **x³/3**. **(i) = 1/3.** **(ii)** x − sin x = x − (x − x³/6) = **x³/6** ⟹ **(ii) = 1/6**. (Series route is the clean one; equivalently apply the standard limits twice with the compound-angle identity sin x − x cos x = x²·(sin x/x)′-type reductions.)

**NEB 2021 (verified PYQ): Evaluate lim_{x→2} (√(7+x) − 3)/(x − 2). (3m)** — 0/0 ⟹ **rationalise:** multiply by (√(7+x) + 3)/(√(7+x) + 3): numerator = (7 + x) − 9 = x − 2, cancelling the denominator (x ≠ 2): 1/(√(7+x) + 3). Limit: 1/(√9 + 3) = **1/6**. (Standard-limit thinking: the conjugate reduction is the root version of the (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) theorem with n = 1/2, a = 2: (1/2)·2^{−1/2} = 1/(2√2)... here the shifted form gives 1/6 — the rationalisation is the honest working.)

## 8. Deep Conceptual — Stars Are Tangent Approximations in Disguise

- Each standard limit is a statement that a complicated function **agrees with a simpler one to first order**: sin u ~ u says the sine curve hugs the line y = u near 0; eᵘ − 1 ~ u says the exponential hugs y = 1 + u; ln(1+u) ~ u says the log hugs y = u. The stars are a table of *local linearisations*.
- **Why radians are non-negotiable:** sin u ~ u is only true when u measures arc length — in degrees the mismatch factor π/180 breaks the star. The radian is the angle unit that makes the sine's slope at 0 equal 1; the star is that geometric fact written as a limit.
- **Composability:** stars compose with the substitution u = g(x) → 0 — sin(3x) ~ 3x, ln(1 + 5x) ~ 5x, e^{−2x} − 1 ~ −2x. One table, unlimited composites; the only care needed is that u genuinely → 0 at the point in question.

## 9. Deep Conceptual — Steering: Manufacturing the Star's Denominator

- The stars have fixed denominators (u, u², u³...), but exam expressions arrive with arbitrary denominators. **Steering** is the craft of multiplying by 1 — rewriting A/B as (A·k)/(B·k) to make the denominator match a star's form, then compensating with the constant.
- **The canonical steering:** to use sin u/u, force the denominator to be exactly the argument of the sine: (sin 5x)/x = 5·(sin 5x)/(5x) → 5·1 = 5. The inserted factor 5x is the star's demanded denominator; the outside 5 pays for it.
- **Higher-order stars decide close races:** when two contestants vanish at the same order (both ~ u), the ratio is a nonzero constant; when one is faster (u² vs u), the ratio is 0 or ∞. Knowing the *order* of each star — sin u ~ u (order 1), 1 − cos u ~ u²/2 (order 2), tan u − u ~ u³/3 (order 3) — tells you which tool resolves which expression before any algebra.

## 10. Deep Conceptual — The Hall of Fame as a Proof Network

- The stars are not independent facts: sin u/u → 1 plus the Pythagorean identity yields (1 − cos u)/u → 0; (eᵘ − 1)/u → 1 plus continuity yields ln(1+u)/u → 1 (inverse function); the compound star ((1+u)^{1/u} → e) is the *definition* of e wearing limit notation.
- **One star, many faces:** lim_{u→0} (1+u)^{1/u} = e is simultaneously the definition of e, the compound-interest limit, and the engine of every 1^∞ power form. Memorising it as three separate facts triples the memorisation and quarters the understanding.
- **Usage discipline:** every star application should be annotated — which star, what u is, why u → 0 (or → ∞ for the e forms). The annotation is the proof; the answer is just its last line.

- The stars are not independent facts: sin u/u → 1 plus the Pythagorean identity yields (1 − cos u)/u → 0; (eᵘ − 1)/u → 1 plus continuity yields ln(1+u)/u → 1 (inverse function); the compound star ((1+u)^{1/u} → e) is the *definition* of e wearing limit notation.
- **One star, many faces:** lim_{u→0} (1+u)^{1/u} = e is simultaneously the definition of e, the compound-interest limit, and the engine of every 1^∞ power form. Memorising it as three separate facts triples the memorisation and quarters the understanding.
- **Usage discipline:** every star application should be annotated — which star, what u is, why u → 0 (or → ∞ for the e forms). The annotation is the proof; the answer is just its last line.
keyPoints: Standard limits (x in radians): sin x/x -> 1; tan x/x -> 1; (1 - cos x)/x^2 -> 1/2; (e^x - 1)/x -> 1; (a^x - 1)/x -> ln a; ln(1+x)/x -> 1; (x^n - a^n)/(x - a) -> n a^(n-1) as x -> a; (1 + x)^(1/x) -> e as x -> 0; (1 + 1/x)^x -> e as x -> inf; ((1+x)^n - 1)/x -> n. Reduction discipline: substitute u -> 0, factor, multiply by 1 to reach a standard form. Radians are mandatory for the trig star. The algebraic star is the derivative of x^n at a in disguise.
importantConcepts: Standard limits are the targets of every transformation: reduce the unknown 0/0 to a known star by substitution, factoring, or multiplying by 1.
examples: ***The radian contract*** - sin x/x -> 1 is arc-versus-chord geometry, valid only in radians; degrees smuggle a pi/180 factor into every trig limit.
universalFacts: Compound interest converging to continuous compounding is (1 + 1/n)^n -> e - the exponential star discovered by bankers.
importantNotes: Verified PYQs: NEB 2022 ((e^x - 1)/x MCQ), NEB 2024 (sin x - x cos x and x - sin x over x^3), NEB 2021 (sqrt(7+x) - 3 over x - 2) - assigned to this row.
examShortTricks: 0/0: hunt for a standard form. Roots: conjugate. Trig: force sin u/u. Exponentials: force (e^u - 1)/u. Series fallback: x - sin x ~ x^3/6, sin x - x cos x ~ x^3/3.
examNotes: Quote the standard limit by name when using it - the citation is the method mark; keep radians explicit in trig limits.
formulas:
- lim_{x→0} sin x/x = 1; tan x/x = 1; (1 − cos x)/x² = 1/2
- lim_{x→0} (eˣ−1)/x = 1; (aˣ−1)/x = ln a; ln(1+x)/x = 1
- lim_{x→a} (xⁿ−aⁿ)/(x−a) = naⁿ⁻¹; lim_{x→0} (1+x)^{1/x} = e
- x − sin x ~ x³/6; sin x − x cos x ~ x³/3 (small x)
practice: State lim_{x→0} (eˣ − 1)/x and identify it as a standard limit.
Evaluate lim_{x→0} (sin x − x cos x)/x³ and lim_{x→0} (x − sin x)/x³.
Evaluate lim_{x→2} (√(7+x) − 3)/(x − 2).
practiceQuestions: **NEB 2022 (verified PYQ): lim_{x→0} (eˣ − 1)/x equals: (a) 0 (b) 1 (c) e (d) ∞ (1m)** — **Recognition:** this is the exponential standard limit: **lim_{x→0} (eˣ − 1)/x = 1 — option (b)**. **Why it is true:** eˣ = 1 + x + x²/2 + ⋯, so eˣ − 1 = x + x²/2 + ⋯ = x(1 + x/2 + ⋯), and dividing by x leaves 1 + x/2 + ⋯ → 1. **Significance:** this limit *is* the statement that eˣ has instantaneous rate 1 at x = 0 — the seed of (eˣ)′ = eˣ, the defining perk of the natural base. (For general base a, (aˣ − 1)/x → ln a; a = e gives ln e = 1.)

**NEB 2024 (verified PYQ): Evaluate (i) lim_{x→0} (sin x − x cos x)/x³ and (ii) lim_{x→0} (x − sin x)/x³. (4m)** — **Series route (small-x expansions, radians):** sin x = x − x³/6 + O(x⁵) and cos x = 1 − x²/2 + O(x⁴). **(i):** sin x − x cos x = (x − x³/6) − x(1 − x²/2) = x − x³/6 − x + x³/2 = x³(1/2 − 1/6) = **x³/3** ⟹ the limit is **1/3**. **(ii):** x − sin x = x − (x − x³/6) = **x³/6** ⟹ the limit is **1/6**. **Standard-limit cross-check for (ii):** x − sin x = x(1 − sin x/x); with sin x/x = 1 − x²/6 + ⋯ (from the half-angle identity 1 − sin x/x... equivalently the cubic term), 1 − sin x/x ~ x²/6, so x(1 − sin x/x)/x³ → 1/6 ✓. Both are higher-order refinements of sin x/x → 1: the leading x-terms cancel, exposing the cubic layer.

**NEB 2021 (verified PYQ): Evaluate lim_{x→2} (√(7+x) − 3)/(x − 2). (3m)** — **Substitution:** (√9 − 3)/0 = **0/0** ⟹ transform. **Rationalise:** multiply by the conjugate (√(7+x) + 3)/(√(7+x) + 3): numerator = (7 + x) − 9 = **x − 2**, which cancels the denominator (licensed for x ≠ 2): the expression becomes **1/(√(7+x) + 3)**. **Substitute:** 1/(√9 + 3) = **1/6**. **Connection:** this is the (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) standard limit with a fractional power — equivalently the derivative of √(7+x) at x = 2, which the chain rule will later confirm as 1/(2√9) = 1/6 ✓. The conjugate is the honest algebraic route before calculus tools are available.

**NEB-style (6m): Evaluate lim_{x→0} (sin 5x − tan 3x)/(2x) using standard limits, annotating each star used.** — **Split the quotient** (both pieces' limits exist — licensed): = lim (sin 5x)/(2x) − lim (tan 3x)/(2x). **First piece (star: sin u/u → 1, u = 5x → 0):** (sin 5x)/(2x) = (5/2)·(sin 5x)/(5x) → (5/2)·1 = **5/2** — the steering factor 5x was manufactured in the denominator, paid for by the outside 5/2. **Second piece (star: tan u/u → 1, u = 3x → 0):** (tan 3x)/(2x) = (3/2)·(tan 3x)/(3x) → (3/2)·1 = **3/2**. **Combine: 5/2 − 3/2 = 1.** **Deep point:** every term was steered to its star's exact denominator and the constant carried outside — the annotation (which star, which u) is the working; the arithmetic is bookkeeping. Note the answer is a clean difference of first-order coefficients, which is the general pattern for same-order contestants.

**NEB-style (6m): Evaluate lim_{x→0} (1 − cos 4x)/(x²) using the standard limit (1 − cos u)/u² → 1/2.** — **Match the star's form:** the star wants u² under (1 − cos u); here u = 4x, so u² = 16x². **Steer:** (1 − cos 4x)/(x²) = 16·(1 − cos 4x)/(16x²) = 16·(1 − cos 4x)/(4x)². **Apply the star** (u = 4x → 0): (1 − cos u)/u² → 1/2 ⟹ the limit = 16·(1/2) = **8**. **Cross-check via the first-order star:** (1 − cos 4x)/(4x) → 0 shows the numerator vanishes faster than x — consistent with the contest being decided at second order, where the u²/2 star operates ✓. **Deep point:** the steering factor is the *square* of the argument's coefficient (16 = 4²) because the star's denominator is quadratic — matching orders of vanishing means matching powers of the steering factor.

**NEB-style (5m): Evaluate lim_{x→∞} (1 + 3/x)^{x}, citing the compound star.** — **Recognise the form:** base → 1, exponent → ∞ — the **1^∞ species**, home of the compound star. **Reshape to the star's exact form:** (1 + 3/x)^{x} = [(1 + 3/x)^{x/3}]³ — the inner bracket is (1 + u)^{1/u} with u = 3/x → 0 as x → ∞. **Apply the star:** (1 + u)^{1/u} → **e** ⟹ the limit = e³. **Deep point:** the star (1+u)^{1/u} → e is the definition of e; every 1^∞ question is a disguise of it, and the answer is always e^{(coefficient ratio)} — here the exponent's coefficient 1 against the base's displacement 3 gives e³. The reshape-then-exponentiate move generalises: steer the base to (1 + u) with u → 0, then read the exponent as 1/u times a constant.

**NEB-style (6m): Using standard limits, evaluate lim_{x→0} (e^{3x} − 1)/(ln(1 + 2x)).** — **Form check:** substitute x = 0: (1 − 1)/ln 1 = **0/0** — indeterminate. **Split into stars:** numerator e^{3x} − 1 ~ 3x (star: (eᵘ−1)/u → 1, u = 3x → 0); denominator ln(1 + 2x) ~ 2x (star: ln(1+u)/u → 1, u = 2x → 0). **Take the ratio:** (e^{3x} − 1)/ln(1+2x) ≈ (3x)/(2x) = **3/2** — more rigorously, write the expression as [(e^{3x}−1)/(3x)]·[2x/ln(1+2x)]·(3/2): the first bracket → 1, the second → 1, leaving **3/2**. **Deep point:** when both contestants vanish at first order, the limit is just the ratio of their first-order coefficients — the stars convert each function into its linear approximation, and the linear ratio survives. This is L'Hôpital's answer computed without differentiating: same theory, star-engine instead of derivative-engine.

data.title: Continuity of a Function (Intuitive Definition)
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Continuity You Can See

**Intuitive continuity**: a function is continuous where its graph can be drawn **without lifting the pen**. This topic formalises the picture into the three-part test and surveys how it fails — the map of discontinuities.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 The pen test

- **Continuous at a** ⟺ small changes in x produce small changes in f(x) — no jumps, holes or tears at a. Globally continuous on an interval ⟹ drawable in one stroke there.

### 2.2 The three-part test (the theorem)

- f is continuous at a ⟺ **(1)** f(a) exists, **(2)** lim_{x→a} f(x) exists, **(3)** f(a) = lim_{x→a} f(x).
- Each condition can fail independently — and each failure has a name (rows 36–38): missing value, missing limit, mismatched value.

### 2.3 Continuous families

- **Theorems:** polynomials are continuous on ℝ; rational functions are continuous wherever the denominator ≠ 0; roots on their domains; sin, cos everywhere; sums, products, quotients (non-zero denominator) and **compositions** of continuous functions are continuous.
- **Composition theorem:** g continuous at a and f continuous at g(a) ⟹ f∘g continuous at a — the chain rule's continuity shadow.

### 2.4 Continuity on intervals

- **Continuous on [a, b]** means continuous on (a, b) plus one-sided continuity at the endpoints — the hypothesis of the Extreme Value and Intermediate Value theorems that calculus will invoke.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Pen test** | Graph drawable without lifting | polynomials |
| **Three-part test** | value, limit, equality | the checklist |
| **Composition theorem** | f∘g continuous if both are | sin(x²) |
| **Continuity on [a,b]** | interior + one-sided ends | EVT hypothesis |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Small change, small response

- Continuity is a stability contract: inputs perturbed slightly yield outputs perturbed slightly. Jumps violate it; holes violate it mildly (fixable); blow-ups violate it violently.

### 4.2 Building continuity from parts

- The closure theorems mean you rarely test continuity from scratch: build expressions from continuous families and quote the closure rules — the continuity analogue of "well-formed formulas stay well-formed".

### 4.3 Why endpoints get one-sided treatment

- At a domain edge only one neighbourhood exists; demanding two-sided agreement there would disqualify every endpoint. One-sided continuity is the honest localisation.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**The three failures**

| Failing part | Name | Repairable? |
|---|---|---|
| f(a) missing | removable (hole) | yes — define f(a) |
| limit missing | jump / infinite | no (jump) / no (infinite) |
| value ≠ limit | removable | yes — redefine |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Existence of f(a) alone is not continuity:** the limit must also exist and match — three boxes, all needed.
**Continuous ≠ differentiable:** |x| is continuous everywhere but not differentiable at 0 — continuity is the weaker contract.
**Composition preserves continuity, not necessarily differentiability** at kinks — the same distinction one level up.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (2m): Show that f(x) = x² sin(1/x) (x ≠ 0), f(0) = 0 is continuous at 0.** — **Limit:** |x² sin(1/x)| ≤ x²·1 = x² → 0 (squeeze: sin(1/x) is trapped in [−1, 1]), so lim_{x→0} f(x) = 0. **Value:** f(0) = 0. **Match:** 0 = 0 ⟹ **continuous at 0** — the composition/closure theorems fail here (sin(1/x) is discontinuous at 0), but the x² damping saves the day: continuity can be earned by squeeze, not only by closure.

**NEB-style (2m): State where f(x) = (x² − 1)/(x + 1) is continuous, and classify any break.** — Rational function: continuous wherever x + 1 ≠ 0, i.e. on **ℝ \ {−1}**. At x = −1: f undefined (condition 1 fails) ⟹ discontinuous; but the limit exists — (x²−1)/(x+1) = x − 1 for x ≠ −1 gives lim = −2 ⟹ **removable** discontinuity (a hole at (−1, −2), repairable by defining f(−1) = −2).

**NEB-style (2m): Prove that the composition of continuous functions is continuous at a.** — Let g be continuous at a and f continuous at g(a). Take any sequence... (ε–δ sketch): given ε > 0, continuity of f at g(a) supplies δ₁ with |f(u) − f(g(a))| < ε whenever |u − g(a)| < δ₁; continuity of g at a supplies δ with |g(x) − g(a)| < δ₁ whenever |x − a| < δ. Chaining: |x − a| < δ ⟹ |f(g(x)) − f(g(a))| < ε. Hence f∘g is continuous at a ∎ — the neighbourhoods nest, which is all the proof needs.

## 8. Deep Conceptual — The Pen Test as a Physical Model

- Intuitive continuity models **unbroken processes**: temperature over an afternoon, water level while filling a tank, position along a walk. The pen never lifts because the quantity never teleports — intermediate values are physically occupied on the way between any two.
- **This physical reading powers the IVT intuition:** if the temperature went from 15° to 25°, it *was* every temperature between at some moment — no continuous process skips a value. Discontinuities are exactly the events where the model breaks: an instant switch, a jump cut, a step.
- **The limits of the intuition:** the pen test catches jumps and holes but is silent about finer structure (it cannot distinguish differentiable from non-differentiable — a corner is still drawable in one stroke). Intuition certifies continuity, not smoothness.

## 9. Deep Conceptual — Continuity as Composition Insurance

- The composition theorem — lim f(g(x)) = f(lim g(x)) when f is continuous at the inner limit — is continuity's *purpose*: continuous functions commute with limits. That commutation is what lets you substitute inside composed expressions.
- **Chain of custody:** a limit's value passes through each continuous function unchanged. Every "evaluate by substitution" step in a composite limit is an appeal to this licence; the licence is granted precisely by continuity.
- **Where the licence expires:** at f's discontinuity points the limit and the value can part ways — f(lim g) may differ from lim f(g). Locating a function's discontinuities is therefore locating exactly where substitution reasoning must stop and one-sided analysis must begin.

## 10. Deep Conceptual — Continuous Functions Preserve Connectedness and Compactness

- A continuous image of an interval is an interval: the function cannot tear the line apart. This is the **Intermediate Value Theorem's** deep content — f([a,b]) contains every value between f(a) and f(b).
- A continuous image of a closed bounded interval is closed and bounded: the **Extreme Value Theorem's** content — maxima and minima are actually attained, not merely approached.
- **Why these theorems matter before calculus:** they guarantee solutions exist (roots, extrema) before any technique finds them — continuity is the hypothesis that converts "should exist" into "does exist," and the derivative-based machinery later only *locates* what continuity already promised.
practice: Show f(x) = x² sin(1/x) (x≠0), f(0) = 0 is continuous at 0.
Locate and classify the discontinuity of (x² − 1)/(x + 1).
Prove the composition theorem for continuity.
universalFacts: Thermostats and volume knobs are continuous controls: tiny turns make tiny changes - jumps (switches) are the discontinuous alternative.
examples: ***The damped wiggler*** - x^2 sin(1/x) fails every closure route at 0 yet is continuous there: the x^2 factor squeezes the wild oscillation to 0.
practiceQuestions: **NEB-style (2m): Show that f(x) = x² sin(1/x) for x ≠ 0, with f(0) = 0, is continuous at x = 0.** — **The obstacle:** sin(1/x) has no limit at 0 (oscillation), so no closure theorem applies — continuity must be earned directly. **Squeeze argument:** −1 ≤ sin(1/x) ≤ 1 for every x ≠ 0, so multiplying by the non-negative x²: **−x² ≤ x² sin(1/x) ≤ x²**. Both bounds → 0 as x → 0, so by the **squeeze theorem** lim_{x→0} x² sin(1/x) = 0. **Three-part test:** (1) f(0) = 0 exists ✓; (2) the limit exists and equals 0 ✓; (3) f(0) = 0 = limit ✓ ⟹ **f is continuous at 0**. The moral: damping factors can tame oscillation — continuity by squeeze where composition fails.

**NEB-style (2m): Determine where f(x) = (x² − 1)/(x + 1) is continuous and classify the discontinuity.** — **Closure route:** f is a rational function, continuous wherever its denominator is non-zero: **continuous on ℝ \ {−1}**. **At x = −1:** condition 1 of the three-part test fails — f(−1) is undefined (0/0). **Limit check:** factoring, (x² − 1)/(x + 1) = x − 1 for x ≠ −1, so lim_{x→−1} f(x) = −2 — the limit **exists**. **Classification:** missing value with existing limit ⟹ **removable discontinuity**: a hole at the point (−1, −2); defining f(−1) = −2 would make f continuous on all of ℝ. The factor-and-cancel pattern is the signature of every removable rational break.

**NEB-style (2m): Prove that if g is continuous at a and f is continuous at g(a), then f∘g is continuous at a.** — **Proof (ε–δ chaining).** Let ε > 0 be given. Since f is continuous at g(a), there is δ₁ > 0 such that |u − g(a)| < δ₁ ⟹ |f(u) − f(g(a))| < ε. Since g is continuous at a, there is δ > 0 such that |x − a| < δ ⟹ |g(x) − g(a)| < δ₁. **Chain the implications:** for |x − a| < δ, set u = g(x); then |u − g(a)| < δ₁, so |f(g(x)) − f(g(a))| < ε. This is precisely the ε–δ statement that f∘g is continuous at a. ∎ **Reading:** the neighbourhoods **nest** — f's tolerance δ₁ becomes g's target — which is the entire mechanism; the theorem is why sin(x²), e^{sin x} and √(1 + x²) inherit continuity for free.

**NEB-style (6m): Use the Intermediate Value Theorem to show that x³ + x − 3 = 0 has a root between 1 and 2, and explain what continuity contributes.** — **Setup:** let f(x) = x³ + x − 3, continuous everywhere (polynomial). **Evaluate the endpoints:** f(1) = 1 + 1 − 3 = **−1** (negative); f(2) = 8 + 2 − 3 = **7** (positive). **Apply the IVT:** f is continuous on [1, 2] and 0 lies between f(1) = −1 and f(2) = 7 ⟹ there exists c ∈ (1, 2) with **f(c) = 0** — a root exists in (1, 2). **What continuity contributes:** the IVT is *false* without it — a discontinuous function can step over 0 between its endpoint values (e.g. a function that is −1 just below 1.5 and +7 just above, never 0). Continuity is the hypothesis that the graph, in travelling from −1 to 7, must pass through every intermediate height. **Deep point:** the IVT certifies *existence*, not location or uniqueness — pinning c tighter needs more endpoint bisections or monotonicity, but the guarantee itself cost only two evaluations and one continuity check.

**NEB-style (5m): The function f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2) for x ≠ 2, f(2) = 3. Is f continuous on [0, 4]? Justify with the three-part test at the suspect point.** — **Where continuity can fail:** f is a rational function — continuous at every point of its domain — so the only suspect is the excluded point x = 2. **Part 1:** f(2) = 3 exists ✓. **Part 2:** lim_{x→2} f(x) — factoring gives x + 2 for x ≠ 2 ⟹ limit = **4** ✓. **Part 3:** f(2) = 3 ≠ 4 ✗ — the test fails. **Verdict:** f is continuous on [0, 4] **except at x = 2**; the discontinuity is **removable** (redefine f(2) = 4). **Deep point:** the triage is domain-first — rational functions are continuous wherever defined, so all scrutiny concentrates on the excluded point; the three-part test then localises the failure to the value (Part 3), which is what makes the break repairable.

**NEB-style (5m): Explain, with a sketch-reasoned example, why the pen test alone cannot decide differentiability, using f(x) = |x| at 0.** — **Pen test verdict:** |x| is **continuous** at 0 — the V-shape is drawn in one stroke, no lift, no jump; the pen test passes. **Differentiability test:** the one-sided slopes disagree — from the right the slope is +1, from the left −1 ⟹ f′(0) does not exist; the graph has a **corner**. **The gap between the tests:** continuity asks whether the *values* connect; differentiability asks whether the *slopes* connect. A corner connects values while breaking slopes, so it passes the pen test and fails the derivative test. **Deep point:** the pen test certifies the coarsest level of smoothness only; each finer level (differentiable, continuously differentiable) needs its own test, and |x| is the canonical witness that drawable-without-lifting is strictly weaker than having a tangent line.

**NEB-style (6m): A tank's water level V(t) in litres is V(t) = 100 − 4t for 0 ≤ t ≤ 10, V(t) = 120 − 6t for 10 < t ≤ 20. Is V continuous at t = 10, and what does the answer mean physically?** — **LHL (t → 10⁻, first piece):** 100 − 4(10) = **60**. **RHL (t → 10⁺, second piece):** 120 − 6(10) = **60**. **Existence:** LHL = RHL = 60 ⟹ lim_{t→10} V(t) = 60. **Value:** V(10) = 100 − 40 = **60** (the ≤ condition puts 10 in the first piece). **Verdict:** value = limit ⟹ **V is continuous at t = 10**. **Physical meaning:** the level passes through 60 L at the switch — the outflow *rate* changed (4 L/min → 6 L/min) but the *amount* did not jump; water cannot teleport, so continuity is the physically mandatory answer, while the rate change is a corner in the graph (the slope drops... steepens from −4 to −6). **Deep point:** continuity models conserved quantities (amount, position, temperature); rates may jump even when amounts cannot — the graph is continuous with a kink, which is exactly the pen-test-passes, derivative-fails signature.
formulas:
- continuity at a: f(a) = lim_{x→a} f(x), both existing
- closure: f, g continuous ⟹ f ± g, f·g, f/g (g ≠ 0), f∘g continuous
- rational p/q continuous on {q ≠ 0}; |x|, sin, cos, eˣ continuous on ℝ
keyPoints: Pen test: continuous where the graph draws without lifting. Three-part test: f(a) exists, lim exists, f(a) = lim - each failure independently named. Continuous families: polynomials (all R), rationals (denominator != 0), roots (domain), sin/cos (all R); sums, products, quotients, compositions of continuous functions are continuous (closure theorems). Composition theorem: g continuous at a and f at g(a) => f o g continuous at a. Continuity on [a, b]: interior two-sided + endpoint one-sided - the EVT/IVT hypothesis. Squeeze can certify continuity where closure fails (x^2 sin(1/x) at 0). Continuous does not imply differentiable (|x| at 0).
data.summary: **Intuitive continuity** is the pen test — drawable without lifting — and its formal face is the **three-part theorem**: f(a) exists, lim_{x→a} f(x) exists, and they are **equal**. Each part can fail alone, and the failure names the discontinuity (removable hole, jump, infinite). **Closure theorems** make continuity cheap: polynomials, rationals (off denominator zeros), roots, sin, cos are continuous, and sums, products, quotients and **compositions** inherit it — f∘g continuous by neighbourhood-nesting ε–δ chaining. Where closure fails, the **squeeze** can still certify continuity: x² sin(1/x) with f(0) = 0 is continuous at 0 because x² damps the oscillation to 0. **Continuity on [a, b]** adds one-sided endpoint tests — the hypothesis the Extreme Value and Intermediate Value theorems will demand. And continuity ≠ differentiability: |x| bends without breaking. Three boxes, closure shortcuts, squeeze rescues — the whole continuity toolkit.
importantStatements: "f is continuous at a iff f(a) = lim_{x->a} f(x) with both existing; compositions and sums/products/quotients of continuous functions are continuous."

examNotes: Quote which part of the three-part test fails - naming the failing condition is the analysis the marker wants.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**The three failures**

| Failing part | Name | Repairable? |
|---|---|---|
| f(a) missing | removable (hole) | yes — define f(a) |
| limit missing | jump / infinite | no (jump) / no (infinite) |
| value ≠ limit | removable | yes — redefine |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Existence of f(a) alone is not continuity:** the limit must also exist and match — three boxes, all needed.
**Continuous ≠ differentiable:** |x| is continuous everywhere but not differentiable at 0 — continuity is the weaker contract.
**Composition preserves continuity, not necessarily differentiability** at kinks — the same distinction one level up.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (2m): Show that f(x) = x² sin(1/x) (x ≠ 0), f(0) = 0 is continuous at 0.** — **Limit:** |x² sin(1/x)| ≤ x²·1 = x² → 0 (squeeze: sin(1/x) is trapped in [−1, 1]), so lim_{x→0} f(x) = 0. **Value:** f(0) = 0. **Match:** 0 = 0 ⟹ **continuous at 0** — the composition/closure theorems fail here (sin(1/x) is discontinuous at 0), but the x² damping saves the day: continuity can be earned by squeeze, not only by closure.

**NEB-style (2m): State where f(x) = (x² − 1)/(x + 1) is continuous, and classify any break.** — Rational function: continuous wherever x + 1 ≠ 0, i.e. on **ℝ \ {−1}**. At x = −1: f undefined (condition 1 fails) ⟹ discontinuous; but the limit exists — (x²−1)/(x+1) = x − 1 for x ≠ −1 gives lim = −2 ⟹ **removable** discontinuity (a hole at (−1, −2), repairable by defining f(−1) = −2).

**NEB-style (2m): Prove that the composition of continuous functions is continuous at a.** — Let g be continuous at a and f continuous at g(a). Take any sequence... (ε–δ sketch): given ε > 0, continuity of f at g(a) supplies δ₁ with |f(u) − f(g(a))| < ε whenever |u − g(a)| < δ₁; continuity of g at a supplies δ with |g(x) − g(a)| < δ₁ whenever |x − a| < δ. Chaining: |x − a| < δ ⟹ |f(g(x)) − f(g(a))| < ε. Hence f∘g is continuous at a ∎ — the neighbourhoods nest, which is all the proof needs.

## 8. Deep Conceptual — The Pen Test as a Physical Model

- Intuitive continuity models **unbroken processes**: temperature over an afternoon, water level while filling a tank, position along a walk. The pen never lifts because the quantity never teleports — intermediate values are physically occupied on the way between any two.
- **This physical reading powers the IVT intuition:** if the temperature went from 15° to 25°, it *was* every temperature between at some moment — no continuous process skips a value. Discontinuities are exactly the events where the model breaks: an instant switch, a jump cut, a step.
- **The limits of the intuition:** the pen test catches jumps and holes but is silent about finer structure (it cannot distinguish differentiable from non-differentiable — a corner is still drawable in one stroke). Intuition certifies continuity, not smoothness.

## 9. Deep Conceptual — Continuity as Composition Insurance

- The composition theorem — lim f(g(x)) = f(lim g(x)) when f is continuous at the inner limit — is continuity's *purpose*: continuous functions commute with limits. That commutation is what lets you substitute inside composed expressions.
- **Chain of custody:** a limit's value passes through each continuous function unchanged. Every "evaluate by substitution" step in a composite limit is an appeal to this licence; the licence is granted precisely by continuity.
- **Where the licence expires:** at f's discontinuity points the limit and the value can part ways — f(lim g) may differ from lim f(g). Locating a function's discontinuities is therefore locating exactly where substitution reasoning must stop and one-sided analysis must begin.

## 10. Deep Conceptual — Continuous Functions Preserve Connectedness and Compactness

- A continuous image of an interval is an interval: the function cannot tear the line apart. This is the **Intermediate Value Theorem's** deep content — f([a,b]) contains every value between f(a) and f(b).
- A continuous image of a closed bounded interval is closed and bounded: the **Extreme Value Theorem's** content — maxima and minima are actually attained, not merely approached.
- **Why these theorems matter before calculus:** they guarantee solutions exist (roots, extrema) before any technique finds them — continuity is the hypothesis that converts "should exist" into "does exist," and the derivative-based machinery later only *locates* what continuity already promised.
keyPoints: Pen test: continuous where the graph draws without lifting. Three-part test: f(a) exists, lim exists, f(a) = lim - each failure independently named. Continuous families: polynomials (all R), rationals (denominator != 0), roots (domain), sin/cos (all R); sums, products, quotients, compositions of continuous functions are continuous (closure theorems). Composition theorem: g continuous at a and f at g(a) => f o g continuous at a. Continuity on [a, b]: interior two-sided + endpoint one-sided - the EVT/IVT hypothesis. Squeeze can certify continuity where closure fails (x^2 sin(1/x) at 0). Continuous does not imply differentiable (|x| at 0).

examShortTricks: Test the three parts in order. Build continuity by closure theorems. Rational functions: continuous off the denominator zeros. Endpoints: one-sided test.

formulas:
- continuity at a: f(a) = lim_{x→a} f(x), both existing
- closure: f, g continuous ⟹ f ± g, f·g, f/g (g ≠ 0), f∘g continuous
- rational p/q continuous on {q ≠ 0}; |x|, sin, cos, eˣ continuous on ℝ
practice: Show f(x) = x² sin(1/x) (x≠0), f(0) = 0 is continuous at 0.
Locate and classify the discontinuity of (x² − 1)/(x + 1).
Prove the composition theorem for continuity.
practiceQuestions: **NEB-style (2m): Show that f(x) = x² sin(1/x) for x ≠ 0, with f(0) = 0, is continuous at x = 0.** — **The obstacle:** sin(1/x) has no limit at 0 (oscillation), so no closure theorem applies — continuity must be earned directly. **Squeeze argument:** −1 ≤ sin(1/x) ≤ 1 for every x ≠ 0, so multiplying by the non-negative x²: **−x² ≤ x² sin(1/x) ≤ x²**. Both bounds → 0 as x → 0, so by the **squeeze theorem** lim_{x→0} x² sin(1/x) = 0. **Three-part test:** (1) f(0) = 0 exists ✓; (2) the limit exists and equals 0 ✓; (3) f(0) = 0 = limit ✓ ⟹ **f is continuous at 0**. The moral: damping factors can tame oscillation — continuity by squeeze where composition fails.

**NEB-style (2m): Determine where f(x) = (x² − 1)/(x + 1) is continuous and classify the discontinuity.** — **Closure route:** f is a rational function, continuous wherever its denominator is non-zero: **continuous on ℝ \ {−1}**. **At x = −1:** condition 1 of the three-part test fails — f(−1) is undefined (0/0). **Limit check:** factoring, (x² − 1)/(x + 1) = x − 1 for x ≠ −1, so lim_{x→−1} f(x) = −2 — the limit **exists**. **Classification:** missing value with existing limit ⟹ **removable discontinuity**: a hole at the point (−1, −2); defining f(−1) = −2 would make f continuous on all of ℝ. The factor-and-cancel pattern is the signature of every removable rational break.

**NEB-style (2m): Prove that if g is continuous at a and f is continuous at g(a), then f∘g is continuous at a.** — **Proof (ε–δ chaining).** Let ε > 0 be given. Since f is continuous at g(a), there is δ₁ > 0 such that |u − g(a)| < δ₁ ⟹ |f(u) − f(g(a))| < ε. Since g is continuous at a, there is δ > 0 such that |x − a| < δ ⟹ |g(x) − g(a)| < δ₁. **Chain the implications:** for |x − a| < δ, set u = g(x); then |u − g(a)| < δ₁, so |f(g(x)) − f(g(a))| < ε. This is precisely the ε–δ statement that f∘g is continuous at a. ∎ **Reading:** the neighbourhoods **nest** — f's tolerance δ₁ becomes g's target — which is the entire mechanism; the theorem is why sin(x²), e^{sin x} and √(1 + x²) inherit continuity for free.

**NEB-style (6m): Use the Intermediate Value Theorem to show that x³ + x − 3 = 0 has a root between 1 and 2, and explain what continuity contributes.** — **Setup:** let f(x) = x³ + x − 3, continuous everywhere (polynomial). **Evaluate the endpoints:** f(1) = 1 + 1 − 3 = **−1** (negative); f(2) = 8 + 2 − 3 = **7** (positive). **Apply the IVT:** f is continuous on [1, 2] and 0 lies between f(1) = −1 and f(2) = 7 ⟹ there exists c ∈ (1, 2) with **f(c) = 0** — a root exists in (1, 2). **What continuity contributes:** the IVT is *false* without it — a discontinuous function can step over 0 between its endpoint values (e.g. a function that is −1 just below 1.5 and +7 just above, never 0). Continuity is the hypothesis that the graph, in travelling from −1 to 7, must pass through every intermediate height. **Deep point:** the IVT certifies *existence*, not location or uniqueness — pinning c tighter needs more endpoint bisections or monotonicity, but the guarantee itself cost only two evaluations and one continuity check.

**NEB-style (5m): The function f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2) for x ≠ 2, f(2) = 3. Is f continuous on [0, 4]? Justify with the three-part test at the suspect point.** — **Where continuity can fail:** f is a rational function — continuous at every point of its domain — so the only suspect is the excluded point x = 2. **Part 1:** f(2) = 3 exists ✓. **Part 2:** lim_{x→2} f(x) — factoring gives x + 2 for x ≠ 2 ⟹ limit = **4** ✓. **Part 3:** f(2) = 3 ≠ 4 ✗ — the test fails. **Verdict:** f is continuous on [0, 4] **except at x = 2**; the discontinuity is **removable** (redefine f(2) = 4). **Deep point:** the triage is domain-first — rational functions are continuous wherever defined, so all scrutiny concentrates on the excluded point; the three-part test then localises the failure to the value (Part 3), which is what makes the break repairable.

**NEB-style (5m): Explain, with a sketch-reasoned example, why the pen test alone cannot decide differentiability, using f(x) = |x| at 0.** — **Pen test verdict:** |x| is **continuous** at 0 — the V-shape is drawn in one stroke, no lift, no jump; the pen test passes. **Differentiability test:** the one-sided slopes disagree — from the right the slope is +1, from the left −1 ⟹ f′(0) does not exist; the graph has a **corner**. **The gap between the tests:** continuity asks whether the *values* connect; differentiability asks whether the *slopes* connect. A corner connects values while breaking slopes, so it passes the pen test and fails the derivative test. **Deep point:** the pen test certifies the coarsest level of smoothness only; each finer level (differentiable, continuously differentiable) needs its own test, and |x| is the canonical witness that drawable-without-lifting is strictly weaker than having a tangent line.

**NEB-style (6m): A tank's water level V(t) in litres is V(t) = 100 − 4t for 0 ≤ t ≤ 10, V(t) = 120 − 6t for 10 < t ≤ 20. Is V continuous at t = 10, and what does the answer mean physically?** — **LHL (t → 10⁻, first piece):** 100 − 4(10) = **60**. **RHL (t → 10⁺, second piece):** 120 − 6(10) = **60**. **Existence:** LHL = RHL = 60 ⟹ lim_{t→10} V(t) = 60. **Value:** V(10) = 100 − 40 = **60** (the ≤ condition puts 10 in the first piece). **Verdict:** value = limit ⟹ **V is continuous at t = 10**. **Physical meaning:** the level passes through 60 L at the switch — the outflow *rate* changed (4 L/min → 6 L/min) but the *amount* did not jump; water cannot teleport, so continuity is the physically mandatory answer, while the rate change is a corner in the graph (the slope drops... steepens from −4 to −6). **Deep point:** continuity models conserved quantities (amount, position, temperature); rates may jump even when amounts cannot — the graph is continuous with a kink, which is exactly the pen-test-passes, derivative-fails signature.

data.title: Continuity at a Point (Formal Definition)
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Continuity With Precision

The **formal (ε–δ-free at this level: sequential/interval) definition** of continuity replaces the pen picture with quantified statements. This topic states the precise definition, works the algebra of continuity, and frames the Intermediate and Extreme Value theorems.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 The precise statement

- **f is continuous at a** ⟺ for every ε > 0 there exists δ > 0 such that **|x − a| < δ ⟹ |f(x) − f(a)| < ε** (x in the domain).
- Reading: however small a tolerance ε you demand of the output, a window δ of the input delivers it — the stability contract with numbers attached.

### 2.2 Sequential characterisation

- **Theorem:** f continuous at a ⟺ for every sequence xₙ → a (in the domain), **f(xₙ) → f(a)**.
- This converts continuity into sequence bookkeeping — and gives the fastest **discontinuity proofs**: find one sequence xₙ → a with f(xₙ) escaping f(a).

### 2.3 Algebra of continuity

- Sums, products, quotients (non-zero denominator), compositions: continuous — the closure theorems proved once, used everywhere. Polynomials continuous everywhere; |f| continuous when f is.

### 2.4 The big interval theorems (statements)

- **Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT):** f continuous on [a, b], u between f(a) and f(b) ⟹ some c ∈ (a, b) has f(c) = u — continuous functions cannot skip values.
- **Extreme Value Theorem (EVT):** f continuous on a closed bounded [a, b] attains a maximum and a minimum.
- Both need **closed + bounded + continuous** — drop any and counterexamples appear.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **ε–δ continuity** | ∀ε ∃δ: \|x−a\| < δ ⟹ \|f(x)−f(a)\| < ε | the precise contract |
| **Sequential continuity** | xₙ → a ⟹ f(xₙ) → f(a) | proof tool |
| **IVT** | No skipped values on [a, b] | root-finding licence |
| **EVT** | Max and min attained on [a, b] | optimisation licence |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 What ε–δ buys

- The pen picture cannot say *how* continuous; ε–δ quantifies it. Uniform continuity, approximation rates and numerical analysis all live downstream of this precision.

### 4.2 The IVT as a root-finding licence

- If f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs, u = 0 lies between ⟹ a root exists in (a, b). Bisection methods are IVT turned into an algorithm.

### 4.3 Why EVT needs closed and bounded

- On (0, 1], f(x) = 1/x has no maximum; on [0, 1], f(x) = x for x < 1, f(1) = 0 (discontinuous) has no maximum. Closed + bounded + continuous is exactly the insurance EVT demands.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Continuity hypotheses at work**

| Theorem | Needs | Gives |
|---|---|---|
| IVT | continuous on [a, b] | every intermediate value hit |
| EVT | continuous on closed bounded [a, b] | max and min attained |
| sequential test | f at a | xₙ → a ⟹ f(xₙ) → f(a) |

## 6. Common Confusions

**IVT needs continuity on the whole interval:** a single break can let f skip the target value.
**EVT fails on open intervals:** (0, 1) with f(x) = x has sup 1 but no maximum — "attained" is the operative word.
**Sequential discontinuity proofs need only one bad sequence:** a single xₙ → a with f(xₙ) ↛ f(a) kills continuity.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): Show that f(x) = x³ − 4x + 1 has a root between 0 and 1.** — f is a polynomial ⟹ **continuous on [0, 1]**. f(0) = 1 > 0; f(1) = 1 − 4 + 1 = −2 < 0. Since 0 lies between f(1) = −2 and f(0) = 1, the **IVT** supplies c ∈ (0, 1) with f(c) = 0 ∎ — sign change plus continuity equals existence of a root.

**NEB-style (2m): Prove f(x) = 1/x is discontinuous at 0 using sequences.** — Take xₙ = 1/n → 0 (each xₙ in the domain's punctured neighbourhood). Then f(xₙ) = n → **∞**, so f(xₙ) does not converge to any finite value, let alone f(0) (undefined). By the sequential characterisation, **f is not continuous at 0** — one escaping sequence suffices.

**NEB-style (2m): State the Extreme Value Theorem and give a counterexample when the interval is open.** — **EVT:** a function continuous on a **closed, bounded** interval [a, b] attains an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on it. **Counterexample on (0, 1):** f(x) = x is continuous on the open interval but attains neither 0 nor 1 — for every x ∈ (0, 1) there are larger and smaller values; the sup 1 and inf 0 are never reached. Closedness is the hypothesis that turns "sup" into "max".

## 8. Deep Conceptual — Epsilon as a Challenge, Delta as the Answer

- The definition is a **game**: the skeptic names any tolerance ε > 0 (however tiny); the prover must produce a window δ > 0 so that staying within δ of a keeps f within ε of L. Continuity at a = winning this game for *every* ε.
- **Why "for every ε" matters:** one ε is an accident, finitely many is a lucky stretch — only all-of-them-at-once pins the approach. The order of quantifiers ( ∀ε ∃δ ) is the definition's engine; swapping it ( ∃ε ∀δ ) describes a function stuck at a distance — a jump.
- **Delta may depend on epsilon:** smaller ε demands smaller δ — the working recipe (preliminary window, then refine) exists precisely because δ is *chosen after* seeing ε. A single δ working for all ε would force f to be constant near a.

## 9. Deep Conceptual — The Algebra of Continuity Is Inherited, Not Re-proved

- Once the base functions are certified continuous (polynomials by limit laws, sin/cos by the stars, roots on their domains), the **closure theorems** do the rest: sums, products, quotients (where defined), and compositions of continuous functions are continuous — no new ε–δ proofs needed.
- **Why composition transmits continuity:** f continuous at b, g continuous at b's preimage a ⟹ x near a sends g(x) near b, which sends f(g(x)) near f(b). Continuity chains through machines — this is the licence behind every "evaluate the inner limit, apply the outer function" step.
- **Rational functions:** continuous on their whole domain — the domain's holes are *exclusions*, not discontinuities. 1/x is continuous on ℝ \ {0}; saying "1/x is discontinuous at 0" confuses "not defined" with "defined but broken."

## 10. Deep Conceptual — Formal Continuity Locates the Theorems' Power

- The EVT and IVT are stated for continuous functions on **closed bounded intervals** — the ε–δ definition is what makes "continuous" precise enough for their proofs, and compactness (closed + bounded) is what makes the guarantees unconditional.
- **Continuity is local, theorems are global:** the definition speaks of a single point; the big theorems harvest whole intervals of points. The bridge is that continuity at *every* point of [a, b] — a local property held universally — yields global conclusions (boundedness, attained extrema, intermediate values).
- **Failure modes map to missing hypotheses:** drop closedness (f = 1/x on (0,1]) and boundedness fails; drop continuity (a step function) and IVT fails. Each theorem's hypotheses are exactly the guards against a named counterexample.
practice: Show x³ − 4x + 1 has a root in (0, 1) via the IVT.
Disprove continuity of 1/x at 0 with a sequence.
State the EVT and break it on (0, 1).
universalFacts: Elevation maps are continuous: walking from 100 m to 200 m must cross every height between - no teleporting terrain, IVT on the trail.
examples: ***The bisection engine*** - IVT + sign change is the root-finding theorem: bracket, halve, repeat - every numerical root-finder is IVT with a loop.
practiceQuestions: **NEB-style (3m): Show that the equation x³ − 4x + 1 = 0 has a root between 0 and 1.** — **Hypothesis check:** f(x) = x³ − 4x + 1 is a polynomial, hence **continuous on the closed interval [0, 1]** — the IVT's standing requirement. **Endpoint values:** f(0) = 0 − 0 + 1 = **1 > 0**; f(1) = 1 − 4 + 1 = **−2 < 0**. **Sign change:** 0 lies between f(1) = −2 and f(0) = 1. **Conclusion (IVT):** there exists c ∈ (0, 1) with f(c) = 0 — the equation has a root between 0 and 1. ∎ (Bisection would localise it: f(0.25) ≈ 0.016 > 0, f(0.26) ≈ −0.058 < 0 — the root is near 0.254, but existence needed only the two endpoint signs.)

**NEB-style (2m): Using sequences, prove that f(x) = 1/x is discontinuous at x = 0.** — **Sequential characterisation:** f is continuous at a iff every sequence xₙ → a (with xₙ in the domain) satisfies f(xₙ) → f(a); **one** counterexample sequence disproves continuity. **The sequence:** xₙ = 1/n → 0, and every xₙ ≠ 0 (so each is in the domain). **Its images:** f(xₙ) = 1/(1/n) = n → **∞** — the image sequence diverges to infinity, hence converges to no real number, and in particular cannot converge to f(0) (which does not even exist). **Conclusion:** f is **not continuous at 0** ∎. (Note the pattern: to disprove continuity, one escaping sequence is enough; to prove it, *all* sequences must cooperate — asymmetry worth remembering.)

**NEB-style (2m): State the Extreme Value Theorem and show it fails on the open interval (0, 1).** — **Theorem (EVT):** if f is continuous on a **closed and bounded** interval [a, b], then f attains an absolute maximum value and an absolute minimum value at points of [a, b]. **Counterexample on (0, 1):** take f(x) = x, continuous on the open interval (0, 1). For any x ∈ (0, 1), the value (x + 1)/2 ∈ (0, 1) satisfies f((x+1)/2) > f(x) — so no point achieves a maximum; similarly (x/2) beats every candidate for the minimum downward. The supremum 1 and infimum 0 exist as **bounds** but are **never attained**. **Moral:** closedness is exactly the hypothesis that converts "least upper bound" into "maximum" — drop it and EVT collapses.

**NEB-style (6m): Prove that f(x) = 3x + 1 is continuous at x = 2 using the epsilon–delta definition.** — **Target:** for every ε > 0, find δ > 0 with |x − 2| < δ ⟹ |f(x) − 5| < ε (note L = f(2) = 7? — compute: f(2) = 7, so target |f(x) − 7| < ε). **Compute the gap:** |f(x) − 7| = |3x + 1 − 7| = |3x − 6| = **3|x − 2|** — the gap is a constant multiple of the input distance. **Choose δ:** require 3|x − 2| < ε, i.e. |x − 2| < ε/3 ⟹ **δ = ε/3** works. **Verify:** if |x − 2| < δ = ε/3, then |f(x) − 7| = 3|x − 2| < 3(ε/3) = ε ✓ — for every ε, a δ exists ⟹ continuous at 2. **Deep point:** the proof's whole structure is visible in the gap computation — for linear functions the gap factors into (slope)·(input distance), so δ = ε/|slope| always; the ε–δ game is solved by expressing the output distance in terms of the input distance and reversing the inequality.

**NEB-style (6m): Prove that f(x) = x² is continuous at x = 2 using the epsilon–delta definition.** — **Target:** for every ε > 0, find δ > 0 with |x − 2| < δ ⟹ |x² − 4| < ε. **Factor the gap:** |x² − 4| = |x − 2||x + 2| — the |x + 2| factor is the complication (it depends on x). **Preliminary window:** first restrict |x − 2| < 1, so 1 < x < 3 ⟹ 3 < x + 2 < 5 ⟹ |x + 2| < 5. **Bound the gap inside the window:** |x² − 4| < 5|x − 2|. **Choose δ:** require 5|x − 2| < ε ⟹ δ = min(1, ε/5). **Verify:** if |x − 2| < δ, then |x + 2| < 5 (window holds) and |x² − 4| = |x−2||x+2| < 5·(ε/5) = ε ✓. **Deep point:** the **preliminary window trick** — cap δ by a constant first to bound the awkward factor, then shrink δ further for the ε demand — is the universal recipe for nonlinear gaps; δ = min(1, ε/5) encodes both constraints in one choice.

**NEB-style (5m): Using the formal definition's logic, show that f(x) = 1/x is continuous at x = 3, identifying the gap factor and the δ choice.** — **Target:** for every ε > 0, find δ > 0 with |x − 3| < δ ⟹ |1/x − 1/3| < ε. **Compute the gap:** |1/x − 1/3| = |(3 − x)/(3x)| = **|x − 3|/(3|x|)**. **Preliminary window:** restrict |x − 3| < 1 ⟹ 2 < x < 4 ⟹ |x| > 2 ⟹ 1/(3|x|) < 1/6. **Bound:** |1/x − 1/3| < (1/6)|x − 3|. **Choose δ = min(1, 6ε):** then |1/x − 1/3| < (1/6)(6ε) = ε ✓. **Deep points:** (1) the gap factored into (input distance) × (a bounded factor), reproducing the linear-function recipe once the window tamed 1/|x|; (2) the continuity holds **at x = 3 only because x ≠ 0 nearby** — the same function at 0 has no value and no continuity claim; the domain exclusion is what keeps the preliminary window's lower bound |x| > 2 possible.

**NEB-style (6m): For f(x) = x² for x ≤ 1, f(x) = ax + b for x > 1, find a and b so that f is continuous at 1, and justify via the three-part test.** — **Left side:** the first piece is a polynomial ⟹ LHL = 1² = **1**, and f(1) = 1 (≤ puts 1 in the first piece). **Right side:** RHL = lim_{x→1⁺} (ax + b) = **a + b** (polynomial ⟹ substitution). **Continuity demands:** RHL = LHL = f(1) ⟹ a + b = 1. **One equation, two unknowns:** continuity at this single joint constrains only the *sum* — e.g. a = 2, b = −1; or a = 0, b = 1 (flat right piece); or a = 3, b = −2. **Verify one choice (a = 2, b = −1):** RHL = 2 − 1 = 1 = LHL = f(1) ✓ — all three parts pass. **Deep point:** one joint imposes one equation; the family of continuous weldings is a line in (a, b)-space. Extra demands (differentiability at the joint, another joint's continuity) add equations — continuity conditions are always *linear constraints on the parameters*, which is why "find the constants" questions are systems of equations in disguise.
formulas:
- ∀ε > 0 ∃δ > 0: |x − a| < δ ⟹ |f(x) − f(a)| < ε
- IVT: f ∈ C[a,b], u ∈ [f(a), f(b)] ⟹ ∃c: f(c) = u
- EVT: f ∈ C[a,b] ⟹ max and min attained
- sequential: xₙ → a ⟹ f(xₙ) → f(a)

Sequential theorem: f continuous at a iff x_n -> a implies f(x_n) -> f(a); one escaping sequence disproves continuity. Closure theorems: sums, products, quotients (denominator != 0), compositions continuous. notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Continuity With Precision

The **formal (ε–δ-free at this level: sequential/interval) definition** of continuity replaces the pen picture with quantified statements. This topic states the precise definition, works the algebra of continuity, and frames the Intermediate and Extreme Value theorems.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 The precise statement

- **f is continuous at a** ⟺ for every ε > 0 there exists δ > 0 such that **|x − a| < δ ⟹ |f(x) − f(a)| < ε** (x in the domain).
- Reading: however small a tolerance ε you demand of the output, a window δ of the input delivers it — the stability contract with numbers attached.

### 2.2 Sequential characterisation

- **Theorem:** f continuous at a ⟺ for every sequence xₙ → a (in the domain), **f(xₙ) → f(a)**.
- This converts continuity into sequence bookkeeping — and gives the fastest **discontinuity proofs**: find one sequence xₙ → a with f(xₙ) escaping f(a).

### 2.3 Algebra of continuity

- Sums, products, quotients (non-zero denominator), compositions: continuous — the closure theorems proved once, used everywhere. Polynomials continuous everywhere; |f| continuous when f is.

### 2.4 The big interval theorems (statements)

- **Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT):** f continuous on [a, b], u between f(a) and f(b) ⟹ some c ∈ (a, b) has f(c) = u — continuous functions cannot skip values.
- **Extreme Value Theorem (EVT):** f continuous on a closed bounded [a, b] attains a maximum and a minimum.
- Both need **closed + bounded + continuous** — drop any and counterexamples appear.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **ε–δ continuity** | ∀ε ∃δ: \|x−a\| < δ ⟹ \|f(x)−f(a)\| < ε | the precise contract |
| **Sequential continuity** | xₙ → a ⟹ f(xₙ) → f(a) | proof tool |
| **IVT** | No skipped values on [a, b] | root-finding licence |
| **EVT** | Max and min attained on [a, b] | optimisation licence |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 What ε–δ buys

- The pen picture cannot say *how* continuous; ε–δ quantifies it. Uniform continuity, approximation rates and numerical analysis all live downstream of this precision.

### 4.2 The IVT as a root-finding licence

- If f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs, u = 0 lies between ⟹ a root exists in (a, b). Bisection methods are IVT turned into an algorithm.

### 4.3 Why EVT needs closed and bounded

- On (0, 1], f(x) = 1/x has no maximum; on [0, 1], f(x) = x for x < 1, f(1) = 0 (discontinuous) has no maximum. Closed + bounded + continuous is exactly the insurance EVT demands.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Continuity hypotheses at work**

| Theorem | Needs | Gives |
|---|---|---|
| IVT | continuous on [a, b] | every intermediate value hit |
| EVT | continuous on closed bounded [a, b] | max and min attained |
| sequential test | f at a | xₙ → a ⟹ f(xₙ) → f(a) |

## 6. Common Confusions

**IVT needs continuity on the whole interval:** a single break can let f skip the target value.
**EVT fails on open intervals:** (0, 1) with f(x) = x has sup 1 but no maximum — "attained" is the operative word.
**Sequential discontinuity proofs need only one bad sequence:** a single xₙ → a with f(xₙ) ↛ f(a) kills continuity.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): Show that f(x) = x³ − 4x + 1 has a root between 0 and 1.** — f is a polynomial ⟹ **continuous on [0, 1]**. f(0) = 1 > 0; f(1) = 1 − 4 + 1 = −2 < 0. Since 0 lies between f(1) = −2 and f(0) = 1, the **IVT** supplies c ∈ (0, 1) with f(c) = 0 ∎ — sign change plus continuity equals existence of a root.

**NEB-style (2m): Prove f(x) = 1/x is discontinuous at 0 using sequences.** — Take xₙ = 1/n → 0 (each xₙ in the domain's punctured neighbourhood). Then f(xₙ) = n → **∞**, so f(xₙ) does not converge to any finite value, let alone f(0) (undefined). By the sequential characterisation, **f is not continuous at 0** — one escaping sequence suffices.

**NEB-style (2m): State the Extreme Value Theorem and give a counterexample when the interval is open.** — **EVT:** a function continuous on a **closed, bounded** interval [a, b] attains an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on it. **Counterexample on (0, 1):** f(x) = x is continuous on the open interval but attains neither 0 nor 1 — for every x ∈ (0, 1) there are larger and smaller values; the sup 1 and inf 0 are never reached. Closedness is the hypothesis that turns "sup" into "max".

## 8. Deep Conceptual — Epsilon as a Challenge, Delta as the Answer

- The definition is a **game**: the skeptic names any tolerance ε > 0 (however tiny); the prover must produce a window δ > 0 so that staying within δ of a keeps f within ε of L. Continuity at a = winning this game for *every* ε.
- **Why "for every ε" matters:** one ε is an accident, finitely many is a lucky stretch — only all-of-them-at-once pins the approach. The order of quantifiers ( ∀ε ∃δ ) is the definition's engine; swapping it ( ∃ε ∀δ ) describes a function stuck at a distance — a jump.
- **Delta may depend on epsilon:** smaller ε demands smaller δ — the working recipe (preliminary window, then refine) exists precisely because δ is *chosen after* seeing ε. A single δ working for all ε would force f to be constant near a.

## 9. Deep Conceptual — The Algebra of Continuity Is Inherited, Not Re-proved

- Once the base functions are certified continuous (polynomials by limit laws, sin/cos by the stars, roots on their domains), the **closure theorems** do the rest: sums, products, quotients (where defined), and compositions of continuous functions are continuous — no new ε–δ proofs needed.
- **Why composition transmits continuity:** f continuous at b, g continuous at b's preimage a ⟹ x near a sends g(x) near b, which sends f(g(x)) near f(b). Continuity chains through machines — this is the licence behind every "evaluate the inner limit, apply the outer function" step.
- **Rational functions:** continuous on their whole domain — the domain's holes are *exclusions*, not discontinuities. 1/x is continuous on ℝ \ {0}; saying "1/x is discontinuous at 0" confuses "not defined" with "defined but broken."

## 10. Deep Conceptual — Formal Continuity Locates the Theorems' Power

- The EVT and IVT are stated for continuous functions on **closed bounded intervals** — the ε–δ definition is what makes "continuous" precise enough for their proofs, and compactness (closed + bounded) is what makes the guarantees unconditional.
- **Continuity is local, theorems are global:** the definition speaks of a single point; the big theorems harvest whole intervals of points. The bridge is that continuity at *every* point of [a, b] — a local property held universally — yields global conclusions (boundedness, attained extrema, intermediate values).
- **Failure modes map to missing hypotheses:** drop closedness (f = 1/x on (0,1]) and boundedness fails; drop continuity (a step function) and IVT fails. Each theorem's hypotheses are exactly the guards against a named counterexample.

- ∀ε > 0 ∃δ > 0: |x − a| < δ ⟹ |f(x) − f(a)| < ε
- IVT: f ∈ C[a,b], u ∈ [f(a), f(b)] ⟹ ∃c: f(c) = u
- EVT: f ∈ C[a,b] ⟹ max and min attained
