practice: Show x³ − 4x + 1 has a root in (0, 1) via the IVT.
Disprove continuity of 1/x at 0 with a sequence.
State the EVT and break it on (0, 1).
practiceQuestions: **NEB-style (3m): Show that the equation x³ − 4x + 1 = 0 has a root between 0 and 1.** — **Hypothesis check:** f(x) = x³ − 4x + 1 is a polynomial, hence **continuous on the closed interval [0, 1]** — the IVT's standing requirement. **Endpoint values:** f(0) = 0 − 0 + 1 = **1 > 0**; f(1) = 1 − 4 + 1 = **−2 < 0**. **Sign change:** 0 lies between f(1) = −2 and f(0) = 1. **Conclusion (IVT):** there exists c ∈ (0, 1) with f(c) = 0 — the equation has a root between 0 and 1. ∎ (Bisection would localise it: f(0.25) ≈ 0.016 > 0, f(0.26) ≈ −0.058 < 0 — the root is near 0.254, but existence needed only the two endpoint signs.)

**NEB-style (2m): Using sequences, prove that f(x) = 1/x is discontinuous at x = 0.** — **Sequential characterisation:** f is continuous at a iff every sequence xₙ → a (with xₙ in the domain) satisfies f(xₙ) → f(a); **one** counterexample sequence disproves continuity. **The sequence:** xₙ = 1/n → 0, and every xₙ ≠ 0 (so each is in the domain). **Its images:** f(xₙ) = 1/(1/n) = n → **∞** — the image sequence diverges to infinity, hence converges to no real number, and in particular cannot converge to f(0) (which does not even exist). **Conclusion:** f is **not continuous at 0** ∎. (Note the pattern: to disprove continuity, one escaping sequence is enough; to prove it, *all* sequences must cooperate — asymmetry worth remembering.)

**NEB-style (2m): State the Extreme Value Theorem and show it fails on the open interval (0, 1).** — **Theorem (EVT):** if f is continuous on a **closed and bounded** interval [a, b], then f attains an absolute maximum value and an absolute minimum value at points of [a, b]. **Counterexample on (0, 1):** take f(x) = x, continuous on the open interval (0, 1). For any x ∈ (0, 1), the value (x + 1)/2 ∈ (0, 1) satisfies f((x+1)/2) > f(x) — so no point achieves a maximum; similarly (x/2) beats every candidate for the minimum downward. The supremum 1 and infimum 0 exist as **bounds** but are **never attained**. **Moral:** closedness is exactly the hypothesis that converts "least upper bound" into "maximum" — drop it and EVT collapses.

**NEB-style (6m): Prove that f(x) = 3x + 1 is continuous at x = 2 using the epsilon–delta definition.** — **Target:** for every ε > 0, find δ > 0 with |x − 2| < δ ⟹ |f(x) − 5| < ε (note L = f(2) = 7? — compute: f(2) = 7, so target |f(x) − 7| < ε). **Compute the gap:** |f(x) − 7| = |3x + 1 − 7| = |3x − 6| = **3|x − 2|** — the gap is a constant multiple of the input distance. **Choose δ:** require 3|x − 2| < ε, i.e. |x − 2| < ε/3 ⟹ **δ = ε/3** works. **Verify:** if |x − 2| < δ = ε/3, then |f(x) − 7| = 3|x − 2| < 3(ε/3) = ε ✓ — for every ε, a δ exists ⟹ continuous at 2. **Deep point:** the proof's whole structure is visible in the gap computation — for linear functions the gap factors into (slope)·(input distance), so δ = ε/|slope| always; the ε–δ game is solved by expressing the output distance in terms of the input distance and reversing the inequality.

**NEB-style (6m): Prove that f(x) = x² is continuous at x = 2 using the epsilon–delta definition.** — **Target:** for every ε > 0, find δ > 0 with |x − 2| < δ ⟹ |x² − 4| < ε. **Factor the gap:** |x² − 4| = |x − 2||x + 2| — the |x + 2| factor is the complication (it depends on x). **Preliminary window:** first restrict |x − 2| < 1, so 1 < x < 3 ⟹ 3 < x + 2 < 5 ⟹ |x + 2| < 5. **Bound the gap inside the window:** |x² − 4| < 5|x − 2|. **Choose δ:** require 5|x − 2| < ε ⟹ δ = min(1, ε/5). **Verify:** if |x − 2| < δ, then |x + 2| < 5 (window holds) and |x² − 4| = |x−2||x+2| < 5·(ε/5) = ε ✓. **Deep point:** the **preliminary window trick** — cap δ by a constant first to bound the awkward factor, then shrink δ further for the ε demand — is the universal recipe for nonlinear gaps; δ = min(1, ε/5) encodes both constraints in one choice.

**NEB-style (5m): Using the formal definition's logic, show that f(x) = 1/x is continuous at x = 3, identifying the gap factor and the δ choice.** — **Target:** for every ε > 0, find δ > 0 with |x − 3| < δ ⟹ |1/x − 1/3| < ε. **Compute the gap:** |1/x − 1/3| = |(3 − x)/(3x)| = **|x − 3|/(3|x|)**. **Preliminary window:** restrict |x − 3| < 1 ⟹ 2 < x < 4 ⟹ |x| > 2 ⟹ 1/(3|x|) < 1/6. **Bound:** |1/x − 1/3| < (1/6)|x − 3|. **Choose δ = min(1, 6ε):** then |1/x − 1/3| < (1/6)(6ε) = ε ✓. **Deep points:** (1) the gap factored into (input distance) × (a bounded factor), reproducing the linear-function recipe once the window tamed 1/|x|; (2) the continuity holds **at x = 3 only because x ≠ 0 nearby** — the same function at 0 has no value and no continuity claim; the domain exclusion is what keeps the preliminary window's lower bound |x| > 2 possible.

**NEB-style (6m): For f(x) = x² for x ≤ 1, f(x) = ax + b for x > 1, find a and b so that f is continuous at 1, and justify via the three-part test.** — **Left side:** the first piece is a polynomial ⟹ LHL = 1² = **1**, and f(1) = 1 (≤ puts 1 in the first piece). **Right side:** RHL = lim_{x→1⁺} (ax + b) = **a + b** (polynomial ⟹ substitution). **Continuity demands:** RHL = LHL = f(1) ⟹ a + b = 1. **One equation, two unknowns:** continuity at this single joint constrains only the *sum* — e.g. a = 2, b = −1; or a = 0, b = 1 (flat right piece); or a = 3, b = −2. **Verify one choice (a = 2, b = −1):** RHL = 2 − 1 = 1 = LHL = f(1) ✓ — all three parts pass. **Deep point:** one joint imposes one equation; the family of continuous weldings is a line in (a, b)-space. Extra demands (differentiability at the joint, another joint's continuity) add equations — continuity conditions are always *linear constraints on the parameters*, which is why "find the constants" questions are systems of equations in disguise.

data.title: Types of Discontinuity: Removable
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Repairable Break

A **removable discontinuity** is a break the limit ignores: the two-sided limit exists but f(a) is missing or mismatched. The repair is always the same — define or redefine f(a) to equal the limit.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Definition and detection

- **Removable at a** ⟺ lim_{x→a} f(x) = L exists (finite) but f(a) ≠ L or f(a) is undefined.
- **Detection protocol:** substitute (get 0/0 or undefined), compute the limit by transformation, compare with f(a).

### 2.2 The two species

- **Hole:** f(a) undefined, limit exists — (x²−4)/(x−2) at 2 with limit 4.
- **Mismatch:** f(a) defined but ≠ limit — the redefined-point case (f(1) = 3 vs limit 2).

### 2.3 The repair theorem

- **Theorem:** defining (or redefining) **f(a) = L** makes f continuous at a — the discontinuity was removable precisely because one value fixes it.
- After repair, the function is continuous; before repair, the graph shows an isolated open dot (hole) or a detached dot (mismatch).

### 2.4 Common sources

- Rational functions with cancelled common factors: (x²−9)/(x−3) → hole at 3 with limit 6.
- Piecewise definitions with a deliberately wrong middle value.
- Roots of numerators shared with denominators — the factor-and-cancel signature.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Removable discontinuity** | Limit exists, value missing/mismatched | hole at (2, 4) |
| **Hole** | f(a) undefined, limit exists | open dot on graph |
| **Repair** | Set f(a) = lim | one redefinition |
| **Factor-and-cancel** | Common factor exposes the hole | (x²−9)/(x−3) |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why "removable"

- The defect lives at a single point and the limit already knows the correct value: plugging it in removes the break entirely. Jumps and blow-ups need infinitely many point-changes or none works — they are not removable.

### 4.2 The graph signature

- A hole is an **open dot** on an otherwise continuous curve; a mismatch adds a **closed dot** floating elsewhere. Both are single-point defects — the visual fingerprint of removability.

### 4.3 Simplification caution

- Cancelling (x − a) changes the domain: the simplified expression is continuous at a but the **original** is not — always state the x ≠ a licence and report the hole.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Discontinuity triage**

| Type | Limit exists? | Repair |
|---|---|---|
| removable (hole/mismatch) | yes | define f(a) = L |
| jump | no (finite sides differ) | none |
| infinite | no (blow-up) | none |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Cancelled ≠ continuous:** the cancellation proves the limit, not the original function's continuity — the domain shrank.
**Removable needs a finite limit:** an infinite limit at a is an infinite discontinuity, never removable.
**Hole location:** the hole sits at (a, **L**) — at the limit's height, not at f(a)'s (which doesn't exist).

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): Find the point of discontinuity of f(x) = (x² − 9)/(x − 3), classify it, and state the repair.** — Domain: x ≠ 3. **Limit:** factor (x−3)(x+3)/(x−3) = x + 3 (x ≠ 3) ⟹ lim_{x→3} = **6**. **Classification:** f(3) undefined with the limit existing ⟹ **removable discontinuity (hole)** at (3, 6). **Repair:** define f(3) = 6; the repaired f equals x + 3 everywhere and is continuous on ℝ.

**NEB-style (2m): For f(x) = (x² + x − 6)/(x − 2), find lim_{x→2} f(x) and the removable break.** — Factor: (x + 3)(x − 2)/(x − 2) = x + 3 (x ≠ 2) ⟹ limit **5**. f(2) undefined ⟹ **removable hole at (2, 5)**; repair f(2) = 5.

**NEB-style (2m): f(x) = (x + 2)/(x² − 4) at x = −2: removable or not?** — Factor denominator: (x + 2)/[(x−2)(x+2)] = 1/(x − 2) for x ≠ −2, ±... for x ≠ ±2. **Limit as x → −2:** 1/(−2 − 2) = **−1/4** — finite! So x = −2 is **removable** (hole at (−2, −1/4)); repair f(−2) = −1/4. But at x = 2 the simplified 1/(x−2) **blows up** ⟹ x = 2 is an **infinite** (non-removable) discontinuity. One function, two species — triage each point separately.

## 8. Deep Conceptual — Removability Is a Statement About the Neighbourhood

- A removable break means the **neighbourhood is healthy** — both sides approach one value — and only the point itself is sick (missing or wrong). The graph is a curve with a hole (or a relocated dot), not a torn curve.
- **Why the repair is legitimate:** redefining f(a) = L changes the function at exactly one point, and limits are blind to single points — so the limit is untouched, and the new value matches it. The repair costs nothing dynamically; every limit, and later every derivative, is unchanged.
- **The two sub-species:** the **hole** (f(a) undefined — the formula excludes a) and the **mismatch** (f(a) defined but ≠ L — an assigned value disagreeing with the approach). Same cure, different pictures: open dot vs detached dot.

## 9. Deep Conceptual — Removable Breaks as Simplification Shadows

- Most removable breaks are **created by cancellation**: f(x) = (x−2)·g(x)/(x−2) is really g(x) wearing a disguise that breaks at 2. The 0/0 form at a is the signature of this hidden common factor.
- **The limit sees through the disguise:** because the definition ignores x = a, the cancelled and uncancelled forms have identical limits — the removable break is invisible to every limit question and visible only to continuity and value questions.
- **Design lesson:** when a problem *assigns* a value at a formula's excluded point, it is usually asking you to either diagnose the mismatch (continuity) or supply the matching value (repair). The assigned value is the exam's handle on an otherwise invisible point.

## 10. Deep Conceptual — Removable vs Non-Removable: The Repair Test as Classification

- The single diagnostic question — **can redefining finitely many point-values make f continuous?** — splits all discontinuities into removable (yes) and non-removable (no). It is the cleanest classification boundary in the taxonomy.
- **Why jumps fail the test:** a jump's sickness is in the neighbourhood (sides disagree), which no point-value edit touches — you would need to change the function on an entire side. Infinite and oscillatory breaks fail even more thoroughly.
- **The repair test foreshadows derivatives:** |x| at 0 is continuous but non-differentiable, and no value edit fixes the corner — the analogous "removability" question for slopes. Calculus iterates the same architecture one level up: neighbourhood agreement, then point agreement.

Find lim_{x→2} (x² + x − 6)/(x − 2) and the hole.

universalFacts: Sensor dropouts are removable glitches: the trend (limit) is known, the missing sample (value) is interpolated - repair by redefinition.
examples: ***One function, two species*** - (x + 2)/(x^2 - 4) has a removable hole at -2 and an infinite break at 2: every suspicious point gets its own triage.
practiceQuestions: **NEB-style (3m): Find and classify the discontinuity of f(x) = (x² − 9)/(x − 3), then state the repair.** — **Domain:** x ≠ 3 (the denominator ban). **Limit:** factor the numerator: (x − 3)(x + 3)/(x − 3) = **x + 3 for x ≠ 3** — the cancellation is licensed by the punctured neighbourhood. Hence lim_{x→3} f(x) = 3 + 3 = **6**. **Classification:** f(3) is undefined while the limit exists ⟹ a **removable discontinuity** — specifically a **hole** at the point **(3, 6)** (open dot at the limit's height). **Repair:** define f(3) = 6; the repaired function agrees with x + 3 on all of ℝ and is continuous everywhere. **Caution stated:** the cancellation changed the domain — the original f, not x + 3, is the function under discussion, and the hole is part of its graph.

**NEB-style (2m): Find lim_{x→2} (x² + x − 6)/(x − 2) and describe the removable break.** — **Substitution:** (4 + 2 − 6)/0 = **0/0** ⟹ transform. **Factor:** x² + x − 6 = (x + 3)(x − 2), so the expression = (x + 3)(x − 2)/(x − 2) = **x + 3 for x ≠ 2**. **Limit:** 2 + 3 = **5**. **Break:** f(2) undefined with limit 5 ⟹ **removable hole at (2, 5)**; the repair f(2) = 5 restores continuity. The factor-and-cancel signature — a shared linear factor — is the universal birthplace of removable rational breaks.

**NEB-style (3m): Triage f(x) = (x + 2)/(x² − 4) at each point of discontinuity.** — **Suspicious points:** zeros of x² − 4 = (x − 2)(x + 2), i.e. x = 2 and x = −2 — triage each separately. **At x = −2:** cancel the common factor: f(x) = 1/(x − 2) for x ≠ ±2; lim_{x→−2} f(x) = 1/(−4) = **−1/4** — finite ⟹ **removable** (hole at (−2, −1/4)); repair f(−2) = −1/4. **At x = 2:** the simplified form 1/(x − 2) has numerator 1 ≠ 0 with denominator → 0 ⟹ **blow-up**: lim_{x→2⁺} = +∞, lim_{x→2⁻} = −∞ ⟹ **infinite discontinuity** — not removable. **Verdict:** one function, two species — the cancelled factor's zero is always the removable candidate; the surviving denominator's zero is always the infinite one.

**NEB-style (6m): For f(x) = (x² − 5x + 6)/(x − 2) for x ≠ 2, f(2) = 1: find the limit at 2, classify the discontinuity, and state the repair value.** — **Diagnose:** substitute x = 2: (4 − 10 + 6)/0 = **0/0** ⟹ a shared root exists. **Factor:** x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3) ⟹ f(x) = x − 3 for x ≠ 2. **Limit:** lim_{x→2} f(x) = **−1**. **Classification:** the limit exists; f(2) = 1 ≠ −1 ⟹ the failure is only at the point's value ⟹ **removable discontinuity** (a detached dot at (2, 1) hovering over the hole at (2, −1)). **Repair:** redefine **f(2) = −1** ⟹ value = limit ⟹ continuous at 2. **Deep point:** the 0/0 diagnosis guaranteed removability before the factoring — a shared root means the neighbourhood's approach is governed by the cancelled quotient, so the break lives at the point, not in the road leading to it.

**NEB-style (5m): For f(x) = (x³ − 27)/(x − 3) for x ≠ 3, determine the value f(3) must have for f to be continuous at 3.** — **Diagnose:** at x = 3: (27 − 27)/0 = **0/0** ⟹ shared root. **Factor (difference of cubes):** x³ − 27 = (x − 3)(x² + 3x + 9) ⟹ f(x) = x² + 3x + 9 for x ≠ 3. **Limit:** 9 + 9 + 9 = **27**. **Required value:** continuity needs f(3) = limit ⟹ **f(3) = 27**. **Check the shape:** the graph is the parabola y = x² + 3x + 9 with a hole at (3, 27); assigning f(3) = 27 fills it exactly. **Deep point:** "the value that makes it continuous" is always **the limit** — the question is the three-part test inverted: instead of checking Part 3, you *engineer* Part 3 to pass by setting the value to what Parts 1 and 2 already produced.

**NEB-style (6m): For f(x) = (x + 2)(x² − 9)/(x² + x − 6) for x ≠ 2 and x ≠ −3: find all removable breaks, the limit at each, and the repaired values.** — **Factor everything:** x² − 9 = (x−3)(x+3); x² + x − 6 = (x+3)(x−2). So f(x) = (x+2)(x−3)(x+3)/[(x+3)(x−2)] = **(x+2)(x−3)/(x−2)** after cancelling (x+3) — licensed for x ≠ −3. **Break at x = −3:** the cancelled factor's root ⟹ **removable**. Limit: (−1)(−6)/(−5) = 6/(−5) = **−6/5** ⟹ repair f(−3) = −6/5. **Break at x = 2:** the surviving denominator's root — check the numerator at 2: (4)(−1) = −4 ≠ 0 ⟹ no cancellation possible ⟹ **non-removable (infinite)**: as x → 2, denominator → 0 with numerator → −4 ⟹ the sides blow up (a wall). **Summary:** one removable break at −3 (limit −6/5, repair value −6/5) and one non-removable wall at 2. **Deep point:** after full factorisation, *cancelled* roots are removable and *surviving denominator* roots are not — the factorisation is simultaneously the limit computation and the discontinuity classification.

**NEB-style (5m): A student says f(x) = (x² − 1)/(x − 1) is discontinuous at x = 1 and therefore lim_{x→1} f(x) does not exist. Assess the claim.** — **The discontinuity claim:** correct in classification — f(1) is undefined (0/0), so f is not continuous at 1. **The limit claim:** wrong — the limit and the value are independent; the limit reads the neighbourhood, which is healthy. **Compute:** (x²−1)/(x−1) = x + 1 for x ≠ 1 ⟹ lim_{x→1} f(x) = **2**. **Correct statement:** f has a **removable** discontinuity at 1 — the limit exists (2) while the value does not; defining f(1) = 2 repairs continuity. **Deep point:** the student treated "discontinuous" as "limit fails," conflating the point with its neighbourhood — the removable/jump/infinite taxonomy exists precisely because discontinuities differ in *where* they live, and only the point-local kind leaves limits intact.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Repairable Break

A **removable discontinuity** is a break the limit ignores: the two-sided limit exists but f(a) is missing or mismatched. The repair is always the same — define or redefine f(a) to equal the limit.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Definition and detection

- **Removable at a** ⟺ lim_{x→a} f(x) = L exists (finite) but f(a) ≠ L or f(a) is undefined.
- **Detection protocol:** substitute (get 0/0 or undefined), compute the limit by transformation, compare with f(a).

### 2.2 The two species

- **Hole:** f(a) undefined, limit exists — (x²−4)/(x−2) at 2 with limit 4.
- **Mismatch:** f(a) defined but ≠ limit — the redefined-point case (f(1) = 3 vs limit 2).

### 2.3 The repair theorem

- **Theorem:** defining (or redefining) **f(a) = L** makes f continuous at a — the discontinuity was removable precisely because one value fixes it.
- After repair, the function is continuous; before repair, the graph shows an isolated open dot (hole) or a detached dot (mismatch).

### 2.4 Common sources

- Rational functions with cancelled common factors: (x²−9)/(x−3) → hole at 3 with limit 6.
- Piecewise definitions with a deliberately wrong middle value.
- Roots of numerators shared with denominators — the factor-and-cancel signature.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Removable discontinuity** | Limit exists, value missing/mismatched | hole at (2, 4) |
| **Hole** | f(a) undefined, limit exists | open dot on graph |
| **Repair** | Set f(a) = lim | one redefinition |
| **Factor-and-cancel** | Common factor exposes the hole | (x²−9)/(x−3) |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why "removable"

- The defect lives at a single point and the limit already knows the correct value: plugging it in removes the break entirely. Jumps and blow-ups need infinitely many point-changes or none works — they are not removable.

### 4.2 The graph signature

- A hole is an **open dot** on an otherwise continuous curve; a mismatch adds a **closed dot** floating elsewhere. Both are single-point defects — the visual fingerprint of removability.

### 4.3 Simplification caution

- Cancelling (x − a) changes the domain: the simplified expression is continuous at a but the **original** is not — always state the x ≠ a licence and report the hole.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Discontinuity triage**

| Type | Limit exists? | Repair |
|---|---|---|
| removable (hole/mismatch) | yes | define f(a) = L |
| jump | no (finite sides differ) | none |
| infinite | no (blow-up) | none |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Cancelled ≠ continuous:** the cancellation proves the limit, not the original function's continuity — the domain shrank.
**Removable needs a finite limit:** an infinite limit at a is an infinite discontinuity, never removable.
**Hole location:** the hole sits at (a, **L**) — at the limit's height, not at f(a)'s (which doesn't exist).

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): Find the point of discontinuity of f(x) = (x² − 9)/(x − 3), classify it, and state the repair.** — Domain: x ≠ 3. **Limit:** factor (x−3)(x+3)/(x−3) = x + 3 (x ≠ 3) ⟹ lim_{x→3} = **6**. **Classification:** f(3) undefined with the limit existing ⟹ **removable discontinuity (hole)** at (3, 6). **Repair:** define f(3) = 6; the repaired f equals x + 3 everywhere and is continuous on ℝ.

**NEB-style (2m): For f(x) = (x² + x − 6)/(x − 2), find lim_{x→2} f(x) and the removable break.** — Factor: (x + 3)(x − 2)/(x − 2) = x + 3 (x ≠ 2) ⟹ limit **5**. f(2) undefined ⟹ **removable hole at (2, 5)**; repair f(2) = 5.

**NEB-style (2m): f(x) = (x + 2)/(x² − 4) at x = −2: removable or not?** — Factor denominator: (x + 2)/[(x−2)(x+2)] = 1/(x − 2) for x ≠ −2, ±... for x ≠ ±2. **Limit as x → −2:** 1/(−2 − 2) = **−1/4** — finite! So x = −2 is **removable** (hole at (−2, −1/4)); repair f(−2) = −1/4. But at x = 2 the simplified 1/(x−2) **blows up** ⟹ x = 2 is an **infinite** (non-removable) discontinuity. One function, two species — triage each point separately.

## 8. Deep Conceptual — Removability Is a Statement About the Neighbourhood

- A removable break means the **neighbourhood is healthy** — both sides approach one value — and only the point itself is sick (missing or wrong). The graph is a curve with a hole (or a relocated dot), not a torn curve.
- **Why the repair is legitimate:** redefining f(a) = L changes the function at exactly one point, and limits are blind to single points — so the limit is untouched, and the new value matches it. The repair costs nothing dynamically; every limit, and later every derivative, is unchanged.
- **The two sub-species:** the **hole** (f(a) undefined — the formula excludes a) and the **mismatch** (f(a) defined but ≠ L — an assigned value disagreeing with the approach). Same cure, different pictures: open dot vs detached dot.

## 9. Deep Conceptual — Removable Breaks as Simplification Shadows

- Most removable breaks are **created by cancellation**: f(x) = (x−2)·g(x)/(x−2) is really g(x) wearing a disguise that breaks at 2. The 0/0 form at a is the signature of this hidden common factor.
- **The limit sees through the disguise:** because the definition ignores x = a, the cancelled and uncancelled forms have identical limits — the removable break is invisible to every limit question and visible only to continuity and value questions.
- **Design lesson:** when a problem *assigns* a value at a formula's excluded point, it is usually asking you to either diagnose the mismatch (continuity) or supply the matching value (repair). The assigned value is the exam's handle on an otherwise invisible point.

## 10. Deep Conceptual — Removable vs Non-Removable: The Repair Test as Classification

- The single diagnostic question — **can redefining finitely many point-values make f continuous?** — splits all discontinuities into removable (yes) and non-removable (no). It is the cleanest classification boundary in the taxonomy.
- **Why jumps fail the test:** a jump's sickness is in the neighbourhood (sides disagree), which no point-value edit touches — you would need to change the function on an entire side. Infinite and oscillatory breaks fail even more thoroughly.
- **The repair test foreshadows derivatives:** |x| at 0 is continuous but non-differentiable, and no value edit fixes the corner — the analogous "removability" question for slopes. Calculus iterates the same architecture one level up: neighbourhood agreement, then point agreement.

data.title: Types of Discontinuity: Jump
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Step in the Graph

A **jump discontinuity** occurs when both one-sided limits exist finitely but **disagree**. The graph steps from one height to another; no redefinition can repair it, because the limit itself does not exist.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Definition and detection

- **Jump at a** ⟺ lim_{x→a⁻} f(x) = L and lim_{x→a⁺} f(x) = M both exist finitely with **L ≠ M**.
- **Detection:** compute both one-sided limits (branch selection for piecewise functions); compare.

### 2.2 Jump size and classification

- **Jump size = M − L** (RHL − LHL) — the height of the step.
- Jump discontinuities are **non-removable**: no single value f(a) can make LHL = RHL.
- **Special case — the Heaviside step:** f(x) = 0 for x < 0, 1 for x ≥ 0: jump of size 1 at 0, the prototype switch.

### 2.3 Where jumps live

- Piecewise-defined functions (tax brackets, shipping rates, sign functions).
- Floor/ceiling functions at every integer.
- Digitised/quantised signals — sampling turns continuous waves into staircases.

### 2.4 One-sided continuity

- A jump function can still be **left-continuous or right-continuous** at the step: f continuous from the right at a ⟺ f(a) = RHL. The Heaviside step is right-continuous at 0.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Jump discontinuity** | Finite one-sided limits that differ | step at 0 |
| **Jump size** | RHL − LHL | 1 for Heaviside |
| **Non-removable** | No single value repairs it | inherent to the sides |
| **Right-continuous** | f(a) = RHL | Heaviside at 0 |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why no repair exists

- Removability needs a limit to copy. Here the two sides report different values — there is no single L to assign; the defect is structural, in the neighbourhoods themselves.

### 4.2 Reading jumps on graphs

- A jump shows as a **vertical gap**: closed dot on the side owning f(a), open dot on the other. The step's height is measurable — RHL − LHL.

### 4.3 Jumps in the wild

- Switches (on/off), thresholds (tax, shipping), quantisation (audio samples): the mathematics of "below vs above" is exactly the theory of jump discontinuities.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Non-removable species**

| Type | Sides | Graph |
|---|---|---|
| jump | finite, unequal | vertical gap |
| infinite | blow-up | asymptote |
| oscillatory | none | dense wiggles |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Finite sides ≠ existence:** the two-sided limit needs *equal* finite sides — unequal finite is still DNE.
**f(a) doesn't matter for the jump:** the step is between the sides; whether f(a) matches one of them decides one-sided continuity, not the jump's existence.
**Jump ≠ hole:** a hole keeps the sides agreeing; a jump breaks the agreement — categorically different repairs (none vs one value).

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): For f(x) = { x + 2 if x < 1; 5 − x if x > 1; 3 if x = 1 }, find both one-sided limits at 1, the jump size, and discuss continuity.** — **LHL:** x + 2 → **3**. **RHL:** 5 − x → **4**. **Jump:** 4 − 3 = **1** — the two-sided limit does not exist ⟹ **jump discontinuity at x = 1**, non-removable. **Value:** f(1) = 3 = LHL ⟹ f is **left-continuous** at 1 but not right-continuous. No repair possible: changing f(1) can match at most one side.

**NEB-style (2m): Show that the floor function f(x) = ⌊x⌋ has a jump discontinuity at every integer.** — At n ∈ ℤ: for x ↑ n, ⌊x⌋ = n − 1 ⟹ **LHL = n − 1**; for x ↓ n, ⌊x⌋ = n ⟹ **RHL = n**. Sides finite but unequal ⟹ **jump of size 1** at every integer; between integers ⌊x⌋ is constant, hence continuous. The staircase graph shows a unit step at each integer — closed dot on the right side (⌊n⌋ = n), open on the left.

**NEB-style (2m): Construct a function with a jump of size 2 at x = 0, right-continuous there.** — Take f(x) = 0 for x < 0 and f(x) = 2 for x ≥ 0. **LHL = 0, RHL = 2**, jump size 2 ✓. **Right-continuity:** f(0) = 2 = RHL ✓ — the closed dot sits on the right branch. (Any pair of constants c, c + 2 with the boundary assigned to the upper branch works.)

## 8. Deep Conceptual — Jumps as Decisions, Not Defects

- Some jumps are *engineered*: tax brackets, postage tiers, signal thresholds, on/off switches. The function's rule legitimately changes at the threshold, and the jump size measures the change. A jump is a defect only when the underlying quantity is conserved (position, money, temperature) — then a jump would mean teleportation.
- **The jump size is data:** J = RHL − LHL quantifies the discontinuity. In piecewise models it is the "fee," "surcharge," or "phase change" magnitude — often the quantity the question actually cares about.
- **One-sided continuity is the natural habitat:** step functions are usually continuous from one side (the dot sits on one end of each segment). Asking "continuous from the left/right" is more informative at a jump than the two-sided verdict "not continuous."

## 9. Deep Conceptual — Jumps Defeat Every Limit Tool, By Design

- No transformation repairs a jump: factoring, conjugates, and stars all assume the neighbourhood is trying to agree. At a jump the sides are *not trying* to agree — the failure is structural, in the definitions, not computational.
- **L'Hôpital does not apply:** the 0/0 and ∞/∞ forms require both contestants to be approaching (the same kind of) trouble. At a jump the one-sided limits are finite and unequal — there is nothing indeterminate to resolve, only a verdict to record.
- **What still works:** one-sided limits fully describe the jump; the existence theorem correctly reports failure; the graph convention (filled dot on the side that owns the value) records the assignment. The tools don't fail — they correctly certify a non-removable break.

## 10. Deep Conceptual — Jumps and the Boundaries of the Big Theorems

## 1. Topic Introduction — The Step in the Graph

A **jump discontinuity** occurs when both one-sided limits exist finitely but **disagree**. The graph steps from one height to another; no redefinition can repair it, because the limit itself does not exist.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Definition and detection

- **Jump at a** ⟺ lim_{x→a⁻} f(x) = L and lim_{x→a⁺} f(x) = M both exist finitely with **L ≠ M**.
- **Detection:** compute both one-sided limits (branch selection for piecewise functions); compare.

### 2.2 Jump size and classification

- **Jump size = M − L** (RHL − LHL) — the height of the step.
- Jump discontinuities are **non-removable**: no single value f(a) can make LHL = RHL.
- **Special case — the Heaviside step:** f(x) = 0 for x < 0, 1 for x ≥ 0: jump of size 1 at 0, the prototype switch.

### 2.3 Where jumps live

- Piecewise-defined functions (tax brackets, shipping rates, sign functions).
- Floor/ceiling functions at every integer.
- Digitised/quantised signals — sampling turns continuous waves into staircases.

### 2.4 One-sided continuity

- A jump function can still be **left-continuous or right-continuous** at the step: f continuous from the right at a ⟺ f(a) = RHL. The Heaviside step is right-continuous at 0.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Jump discontinuity** | Finite one-sided limits that differ | step at 0 |
| **Jump size** | RHL − LHL | 1 for Heaviside |
| **Non-removable** | No single value repairs it | inherent to the sides |
| **Right-continuous** | f(a) = RHL | Heaviside at 0 |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why no repair exists

- Removability needs a limit to copy. Here the two sides report different values — there is no single L to assign; the defect is structural, in the neighbourhoods themselves.

### 4.2 Reading jumps on graphs

- A jump shows as a **vertical gap**: closed dot on the side owning f(a), open dot on the other. The step's height is measurable — RHL − LHL.

### 4.3 Jumps in the wild

- Switches (on/off), thresholds (tax, shipping), quantisation (audio samples): the mathematics of "below vs above" is exactly the theory of jump discontinuities.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Non-removable species**

| Type | Sides | Graph |
|---|---|---|
| jump | finite, unequal | vertical gap |
| infinite | blow-up | asymptote |
| oscillatory | none | dense wiggles |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Finite sides ≠ existence:** the two-sided limit needs *equal* finite sides — unequal finite is still DNE.
**f(a) doesn't matter for the jump:** the step is between the sides; whether f(a) matches one of them decides one-sided continuity, not the jump's existence.
**Jump ≠ hole:** a hole keeps the sides agreeing; a jump breaks the agreement — categorically different repairs (none vs one value).

## 7. Exam Application

No repair possible: changing f(1) can match at most one side.

**NEB-style (2m): Show that the floor function f(x) = ⌊x⌋ has a jump discontinuity at every integer.** — At n ∈ ℤ: for x ↑ n, ⌊x⌋ = n − 1 ⟹ **LHL = n − 1**; for x ↓ n, ⌊x⌋ = n ⟹ **RHL = n**. The staircase graph shows a unit step at each integer — closed dot on the right side (⌊n⌋ = n), open on the left.

**NEB-style (2m): Construct a function with a jump of size 2 at x = 0, right-continuous there.** — Take f(x) = 0 for x < 0 and f(x) = 2 for x ≥ 0. **LHL = 0, RHL = 2**, jump size 2 ✓. **Right-continuity:** f(0) = 2 = RHL ✓ — the closed dot sits on the right branch. ## 8. Deep Conceptual — Jumps as Decisions, Not Defects

- Some jumps are *engineered*: tax brackets, postage tiers, signal thresholds, on/off switches. The function's rule legitimately changes at the threshold, and the jump size measures the change. A jump is a defect only when the underlying quantity is conserved (position, money, temperature) — then a jump would mean teleportation.

## 9. Deep Conceptual — Jumps Defeat Every Limit Tool, By Design

- No transformation repairs a jump: factoring, conjugates, and stars all assume the neighbourhood is trying to agree. At a jump the sides are *not trying* to agree — the failure is structural, in the definitions, not computational.
- **L'Hôpital does not apply:** the 0/0 and ∞/∞ forms require both contestants to be approaching (the same kind of) trouble. At a jump the one-sided limits are finite and unequal — there is nothing indeterminate to resolve, only a verdict to record.

- **Derivatives cannot jump (Darboux):** derivatives, though possibly discontinuous, never have jump discontinuities — they satisfy the intermediate value property themselves. Jumps belong to functions, not to their rates; the asymmetry is a deep structural fact.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Vertical Wall

An **infinite discontinuity** occurs when f blows up at a: at least one one-sided limit is ±∞. The graph sprouts a **vertical asymptote** x = a — the line the curve approaches but never touches.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Definition and detection

- **Infinite discontinuity at a** ⟺ lim_{x→a⁻} f(x) or lim_{x→a⁺} f(x) is **+∞ or −∞**.
- **Detection:** c/0 forms (numerator → c ≠ 0, denominator → 0); also log x at 0⁺, and unbounded growth like e^{1/x} compositions.

### 2.2 The two species of blow-up

- **Split asymptote:** sides infinite with **opposite** signs — 1/x at 0 (−∞ left, +∞ right); caused by **odd-multiplicity** zeros of the denominator.
- **Unified blow-up:** both sides the same infinity — 1/x² at 0 (+∞ both); **even multiplicity** zeros.
- Either way the two-sided limit **does not exist** — infinity is not a value.

### 2.3 The vertical asymptote

- **x = a is a vertical asymptote** ⟺ |f(x)| → ∞ as x → a from at least one side. The curve hugs the line without meeting it (or crosses it far away — asymptotes describe local behaviour).
- Denominator zeros of rational functions (after cancelling common factors) are the standard asymptote factories.

### 2.4 Non-removability

- No redefinition helps: the neighbourhood values are unbounded, so no finite f(a) reconciles them. Infinite discontinuities are **non-removable** by nature.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Infinite discontinuity** | A one-sided limit is ±∞ | 1/x at 0 |
| **Vertical asymptote** | \|f\| → ∞ at x = a | x = 0 for 1/x |
| **Split vs unified** | Opposite vs same infinities | 1/x vs 1/x² |
| **Multiplicity rule** | Odd zero splits, even unifies | (x−a)³ vs (x−a)² |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Multiplicity is the sign story

- Near a, (x − a)ᵐ changes sign across a iff m is odd. Dividing c by it: odd m ⟹ the sides split (±∞); even m ⟹ they unify (+∞ after squaring). The multiplicity of the denominator zero is the entire classification.

### 4.2 Cancel first, then triage

- Cancel common factors (removable holes at those zeros), then the surviving denominator zeros give asymptotes. The (x+2)/(x²−4) pattern: hole at −2, wall at 2.

### 4.3 Logs and composites

- ln x → −∞ as x → 0⁺: a one-sided wall at the domain edge. Compositions inherit blow-ups: e^{1/x} → ∞ from the right, → 1·... → e^{−∞} = 0 from the left — walls can wear disguises.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Blow-up atlas**

## 6. Common Confusions

**∞ is not a limit value:** "limit = ∞" is shorthand for unbounded behaviour; the two-sided limit still DNE.
**Every denominator zero is an asymptote:** only after cancelling common factors — shared zeros are holes first.

## 7. Exam Application

Both are infinite discontinuities; f → ±∞ near each.

**NEB-style (2m): Show that lim_{x→0⁺} ln x = −∞ and interpret graphically.** — For x → 0⁺, ln x = −|ln x| → **−∞**: the log dives without bound at its domain's left edge. **Graph:** x = 0 (the y-axis) is a **one-sided vertical asymptote** — the curve hugs it downward; no left side exists (domain x > 0), so the wall is visible only from the right.

**NEB-style (2m): Discuss lim_{x→0} e^{1/x}.** — **Right side:** x → 0⁺ ⟹ 1/x → +∞ ⟹ e^{1/x} → **+∞**. **Left side:** 1/x → −∞ ⟹ e^{1/x} → **e^{−∞} = 0**. **Verdict:** RHL = +∞ (infinite), LHL = 0 — the right side blows up ⟹ **infinite discontinuity at 0** (non-removable), with a disguised wall: the exponential turns the split of 1/x into a one-sided blow-up against a finite left approach.

## 8. Deep Conceptual — Walls Are Real Features, Not Failures of Nerve

- An infinite discontinuity encodes **unboundedness**, which is genuine mathematical information: near a wall the function takes arbitrarily large values. Writing "the limit is ∞" is a *description* of that behaviour; writing "the limit does not exist" is the *strict verdict* — ∞ is not a real number, so the limit still fails to exist. Both statements belong in a full answer.

## 9. Deep Conceptual — Infinite Limits Compose With the Algebra of Signs

- The limit laws partially extend to infinities: ∞ + c = ∞, ∞·c > 0 = ∞, ∞/c = ∞ — but **∞ − ∞, 0·∞, ∞/∞ stay indeterminate**: two infinities can compete, and their race's outcome needs the rates, not the signs.

**NEB-style (5m): For f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x² − 4x + 4), classify the discontinuity at x = 2 completely.** — **Factor:** numerator (x−2)(x+2); denominator (x−2)² ⟹ f(x) = (x+2)/(x−2) for x ≠ 2. **One factor cancelled, one survived:** the cancelled (x−2) would have been removable, but the surviving (x−2) in the denominator dominates. **Behaviour at 2:** numerator → 4 ≠ 0; denominator → 0⁺ from both sides (a square) ⟹ f → **+∞ from both sides** — a **unifying wall** (even power), lim = +∞ (description), limit does not exist (verdict). **Classification: infinite (non-removable) discontinuity** at x = 2. **Deep point:** when a root appears in both numerator and denominator, compare powers: numerator's power 1 vs denominator's power 2 ⟹ one power cancels, one remains ⟹ the break is infinite, not removable — removability requires the denominator's root to be *fully* cancelled.

**NEB-style (6m): Evaluate the one-sided limits of f(x) = 1/(x − 2)² + 3 at x = 2 and sketch-reason the graph's behaviour there.** — **Both sides:** (x − 2)² > 0 for every x ≠ 2, regardless of side ⟹ 1/(x−2)² → **+∞** from both the left and the right. **Shift:** adding 3 does not change the blow-up — f → **+∞ from both sides**; the limit does not exist (no finite value), but the wall is **unifying** (even power) rather than splitting. **Graph reading:** both branches of the curve rise along the vertical line x = 2, hugging it upward; the +3 lifts the branches' tails so the curve tends to the horizontal level y = 3 far from the wall. **Deep point:** the even power makes the two sides *agree* at infinity — a rare case where the existence theorem's agreement condition is satisfied at an infinite level; convention records this as lim = +∞ while the strict finite-limit verdict remains "does not exist."

**NEB-style (5m): A student applies L'Hôpital's rule to lim_{x→0⁺} 1/x and obtains lim (0)/(−1/x²) = 0. Diagnose the error completely.** — **The form check fails:** at x → 0⁺, the numerator 1 is a **nonzero constant**, the denominator x → 0 — the form is **c/0⁺ → +∞**, not 0/0 and not ∞/∞. **L'Hôpital's hypotheses:** the rule applies only to 0/0 or ∞/∞; applying it to c/0 is outside its licence, so the "answer" 0 is meaningless. **Correct evaluation:** numerator positive constant, denominator small positive ⟹ quotient large positive ⟹ **lim_{x→0⁺} 1/x = +∞** (blow-up; the limit does not exist as a finite value). **Deep point:** the form check is not paperwork — it is the *hypothesis test* that gates the rule; every L'Hôpital solution must open by naming the indeterminate form, and c/0 is precisely the common case where a student's shortcut manufactures a wrong finite answer from a genuine wall.

## 1. Topic Introduction — Trigonometry Meets 0/0

**Trigonometric limits** deploy the sin x/x star and its relatives: sin kx/x, tan kx/x, (1 − cos x)/x², and compound-angle constructions. The craft is steering every unknown 0/0 into a standard form.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 The core star and its rescalings

- **lim_{u→0} sin u/u = 1** (radians). **Rescaling theorem:** lim_{x→0} sin(kx)/x = k, since sin(kx)/x = k·sin(kx)/(kx) with kx → 0.
- **lim_{x→0} sin(kx)/(mx) = k/m** — the general ratio form.
- **lim_{x→0} tan(kx)/x = k** (tan u/u → 1 via sin/cos).

### 2.2 The cosine-squared family

- **lim_{x→0} (1 − cos x)/x² = 1/2** — via 1 − cos x = 2sin²(x/2): the expression becomes 2sin²(x/2)/x² = ½·[sin(x/2)/(x/2)]² → ½·1 = ½.
- **lim_{x→0} (1 − cos kx)/x² = k²/2** — same route with the rescaling.

### 2.3 Compound-angle steering

- Expressions like sin 3x/sin 5x, (1 − cos 2x)/x sin x, sin(x + a) − sin a: rewrite with identities (sin A − sin B = 2 cos((A+B)/2) sin((A−B)/2)), split into standard ratios, and multiply by 1 (form kx/kx factors).

### 2.4 The squeeze safety net

- When steering stalls, squeeze: |sin u| ≤ |u| bounds the expression. The sandwich proof of sin x/x → 1 is the template: (cos x)·... sin x/x is trapped between cos x and 1.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Standard trig star** | sin u/u → 1 (radians) | the anchor |
| **Rescaling** | sin(kx)/x → k | insert kx/kx |
| **Half-angle route** | 1 − cos x = 2sin²(x/2) | powers the ½ |
| **Squeeze** | Trap between two known limits | sin x/x proof |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why radians are non-negotiable

- sin x/x → 1 equates arc and chord asymptotics; degrees carry π/180 in every derivative and limit. Convert first, compute second.

### 4.2 The kx/kx insertion

- The universal move: multiply and divide by the argument's coefficient. sin 5x/sin 3x = [5x·sin5x/(5x)]/[3x·sin3x/(3x)] → (5·1)/(3·1) = 5/3 — steering by bookkeeping.

### 4.3 Identities as reducers

- Compound angles and half-angles convert unfamiliar trig expressions into products of standard ratios. Keep the identity sheet beside every trig limit.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Trig limit shelf**

| Limit | Value | Route |
|---|---|---|
| sin kx/x | k | kx/kx insertion |
| tan kx/x | k | sin/cos split |
| (1 − cos x)/x² | 1/2 | half-angle |
| (1 − cos kx)/x² | k²/2 | half-angle + rescale |
| sin kx/sin mx | k/m | double insertion |

## 6. Common Confusions

**Degrees again:** every trig limit in this topic assumes radians — state it.
%%**
**Half-angle factor:** (1 − cos x)/x² is ½, not 1 — the 2sin²(x/2) identity carries the ½.
**sin kx/x vs sin x/x:** the coefficient k survives as a factor — forgetting it halves marks on rescaled forms.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): Evaluate lim_{x→0} sin 5x/sin 3x.** — Insert the rescalings: sin 5x/sin 3x = [5x·(sin 5x/5x)]/[3x·(sin 3x/3x)] = (5/3)·[sin 5x/5x]/[sin 3x/3x]. As x → 0 both bracketed stars → 1 ⟹ limit = **5/3**. (General rule: sin kx/sin mx → k/m.)

**NEB-style (3m): Evaluate lim_{x→0} (1 − cos 4x)/x².** — Half-angle: 1 − cos 4x = 2sin²(2x). Expression = 2sin²(2x)/x² = 2·[sin 2x/(2x)]²·4 = 8·[sin 2x/2x]² → 8·1 = **8** — matching the formula k²/2 = 16/2 = 8 ✓.

**NEB-style (3m): Evaluate lim_{x→0} (x − sin x)/x³.** — Direct forms stall; use the cubic refinement **x − sin x ~ x³/6** (from sin x = x − x³/6 + ⋯): the limit is **1/6**. Derivation without series: x − sin x = x(1 − sin x/x), and 1 − sin x/x = [x − sin x]/x — circular; the honest elementary route applies the standard limits twice via sin x − sin y identities or accepts the known refinement — quote it as a standard result.

## 8. Deep Conceptual — The Sine Star as a Geometry Theorem

- sin u/u → 1 is not algebra — it is the **squeeze theorem applied to geometry**: for small positive u, the areas/lengths give sin u < u < tan u, and dividing by sin u pins 1 < u/sin u < 1/cos u → 1. The star is a squeeze result wearing a trig costume.
- **Why radians are structural:** the inequality sin u < u compares a chord-vertical to an *arc*, and arcs are measured in radians. In degrees the star reads sin u°/(u°·π/180) — the π/180 factor is the residue of the wrong unit; radians are the unit where geometry and limits coincide.
- **The star's corollaries cascade:** (1 − cos u)/u → 0 (Pythagorean identity), tan u/u → 1 (quotient of stars), (1 − cos u)/u² → 1/2 (second-order refinement). One geometric fact powers the whole trig-limit table.

## 9. Deep Conceptual — Orders of Vanishing: The Trig Hierarchy

- Near 0, the trig functions die at **different speeds**: sin u ~ u (order 1), 1 − cos u ~ u²/2 (order 2), u − sin u ~ u³/6 (order 3), tan u − u ~ u³/3 (order 3). The order is the exponent of the leading term — the function's "vanishing exponent."
- **Reading races by order:** in a quotient, same-order contestants leave a nonzero constant (sin 3x/tan 3x → 3x/3x = 1); a higher-order numerator dies faster ⟹ limit 0; a higher-order denominator ⟹ ±∞. The order comparison decides the limit before any computation.
- **Why the hierarchy matters for L'Hôpital:** each order of vanishing is one derivative pass — sin u/u resolves in one pass, (1−cos u)/u² in two, (u − sin u)/u³ in three. The hierarchy is the map of how much work each 0/0 form will cost.

## 10. Deep Conceptual — Substitution Depth: Nesting Trig Stars

- The stars compose: with u = g(x) → 0, sin(g(x)) ~ g(x) — so sin(x²) ~ x², sin(tan x) ~ tan x ~ x. Each nesting adds a layer but the *leading-order* behaviour is governed by the innermost argument's approach to 0.
- **The classic trap — sin of something not → 0:** sin u/u → 1 needs u → 0. For sin(1/x)/x-type expressions the star does not apply; the squeeze theorem or damping is needed instead. Always annotate what u is and why it → 0.
- **Steering with trig identities:** when the expression resists direct star-matching, identities (double-angle, Pythagorean, sum-to-product) reshape it into star form — e.g. 1 − cos 2x = 2sin²x converts a second-order problem into two first-order stars squared.

Squeeze safety net: |sin u| <= |u|. Cubic refinements: x - sin x ~ x^3/6; sin x - x cos x ~ x^3/3. Degrees break every trig limit - convert first.
importantConcepts: The kx/kx insertion is the universal steering move: multiply and divide by the coefficient so every factor becomes a standard star.
examples: ***The half-angle halving*** - 1 - cos x = 2 sin^2(x/2) is why the cosine family limits carry 1/2 and k^2/2: the identity does the arithmetic.
universalFacts: Small-angle approximations in optics and pendulum motion (sin th ~ th) are sin x/x -> 1 in engineering clothing.

examShortTricks: Insert kx/kx. Half-angle for 1 - cos. Compound-angle identities for differences. Quote radians. Fallback: cubic refinements x - sin x ~ x^3/6.

- lim_{x→0} sin(kx)/x = k; sin(kx)/(mx) = k/m; tan(kx)/x = k
- lim_{x→0} (1 − cos x)/x² = 1/2; (1 − cos kx)/x² = k²/2

Evaluate lim_{x→0} (1 − cos 4x)/x².

practiceQuestions: **NEB-style (3m): Evaluate lim_{x→0} sin 5x/sin 3x.** — **Steering by insertion:** multiply and divide each sine by its own argument: sin 5x/sin 3x = [5x · (sin 5x)/(5x)] / [3x · (sin 3x)/(3x)] = (5/3) · [(sin 5x)/(5x)] / [(sin 3x)/(3x)]. **Apply the star:** as x → 0, both 5x → 0 and 3x → 0, so (sin 5x)/(5x) → 1 and (sin 3x)/(3x) → 1 (radians throughout). **Result:** (5/3)·(1/1) = **5/3**. **General rule harvested:** lim_{x→0} sin(kx)/sin(mx) = k/m — the double insertion turns any sine ratio into a coefficient ratio.

**NEB-style (3m): Evaluate lim_{x→0} (1 − cos 4x)/x².** — **Half-angle identity:** 1 − cos θ = 2sin²(θ/2), so 1 − cos 4x = **2sin²(2x)**. **Rewrite:** (1 − cos 4x)/x² = 2sin²(2x)/x² = 2 · [sin 2x/(2x)]² · (2x)²/x² = 2 · [sin 2x/(2x)]² · 4 = **8·[sin 2x/(2x)]²**. **Apply the star:** sin 2x/(2x) → 1 as x → 0 ⟹ the limit is 8·1² = **8**. **Formula check:** the general result (1 − cos kx)/x² → k²/2 gives 4²/2 = 16/2 = 8 ✓ — the half-angle identity is exactly where the ½ and the k² come from.

**NEB-style (3m): Evaluate lim_{x→0} (x − sin x)/x³.** — **Why steering stalls:** both x − sin x and x³ vanish to third order — the first-order standard limits cancel out, exposing the cubic layer. **Cubic refinement (standard result):** from the small-x expansion sin x = x − x³/6 + O(x⁵) (radians), **x − sin x = x³/6 + O(x⁵) ~ x³/6**. **Limit:** (x − sin x)/x³ → (x³/6)/x³ = **1/6**. **Consistency:** the companion limit (sin x − x cos x)/x³ = 1/3 (NEB 2024) satisfies the identity (x − sin x) + (sin x − x cos x) = x(1 − cos x) ~ x³/2, and 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2 ✓ — the three refinements interlock. At this level the refinement is quoted as a standard result derived from the sin x/x machinery.

**NEB-style (6m): Evaluate lim_{x→0} (sin 3x · tan 5x)/(x²), annotating every star used.** — **Split the product** (limits of the factors exist — licensed): = lim (sin 3x)/x · lim (tan 5x)/x. **First factor (star sin u/u → 1, u = 3x → 0):** (sin 3x)/x = 3·(sin 3x)/(3x) → **3**. **Second factor (star tan u/u → 1, u = 5x → 0):** (tan 5x)/x = 5·(tan 5x)/(5x) → **5**. **Product: 3 × 5 = 15.** **Order reading:** sin 3x ~ 3x (order 1), tan 5x ~ 5x (order 1) ⟹ numerator ~ 15x², matching the x² denominator exactly ⟹ a nonzero constant was guaranteed before any steering. **Deep point:** the order comparison predicted the answer's *type* (finite nonzero), and the steering factors (3 and 5) delivered its *value* — annotate the star, name the u, then multiply constants.

**NEB-style (6m): Evaluate lim_{x→0} (1 − cos 3x)/(x·sin 2x).** — **Order diagnosis first:** 1 − cos 3x ~ (3x)²/2 = 9x²/2 (order 2); x·sin 2x ~ x·2x = 2x² (order 2) — **same order** ⟹ a nonzero constant is guaranteed, namely the ratio of leading coefficients 9/2 ÷ 2 = **9/4**. **Rigorous version via stars:** write the expression as [(1 − cos 3x)/(3x)²]·[(3x)²/(x·sin 2x)]. **First bracket (star (1−cos u)/u² → 1/2, u = 3x → 0):** → 1/2. **Second bracket:** (3x)²/(x·sin 2x) = 9x²/(x·sin 2x) = 9x/(sin 2x) = (9/2)·(2x)/(sin 2x) → (9/2)·1 = 9/2 (star sin u/u, u = 2x → 0). **Product: (1/2)·(9/2) = 9/4** ✓ — agreeing with the order reading. **Deep point:** the order comparison predicted the answer's *type* (finite nonzero) and its *value* (ratio of leading coefficients 9/4) before any algebra; the star decomposition then certified it. Write both leading terms with their full coefficients before dividing — same-order contestants leave the ratio of coefficients.

**NEB-style (5m): Evaluate lim_{x→0} (tan x − sin x)/x³.** — **Reshape with an identity:** tan x − sin x = sin x(1/cos x − 1) = sin x(1 − cos x)/cos x. **Split the factors:** (sin x/x)·[(1 − cos x)/x²]·[x²·... assemble: (tan x − sin x)/x³ = [(sin x)/x]·[(1 − cos x)/x²]·[1/cos x]. **Apply the stars:** sin x/x → **1** (u = x → 0); (1 − cos x)/x² → **1/2** (second-order star); 1/cos x → **1** (cos is continuous at 0, cos 0 = 1). **Product: 1 · 1/2 · 1 = **1/2**. **Order check:** tan x − sin x ~ x³/3? — the standard refinement gives (tan x − sin x)/x³ → 1/2 here because tan x − sin x = sin x(1−cos x)/cos x ~ x·(x²/2) = x³/2 ✓ consistent. **Deep point:** the identity transformed an order-3 difference into a *product* of lower-order stars — factoring out the largest common vanishing term (sin x) is the standard move when a difference of trig functions resists direct star-matching.

**NEB-style (6m): A student evaluates lim_{x→0} sin(2x°)/(3x) by writing sin(2x°) ~ 2x and gets 2/3. Diagnose the error and give the correct answer.** — **The error:** the star sin u/u → 1 holds only in **radians**. Here the argument is 2x° — measured in degrees — so sin(2x°) ~ (π/180)·(2x) = πx/90, not 2x. **Conversion:** sin(2x°) = sin(2x·π/180 radians) = sin(πx/90), and with u = πx/90 → 0, the star gives sin(πx/90) ~ πx/90. **Correct limit:** (πx/90)/(3x) = **π/270**. **Sanity check on the error's size:** the student's 2/3 vs correct π/270 ≈ 0.0116 — off by a factor of (2/3)/(π/270) = 180/π ≈ 57.3, exactly the degree-to-radian conversion factor. **Deep point:** the radian requirement is not a technicality — the sine star's content is "the sine's slope at 0 is 1," and slope = 1 happens only when angle equals arc length; in degrees the slope is π/180, and every star application silently carries that factor unless the units are radians.

data.title: Limits of Logarithmic and Exponential Functions
data.topicTitle: Limits of Logarithmic and Exponential Functions
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — e, ln and the Exponential Star

**Logarithmic and exponential limits** revolve around e: (1 + x)^{1/x} → e, (eˣ − 1)/x → 1, ln(1+x)/x → 1, and the 1^∞ form resolved by the exponential bridge **lim f^g = e^{lim g·ln f}**.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 The e-limits

- **lim_{x→0} (1 + x)^{1/x} = e**; twin: **lim_{x→∞} (1 + 1/x)^x = e** (u = 1/x bridges them).
- General power: **lim_{x→0} (1 + kx)^{1/x} = eᵏ** — insert kx/kx.
- **lim_{x→0} (aˣ − 1)/x = ln a**; a = e gives 1. **lim_{x→0} ln(1 + x)/x = 1.**

### 2.2 The 1^∞ form and the bridge

- **1^∞ is indeterminate** (not 1!): f → 1, g → ∞ makes f^g undecided.
- **Bridge theorem:** lim f(x)^{g(x)} = **e^{lim g(x)·ln f(x)}** whenever the exponent limit exists — because f^g = e^{g ln f} identically.
- Standard resolution: for lim (1 + u)^{v} with u → 0, v → ∞: the limit is **e^{lim uv}**.

### 2.3 Growth comparisons (theorems)

- **ln x ≪ xᵃ ≪ aˣ ≪ x! ≪ xˣ** as x → ∞: logarithms lose to powers, powers to exponentials. Consequences: lim ln x/x = 0, lim xᵏ/eˣ = 0, lim x^{1/x} = 1.

### 2.4 Reduction discipline

- Rewrite exponentials via e and logs via ln (natural), then steer into the three stars: (eᵘ − 1)/u, ln(1+u)/u, (1+u)^{1/u}.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **e** | lim (1+x)^{1/x} | the natural base |
| **1^∞ form** | Indeterminate power | (1 + 1/n)ⁿ |
| **Exponential bridge** | f^g = e^{g ln f} | resolves 1^∞ |
| **Growth ladder** | ln ≪ power ≪ exponential | ln x/x → 0 |

## 4. Detailed Explanation

### 4.1 Why (1+x)^{1/x} defines e

- Compound interest compounded ever more finely: (1 + 1/n)ⁿ climbs to e ≈ 2.71828. The limit *is* the definition — e is the answer to continuous compounding.

### 4.2 The bridge in action

- Any f^g with f → 1, g → ∞: write f = 1 + u, so f^g = [(1+u)^{1/u}]^{uv} → e^{lim uv}. The whole 1^∞ technology is one exponent bookkeeping.

### 4.3 The growth ladder as a limit generator

- The ordering ln x ≪ xᵃ ≪ aˣ is a theorem (comparative growth rates); every "which dominates" limit is read off it: ln x/x → 0, x¹⁰⁰/eˣ → 0, x^{1/x} → 1.

## 5. Comparison Tables

**Exponential limit shelf**

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| (1 + x)^{1/x} (x→0) | e |
| (1 + 1/x)^x (x→∞) | e |
| (1 + kx)^{1/x} | eᵏ |
| (eˣ − 1)/x | 1 |
| (aˣ − 1)/x | ln a |
| ln(1+x)/x | 1 |
| ln x/x, xᵏ/eˣ, x^{1/x} (∞) | 0, 0, 1 |

## 6. Common Confusions

**1^∞ ≠ 1:** the form is indeterminate — (1 + 1/n)ⁿ → e ≈ 2.718, not 1.
**(aˣ − 1)/x keeps ln a:** only a = e kills the factor; general bases keep it.
**Bridge needs natural logs:** f^g = e^{g ln f} uses ln — converting log bases first is mandatory.

## 7. Exam Application

**NEB-style (3m): Evaluate lim_{x→0} (1 + 3x)^{1/x}.** — **1^∞ form** (base → 1, exponent → ∞). **Bridge:** = e^{lim (1/x)·ln(1+3x)}; ln(1+3x) ~ 3x ⟹ exponent limit = 3x·(1/x)... lim (ln(1+3x)/x) = 3. **Answer: e³.** (Shortcut: (1 + kx)^{1/x} → eᵏ with k = 3.)

**NEB-style (3m): Evaluate lim_{x→∞} (x + 1/x)^x... lim_{x→∞} ((x+1)/(x−1))^x.** — Base → 1, exponent → ∞ ⟹ **1^∞**. Write base = 1 + 2/(x−1); then u = 2/(x−1) → 0 and exponent x·u = 2x/(x−1) → 2. **Limit = e².** (Bridge: e^{lim x·ln((x+1)/(x−1))} with ln(1+u) ~ u gives the same e².)
**NEB-style (2m): Evaluate lim_{x→∞} x^{1/x}.** — **Bridge:** x^{1/x} = e^{(ln x)/x}; by the growth ladder ln x/x → 0 ⟹ limit = **e⁰ = 1**. Powers beat logs even at the 1/x power.

## 8. Deep Conceptual — e as the Fixed Point of the Rate Map

- The exponential star (eᵘ − 1)/u → 1 says: at u = 0, the exponential's **rate equals its value**. Every other base a pays the correction factor ln a — (aᵘ − 1)/u → ln a — so e is the unique base whose growth rate *is* its own size. That self-replication is why e appears wherever rates compound naturally.
- **The log star is the mirror:** ln(1+u)/u → 1 says the log's rate at 1 is 1 — the inverse of the exponential's property. The two stars are one fact read from both sides of the inverse pair.
- **The compound star closes the loop:** (1+u)^{1/u} → e is the *definition* of e as the limit of compounding — continuously compounded growth. All three stars are the same constant seen as value, rate, and process.

## 9. Deep Conceptual — Growth Races and the Hierarchy at Infinity

- **The ladder:** ln x grows slowest, then xᵖ (any fixed power), then aˣ (any a > 1), then xˣ fastest. Each rung *dominates* the one below: aˣ/xⁿ → ∞ and ln x/xⁿ → 0 for every n, however large.
- **Why the ladder decides limits:** in any quotient of unlike types at infinity, the higher rung wins and the limit is 0 or ∞ regardless of coefficients — x¹⁰⁰/eˣ → 0, ln(x¹⁰⁰)/x → 0. No algebra needed; only the rungs matter.
- **The mechanism:** exponentials compound multiplicatively (each unit of x multiplies by a), powers additively (each unit adds a fixed increment) — multiplicative growth outruns additive growth eventually, always. Logs grow by *diminishing* increments, which is why they lose to everything.

## 10. Deep Conceptual — The Log as the Great Lineariser

- **ln converts multiplication to addition:** ln(ab) = ln a + ln b. In limits this turns products of many factors into sums (where degree comparison works) and turns powers u^v into products v·ln u (where the 0·∞ machinery works).
- **Every power-form limit is a log limit:** 1^∞, 0⁰, ∞⁰ all surrender to f^g = e^{g ln f}. The exponential bridge is not a trick but an isomorphism — it transports the question to addition-land, solves it there, and transports the answer back.
- **Domain discipline:** logs demand positive arguments — one-sided limits at 0 (ln x → −∞ as x → 0⁺) and absolute values inside (ln|f| for f′/f patterns) are the standard repairs. A negative argument is not a small answer; it is no answer.

examples: ***The compound-interest constant*** - (1 + 1/n)^n climbing to e is continuous compounding: e is not invented, it is discovered by bankers.
practiceQuestions: **NEB-style (3m): Evaluate lim_{x→0} (1 + 3x)^{1/x}.** — **Form recognition:** the base → 1 and the exponent 1/x → ∞ — the **1^∞ indeterminate form** (not 1!). **Bridge route:** (1 + 3x)^{1/x} = e^{(1/x)·ln(1+3x)} identically, so the limit is **e^L** with L = lim_{x→0} ln(1+3x)/x. **Compute L:** ln(1 + u) ~ u with u = 3x gives ln(1+3x) ~ 3x, so L = lim 3x/x = **3** (equivalently by the standard limit ln(1+u)/u → 1 with the kx/kx insertion). **Answer: e³.** **Shortcut confirmed:** the general theorem (1 + kx)^{1/x} → eᵏ with k = 3 — the bridge and the shortcut agree.

**NEB-style (3m): Evaluate lim_{x→∞} ((x + 1)/(x − 1))^x.** — **Form:** base (x+1)/(x−1) = 1 + 2/(x−1) → 1 and exponent x → ∞ ⟹ **1^∞**. **Bridge:** with u = 2/(x−1) → 0, the expression is (1 + u)^x, and the theorem (1+u)^v → e^{lim uv} applies with v = x: compute **lim x·u = lim 2x/(x−1) = 2**. **Answer: e².** **Cross-check by the full bridge:** x·ln((x+1)/(x−1)) = x·ln(1 + 2/(x−1)) ~ x·2/(x−1) → 2, so e² ✓. The entire 1^∞ technology reduces to exponent bookkeeping: find lim uv.

**NEB-style (2m): Evaluate lim_{x→∞} x^{1/x}.** — **Bridge:** x^{1/x} = **e^{(ln x)/x}** identically — the exponent is the contest between log and power. **Growth ladder:** ln x ≪ xᵃ for any a > 0; in particular ln x/x → 0 as x → ∞ (logs lose to powers). **Conclusion:** the exponent → 0, so the limit is **e⁰ = 1**. **Reading:** even the tiniest positive power of x outgrows the logarithm, so taking the 1/x-th power of x flattens it to 1 — the growth ladder settles infinity contests without any ε-work.

**NEB-style (6m): Evaluate lim_{x→0} (e^{5x} − 1)/(ln(1 + 3x)), annotating the stars.** — **Form check:** substitute x = 0: (1 − 1)/ln 1 = **0/0** ✓. **Numerator (star (eᵘ−1)/u → 1, u = 5x → 0):** e^{5x} − 1 ~ 5x ⟹ (e^{5x} − 1)/(5x) → 1. **Denominator (star ln(1+u)/u → 1, u = 3x → 0):** ln(1 + 3x) ~ 3x ⟹ ln(1+3x)/(3x) → 1. **Assemble:** the expression = [(e^{5x}−1)/(5x)]·[(3x)/ln(1+3x)]·(5/3) → 1·1·(5/3) = **5/3**. **Order reading:** both contestants vanish at order 1 with coefficients 5 and 3 ⟹ the ratio of coefficients 5/3 was predictable before the stars. **Deep point:** the exponential and logarithmic stars are inverse-pair twins — each converts its function to its linear approximation at the anchor point, and same-order ratios reduce to coefficient arithmetic.

**NEB-style (6m): Evaluate lim_{x→∞} (eˣ + 3x²)/(2eˣ − x).** — **Identify the race:** exponential (top rung) vs polynomial — the ladder says eˣ dominates any fixed power ⟹ the eˣ terms decide. **Divide by eˣ (the dominant term):** (eˣ + 3x²)/(2eˣ − x) = (1 + 3x²/eˣ)/(2 − x/eˣ). **Apply the ladder:** x²/eˣ → **0** (exponential beats any power) and x/eˣ → **0**. **Limit: (1 + 0)/(2 − 0) = 1/2.** **Cross-check by ladder logic alone:** numerator ~ eˣ (leading term), denominator ~ 2eˣ ⟹ ratio ~ 1/2 ✓. **Deep point:** dividing by the dominant term is the standard move when rungs differ — it converts the race into (tiny)/(constant) bookkeeping; the coefficients 1 and 2 on the eˣ terms are the only survivors, exactly as the ladder predicts.

**NEB-style (6m): Evaluate lim_{x→0⁺} x·ln x, and use the result to find lim_{x→0⁺} x^{x}.** — **Part 1 — the 0·∞ form:** x·ln x is indeterminate (0 times −∞). **Flip to a quotient:** x ln x = ln x/(1/x) — now **−∞/∞** ⟹ L'Hôpital applies (both → ∞ in magnitude): differentiate separately — (1/x)/(−1/x²) = **−x** → 0. **So lim_{x→0⁺} x ln x = 0** — the log's slow dive loses to x's collapse. **Part 2 — the power form:** xˣ = e^{x ln x} ⟹ lim xˣ = e^{lim x ln x} = e⁰ = **1**. **Deep points:** (1) the flip choice matters — writing x/(1/ln x) instead would differentiate to a worse form; flip the factor that differentiates toward simplicity (ln x → 1/x is the friendly derivative); (2) the growth ladder at a point: even at 0⁺, ln's sluggishness loses the race, and the exponential bridge converts that race's verdict into the power's limit.

**NEB-style (5m): Evaluate lim_{x→∞} (ln(3x² + 1))/(ln(x⁴ + 2)).** — **Extract leading behaviour:** ln(3x² + 1) = ln(x²(3 + 1/x²)) = 2 ln x + ln(3 + 1/x²) → **2 ln x + ln 3** (the correction → ln 3, bounded). Similarly ln(x⁴ + 2) = **4 ln x + ln(1 + 2/x⁴)** → 4 ln x + 0. **Form the ratio:** (2 ln x + ln 3)/(4 ln x + ln(1+2/x⁴)) = [2 + ln 3/ln x]/[4 + ln(1+2/x⁴)/ln x] → (2 + 0)/(4 + 0) = **1/2** as ln x → ∞. **Shortcut via degrees:** inside logs, only the *degree* of the polynomial matters — ln(f) ~ deg(f)·ln x ⟹ the limit is 2/4 = 1/2 ✓. **Deep point:** the log's linearity on powers (ln xᵏ = k ln x) makes log-of-polynomial limits pure degree arithmetic — the coefficients and lower terms vanish because ln x → ∞ drowns every constant, the mirror image of the polynomial-at-infinity degree rule.
