data.title: Poisson's Ratio

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Stretch Here, Shrink There

Stretch a rubber band and it visibly thins; stretch a cork and it barely changes width. Poisson's ratio captures this sideways response — the lateral contraction that accompanies every longitudinal stretch — and it is dimensionless because it compares strain with strain.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2024)

### 2.1 Definition

When a wire is stretched longitudinally, its diameter decreases laterally. **Poisson's ratio (σ)** is the ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain:
$$\sigma = \frac{\text{lateral strain}}{\text{longitudinal strain}} = \frac{-\Delta D/D}{\Delta L/L}$$

### 2.2 Why is it dimensionless? (NEB 2024)

Both numerator and denominator are **strains** — ratios of like quantities (length/length) — so their ratio is a pure number with no units.

### 2.3 Typical values and theoretical limits

| Material | σ |
|---|---|
| Cork | ≈ 0 (barely thins — why cork seals bottles) |
| Metals (steel, copper) | 0.25 – 0.34 |
| Rubber | ≈ 0.5 (nearly incompressible) |
| Theoretical limits | −1 ≤ σ ≤ 0.5 (isotropic materials) |

For most metals σ ≈ 0.3. Rubber's σ ≈ 0.5 means volume is nearly conserved under stretch.

### 2.4 Worked numerical

**Q (NEB-style):** A wire of diameter 2 mm stretches by 0.1% longitudinally. If σ = 0.3, find the percentage change in diameter.
Lateral strain = σ × longitudinal strain = 0.3 × 0.001 = 3×10⁻⁴ → diameter decreases by **0.03%** (ΔD = 0.0006 mm).

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 40:** σ links the three moduli: $Y = 2\eta(1+\sigma) = 3K(1-2\sigma)$.
- **To volume conservation:** σ = 0.5 → no volume change on stretching; σ < 0.5 → volume increases slightly.
- **To auxetic materials:** σ < 0 (they get *fatter* when stretched) — engineered metamaterials.

## 4. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 4.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

| Year | Unit | Topic | Question | Marks | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2080/2024 | Mechanics | Elasticity | Define bulk modulus and Poisson's ratio. Why is Poisson's ratio dimensionless? | 3 | Definition |

### 4.2 Model answer

**Q (3m, 2024):** **Poisson's ratio** is the ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain for a stretched body: $\sigma = \frac{-\Delta D/D}{\Delta L/L}$. **Bulk modulus** is the ratio of volumetric stress to volumetric strain: $K = -\Delta P/(\Delta V/V)$. Poisson's ratio is **dimensionless** because it is a ratio of two strains, each itself a dimensionless ratio of length to length.

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Giving σ units (Pa) — it has none.
2. Forgetting the negative sign convention (lateral strain opposes longitudinal).
3. Quoting σ > 0.5 for ordinary materials — impossible for isotropic solids.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Stretch Here, Shrink There

Stretch a rubber band and it visibly thins; stretch a cork and it barely changes width. Poisson's ratio captures this sideways response — the lateral contraction that accompanies every longitudinal stretch — and it is dimensionless because it compares strain with strain.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2024)

### 2.1 Definition

When a wire is stretched longitudinally, its diameter decreases laterally. **Poisson's ratio (σ)** is the ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain:
$$\sigma = \frac{\text{lateral strain}}{\text{longitudinal strain}} = \frac{-\Delta D/D}{\Delta L/L}$$

### 2.2 Why is it dimensionless? (NEB 2024)

Both numerator and denominator are **strains** — ratios of like quantities (length/length) — so their ratio is a pure number with no units.

### 2.3 Typical values and theoretical limits

| Material | σ |
|---|---|
| Cork | ≈ 0 (barely thins — why cork seals bottles) |
| Metals (steel, copper) | 0.25 – 0.34 |
| Rubber | ≈ 0.5 (nearly incompressible) |
| Theoretical limits | −1 ≤ σ ≤ 0.5 (isotropic materials) |

For most metals σ ≈ 0.3. Rubber's σ ≈ 0.5 means volume is nearly conserved under stretch.

### 2.4 Worked numerical

**Q (NEB-style):** A wire of diameter 2 mm stretches by 0.1% longitudinally. If σ = 0.3, find the percentage change in diameter.
Lateral strain = σ × longitudinal strain = 0.3 × 0.001 = 3×10⁻⁴ → diameter decreases by **0.03%** (ΔD = 0.0006 mm).

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 40:** σ links the three moduli: $Y = 2\eta(1+\sigma) = 3K(1-2\sigma)$.
- **To volume conservation:** σ = 0.5 → no volume change on stretching; σ < 0.5 → volume increases slightly.
- **To auxetic materials:** σ < 0 (they get *fatter* when stretched) — engineered metamaterials.

## 4. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 4.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

| Year | Unit | Topic | Question | Marks | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2080/2024 | Mechanics | Elasticity | Define bulk modulus and Poisson's ratio. Why is Poisson's ratio dimensionless? | 3 | Definition |

### 4.2 Model answer

**Q (3m, 2024):** **Poisson's ratio** is the ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain for a stretched body: $\sigma = \frac{-\Delta D/D}{\Delta L/L}$. **Bulk modulus** is the ratio of volumetric stress to volumetric strain: $K = -\Delta P/(\Delta V/V)$. Poisson's ratio is **dimensionless** because it is a ratio of two strains, each itself a dimensionless ratio of length to length.

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Giving σ units (Pa) — it has none.
2. Forgetting the negative sign convention (lateral strain opposes longitudinal).
3. Quoting σ > 0.5 for ordinary materials — impossible for isotropic solids.

data.title: Elastic Potential Energy

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Energy in a Stretched Wire

Stretch a spring and it stores energy — recoverable, mechanical, ready. The work done against the restoring force accumulates as **elastic potential energy**, the quantity that powers bows, catapults, clock springs and the recoil of every impact.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2024)

### 2.1 Derivation

The restoring force grows linearly with extension (Hooke's law): at extension $x$, force $= kx$. Work done to stretch from 0 to $x$:
$$U = \int_0^x kx'\,dx' = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$$
Equivalently, the area under the F–x graph is a triangle: $U = \frac{1}{2} \times F \times x = \frac{1}{2}Fx$ (since F = kx).

### 2.2 Forms of the energy density

For a wire of volume $AL$:
$$u = \frac{U}{\text{volume}} = \frac{\frac{1}{2}F\Delta L}{AL} = \frac{1}{2}\,\sigma\,\epsilon = \frac{\sigma^2}{2Y}$$
— energy per unit volume in terms of stress and strain.

### 2.3 Worked numericals (NEB 2024)

**Q (3m, 2024):** How much energy is stored in the wire of the previous question when stretched by the 50 N load? (2 m wire, 2 mm extension, k = 2.5×10⁴ N/m)
$$U = \frac{1}{2}Fx = \frac{1}{2} \times 50 \times 2\times10^{-3} = 0.05 \text{ J}$$
(equivalently $\frac{1}{2}kx^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 2.5\times10^4 \times (2\times10^{-3})^2 = 0.05$ J ✓)

**Q (NEB-style):** A spring of k = 200 N/m is compressed 10 cm. Find the stored energy and the average force during compression.
$U = \frac{1}{2} \times 200 \times 0.01 = 1$ J; average force = $F_{max}/2 = 20/2 = 10$ N.

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 38:** U = ½kx² is the integral of Hooke's law.
- **To Work-energy theorem (Topic 18):** the stored energy converts to kinetic energy on release.
- **To collisions (Topic 21):** during impact, KE temporarily stores as elastic deformation energy.
- **To spring PE in gravity problems:** bungee and catapult energy chains.

## 4. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

notes: **Elastic Potential Energy (U):** The energy stored in a deformed elastic body (like a spring or stretched wire) due to the work done against internal restoring forces. For a spring, $U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$.

**Energy Density (u):** The elastic potential energy stored per unit volume. For a wire under tension, $u = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{stress} \times \text{strain} = \frac{1}{2} \sigma \epsilon = \frac{1}{2} \frac{\sigma^2}{E} = \frac{1}{2} E \epsilon^2$.
**Work Done:** The work done to stretch a spring by $x$ is the area under the $F-x$ graph: $W = \int_0^x F dx = \int_0^x kx dx = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$.

**Hysteresis:** In some materials, the loading and unloading stress-strain curves do not coincide. The area enclosed by the loop represents energy dissipated as heat per unit volume per cycle. This is crucial for shock absorbers and rubber components.
**NEB exam focus:** Derive $U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$; calculate energy stored in springs and wires; understand energy density; explain hysteresis loops.
confusion: ❌ 'Energy stored is $kx^2$.' ✅ It is $\frac{1}{2}kx^2$ — the factor of 1/2 comes from the average force $\bar{F} = (0+kx)/2 = kx/2$.
❌ 'Energy density is $\sigma \epsilon$.' ✅ It is $\frac{1}{2} \sigma \epsilon$ — again, the 1/2 factor from the triangular area under the stress-strain curve.
❌ 'Hysteresis loop area is energy stored.' ✅ It is energy DISSIPATED (lost as heat) per cycle.
❌ 'Elastic potential energy is only for springs.' ✅ It applies to any elastic deformation (wires, beams, bulk compression) where work is done against restoring forces.

data.title: Electric charges
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Spark That Starts Electricity

Rub a balloon on your hair and it sticks to the wall. That invisible "something" is electric charge — a fundamental property of matter, quantised in units of e, conserved in every interaction, and the protagonist of all of electrostatics.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2021)

### 2.1 Electric charge and its properties

- **Charge** is the intrinsic property of matter responsible for electric forces; carried by protons (+e) and electrons (−e).
- **Two kinds:** positive and negative — like charges repel, unlike attract.
- **Additivity:** total charge is the algebraic sum of individual charges.
- **Quantisation (NEB 2021, 3m):** all charges are integer multiples of the elementary charge:
$$q = ne, \qquad e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\text{ C}$$
Possible charges: …, −2e, −e, 0, +e, +2e, … — a charge of 2.5e can **never** be observed, because charge is carried in discrete packets (electrons/protons; quarks carry fractional charge but are always confined inside whole hadrons).
- **Conservation:** the total charge of an isolated system never changes — charging merely separates equal amounts of + and −.
- **Invariance:** charge is the same in every reference frame.

### 2.2 Charging methods

- **Friction (rubbing):** transfer of electrons between surfaces (comb–hair, silk–glass).
- **Conduction (contact):** touching a charged body to a neutral one shares the charge.
- **Induction:** charging *without contact* by redistributing charge with a nearby charged body and earthing (Topic 84).

### 2.3 Worked numerical

**Q (NEB-style):** How many electrons make a charge of −1 C?
$n = \frac{q}{e} = \frac{1}{1.6\times10^{-19}} = 6.25\times10^{18}$ electrons.

**Q (NEB-style):** A body gains 10⁹ electrons. Find its charge.
$q = ne = 10^9 \times (-1.6\times10^{-19}) = -1.6\times10^{-10}$ C.

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 85:** Coulomb's law quantifies the force between these charges.
- **To atomic structure:** protons/electrons carry ±e; the neutron carries none.
- **To nuclear physics (Unit 26):** charge conservation rules every nuclear reaction.

## 4. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 4.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

| Year | Unit | Topic | Question | Marks | Type |

| 2077/2021 | Electricity | Charge | What is meant by quantisation of electric charge? Explain why a charge of 2.5 e can never be observed. | 3 | Explanation |

2. Electron-count numerical (2m).
3. State the law of conservation of charge with an example (2m).

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

2. Saying friction "creates" charge — it only transfers electrons.
3. Using e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ without units.

data.title: Charging by induction
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Charging Without Touching

Bring a charged rod near a metal sphere and the sphere's own charges rearrange: the near side turns opposite, the far side same. Earth the sphere at the right moment and it keeps a permanent charge — all without contact. That is induction, the trick behind electrostatic generators and lightning safety.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 What is charging by induction?

**Induction** charges a body **without contact** with a charged object: a nearby charge *redistributes* the free electrons of a conductor. The net charge of the pair is unchanged — induction separates charge, it never creates it.

### 2.2 The four-step process

Charging a metal sphere positively with a negatively charged rod:
1. Bring the charged rod **near** (not touching) the sphere — electrons in the sphere are repelled to the far side; the near side becomes positive (charge **polarisation**).
2. **Earth** the far side — repelled electrons flow away to the ground through the earth wire.
3. **Remove the earth connection** first — the sphere is left electron-deficient.
4. **Remove the rod** — the sphere is left with a uniform **positive** charge.

Key sequencing: earth *while* the rod is near; disconnect the earth *before* removing the rod.

### 2.3 Everyday evidence

- A charged comb attracts neutral paper: the paper's charges polarise, the nearer opposite charge feels a stronger pull.
- A charged balloon sticks to a neutral wall.
- Electrostatic induction underlies the Wimshurst/van de Graaff generators and the gold-leaf electroscope's response.

### 2.4 Worked reasoning

**Q (NEB-style):** Why does a negatively charged rod attract a neutral conducting ball?
The rod's negative charge repels free electrons to the ball's far side, leaving positive charge on the near side. The nearer positive charge feels a stronger attraction than the farther negative charge feels repulsion — net attraction.

**Q (NEB-style):** Why must the earth wire be removed before the charged rod?
Removing the rod first would let electrons flow back from the earth and neutralise the sphere — the induced charge exists only while the rod's field is present.

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 83:** induction conserves charge — it only separates it.
- **To conductors vs insulators:** induction needs mobile electrons; insulators polarise only molecularly.
- **To lightning protection:** earthing provides a charge reservoir — the same physics in reverse.

## 4. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 4.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

No verified PYQ for this exact topic in the bank. Practise the step-by-step induction process and the "attracts neutral bodies" reasoning as **NEB-style practice** (2–3m).

### 4.2 Likely question forms

1. Describe charging a conductor positively by induction (3m).
2. Why does a charged rod attract a neutral paper? (2m)
3. Why is earthing done while the rod is nearby? (2m)

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Saying induction "transfers charge from the rod" — the rod never touches and keeps its charge.
2. Getting the order wrong: earth first, disconnect earth, then remove the rod.
3. Claiming insulators charge easily by induction — they lack free electrons.

data.summary: **Charging by induction** gives a conductor a permanent charge **without contact**: a nearby charged rod polarises the conductor's free electrons; earthing lets the repelled charge escape to ground; disconnecting the earth and then removing the rod leaves a net charge of the opposite sign to the rod. Charge is only redistributed — never created (conservation). The same polarisation explains why a charged comb attracts neutral paper and why electroscopes and electrostatic generators work. data.title: Coulomb's Law
data.topicTitle: Coulomb's law; force between multiple charges
notes: **Coulomb's Law of Electrostatics:** Formulated by Charles-Augustin de Coulomb in 1785, the electrostatic force between two stationary point charges is directly proportional to the product of the magnitudes of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them: $F = k \frac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^2}$. The electrostatic force acts along the line connecting the centers of the two charges, being repulsive for like charges ($q_1 q_2 > 0$) and attractive for unlike charges ($q_1 q_2 < 0$).

**Electrostatic Constant & Permittivity of Free Space:** The proportionality constant in vacuum/air is $k = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \approx 8.98755 \times 10^9\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2 \approx 9 \times 10^9\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2$. Here $\varepsilon_0$ denotes the electric permittivity of free space, with value $\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{C}^2/(\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2) = 8.854 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{F/m}$ and dimensions $[M^{-1} L^{-3} T^4 I^2]$.

**Vector Formulation & Newton's Third Law:** In vector notation, the force $\vec{F}_{12}$ exerted on charge $q_1$ by charge $q_2$ located at position vector $\vec{r}_2$ is: $\vec{F}_{12} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{|\vec{r}_1 - \vec{r}_2|^3} (\vec{r}_1 - \vec{r}_2) = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2} \hat{r}_{21}$. Because $\hat{r}_{12} = -\hat{r}_{21}$, it follows rigorously that $\vec{F}_{12} = -\vec{F}_{21}$. Thus, electrostatic forces between two charges constitute an action-reaction pair satisfying Newton's Third Law in its strong central-force form.

**Dielectric Medium & Relative Permittivity:** When point charges are embedded within an insulating medium of permittivity $\varepsilon$, dielectric polarization shields the charges, reducing the net force to $F_m = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon} \frac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^2} = \frac{F_0}{\varepsilon_r} = \frac{F_0}{\kappa}$. The dimensionless quantity $\kappa = \varepsilon_r = \frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon_0} \ge 1$ is the dielectric constant (relative permittivity) of the medium (for vacuum $\kappa = 1$, dry air $\approx 1.0006$, water $\approx 80$, ideal conductor $\kappa \to \infty$).

**Principle of Linear Superposition:** Electrostatic interaction between any pair of charges is completely unaffected by the presence of other surrounding charges. Consequently, the net electrostatic force on a test charge $q_0$ due to a discrete distribution of $N$ point charges $q_1, q_2, \dots, q_N$ is the vector sum: $\vec{F}_{net} = \sum_{i=1}^N \vec{F}_{0i} = \frac{q_0}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{q_i}{|\vec{r}_0 - \vec{r}_i|^3} (\vec{r}_0 - \vec{r}_i)$.

**Electrostatic Equilibrium & Earnshaw's Theorem:** A system of charges is in equilibrium if the net electrostatic force on each constituent charge vanishes ($\sum \vec{F} = 0$). By Earnshaw's theorem (derived from Gauss's law $\vec{\nabla} \cdot \vec{E} = 0$ in charge-free regions), a collection of stationary point charges cannot be maintained in a state of stable equilibrium solely under the influence of inverse-square electrostatic interactions.
confusion: Adding electrostatic forces as scalar algebraic quantities: Electric forces are vectors! When calculating the net force exerted by multiple charges, one must resolve each pairwise force into Cartesian orthogonal components ($F_x, F_y$) before summing: $F_{net} = \sqrt{(\sum F_x)^2 + (\sum F_y)^2}$.

Ignoring the medium's dielectric screening: In water ($\kappa \approx 80$), the electrostatic force between ions drops to $\frac{1}{80}$ of its vacuum value, explaining why table salt ($NaCl$) spontaneously dissociates into hydrated $Na^+$ and $Cl^-$ ions in water.

Applying Coulomb's law to extended charge distributions at close range: Coulomb's inverse-square formula applies strictly to point charges or non-overlapping spherical charge distributions (via Shell Theorem). At close range, induction distorts charge distribution on real conductors.
practice: Two identical positive point charges $q_1 = q_2 = +2.0\,\mu\text{C}$ are placed at coordinates $(0, 0.3\text{ m})$ and $(0, -0.3\text{ m})$ along the y-axis. A third point charge $q_0 = +4.0\,\mu\text{C}$ is placed on the x-axis at $(0.4\text{ m}, 0)$. Find the magnitude and direction of the net electrostatic force acting on $q_0$. Solution: Distance from each charge to $q_0$ is $r = \sqrt{0.4^2 + 0.3^2} = 0.5\text{ m}$. Force magnitude from one charge: $F_1 = \frac{(9 \times 10^9)(2 \times 10^{-6})(4 \times 10^{-6})}{(0.5)^2} = \frac{0.072}{0.25} = 0.288\text{ N}$. Angle with x-axis: $\cos\theta = 0.4 / 0.5 = 0.8$, $\sin\theta = 0.3 / 0.5 = 0.6$. By symmetry, vertical components cancel ($F_{1y} - F_{2y} = 0$). Net horizontal force: $F_{net} = 2 F_1 \cos\theta = 2(0.288)(0.8) = 0.461\text{ N}$ directed along $+x$ axis.
universalFacts: The electrostatic force between two protons inside a nucleus is approximately $10^{36}$ times stronger than the gravitational force between them: $\frac{F_e}{F_g} = \frac{e^2 / (4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2)}{G m_p^2 / r^2} \approx 1.24 \times 10^{36}$, showing the colossal dominance of electromagnetism over gravity at microscopic scales.

Coulomb's law has been tested experimentally to an accuracy of better than 1 part in $10^{16}$, establishing the inverse power $r^{-(2+\delta)}$ with $|delta| < 10^{-16}$, proving the photon has zero rest mass.
examples: Ionic lattice cohesion in minerals: Table salt crystals ($NaCl$) are held together by Coulomb attraction between alternating $Na^+$ cations and $Cl^-$ anions, providing a high melting point of 801 °C.

Atomic electron orbitals: In Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom, the electrostatic Coulomb attraction between the single proton nucleus and orbiting electron ($F = \frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2}$) provides the required centripetal acceleration ($m v^2 / r$).

Dissolution in polar solvents: The high dielectric constant of liquid water ($\kappa \approx 80$) reduces ionic attraction by a factor of 80, permitting thermal agitation to break ionic bonds and dissolve salts.
practiceQuestions: Q1. State Coulomb's law in electrostatics. Express it in vector form and show that it satisfies Newton's third law of motion.
Q2. Define the SI unit of electric charge (1 Coulomb) in terms of Coulomb's law.

Q3. Two point charges $+4q$ and $+q$ are fixed at a distance $L$ apart. Where should a third charge $Q$ be placed on the line joining them so that the entire system remains in electrostatic equilibrium?

Q4. Explain the principle of linear superposition of electrostatic forces and describe how to calculate the net force on a charge located at the vertex of an equilateral triangle with charges at the other two vertices.
formulas: Coulomb's Law (magnitude): $F = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^2}$
Coulomb's Law (vector form): $\vec{F}_{12} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}\hat{r}_{21} = -\vec{F}_{21}$
Force in dielectric medium: $F_m = \frac{F_0}{\varepsilon_r} = \frac{F_0}{\kappa} = \frac{1}{4\pi\kappa\varepsilon_0} \frac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^2}$
Principle of Superposition: $\vec{F}_{net} = \sum_{i=1}^N \vec{F}_i$
Proportionality constant in vacuum: $k = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \approx 8.99 \times 10^9\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2$
keyPoints: Coulomb's law is an inverse-square central force acting along the line connecting two stationary point charges.
Vector formulation demonstrates mutual symmetry: $\vec{F}_{12} = -\vec{F}_{21}$, fulfilling Newton's third law.
Presence of a dielectric medium with relative permittivity $\kappa > 1$ reduces electrostatic force by a factor of $\kappa$.
The principle of superposition allows independent pairwise summation of forces in multi-charge configurations.
Earnshaw's theorem establishes that stable electrostatic equilibrium of stationary point charges is impossible without non-electrostatic constraints.
data.summary: Coulomb's Law quantifies the electrostatic force between two stationary point charges as directly proportional to the product of charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation: F = k|q₁q₂|/r². In vector form, forces obey Newton's third law (F₁₂ = -F₂₁). When immersed in a dielectric medium of relative permittivity κ, the force reduces to F₀/κ. For multiple charges, the net force is determined via the principle of linear superposition by vector addition of all individual pairwise interactions.
specialNotes: Coulomb's law is strictly valid only for stationary point charges in an inertial reference frame. Accelerating charges radiate electromagnetic energy.
Definition of 1 Coulomb: That charge which, when placed in vacuum at a distance of 1 meter from an identical charge, repels it with a force of 9 × 10⁹ N.
importantStatements: Statement 1: The electrostatic force between two stationary point charges varies inversely with the square of the distance between them.
Statement 2: Electrostatic forces are central forces acting strictly along the straight line joining the centers of two interacting charges.
Statement 3: Electrostatic forces satisfy Newton's third law: the force on charge 1 by charge 2 is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force on charge 2 by charge 1.
Statement 4: The electrostatic force between two charges is independent of the presence of any other surrounding charges.
Statement 5: In any dielectric medium with relative permittivity κ, the electrostatic force between two charges is attenuated by a factor of κ.
importantNotes: Remember that the permittivity of free space ε₀ has SI units of C²/(N·m²) or F/m, with value 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m.
examShortTricks: Equilibrium between like charges q₁ and q₂ at distance L: Third charge of opposite sign placed at x = L / (√(q₂/q₁) + 1) from q₁ achieves equilibrium.
Ratio of forces in dielectric medium: F_air / F_medium = κ.
Two identical charges in symmetrical polygons: Net electrostatic force at the geometric center of any regular polygon with equal vertices charges is identically ZERO.
examNotes: State Coulomb's law in vector form and derive the condition for third charge equilibrium along a line joining two point charges (frequent 3-4 mark NEB question).

mcs.question: Two point charges placed at a distance r in air experience a force F. If they are immersed in a medium of dielectric constant κ = 4 at the same distance, the new force is:
mcs.explanation: In a dielectric medium, the force is reduced by the relative permittivity: F_medium = F_air / κ = F / 4.

mcs.explanation: The force on charge 1 due to charge 2 acts along the unit vector from charge 2 to charge 1 (r̂₂₁): F⃗₁₂ = (1/4πε₀) · (q₁q₂/r²) r̂₂₁.

mcs.question: Four equal positive charges +q are fixed at the four corners of a square of side a. The net force on a test charge placed at the center of the square is:
mcs.explanation: By diagonal symmetry, forces exerted by pairs of charges located at opposite corners are equal in magnitude and oppositely directed, canceling to exactly zero.

Coulomb's law in vector form satisfying Newton's third law (central force).
Dielectric screening effect and definition of relative permittivity κ = ε/ε₀.

data.title: Coulomb's law: force between two point charges
data.topicTitle: Coulomb's law: force between two point charges
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Inverse Square Law of Charge

Two centuries before electrons were discovered, Coulomb measured with a torsion balance how charged bodies push and pull: a force proportional to each charge, inversely proportional to the square of the separation. That law is the electrostatic twin of Newton's gravitation.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2022, 2024)

### 2.1 Statement and formula

**Coulomb's law:** the electrostatic force between two point charges acts along the line joining them, is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation:
$$F = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q_1q_2}{r^2} = k\frac{q_1q_2}{r^2}$$
- $k = 9\times10^9$ N m²C⁻² (in air/vacuum); $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}$ C²N⁻¹m⁻² (permittivity of free space).
- **Like charges repel, unlike attract** — the sign of the product sets the direction.
- In a dielectric medium: $F = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r}\frac{q_1q_2}{r^2}$ — the force shrinks by the relative permittivity.

### 2.2 Comparison with gravitation

| Feature | Coulomb force | Gravitational force |
|---|---|---|
| Source | Charge | Mass |
| Sign | Attractive or repulsive | Always attractive |
| Strength | ~10³⁹ times stronger (for e pairs) | Very weak |
| Dependence | 1/r² | 1/r² |
| Medium | Affected by dielectric | Unaffected |

### 2.3 Worked numericals

**Q (3m, 2024):** State Coulomb's law. Calculate the force between two charges of 2 μC and 3 μC placed 0.1 m apart in air.
$$F = \frac{9\times10^9 \times 2\times10^{-6} \times 3\times10^{-6}}{(0.1)^2} = \frac{5.4\times10^{-2}}{10^{-2}} = 5.4 \text{ N (repulsive)}$$

**Q (1m, 2022 — MCQ):** Two charges of +2 μC and −3 μC are 0.6 m apart. The force between them is:
$$F = 9\times10^9 \times \frac{6\times10^{-12}}{0.36} = 0.15 \text{ N — attractive}$$

**Q (NEB-style):** How far apart must two 1 C charges be for the force to be 1 N?
$r = \sqrt{kq_1q_2/F} = \sqrt{9\times10^9} ≈ 9.5\times10^4$ m — nearly 95 km!

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 83:** the law quantifies the interactions of quantised, conserved charges.
- **To Topic 86:** superposition extends the two-charge law to systems.
- **To gravitation (Unit 7):** same inverse-square mathematics, different source and strength.

## 4. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 4.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

| Year | Unit | Topic | Question | Marks | Type |

| 2078/2022 | Electricity | Coulomb | Two charges of +2 μC and −3 μC are placed 0.6 m apart. The force between them is: (a) 0.15 N attractive … | 1 | MCQ |
| 2080/2024 | Electricity | Coulomb | State Coulomb's law. Calculate the force between two charges of 2 μC and 3 μC placed 0.1 m apart in air. | 3 | Statement + numerical |

### 4.2 Likely additional forms (NEB-style)

1. Compare Coulomb's law with Newton's law of gravitation (3m).
2. Distance-ratio numerical (2m).
3. Effect of a dielectric medium (2m).

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Using μC directly without converting (1 μC = 10⁻⁶ C).
2. Forgetting to square r.
3. Quoting k as 9×10⁹ without units.

data.title: Force between multiple electric charges
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Superposition: Adding Forces Vectorially

With three or more charges, every pair interacts independently. Coulomb's law plus the **principle of superposition** — add all pairwise forces as vectors — handles any configuration, from electron clouds to charged spheres.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Principle of superposition

The force on any charge in a system equals the **vector sum** of the forces each other charge would exert alone:
$$\vec{F}_1 = \vec{F}_{12} + \vec{F}_{13} + \vec{F}_{14} + \cdots$$
- Each pairwise force obeys Coulomb's law independently — the presence of other charges does not modify any single pair's force.
- Forces add **as vectors**: resolve into components when directions differ.

### 2.2 Worked numericals

**Q (NEB-style):** Charges q₁ = +2 μC and q₂ = +2 μC sit 0.2 m apart on the x-axis; q₃ = +1 μC sits at the midpoint. Find the net force on q₃.
- Forces from q₁ and q₂ on q₃: equal magnitude, opposite directions → **cancel**.
- $F_{13} = F_{23} = \frac{9\times10^9 \times 2\times10^{-6}\times10^{-6}}{(0.1)^2} = 1.8$ N each, opposite → net force = **0**.

**Q (NEB-style):** Two charges +4 μC and −4 μC are 0.3 m apart. Find the field point force on a +1 μC test charge placed 0.1 m from +4 μC along the line beyond the −4 μC charge... simpler: find the net force on a charge placed at the midpoint of an *unlike* pair.
- Unlike pair ±4 μC, 0.3 m apart, midpoint: both forces point the same way (toward the negative).
- $F_{each} = \frac{9\times10^9 \times 4\times10^{-6}\times1\times10^{-6}}{(0.15)^2} = 1.6$ N → net = **3.2 N toward the negative charge**.

**Q (NEB-style):** Three equal charges q at the corners of an equilateral triangle: force on each?
Each charge feels two forces of magnitude $\frac{kq^2}{a^2}$ at 60° apart; the resultant has magnitude $\sqrt{3}\frac{kq^2}{a^2}$ directed away from the triangle's centre (for like charges).

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 85:** superposition takes Coulomb's two-charge law as its building block.
- **To electric field (Unit 20):** the same superposition principle applies to field vectors.
- **To vectors (Unit 2):** component resolution is the practical tool.

## 4. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 4.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

No verified PYQ for this exact topic in the bank. Practise superposition numericals and the equilateral-triangle result as **NEB-style practice** (3–4m).

### 4.2 Likely question forms

1. State the principle of superposition (2m).
2. Net force at the midpoint/vertex of a charge arrangement (3–4m).

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Superposition: Adding Forces Vectorially

With three or more charges, every pair interacts independently. Coulomb's law plus the **principle of superposition** — add all pairwise forces as vectors — handles any configuration, from electron clouds to charged spheres.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Principle of superposition

The force on any charge in a system equals the **vector sum** of the forces each other charge would exert alone:
$$\vec{F}_1 = \vec{F}_{12} + \vec{F}_{13} + \vec{F}_{14} + \cdots$$
- Each pairwise force obeys Coulomb's law independently — the presence of other charges does not modify any single pair's force.
- Forces add **as vectors**: resolve into components when directions differ.

### 2.2 Worked numericals

**Q (NEB-style):** Charges q₁ = +2 μC and q₂ = +2 μC sit 0.2 m apart on the x-axis; q₃ = +1 μC sits at the midpoint. Find the net force on q₃.
- Forces from q₁ and q₂ on q₃: equal magnitude, opposite directions → **cancel**.
- $F_{13} = F_{23} = \frac{9\times10^9 \times 2\times10^{-6}\times10^{-6}}{(0.1)^2} = 1.8$ N each, opposite → net force = **0**.

**Q (NEB-style):** Two charges +4 μC and −4 μC are 0.3 m apart. Find the field point force on a +1 μC test charge placed 0.1 m from +4 μC along the line beyond the −4 μC charge... simpler: find the net force on a charge placed at the midpoint of an *unlike* pair.
- Unlike pair ±4 μC, 0.3 m apart, midpoint: both forces point the same way (toward the negative).
- $F_{each} = \frac{9\times10^9 \times 4\times10^{-6}\times1\times10^{-6}}{(0.15)^2} = 1.6$ N → net = **3.2 N toward the negative charge**.

**Q (NEB-style):** Three equal charges q at the corners of an equilateral triangle: force on each?
Each charge feels two forces of magnitude $\frac{kq^2}{a^2}$ at 60° apart; the resultant has magnitude $\sqrt{3}\frac{kq^2}{a^2}$ directed away from the triangle's centre (for like charges).

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 85:** superposition takes Coulomb's two-charge law as its building block.
- **To electric field (Unit 20):** the same superposition principle applies to field vectors.
- **To vectors (Unit 2):** component resolution is the practical tool.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Invisible Field Around a Charge

A charge warps the space around it: any other charge placed nearby feels a force. Describing that influence as an **electric field** — force per unit positive test charge — lets us map, add and predict electric effects without touching the source.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2020, 2023, 2024)

### 2.1 Electric field and intensity

**Electric field** at a point is the force experienced by a unit positive test charge placed there:
$$\vec{E} = \frac{\vec{F}}{q_0} \qquad \text{unit: N/C (or V/m)}$$
- Due to a **point charge**: $E = \dfrac{kq}{r^2}$, directed radially away from a positive charge and toward a negative one.
- Fields add by **superposition** (vector sum).

### 2.2 Electric field lines

**Properties (NEB 2024, 2m):**
1. Lines start on **positive** charges and end on **negative** charges (or infinity).
2. Lines **never cross** — crossing would mean two field directions at one point.
3. **Density** of lines measures field strength (crowded = strong).
4. Lines meet a conductor's surface **perpendicular**; no lines inside a conductor in equilibrium.

### 2.3 Worked numericals

**Q (3m, 2023):** Find the electric field intensity at a point 2 m from a point charge of +4 μC. (k = 9×10⁹ N m²C⁻²)
$$E = \frac{kq}{r^2} = \frac{9\times10^9 \times 4\times10^{-6}}{2^2} = \frac{3.6\times10^4}{4} = 9\times10^3 \text{ N/C}$$

**Q (2m, 2024):** Calculate the electric field strength at 0.3 m from a point charge of 6 μC in air.
$$E = \frac{9\times10^9 \times 6\times10^{-6}}{0.09} = 6\times10^5 \text{ N/C, directed away from the charge}$$

**Q (3m, 2020):** Two equal charges of +2 μC each are placed 10 cm apart. Find the electric field intensity at the midpoint.
- Midpoint: r = 5 cm from each; $E_1 = \frac{9\times10^9 \times 2\times10^{-6}}{(0.05)^2} = 7.2\times10^6$ N/C
- The two fields are equal and **opposite** → net E = **0**.

**Q (3m, 2024):** An electric dipole of +4 μC and −4 μC charges 0.2 m apart: find its dipole moment and the field on its axis 0.5 m from its centre.
- $p = qd = 4\times10^{-6} \times 0.2 = 8\times10^{-7}$ C·m
- $E_{axial} = \dfrac{2kp}{r^3} = \dfrac{2 \times 9\times10^9 \times 8\times10^{-7}}{0.125} = 1.15\times10^5$ N/C along the axis.

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 85/86:** E is Coulomb force per unit charge; fields superpose like forces.
- **To Topic 88/89:** Gauss's law computes E for symmetric charge distributions.
- **To potential (Unit 21):** E is the negative potential gradient.

2. Stating the direction of E wrongly — away from positive, toward negative.
3. Field-line properties: omitting "lines never cross" or "no lines inside a conductor".

data.topicTitle: Electric field due to point charges and field lines
notes: **Electric Field Concept & Definition:** An electric field $\vec{E}$ is an intrinsic vector property of space surrounding any charged distribution. It is defined quantitatively as the electrostatic force experienced per unit positive infinitesimal test charge placed at that location: $\vec{E} = \lim_{q_0 \to 0} \frac{\vec{F}}{q_0}$. The limiting operation $q_0 \to 0$ ensures the test charge does not disturb the source charge configuration. The SI unit of electric field is Newton per Coulomb ($\text{N/C}$) or equivalently Volt per meter ($\text{V/m}$), with dimensional formula $[M L T^{-3} I^{-1}]$.

**Electric Field due to an Isolated Point Charge:** Applying Coulomb's law to a source charge $q$ at position vector $\vec{r}'$ and test charge $q_0$ at field point $\vec{r}$, the electric field is: $\vec{E}(\vec{r}) = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q}{|\vec{r} - \vec{r}'|^3} (\vec{r} - \vec{r}') = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q}{r^2}\hat{r}$. The electric field radiates spherically outward in all directions for a positive source charge ($q > 0$) and converges radially inward for a negative source charge ($q < 0$), exhibiting strict inverse-square attenuation with radial distance $r$.

**Superposition Principle for Discrete & Continuous Charges:** The net electric field created by an ensemble of $N$ discrete point charges is the vector sum of individual fields: $\vec{E}_{net} = \sum_{i=1}^N \vec{E}_i = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{q_i}{r_i^2}\hat{r}_i$. For continuous charge distributions, summation transitions to volume, surface, or linear integrals: $\vec{E} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \int \frac{dq}{r^2}\hat{r}$, where $dq = \lambda dl$ (linear charge density), $dq = \sigma dA$ (surface charge density), or $dq = \rho dV$ (volume charge density).

**Properties of Electric Field Lines:** Introduced by Michael Faraday, electric field lines (lines of force) provide an intuitive geometric mapping of electrostatic vector fields: (1) Lines originate perpendicularly on positive charges and terminate on negative charges (or extend to infinity); (2) The tangent to a field line at any point indicates the direction of $\vec{E}$ at that point; (3) Two field lines can NEVER cross, because intersecting lines would imply two distinct field vectors at the same spatial coordinate; (4) The local areal density of lines is directly proportional to field magnitude $E$; (5) Electrostatic field lines never form closed loops, reflecting the conservative nature of electrostatic forces ($\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{r} = 0$).

**Electric Dipole & Dipole Moment:** An electric dipole consists of two equal and opposite point charges $\pm q$ separated by a small distance $2a$. The electric dipole moment vector is defined as $\vec{p} = q(2\vec{a})$, directed by convention from the negative charge $-q$ to positive charge $+q$, with SI unit $\text{C}\cdot\text{m}$. In an external electric field $\vec{E}$, a dipole experiences a net aligning torque $\vec{\tau} = \vec{p} \times \vec{E}$ and possesses electrostatic potential energy $U = -\vec{p} \cdot \vec{E}$. In a non-uniform field, it experiences both torque and a net translational force $\vec{F} = (\vec{p} \cdot \vec{\nabla})\vec{E}$.

**Electric Field of a Dipole at Axial & Equatorial Points:** For a dipole of moment $p = 2qa$ at distances $r \gg a$: (1) **Axial point (End-on position):** $\vec{E}_{axial} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{2\vec{p}}{r^3}$, parallel to $\vec{p}$; (2) **Equatorial point (Broadside-on position):** $\vec{E}_{equatorial} = -\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{\vec{p}}{r^3}$, antiparallel to $\vec{p}$. Notice that for any dipole, $E \propto 1/r^3$ (faster fall-off than a point charge's $1/r^2$), and $E_{axial} = 2 E_{equatorial}$ at the same radial distance $r$.
confusion: Confusing field line direction with trajectory of a moving charge: An electric field line represents the direction of electrostatic force on a stationary positive charge, NOT the trajectory of a moving charge. A moving charge accelerates along $\vec{F} = q\vec{E}$, so velocity and field vectors generally diverge due to inertia.

Assuming field lines can intersect: If two field lines crossed, a test charge at the intersection would experience two distinct electrostatic forces in different directions simultaneously, which violates the uniqueness theorem of vector fields.

Confusing the radial fall-off of dipoles versus point charges: Point charge field scales as $1/r^2$, whereas an electric dipole field decays as $1/r^3$ because the positive and negative charges largely cancel each other out at long distances ($r \gg a$).
practice: Two point charges $q_1 = +5.0\,\mu\text{C}$ and $q_2 = -5.0\,\mu\text{C}$ are separated by $10\text{ cm}$ along the x-axis ($2a = 0.1\text{ m}$). (a) Find the electric dipole moment. (b) Find the electric field magnitude at an axial point $20\text{ cm}$ from the dipole center. Solution: (a) $p = q(2a) = (5.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ C})(0.1\text{ m}) = 5.0 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{C}\cdot\text{m}$. (b) Using the axial field formula with $r = 0.2\text{ m}$ ($r \gg a$ approximation): $E_{axial} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{2p}{r^3} = \frac{(9 \times 10^9)(2 \times 5.0 \times 10^{-7})}{(0.2)^3} = \frac{9000}{0.008} = 1.125 \times 10^6\,\text{N/C}$, directed along the dipole axis in the direction of $\vec{p}$.
universalFacts: The terrestrial fair-weather atmosphere maintains a downward-directed vertical electric field of approximately $100\,\text{to}\,150\,\text{V/m}$ near the Earth's surface due to the global electrical thunderstorm battery circuit.

Electric fields in nerve cells (action potentials) reach immense intensities of roughly $10^7\,\text{V/m}$ across thin ($7\text{ nm}$) phospholipid bilayer cell membranes, driving ion pumps that enable animal thought and heartbeat.
examples: Inkjet printers: Electrically deflected microscopic ink droplets pass between high-voltage deflection plates generating a uniform electric field, steering droplets precisely onto paper to render text and images.

Cathode Ray Oscilloscope (CRO): An electron beam accelerated by an electron gun is deflected horizontally and vertically by orthogonal electric fields between parallel plates, projecting waveforms onto a fluorescent screen.
Laser toner transfer: Controlled electrostatic fields attract charged polymer toner particles from the photoconductor drum onto paper, which is subsequently thermally fused.
practiceQuestions: Q1. Define electric field intensity. Derive an expression for the electric field at a distance r due to an isolated point charge Q in vacuum.
Q2. State four essential characteristics of electric field lines and explain why two field lines can never intersect each other.
Q3. Define electric dipole moment. Derive expressions for the electric field intensity due to a short electric dipole at (a) an axial point, and (b) an equatorial point.
Q4. An electron is released from rest in a uniform horizontal electric field of intensity 2.0 × 10⁴ N/C. Calculate its acceleration and the time taken to travel a distance of 1.5 cm.
formulas: Electric field definition: $\vec{E} = \frac{\vec{F}}{q_0}$
Field of a point charge: $\vec{E} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q}{r^2}\hat{r}$
Electric dipole moment: $\vec{p} = q(2\vec{a})$
Dipole field (axial, $r \gg a$): $\vec{E}_{axial} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{2\vec{p}}{r^3}$
Dipole field (equatorial, $r \gg a$): $\vec{E}_{equatorial} = -\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{\vec{p}}{r^3}$
Dipole torque in uniform field: $\vec{\tau} = \vec{p} \times \vec{E}$
Dipole potential energy: $U = -\vec{p} \cdot \vec{E}$
keyPoints: Electric field intensity is force per unit positive test charge ($E = F/q_0$) in N/C or V/m.
Point charge field obeys inverse square law ($E \propto 1/r^2$); short dipole field obeys inverse cube law ($E \propto 1/r^3$).
Field lines point outward from positive charges and inward toward negative charges, never intersecting.
Axial field of a short dipole is exactly twice the magnitude of equatorial field at equal distance ($E_{axial} = 2 E_{equatorial}$).
In a uniform electric field, an electric dipole experiences zero net force but a restoring torque $\vec{\tau} = \vec{p} \times \vec{E}$.
data.summary: The electric field E is a vector field describing electrostatic force per unit test charge (E = F/q₀). Point charges produce radially symmetric fields falling off as 1/r², mapped visually by continuous non-intersecting field lines originating on positive and terminating on negative charges. Electric dipoles (p = 2qa) generate fields decaying as 1/r³, with axial field intensity twice that of the equatorial position at the same large distance, experiencing aligning torque τ = p × E in an external field.
specialNotes: Electrostatic field lines do not form closed loops because electrostatic fields are conservative: the closed loop line integral ∮ E · dr = 0.
A charged particle projected perpendicularly into a uniform electric field follows a parabolic trajectory, analogous to projectile motion in a uniform gravitational field.
importantStatements: Statement 1: The electric field at any point in space is the electrostatic force experienced per unit infinitesimal positive test charge.
Statement 2: Electric field lines originate on positive charges, terminate on negative charges, and cannot intersect at any point.
Statement 3: The electric field due to a point charge obeys an inverse-square distance relationship (E ∝ 1/r²).
Statement 4: The electric field due to a short electric dipole decays inversely with the cube of distance (E ∝ 1/r³).
Statement 5: In a uniform electric field, an electric dipole experiences zero translational net force but a net aligning torque τ = p × E.
importantNotes: Remember that the SI units N/C and V/m are completely interchangeable: 1 N/C = 1 (J/m) / C = 1 (J/C) / m = 1 V/m.
examShortTricks: Dipole field ratio trick: At identical large distance r, E_axial / E_equatorial = 2.
Neutral point between like charges: E_net = 0 lies between them at distance x = d / (√(q₂/q₁) + 1) from q₁.
Acceleration of charged particle in field: a = qE / m (direction along E for positive charge, opposite E for electron).

mcs.question: The electric field intensity at an axial point distance r from a short electric dipole is E. The electric field at an equatorial point at the same distance r is:
mcs.explanation: For a short dipole (r ≫ a), E_axial = 2kp/r³ and E_equatorial = kp/r³. Therefore, E_equatorial = E_axial / 2 = E / 2.

mcs.question: An electric dipole placed in a uniform electric field experiences:
options: both a net force and a torque
a net force only, but no torque
a torque only, but no net force
neither a net force nor a torque
mcs.explanation: In a uniform field, equal and opposite forces act on +q and -q (+qE and -qE), so net force is zero. However, their lines of action do not coincide, producing a net torque τ = p × E.

mcs.question: Electric field lines can never intersect each other because:
options: at the point of intersection, the electric field would have two distinct directions
they form closed loops in vacuum
mcs.explanation: The tangent to a field line gives the direction of E. If two lines intersect, there would be two tangents, meaning two distinct field directions at a single point, which is physically impossible.

data.title: Gauss law: electric flux
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Counting Field Lines Through a Surface

Gauss's law links the electric flux through any closed surface to the charge it encloses. With symmetry — a sphere, a line, a sheet — it turns hard integrations into one-line answers. NEB 2023 and 2024 both carried it as a 5-mark question.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2023, 2024)

### 2.1 Electric flux

**Electric flux** through an area A in a uniform field E:
$$\Phi = EA\cos\theta = \vec{E}\cdot\vec{A} \qquad \text{unit: N m}^2\text{C}^{-1}$$
θ is the angle between E and the area's normal. Flux measures "how many field lines pierce" the surface.

### 2.2 Gauss's law (NEB 2023, 2024, 5m)

**Statement:** the total electric flux through any closed surface equals $\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}$ times the net charge enclosed:
$$\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{q_{enclosed}}{\varepsilon_0}$$
- The **Gaussian surface** is imaginary and chosen to exploit symmetry.
- The law holds for *any* closed surface; only flux *leaving* the surface counts — charges outside contribute zero net flux.
- Gauss's law is equivalent to Coulomb's law plus the inverse-square geometry.

### 2.3 Application: infinite plane sheet of charge (NEB 2023, 2024)

For a sheet of surface charge density σ, take a **cylindrical Gaussian pillbox** piercing the sheet:
- Flux leaves through both flat faces: $\Phi = EA + EA = 2EA$
- Enclosed charge: $q = \sigma A$
$$2EA = \frac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0} \Rightarrow \boxed{E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}}$$
— uniform, independent of distance from the sheet, pointing away on both sides.

### 2.4 Worked numerical

**Q (NEB-style):** A spherical Gaussian surface of radius 0.2 m encloses 2 μC. Find the flux through it.
$$\Phi = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} = \frac{2\times10^{-6}}{8.85\times10^{-12}} ≈ 2.26\times10^5 \text{ N m}^2\text{C}^{-1}$$

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 87:** flux counts field lines through a surface.
- **To Topic 89:** the sphere, line and sheet results are Gauss's law's standard applications.
- **To conductors:** zero field inside a conductor follows immediately from Gauss's law.

## 4. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

| 2079/2023 | Electricity | Gauss | State Gauss's law. Use it to find the electric field due to an infinite plane sheet of charge. | 5 | Statement + derivation |
| 2080/2024 | Electricity | Gauss | State Gauss's law. Use it to find the electric field due to an infinite plane sheet of charge. | 5 | Statement + derivation |

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

2. Using the total charge instead of the *enclosed* charge.
3. Omitting the cos θ in flux through an inclined surface.

data.title: Application of Gauss Law: Field of a Charge Sphere, Line Charge, Charged Plane Conductor
data.topicTitle: Application of Gauss law: field of a charge sphere, line charge, charged plane conductor
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Three Results Every Physicist Knows

Gauss's law plus symmetry delivers the three canonical fields: a charged **sphere** (acts like a point outside, zero inside), an infinite **line** (falls as 1/r), and a charged **conducting plane** (σ/ε₀, constant). These are the 5-mark derivations NEB keeps returning to.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2024)

### 2.1 Uniformly charged spherical shell (NEB 2024, 5m)

Shell of radius R carrying charge Q:
- **Outside (r > R):** spherical Gaussian surface encloses all Q:
$$E \cdot 4\pi r^2 = \frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0} \Rightarrow E = \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2}$$
— the shell acts as if all charge sat at its centre.
- **Inside (r < R):** the Gaussian surface encloses no charge → $E = 0$ everywhere inside.
- On the surface: E = Q/4πε₀R² (maximum).

### 2.2 Infinite line charge

Linear density λ, cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r, length l:
$$E \cdot 2\pi r l = \frac{\lambda l}{\varepsilon_0} \Rightarrow E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$$
— falls as **1/r**, radial direction.

### 2.3 Charged conducting plane (conductor surface)

For a conductor's surface with charge density σ, the field just outside:
$$E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$$
— twice the infinite-sheet value, because all flux leaves through the *outer* face only (no field inside the conductor).

### 2.4 Worked numericals

**Q (NEB-style):** A shell of radius 10 cm carries 4 μC. Find E at r = 20 cm and at the centre.
- Outside: $E = \frac{9\times10^9 \times 4\times10^{-6}}{0.04} = 9\times10^5$ N/C
- Inside: **E = 0**.

**Q (NEB-style):** A long wire has λ = 2 μC/m. Find E at 5 cm.
$E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r} = \frac{2\times10^{-6}}{2\pi \times 8.85\times10^{-12} \times 0.05} ≈ 7.2\times10^5$ N/C.

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 88:** each result is the flux identity ∮E·dA = q/ε₀ with a symmetry-matched surface.
- **To conductors:** E = 0 inside any conductor in equilibrium — the basis of electrostatic shielding.
- **To Topic 87:** outside a sphere, the field matches a point charge — Coulomb's law recovered.

## 4. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 4.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

| Year | Unit | Topic | Question | Marks | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2080/2024 | Electricity | Gauss | Use Gauss's law to find the electric field due to a uniformly charged spherical shell of radius R carrying charge Q, at points outside and inside the shell. | 5 | Derivation |
| 2080/2024 | Electricity | Gauss | Why is the electric field zero everywhere inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium? | 2 | Reasoning |

### 4.2 Likely additional forms (NEB-style)

1. Derive E for an infinite line charge (5m).
2. Field of a charged conducting plane (3m).
3. Shell numericals inside/outside (3m).

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Writing E = σ/2ε₀ for a *conductor's* surface — it is σ/ε₀ (single face).
2. Forgetting the shell's inside field is zero, not kQ/R².
3. Mixing up the line charge's 2πrl surface area.
specificConditions: Symmetry Required: Gauss's law is always true but practically useful only for spherical, cylindrical, or planar symmetry where E is constant over the Gaussian surface.
Conductor vs Insulator: For conducting sphere, charge resides on surface → E = 0 inside. For insulating sphere with uniform volume charge, E grows linearly from center.
Infinite Approximation: Line charge formula $E = \lambda/(2\pi\varepsilon_0 r)$ assumes infinite length — valid near middle of long wire, not near ends.

- Shell: E = Q/4πε₀r² (r > R); E = 0 (r < R)
- Line: E = λ/2πε₀r
- Conductor surface: E = σ/ε₀
keyPoints: Shell: E = Q/4πε₀r² outside, 0 inside. Line: λ/2πε₀r. Conductor surface: σ/ε₀.
importantStatements: "The electric field inside a charged conducting shell is zero at every point."

examNotes: State directions (radial outward for Q > 0) and the r-dependence in words.
examples: ***Faraday cage*** — E = 0 inside a conductor shields whatever is inside.
practiceQuestions: **Numerical (3m): A shell of radius 5 cm carries 2 μC. Find E at 10 cm from the centre.** — Outside: E = 9×10⁹ × 2×10⁻⁶/0.01 = 1.8×10⁶ N/C, radial outward.
practice: How does a car protect occupants from lightning?
universalFacts: Outside a uniformly charged shell the field is exactly that of a point charge at the centre — the electrostatic analogue of Newton's shell theorem.

**Inside a shell E = 0** — the shell theorem's most surprising half.

mcs.question: Electric field inside a charged conducting spherical shell is:
mcs.explanation: Charge resides on surface; by Gauss's law with Gaussian surface inside, Q_enc = 0, so E = 0.

mcs.question: Electric field due to infinite line charge at distance r is proportional to:
mcs.explanation: Cylindrical symmetry gives E = λ/(2πε₀r) — inverse first power.

mcs.question: Electric field near infinite plane sheet with charge density σ is:
mcs.explanation: Pillbox Gaussian surface gives E = σ/(2ε₀) on each side of the sheet.

mcs.question: For a uniformly charged solid insulating sphere, field inside at distance r from center:
mcs.explanation: Inside uniform sphere, Q_enc ∝ r³ and area ∝ r², so E ∝ r: E = kQr/R³.

mcs.question: Gauss's law is most useful when charge distribution has:
mcs.explanation: High symmetry lets us assume E is constant over Gaussian surface and pull it outside the integral.

data.summary: Gauss's law's standard applications: a **uniformly charged spherical shell** (Q, radius R) gives $E = Q/4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2$ outside — as if the charge were a point at the centre — and **E = 0 everywhere inside** (NEB 2024, 5m); free electrons in a conductor in equilibrium move until the internal field vanishes, which is why conductors shield their interiors and charge resides on the outer surface (NEB 2024, 2m). An **infinite line charge** (λ) gives $E = \lambda/2\pi\varepsilon_0 r$ (1/r falloff), and a **charged conducting plane** gives $E = \sigma/\varepsilon_0$ just outside — double the infinite-sheet value because flux leaves through one face only. Symmetry plus one flux identity replaces pages of integration.

**Q (NEB-style):** A shell of radius 10 cm carries 4 μC. Find E at r = 20 cm and at the centre.
- Outside: $E = \frac{9\times10^9 \times 4\times10^{-6}}{0.04} = 9\times10^5$ N/C
- Inside: **E = 0**.

**Q (NEB-style):** A long wire has λ = 2 μC/m. Find E at 5 cm.
$E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r} = \frac{2\times10^{-6}}{2\pi \times 8.85\times10^{-12} \times 0.05} ≈ 7.2\times10^5$ N/C.

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 88:** each result is the flux identity ∮E·dA = q/ε₀ with a symmetry-matched surface.
- **To conductors:** E = 0 inside any conductor in equilibrium — the basis of electrostatic shielding.
- **To Topic 87:** outside a sphere, the field matches a point charge — Coulomb's law recovered.

### 4.2 Likely additional forms (NEB-style)

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

2. Forgetting the shell's inside field is zero, not kQ/R².

data.title: Applications of Gauss Law
notes: **Overview of Gauss's Law Applications:** Gauss's law provides an elegant and straightforward analytical method for determining electric fields produced by symmetric charge distributions where direct Coulomb integration is cumbersome. The three standard canonical geometries required by the NEB curriculum are: (1) an infinitely long straight line of charge (cylindrical symmetry); (2) an infinite uniformly charged plane sheet (planar symmetry); and (3) a uniformly charged spherical shell or conducting sphere (spherical symmetry).

**Electric Field of an Infinitely Long Straight Wire (Line Charge):** Consider a straight thin wire of infinite length having uniform linear charge density $\lambda$ ($\text{C/m}$). By cylindrical symmetry, the electric field is purely radial, pointing perpendicular to the wire. Construct a coaxial Gaussian cylinder of radius $r$ and length $L$. The electric flux through the two circular flat end caps is zero because $\vec{E} \perp d\vec{A}$ ($\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = 0$). Through the curved cylindrical surface of area $2\pi r L$, $\vec{E}$ is parallel to $d\vec{A}$ everywhere and constant in magnitude: $\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = E (2\pi r L)$. Enclosed charge is $Q_{enc} = \lambda L$. Applying Gauss's law: $E(2\pi r L) = \frac{\lambda L}{\varepsilon_0} \implies E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r} = \frac{2k\lambda}{r}$. The field decays inversely with distance ($E \propto 1/r$).

**Electric Field due to an Infinite Uniform Plane Sheet of Charge:** Consider an infinite non-conducting thin plane sheet carrying uniform surface charge density $\sigma$ ($\text{C/m}^2$). By symmetry, $\vec{E}$ is everywhere perpendicular to the sheet, directed away from both faces if $\sigma > 0$. Construct a Gaussian pillbox (a cylinder of cross-sectional area $A$ piercing perpendicular to the sheet with ends parallel to it). Flux through the curved surface is zero as $\vec{E}$ is parallel to the surface. Flux through the two end caps is $\Phi = E A + E A = 2 E A$. Enclosed charge is $Q_{enc} = \sigma A$. By Gauss's law: $2 E A = \frac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0} \implies E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$. Crucially, the electric field is completely independent of distance $r$ from the sheet, forming a perfectly uniform field.

**Electric Field of a Charged Conducting Plate & Between Parallel Plates:** For a conducting plate of finite thickness, mobile free electrons ensure that the internal electric field is strictly zero ($E_{inside} = 0$). The charge redistributes onto both outer faces with surface density $\sigma$. Constructing a pillbox with one face inside the conductor and one outside yields $E A = \frac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0} \implies E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$ (twice that of an isolated non-conducting sheet). For two oppositely charged parallel conducting plates ($\pm \sigma$), fields add constructively between plates: $E_{between} = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} + \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$, while cancelling outside: $E_{outside} = 0$.

**Electric Field due to a Uniformly Charged Thin Spherical Shell:** Consider a thin spherical shell of radius $R$ carrying total charge $Q$ distributed uniformly with surface density $\sigma = \frac{Q}{4\pi R^2}$. Construct a concentric spherical Gaussian surface of radius $r$: (1) **Outside the shell ($r > R$):** $\oint E\,dA = E(4\pi r^2) = \frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0} \implies E = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q}{r^2} = \frac{\sigma R^2}{\varepsilon_0 r^2}$. The shell acts as if all its charge were concentrated at the geometric center; (2) **On the surface ($r = R$):** $E_{surface} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q}{R^2} = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$ (maximum magnitude); (3) **Inside the shell ($r < R$):** The Gaussian surface encloses zero charge ($Q_{enc} = 0$), so $E(4\pi r^2) = 0 \implies E_{inside} = 0$.

**Electric Field of a Uniformly Charged Non-Conducting Solid Sphere:** For an insulating solid sphere of radius $R$ with uniform volume charge density $\rho = \frac{Q}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3}$: (1) **Outside ($r \ge R$):** $E = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{r^2}$; (2) **Inside ($r < R$):** A concentric Gaussian sphere of radius $r$ encloses charge $Q_{enc} = \rho \left(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\right) = Q \left(\frac{r^3}{R^3}\right)$. Applying Gauss's law: $E(4\pi r^2) = \frac{Q r^3}{\varepsilon_0 R^3} \implies E = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q r}{R^3} = \frac{\rho r}{3\varepsilon_0}$. Thus, the electric field increases linearly with radial distance $r$ from zero at the center up to maximum at the surface ($E \propto r$ for $r \le R$), then decays as $1/r^2$ for $r > R$.
confusion: Confusing field of a non-conducting infinite sheet with a conducting plate: An isolated non-conducting sheet has $E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$ on both sides because charge is embedded in a single layer. A conducting plate has charge on two separate faces; just outside any conducting surface, the boundary condition gives $E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$.

Assuming field inside a charged sphere is always zero: Inside a hollow shell or conductor, $E = 0$. However, inside a uniformly charged *non-conducting solid sphere*, the field increases linearly with radius: $E = \frac{\rho r}{3\varepsilon_0} = \frac{k Q r}{R^3}$.

Neglecting Gaussian end-caps in line charge: Students often forget to justify why the two flat circular ends of a Gaussian cylinder contribute zero flux (because $\vec{E} \perp d\vec{A}$, making $\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = 0$).
practice: An infinite line of charge produces an electric field of $9.0 \times 10^4\,\text{N/C}$ at a perpendicular distance of $2.0\text{ cm}$ in air. Calculate the linear charge density $\lambda$. Solution: The electric field of a long wire is $E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r} = \frac{2k\lambda}{r}$. Rearranging for $\lambda$: $\lambda = \frac{E \cdot r}{2k} = \frac{(9.0 \times 10^4\,\text{N/C})(0.02\text{ m})}{2 \times (9.0 \times 10^9\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2)} = \frac{1800}{1.8 \times 10^{10}} = 1.0 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{C/m} = 0.10\,\mu\text{C/m}$.
universalFacts: Electrostatic shielding (Faraday cage effect) is an exact consequence of Gauss's law: because $E = 0$ inside any empty conducting cavity, sensitive electronics or occupants in an automobile or airplane are immune to external high-voltage discharges and lightning.

The linear dependence of electric field $E \propto r$ inside a uniform non-conducting charge sphere is mathematically identical to the gravitational acceleration $g(r) \propto r$ inside a hypothetical uniform planetary Earth.
examples: Van de Graaff Generator: Charges carried to the hollow metallic upper terminal immediately transfer to the outer sphere surface because E = 0 inside, allowing accumulation of potentials up to millions of volts.

Electrostatic air precipitators: High-voltage central wire electrodes generate intense radial fields (E ∝ 1/r) that ionize air molecules, charging smoke particles which then migrate to grounded collection plates.

Coaxial cable design: In transmission lines, the electric field is strictly contained between the inner cylinder and outer grounded shielding conductor (E = λ / (2πε₀r)), preventing signal radiation and electromagnetic interference.
practiceQuestions: Q1. Using Gauss's law, derive an expression for the electric field intensity at a distance r from an infinitely long straight wire carrying uniform linear charge density λ.
Q2. Derive an expression for the electric field intensity due to an infinite plane sheet of charge with uniform surface charge density σ. Why is this field uniform?

Q3. Apply Gauss's law to find the electric field intensity due to a uniformly charged thin spherical shell of radius R at points (a) outside the shell (r > R), (b) on the surface (r = R), and (c) inside the shell (r < R). Sketch a graph of E versus r.

Q4. A spherical conductor of radius 10 cm has a charge of 3.2 × 10⁻⁷ C distributed uniformly on its surface. What is the electric field at (a) a point 15 cm from the center, and (b) inside the conductor at 5 cm from the center?
formulas: Infinite line charge: $E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r} = \frac{2k\lambda}{r}$
Infinite non-conducting plane sheet: $E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$
Conducting surface boundary: $E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$
Between oppositely charged plates: $E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$
Spherical shell (outside, $r \ge R$): $E = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{r^2}$
Spherical shell (inside, $r < R$): $E = 0$
Non-conducting sphere (inside, $r \le R$): $E = \frac{\rho r}{3\varepsilon_0} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q r}{R^3}$
keyPoints: Line charge field decreases inversely with radial distance: $E \propto 1/r$.
Infinite sheet field is completely uniform and distance-independent: $E = \sigma / (2\varepsilon_0)$.
Inside any hollow conductor or spherical shell in electrostatic equilibrium, $E = 0$ (electrostatic shielding).
Outside a spherical charge distribution, the field behaves as if all charge is concentrated at the center ($E \propto 1/r^2$).
Inside a uniformly charged solid dielectric sphere, field increases linearly from center to surface ($E \propto r$).
data.summary: Gauss's law enables straightforward derivation of electric fields for symmetric charge systems: an infinite line charge yields E = λ / (2πε₀r) showing inverse distance decay; an infinite planar sheet produces a uniform, distance-independent field E = σ / (2ε₀); and a spherical shell creates an inverse-square field externally (E = Q / (4πε₀r²)) while maintaining strictly zero internal field (E = 0), establishing electrostatic shielding.
specialNotes: The electric field just outside any arbitrarily shaped conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is always perpendicular to the surface and has magnitude E = σ / ε₀.
A graph of E versus r for a thin spherical shell shows zero field for 0 ≤ r < R, a step discontinuity to E_max = kQ/R² at r = R, and smooth 1/r² decay for r > R.
importantStatements: Statement 1: The electric field due to an infinitely long straight wire carrying uniform linear charge density is inversely proportional to distance from the wire (E ∝ 1/r).
Statement 2: The electric field due to an infinite plane sheet of charge is uniform and completely independent of the distance from the sheet.
Statement 3: The electric field inside a uniformly charged conducting spherical shell is identically zero everywhere.
Statement 4: Outside a spherically symmetric charge distribution, the field is identical to that of a point charge located at the sphere's geometric center.
Statement 5: Inside a uniformly charged non-conducting sphere, the electric field increases linearly with radial distance from the center (E ∝ r).
importantNotes: Contrast the distance dependencies: point charge E ∝ 1/r², dipole E ∝ 1/r³, line charge E ∝ 1/r, infinite plane sheet E ∝ r⁰ (independent of distance).
examShortTricks: Distance dependency table: Infinite Sheet (E ∝ r⁰), Infinite Line (E ∝ 1/r), Point Charge (E ∝ 1/r²), Dipole (E ∝ 1/r³).
Hollow shell inside: E = 0 always; potential V = constant = kQ/R.
Solid dielectric sphere inside: E(r) = (r / R) · E_surface.

data.title: Newton's Law of Gravitation

notes: **Law statement:** every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force that is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres: $F = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$.

**The universal constant G:** $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11} \text{ N m}^2/\text{kg}^2$. It is the same everywhere in the universe (hence 'universal') and was first measured by Cavendish (1798) using a torsion balance. G is very small, which is why the gravitational attraction between everyday objects is imperceptible.

**Vector form & direction:** the force on mass m₁ due to m₂ is $F_{12} = -G\frac{m_1m_2}{r^2} \hat{r}_{12}$, directed along the line joining the centres, always attractive. Newton's third law applies: $F_{12} = -F_{21}$.

**Superposition:** when several masses act on one particle, the net force is the vector sum of the individual forces: $F_{\text{net}} = \sum F_i$. Each pair obeys the inverse-square law independently.

**Worked example — Earth and Moon:** $m_{\text{Earth}} = 6\times 10^{24} \text{ kg}$, $m_{\text{Moon}} = 7.4\times 10^{22} \text{ kg}$, $r = 3.84\times 10^8 \text{ m}$. $F = \frac{6.67\times 10^{-11} \times 6\times 10^{24} \times 7.4\times 10^{22}}{(3.84\times 10^8)^2} = 2.0\times 10^{20} \text{ N}$ — enough to hold the Moon in orbit.

**Gravitational field strength:** $g = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{GM}{r^2}$, the force per unit mass at a distance r from mass M. On Earth's surface $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$, which gives Earth's mass: $M = \frac{gR^2}{G} \approx 5.97\times 10^{24} \text{ kg}$.

**Why G is used in orbits:** equating gravitational force to centripetal force ($\frac{GMm}{r^2} = \frac{mv^2}{r}$) gives orbital velocity $v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$ and period $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^3}{GM}}$ — Kepler's third law follows directly.

**Important comparisons:** gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces — between two protons the gravitational force is $\sim 10^{-36}$ times the electric force — yet it dominates cosmology because mass adds up while electric charges cancel.
confusion: ❌ 'There is a force of gravity only near Earth.' ✅ Gravity acts between ANY two masses anywhere in the universe — it never switches off, it only weakens with the square of distance.
❌ 'G can change with temperature or medium.' ✅ G is a universal constant — independent of temperature, pressure, medium, or the objects involved.
❌ 'The force depends on the square of the distance — it dies quickly.' ✅ It dies as 1/r² but never reaches zero; at double distance the force is a quarter, at ten times it is one-hundredth.

❌ 'Heavier objects fall faster because gravity pulls them harder.' ✅ Gravity pulls harder on heavier objects ($F = mg$), but their acceleration is the same: $a = F/m = g$, hence all bodies in free fall accelerate equally (ignoring air resistance).

❌ 'Earth pulls the Moon but the Moon does not pull Earth.' ✅ The forces are equal and opposite (Newton's third law). Earth and Moon pull on each other with equal forces — the Moon's acceleration is larger because its mass is smaller.
❌ 'Inside Earth gravity stops.' ✅ Inside a uniform sphere, g decreases linearly with distance from the centre, reaching zero at the centre — it is not zero except exactly at the centre.

universalFacts: Isaac Newton published the law of gravitation in his Principia (1687), synthesising the work of Kepler and Galileo — it was the first unified theory of terrestrial and celestial mechanics.
The modern value of $G = 6.674\times 10^{-11}$ is still the least precisely known fundamental constant because gravity is so weak.
The inverse-square character of gravity was seen by Newton as proof that planets are pulled toward the Sun rather than pushed.
Gravity's weakness explains why everyday objects attract negligibly but planets, stars, and galaxies dominate large-scale structure.
The same law that keeps you on the ground also governs satellite orbits, tidal effects, and the orbits of binary stars.

notes: **Law statement:** every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force that is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres: $F = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$.

**The universal constant G:** $G = 6.67\times 10^{-11} \text{ N m}^2/\text{kg}^2$. It is the same everywhere in the universe (hence 'universal') and was first measured by Cavendish (1798) using a torsion balance. G is very small, which is why the gravitational attraction between everyday objects is imperceptible.

**Vector form & direction:** the force on mass m₁ due to m₂ is $F_{12} = -G\frac{m_1m_2}{r^2} \hat{r}_{12}$, directed along the line joining the centres, always attractive. Newton's third law applies: $F_{12} = -F_{21}$.

**Superposition:** when several masses act on one particle, the net force is the vector sum of the individual forces: $F_{\text{net}} = \sum F_i$. Each pair obeys the inverse-square law independently.

**Worked example — Earth and Moon:** $m_{\text{Earth}} = 6\times 10^{24} \text{ kg}$, $m_{\text{Moon}} = 7.4\times 10^{22} \text{ kg}$, $r = 3.84\times 10^8 \text{ m}$. $F = \frac{6.67\times 10^{-11} \times 6\times 10^{24} \times 7.4\times 10^{22}}{(3.84\times 10^8)^2} = 2.0\times 10^{20} \text{ N}$ — enough to hold the Moon in orbit.

**Gravitational field strength:** $g = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{GM}{r^2}$, the force per unit mass at a distance r from mass M. On Earth's surface $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$, which gives Earth's mass: $M = \frac{gR^2}{G} \approx 5.97\times 10^{24} \text{ kg}$.

**Why G is used in orbits:** equating gravitational force to centripetal force ($\frac{GMm}{r^2} = \frac{mv^2}{r}$) gives orbital velocity $v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$ and period $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^3}{GM}}$ — Kepler's third law follows directly.

**Important comparisons:** gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces — between two protons the gravitational force is $\sim 10^{-36}$ times the electric force — yet it dominates cosmology because mass adds up while electric charges cancel.

❌ 'The force depends on the square of the distance — it dies quickly.' ✅ It dies as 1/r² but never reaches zero; at double distance the force is a quarter, at ten times it is one-hundredth.

data.title: Newton's Law of Gravitation

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — One Law for the Universe

An apple falls and the Moon orbits by the same rule. Newton's law of gravitation states that every particle attracts every other with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation — the first law that explained both heaven and Earth.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2019, 2024)

### 2.1 Statement

**Every particle of matter in the universe attracts every other particle with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.**
$$F = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$$
directed along the line joining the two particles.

### 2.2 The gravitational constant G

$G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$ N m² kg⁻² — the force between two 1 kg masses 1 m apart. It is a **universal constant** (same everywhere, for any pair of masses), measured by Cavendish using a torsion balance. Contrast with $g = 9.8$ m/s², which is local and varies.

### 2.3 Does it obey Newton's third law? (NEB 2019)

**Yes.** The force $m_1$ exerts on $m_2$ is equal in magnitude ($Gm_1m_2/r^2$), opposite in direction, and acts along the same line — even when the masses are wildly unequal. Earth pulls you down with 600 N; you pull Earth up with 600 N (Earth's enormous inertia makes the effect invisible).

### 2.4 Properties of the gravitational force

| Property | Detail |
|---|---|
| Always attractive | Unlike electric forces, never repulsive |
| Central | Acts along the line of centres |
| Inverse-square | $F \propto 1/r^2$ |
| Independent of medium | Unaffected by intervening material |
| Weakest of the fundamental forces | ~10³⁸ times weaker than the strong force, yet dominates at astronomical scales |
| Long-range | Infinite range; no shielding possible |

### 2.5 Worked numerical

**Q (NEB-style):** Two 100 kg spheres sit 1 m apart. Find the attraction.
$F = \dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 100 \times 100}{1^2} = 6.67 \times 10^{-7}$ N — tiny: gravity only matters when a planet-scale mass is involved.

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 31:** $g = GM/R^2$ follows by equating $mg = GMm/R^2$.
- **To Unit 4 (Newton's laws):** the third-law symmetry verified here.
- **To Kepler's laws:** the inverse-square law yields elliptical orbits and $T^2 \propto r^3$.

### 4.2 Model answers

**Q (2m, 2024):** Every particle attracts every other particle with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation: $F = Gm_1m_2/r^2$. **G** is the universal gravitational constant, $6.67 \times 10^{-11}$ N m² kg⁻² — the force between two unit masses separated by 1 m.

**Q (2m, 2019):** Yes — the two forces are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction and act along the line joining the particles, exactly as the third law requires.

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Confusing $G$ (universal constant) with $g$ (local acceleration).
2. Writing $F \propto m_1m_2/r$ — the distance is **squared**.
