data.title: Nuclear Fission and Fusion
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Splitting and Joining for Energy

Both routes to nuclear energy walk up the binding-energy curve toward iron: **fission** splits a heavy nucleus, **fusion** joins light ones. Each gram of fuel converts milligrams of mass into energy millions of times beyond any chemical reaction.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2022)

### 2.1 Nuclear fission

A heavy nucleus (A > 200) absorbs a neutron and splits into two medium nuclei plus neutrons and energy:
$$^{235}_{92}U + n \rightarrow ^{141}_{56}Ba + ^{92}_{36}Kr + 3n + \text{energy}$$
- The fragments have higher BE/A than uranium — the mass difference appears as ~200 MeV per fission.
- Released neutrons can trigger further fissions: a **chain reaction** (controlled in reactors via moderators and control rods; uncontrolled in weapons).
- Used in nuclear reactors.

### 2.2 Nuclear fusion

Two light nuclei merge into a heavier one, releasing energy:
$$^{2}_{1}H + ^{3}_{1}H \rightarrow ^{4}_{2}He + n + 17.6 \text{ MeV}$$
- Requires enormous temperature (~10⁸ K) to overcome Coulomb repulsion — hence "thermonuclear".
- Powers the Sun and stars; the goal of fusion reactors (plasma confinement). Per kilogram, fusion releases more energy than fission.

### 2.3 Why both release energy (NEB 2022, 3m)

The BE/A curve peaks at iron-56. Heavy nuclei fission and light nuclei fuse — each move **toward the iron peak raises BE/A**, and the increase times the nucleon count is the energy released, supplied by the corresponding mass loss (Δm c²).

### 2.4 Comparison (NEB 2022, 3m)

| | Fission | Fusion |
|---|---|---|
| Process | Heavy nucleus splits | Light nuclei combine |
| Example | ²³⁵U + n → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3n | ²H + ³H → ⁴He + n |
| Conditions | Neutron capture; possible at room T | ~10⁸ K (thermonuclear) |
| Energy per event | ~200 MeV | 17.6 MeV (but higher per kg) |
| By-products | Radioactive waste | Mostly harmless helium |
| Application | Reactors | Stars; experimental reactors |

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 109:** the BE/A curve is the master explanation of both processes.
- **To Topic 108:** the released energy equals the mass loss × c².
- **To Topic 107:** fission fragments are radioactive isotopes with their own half-lives.

## 4. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 4.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

| Year | Unit | Topic | Question | Marks | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2078/2022 | Nuclear physics | Fission & fusion | Distinguish between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion with one example each. | 3 | Comparison |

### 4.2 Likely additional forms (NEB-style)

1. Explain the chain reaction and reactor control (3m).
2. Mass-to-energy numerical for a fission event (3m).
3. Why does the Sun need fusion, not fission? (2m)

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Forgetting the example equations — they carry marks in the 3m comparison.
2. Saying fusion happens "at room temperature" — the Coulomb barrier demands ~10⁸ K.
3. Claiming fission yields more energy *per kilogram* — fusion wins per kg, fission per event.

data.title: Optics — Introduction
data.summary: Geometrical (ray) optics and wave optics: light obeys reflection and refraction (Snell's law) derived from Fermat's principle; interference, diffraction and polarization demand the wave picture. Ray optics is valid while object sizes and apertures are much greater than the wavelength.
notes: Nature of Light: Light is an electromagnetic wave that exhibits both wave and particle (photon) behavior. Speed of light in vacuum c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

Ray Optics (Geometrical Optics): Light travels in straight lines in a homogeneous medium. Valid when object sizes and apertures are much larger than the wavelength λ. Deals with reflection, refraction, and image formation by mirrors and lenses.
Wave Optics (Physical Optics): Explains interference, diffraction, and polarization — phenomena that cannot be explained by ray optics alone. Required when apertures or obstacles are comparable to λ.
Fermat's Principle of Least Time: Light travels between two points along the path that takes the least time. This principle derives both the law of reflection and Snell's law of refraction.
Reflection: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection (i = r). The incident ray, reflected ray, and normal all lie in the same plane.
Refraction: When light passes from one medium to another, it bends. Snell's law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, where n is the refractive index of the medium.
Refractive Index: n = c/v, where v is the speed of light in the medium. Absolute refractive index is relative to vacuum. Relative refractive index ⁿ₂n₁ = v₁/v₂ = n₂/n₁.
specificConditions: Optical Principles: The behavior of light is governed by the laws of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection) and refraction (Snell's law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂). These laws derive from Fermat's principle of least time.

Wave Nature of Light: Light exhibits wave phenomena including interference, diffraction, and polarization. These cannot be explained by ray optics alone and require wave optics. The wavelength λ and frequency f are related by c = λf.

Approximations and Validity: Ray optics (geometrical optics) is valid when object sizes are much greater than wavelength λ. Wave optics is required when apertures or obstacles are comparable to λ. Quantum optics is needed for single-photon phenomena.
formulas: Speed of light: c = λf, where c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum
Refractive index: n = c/v, where v is speed of light in the medium
Snell's law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂
Law of reflection: angle of incidence i = angle of reflection r
Relative refractive index: ⁿ₂n₁ = v₁/v₂ = n₂/n₁
keyPoints: Light exhibits both wave and particle (photon) dual nature.
Ray optics is valid when object sizes ≫ wavelength λ.
Wave optics explains interference, diffraction, and polarization.
Fermat's principle of least time derives reflection and refraction laws.
Refractive index n = c/v measures how much light slows in a medium.
importantStatements: Statement 1: The speed of light in vacuum is approximately 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
Statement 2: Snell's law states n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ for refraction at an interface.
Statement 3: The law of reflection states angle of incidence equals angle of reflection.
Statement 4: Fermat's principle of least time is the foundation of geometrical optics.
Statement 5: Wave optics is needed when apertures are comparable to the wavelength.
importantNotes: Refractive index is dimensionless and has no units.
When light enters a denser medium, it bends towards the normal.
When light enters a rarer medium, it bends away from the normal.
The frequency of light remains unchanged during refraction; wavelength and speed change.
Total internal reflection occurs when light travels from denser to rarer medium beyond the critical angle.
examShortTricks: n = c/v — higher n means slower light in medium.
Denser to rarer → bends away from normal.
Rarer to denser → bends towards normal.
i = r for reflection — always measure from normal.
c = λf — frequency stays constant across media.
examNotes: NEB frequently asks to state and explain Snell's law and the laws of reflection.
Refractive index numericals: n = c/v, real depth/apparent depth = n.

data.title: Mirrors and Lenses
data.summary: Mirrors and lenses form images by reflection and refraction. Plane mirrors form virtual images; spherical mirrors (concave/convex) and lenses use the mirror/lens formula with sign conventions to determine image position, size, and nature.
notes: Plane Mirror: Forms a virtual, erect, same-sized image behind the mirror. Image distance equals object distance. Lateral inversion occurs (left-right reversed).
Spherical Mirrors: Concave (converging) and convex (diverging) mirrors. Key terms: pole (P), center of curvature (C), radius of curvature (R), focus (F), focal length (f = R/2), principal axis.
Mirror Formula: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u, where u = object distance, v = image distance, f = focal length. Sign convention: distances measured from pole; positive in direction of incident light.
Magnification: m = -v/u = h_i/h_o, where h_i is image height and h_o is object height. Negative m means inverted image.
Convex Lens: Converging lens. Thicker at center. Forms real inverted images (except when object within focal length). Lens formula: 1/f = 1/v - 1/u.
Concave Lens: Diverging lens. Thinner at center. Always forms virtual, erect, diminished images.
Power of Lens: P = 1/f (f in meters), unit: diopter (D). Convex lens: P > 0. Concave lens: P < 0. Lenses in contact: P = P₁ + P₂ + ...
Spherical Aberration: Marginal rays focus at different points than paraxial rays. Minimized by using small apertures or parabolic mirrors.
specificConditions: Thin Lens/Mirror Approximation: The mirror equation (1/f = 1/u + 1/v) and lens formula (1/f = 1/v - 1/u) assume thin optics where thickness is negligible. For thick lenses, principal planes must be used. Sign convention (Cartesian): distances measured from pole/lens center; positive in direction of incident light for u, opposite for v/f.

Spherical Aberration: Paraxial rays (close to axis) follow the simple formulas. Non-paraxial rays focus at different points, causing spherical aberration. The formulas assume paraxial approximation (small angles, sin θ ≈ θ).

Lens/Mirror Power: Power P = 1/f (meters) in diopters. Converging (convex lens, concave mirror): P > 0. Diverging (concave lens, convex mirror): P < 0. Powers add for thin lenses in contact: P_total = Σ P_i.

data.title: Potential Difference and Point Charge
data.topicTitle: Potential difference, potential due to point charge, potential energy and electron volt
notes: **Electrostatic Potential & Potential Difference:** Electric potential at a point P is defined as the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a test charge q₀ from infinity to P against the electrostatic force of the source distribution, without altering the field: $V = \frac{W}{q_0} = -\int_\infty^P \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{r}$. Potential difference between two points A and B is $\Delta V = V_B - V_A = -\int_A^B \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{r}$. Both V and ΔV are scalars, have SI unit volt (V), where $1\,\text{V} = 1\,\text{J/C}$, and are path-independent because the electrostatic field is conservative ($\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{r} = 0$).

**Potential due to an Isolated Point Charge:** For a source charge Q at the origin, the work done in bringing q₀ from infinity to distance r is $W = -\int_\infty^r \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 x^2} dx = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{Q q_0}{r}$. Dividing by q₀ gives the potential: $V(r) = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q}{r} = k\frac{Q}{r}$. Unlike electric field (which is a vector falling off as 1/r²), potential is a scalar that falls off only as 1/r. For an ensemble of point charges, superposition applies algebraically: $V = k \sum_i \frac{q_i}{r_i}$.

**Relation between Electric Field and Potential Gradient:** The electric field and potential are intrinsically related. Since $V = -\int \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{r}$, we obtain $\vec{E} = -\vec{\nabla}V$. For a uniform field directed along the x-axis: $E = -\frac{dV}{dx}$. This is the foundational link that converts every electrostatic field formula into a corresponding potential formula, always by substituting $E \propto 1/r^2$ with $V \propto 1/r$.

**Potential of Standard Charge Distributions:** (1) **Line charge:** $V = -\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\ln(r/r_0)$; (2) **Infinite plane sheet:** $V = -\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}x$ (linear decrease, since E is constant); (3) **Charged conducting shell (radius R, charge Q):** $V = kQ/R$ everywhere inside and on the surface, jumping to $V = kQ/r$ outside — a discontinuity of exactly $E R = \sigma R/\varepsilon_0$; (4) **Two parallel plates separated by d:** $E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$ and $V_{AB} = -Ed = -\frac{\sigma d}{\varepsilon_0}$.

**Potential Energy of a System of Charges:** The potential energy of a charge q brought from infinity into the field of source charge Q is $U = qV = k\frac{qQ}{r}$. For two like charges ($qQ > 0$), U is positive, meaning work must be done against repulsion; for two unlike charges ($qQ < 0$), U is negative, indicating the system is bound and energy is released on assembly. For multiple charges, the total energy is the sum over all distinct pairs: $U = k \sum_{i<j} \frac{q_i q_j}{r_{ij}}$. Energy is a scalar and must never be computed by summing $\vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r}$ naively over individual pairs for conservative systems.

**Equivalence of Potential Energy and Force:** By the work-energy theorem, the work done by the electrostatic force in moving a charge slowly from A to B is $W = q(V_A - V_B) = -\Delta U$. Therefore $\Delta U = -W_{electric}$, proving that $\Delta U = -\int \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r}$. This means a force always acts to reduce potential energy: a positive charge accelerates toward lower V, and a negative charge accelerates toward higher V.

**Electron Volt (eV) — Energy Unit Conversion:** The electron volt is the energy gained by a particle of charge e when accelerated through a potential difference of one volt: $1\,\text{eV} = e \times 1\,\text{V} = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C} \times 1\,\text{J/C} = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$. Convenient conversion factors: $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$ and $1\,\text{J} = 6.242 \times 10^{18}\,\text{eV}$. Multiples are commonly used: $1\,\text{keV} = 10^3\,\text{eV}$ (X-rays), $1\,\text{MeV} = 10^6\,\text{eV}$ (particle accelerators, nuclear binding), and $1\,\text{GeV} = 10^9\,\text{eV}$ (collider experiments). Note that electron volt is an energy unit, not a charge or potential unit.
confusion: Treating potential as a vector and adding components: Potential V is a scalar. Only in a region with a clear directional symmetry (e.g. along the axis of a line charge) is it meaningful to write $V = -Ex$; you must never resolve V into vector components like x, y, z components.

Confusing potential difference with potential: Potential difference is a change $\Delta V = V_B - V_A$ between two points and can be positive or negative. Potential V itself is defined relative to infinity ($V_\infty = 0$), so a positive charge gives positive V while an electron gives negative V.

Believing the electron volt is a unit of charge or potential: The electron volt (eV) is a unit of ENERGY, defined as the energy of a charge of magnitude e accelerated through 1 V. 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

Computing total potential energy by summing over all ordered pairs (i, j) instead of distinct pairs (i < j): Every interaction must be counted exactly once; summing both $q_i q_j$ and $q_j q_i$ double-counts each pair energy.
practice: Two charges $q_1 = +2\,\mu\text{C}$ and $q_2 = -3\,\mu\text{C}$ are separated by $30\,\text{cm}$ in vacuum. (a) Find the potential at the midpoint. (b) Find the potential energy of the system. Solution: (a) At the midpoint, $r_1 = r_2 = 0.15\,\text{m}$, so $V = k\left(\frac{q_1}{r_1} + \frac{q_2}{r_2}\right) = (9 \times 10^9)\left(\frac{2 \times 10^{-6} - 3 \times 10^{-6}}{0.15}\right) = (9 \times 10^9)\left(\frac{-1 \times 10^{-6}}{0.15}\right) = (9 \times 10^9)(-6.67 \times 10^{-6}) = -6.0 \times 10^4\,\text{V}$. (b) $U = k\frac{q_1 q_2}{r} = (9 \times 10^9)\frac{(2 \times 10^{-6})(-3 \times 10^{-6})}{0.30} = (9 \times 10^9)(-2 \times 10^{-11}) = -1.8 \times 10^{-1}\,\text{J} = -0.18\,\text{J}$.
universalFacts: The electron volt is named after the electron but is a universal energy unit: an alpha particle with charge +2e accelerated through 1 V gains 2 eV, while a proton accelerated through the same 1 V gains 1 eV.

The resting membrane potential of a human nerve axon (about −70 mV measured inside relative to outside) corresponds to a stored energy of roughly 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰ J per ion crossing the membrane, which is the physical basis of neural signaling.
examples: Electron gun in a cathode ray tube: Electrons accelerated through a potential difference V gain kinetic energy eV. For V = 10 kV, each electron gains 10 keV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ J, which determines the spot size on the fluorescent screen.

Photocell and photoelectric effect: Incoming photons with energies quoted in electron volts (visible light ≈ 1.5–3 eV, UV up to tens of eV) eject photoelectrons only if the photon energy exceeds the work function, the basis of all photoelectric devices.

Nucleosome-free grounding of tall buildings: Lightning-induced potential differences of 10⁸ V are bled harmlessly to earth through lightning rods and thick grounding strips, since $W = qV$ for a large charge at huge potential would otherwise be catastrophic.
practiceQuestions: Q1. Define electrostatic potential at a point. State its SI unit and dimensional formula, and explain why electric potential is a scalar while electric field is a vector.
Q2. Derive an expression for the potential at a point due to a point charge Q, and compare its distance dependence with that of the electric field.
Q3. A charge q is brought from infinity to a point in the field of a dipole of moment p placed along the x-axis. Show that the potential energy is $U = -kq p \cos\theta / r^2$.

Q4. An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 500 V. Calculate the energy gained in joules and in electron volts, and the resulting speed. (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg)
formulas: Potential: $V = \frac{W}{q_0} = -\int_\infty^P \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{r}$
Potential difference: $\Delta V = V_B - V_A = -\int_A^B \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{r}$
Potential due to point charge: $V = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q}{r} = k\frac{Q}{r}$
Field–potential link: $\vec{E} = -\vec{\nabla}V$
Potential energy of two charges: $U = k\frac{q_1 q_2}{r}$
System potential energy: $U = k\sum_{i<j} \frac{q_i q_j}{r_{ij}}$
Energy–work relation: $\Delta U = -W_{electric}$
Electron volt: $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$
keyPoints: Potential V is work done per unit positive charge; SI unit is volt (1 V = 1 J/C).
Potential is a path-independent scalar; electric field is a vector with direction given by -∇V.
Potential due to a point charge falls as 1/r, while its electric field falls as 1/r².
Like charges give positive U (repulsive, unbound); unlike charges give negative U (attractive, bound).
1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, an energy unit; 1 MeV = 10⁶ eV is standard in nuclear physics.
data.summary: Electrostatic potential V is the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a test charge from infinity, given by V = -∫E·dr, with SI unit the volt. A point charge Q produces V = kQ/r, falling as 1/r (compared with the field's 1/r²), and fields and potentials are linked by E = -∇V. The potential energy of a charge system is U = kΣqᵢqⱼ/rᵢⱼ, positive for like charges and negative for unlike charges, with ΔU = -W_electric. The electron volt is an energy unit where 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
specialNotes: Electric potential can be zero at a point even where the field is non-zero (the equatorial point of a dipole, and the null point of a dipole field). Only the electric field is guaranteed to be non-zero wherever a charge feels a force.
Inside a hollow charged conductor the potential is constant (not zero): V = kQ/R, whereas the electric field there is zero. Zero field does not imply zero potential.

Because V depends on position but not on the path taken, a charge can reach a point via any route with identical work done, which is why parallel-plate capacitor calculations ignore the fringing geometry at the edges.
importantStatements: Statement 1: Electric potential at a point is defined as the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a test charge from infinity to that point.
Statement 2: The potential due to a point charge varies inversely with distance (V ∝ 1/r), whereas the electric field varies inversely with distance squared (E ∝ 1/r²).
Statement 3: The electric field at any point is the negative gradient of the potential at that point (E = -∇V).

Statement 4: The potential energy of two like charges is positive, indicating a repulsive, unbound configuration, whereas for two unlike charges it is negative, indicating an attractive, bound configuration.
Statement 5: One electron volt is the energy gained by an electron accelerated through a potential difference of one volt, equal to 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
importantNotes: The SI unit of potential is the volt (V), where 1 V = 1 J/C, and its dimensional formula is [M L² T⁻³ I⁻¹], identical to that of energy per unit charge.
examShortTricks: Field-to-potential conversion trick: whenever E ∝ 1/r², the corresponding potential is V ∝ 1/r; whenever E ∝ 1/r, the potential is V ∝ ln r.
Sign check: a positive charge always moves toward lower V, while a negative charge moves toward higher V, since force always acts to reduce potential energy.
eV conversion: multiply eV by 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ to get joules, or divide joules by 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ to get eV.

mcs.explanation: Energy gained = qV = (1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)(100 V) = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁷ J, which is equivalent to 100 eV.

mcs.question: Two charges +2 μC and -2 μC are separated by 1 m. The potential energy of the system is:

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Energy Landscape of Charge

Electric potential is electrostatics' energy language: instead of asking how strongly a charge is pushed, we ask how much work it takes to move it. Volts, electron-volts and the kq/r formula make field problems as easy as bookkeeping.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024)

### 2.1 Potential and potential difference

- **Electric potential at a point:** the work done per unit positive charge in bringing it from infinity to that point without acceleration:
$$V = \frac{W}{q} \qquad \text{SI unit: volt (V) = J C}^{-1}$$
- **Potential difference** between two points: work per unit charge moving *between* them — 1 volt = 1 joule per coulomb (NEB 2023, 1m MCQ).
- **Work–charge relation:** $W = qV$; for n electrons, $W = neV$ (NEB 2022, 4m).

### 2.2 Potential due to a point charge

$$V = \frac{kq}{r} = \frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}$$
— a scalar, so potentials from several charges add **algebraically** (signs included). Zero taken at infinity.

### 2.3 Potential energy of a pair of charges

$$U = \frac{kq_1q_2}{r}$$
— negative for unlike charges (bound system), positive for like charges (work needed to assemble).

### 2.4 The electron volt

**1 eV** = the kinetic energy gained by an electron crossing a potential difference of 1 V:
$$1 \text{ eV} = e \times 1\text{ V} = 1.6\times10^{-19} \text{ J}$$

### 2.5 Worked numericals

**Q (2m, 2024):** Calculate the electric potential at 0.5 m from a point charge of 2 μC in air.
$$V = \frac{kq}{r} = \frac{9\times10^9 \times 2\times10^{-6}}{0.5} = 3.6\times10^4 \text{ V} = 36 \text{ kV}$$

**Q (3m, 2020):** Find the work done in moving a charge of 2×10⁻¹⁹ C through 300 V; express in electron volts.
- $W = qV = 2\times10^{-19} \times 300 = 6.0\times10^{-17}$ J
- $W = \frac{6.0\times10^{-17}}{1.6\times10^{-19}} = 375$ eV

**Q (3m, 2024):** Two charges +3 μC and −2 μC are 0.3 m apart. Calculate the potential energy.
$$U = \frac{kq_1q_2}{r} = \frac{9\times10^9 \times 3\times10^{-6} \times (-2\times10^{-6})}{0.3} = -0.18 \text{ J}$$
— negative: work must be done to *separate* them; opposite charges bind.

**Q (2m, 2024):** Define the electron-volt; convert 1 eV into joules. — see §2.4.

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 87:** V is the line integral of E; E is the gradient of V.
- **To Topic 91:** equipotential surfaces are V = constant maps.
- **To capacitors (Unit 24):** U = ½CV² stores energy in the same language.

data.title: Equipotential Lines and Surfaces
notes: **Definition of an Equipotential Surface:** An equipotential surface (or equipotential line in two dimensions) is a geometrical surface on which the electric potential V is the same at every point. Since $\Delta V = 0$ between any two points on it, no work is done by the electrostatic field in moving a charge anywhere along the surface: $W = q\Delta V = 0$. Every equipotential surface is a level surface of the scalar potential field, just as contour lines on a topographic map join points of equal height.

**Fundamental Properties of Equipotential Surfaces:** (1) **No work is done** on a charge moving along the surface ($W = q\Delta V = 0$); (2) **They are always perpendicular to electric field lines** wherever the field is non-zero; (3) **They never intersect one another** — two intersecting surfaces would assign two different potentials to the same point; (4) **The spacing between successive equipotential surfaces indicates field strength** — closely spaced surfaces signify a strong electric field and rapidly changing potential; (5) **A conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is a single equipotential surface**, since free charges redistribute until the internal field vanishes.

**Proof that Equipotential Surfaces are Perpendicular to Field Lines:** Let A and B be two points a distance $\Delta s$ apart on the same equipotential surface, so $\Delta V = 0$. The change in potential along a displacement is $\Delta V = -\vec{E} \cdot \Delta\vec{s} = -E\,\Delta s\cos\theta$. Since $\Delta V = 0$, we must have $\cos\theta = 0$, meaning $\theta = 90^\circ$. Therefore the displacement $\Delta\vec{s}$ (which lies along the equipotential surface) is always perpendicular to $\vec{E}$, confirming that equipotential surfaces and field lines intersect at right angles everywhere.

**Equipotential Surfaces for Standard Charge Configurations:** (1) **Isolated point charge Q:** $V = kQ/r$ is constant on a sphere of radius r, so equipotentials are concentric spheres, and the normal to each sphere is radial, exactly along the field lines. (2) **Infinite line charge λ:** $V = -\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\ln\frac{r}{r_0}$, so equipotentials are coaxial cylinders of radius r, with field lines radial and perpendicular. (3) **Infinite plane sheet with surface density σ:** $V = -\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}x$, so equipotentials are infinite planes parallel to the sheet, uniformly spaced since E is constant. (4) **Two parallel plates:** planes parallel to the plates, densely packed between the plates (where E is large) and widely spaced outside (where E is zero).

**Equipotential Surface of a Conducting Sphere:** For a conducting sphere of radius R carrying charge Q, the entire surface of the sphere is at a single potential $V = kQ/R$. Taking the outside potential, $V(r) = kQ/r$, the equipotentials are concentric spheres of radius r ≥ R, all larger than the sphere itself. Inside the hollow conductor, V is constant at $kQ/R$ for every point $r < R$, so the entire interior cavity constitutes one equipotential region. Because E = 0 inside, there is no field direction to define, and the conductor plus its interior forms a single continuous equipotential volume.

**Work and Energy Relations for Equipotential Surfaces:** Moving a charge q from equipotential surface V₁ to V₂ requires external work $W_{ext} = q\Delta V = q(V_2 - V_1)$ and changes the system's potential energy by exactly the same amount: $\Delta U = q\Delta V$. For a positive charge, work is required to move it to a higher potential; for an electron (negative charge), it is spontaneous. Two equipotential surfaces at potentials differing by 1 volt, for a single electron, differ in potential energy by exactly 1 eV — this is precisely why the electron volt is the natural energy unit when discussing potential differences.
confusion: Mistaking equipotential surfaces for field lines: Field lines show the direction of the force on a positive test charge; equipotential surfaces join points of equal potential. The two families are always mutually perpendicular, never parallel.

Believing that equipotential surfaces are widely spaced where the field is weak: Spacing is inversely related to field strength. Close spacing means a large potential change over a short distance, i.e. a strong field (E = -ΔV/Δs).

Assuming the potential on the surface of a charged conductor varies with position: In electrostatic equilibrium, free charges redistribute until the interior field is zero, making the entire conductor surface a single equipotential at V = kQ/R.
practice: A point charge q = 4 μC is located at the origin. (a) What is the potential on a sphere of radius 5 cm? (b) What is the work required to move a test charge of 2 μC from that sphere to a sphere of radius 10 cm? Solution: (a) $V = kq/r = (9 \times 10^9)(4 \times 10^{-6})/0.05 = 36000/0.05 = 7.2 \times 10^5\,\text{V}$. (b) $W = q_0\Delta V$ where $\Delta V = kq(1/r_2 - 1/r_1) = (9 \times 10^9)(4 \times 10^{-6})(10 - 20) = 36000 \times (-10) = -3.6 \times 10^5\,\text{V}$. Thus $W = (2 \times 10^{-6})(-3.6 \times 10^5) = -0.72\,\text{J}$. The negative sign indicates the field does this work spontaneously as the test charge moves outward against the repulsion of the positive source.
universalFacts: The human heart, whose electrical activity is measured by electrocardiograms (ECGs), depends on the heart muscle cells generating potential differences of about 1 mV at the body surface — an equipotential mapping problem in three dimensions.

Equipotential mapping of underground rock and soil resistivity is a standard geophysical prospecting technique: injecting current into the ground and mapping constant-potential contours reveals buried ore deposits, voids, and groundwater.
examples: Cathode ray oscilloscope (CRO): The vertical deflection plates are connected to an amplifier so the electron beam passes through a controlled electric field, but the calibration relies on the beam travelling along a path of constant potential between the plates.

Electrostatic loudspeaker drivers: A charged cone suspended in a radial field moves along paths near-constant potential, so almost no additional energy is required for the cone's travel and the efficiency stays high.

Tectonic stress mapping in geophysics: Repeated surveys of Earth's surface potential (equipotential contours) show slow drift of surface charge, a possible precursor to earthquakes as stressed rock begins to release charge.
practiceQuestions: Q1. Define an equipotential surface. State and prove any three properties of equipotential surfaces.

Q2. Show that equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to the lines of force. Deduce the shape of the equipotential surfaces for (a) a point charge, (b) a long straight wire, and (c) an infinite plane sheet of charge.
Q3. A conducting sphere of radius 10 cm carries a charge of 1 μC. Find the potential (a) on the surface, (b) at a point 15 cm from the centre, and (c) at a point 5 cm from the centre.

Q4. Two equipotential surfaces of an electric field are at 10 V and 40 V. How much work is required to move a charge of 2 μC from the first surface to the second, and what is the change in its potential energy?
formulas: Equipotential condition: $\Delta V = 0$
Perpendicularity condition: $\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{l} = -dV = 0$
Field from potential spacing: $E \approx \frac{\Delta V}{\Delta s}$
Work to move charge between surfaces: $W = q\Delta V$
Potential change: $\Delta U = q\Delta V$
keyPoints: No work is done by the electric field in moving a charge along an equipotential surface (W = qΔV = 0).
Equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to electric field lines.
Two equipotential surfaces can never intersect one another.
Closely spaced equipotential surfaces indicate a strong electric field; widely spaced ones indicate a weak field.
A conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is a single equipotential surface at constant V = kQ/R.
data.summary: An equipotential surface is a locus of points at identical potential V, so no work is done by the field along it (W = qΔV = 0). Equipotential surfaces can never intersect and are always perpendicular to electric field lines, since dV = -E·dl = 0 forces the displacement along the surface to be normal to E. Their spacing indicates field strength: close spacing means a strong field. For a point charge they are concentric spheres, for a line charge coaxial cylinders, and for an infinite plane sheet parallel planes.
specialNotes: Inside a charged conductor there is no field direction, so the concept of perpendicularity does not apply there; the whole cavity is simply at the constant potential of the conductor's surface.
For a dipole, the V = 0 equipotential surface is the perpendicular bisector plane of the axis — the only region in the dipole's field where V is exactly zero, though E is non-zero there.
importantStatements: Statement 1: No work is done by the electrostatic field in moving a charge along an equipotential surface, since W = qΔV = 0.
Statement 2: Equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to the electric field lines at the points of intersection.
Statement 3: Two distinct equipotential surfaces can never intersect each other.
Statement 4: The closeness of successive equipotential surfaces is inversely proportional to the strength of the electric field in that region.
Statement 5: The entire surface of a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is at a single constant potential.
importantNotes: Equipotential surfaces are the two-dimensional analogue of contour lines on a topographic map: equal potential means equal 'height' of the potential field, and gradient magnitude equals field magnitude.
examShortTricks: Shape recall: point charge → concentric spheres; line charge → coaxial cylinders; plane sheet → parallel planes; conducting shell → sphere plus a constant interior region.
Quick check of perpendicularity: if E had a component along the equipotential surface, moving along it would change V, contradicting ΔV = 0.

mcs.question: The work done in moving a charge q from one equipotential surface to another surface at a higher potential is:
mcs.explanation: W = qΔV where ΔV is the potential difference between the two surfaces. This is non-zero because the surfaces are not equipotential with each other.

mcs.question: Equipotential surfaces of a point charge are:
mcs.explanation: Since V = kQ/r, V is constant for a fixed value of r, which is the equation of a sphere centred on the charge. Hence equipotentials are concentric spheres.

mcs.question: The spacing between two consecutive equipotential surfaces in a region is small. This indicates that the electric field in that region is:
mcs.explanation: A small separation for a fixed potential difference means a large gradient, E = -ΔV/Δs, so the field is very large in that region.

data.title: Potential Gradient
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — From Potential to Field

The electric field and the potential are two views of one thing: E is the *slope* of V. Where potential drops fastest, the field is strongest — a relation that turns every potential map into a force map, and explains why the inside of a charged shell is field-free.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2024)

### 2.1 The relation E = −dV/dr

The **potential gradient** is the rate of change of potential with distance:
$$E = -\frac{dV}{dr} \qquad \text{unit: V/m} \equiv \text{N/C}$$
- The **minus sign**: the field points in the direction of *decreasing* potential — from high V to low V.
- Magnitude: the steepest slope of the potential landscape.
- For a uniform field between plates: $E = \frac{V}{d}$ — potential difference per unit separation.

### 2.2 Statement form (NEB 2024, 3m)

**Electric potential** is work per unit charge from infinity (SI unit volt); **the relation between field and potential** is $E = -dV/dr$ — the field points down the steepest potential slope. NEB 2024 asked exactly this trio: definition, unit, relation.

### 2.3 Worked reasoning and numericals

**Q (3m, 2024):** Show that the electric potential everywhere inside a uniformly charged hollow sphere equals its surface value.
- Inside the shell E = 0 (Gauss's law — no enclosed charge).

- Continuity at the surface forces that constant to be $V = \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R}$ — the surface value. The interior is one equipotential region.

$E = -\frac{dV}{dx} = -4x$ → at x = 1: E = −4 V/m (4 V/m in the −x direction).

data.title: Heat (H) - Mass and Temperature Dependency
data.topicTitle: Quantity of heat (H) - mass and temperature dependency
notes: **Heat is energy in transit:** Heat ($H$) is the thermal energy transferred between systems due to a temperature difference. It is NOT a property of a body - you cannot say "a body contains heat." A body contains internal energy; heat is the transfer of that energy.

**Mass dependency (H ∝ m):** For a given substance and temperature change, the heat required is directly proportional to the mass: $H \propto m$. Doubling the mass doubles the heat needed. This is because more molecules means more total kinetic energy must change.

**Temperature dependency (H ∝ Δθ):** For a given mass, heat is directly proportional to the temperature change: $H \propto \Delta\theta$, where $\Delta\theta = \theta_f - \theta_i$ (final − initial). Heating water from 20°C to 80°C requires 3× the heat of heating from 20°C to 40°C.

**Combined relation:** Combining both: $H \propto m \cdot \Delta\theta$. Introducing the constant of proportionality - the specific heat capacity ($c$) - gives the fundamental equation: **$H = m \cdot c \cdot \Delta\theta$**

**Sign convention:** When heat is absorbed (temperature rises), $H > 0$ and $\Delta\theta > 0$. When heat is released (temperature falls), $H < 0$ and $\Delta\theta < 0$. The sign tells you the direction of energy flow.

**Units of heat:** SI unit is the **joule (J)**. The CGS unit is the **calorie (cal)**. Conversion: $1\text{ cal} = 4.184\text{ J}$ (thermochemical calorie). Another unit, the BTU (British Thermal Unit), is used in engineering: $1\text{ BTU} \approx 1055\text{ J}$.

**Heat vs. Temperature:** Temperature ($\theta$) is an intensive property - it doesn't depend on the amount of substance. Heat ($H$) is extensive - it depends on mass. A cup of water at 80°C has a higher temperature than a bathtub at 50°C, but the bathtub has more thermal energy (and more heat to transfer if cooled).

**Heat vs. Internal Energy:** Internal energy ($U$) is the total energy stored in a system's molecules. Heat ($H$) is the energy TRANSFERRED. When you heat a body, its internal energy increases: $\Delta U = H$ (at constant volume, no work done).

**Real-world analogy:** Think of water flowing from a high tank to a low tank. Temperature is like water level (height), heat is like the amount of water that flows. Two tanks at the same height have the same temperature, but the larger tank has more water (more heat capacity).

**Calorimetry context:** In all calorimetry problems, the equation $H = mc\Delta\theta$ is applied to EACH substance separately. Hot body: $H_{lost} = m_h c_h (\theta_h - \theta_{eq})$. Cold body: $H_{gained} = m_c c_c (\theta_{eq} - \theta_c)$. Set $H_{lost} = H_{gained}$.

**Common values of c (for reference):** Water: $c = 4200\text{ J/kg·K}$. Ice: $c = 2100\text{ J/kg·K}$. Copper: $c = 390\text{ J/kg·K}$. Aluminum: $c = 900\text{ J/kg·K}$. Iron: $c = 450\text{ J/kg·K}$. Lead: $c = 130\text{ J/kg·K}$. Higher $c$ means more heat needed per degree.

**Why water is special:** Water has the highest specific heat among common liquids ($4200\text{ J/kg·K}$). This means it absorbs huge amounts of heat with minimal temperature change - why it's used as a coolant in car radiators, power plants, and why coastal climates are moderate.

**Quick estimation rule:** For a 1 kg mass of water, raising temperature by 1°C requires 4200 J. So heating 2 kg by 50°C requires $H = 2 \times 4200 \times 50 = 420{,}000\text{ J} = 420\text{ kJ}$. This is roughly the energy in 100 g of sugar.
**Dimensional check:** $[H] = [M][L]^2[T]^{-2}$ (energy). $[mc\Delta\theta] = [M] \cdot [L]^2[T]^{-2}[\Theta]^{-1} \cdot [\Theta] = [M][L]^2[T]^{-2}$. ✓ Dimensions match.

**Power and heat rate:** If heat is supplied at a constant rate (power $P$), then $H = Pt$. So $Pt = mc\Delta\theta$, which gives $\Delta\theta/t = P/(mc)$. A 1500 W kettle heats 1 kg of water at $\Delta\theta/t = 1500/(1 \times 4200) = 0.357\text{ °C/s}$.
confusion: ❌ Heat and temperature are the same thing. ✅ Temperature is the average molecular kinetic energy (intensive). Heat is the total energy transferred (extensive). A spark at 2000°C has tiny heat content; a bathtub at 40°C has huge heat content.

❌ A body "contains" heat. ✅ A body contains internal energy (kinetic + potential of its molecules). Heat is the TRANSFER of energy due to temperature difference. Once energy is in the body, it's no longer "heat." Think of it like "payment" - once received, it's no longer a payment; it's just money in your account.

❌ All materials heat up at the same rate with the same power. ✅ Different materials have different specific heats. 1 kW heats 1 kg of aluminum ($c=900$) much faster than 1 kg of water ($c=4200$). The aluminum's temperature rises ~4.7× faster.

❌ The formula H = mcΔθ works for phase changes too. ✅ This formula ONLY works when temperature changes WITHOUT a phase change. During melting (ice → water at 0°C) or boiling (water → steam at 100°C), temperature stays constant - you need $H = mL$ instead.

❌ Specific heat capacity depends on the amount of substance. ✅ Specific heat capacity is an INTENSIVE property - it depends only on the MATERIAL, not the mass. 1 kg of copper has $c = 390\text{ J/kg·K}$, same as 1 g of copper.

❌ Heat always flows from hot to cold, so a cold object can never lose heat to a hot one. ✅ Heat naturally flows from hot to cold. However, a refrigerator CAN move heat from cold to hot - but only by doing external work (compressor). This doesn't violate the second law.

❌ If you add heat, temperature always rises. ✅ During a phase change (melting, boiling, sublimation), added heat goes into breaking intermolecular bonds (increasing potential energy), NOT increasing kinetic energy. Temperature stays constant during the transition.
practice: How much heat is required to raise the temperature of 2.5 kg of water from 20°C to 80°C? $H = mc\Delta\theta = 2.5 \times 4200 \times 60 = 630{,}000\text{ J} = 630\text{ kJ}$.

A 500 g copper block at 100°C is placed in 200 g of water at 20°C. If no heat is lost, what is the final temperature? Set $m_{Cu}c_{Cu}(100 - T) = m_w c_w(T - 20)$. $0.5 \times 390 \times (100-T) = 0.2 \times 4200 \times (T-20)$. $195(100-T) = 840(T-20)$. $19500 - 195T = 840T - 16800$. $1035T = 36300 \Rightarrow T \approx 35.1°\text{C}$.

An electric heater supplies 840 J/s to 2 kg of water. How long to raise the temperature from 25°C to 75°C? $H = mc\Delta\theta = 2 \times 4200 \times 50 = 420{,}000\text{ J}$. Time $t = H/P = 420000/840 = 500\text{ s} \approx 8\text{ min } 20\text{ s}$.

What mass of iron ($c = 450\text{ J/kg·K}$) at 100°C is needed to raise 0.5 kg of water from 15°C to 25°C? $m_{Fe} \times 450 \times (100-25) = 0.5 \times 4200 \times 10$. $m_{Fe} \times 33750 = 21000$. $m_{Fe} = 0.622\text{ kg} = 622\text{ g}$.

A 0.2 kg aluminum calorimeter contains 0.3 kg of water at 20°C. A 0.1 kg copper block at 90°C is dropped in. Find the equilibrium temperature ($c_{Al} = 900$, $c_{Cu} = 390$). Heat gained: $(0.3 \times 4200 + 0.2 \times 900)(T-20) = 1440(T-20)$. Heat lost: $0.1 \times 390 \times (90-T) = 39(90-T)$. $1440(T-20) = 3510 - 39T$. $1479T = 6390 \Rightarrow T \approx 4.32°\text{C}$ - wait, that's too low. Recalculate: $1440T - 28800 = 3510 - 39T$. $1479T = 32310 \Rightarrow T \approx 21.85°\text{C}$.
universalFacts: The calorie was originally defined as the heat needed to raise 1 gram of water by 1°C - specifically from 14.5°C to 15.5°C, since water's specific heat varies slightly with temperature. The modern value is $1\text{ cal} = 4.184\text{ J}$ (exact).

Water's anomalously high specific heat ($4200\text{ J/kg·K}$) is due to hydrogen bonding. Breaking these bonds requires extra energy, so more heat goes into the system without raising temperature. This is why oceans moderate Earth's climate.

The concept of "heat" as a form of energy was established by James Prescott Joule in the 1840s. His famous paddle-wheel experiment showed that mechanical work could be converted to heat, establishing the mechanical equivalent of heat: $1\text{ J} \leftrightarrow$ temperature rise.

Joseph Black (1728-1799) was the first to distinguish between "heat" and "temperature." He observed that melting ice absorbs heat without changing temperature - this led to the concept of "latent heat" and the caloric theory of heat.

Specific heat capacity determines how quickly a material heats up or cools down. Metals (low $c$) heat up fast; water (high $c$) resists temperature change. This is why a metal spoon gets hot quickly in soup, but the soup itself takes minutes to cool.
specificConditions: **Heat as Energy Transfer:** Heat ($H$) is energy in transit due to temperature difference, not a property of a system. A body contains internal energy $U$; heat is the transfer $\Delta U = H$ (at constant volume, no work).

**Proportionality Law:** $H \propto m \Delta\theta$ for a given substance. This linearity holds only within a single phase (no phase change). During phase transitions, $H = mL$ with constant $\theta$ — the $H \propto \Delta\theta$ relation breaks down.

**Specific Heat Capacity Definition:** $c = H/(m\Delta\theta)$ is the proportionality constant. It is an *intensive* property (independent of mass). The SI unit is J/kg·K. Specific heat varies slightly with temperature for real materials; the constant-$c$ approximation is valid for small $\Delta\theta$.

data.title: Newton's Law of Cooling
notes: **Purpose of Newton's law of cooling:** The law provides a simple mathematical model to predict how the temperature of a body changes with time when it is placed in a surroundings of constant temperature.

**Forensic science — estimating time of death:** A corpse cools according to Newton's law after death (the "algor mortis" process). If body temperature is measured at time $t$, and the ambient temperature is known, the law estimates how long ago death occurred: $\theta(t) = \theta_0 + (\theta_{body} - \theta_0)e^{-K't}$.

**Engineering — cooling system design:** Engineers use Newton's law to size radiators, heat sinks, and cooling fans. For a component dissipating power $P$, the steady-state temperature rise is $\Delta T = P/(kA)$, where $k$ is the heat transfer coefficient.

**Food industry — pasteurization and chilling:** After pasteurization, milk must be cooled to below 4°C within a specified time to prevent bacterial growth. Newton's law calculates the required cooling time and the size of the heat exchanger.

**Everyday life — coffee and tea:** A hot cup of coffee cools faster when the room is cold and slower when the room is warm. The law explains why adding cold milk immediately (rather than waiting) keeps coffee hotter longer — the milk lowers the initial temperature, reducing the rate of heat loss.

**Metallurgy — quenching and annealing:** The rate of cooling a hot metal determines its microstructure and hardness. Quenching in water (large $k$) produces hard martensite; slow cooling in oil or air (smaller $k$) produces softer phases. Newton's law approximates the cooling curve.

**Climate and building science — thermal mass:** Walls and floors with high heat capacity (large $mc$) change temperature slowly. Newton's law predicts how quickly a building cools after the heating is turned off, helping design energy-efficient HVAC systems.

**Weather forecasting — radiation fog:** On clear nights, the ground loses heat by radiation. Newton's law approximates how quickly surface temperature drops. When it falls below the dew point, fog forms. This is used in agricultural frost warnings.

**Electronic devices — CPU thermal management:** A processor generates heat at rate $P$. Without cooling, its temperature rises until heat loss balances power input. With a heatsink, Newton's law predicts the equilibrium temperature: $T_{eq} = T_{ambient} + P/k$.

**Calorimetry corrections — radiation loss:** In precision calorimetry, heat loss to surroundings causes systematic errors. Newton's law allows correction: the heat lost during an experiment is $\int k(\theta - \theta_0)\,dt$, which can be estimated from the cooling curve.

**Medicine — therapeutic hypothermia:** After cardiac arrest, patients are cooled to 32–34°C to reduce brain damage. Newton's law guides the cooling protocol, predicting how long ice packs or cooling blankets must be applied.

**Photography — darkroom processing:** Chemical baths in photography must be kept at a precise temperature. Newton's law predicts how quickly a fresh bath reaches the target temperature when moved from a warm storage area.

**Automotive — engine warm-up and cooling:** A car engine reaches operating temperature faster in cold weather (larger $\theta - \theta_0$) but the cooling system must dissipate more heat. Newton's law models both warm-up and cooling phases.

**NEB exam applications:** Identify real-world situations where Newton's law applies. Explain how the law is used in forensic time-of-death estimation and in finding unknown specific heats by the method of cooling.

**Limitation reminder:** Newton's law is an approximation. Real cooling involves radiation ($\propto T^4 - T_0^4$), convection, and conduction simultaneously. The law is most accurate when temperature differences are moderate (20–50°C) and convection dominates.
**Newton's Law of Cooling:** This topic covers the fundamental concepts of newton's law of cooling in the physics curriculum.
Understanding newton's law of cooling is essential for solving problems and building higher-level mathematical skills.
Key definitions and theorems related to newton's law of cooling should be memorized and practiced regularly.
confusion: ❌ Newton's law of cooling tells you the exact time of death. ✅ It gives an ESTIMATE. The model ignores many factors (clothing, body size, air movement, humidity) that affect real cooling rates.

❌ The law works equally well for very large temperature differences (e.g., a red-hot iron in air). ✅ For large $\Delta T$, radiation ($\propto T^4$) dominates over convection, and Newton's linear law becomes inaccurate.
❌ A larger object always cools faster. ✅ Larger objects have larger heat capacity ($mc$), which slows cooling. The cooling RATE depends on the ratio $k/(mc)$, not just on size.

❌ Newton's law of cooling is the same as the Stefan-Boltzmann law. ✅ Newton's law is linear ($d\theta/dt \propto \theta - \theta_0$). Stefan-Boltzmann is quartic ($\propto T^4 - T_0^4$). Newton's law is an approximation valid for small $\Delta T$.

❌ The cooling constant $k$ is a property of the material. ✅ $k$ depends on the SURFACE properties (area, texture, air flow), not the material inside. Two objects of the same material but different shapes have different $k$.

❌ Once a body reaches room temperature, it stays there forever. ✅ It reaches thermal equilibrium asymptotically — it gets arbitrarily close but never exactly reaches $\theta_0$ in finite time (though for practical purposes it appears to).

❌ The method of cooling (comparing cooling rates) gives the exact specific heat. ✅ It gives an approximate value. Errors arise from non-identical conditions, radiation losses, and the approximation that $k$ is constant.
Carefully distinguish between similar-looking concepts in newton's law of cooling.
Pay attention to the conditions under which formulas and theorems apply.
Practice with multiple examples to solidify your understanding.
practice: A body cools from 80°C to 50°C in 3 min in a 20°C room. How long to cool from 50°C to 35°C? $K' = \frac{1}{3}\ln\frac{60}{30} = \frac{\ln 2}{3} = 0.231\text{ min}^{-1}$. Time 50→35: $t = \frac{1}{K'}\ln\frac{30}{15} = \frac{\ln 2}{0.231} = 3\text{ min}$. Same time because the ratio of excesses is the same (2:1).

A cup of tea at 95°C cools to 75°C in 4 min in a 20°C room. How long until it reaches 40°C (drinkable)? $K' = \frac{1}{4}\ln\frac{75}{55} = \frac{\ln 1.364}{4} = 0.0783\text{ min}^{-1}$. Time to 40°C: $t = \frac{1}{0.0783}\ln\frac{75}{20} = 12.77 \times 1.322 = 16.9\text{ min}$ from start.

Why does adding cold milk to coffee keep it warmer longer? Without milk: coffee at 85°C, excess = 65°C. With milk added immediately: coffee at 70°C, excess = 50°C. The rate of cooling is proportional to excess, so the milk-added coffee cools at a slower RATE from the start, and stays above any given temperature longer.

A forge-cooled CPU has $k = 0.5\text{ W/K}$ and dissipates 65 W. If ambient is 25°C, what is the steady-state temperature? At equilibrium, heat generated = heat lost: $P = k(T_{eq} - T_0)$. $65 = 0.5(T_{eq} - 25)$. $T_{eq} = 25 + 130 = 155°C$. This is dangerously hot — a larger heatsink (larger $k$) is needed.

A metal sphere and a metal cube of the same material and same mass are heated to the same temperature and allowed to cool. Which cools faster? The sphere has the smallest surface area for a given volume. The cube has more surface area. Since $K' = k/(mc)$ and $k \propto$ surface area, the cube cools faster (larger $A$ → larger $k$).

In a calorimetry experiment, a hot metal sample is dropped into water. Heat loss to the room causes the measured equilibrium temperature to be lower than the true value. How does Newton's law help correct this? By recording the temperature before and after mixing, you can estimate the heat lost: $Q_{lost} = \int k(\theta - \theta_0)dt \approx k(\theta_{avg} - \theta_0)\Delta t$. Adding this to the energy balance gives a more accurate specific heat.

universalFacts: Newton's law of cooling is an example of a "linear first-order differential equation" — the same mathematical form appears in RC circuits ($dQ/dt = -Q/RC$), radioactive decay ($dN/dt = -\lambda N$), and chemical reaction kinetics.

The time constant $\tau = mc/k$ has units of time and appears in countless physical, chemical, and biological processes. It characterizes how "inertial" a thermal system is — large $\tau$ means slow response.

Forensic use of Newton's law for time-of-death estimation was described by Poisson in 1829. Modern forensic science combines it with more sophisticated models that account for body composition, clothing, and air movement.

The law is named after Isaac Newton, who first published it in 1701 in "Scala Graduum Caloris". However, the principle was likely known to earlier natural philosophers and was studied independently by several scientists.

In electronics, the thermal time constant of a CPU heatsink is typically 10–100 seconds. This means it takes about 50–500 seconds (1–8 minutes) for the CPU to reach near its steady-state temperature after a sudden power increase.

data.topicTitle: Measurement of specific heat capacity of solids and liquids
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — How Much Heat for One Degree?

Water needs 4186 J to raise one kilogram by one kelvin; copper needs barely a tenth of that. Specific heat capacity quantifies this appetite for heat — and the principle of calorimetry (heat lost = heat gained) turns mixtures into measurement instruments.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2020, 2023, 2024)

### 2.1 Definitions

**Quantity of heat:** the energy transferred because of temperature difference; measured in joules.

**Specific heat capacity (c):** the heat required to raise the temperature of **1 kg** of a substance by **1 K**:
$$Q = mc\Delta T \qquad c \text{ in J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

**Thermal (heat) capacity:** heat to raise a *whole body* by 1 K: $C = mc$ (J/K).

Water's c = 4186 J kg⁻¹K⁻¹ — exceptionally high (hydrogen bonding), which is why water is the coolant of engines and the climate buffer of coastal cities.

### 2.2 Principle of calorimetry

$$\text{Heat lost by hot body} = \text{Heat gained by cold body}$$
$$m_1c_1(T_1 - T) = m_2c_2(T - T_2)$$
(neglecting losses) — the working equation of the **method of mixtures**.

### 2.3 Measurement of specific heat — method of mixtures

1. A known mass of the solid is heated in boiling water (to a known temperature $T_1$).
2. It is quickly transferred into a **calorimeter** (known mass $m_c$, specific heat $c_c$) containing known mass $m_w$ of water at $T_2$.
3. The final common temperature $T$ is read.
4. Energy balance (including the calorimeter):
$$m_s c_s (T_1 - T) = (m_w c_w + m_c c_c)(T - T_2) \Rightarrow c_s = \frac{(m_w c_w + m_c c_c)(T - T_2)}{m_s (T_1 - T)}$$

### 2.4 Worked numericals

**Q (3m, 2024):** Define specific heat capacity. A 200 g block of aluminium is heated from 20 °C to 100 °C. How much heat is absorbed? (c = 0.897×10³ J kg⁻¹K⁻¹... as given: 0.897 J/g°C)
- Definition as above. $Q = mc\Delta T = 0.2 \times 897 \times 80 = 1.44 \times 10^4$ J ≈ **14.4 kJ**

**Q (3m, 2020):** Calculate the heat required to raise the temperature of 500 g of water from 20 °C to 60 °C. (c = 4200 J kg⁻¹K⁻¹)
$$Q = mc\Delta T = 0.5 \times 4200 \times 40 = 8.4 \times 10^4 \text{ J}$$

**Q (NEB-style):** A 100 g copper calorimeter (c = 385) contains 200 g water at 20 °C. A 50 g metal at 100 °C is dropped in; final temperature 22.5 °C. Find c of the metal.
- Lost: 0.05 c (77.5). Gained: (0.2×4186 + 0.1×385)(2.5) = (837.2+38.5)(2.5) = 2194 J.
- $c = 2194/(0.05 \times 77.5) = 566$ J kg⁻¹K⁻¹.

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 50:** cooling corrections refine the final temperature reading.
- **To Topic 52/53:** latent-heat terms enter the calorimetry equation during phase changes.
- **To first law:** at constant volume (solids/liquids), heat = change in internal energy.

1. Mixing grams and kilograms in Q = mcΔT.
2. Omitting the calorimeter's heat capacity in mixture problems.
3. Writing c's unit as J/K (that is heat capacity C, not specific heat c).

data.title: Change of Phases and Latent Heat
data.topicTitle: Change of Phases and Latent Heat
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Heat That Changes State, Not Temperature

Boil a kettle and the thermometer freezes at 100 °C while the burner pours in energy. During a phase change every joule goes into breaking molecular bonds, not raising temperature — that hidden energy is **latent heat**, the reason steam burns and ice cools.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2017, 2023)

### 2.1 Change of phase

Matter changes phase — solid ↔ liquid ↔ gas — at characteristic temperatures (melting point, boiling point) for a given pressure. During the change:
- **Temperature stays constant** even though heat is continuously supplied.
- The supplied energy goes into **increasing intermolecular potential energy** (breaking bonds/overcoming attractions), not into kinetic energy.

### 2.2 Latent heat

**Latent heat** is the quantity of heat absorbed or released during a change of phase, **without any change in temperature**.

**Specific latent heat (L):** heat required to change the phase of **1 kg** of a substance at constant temperature:
$$Q = mL \qquad L \text{ in J/kg}$$

### 2.3 Latent heat of fusion vs vaporization (NEB 2023)

| | Latent heat of fusion ($L_f$) | Latent heat of vaporization ($L_v$) |
|---|---|---|
| Change | solid ↔ liquid | liquid ↔ gas |
| For water | 3.34×10⁵ J/kg | 2.26×10⁶ J/kg |
| Direction | absorbed on melting, released on freezing | absorbed on boiling, released on condensing |
| Magnitude | smaller (few bonds broken) | larger (all remaining attractions overcome) |

$L_v > L_f$ because vaporization must completely separate molecules, while melting only loosens the lattice.

### 2.4 Why temperature stays constant during a phase change (NEB 2017)

The kinetic energy of molecules (which *is* temperature) does not change; all the supplied heat raises the **potential energy** of the molecules as bonds loosen or break. The energy is "latent" — hidden in molecular configuration, recoverable on the reverse change.

### 2.5 Worked numericals

**Q (NEB-style):** How much heat melts 500 g of ice at 0 °C? ($L_f$ = 3.34×10⁵ J/kg)
$Q = mL = 0.5 \times 3.34\times10^5 = 1.67 \times 10^5$ J.

**Q (NEB-style):** 20 g of steam at 100 °C condenses on skin. How much energy is released beyond that of 20 g of water at 100 °C?
Extra = $mL_v = 0.02 \times 2.26\times10^6 = 4.52 \times 10^4$ J — why steam scalds so badly.

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 51:** calorimetry problems add mL terms alongside mcΔT.
- **To Topic 53:** measurement of L by mixture and electrical methods.
- **To pressure effects:** melting point of ice drops under pressure (regelation); boiling point rises with pressure (pressure cooker).

## 4. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 4.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

| Year | Unit | Topic | Question | Marks | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2073/2017 | Heat | Latent heat | What is latent heat of fusion? Why does the temperature of a substance not change during a phase change? | 2 | Definition + reasoning |
| 2079/2023 | Heat | Latent heat | What is latent heat? Distinguish between latent heat of fusion and latent heat of vaporization. | 3 | Definition + difference |

### 4.2 Model answers

**Q (2m, 2017):** Latent heat of fusion is the heat required to change unit mass of a solid into liquid at its melting point without temperature change. Temperature stays constant during a phase change because the supplied energy increases the **potential energy** of molecules (breaking intermolecular bonds) rather than their kinetic energy, which is what temperature measures.

**Q (3m, 2023):** Latent heat is the heat absorbed or released during a phase change without temperature change ($Q = mL$). **Fusion:** solid ↔ liquid, for water 3.34×10⁵ J/kg. **Vaporization:** liquid ↔ gas, for water 2.26×10⁶ J/kg — larger because vaporization must completely separate the molecules, while melting only loosens the lattice.

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Saying temperature "pauses" because heating stops — heat supply continues.
2. Swapping the values of $L_f$ and $L_v$.
3. Writing L's unit as J (it is J/kg).

The reverse changes release the same heat: steam scalds, sweat cools, ice packs freeze injuries.

### 2.4 Why temperature stays constant during a phase change (NEB 2017)

The kinetic energy of molecules (which *is* temperature) does not change; all the supplied heat raises the **potential energy** of the molecules as bonds loosen or break. The energy is "latent" — hidden in molecular configuration, recoverable on the reverse change.

### 2.5 Worked numericals

**Q (NEB-style):** How much heat melts 500 g of ice at 0 °C? ($L_f$ = 3.34×10⁵ J/kg)
$Q = mL = 0.5 \times 3.34\times10^5 = 1.67 \times 10^5$ J.

**Q (NEB-style):** 20 g of steam at 100 °C condenses on skin. How much energy is released beyond that of 20 g of water at 100 °C?
Extra = $mL_v = 0.02 \times 2.26\times10^6 = 4.52 \times 10^4$ J — why steam scalds so badly.

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 51:** calorimetry problems add mL terms alongside mcΔT.
- **To Topic 53:** measurement of L by mixture and electrical methods.
- **To pressure effects:** melting point of ice drops under pressure (regelation); boiling point rises with pressure (pressure cooker).

| 2073/2017 | Heat | Latent heat | What is latent heat of fusion? Why does the temperature of a substance not change during a phase change? | 2 | Definition + reasoning |
| 2079/2023 | Heat | Latent heat | What is latent heat? Distinguish between latent heat of fusion and latent heat of vaporization. | 3 | Definition + difference |

### 4.2 Model answers

**Q (2m, 2017):** Latent heat of fusion is the heat required to change unit mass of a solid into liquid at its melting point without temperature change. Temperature stays constant during a phase change because the supplied energy increases the **potential energy** of molecules (breaking intermolecular bonds) rather than their kinetic energy, which is what temperature measures.

**Q (3m, 2023):** Latent heat is the heat absorbed or released during a phase change without temperature change ($Q = mL$). **Fusion:** solid ↔ liquid, for water 3.34×10⁵ J/kg. **Vaporization:** liquid ↔ gas, for water 2.26×10⁶ J/kg — larger because vaporization must completely separate the molecules, while melting only loosens the lattice.

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Saying temperature "pauses" because heating stops — heat supply continues.
2. Swapping the values of $L_f$ and $L_v$.
3. Writing L's unit as J (it is J/kg).

data.title: Heat Capacity (Thermal Capacity, C')
notes: **Definition:** Heat capacity (also called thermal capacity), denoted $C'$ or simply $C$, is the amount of heat energy required to raise the temperature of an **entire object** (not a unit mass) by 1 K (or 1°C).

**Formula:** $C' = m \cdot c$, where $m$ is the mass of the object and $c$ is the specific heat capacity of the material. Alternatively, $C' = H/\Delta\theta$ - heat required per degree of temperature rise.
**Heat exchanged using C':** $H = C' \cdot \Delta\theta$. This is simpler than $H = mc\Delta\theta$ when you already know the heat capacity of the object.
**SI unit:** $\text{J/K}$ (joule per kelvin) or $\text{J/°C}$. Since a kelvin and a degree Celsius have the same size, $\text{J/K} = \text{J/°C}$ numerically.
**CGS unit:** $\text{cal/°C}$ (calorie per degree Celsius). Water's heat capacity is $1\text{ cal/°C}$ per gram, or $4.186\text{ J/°C}$ per gram.

**Key distinction - C' vs c:** $c$ (specific heat) is an INTENSIVE property - it depends only on the MATERIAL (e.g., copper always has $c = 390\text{ J/kg·K}$). $C'$ (heat capacity) is an EXTENSIVE property - it depends on both the material AND the mass of the object. A 2 kg copper block has $C' = 2 \times 390 = 780\text{ J/K}$.
**Dimensional formula:** $[C'] = [M] \cdot [L^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}] = [ML^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}]$. Unlike $c$, the mass dimension $[M]$ does NOT cancel.

**Water equivalent connection:** Heat capacity is directly related to water equivalent: $C' = W \cdot c_w$, where $W$ is the water equivalent mass and $c_w$ is water's specific heat. So $C' = W \times 4186\text{ J/K}$.

**Calorimeter heat capacity:** A calorimeter has its own heat capacity $C'_{cal} = m_{cal} \cdot c_{cal}$. In calorimetry problems, this must be included: $H_{gained} = (m_{liquid}c_{liquid} + C'_{cal})\Delta\theta_{liquid}$.

**Practical examples:** A 500 g aluminum pot ($c = 900$): $C' = 0.5 \times 900 = 450\text{ J/K}$. A 2 kg iron pan ($c = 450$): $C' = 2 \times 450 = 900\text{ J/K}$. The iron pan needs more heat for the same temperature rise - despite iron's lower $c$, its larger mass wins.

**Why it matters in experiments:** When measuring specific heat using the method of mixtures, you must account for the heat capacity of the container. Neglecting $C'_{cal}$ is a common source of error.
**Thermal mass:** In building physics
thermal mass" is the aggregate heat capacity of a building's materials (walls, floors, furniture). High thermal mass means the building heats and cools slowly - beneficial for passive solar design.

**Comparison table:** Substance | Mass | c (J/kg·K) | C' (J/K)
Water (1 L) | 1 kg | 4200 | 4200
Aluminum pot (0.5 kg) | 0.5 kg | 900 | 450
Iron pan (2 kg) | 2 kg | 450 | 900
Lead weight (1 kg) | 1 kg | 130 | 130

**NEB exam tip:** Distinguish clearly between $c$ (specific heat, per kg) and $C'$ (heat capacity, for the whole object). Many exam questions give $C'$ directly and ask you to find $c$, or vice versa. Remember: $C' = mc$ and $c = C'/m$.

**Relationship to Newton's law of cooling:** In Newton's law, the cooling constant $K$ is often written as $K = hA/C'$, where $h$ is the surface heat transfer coefficient and $A$ is the surface area. A larger $C'$ means slower cooling.
confusion: ❌ Heat capacity and specific heat are the same thing. ✅ Heat capacity ($C'$) depends on the object's mass; specific heat ($c$) is a property of the material alone. $C' = mc$ - they are related but not identical.

❌ A larger object always has a larger heat capacity. ✅ For the SAME material, yes. But a small lead weight ($c=130$) may have a smaller $C'$ than a large aluminum block ($c=900$) even if the lead is more massive.
❌ Heat capacity has no units. ✅ Heat capacity has units: J/K (SI) or cal/°C (CGS). Specific heat has units J/kg·K or cal/g·°C. The units are different by a factor of mass.
❌ Heat capacity is the same for all objects of the same material. ✅ Heat capacity depends on BOTH material and mass. Two copper objects have the same $c$ but different $C'$ if their masses differ.

❌ The dimensional formula of heat capacity is $[M^0L^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}]$. ✅ Heat capacity includes mass: $[C'] = [ML^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}]$. The $[M]$ does NOT cancel because $C'$ depends on the amount of substance.

❌ You can use $C'$ in place of $c$ in all formulas. ✅ In $H = mc\Delta\theta$, replace $mc$ with $C'$: $H = C'\Delta\theta$. But if you need $c$ itself (e.g., to identify the material), you must divide: $c = C'/m$.
❌ Water equivalent has units of J/K. ✅ Water equivalent ($W$) has units of MASS (kg or g). Heat capacity has units of J/K. They are related by $C' = W \cdot c_w$, where $c_w = 4186\text{ J/kg·K}$.
practice: A 2 kg iron block ($c = 450\text{ J/kg·K}$) is heated from 20°C to 80°C. Find its heat capacity and the heat required. $C' = 2 \times 450 = 900\text{ J/K}$. $H = 900 \times 60 = 54{,}000\text{ J} = 54\text{ kJ}$.
An object has heat capacity 840 J/K. How much heat raises its temperature by 15°C? $H = C'\Delta\theta = 840 \times 15 = 12{,}600\text{ J} = 12.6\text{ kJ}$.

A calorimeter has mass 0.05 kg and $c = 400\text{ J/kg·K}$. Find its heat capacity and water equivalent. $C' = 0.05 \times 400 = 20\text{ J/K}$. $W = C'/c_w = 20/4186 = 0.00478\text{ kg} = 4.78\text{ g}$.

Two objects A and B have the same heat capacity. Object A is 0.5 kg of aluminum ($c=900$). Object B is 1.0 kg of an unknown material. Find B's specific heat. $C'_A = 0.5 \times 900 = 450\text{ J/K}$. Since $C'_B = C'_A$: $1.0 \times c_B = 450 \Rightarrow c_B = 450\text{ J/kg·K}$ (iron).

A copper calorimeter ($m = 0.1\text{ kg}$, $c = 390$) contains 0.2 kg of water. Find the total heat capacity of the system. $C'_{cal} = 0.1 \times 390 = 39\text{ J/K}$. $C'_{water} = 0.2 \times 4200 = 840\text{ J/K}$. $C'_{total} = 39 + 840 = 879\text{ J/K}$.

An object's temperature rises by 10 K when 2000 J of heat is supplied. Find its heat capacity, water equivalent, and the mass if it's made of copper ($c=390$). $C' = 2000/10 = 200\text{ J/K}$. $W = 200/4186 = 0.0478\text{ kg} = 47.8\text{ g}$. $m = C'/c = 200/390 = 0.513\text{ kg}$.
universalFacts: Heat capacity is sometimes called "thermal mass" in engineering. A brick wall has high thermal mass - it absorbs heat during the day and releases it at night, moderating indoor temperatures.
The concept of heat capacity was developed by Joseph Black in the 1760s. He realized that "heat content
(what he called
quantity of heat
) is different from
temperature" - two objects at the same temperature can have different heat capacities.

In chemistry, the molar heat capacity ($C_m$) is more useful than mass heat capacity. For gases, $C_p$ (constant pressure) and $C_v$ (constant volume) are both molar heat capacities and differ by $R = 8.314\text{ J/mol·K}$.

Phase changes involve enormous heat capacities in a sense - during melting, temperature doesn't change despite continuous heat input, so $C' = H/\Delta\theta \to \infty$. This is why the concept of heat capacity breaks down at phase transitions.

The heat capacity of the Earth's oceans ($\sim 1.4 \times 10^{21}\text{ J/K}$) is so large that absorbing 1 W per square meter of ocean surface raises the ocean temperature by only about 0.02 K per century - yet this small change drives global sea level rise through thermal expansion.

data.title: Specific latent heat of fusion and vaporization
data.topicTitle: Specific latent heat of fusion and vaporization
notes: Specific latent heat L is the heat absorbed or released when 1 kg of a substance changes state at constant temperature. The heat is Q = m L, and there is no Δθ term while the change of state is going on.
The specific latent heat of fusion, L_f, is for melting or freezing. For ice at 0°C it is about 3.34 × 10^5 J/kg. Melting absorbs this heat. Freezing releases it.

The specific latent heat of vaporization, L_v, is for boiling or condensation. For water at 100°C it is about 2.26 × 10^6 J/kg, several times larger than L_f, because the molecules must be separated much further.

During melting the temperature stays at the melting point until all the solid has changed. The supplied energy increases the potential energy of the molecules, not the average kinetic energy that temperature tracks.
A warming problem that crosses a change of state is done in pieces: mc Δθ up to the change point, then m L, then mc Δθ in the new state. Leaving out m L is the usual error.
The same L applies to the reverse change. Condensing 1 kg of steam at 100°C releases m L_v, which is why a steam burn is severe compared with a burn from water at the same temperature.

data.topicTitle: Measurement of specific latent heat of fusion and vaporization
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Measuring the Hidden Heat

Latent heat cannot be read on a thermometer; it must be *weighed out* in energy balances. Drop melting ice into warm water, or pass steam through it, and calorimetry converts temperature changes into L_f and L_v — the numbers behind refrigeration, steam engines and weather.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2021)

### 2.1 Specific latent heat of fusion and vaporization

- **Specific latent heat of fusion ($L_f$):** heat required to convert 1 kg of a solid to liquid at its melting point, with no temperature change. Water: $3.34 \times 10^5$ J/kg.
- **Specific latent heat of vaporization ($L_v$):** heat required to convert 1 kg of liquid to vapour at its boiling point. Water: $2.26 \times 10^6$ J/kg.
$$Q = mL$$

### 2.2 Measurement of L_f (method of mixtures)

A calorimeter (mass $m_c$, specific heat $c_c$) contains warm water ($m_w$, $T_2$). Dry ice ($m$, at 0 °C) is added; final temperature $T$:
$$mL_f + mc_w(T - 0) = (m_wc_w + m_cc_c)(T_2 - T)$$
$$L_f = \frac{(m_wc_w + m_cc_c)(T_2 - T) - mc_wT}{m}$$
(ice must be *dry* — any attached water adds unaccounted mc_w(T−0) on the wrong side).

### 2.3 Measurement of L_v (condensation method)

Steam at 100 °C is passed into cold water in a calorimeter; mass of steam condensed = m (weighed before/after):
$$mL_v + mc_w(100 - T) = (m_wc_w + m_cc_c)(T - T_2)$$
$$L_v = \frac{(m_wc_w + m_cc_c)(T - T_2) - mc_w(100 - T)}{m}$$

### 2.4 Worked numerical (NEB 2021, 5m)

**Q (5m, 2021):** A mass of steam at 100 °C is passed into water at 30 °C. If 5 g of steam condenses to raise 50 g of water from 30 °C to 50 °C, calculate the specific latent heat of vaporization of water.
- Heat gained by water: $0.05 \times 4200 \times (50-30) = 4200$ J
- Heat lost by steam: $mL_v + mc_w(100-50) = 0.005\,L_v + 0.005 \times 4200 \times 50 = 0.005\,L_v + 1050$
- Balance: $0.005\,L_v + 1050 = 4200 \Rightarrow L_v = \dfrac{3150}{0.005} = 6.3 \times 10^5$ J/kg

### 2.5 Second worked numerical (NEB-style)

**Q (NEB-style):** 40 g of ice at 0 °C is added to 200 g of water at 30 °C in a 60 g copper calorimeter (c = 385). Final temperature 15 °C. Find L_f.
- Gained: $0.04L_f + 0.04 \times 4200 \times 15$
- Lost: $(0.2 \times 4200 + 0.06 \times 385)(30 - 15) = (840 + 23.1) \times 15 = 12947$ J
- $0.04L_f + 2520 = 12947 \Rightarrow L_f = 260675 \approx 2.6 \times 10^5$ J/kg (close to 3.34×10⁵; difference = experimental losses).

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 52:** these measurements quantify the latent heats defined there.
- **To Topic 51:** the same calorimetric balance with an added mL term.
- **To engineering:** L_v powers steam engines and refrigeration cycles (compression/condensation).

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Forgetting the $mc_w(100 - T)$ condensation-cooling term (steam ends as water at T, not 100 °C).
2. Using wet ice — unaccounted water corrupts L_f.
3. Mixing grams and kilograms.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Measuring the Hidden Heat

Latent heat cannot be read on a thermometer; it must be *weighed out* in energy balances. Drop melting ice into warm water, or pass steam through it, and calorimetry converts temperature changes into L_f and L_v — the numbers behind refrigeration, steam engines and weather.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2021)

### 2.1 Specific latent heat of fusion and vaporization

- **Specific latent heat of fusion ($L_f$):** heat required to convert 1 kg of a solid to liquid at its melting point, with no temperature change. Water: $3.34 \times 10^5$ J/kg.
- **Specific latent heat of vaporization ($L_v$):** heat required to convert 1 kg of liquid to vapour at its boiling point. Water: $2.26 \times 10^6$ J/kg.
$$Q = mL$$

### 2.2 Measurement of L_f (method of mixtures)

A calorimeter (mass $m_c$, specific heat $c_c$) contains warm water ($m_w$, $T_2$). Dry ice ($m$, at 0 °C) is added; final temperature $T$:
$$mL_f + mc_w(T - 0) = (m_wc_w + m_cc_c)(T_2 - T)$$
$$L_f = \frac{(m_wc_w + m_cc_c)(T_2 - T) - mc_wT}{m}$$
(ice must be *dry* — any attached water adds unaccounted mc_w(T−0) on the wrong side).

### 2.3 Measurement of L_v (condensation method)

Steam at 100 °C is passed into cold water in a calorimeter; mass of steam condensed = m (weighed before/after):
$$mL_v + mc_w(100 - T) = (m_wc_w + m_cc_c)(T - T_2)$$
$$L_v = \frac{(m_wc_w + m_cc_c)(T - T_2) - mc_w(100 - T)}{m}$$

### 2.4 Worked numerical (NEB 2021, 5m)

**Q (5m, 2021):** A mass of steam at 100 °C is passed into water at 30 °C. If 5 g of steam condenses to raise 50 g of water from 30 °C to 50 °C, calculate the specific latent heat of vaporization of water.
- Heat gained by water: $0.05 \times 4200 \times (50-30) = 4200$ J
- Heat lost by steam: $mL_v + mc_w(100-50) = 0.005\,L_v + 0.005 \times 4200 \times 50 = 0.005\,L_v + 1050$
- Balance: $0.005\,L_v + 1050 = 4200 \Rightarrow L_v = \dfrac{3150}{0.005} = 6.3 \times 10^5$ J/kg

### 2.5 Second worked numerical (NEB-style)

**Q (NEB-style):** 40 g of ice at 0 °C is added to 200 g of water at 30 °C in a 60 g copper calorimeter (c = 385). Final temperature 15 °C. Find L_f.
- Gained: $0.04L_f + 0.04 \times 4200 \times 15$
- Lost: $(0.2 \times 4200 + 0.06 \times 385)(30 - 15) = (840 + 23.1) \times 15 = 12947$ J
- $0.04L_f + 2520 = 12947 \Rightarrow L_f = 260675 \approx 2.6 \times 10^5$ J/kg (close to 3.34×10⁵; difference = experimental losses).

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 52:** these measurements quantify the latent heats defined there.
- **To Topic 51:** the same calorimetric balance with an added mL term.
- **To engineering:** L_v powers steam engines and refrigeration cycles (compression/condensation).

## 4. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 4.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

| Year | Unit | Topic | Question | Marks | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2077/2021 | Heat | Latent heat | A mass of steam at 100 °C is passed into water at 30 °C. If 5 g of steam condenses to raise 50 g of water from 30 °C to 50 °C, calculate the specific latent heat of vaporization of water. | 5 | Numerical |

### 4.2 Likely additional forms (NEB-style)

1. Describe the method of mixtures to determine L_f of ice (4m).
2. Ice-in-water calorimetry numerical (4m).

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Forgetting the $mc_w(100 - T)$ condensation-cooling term (steam ends as water at T, not 100 °C).
2. Using wet ice — unaccounted water corrupts L_f.
3. Mixing grams and kilograms.
