**The three classic cases — what was claimed and how it ended**

| Case | What was patented / claimed | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Turmeric | US patent (1995) on wound-healing use of turmeric | Revoked 1997 — CSIR produced ancient Sanskrit medical texts as prior art |
| Neem | European patent on neem-based fungicide/pesticide | Opposed by India + Green Party; patent revoked (2000, upheld 2005) |
| Basmati | US firm's claim to 'basmati' rice varieties and the name | Claim narrowed; India won protection of the name in key markets |
| General rule | Life forms and traditional knowledge are NOT free for the taking | CBD 1992: national sovereignty + benefit sharing; TKDL documents 1000s of remedies |

notes: Biotechnology in this chapter rests on two ideas used together. Genetic engineering changes the genetic material so a cell can make something it did not make before. Bioprocess engineering grows that cell in large, clean cultures and recovers the product.

A changed gene in a test tube is not yet a medicine. The host has to be multiplied without contamination, and the protein has to be separated from thousands of other molecules. Sterile culture is part of the principle, not a side comment. One unwanted microbe can outgrow the production strain.

The genetic-engineering sequence is: isolate the DNA, cut out the wanted piece with a restriction enzyme, join it to a vector with ligase, put the recombinant vector into a host, and select the cells that received it. Each step fails for a different reason, so each has its own check.

The host must be competent, able to take DNA in. For a product that needs human-like sugar chains, a bacterial host may be the wrong choice even if it grows fast. Insulin can be made in E. coli. Some other human proteins need mammalian cells. The host is chosen for the product, not from habit.

Downstream processing is the recovery half of bioprocess engineering. Cells are separated from the broth, the product is extracted, and it is purified until it is safe to use. A culture that made the protein but was never purified has not finished the process.

The same recombinant molecule can be copied only because the vector has an origin of replication and the culture is kept free of competitors. Genetic engineering supplies the instruction. Bioprocess engineering supplies the mass of cells and the clean product. Neither idea alone is the technology.

# Principles of biotechnology — recombinant DNA technology

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Principles of biotechnology — recombinant DNA technology** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Biotechnology — Principles and Processes fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Principles of biotechnology — recombinant DNA technology

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

**Recombinant DNA (rDNA) technology** splices a gene from one organism into the DNA of another, so the recipient makes a protein it could never make alone. Three core principles make it work: (1) restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sequences, (2) DNA ligase stitches pieces together, and (3) a vector carries the recombinant DNA into a host that then replicates and expresses it. Human insulin in bacteria is the textbook product.

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Key ideas and worked angles**

**Table 2 — Key ideas and worked angles**

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — the seven steps of gene cloning (study in this order)**

| Step | Action | Tool used |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Identify and isolate the gene of interest | Restriction enzymes, mRNA → cDNA |
| 2 | Cut the vector (plasmid) with the same enzyme | Restriction enzyme — matching sticky ends |
| 3 | Insert the gene into the vector (ligation) | DNA ligase |
| 4 | Transfer the recombinant DNA into the host | Transformation, microinjection, gene gun |
| 5 | Select the cells that took up the construct | Antibiotic-resistance marker |
| 6 | Scale up and express | Fermenter; host transcribes and translates the gene |
| 7 | Harvest and purify the product | Downstream processing |

**The three founding principles — who showed what**

| Principle | Discovery | Significance |
|---|---|---|
| Cutting DNA at specific sites | Restriction enzymes; Cohen and Boyer's 1972–73 experiments | Precise, reproducible cuts with matching 'sticky ends' |
| Joining DNA pieces | DNA ligase | Seals the sugar-phosphate backbone — makes the construct permanent |
| Carrying DNA into a host | Plasmids and phage as vectors; Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer built the first recombinant plasmid | The construct replicates and is expressed inside the host |

**Worked example — why the same enzyme must cut both pieces.** EcoRI recognises GAATTC and cuts between G and A, leaving staggered 'sticky ends'. If the human DNA and the plasmid are both cut with EcoRI, every fragment ends with the same complementary overhang, so any gene can anneal into any plasmid — ligase then seals it permanently. Use two different enzymes and the ends will not match: no clone. Sticky ends are the Morse code that makes recombination specific.

**Summary.** rDNA technology = cut (restriction enzymes) + join (ligase) + carry (vector) + express (host). Every biotech product, from insulin to Bt cotton, is this one logic at different scales. **Self-check:** can you list the seven steps from memory and say which enzyme does steps 2 and 3?

Sterile does not mean 'no living cells'. It means no cells other than the production strain.
E. coli is not the right host for every human protein. Glycoproteins often need animal cells.
Downstream processing is not the same step as ligation. Ligation builds the DNA. Downstream processing collects the product.

# Tools: restriction enzymes, vectors, competent host

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Tools** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Biotechnology — Principles and Processes fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Tools: restriction enzymes
### vectors
### competent host

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

Genetic engineering needs a standard toolkit. **Restriction enzymes** — the molecular scissors — recognise specific palindromic sequences and cut, leaving sticky or blunt ends. **Vectors** — plasmids, phage, cosmids — carry the gene into cells and replicate there; they need an origin of replication, a selectable marker and cloning sites. The **competent host** (usually *E. coli*) is made permeable so it can take up the recombinant DNA.

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 2 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 3 — Summary and marks map**

| Sub-topic | One-line essence | NEB marks trend |
| --- | --- | --- |

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — the toolkit in working order (study in this order)**

| Step | Tool | Job |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Restriction enzyme (e.g. EcoRI) | Cuts source DNA and vector at the same recognition site |
| 2 | DNA ligase | Seals insert into vector |
| 3 | Vector (plasmid pBR322, phage lambda) | Replicates inside the host; carries selectable marker |
| 4 | Competent host (E. coli) | Takes up the recombinant DNA and expresses it |
| 5 | Selectable marker | Antibiotic resistance lets only transformed cells survive |

**Restriction enzymes — naming, recognition and cut types**

| Feature | Detail | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Naming | First letter = genus, next two = species, then strain/number | EcoRI = E. coli R strain, enzyme I |
| Recognition site | Palindromic sequence, 4–8 bp | EcoRI: GAATTC; BamHI: GGATCC |
| Sticky ends | Staggered cut leaves single-stranded overhangs | EcoRI cuts G^AATTC — the classic exam enzyme |
| Blunt ends | Straight cut across both strands | SmaI: CCC^GGG |
| Why 'restriction' | Bacteria use them to restrict invading phage DNA; they protect their own DNA by methylation | Part of the bacterial immune system |

**Vectors — requirements and types**

| Feature / type | What it provides | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Origin of replication (ori) | The vector copies itself inside the host | Every plasmid has one; copy number varies |
| Selectable marker | Distinguishes transformed cells (antibiotic resistance) | ampR, tetR genes on pBR322 |
| Cloning sites (MCS) | Recognised cutting sites for inserting the gene | Cluster of restriction sites |
| Plasmid | Small circular DNA; workhorse of cloning | pBR322, pUC |
| Phage lambda | Infects bacteria efficiently; carries larger inserts | Lambda derivatives |
| Cosmid / BAC / YAC | Carries very large DNA fragments | Used in genome projects |

**Worked example — reading a plasmid map.** pBR322 carries ampR and tetR. The gene is inserted at a site inside tetR. Cells grown on ampicillin survive if they carry any plasmid; cells grown on tetracycline die if the insert disrupted tetR. So the clone of interest is: ampicillin-resistant AND tetracycline-sensitive. This is **insertional inactivation** — using the disruption of a marker gene as the selection signal.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Restriction enzymes: cut palindromic sites; EcoRI = E. coli restriction I; produce sticky ends (5' overhangs) — the nomenclature and sticky ends are the marks.
Trick 2: Vector requirements: origin of replication (ori), selectable marker (antibiotic resistance), cloning site (MCS), small size, high copy number — five criteria.
Trick 3: Competent host: CaCl2 + cold shock (0 °C → 42 °C) makes E. coli take up plasmids; alternatives: microinjection, gene gun (biolistics), electroporation — the methods list.
Trick 4: Insertional inactivation: insert in lacZ/blue-white screening — the selection trick worth a mark.

# Processes: DNA isolation, PCR, gel electrophoresis, gene transfer

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Processes** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Biotechnology — Principles and Processes fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Processes: DNA isolation
### PCR
### gel electrophoresis
### gene transfer

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

The working processes of biotech: **DNA isolation** (lyse cells, remove proteins, precipitate pure DNA), **PCR** (polymerase chain reaction — amplify a DNA segment a billion-fold in hours using Taq polymerase through denaturation, primer annealing and extension cycles), **gel electrophoresis** (separate DNA fragments by size through an agarose gel — DNA is negative, so it runs to the anode), and **gene transfer** into hosts or plants.

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Process steps**

| Step | What happens | Where | Key enzyme or number |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 2 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 3 — Summary and marks map**

| Sub-topic | One-line essence | NEB marks trend |
| --- | --- | --- |

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — the processes in the order a cloning project uses them (study in this order)**

| Step | Process | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | DNA isolation | Extract clean DNA from cells (lysis → RNase/protease → ethanol precipitation) |
| 2 | Cutting with restriction enzymes | Produce fragments with usable ends |
| 3 | PCR | Amplify the specific fragment a billion-fold |
| 4 | Gel electrophoresis | Check fragment sizes; recover the right band |
| 5 | Ligation into vector | Build the recombinant DNA |
| 6 | Gene transfer | Deliver the construct to host or plant cells |

**PCR — the three temperatures and what happens at each**

| Step | Temperature | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Denaturation | ~94–95°C | Double helix separates into two single strands |
| 2. Primer annealing | ~50–60°C | Short primers bind the flanking sequences of the target |
| 3. Extension | ~72°C | Taq polymerase builds the new strand from the primers |
| Result after n cycles | — | Target copies ≈ 2ⁿ; 30 cycles → over a billion copies |
| Why Taq polymerase | From Thermus aquaticus (hot-spring bacterium) | Survives the denaturation step — the enzyme does not need re-adding |

**Gene transfer methods — classified**

| Method | How it works | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| Transformation (CaCl2 + heat shock) | Cold calcium makes membranes permeable; brief heat shock lets DNA in | Bacteria (E. coli) |
| Electroporation | Electric pulses open temporary pores | Bacteria, plant cells |
| Microinjection | DNA injected directly into the cell/nucleus with a fine needle | Animal cells, embryos |
| Biolistics (gene gun) | Gold/tungsten particles coated with DNA shot into cells | Plant cells |
| Agrobacterium tumefaciens | Disarmed Ti plasmid carries the gene into plant genome naturally | Dicot plants — nature's own genetic engineer |

**Worked example — PCR maths.** Starting with 1 copy and running 30 cycles: copies = 2³⁰ ≈ 1.07 billion. With 20 cycles: 2²⁰ ≈ 1 million. So the choice of cycle count sets sensitivity — forensic and diagnostic PCR use 30–40 cycles to detect vanishingly small starting amounts, which is also why contamination is fatal: one stray molecule becomes a billion too.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: DNA isolation: cell lysis (lysozyme/EDTA/detergent) → protease/RNase → chilled ethanol precipitation ('spooling') — the three-step order.

data.title: Applications of recombinant DNA technology

visualization.desc: Applications of recombinant DNA all start from a gene carried on a double helix the host can copy.

notes: Recombinant DNA is used wherever a cell can be instructed to make a molecule that is hard to collect from its natural source. The applications sit in medicine, farming, industry and the cleanup of pollutants.

In medicine the landmark product is human insulin made in E. coli, approved as Humulin in 1982. The amino-acid sequence is the human one, so the immune reactions that came with some animal insulins became less of a problem. The same logic produces other proteins: human growth hormone, and vaccines such as the hepatitis B surface antigen made in yeast.

Diagnosis uses the same toolkit. PCR amplifies a pathogen's DNA until a test can see it. ELISA detects an antigen or an antibody with an enzyme-linked reaction. One finds nucleic acid. The other finds protein. They answer different clinical questions.

Gene therapy delivers a working copy of a defective gene into a patient's somatic cells. The correction is for that person. It is not passed to children, because the germline is not the target of the permitted treatments. The first approved attempt, in 1990, was for ADA deficiency.

In agriculture the same technology produces Bt crops and other modified plants. In the environment, microbes have been designed or selected to break down oil and other pollutants, which is bioremediation. The microbe eats the waste. It does not make the waste vanish by a physical filter alone.

Every application still depends on the pipeline: a correct gene, a host that can express it, and a product that has been checked. A recombinant protein is not automatically safe or correctly folded. Purification and testing are part of the application, not paperwork after the science.

# Applications of recombinant DNA technology

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Applications of recombinant DNA technology** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). ## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Applications of recombinant DNA technology

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

rDNA technology turned biology into an industry. Its products span medicine (human insulin, growth hormone, vaccines, interferon), agriculture (Bt crops, golden rice, herbicide tolerance), industry (enzymes for detergents and food) and research (gene therapy, DNA fingerprints, transgenic animals). The common thread: a gene, once cloned, can be manufactured in fermenters at scale.

| 2 | Agriculture | Bt cotton/brinjal (insect resistance), golden rice (pro-vitamin A), herbicide-tolerant soybean |
| 3 | Industry and environment | Detergent enzymes (lipase, protease), cheese rennet (chymosin), oil-eating bacteria |
| 4 | Diagnostics and research | DNA fingerprinting, PCR-based disease tests, gene therapy trials, transgenic animals |

**Flagship products — gene, host and benefit**

| Product | Gene / source | Production host | Benefit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Human insulin (Humulin, 1982) | Human insulin gene | E. coli / yeast fermenters | Replaced pancreas-extracted insulin; unlimited, safe supply for diabetics |
| Growth hormone (hGH) | Human GH gene | E. coli | Treats pituitary dwarfism without cadaver-derived hormone |
| Hepatitis B vaccine | HBsAg surface antigen gene | Yeast | Safe vaccine with no live virus |
| Bt cotton | cry genes from Bacillus thuringiensis | Cotton plant itself | Built-in bollworm resistance; less insecticide |
| Golden rice | Beta-carotene pathway genes | Rice plant | Fights vitamin-A deficiency blindness |
| Chymosin (rennet) | Calf chymosin gene | Microbes | Vegetarian-safe cheese at industrial scale |

**Worked example — insulin, the first blockbuster.** Before 1982, insulin came from pig and cattle pancreases — limited supply, occasional allergic reactions. Genentech and Eli Lilly cloned the human insulin genes A and B into E. coli; fermenters now produce it in tonnes. The scientific trick: express the two chains separately, then join them, or express pro-insulin and cleave it. Humulin (1982) was the first FDA-approved recombinant drug — the moment biotech became an industry.

confusion: Humulin is human-sequence insulin from a microbe. It is not insulin extracted from cattle.
ELISA and PCR are not two names for one test. PCR copies DNA. ELISA detects antigen or antibody.
Somatic gene therapy is not inherited. Germline alteration is a different, and clinically disallowed, act.
Bioremediation uses living metabolism. It is not the same thing as Bt cotton.

data.title: Air and Water Pollution
notes: Air pollution is the addition of gases and particles that harm health, crops or buildings. The main primary pollutants in this course are sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, unburnt hydrocarbons and particulate matter. Vehicles, coal, industry and, in many Nepali towns, brick kilns are the sources to name.

Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin as carboxyhaemoglobin and so blocks oxygen transport. Fine particles, especially those small enough to reach the alveoli, damage lungs. Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides irritate the airway and, dissolved in cloud water, become acid rain. Nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbons in sunlight also make ground-level ozone, which is a smog pollutant, not the stratospheric shield.

Control follows the pollutant. An electrostatic precipitator charges dust and collects it on plates, so it suits particulates from a chimney. A scrubber sprays liquid through the gas and takes out sulphur dioxide. A catalytic converter, using platinum, palladium and rhodium, turns carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides and unburnt hydrocarbons into carbon dioxide, nitrogen and water. Lead in petrol poisons that catalyst, which is why the fuel has to be unleaded. Compressed natural gas burns with less smoke than petrol or diesel and has been used to clean city bus fleets.

Water pollution is the addition of sewage, industrial chemicals, detergents, farm runoff or heat until the water can no longer support its normal life. Organic sewage is measured by biochemical oxygen demand: the oxygen microbes need to oxidise the organic matter in a litre of water, usually over five days at 20 °C. A high BOD means the waste will strip dissolved oxygen from the river.

Nitrates and phosphates from fertiliser and detergents drive eutrophication. Algae bloom, die, and bacteria decay them. Dissolved oxygen collapses and fish die. Non-biodegradable poisons take a different path. DDT and mercury build up in tissues and become more concentrated at each higher trophic level, which is biomagnification. The Minamata mercury poisoning is the human example of that concentration.

Sewage is treated in stages. Primary treatment settles solids. Secondary treatment uses microbes to lower the BOD. Tertiary treatment, where it exists, strips nutrients that would otherwise feed an algal bloom. None of that works if untreated sewage is still discharged beside the plant. Using less phosphate in detergents and less excess fertiliser cuts the problem before the pipe.
confusion: Ground-level ozone in smog is a pollutant. It is not the ozone layer.
A high BOD means the water is more polluted with organic matter, not that the water is richer in oxygen.
Biomagnification is not the same as a large spill. It is the rise in concentration along a food chain.
A catalytic converter does not remove carbon dioxide as its job. It makes carbon dioxide from carbon monoxide.

data.title: Solid Waste Management
notes: This note is about what to do with solid waste after it exists. The health risk and the treatment method depend on whether the waste can rot, whether it can be recycled, or whether it is infectious or full of metals. A single pit for everything fails all three.

Biodegradable waste is food, garden cuttings and paper that microbes can break down. If it is kept clean of plastic and glass it becomes compost, or it can go into a biogas digester where air-free decay produces methane that is burned as fuel and a slurry that can fertilise a field. That is recovery, not dumping.

Non-biodegradable waste does not join the compost. Glass, metal and many plastics are recycled only when they are dry and sorted. A plastic bottle in a compost heap does not become soil. It has to be collected as plastic. Contaminated recyclables, soaked in food, are often rejected and end up buried anyway, which is why the wet bin and the dry bin are separated at home.

Disposal of what cannot be recycled uses a sanitary landfill or a controlled incinerator. The landfill is lined, the leachate is taken out, the waste is covered, and the gas is managed. Incineration shrinks the volume and can heat water for electricity, but only if the temperature is high and the smoke is cleaned. Incomplete burning makes poisonous organic products and leaves a toxic ash that still needs a landfill.

Two streams injure people if they are treated as ordinary rubbish. Biomedical waste carries pathogens. It is autoclaved or burned in a dedicated incinerator, and sharps are contained so nobody is stuck by a needle. Electronic waste carries lead, mercury and cadmium. Informal open burning, which has been common where repair shops dump boards, puts those metals into the air and the ash. Recovery has to be a controlled process.

The public-health chain from a bad dump is short. Flies and rats move between waste and kitchens. Leachate reaches wells. Methane collects in pockets and can burn. Plastic blocks drains, so the next rain floods the lane with the same dirty water. Integrated management is just the decision to use compost, recycling, a proper landfill and special streams together, instead of one smoking pile.
confusion: Biogas is not compost. Biogas is methane from air-free decay. Compost is aerobic rotting that makes a soil conditioner.
Incineration does not make waste vanish. It makes ash, and bad incineration makes toxic smoke.
Paper can be recycled or composted. Soft plastic film is a different material and often is not composted.
Autoclaving hospital waste sterilises it. It does not recycle it into compost for vegetable beds.
keyPoints: Biodegradable → compost or biogas.
Dry recyclables → recycling, only if they were kept clean.
Sanitary landfill: liner, leachate collection, cover, gas control.
Incineration needs high temperature and smoke cleaning, and it still leaves ash.
Biomedical waste is sterilised or incinerated. E-waste metals are recovered, not openly burned.
importantStatements: The treatment is chosen from the kind of waste, not from whichever truck arrived.
Methane is a useful fuel inside a digester and a hazard inside a dump.
Ash from an incinerator is still waste.
examples: A household wet bin of vegetable peels feeds a community compost pit.
A capped sanitary landfill pipes its gas away instead of letting it seep into nearby basements.
A broken phone sent to an open fire releases lead and plastic fumes. The same phone in a recovery line yields metals and a smaller residue.
universalFacts: Anaerobic digestion of organic waste produces methane.
Autoclave conditions used to sterilise infectious waste are moist heat under pressure, classically 121 °C.
formulas: Organic waste + air → compost. Organic waste without air → biogas (methane) + slurry.
Integrated route: segregate → compost or biogas, recycle, sanitary landfill or controlled incineration, separate biomedical and e-waste.

specialNotes: 121 °C is the autoclave figure for sterilising infectious material. Do not quote it as a compost temperature.

data.title: Climate Change and Greenhouse Effect

visualization.desc: This topic is the left panel: greenhouse gases and warming. The ozone panel is a different chapter.

notes: Climate change in this chapter means the warming and the shifted rainfall that follow an enhanced greenhouse effect. The effect itself is natural. Carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, water vapour and CFCs absorb infrared radiation leaving the Earth, so the surface is warmer than it would be. Without them the mean temperature would be about −18 °C rather than about +15 °C.

People have thickened that blanket. Carbon dioxide has risen from about 280 ppm before industry to a little above 420 ppm, which is about 0.04 percent of air. The added carbon dioxide comes from coal, oil, gas and from forests that were cut and burned. Methane comes from livestock, flooded rice fields and rotting waste. Nitrous oxide comes from fertilised soils. These are the gases to write down. Water vapour amplifies warming, but it is not the gas the policies are aimed at.

The results are not only a higher thermometer reading. Ice melts and sea level rises. Heatwaves and heavy rain become more likely. Crop zones move. Disease vectors move with the temperature. In the Himalaya, glaciers retreat and glacial lakes can burst. That is the Nepali form of the same global change, and it is about water and slopes, not about a hole in the ozone layer.

Mitigation means cutting the cause. Burn less fossil fuel, waste less energy, stop clearing forests, and store carbon in vegetation and soil. A landfill that captures methane, or a herd and a rice system that emit less of it, is mitigation of a greenhouse gas. Adaptation means living with the change that is already arriving: crop varieties that tolerate heat or a late monsoon, flood protection, and settlements that are not sitting under an unstable glacial lake.

International targets are part of the answer. The Paris Agreement asks countries to hold warming well below 2 °C and to pursue 1.5 °C above the pre-industrial temperature. A target is not a fall in carbon dioxide by itself. The fall comes from the fuels and the forests.

Ozone depletion is the trap answer. It is caused mainly by chlorine and bromine compounds, it is measured in Dobson units, and it increases ultraviolet-B. Some CFCs do warm the climate and also destroy ozone, but carbon dioxide does not punch the ozone hole, and chlorine is not the reason glaciers retreat. Write them as neighbours, not as synonyms.

Climate change and the ozone hole are not the same measurement and not the same gases.
Mitigation is not adaptation. One cuts emissions. The other copes with impacts.
Water vapour is a greenhouse gas, but listing only water vapour misses the gases people have increased.
keyPoints: Natural warming is about 33 °C, from about −18 °C to about +15 °C.
CO2: about 280 ppm pre-industrial, a little above 420 ppm now.
Main added gases: CO2, methane, nitrous oxide.
Mitigation cuts emissions. Adaptation reduces harm.
Paris range: pursue 1.5 °C and hold warming well below 2 °C.
importantStatements: Infrared is what the greenhouse gases trap. Sunlight mostly gets in.
Himalayan glacier loss and glacial-lake floods are the regional impact to mention.
A CFC can affect both climate and ozone, which does not make CO2 an ozone-depleting gas.
examples: Coal-fired electricity raises CO2. Methane from a landfill raises a more potent greenhouse gas in smaller amounts.
A village that moves its houses off a glacial-lake flood path is adapting. A village that replaces diesel with a cleaner supply is mitigating.
A late monsoon and a hotter wheat season are agricultural faces of the same warming.
universalFacts: Pre-industrial carbon dioxide was about 280 ppm.
The Paris temperature figures are measured against the pre-industrial baseline, not against last year.
formulas: Enhanced greenhouse: extra CO2, CH4 and N2O → more infrared trapped → higher mean temperature.
About 420 ppm CO2 ≈ 0.04 percent of air.

If you mention CFCs, immediately say that CO2 is still the main warming gas and chlorine is the ozone story.
examShortTricks: 280 then about 420. 1.5 and 2. −18 and +15.
Mitigate = less gas. Adapt = live with the impact.
specialNotes: Do not quote a single 'exact' current ppm as if it never moves. 'A little above 420 ppm' matches the course figure.
Glacial-lake outburst floods are a consequence to name. They are not a greenhouse gas.
importantNotes: Deforestation raises atmospheric CO2 both by burning and by losing a sink.
Methane is stronger per molecule than CO2, but CO2 is the larger share of the extra warming because so much of it is emitted.

# Air pollution — causes, effects, and control

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Air pollution — causes** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Environmental Issues fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Air pollution — causes
### effects
### and control

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

Air pollution is the addition of harmful substances to the atmosphere — gases (CO, SO2, NOx), particulates (PM2.5, PM10) and secondary products (photochemical smog, acid rain). Sources are combustion, industry and vehicles; effects range from respiratory disease to acid rain and global climate change. Control combines technology (filters, converters), fuel policy and law.

## 3. Classified tables

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — from source to control (study in this order)**

| Step | Concept | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Primary pollutants emitted directly | CO from vehicles; SO2 from coal; PM from dust and diesel |
| 2 | Secondary pollutants formed in air | Ozone and PAN in photochemical smog; H2SO4 in acid rain |
| 3 | Effects on health | Asthma, bronchitis, heart disease; PM2.5 reaches deep lung tissue |
| 4 | Effects on environment | Acid rain damages lakes and forests; smog damages crops |
| 5 | Control at source | Electrostatic precipitators, scrubbers, catalytic converters, cleaner fuels |
| 6 | Control by policy | Emission norms (Euro/BS standards), lead-free petrol, air-quality monitoring |

**Major air pollutants — source and effect**

| Pollutant | Main source | Main harm |
|---|---|---|
| Carbon monoxide (CO) | Incomplete combustion in engines | Binds haemoglobin — carbon monoxide poisoning, suffocation |
| Sulphur dioxide (SO2) | Coal-burning power plants, smelters | Acid rain; respiratory irritation |
| Nitrogen oxides (NOx) | Vehicle engines, high-temperature combustion | Smog and acid rain; lung inflammation |
| Particulates (PM2.5/PM10) | Diesel, dust, construction, burning biomass | Deep-lung and cardiac damage; visibility loss |
| Ozone (ground-level, O3) | Secondary — sunlight + NOx + hydrocarbons | Photochemical smog; crop damage, eye irritation |
| Lead | Old petrol, battery recycling | Neurotoxic — learning impairment in children |

**Control technologies — what each device removes**

| Device / measure | Where used | What it removes |
|---|---|---|
| Electrostatic precipitator | Power-plant chimneys | Charged particles attracted to plates — up to 99% of particulates |
| Scrubber | Industrial stacks | SO2 and other gases washed out by lime-water spray |
| Catalytic converter | Vehicle exhausts | Converts CO, NOx and unburnt hydrocarbons to CO2, N2 and water — needs lead-free petrol |
| Fuel policy | Cities, refineries | Low-sulphur and unleaded fuel; CNG for buses |
| Standards and monitoring | National level | Emission norms (BS/Euro), AQI public reporting |

**Worked example — why lead killed catalytic converters.** A catalytic converter uses platinum-group catalysts to finish the combustion of CO and NOx. Lead in old petrol coats the catalyst surface in weeks and destroys it — which is why unleaded petrol was a precondition for converter-based emission norms everywhere. One pollutant (lead) had to be removed to control three others.

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Water pollution — causes** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Environmental Issues fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Water pollution — causes
### effects
### and control

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

Water pollution is any change in water quality that harms life or usefulness. The big concepts: **BOD** (biochemical oxygen demand — the oxygen microbes need to decompose the waste; high BOD = dirty water), **eutrophication** (nutrient enrichment → algal bloom → oxygen crash), and **biomagnification** (toxics like DDT and mercury climbing the food chain). Control runs through sewage treatment and watershed management.

| 3 | BOD as the measuring stick | More organic waste → more microbial oxygen demand → lower dissolved O2 |
| 4 | Eutrophication sequence | N + P enrich → algal bloom → bloom dies → decomposition eats O2 → fish kill |
| 5 | Biomagnification | DDT/mercury concentration multiplies ~10× per trophic level — top predators worst hit |
| 6 | Control | Sewage treatment (primary/secondary/tertiary), effluent norms, watershed protection |

**Water pollutants and their signature effects**

| Pollutant | Source | Signature effect |
|---|---|---|
| Organic sewage | Homes, food industry | High BOD, oxygen depletion, foul smell |
| Nitrates and phosphates | Fertiliser runoff, detergents | Eutrophication and algal blooms |
| Mercury | Industry (Minamata) | Biomagnified nerve poison in fish and humans |
| DDT and pesticides | Agriculture | Biomagnification; thin eggshells in birds of prey |
| Thermal discharge | Power plants | Warm water holds less O2 — aquatic stress |
| Pathogens | Untreated sewage | Cholera, typhoid, jaundice outbreaks |

**Sewage treatment — the three stages**

| Stage | What it removes | How |
|---|---|---|
| Primary | Large solids and grit | Screening, grit chamber, sedimentation |
| Secondary (biological) | Dissolved organic matter — the BOD | Aeration tank with microbial floc (activated sludge) or trickling filter; floc settles as sludge, partly recycled |
| Tertiary / final | Nutrients, pathogens, residual solids | Chlorination/UV, chemical precipitation; sludge digested anaerobically → biogas |

**Worked example — reading a BOD test.** Sample A: BOD 5 mg/L, dissolved oxygen 8 mg/L. Sample B: BOD 300 mg/L, dissolved oxygen 2 mg/L. Trick 2: BOD: oxygen needed by microbes to decompose organic matter — higher BOD = more pollution; clean water BOD < 5 ppm; sewage treatment uses BOD reduction as its goal.

data.title: Solid waste management
notes: Solid waste is the solid material a household, shop, farm, hospital or factory throws away. Managing it means collecting it, keeping the dangerous fractions apart, and only then burying, burning or recycling what is left. A roadside heap is not management.

The useful split is by what the waste is. Wet organic waste, such as food scraps, can rot. Dry recyclable waste includes paper, glass, metal and many plastics. Biomedical waste from clinics carries infection. Electronic waste carries lead, mercury and cadmium. Industrial hazardous waste may be corrosive or toxic. Mixing these in one bag makes every later step worse.

An open dump breeds flies and rats, blows plastic into drains, and leaks a dirty liquid called leachate into soil and groundwater. Buried organic waste without air control also makes methane, which is flammable and a strong greenhouse gas. The smell is the least of the damage.

A sanitary landfill is a different structure. The base is lined so leachate can be collected rather than soaked away. Waste is compacted and covered. Gas is vented or burned. It still uses land, and it still needs watching, but it is not a hole in the ground.

The order that cuts the problem is reduce, then reuse, then recycle, and only then recover energy or dispose. Segregation at the house is what makes composting, recycling and safe medical disposal possible. A mixed truckload cannot be unsorted cheaply at the dump.

Hospitals must not send dressings, needles and cultures out with kitchen waste. Those items are incinerated at high temperature or sterilised. Electronic goods should go to a recovery workshop that captures the metals. Burning phones and cables in the open releases the metals and the plastic fumes together.

# Solid waste management

## 1. Introduction

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Solid waste management

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

Solid waste is everything we throw away — household garbage, hospital waste, e-waste, construction debris. Management follows a hierarchy: **reduce → reuse → recycle → compost → energy recovery → landfill** as the last resort. Segregation at source (biodegradable vs non-biodegradable) is the step that makes everything else possible.

**Concept flow — from generation to disposal (study in this order)**

| Step | Stage | Key action |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Generation and segregation | Separate biodegradable, recyclable and hazardous waste at source |
| 2 | Collection and transport | Door-to-door collection, transfer stations |
| 3 | Processing — biological | Composting and vermicomposting of wet waste |
| 4 | Processing — material recovery | Recycling of paper, glass, metal, plastics |
| 5 | Energy recovery | Incineration with energy capture; refuse-derived fuel |
| 6 | Final disposal | Sanitary landfill with liner and leachate collection — the last resort |

**Waste classified by type and the right handling for each**

| Type | Examples | Correct handling |
|---|---|---|
| Biodegradable (wet) | Food scraps, garden waste | Composting / vermicomposting — becomes fertiliser |
| Recyclable (dry) | Paper, glass, metal, some plastics | Segregated, sold to recyclers — re-enters industry |
| Hazardous / biomedical | Needles, expired drugs, batteries | Segregated, autoclaved or incinerated at certified plants |
| E-waste | Old phones, computers | Formal recycling for metals; informal burning is toxic |
| Inert / residual | Ash, construction debris | Sanitary landfill — engineered, lined, covered |

**Composting vs vermicomposting vs incineration vs landfill**

| Method | Best for | Advantage | Drawback |
|---|---|---|---|
| Composting | Wet organic waste | Cheap, makes fertiliser, cuts landfill volume | Needs segregation and time |
| Vermicomposting | Kitchen waste | Faster, richer compost (earthworms) | Needs worm care, moisture control |
| Incineration | Biomedical, low-volume waste | Huge volume reduction, energy recovery | Air pollution if unfiltered; costly |
| Sanitary landfill | Residual inert waste | Simple, large capacity | Land use, methane leak, leachate risk |

# Nuclear radiation hazards

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Nuclear radiation hazards** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Environmental Issues fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Nuclear radiation hazards

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

Ionising radiation — alpha, beta, gamma, X-rays — strips electrons from atoms, breaking DNA and killing or mutating cells. Sources are natural (cosmic rays, radon, rocks) and man-made (reactors, weapons, medical use, waste). Hazard depends on dose, duration and penetration; protection rests on **time, distance and shielding**.

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |

**Table 2 — Key ideas and worked angles**

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — from source to safety rule (study in this order)**

| Step | Concept | Key fact |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Natural background | Cosmic rays, radon gas from rock, K-40 in food — always present |
| 2 | Man-made sources | Medical X-rays (largest artificial dose), reactors, weapons testing, radioisotopes |
| 3 | Biological damage | Ionisation breaks DNA: cell death, mutations, cancer |
| 4 | Acute vs chronic exposure | High short dose → radiation sickness; low long dose → cancer risk |
| 5 | Penetration rules | Alpha stopped by paper; beta by aluminium; gamma needs thick lead/concrete |
| 6 | Protection triad | Minimise TIME, maximise DISTANCE, use SHIELDING |
| 7 | Waste problem | Spent fuel stays dangerous for thousands of years — deep geological storage |

**Alpha, beta, gamma — the three radiations compared**

| Property | Alpha (α) | Beta (β) | Gamma (γ) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nature | Helium nucleus (2p + 2n) | Fast electron | High-energy electromagnetic wave |
| Penetration | Stopped by paper or skin | Stopped by a few mm of aluminium | Needs thick lead or concrete |
| Internal hazard | Most dangerous if INHALED/ingested | Moderate | Dangerous from outside — deep penetration |
| Ionising power | Highest | Moderate | Lowest per interaction |
| Example source | Radon, americium in smoke detectors | Sr-90, C-14 | Co-60, Cs-137 |

**Radiation effects classified by dose and timing**

| Exposure | Effect | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Acute, whole body, very high | Radiation sickness: nausea, hair loss, marrow failure, death | Reactor accidents (Chernobyl firefighters) |
| Chronic, low level | Raised cancer risk over years; mutations in gametes | Survivors near test sites; occupational exposure |
| Localised | Skin burns, local tissue death | Industrial source mishandling |
| In utero | Developmental damage | Medical exposure of pregnant women — avoided |

# Greenhouse effect, global warming, climate change

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Greenhouse effect** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Environmental Issues fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Greenhouse effect
### global warming
### climate change

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

The **greenhouse effect** is natural and life-giving: CO2, CH4, water vapour and other gases let sunlight in but slow the infrared escape, keeping Earth ~33°C warmer than it would be. The problem is the **enhanced** effect: fossil fuel burning and deforestation have raised CO2 from ~280 to over 420 ppm, driving **global warming** and with it **climate change** — shifting rainfall, melting ice, rising seas.

## 3. Classified tables

**Concept flow — from physics to politics (study in this order)**

| Step | Concept | Key fact |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Natural greenhouse effect | Shortwave in, longwave (IR) partially trapped — Earth would be −18°C without it |
| 2 | Enhanced effect | More CO2/CH4 → more IR trapped → surface warms |
| 3 | Main human causes | Fossil fuels, deforestation, cement, agriculture (CH4, N2O) |
| 4 | Observed warming | ~1.1–1.2°C above pre-industrial average |
| 5 | Consequences | Ice melt, sea-level rise, extreme weather, coral bleaching, shifting crop zones |
| 6 | Mitigation | Cut emissions: renewables, efficiency, afforestation, carbon pricing |
| 7 | Adaptation | Adjust to what is locked in: flood defences, drought-tolerant crops |

**The major greenhouse gases**

| Gas | Main human source | Notable point |
|---|---|---|
| CO2 | Fossil-fuel burning, deforestation, cement | Largest contributor by volume — the benchmark gas |
| CH4 (methane) | Livestock, rice paddies, landfills, gas leaks | Far stronger than CO2 per molecule (~25× over a century) |
| N2O | Nitrogen fertilisers, combustion | Also damages the ozone layer |
| CFCs (now phased down) | Old refrigerants and aerosols | Banned by the Montreal Protocol — also ozone destroyers |
| Water vapour | Evaporation (natural) | Most abundant greenhouse gas — a feedback, not a primary driver |

**Mitigation vs adaptation — the two responses**

| Response | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Mitigation | Reduce the cause — cut emissions | Solar and wind power, energy-efficient buildings, afforestation, electric transport, methane capture |
| Adaptation | Reduce the harm — adjust to change | Flood embankments, drought-tolerant crop varieties, early-warning systems, water storage |
| International frameworks | Shared targets | Kyoto Protocol (1997, binding targets), Paris Agreement (2015, well below 2°C, efforts toward 1.5°C) |

data.title: Ozone layer depletion

visualization.desc: The right-hand panel is this topic: stratospheric ozone, Dobson units, and chlorine from CFCs. Warming is the other panel.

notes: Ozone in the stratosphere, about 15 to 35 km above the surface, absorbs ultraviolet-B that would otherwise reach living tissue. The amount in a vertical column is measured in Dobson units. One DU is a layer 0.01 mm thick at standard temperature and pressure. A normal column is about 300 DU.

Ozone is made and destroyed all the time. Ultraviolet light splits O2 into oxygen atoms, and an atom joining another O2 makes O3. Left alone, formation and breakdown stay in balance. The layer is not a fixed shell of gas that never changes. It is a balance.

CFCs upset that balance. They are stable near the ground and drift upward for years. High in the stratosphere, ultraviolet light breaks a chlorine atom off. Chlorine reacts with ozone to make chlorine monoxide and oxygen, then chlorine monoxide reacts with a free oxygen atom and releases the chlorine again. The chlorine is a catalyst. One atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules. Halons, carbon tetrachloride, methyl bromide and nitrogen oxides do related damage. Halons are harsher per molecule than CFCs.

The Antarctic hole appears in spring. Winter cold forms polar stratospheric clouds. On those icy surfaces, chlorine compounds are converted into forms that sunlight can activate. When the sun returns, ozone falls quickly. A column below about 220 DU is called a hole. The Arctic can thin too, but the classic hole is Antarctic.

More ultraviolet-B means more skin cancer and cataracts, a weaker immune response, and damage to phytoplankton, which are the producers of the sea. Crops can be injured as well. None of this is the same process as the greenhouse effect. Carbon dioxide warms the lower air. Chlorine thins the high ozone. A CFC happens to do both jobs, which is why the two stories get mixed.

The Montreal Protocol, agreed in 1987, cut and then phased out the main ozone-depleting chemicals. Substitutes have their own problems, including a greenhouse effect for some of them, but the protocol is the reason stratospheric chlorine has started to decline. Ground-level ozone, made in smog, is still a pollutant. It does not replace the shield 15 km up.

# Ozone layer depletion

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Ozone layer depletion** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Environmental Issues fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Ozone layer depletion

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

The ozone layer (O3, stratosphere, ~25–30 km) absorbs the Sun's harmful UV-B and UV-C. **CFCs** — once used in refrigerators, ACs and aerosols — drift up unreactive, and in the stratosphere UV light snaps off a chlorine atom; one Cl atom then destroys tens of thousands of ozone molecules in a catalytic chain. Result: the Antarctic 'ozone hole'. The **Montreal Protocol (1987)** phased CFCs out — the most successful environmental treaty ever.

| 2 | CFCs released | Refrigerants, aerosols, foam-blowing — inert enough to survive the troposphere |
| 3 | UV splits CFC | Cl atom freed in the stratosphere |
| 4 | Catalytic destruction | Cl + O3 → ClO + O2; ClO + O → Cl + O2 — one Cl kills ~100,000 O3 |
| 5 | Antarctic hole | Polar stratospheric clouds free chlorine in spring — discovered 1985 (Farman) |
| 6 | The fix | Montreal Protocol 1987: phase out CFCs; HCFC/HFC substitutes; hole now slowly healing |

**Ozone-depleting substances — where they came from**

| Substance | Former use | Status |
|---|---|---|
| CFC-11, CFC-12 | Refrigerators, air conditioners, aerosol propellants, foams | Banned under Montreal Protocol |
| Halons | Fire extinguishers | Banned — contain bromine, even more destructive per atom |
| Carbon tetrachloride, methyl chloroform | Solvents, cleaning | Banned |
| HCFCs (transitional) | Replacement refrigerants | Being phased out — lower but not zero ODP |
| HFCs | Current refrigerants | Ozone-safe BUT potent greenhouse gases — Kigali Amendment (2016) phases them down |

**Worked example — why the hole is over Antarctica.** CFCs are released worldwide, yet the hole is polar. In the Antarctic winter, polar stratospheric clouds form at −80°C and hold chlorine reservoirs on their surfaces; spring sunlight then releases the chlorine in a burst. Geography + chemistry + season — the hole is where all three align. The same catalytic logic explains why a few parts per billion of chlorine could matter at all.

data.title: Rainwater harvesting and wasteland development
notes: Rainwater harvesting is the deliberate collection of rain before it runs off into a drain and is lost. The water is stored in a tank or guided underground so a well or a spring can use it later. It is a way of keeping a local water supply, not a new source of river water from far away.

A common design catches rain on a roof, sends it through a first-flush or a simple filter that drops leaves and grit, and then either fills a tank or leads the water into a recharge pit, a trench or an abandoned well. Check dams and percolation ponds do the same job for a slope: they slow the runoff so it soaks in instead of racing away.

The gains are practical. The local water table rises, wells last longer into the dry months, and a sudden storm is less likely to flood the street because some of the water was held. In dry districts, traditional tanks and ponds did this long before the modern name. Rooftop collection has also been made compulsory in places such as Tamil Nadu. In Nepal the same idea appears as community ponds and as rooftop tanks.

Wasteland, in this chapter, is land so degraded that it no longer supports the use it once had. Gullied hills, salinity from bad irrigation, mining spoil, waterlogged soil and heavily overgrazed slopes are typical. It is not a wilderness that was always bare. It is land people damaged.

The causes sit in how the land was used. Trees cut from a slope let rain tear the soil. Too many animals remove the cover. Irrigation water that cannot drain leaves salt at the surface. A mine leaves a pile that plants cannot root in. Each cause points at a repair, not at a single universal machine.

Development of that land means putting cover and water control back. Trees and grasses are planted. Contour bunds and check dams slow runoff. Waterlogged ground is drained. Salty ground is leached only where drainage exists, or it is given salt-tolerant plants. Grazing is held off until the cover returns. The aim is a soil that holds water and a plant community that holds the soil.

# Rainwater harvesting and wasteland development

## 1. Introduction

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point

**Worked example — sizing a rooftop tank.** A school roof of 200 m² receives 800 mm of rain a year. Harvestable water ≈ 200 × 0.8 = 160 m³ = **160,000 litres** (before losses). With a 20,000-litre tank cycled through the dry season, the school covers drinking and toilet flushing for months — and the overflow goes to a recharge pit. The arithmetic is why rooftop harvesting is the cheapest water infrastructure a building can have.

data.title: Plant Breeding

visualization.desc: Five steps in order: collect germplasm, choose parents, cross them, keep the best progeny, then test and release the variety.

notes: Plant breeding is the deliberate production of a crop that is more useful than its parents. The usefulness is a stated target: more grain, a shorter plant that does not lodge, resistance to a named disease, a duration that fits the monsoon, or a seed with more protein. Simply keeping the heaviest heads from a field is selection. Breeding adds a controlled cross so that characters from two parents finish in one line.

The work has five steps, and the order is the answer. First the variability is collected. That collection is the germplasm: local varieties, old farmer seed, and wild relatives that still carry disease resistance the crop has lost. Second, the collection is evaluated and the parents are chosen, one of them usually the adapted crop, the other the donor of the missing character. Third, those parents are cross-pollinated. The flower that will be the female is emasculated before its own pollen is shed, dusted with the chosen pollen, and bagged so stray pollen cannot land. Fourth, the progeny are grown on and only the plants that actually combined the characters are kept. That selection is repeated down the generations until the line is stable. Fifth, the line is tested in more than one place and more than one season, released under a name, and the seed is multiplied for farmers.

The green-revolution cereals are the examples to attach to those steps. Semi-dwarf wheat, from programmes associated with Norman Borlaug, yielded heavily and stayed short enough not to fall over. Sonalika and Kalyan Sona are the wheat names used in this course. Semi-dwarf rice did the same for paddy: IR-8, Jaya and Ratna. Sugarcane shows a cross made for a region rather than for a single gene. Saccharum officinarum has thick stems and high sugar. Saccharum barberi grows in the north of the subcontinent. The hybrid was bred to keep the sugar and the thick stem and still grow in the north.

Disease resistance uses the same five steps with a resistant parent, often a wild relative. Himgiri wheat was produced against leaf rust, stripe rust and hill bunt. If no parent has the character, mutation breeding is the other door. Seeds or buds are treated with a chemical mutagen or with radiation, and a large number of plants are screened. Most are useless. A few carry a new resistant allele. Mung bean varieties resistant to yellow mosaic virus and powdery mildew were recovered that way. The mutagen does not aim the mutation. The screen does the choosing.

Biofortification aims the same method at nutritional quality instead of tonnes alone: more protein, a better amino-acid balance, more oil, more vitamins, or more iron and zinc. Atlas 66 is the high-protein wheat quoted for this. The plant is still bred by collection, choice of parents, crossing, selection and release. A transgenic line such as vitamin-A rice is a biotechnology product. It is worth knowing as a contrast, and it is not required to explain conventional breeding.

The steps fail in known ways. If the female flower is not emasculated in time, the seed is a self-pollination and the donor character never enters. If the two parents flower weeks apart, the cross cannot be made unless pollen is stored or the sowing dates are staggered. A line that tops the trial in one district can collapse in another because the rust race or the day length is different. The multi-location trial exists to catch that before the variety is named and sold.

exercises.question: A breeder wants a rice that keeps a local variety's taste and gains a short stem from a donor. List the steps and the one action that stops self-pollination.

Evaluate both and choose them as parents.

data.title: Single Cell Protein

visualization.desc: Three single-cell protein sources side by side: Spirulina, Methylophilus methylotrophus, and mushrooms.

notes: Single cell protein is microbial biomass grown to be eaten, by people or by livestock, because the cells are rich in protein. The product is the cell mass itself, dried or processed. It is not a purified enzyme and not a single amino acid. The point of the method is that microbes multiply in hours in a tank, so protein can be produced without waiting for a crop season or dedicating a large field.

The organisms in the course are a cyanobacterium, a bacterium, and fungi that people already accept as food. Spirulina grows by photosynthesis and is produced as a supplement. It can be cultured on starch, molasses, and waste water from processing plants, so the same tank that grows food also uses a waste. Methylophilus methylotrophus grows on methanol. The comparison used in class is that a culture of about 250 grams of this bacterium can be expected to produce about 25 tonnes of protein, because the cells grow so fast and so much of their dry mass is protein. Mushrooms are fungi. They are SCP in the technical sense, and they are the form that has already become an ordinary food.

Yeasts, including Saccharomyces, are used in the same way, often for animal feed. Other bacterial and algal biomasses have been tried on whey, molasses, and sewage. The shared advantage is the feedstock. Materials that would otherwise be dumped become the carbon source. A fermenter on a small plot can outproduce a field of pulses in kilograms of protein per day, which is the calculation that made SCP attractive as a food strategy.

The biomass supplies protein as the main nutrient, with some fat, minerals and B vitamins depending on the species. It can be mixed into food or fed to animals whose meat, milk or eggs then carry the protein onward. In either use it is a supplement to crops, not a replacement for plant breeding. Breeding changes a plant. SCP adds a different organism.

The limits are practical and chemical. Bacterial cells contain a large amount of nucleic acid. In a human diet that load has to be reduced by processing, because purines from nucleic acids are not wanted in high amounts. The product also has to be free of toxins and of contaminating microbes, and it has to be something people will actually swallow. Mushrooms passed that test. A pale bacterial powder often did not, which is why much of the industrial output is discussed as feed. Cost matters as well: the protein is only useful if it is cheaper than the pulse or the fish meal it is meant to spare.

Set beside plant breeding, SCP skips land, season and rainfall, and it can run on waste. It fails when the biomass is unsafe, too high in nucleic acid, or rejected as food. Breeding fails when the new variety does not suit the district. A food system can use both: a better rice in the field, and a fermenter turning a waste stream into protein beside it.

data.title: Animal Husbandry

visualization.desc: Four managed products: dairy for milk, poultry for eggs and meat, fishery for capture or culture, and apiculture for honey.

notes: Animal husbandry is the managed breeding, feeding and health care of animals so that they yield milk, meat, eggs, fibre, honey or work. The population is a herd, a flock, a stocked pond or a hive. It is not a wild population that happens to be hunted. Management matters as much as the breed. A good genotype with dirty water and no vaccination does not give the yield the breed was chosen for.

Dairying keeps cattle and buffaloes for milk. Milch breeds are selected for milk, draught breeds for pulling, and dual-purpose breeds for both. Sahiwal and Red Sindhi are the milch cattle named in the course. Murrah is the buffalo example with a high milk yield. In Nepal most milk comes from buffaloes. Lime and Parkote are the indigenous buffalo breeds, and in the high mountains the chauri, a yak-cattle hybrid, supplies milk and also carries loads. Housing has to be clean and ventilated, water has to be clean, and the ration needs both roughage and a concentrate. Vaccination and quick treatment of mastitis and foot problems protect the yield. Breed choice without that care does not.

Poultry splits by product. Layers are kept for eggs. Broilers are kept for meat and are marketed young. White Leghorn is the layer example to remember. Chicks need heat, dry litter and a feed that changes with age. Respiratory disease moves quickly through a crowded house, so the management points are space, dry flooring, and removal of sick birds, not only the name of the strain. The same farm can keep both types. It should not feed them as if they were the same animal.

Fishery is either capture, taking fish from rivers and lakes, or culture, growing them in a managed pond. Composite carp culture stocks species that feed at different levels so the same pond yields more than one species without them all competing for one food. Catla feeds near the surface, Rohu in the water column, and Mrigal on the bottom. That vertical split is the reason the combination works. Cold, oxygen-rich hill water is a different culture, used for trout, and it should not be described as a carp pond. Apiculture keeps Apis cerana, the local honey bee, or Apis mellifera, the introduced one. Honey and wax are the products, and the flowers within flight range, the pasturage, decide how much honey arrives. The bees also pollinate nearby crops, which is an agricultural benefit even in a week when little honey is taken.

Breeding methods change the herd on purpose. Inbreeding, the mating of close relatives, makes the offspring more homozygous and can fix a desired character. It also produces inbreeding depression: fertility and general vigour fall. The remedy is an outcross, a mating with an unrelated superior animal of the same breed. Outbreeding covers that outcross, cross-breeding between two breeds, and crosses between species. Hisardale sheep were produced by crossing Merino rams with Bikaneri ewes. A mule, from a male donkey and a female horse, is the interspecific example, and it is sterile because the chromosomes do not pair at meiosis. Artificial insemination lets semen from one selected male serve many females, so the male does not have to be moved and the gain from his genotype spreads in one season.

MOET, multiple ovulation embryo transfer, speeds the female side in the same spirit. A chosen cow is treated with hormones that act like FSH, so she sheds several eggs instead of one. Those eggs are fertilised, commonly with semen from a proven bull. The young embryos are flushed out and transferred into surrogate cows of ordinary merit. The genetic mother does not have to carry each calf, and she can be superovulated again. One elite female thus contributes many more offspring than a single calf a year. Selection then keeps working on a larger set of progeny.

practice: Distinguish milch, draught and dual-purpose with one use each.
Explain composite culture in three lines, one per fish.

examShortTricks: Top Catla, middle Rohu, bottom Mrigal.

Apis dorsata is the rock bee and is not the usual hive species. Cerana and mellifera are the managed ones.

Layers and broilers

Write MOET as four numbered steps and mark which animal is the genetic mother.

exercises.question: A herd has become weak after several generations of mating close relatives. State the name of the problem and one breeding action that corrects it. Then say how MOET would be used if one cow in the herd is still outstanding.
steps: The weakness and loss of fertility after repeated mating of relatives is inbreeding depression.
The correction is an outcross: mate the animals to an unrelated, superior member of the same breed.
The outstanding cow is the genetic mother for MOET. She is treated so that she superovulates.
Her eggs are fertilised with semen from a selected bull, and the embryos are recovered.
Those embryos are transferred into surrogate cows. The surrogates carry the calves. They do not supply the elite genotype.
exercises.answer: Inbreeding depression, corrected by outcrossing. MOET then superovulates the outstanding cow and transfers her embryos to surrogates.

bounds: Plant breeding and single cell protein are the neighbouring notes. This note is animals, fish and bees.
Breed lists are the course examples plus the Nepali buffalo and chauri cases. It is not a national herd book.
data.summary: Animal husbandry manages breeding, feed and health for milk, meat, eggs, fish or honey. Sahiwal, Red Sindhi and Murrah are the dairy examples, with Lime and Parkote buffaloes and the high-mountain chauri in Nepal. notes:
# Mendel's laws of inheritance — monohybrid and dihybrid cross

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Mendel's laws of inheritance — monohybrid and dihybrid cross** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Heredity and Evolution fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Mendel's laws of inheritance — monohybrid and dihybrid cross

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

Gregor Mendel (1822–1884), a monk in Brno, bred garden peas (*Pisum sativum*) from 1856–1863 and published in 1866. Peas were the right organism: true-breeding varieties, seven clearly contrasting traits, short life cycle, large numbers of offspring, and easy self- plus cross-pollination. He counted thousands of offspring and used mathematics — the first quantitative study of heredity. His work was ignored until 1900, when Correns, de Vries and Tschermak rediscovered it.

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 2 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 3 — Summary and marks map**

| Sub-topic | One-line essence | NEB marks trend |
| --- | --- | --- |

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — how Mendel built the two laws (study in this order)**

| Step | What Mendel did | Result | What it proved |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Grew true-breeding (pure) lines for 7 traits for 2 years | Every line bred true | A clean starting material |
| 2 | Crossed pure tall (TT) × pure dwarf (tt) — the P generation | All F₁ plants tall (Tt) | One trait can mask the other → dominance |
| 3 | Self-pollinated the F₁ — the F₂ generation | 787 tall : 277 dwarf ≈ 3 : 1 | The dwarf factor had not vanished, only hidden → segregation |
| 4 | Self-pollinated the F₂ tall plants | 1/3 bred true (TT), 2/3 split 3:1 (Tt) | Genotype ≠ phenotype — two kinds of tall plants |
| 5 | Crossed F₁ back to the recessive parent (test cross) | 1 tall : 1 dwarf | Confirms F₁ carries both factors |
| 6 | Crossed pure round-yellow × pure wrinkled-green (dihybrid) | F₁ all round-yellow | Dominance holds per trait |
| 7 | Self-pollinated the dihybrid F₁ | F₂ = 315:108:101:32 ≈ 9:3:3:1 | Traits assort independently → second law |
| 8 | Test-crossed the dihybrid F₁ | 1:1:1:1 | Four gamete types in equal numbers |

**Monohybrid vs dihybrid cross — classified side by side**

| Feature | Monohybrid cross | Dihybrid cross |
|---|---|---|
| Traits tracked | One pair of contrasting traits (height) | Two pairs (seed shape + seed colour) |
| Pure parents | TT × tt | RRYY × rryy |
| F₁ genotype | Tt | RrYy |
| F₁ gametes | T and t (2 types) | RY, Ry, rY, ry (4 types) |
| F₂ genotypic ratio | 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt | 1:2:1:2:4:2:1:2:1 (9 classes) |
| F₂ phenotypic ratio | 3 tall : 1 dwarf | 9 round-yellow : 3 round-green : 3 wrinkled-yellow : 1 wrinkled-green |
| Law demonstrated | Law of Segregation (dominance shows in the 3:1) | Law of Independent Assortment |

**Worked example.** A tall pea plant of unknown genotype is test-crossed with a dwarf plant (tt). The offspring are 58 tall and 54 dwarf. Because dwarf offspring (tt) can only receive a **t** from each parent, the unknown parent must have supplied **t** gametes — so it was **Tt** (heterozygous), not TT. A 1:1 test-cross result is the standard proof of heterozygosity. If all offspring had been tall, the parent would have been homozygous TT.

(2) Why did Mendel succeed where others failed — pure lines, discrete traits, large numbers, counting, mathematics. (3) Define test cross and back cross and give the expected ratios. 5–10 line chapter summary, self-check questions and the common-confusions list (block VIII) — completed in the unit fill pass.

**Summary.** Mendel's factors (genes) occur in pairs, separate cleanly during gamete formation (Law of Segregation — 3:1, 1:2:1), and pairs for different traits assort independently (Law of Independent Assortment — 9:3:3:1). Dominance hides recessive alleles in the phenotype but never destroys them. **Self-check:** can you reproduce the 2×2 and 4×4 grids from memory, and explain why the test cross is the single most useful cross in genetics?

# Incomplete dominance and codominance

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Incomplete dominance and codominance** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Heredity and Evolution fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Incomplete dominance and codominance

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

Mendel's peas showed **complete dominance**: the heterozygote looks exactly like the dominant parent. Most genes are not that polite. When the heterozygote is intermediate, the inheritance is **incomplete dominance**; when both alleles are fully and separately visible, it is **codominance**. Neither pattern breaks the Law of Segregation — in both, the F₂ genotypic ratio is still 1:2:1. What changes is that phenotype now reveals genotype.

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 2 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 3 — Summary and marks map**

| Sub-topic | One-line essence | NEB marks trend |
| --- | --- | --- |

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — from Mendel to the exceptions (study in this order)**

| Step | Concept | Classic example | Key observation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Complete dominance (the Mendelian baseline) | Tall vs dwarf pea | Tt looks like TT — recessive hidden |
| 2 | Incomplete dominance | Snapdragon / 4-o'clock flower colour | Red × white → pink F₁; F₂ = 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white |
| 3 | Codominance | ABO blood group, roan cattle | IA IB → AB blood group shows BOTH antigens |
| 4 | Multiple alleles | ABO series: IA, IB, i | More than two alleles in the population, two per person |
| 5 | Why 1:2:1 matters | F₂ of snapdragon | Phenotypic ratio = genotypic ratio — genotype is visible |

**Complete dominance vs incomplete dominance vs codominance**

| Feature | Complete dominance | Incomplete dominance | Codominance |
|---|---|---|---|
| Heterozygote phenotype | Looks like the dominant parent | Intermediate blend of both | Shows BOTH characters side by side |
| F₂ phenotypic ratio | 3 : 1 | 1 : 2 : 1 | 1 : 2 : 1 |
| F₂ genotypic ratio | 1 : 2 : 1 | 1 : 2 : 1 | 1 : 2 : 1 |
| Can you tell genotype from phenotype? | No — TT and Tt look alike | Yes — every genotype is visible | Yes — every genotype is visible |
| Textbook example | Tall × dwarf pea → all tall | Red × white snapdragon → pink | IA × IB → blood group AB; red × white roan cattle |
| Effect on the recessive allele | Completely masked | Partly expressed (diluted) | Fully expressed in a different place |

**ABO blood groups — the codominance + multiple-allele classic**

| Blood group | Genotypes | Antigen on RBC | Antibody in plasma | Can donate to |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | IAIA, IAi | A | anti-B | A, AB |
| B | IBIB, IBi | B | anti-A | B, AB |
| AB | IAIB | A and B (both expressed — codominance) | none — universal recipient | AB only |
| O | ii | none | anti-A and anti-B | O, A, B, AB — universal donor |
| Rule | IA and IB are dominant over i | i is recessive | IA and IB are codominant with each other | — |

## 6. Key terms and statements

**Worked example.** In 4-o'clock plants, red (RR) × white (rr) gives all pink Rr. Selfing the pink F₁ gives 1 RR red : 2 Rr pink : 1 rr white. A pink plant crossed with a red plant gives 1 red : 1 pink — a 1:1 ratio that proves the pink plant was the heterozygote. **Exam trap:** in incomplete dominance the heterozygote is *not* a new allele; the pink is simply one red dose expressing at half strength.

## 7. Exam Zone
NEB past-question map (long/short), topic-wise MCQs with explanations, and short tricks (block VII). Existing entrance-exam (CEE) material stays where it is; this zone grows around it — see the seeded exam fields of this file when present.

**Most-asked points (NEB).** (1) Distinguish incomplete dominance from codominance with one example each. (2) Why is the F₂ phenotypic ratio 1:2:1 instead of 3:1? (3) ABO blood group genotypes and transfusion compatibility. (4) Explain why codominance is not incomplete dominance — in AB blood the A and B antigens are both fully present, not blended into something weaker. (5) Roan cattle: red and white hairs both grow — a patchwork, not a blend.

## 8. Summary and self-check
5–10 line chapter summary, self-check questions and the common-confusions list (block VIII) — completed in the unit fill pass.

**Summary.** Dominance is a matter of degree. Incomplete dominance dilutes the heterozygote (pink snapdragon), codominance displays both alleles at once (AB blood). Both keep the 1:2:1 genotypic ratio and both make genotype readable from phenotype. **Self-check:** given a pink flower, can you state its genotype, and predict the offspring of pink × white?
