# Linkage and crossing over

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Linkage and crossing over** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Heredity and Evolution fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Linkage and crossing over

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

Mendel's second law assumes genes assort independently — but genes live on chromosomes, and a chromosome carries hundreds of them. Genes on the **same chromosome** tend to be inherited together: this is **linkage**, and it was proved by T. H. Morgan's work on *Drosophila* (1910–1915). During prophase I of meiosis, homologous chromosomes swap segments at chiasmata — **crossing over** — which breaks linkage apart in proportion to the distance between the genes. Recombination frequency became the ruler of the genetic map.

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 2 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 3 — Summary and marks map**

| Sub-topic | One-line essence | NEB marks trend |
| --- | --- | --- |

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — from Mendel's exception to the genetic map (study in this order)**

| Step | Concept | Who / when | Key result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Chromosomes carry Mendel's factors | Sutton & Boveri, 1902–03 | Gene behaviour parallels chromosome behaviour |
| 2 | Two genes on one chromosome stay together | Bateson & Punnett (sweet pea) | Deviations from 9:3:3:1 toward parental types |
| 3 | Sex-linkage proves genes ride on chromosomes | Morgan, white-eyed fly, 1910 | Eye colour inherited with sex |
| 4 | Complete linkage — no recombination | Morgan's mutant strains | Only parental gametes |
| 5 | Crossing over at chiasma in prophase I | Cytology of meiosis | Recombinant gametes appear |
| 6 | Recombination frequency ∝ distance | Sturtevant, 1913 | First genetic map, 6 loci on the X chromosome |
| 7 | 1% recombination = 1 map unit (centimorgan) | Modern usage | Map distance, not physical distance |

**Complete vs incomplete linkage — classified comparison**

| Feature | Complete linkage | Incomplete linkage |
|---|---|---|
| Crossing over | Does not occur between the genes | Occurs between them at a chiasma |
| Gamete types | Only 2 parental types (AB, ab) | All 4: parental (AB, ab) + recombinant (Ab, aB) |
| Recombinant frequency | 0% | Between 0% and 50% |
| F₂ ratio | Not 9:3:3:1 — only parental phenotypes | 9:3:3:1 distorted toward parental classes |
| Distance between genes | Very close on the chromosome | Far enough apart for a chiasma in between |
| Example | Genes inside a Y chromosome or pericentric inversion | Most autosomal gene pairs in Drosophila |

**Coupling vs repulsion phase — how the alleles sit on the chromosomes**

| Feature | Coupling (cis) | Repulsion (trans) |
|---|---|---|
| Arrangement | Dominant alleles on one homologue: AB / ab | Dominant alleles on different homologues: Ab / aB |
| Parental gametes | AB and ab | Ab and aB |
| Recombinant gametes | Ab and aB | AB and ab |
| Test-cross offspring | Mostly round-yellow and wrinkled-green | Mostly round-green and wrinkled-yellow |
| How to tell them apart | Phenotypes of the most frequent progeny | Same rule — the frequent classes are the parentals |

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example.** A test cross of a female *Drosophila* heterozygous for b (black body) and vg (vestigial wings) gives: b+vg+ 860, b vg 880, b+ vg 45, b vg+ 40. The two large classes are the parentals; the two small classes are recombinants. Recombination frequency = (45 + 40) / 1825 ≈ **4.7%**, so b and vg are about **4.7 map units** apart. The farther apart two genes are, the more often a chiasma falls between them — up to a maximum of 50 cM, where the genes behave as if unlinked.

(5) State the chromosome theory of inheritance and how Morgan's white-eyed male supported it.

## 8. Summary and self-check
5–10 line chapter summary, self-check questions and the common-confusions list (block VIII) — completed in the unit fill pass.

**Summary.** Genes on the same chromosome are linked; crossing over in prophase I breaks the linkage in proportion to distance, and the recombination percentage is the map distance in centimorgans. Linkage is the great exception to independent assortment — and the tool that let Sturtevant draw the first chromosome map. **Self-check:** from a test-cross table, can you spot the parentals, count the recombinants and compute the cM distance?

# Sex determination and sex-linked disorders

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Sex determination and sex-linked disorders** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Heredity and Evolution fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Sex determination and sex-linked disorders

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

In humans and most mammals, sex is fixed at fertilisation by the sex chromosomes: **XX** = female, **XY** = male. The Y chromosome carries **SRY**, the master switch that turns the embryonic gonads into testes; without it, development defaults to female. Because the X carries hundreds of genes the Y lacks, alleles on the X show **sex-linked inheritance**: a recessive allele that a heterozygous mother carries shows itself in sons, who have only one X.

## 3. Classified tables

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — from chromosomes to haemophilia (study in this order)**

| Step | Concept | Key fact |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sex chromosomes vs autosomes | 22 pairs of autosomes + 1 pair of sex chromosomes in humans |
| 2 | XX / XY system | The ovum is always X; the sperm is X or Y — the father determines sex |
| 3 | SRY gene on Y | Triggers testis development; without it, ovaries form |
| 4 | X-linked recessive inheritance | Haemophilia A, colour blindness — mostly males affected |
| 5 | X-linked dominant inheritance | Vitamin-D-resistant rickets — affected father passes it to ALL daughters |
| 6 | Y-linkage | Only father-to-son; e.g., hairy ears trait |
| 7 | Lyonisation | One X in each female cell is inactivated — the Barr body |

**Sex determination systems across organisms**

| Organism / group | System | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Humans, most mammals | XX / XY | Y chromosome with SRY determines maleness |
| Birds, butterflies | ZZ / ZW | The FEMALE is the heterogametic sex (ZW) |
| Honeybee | Haplodiploidy | Fertilised eggs (2n) = females; unfertilised (n) = males |
| Some reptiles (turtle, crocodile) | Temperature-dependent | Incubation temperature of the egg decides sex |
| Drosophila | XX / XY | Sex is set by the RATIO of X chromosomes to autosome sets, not by the Y |

**X-linked recessive vs X-linked dominant inheritance**

| Feature | X-linked recessive | X-linked dominant |
|---|---|---|
| Who is affected more | Males far more (only one X) | Females slightly more (two chances to inherit) |
| Carrier state | Heterozygous females are silent carriers | No silent carriers — one allele is enough |
| Affected father's sons | NONE affected (Y goes to sons) | ALL daughters affected, no sons |
| Affected father's daughters | All carriers (if mother normal) | All affected |
| Transmission pattern | Mother → son; skips generations | Can be passed by either parent |
| Examples | Haemophilia A, red-green colour blindness, Duchenne MD | Vitamin-D-resistant rickets, Rett syndrome |

# Chromosome theory of inheritance

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Chromosome theory of inheritance** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Heredity and Evolution fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Chromosome theory of inheritance

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

Mendel's factors were invisible abstractions in 1866. Forty years later, two young researchers — **Walter Sutton** (USA) and **Theodor Boveri** (Germany), working independently in 1902–1903 — pointed out that Mendel's factors behave *exactly* like chromosomes do during meiosis. This is the **chromosome theory of inheritance (Sutton–Boveri theory)**: genes are carried on chromosomes. Thomas Hunt Morgan's white-eyed *Drosophila* mutant (1910) and Calvin Bridges' nondisjunction proof (1916) turned the theory into fact.

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 2 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 3 — Summary and marks map**

| Sub-topic | One-line essence | NEB marks trend |
| --- | --- | --- |

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — how the theory was built (study in this order)**

| Step | Event | Year | Contribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Mendel publishes his laws | 1866 | Factors in pairs, segregation, independent assortment |
| 2 | Chromosomes described in dividing cells | 1880s (Flemming, Waldeyer) | Mitosis and meiosis worked out cytologically |
| 3 | Boveri's sea-urchin experiments | 1902 | Embryos need the FULL chromosome set — each chromosome is distinct |
| 4 | Sutton's grasshopper meiosis study | 1902–03 | Chromosome behaviour during meiosis parallels Mendel's factors |
| 5 | Chromosome theory stated | 1903 | Genes are located on chromosomes |
| 6 | Morgan's white-eyed male fly | 1910 | First gene assigned to a specific chromosome (the X) |
| 7 | Bridges' nondisjunction proof | 1916 | Exceptional offspring had exceptional chromosomes — final proof |

**The four parallels — Mendel's factors vs chromosome behaviour**

| Mendelian factor behaviour | Chromosome behaviour during meiosis |
|---|---|
| Factors occur in pairs (alleles) | Chromosomes occur in homologous pairs (diploid set) |
| One factor per gamete (segregation) | Homologues separate in anaphase I — one per gamete |
| Each pair segregates independently of the others | Each homologous pair orients independently at metaphase I |
| A factor from each parent unites at fertilisation | One paternal + one maternal chromosome reunite at fertilisation |

**Evidence classified — what proved genes ride on chromosomes**

| Type of evidence | Experiment | What it showed |
|---|---|---|
| Cytological parallel | Sutton's meiosis drawings | Factor behaviour = chromosome behaviour |
| Embryological | Boveri's sea urchins | Every chromosome carries something essential |
| Genetic (sex-linkage) | Morgan's white-eyed male | Eye-colour gene inherited WITH the X chromosome |
| Genetic + cytological (the clincher) | Bridges' nondisjunction | Rare exceptional phenotypes came with exceptional chromosome counts |

# Molecular basis of inheritance: DNA structure, replication, transcription, translation, gene regulation

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Molecular basis of inheritance** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Heredity and Evolution fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Molecular basis of inheritance: DNA structure
### replication
### transcription
### translation
### gene regulation

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

Heredity is chemistry. DNA was found in 1869 (Miescher), shown to be the transforming principle in 1944 (Avery), confirmed by the Hershey–Chase blender experiment in 1952, and its double helix solved by **Watson and Crick in 1953** using Chargaff's base rules and Franklin's X-ray photo. From that structure follow everything: semi-conservative replication, the central dogma DNA → RNA → protein, the genetic code, and gene regulation (the lac operon as the model).

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Characteristics**

| Part | Structure | Function | Exam note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 2 — Process steps**

| Step | What happens | Where | Key enzyme or number |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 3 — Summary and marks map**

| Sub-topic | One-line essence | NEB marks trend |
| --- | --- | --- |

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — the experiments that made DNA the genetic material (study in this order)**

| Step | Experiment | Year | What it proved |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Miescher isolates 'nuclein' from pus cells | 1869 | DNA exists as a distinct chemical |
| 2 | Griffith's transformation in pneumococcus | 1928 | A 'transforming principle' passes heritable traits between bacteria |
| 3 | Avery–MacLeod–McCarty | 1944 | The transforming principle is DNA (destroyed by DNase only) |
| 4 | Chargaff's rules | 1950 | A = T and G = C in any species' DNA |
| 5 | Hershey–Chase blender experiment | 1952 | Only the DNA of T2 phage enters E. coli — DNA is the genetic material |
| 6 | Watson–Crick double helix (+ Franklin's Photo 51) | 1953 | Structure suggests a copying mechanism |
| 7 | Meselson–Stahl density labelling | 1958 | Replication is semi-conservative, exactly as predicted |

**DNA vs RNA — classified comparison**

| Feature | DNA | RNA |
|---|---|---|
| Sugar | Deoxyribose (no 2'-OH) | Ribose |
| Bases | A, G, C, T | A, G, C, U |
| Strands | Double helix (two antiparallel strands) | Usually single-stranded |
| Stability | Very stable — archival store | Less stable — working copy |
| Location (eukaryote) | Nucleus, mitochondria, chloroplasts | Nucleus and cytoplasm |
| Types | One (genomic; + organellar) | mRNA, tRNA, rRNA, snRNA, miRNA |
| Job | Store and transmit heredity | Express it: message, adapter, factory |

**Replication vs transcription vs translation — the three engines of the central dogma**

| Feature | Replication | Transcription | Translation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Template | Both DNA strands | One DNA strand (the template strand) | mRNA |
| Enzyme | DNA polymerase (+ helicase, primase, ligase) | RNA polymerase | Ribosome + peptidyl transferase (rRNA enzyme) |
| Raw material | dNTPs (dATP, dTTP, dGTP, dCTP) | NTPs (ATP, UTP, GTP, CTP) | Aminoacyl-tRNAs |
| Start signal | Origin of replication | Promoter + start site | AUG start codon |
| Stop signal | Termination sites | Terminator | UAA / UAG / UGA stop codons |
| Product | Two identical DNA duplexes (semi-conservative) | mRNA (5'→3') | Polypeptide (N→C) |
| Proofreading | Yes — polymerase 3'→5' exonuclease | No significant proofreading | None |
| Where (eukaryote) | Nucleus (S phase) | Nucleus | Cytoplasm, on ribosomes |

## 5. Worked examples and applications
≥ 6 worked examples with solved steps, live examples and Nepal-context applications (biology-plan.md §3.1, block V) — written in the unit fill pass.

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example — reading the code.** A template DNA strand reads 3'-TAC GGA TTA-5'. The mRNA is 5'-AUG CCU AAU-3' (U replaces T; transcription starts at the promoter, not at AUG by chance). Reading in frame: AUG = methionine (start), CCU = proline, AAU = asparagine — peptide Met-Pro-Asn. Note the logic: complement the template, then translate the mRNA, never the DNA directly.

## 7. Exam Zone
NEB past-question map (long/short), topic-wise MCQs with explanations, and short tricks (block VII). Existing entrance-exam (CEE) material stays where it is; this zone grows around it — see the seeded exam fields of this file when present.

**Most-asked points (NEB).** (1) Describe the Watson–Crick model with base-pairing rules and antiparallel direction. (2) Why is replication called semi-conservative — and how did Meselson–Stahl prove it? (3) List the differences between DNA and RNA. (4) Compare replication, transcription and translation (template, enzyme, product). (5) Explain lac operon regulation: repressor, inducer (allolactose), negative control. (6) Properties of the genetic code: triplet, degenerate, non-overlapping, universal.

## 8. Summary and self-check
5–10 line chapter summary, self-check questions and the common-confusions list (block VIII) — completed in the unit fill pass.

**Summary.** DNA stores information as base sequence; replication copies it semi-conservatively; transcription and translation express it through the central dogma; operons regulate expression. Every hereditary ratio Mendel saw is, at bottom, the chemistry of complementary base pairing. **Self-check:** can you transcribe and translate a 6-base template strand without notes?

# Human genome project — objectives and significance

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Human genome project — objectives and significance** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Heredity and Evolution fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Human genome project — objectives and significance

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

The **Human Genome Project (HGP)** was the biggest single project in biology: an international, publicly funded effort (launched 1990, DOE + NIH, James Watson first head) to read the complete sequence of the human genome — all ~3.1 billion base pairs — plus the genomes of model organisms. A private competitor (Celera, Craig Venter, 1998) raced it using shotgun sequencing; both published a draft together in **February 2001**, and the 'complete' reference sequence was declared in **April 2003**.

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 2 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 3 — Summary and marks map**

| Sub-topic | One-line essence | NEB marks trend |
| --- | --- | --- |

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — the HGP from idea to finished genome (study in this order)**

| Step | Milestone | Year | Detail |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Idea proposed at DOE meetings | 1985–86 | Detecting radiation-induced mutations motivated sequencing |
| 2 | HGP officially launched | 1990 | DOE + NIH; 15-year, $3-billion plan; Watson first director |
| 3 | Model organisms sequenced in parallel | 1996–2000 | Yeast (1996), C. elegans (1998), Drosophila (2000) |
| 4 | Celera Genomics enters the race | 1998 | Whole-genome shotgun sequencing vs the clone-by-clone map |
| 5 | Working draft announced jointly | June 2000 / Feb 2001 | Clinton + Blair announcement; papers in Nature (public) and Science (Celera) |
| 6 | 'Complete' reference sequence | April 2003 | 99.99% accurate, essentially all euchromatic DNA |
| 7 | Truly telomere-to-telomere genome | 2022 | T2T consortium closed the last gaps with long-read sequencing |

**HGP goals vs the methods that met them**

| Goal | Method used |
|---|---|
| Identify all ~20,000–25,000 human genes | cDNA/EST mapping + gene prediction |
| Determine the sequence of all 3.1 billion base pairs | Clone-by-clone (BAC contigs) + Sanger sequencing; Celera used shotgun |
| Improve sequencing tools and cost | Automated capillary sequencers, bioinformatics (BLAST era) |
| Sequence model organisms (E. coli, yeast, worm, fly, mouse) | Parallel comparative-genomics tracks |
| Address ethics, legal and social issues (ELSI) | 5% of budget reserved — the first project with a built-in ethics arm |
| Store everything in free public databases | GenBank / EMBL / DDBJ — data released within 24 h (Bermuda Principles) |

**Significance of the HGP — classified by field**

| Field | Impact |
|---|---|
| Medicine | Genetic testing, carrier screening, pharmacogenomics (drug response by genotype), cancer genomics |
| Basic biology | Gene number (~20k, fewer than rice), gene families, non-coding RNA, regulatory elements mapped |
| Evolution | Human–chimp–mouse comparisons; conserved vs diverged regions; 'Out of Africa' genomic evidence |
| Technology | Sequencing cost fell from ~$3 billion to under $1,000 — the basis of today's genomic medicine |
| Forensics and identity | STR profiling standards, mitochondrial DNA databases |
| Ethics (ELSI) | GINA-type genetic-discrimination law, privacy of genetic data, informed consent standards |

## 5. Worked examples and applications
≥ 6 worked examples with solved steps, live examples and Nepal-context applications (biology-plan.md §3.1, block V) — written in the unit fill pass.

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example — what the numbers taught us.** Before the HGP, estimates of human gene count ran to 100,000. The finished sequence revealed roughly **20,000–25,000** protein-coding genes — fewer than rice — while ~98% of the genome does NOT code for protein. The lesson: complexity comes less from gene count and more from regulation, alternative splicing and non-coding RNA. This single surprise redirected a decade of biology.

## 7. Exam Zone
NEB past-question map (long/short), topic-wise MCQs with explanations, and short tricks (block VII). Existing entrance-exam (CEE) material stays where it is; this zone grows around it — see the seeded exam fields of this file when present.

**Most-asked points (NEB).** (1) State the goals of the HGP. (2) Give the key dates: 1990 launch, 2001 draft, 2003 completion. (3) What was ELSI and why was it funded? (4) Name the model organisms sequenced alongside human. (5) Method contrast: clone-by-clone vs whole-genome shotgun. (6) Two significance points: pharmacogenomics and the true gene count.

**Summary.** The HGP read all 3.1 billion base pairs of the human genome (1990–2003), discovered the real gene count, spun off cheap sequencing, comparative genomics and genomic medicine, and pioneered project-level ethics (ELSI). **Self-check:** can you name one goal, one method and one significance point for each of medicine, biology and ethics?

# Evolution: evidences, adaptive radiation, Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, human evolution

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Evolution** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Heredity and Evolution fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point

### Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium
### human evolution

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

Darwin's 1859 theory — descent with modification by natural selection — is supported by evidence from every branch of biology. Population genetics later gave it a mathematical spine: the **Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium** defines the genetic baseline of a population that is NOT evolving, so any deviation names the evolutionary force at work. **Adaptive radiation** (Darwin's finches) shows one ancestor diversifying into many niches, and the fossil record of human ancestors shows our own radiation.

**Concept flow — from Darwin to human origins (study in this order)**

| Step | Concept | Key idea |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Natural selection (Darwin, 1859) | Variation + overproduction + struggle → survival of the fittest → new species |
| 2 | Evidence for evolution | Fossils, embryology, comparative anatomy, molecular homology, biogeography |
| 3 | Population genetics | Allele frequencies describe evolution mathematically |
| 4 | Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium | p² + 2pq + q² = 1 in a non-evolving population |
| 5 | Five evolutionary forces | Mutation, gene flow, genetic drift, non-random mating, natural selection |
| 6 | Adaptive radiation | One ancestor → many niches (Darwin's finches, marsupials of Australia) |
| 7 | Human evolution | Australopithecus → Homo habilis → H. erectus → Neanderthal → H. sapiens |

**Evidence for evolution — classified by source**

| Type of evidence | Classic example | What it shows |
|---|---|---|
| Palaeontological (fossils) | Archaeopteryx (reptile + bird); horse series | Life changed through time; transitional forms exist |
| Embryological | Vertebrate embryos share gill pouches and tail | Common ancestry in early development |
| Comparative anatomy — homology | Forelimb of human, whale, bat, horse — same bones, different jobs | Divergent evolution from a common ancestor |
| Comparative anatomy — analogy | Wings of bat and insect | Convergent evolution — similar function, different origin |
| Molecular | Same genetic code; cytochrome-c similarity ranks | The closer two species, the fewer molecular differences |
| Biogeographical | Marsupials radiated in isolated Australia | Isolation + time = independent radiations |

**Hardy–Weinberg — the five conditions and the force each one hides**

| Condition for equilibrium | If violated, the force at work is | Effect on allele frequencies |
|---|---|---|
| No mutation | Mutation | Creates new alleles directly |
| No migration (large population) | Gene flow | Alleles move between populations |
| Very large population | Genetic drift | Random change; strongest in small populations |
| Random mating | Non-random mating (inbreeding, assortative) | Changes genotype frequencies, not allele frequencies |
| No natural selection | Natural selection | Non-random, directional change — the only adaptive force |

**Human evolution — the main stages in order**

| Stage | Approx. age | Brain capacity | Key features |
|---|---|---|---|
| Australopithecus (e.g. 'Lucy', A. afarensis) | 4–2 million yrs ago | 400–500 cc | Bipedal but small-brained; ape-like face; East Africa |
| Homo habilis | 2.4–1.4 million yrs ago | 600–750 cc | First stone tools (Oldowan); 'handy man' |
| Homo erectus | 1.8 million–110,000 yrs ago | 900–1100 cc | Fire, Acheulean tools, first migration out of Africa (Java, Peking man) |
| Neanderthal man (H. neanderthalensis) | 400,000–40,000 yrs ago | 1300–1600 cc | Cold-adapted Europe; burials, Mousterian tools; interbred with sapiens |
| Homo sapiens (Cro-Magnon) | 300,000 yrs ago – present | 1350–1500 cc | Art, language, agriculture; spread worldwide from Africa |

## 5. Worked examples and applications
≥ 6 worked examples with solved steps, live examples and Nepal-context applications (biology-plan.md §3.1, block V) — written in the unit fill pass.

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example — Hardy–Weinberg.** In a population of 1,000 people, 160 cannot roll the tongue (recessive, tt). q² = 160/1000 = 0.16, so q = 0.4 and p = 0.6. Carriers 2pq = 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.48 → **480 carriers**, TT = p² = 360. Check: 360 + 480 + 160 = 1,000. If next generation shows the same frequencies, the population is in equilibrium; if not, name the force that moved them.

## 7. Exam Zone
NEB past-question map (long/short), topic-wise MCQs with explanations, and short tricks (block VII). Existing entrance-exam (CEE) material stays where it is; this zone grows around it — see the seeded exam fields of this file when present.

**Most-asked points (NEB).** (1) List the five lines of evidence for evolution with one example each. (2) Homology vs analogy with examples. (3) State the Hardy–Weinberg law and solve for carrier frequency. (4) Name the five forces that break equilibrium. (5) What is adaptive radiation — give Darwin's finches AND Australian marsupials. (6) Order the human ancestors with brain capacities.

## 8. Summary and self-check
5–10 line chapter summary, self-check questions and the common-confusions list (block VIII) — completed in the unit fill pass.

**Summary.** Evolution is documented (evidence), mechanised (selection) and measured (Hardy–Weinberg). Equilibrium is the null hypothesis; the five forces are the alternatives; adaptive radiation is natural selection at high speed; the human fossil record is radiation applied to ourselves. **Self-check:** can you solve a 2pq problem and place Australopithecus, habilis, erectus, Neanderthal and sapiens in order?

notes:
# Pathogens and diseases: malaria, dengue, filariasis, ascariasis, pneumonia, typhoid, tuberculosis, common cold, AIDS, ringworm

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Pathogens and diseases** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Human Health and Diseases fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Pathogens and diseases: malaria
### dengue
### filariasis
### ascariasis
### pneumonia
### typhoid
### tuberculosis
### common cold
### AIDS
### ringworm

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

A **pathogen** is any organism or agent that causes disease — viruses, bacteria, protozoa, helminth worms and fungi. For every disease in the NEB list you need five facts: the pathogen (with its type), how it spreads, the main symptom, how it is diagnosed, and how it is prevented or treated. The tables below carry all five columns for all ten diseases.

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 2 — Key ideas and worked angles**

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — how any infectious disease is analysed (study in this order)**

| Step | Question | Example (malaria) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | What is the pathogen? | Plasmodium — a protozoan parasite |
| 2 | How is it transmitted? | Bite of female Anopheles mosquito |
| 3 | What does it attack? | Liver cells, then red blood cells |
| 4 | Main symptoms? | Recurring fever with shaking chills every 3–4 days |
| 5 | How is it diagnosed? | Blood smear under the microscope |
| 6 | How is it controlled? | Antimalarial drugs + mosquito control (drains, nets, sprays) |

**The ten NEB diseases — master table**

| Disease | Pathogen (type) | Transmission | Key symptom / damage | Control |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Malaria | Plasmodium vivax / falciparum (protozoan) | Female Anopheles mosquito bite | Recurring fever with chills; RBC destruction | Quinine/antimalarials; mosquito control |
| Dengue | Dengue virus (RNA virus) | Female Aedes aegypti mosquito | High fever, severe joint-muscle pain, bleeding, platelet drop | No vaccine for routine use; Aedes control, avoid stagnant water |
| Filariasis (elephantiasis) | Wuchereria bancrofti (nematode) | Culex / Anopheles mosquito bite | Lymph vessel blockage → gross swelling of limbs/genitals | Antifilarial drugs; mosquito control |
| Ascariasis | Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm) | Faecal contamination of food/water; eggs swallowed | Abdominal pain, blockage of intestinal passage | Deworming; sanitation |
| Typhoid | Salmonella typhi (bacterium) | Contaminated food and water | Sustained high fever, weakness, stomach pain, constipation; Widal test | Chloramphenicol/antibiotics; safe water, sanitation |
| Pneumonia | Streptococcus pneumoniae / Haemophilus influenzae (bacteria) | Inhaling droplets/aerosols | Alveoli fill with fluid; fever, chills, cough, headache | Antibiotics; vaccination of children and elderly |
| Tuberculosis | Mycobacterium tuberculosis (bacterium) | Airborne droplets from cough/sneeze | Chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats; lung damage | DOTS course of several antibiotics for months; BCG vaccine |
| Common cold | Rhinoviruses (group of viruses) | Droplets and contaminated surfaces | Nasal congestion, sore throat, cough, sneezing — self-limiting | Rest and symptomatic care; hygiene |
| AIDS | HIV (retrovirus, RNA) | Sexual contact, infected blood, shared needles, mother-to-child | Attacks helper T cells → immune failure, opportunistic infections | No cure; ART drugs slow it; safe practices, screened blood |
| Ringworm | Microsporum / Trichophyton (fungi) | Direct contact, shared towels/clothes | Dry scaly round lesions with intense itch on skin, scalp, nails | Antifungal creams; personal hygiene |

**Pathogens classified by type — what each group is and how it is fought**

| Pathogen type | Diseases in the list | Why it matters for treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Virus (RNA/DNA) | Dengue, common cold, AIDS | Live inside host cells — antibiotics useless; vaccines and antivirals |
| Bacterium | Typhoid, pneumonia, tuberculosis | Antibiotics work; resistance (MDR-TB) is the danger |
| Protozoan | Malaria | Antiprotozoal drugs; vector control is decisive |
| Helminth (nematode) | Filariasis, ascariasis | Anthelmintic drugs; sanitation breaks the cycle |
| Fungus | Ringworm | Antifungals; spreads by contact — hygiene matters |

**Worked example — reading a case.** A patient has fever that returns every 48 hours with violent shills, lives near a stagnant pond, and a blood smear shows parasites inside red blood cells. Control: antimalarial drug + drain the pond + bed nets. **Exam trap:** only the female mosquito bites (needs blood for eggs); the male feeds on plant sap.

# Immune system — innate and adaptive immunity

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Immune system — innate and adaptive immunity** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Human Health and Diseases fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Immune system — innate and adaptive immunity

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

The immune system is the body's defence network, arranged in layers. **Innate immunity** is inborn, non-specific and immediate — barriers, phagocytes, inflammation. **Adaptive (acquired) immunity** is specific to each antigen, learns, remembers, and is carried by lymphocytes (B and T cells). Cell-mediated immunity (T cells) kills infected cells; humoral immunity (B cells → antibodies) neutralises free pathogens.

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Characteristics**

| Part | Structure | Function | Exam note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 2 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 3 — Summary and marks map**

| Sub-topic | One-line essence | NEB marks trend |
| --- | --- | --- |

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — the layers of defence (study in this order)**

| Step | Layer | What it does | Speed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Physical / chemical barriers | Skin, mucus, cilia, stomach acid, saliva, tears | Instant — blocks entry |
| 2 | Innate cellular defence | Neutrophils, macrophages, NK cells phagocytose / kill; inflammation and fever | Minutes to hours |
| 3 | Humoral adaptive immunity | B lymphocytes → plasma cells → antibodies neutralise free antigen | Days on first meeting |
| 4 | Cell-mediated adaptive immunity | Cytotoxic T cells destroy virus-infected and cancer cells; helper T cells coordinate | Days on first meeting |
| 5 | Immunological memory | Memory B and T cells — the basis of vaccination | Hours on re-exposure |

**Innate vs adaptive immunity — classified comparison**

| Feature | Innate immunity | Adaptive immunity |
|---|---|---|
| Origin | Present from birth | Develops after exposure to antigen |
| Specificity | Non-specific — attacks anything foreign | Specific to one antigen (epitope) |
| Memory | None — same response every time | Memory cells — faster and stronger on re-exposure |
| Main players | Skin, mucus, acid, phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages), NK cells | B lymphocytes (antibodies), T lymphocytes (helper, cytotoxic) |
| Speed | Immediate | Slow on first exposure (primary), rapid afterwards (secondary) |
| Diversity | Fixed set of receptors | Millions of antigen receptors by rearrangement |

**Cells of the immune system — who does what**

| Cell | Class | Job |
|---|---|---|
| Neutrophil | Innate, phagocyte | First responder; engulfs bacteria at wounds |
| Macrophage | Innate, phagocyte | Engulfs debris and pathogens; presents antigen to T cells |
| Natural killer (NK) cell | Innate, cytotoxic | Kills virus-infected and tumour cells without prior exposure |
| B lymphocyte | Adaptive, humoral | Makes antibodies; becomes memory B cell |
| Helper T cell (CD4) | Adaptive, coordinator | Activates B cells and cytotoxic T cells — the cell HIV destroys |
| Cytotoxic T cell (CD8) | Adaptive, cell-mediated | Punches holes in infected / cancerous cells (perforin) |
| Memory B / T cell | Adaptive, memory | Persists for years; drives the fast secondary response |

- **D2** — Immune system — innate and adaptive immunity — process or life-cycle flow (authored SVG — English labels)

≥ 6 worked examples with solved steps, live examples and Nepal-context applications (biology-plan.md §3.1, block V) — written in the unit fill pass.

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example.** A splinter enters the skin. Barriers fail (step 1). Neutrophils and macrophages arrive within hours; the area reddens and swells — inflammation (step 2). Macrophages present antigen to helper T cells, which activate B cells; antibodies appear after ~5–7 days (step 3). Cytotoxic T cells clear any infected cells (step 4). Memory cells persist — a second splinter with the same bacteria is cleared in 1–2 days (step 5).

NEB past-question map (long/short), topic-wise MCQs with explanations, and short tricks (block VII). Existing entrance-exam (CEE) material stays where it is; this zone grows around it — see the seeded exam fields of this file when present.

**Most-asked points (NEB).** (1) Differentiate innate and adaptive immunity in five points. (2) Name the two arms of adaptive immunity and their effector cells. (3) Which cell does HIV attack and why does that collapse the whole adaptive response? (4) What is cell-mediated immunity — give one situation where it matters (transplant rejection, tumour surveillance). (5) Define immunological memory.

## 8. Summary and self-check
5–10 line chapter summary, self-check questions and the common-confusions list (block VIII) — completed in the unit fill pass.

**Summary.** Defence is layered: instant barriers, fast non-specific innate cells, then specific adaptive humoral and cell-mediated arms that remember. Vaccination works because of that memory. **Self-check:** can you place neutrophil, B cell, helper T cell and NK cell in the right layer from memory?

# Antigens and antibodies, immune response

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Antigens and antibodies** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Human Health and Diseases fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Antigens and antibodies
### immune response

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

An **antigen** is any substance that the immune system recognises as foreign and reacts against (toxin, protein on a pathogen surface, pollen). An **antibody (immunoglobulin)** is the Y-shaped protein a plasma B cell secretes to bind that antigen specifically. Antibodies never kill directly — they tag: neutralise toxins, coat pathogens for phagocytes (opsonisation), clump them (agglutination), or trigger complement.

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 2 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 3 — Summary and marks map**

| Sub-topic | One-line essence | NEB marks trend |
| --- | --- | --- |

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — from antigen encounter to immune memory (study in this order)**

| Step | Event | Key cell / molecule |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Antigen enters and is captured | Macrophage / dendritic cell presents it |
| 2 | Helper T cell activates the right clone | CD4 helper T + interleukins |
| 3 | B cells divide into plasma cells | Clonal selection and expansion |
| 4 | Antibodies flood the blood (primary response) | IgM first, then IgG |
| 5 | Antigen cleared; most plasma cells die | Feedback shuts the response off |
| 6 | Memory B and T cells persist | Years of protection |
| 7 | Re-exposure → fast, massive secondary response | IgG dominated, no illness |

**The five antibody classes — classified by structure and role**

| Class | Structure | Where found | Main role |
|---|---|---|---|
| IgG | Monomer | Blood, tissue fluid, crosses placenta | Main defender of secondary response; gives newborn passive immunity |
| IgM | Pentamer (5 Y units) | Blood — first on the scene | First antibody of the primary response; powerful agglutinator |
| IgA | Dimer (2 Y units) | Tears, saliva, milk, gut mucus | Mucosal defence; protects the newborn via colostrum |
| IgE | Monomer | Mast cells and basophils | Allergy and anti-parasite response; triggers histamine release |
| IgD | Monomer | B cell surface | B cell receptor — antigen recognition |

**Primary vs secondary immune response; active vs passive immunity**

| Feature | Primary response | Secondary response |
|---|---|---|
| Trigger | First meeting with the antigen | Re-exposure to the same antigen |
| Lag period | 5–7 days or more | 1–2 days |
| Main antibody | IgM, then some IgG | Massive IgG |
| Magnitude | Moderate, short-lived | Much larger, long-lasting |
| Driving cells | Naive B cells | Memory B cells |

≥ 6 worked examples with solved steps, live examples and Nepal-context applications (biology-plan.md §3.1, block V) — written in the unit fill pass.

Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example — reading an antibody titre.** A patient's blood shows high IgM against a virus but almost no IgG: the infection is **new** (primary response). A second sample two weeks later shows IgM falling and IgG rising steeply: the patient is clearing the infection and has gained memory. If the first sample already had high IgG with no IgM, the infection was old or the patient was vaccinated — IgG tells history, IgM tells news.

# Vaccination and immunization

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Vaccination and immunization** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Human Health and Diseases fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Vaccination and immunization

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

A **vaccine** is a preparation of antigen — killed, weakened, fragmented or synthesized — that trains the immune system without causing disease. Immunization is the process of becoming protected. The principle is Edward Jenner's (cowpox → smallpox, 1796): a mild first encounter produces memory cells, so the real pathogen meets a fast, massive secondary response.

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 2 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 3 — Summary and marks map**

| Sub-topic | One-line essence | NEB marks trend |
| --- | --- | --- |

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — how a vaccine becomes protection (study in this order)**

| Step | Event | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Vaccine antigen delivered (injection / oral) | Antigen reaches lymphoid tissue |
| 2 | B and T cells with matching receptors activate | Clonal expansion |
| 3 | Antibodies produced; antigen cleared | Mild or no symptoms |
| 4 | Memory B and T cells form | Long-term armed state |
| 5 | Real pathogen arrives months or years later | Secondary response in 1–2 days — pathogen destroyed before disease |

**Types of vaccines — classified with examples**

| Type | What it contains | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Live attenuated | Weakened living pathogen | BCG (TB), MMR, oral polio (OPV) | Strong, long-lasting immunity; caution in immune-suppressed people |
| Killed / inactivated | Pathogen killed by heat or chemicals | Injectable polio (IPV), rabies, whole-cell pertussis | Safer, but usually needs boosters |
| Toxoid | Inactivated toxin | Tetanus, diphtheria | Trains the body against the toxin, not the bacterium |
| Subunit / conjugate | Purified protein or sugar-protein piece | Hepatitis B (surface antigen), Hib, pneumococcal | No live material at all — safest for the immune-compromised |
| mRNA / vector | Instructions for cells to make one viral protein | COVID-19 mRNA vaccines | Newest class; rapid development |

**Active vs passive immunization — the two ways to protect**

| Feature | Active immunization (vaccination) | Passive immunization |
|---|---|---|
| What is given | Antigen | Ready-made antibodies |
| Example | Polio drops, BCG, tetanus toxoid | Antivenom for snake bite, antitetanus serum, colostrum IgA |
| Onset of protection | Days to weeks (body must respond) | Immediate |
| Duration | Years — memory cells persist | Short — antibodies decay, no memory |
| Use case | Routine prevention | Emergency after exposure, or people who cannot be vaccinated |

## 4. Diagrams and figures

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example.** A child receives DPT at 6, 10 and 14 weeks. The first dose is the primary response — antibodies appear after about a week and fade. The second and third doses act as boosters: each triggers a bigger, faster IgG response and a larger memory pool. That is why the schedule has three doses, and why a tetanus booster every few years keeps protection high. A person stepped on a rusty nail who was never vaccinated gets **antitetanus serum** — passive immunization, immediate but temporary.

notes:
# Allergy and autoimmune diseases

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Allergy and autoimmune diseases** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Human Health and Diseases fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Allergy and autoimmune diseases

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

The immune system can fail in two opposite directions. **Allergy** is an over-reaction to a harmless antigen (pollen, dust, food) — IgE-coated mast cells dump histamine. **Autoimmunity** is the loss of self-tolerance: the immune system attacks the body's own tissues (rheumatoid arthritis, Type 1 diabetes). One is an attack on something harmless; the other on something that is self.

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 2 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 3 — Summary and marks map**

| Sub-topic | One-line essence | NEB marks trend |
| --- | --- | --- |

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — the two failures of recognition (study in this order)**

| Step | Concept | Key event |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Normal tolerance | Self-reactive lymphocytes deleted or silenced in development |
| 2 | Allergy: false alarm | IgE made against a harmless allergen; mast cells armed |
| 3 | Re-exposure → degranulation | Histamine, serotonin released → symptoms |
| 4 | Anaphylactic shock (extreme allergy) | Whole-body histamine → airway constriction, BP collapse; adrenaline is the rescue drug |
| 5 | Autoimmunity: wrong target | Self-tolerance breaks; immune attack on own organs |
| 6 | Management | Allergy: antihistamines, avoid allergen; autoimmunity: immunosuppression |

**Allergy vs autoimmune disease — classified comparison**

| Feature | Allergy | Autoimmune disease |
|---|---|---|
| Target | Harmless external antigen (allergen) | The body's own cells and tissues |
| Immune players | IgE antibodies on mast cells | Autoantibodies and self-reactive T cells |
| Mediator | Histamine, serotonin from mast cell granules | Chronic inflammation, tissue destruction |
| Onset | Minutes after exposure | Slow, chronic, relapsing |
| Common examples | Hay fever, asthma, eczema, peanut allergy | Rheumatoid arthritis, Type 1 diabetes, Graves' disease, lupus, multiple sclerosis |
| Treatment logic | Antihistamines, adrenaline for shock, avoidance | Immunosuppressant drugs; replace what is lost (insulin) |

**Major autoimmune diseases — what is attacked and the result**

| Disease | Target attacked | Main result |
|---|---|---|
| Rheumatoid arthritis | Joint lining (synovium) | Painful, swollen, deforming joints |
| Type 1 (insulin-dependent) diabetes | Insulin-producing beta cells of pancreas | No insulin → high blood sugar, insulin injections for life |
| Graves' disease | TSH receptor on thyroid | Overactive thyroid — hyperthyroidism, eye protrusion |
| Systemic lupus erythematosus | Widespread nuclear antigens | Multi-organ inflammation; skin, joints, kidneys |
| Multiple sclerosis | Myelin sheath of neurons | Slowed nerve signals — weakness, vision problems |

## 5. Worked examples and applications
≥ 6 worked examples with solved steps, live examples and Nepal-context applications (biology-plan.md §3.1, block V) — written in the unit fill pass.

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example.** A teenager wheezes every spring and a skin-prick test raises a red weal within minutes for grass pollen. Mechanism: first exposures made IgE against pollen; the IgE now sits on mast cells in the airway; each spring the allergen bridges two IgE molecules, the mast cell degranulates, and histamine causes bronchoconstriction. Treatment: antihistamine blocks receptors; inhaled steroids calm the chronic inflammation; adrenaline is reserved for anaphylaxis.

(3) Define autoimmunity and give two diseases with the tissue attacked. (4) Contrast allergy and autoimmunity in four points. (5) Which immune failure is an over-reaction and which a loss of tolerance?

**Summary.** Allergy = IgE + mast cells + histamine aimed at a harmless target; autoimmunity = tolerance lost, self attacked. Both are failures of recognition, in opposite directions. **Self-check:** can you name the antibody in allergy and the destroyed cells in Type 1 diabetes?

# Microorganisms in household products

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Microorganisms in household products** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Microbes in Human Welfare fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Microorganisms in household products

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

Fermentation is household chemistry. *Lactobacillus* turns milk into curd; yeast raises dough and ferments drinks; bacteria and fungi ripen cheese. Every one of these is a microbe digesting sugar and, as a by-product, changing the food — adding flavour, texture, preservation, and in the case of curd, nutrition (vitamin B12).

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Characteristics**

| Part | Structure | Function | Exam note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 2 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 3 — Summary and marks map**

| Sub-topic | One-line essence | NEB marks trend |
| --- | --- | --- |

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — one principle behind every household fermentation (study in this order)**

| Step | Principle | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Microbes are grown on a sugar-rich food | Milk lactose, flour starch, fruit juice |
| 2 | They metabolise it anaerobically (or semi-anaerobically) | Yeast respires without oxygen |
| 3 | The products are acids, alcohol and CO2 | Lactic acid, ethanol, carbon dioxide |
| 4 | The products change the food | Curd sets, dough rises, drinks fizz |
| 5 | Acid / alcohol also preserve the food | Low pH inhibits spoilage bacteria |

**Microbes in household food products — the master table**

| Product | Microbe used | What the microbe does |
|---|---|---|
| Curd / yoghurt | Lactobacillus (lactic acid bacteria) | Converts lactose to lactic acid; acid coagulates milk protein (casein); also increases vitamin B12 |
| Bread, dough | Saccharomyces cerevisiae (baker's yeast) | Ferments sugar to CO2; gas bubbles leaven the dough |
| Idli, dosa batter | Yeasts + lactic acid bacteria | Fermentation makes the batter rise and adds sour flavour |
| Swiss cheese | Propionibacterium shermanii | Produces CO2 holes and the characteristic flavour |
| Roquefort / blue cheese | Penicillium roqueforti (a fungus) | Grows through the cheese, ripens it with blue veins and sharp taste |
| Toddy (traditional drink) | Yeasts (natural fermentation) | Ferments sap of palm trees into an alcoholic drink |
| Dough for dosa kept overnight | Mixed natural flora | Souring + leavening in one step |

## 5. Worked examples and applications
≥ 6 worked examples with solved steps, live examples and Nepal-context applications (biology-plan.md §3.1, block V) — written in the unit fill pass.

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example.** Milk kept warm with a spoonful of curd sets in 4–6 hours, but the same milk left alone spoils instead. The difference is the **starter**: the inoculum gives lactic acid bacteria a huge head start, so they acidify the milk before spoilage organisms can take over. This is the whole logic of controlled fermentation — the right microbe, first and fast. It also explains why curd is safer than raw milk in places without refrigeration.

## 7. Exam Zone
NEB past-question map (long/short), topic-wise MCQs with explanations, and short tricks (block VII). Existing entrance-exam (CEE) material stays where it is; this zone grows around it — see the seeded exam fields of this file when present.

**Most-asked points (NEB).** (1) Name the microbe and the reaction in curd formation. (2) Why does dough rise — name the gas and the organism. (3) Which microbes ripen Swiss cheese and blue cheese? (4) What is toddy? (5) Why does curd formation improve nutrition (vitamin B12) and safety?

## 8. Summary and self-check
5–10 line chapter summary, self-check questions and the common-confusions list (block VIII) — completed in the unit fill pass.

**Summary.** Household fermentation is one principle in many costumes: the right microbe on a sugary food produces acid, alcohol or CO2 that textures, flavours and preserves the product. **Self-check:** can you match all seven products in the master table to their microbes?

# Industrial production of antibiotics, alcoholic beverages, citric acid

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Industrial production of antibiotics** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Microbes in Human Welfare fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Industrial production of antibiotics
### alcoholic beverages
### citric acid

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

The same fermentation principle, scaled to tonnes: a **fermenter** (bioreactor) grows the microbe under controlled temperature, pH and aeration, and the product is harvested, purified and marketed. The three NEB exemplars: **penicillin** (the first antibiotic, discovered by Fleming in 1928, mass-produced in WWII), **ethanol** for beverages (*Saccharomyces*), and **citric acid** (*Aspergillus niger*).

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 2 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 3 — Summary and marks map**

| Sub-topic | One-line essence | NEB marks trend |
| --- | --- | --- |

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — from lab discovery to industrial fermenter (study in this order)**

| Step | Stage | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Discovery | Fleming notices Penicillium killing staphylococci (1928); Florey and Chain purify it (1940s) |
| 2 | Strain selection and improvement | Highest-yielding strain chosen; mutated for more product |
| 3 | Medium preparation | Sterilised nutrient broth (sugar, nitrogen, minerals) loaded into the fermenter |
| 4 | Inoculation and growth | Pure culture added; temperature, pH, oxygen controlled by probes |
| 5 | Production phase | Microbe secretes the product into the broth (or into cells) |
| 6 | Downstream processing | Filtration, extraction, purification, drying, quality control, packaging |

**Industrial products — microbe, substrate and product**

| Product | Microbe | Substrate / process | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Penicillin | Penicillium notatum / chrysogenum (fungus) | Aerobic fermentation on corn-steep liquor medium | Antibiotic against Gram-positive bacteria |
| Ethanol (beer, wine) | Saccharomyces cerevisiae (yeast) | Barley malt (beer) or grape juice (wine), anaerobic fermentation | Alcoholic beverages; industrial ethanol |
| Citric acid | Aspergillus niger (fungus) | Aerobic fermentation on molasses/sugar | Food preservative, flavouring, soft drinks |
| Note — antibiotics kill other microbes | Selected strains yield the most drug per litre | Fermenter keeps conditions at the optimum | Downstream purification is half the cost |

**Inside the fermenter — the parts and their jobs**

| Part | Job |
|---|---|
| Stirrer (impeller) | Mixes the broth evenly; keeps microbes suspended |
| Sparger / aeration system | Delivers sterile air or oxygen for aerobic fermentations |
| Temperature and pH probes | Keep conditions at the optimum for the strain |
| Sterile inlet / inoculum port | Lets the pure culture in without contamination |
| Harvest outlet / product drain | Removes broth for downstream processing |
| Cooling jacket | Carries away metabolic heat — fermentation is exothermic |

## 4. Diagrams and figures
- **D1** — Industrial production of antibiotics — structure (authored SVG — English labels, viewBox 900×640)
- **D2** — Industrial production of antibiotics — process or life-cycle flow (authored SVG — English labels)

stirrer keeps cells</text><text x="120" y="180" font-size="12" fill="#475569">suspended and oxygen</text><text x="120" y="200" font-size="12" fill="#475569">dissolved evenly.</text><text x="320" y="358" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#4b5563">Same vessel makes penicillin, ethanol or citric acid — only microbe and medium change.</text></svg>

## 5. Worked examples and applications
≥ 6 worked examples with solved steps, live examples and Nepal-context applications (biology-plan.md §3.1, block V) — written in the unit fill pass.

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example — penicillin's scale-up.** Fleming's plate gave a halo of killed bacteria around a *Penicillium* colony, but the yield was tiny. Industrial production needed: (1) a higher-yielding strain (from *P. notatum* to *P. chrysogenum*, then X-ray-mutated strains), (2) a better medium (corn-steep liquor), (3) aerated stirred fermenters, because the mould is aerobic, and (4) downstream extraction. Lesson: a discovery becomes a drug only when the fermenter economics work — strain, medium and engineering all three.

## 7. Exam Zone
NEB past-question map (long/short), topic-wise MCQs with explanations, and short tricks (block VII). Existing entrance-exam (CEE) material stays where it is; this zone grows around it — see the seeded exam fields of this file when present.

**Most-asked points (NEB).** (1) Name the microbe for penicillin, ethanol and citric acid. (2) Draw and label a fermenter. (3) Why must the fermenter be aerated for penicillin but not for ethanol? (4) List the stages from discovery to market. (5) What is downstream processing?

## 8. Summary and self-check
5–10 line chapter summary, self-check questions and the common-confusions list (block VIII) — completed in the unit fill pass.

**Summary.** Industrial fermentation = strain + medium + controlled bioreactor + downstream processing. Penicillin (fungus, aerobic), ethanol (yeast, anaerobic) and citric acid (fungus, aerobic) are the three exemplars. **Self-check:** can you label six parts of a fermenter and state each one's job?

# Microbes as biocontrol agents and biofertilizers

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Microbes as biocontrol agents and biofertilizers** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Microbes in Human Welfare fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Microbes as biocontrol agents and biofertilizers

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

Chemical pesticides and fertilisers pollute and cost energy. The biological alternative uses living microbes: **biocontrol agents** are microbes (or their predators) that kill pests and weeds; **biofertilizers** are microbes that supply plant nutrients, chiefly by fixing atmospheric nitrogen. Both are the backbone of organic farming.

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 2 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 3 — Summary and marks map**

| Sub-topic | One-line essence | NEB marks trend |
| --- | --- | --- |

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — from chemical dependence to biological control (study in this order)**

| Step | Concept | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | The problem with chemicals | Residues, resistance, killing of non-target insects, eutrophication from fertiliser runoff |
| 2 | Biocontrol with bacteria | Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) toxin kills caterpillars; gene now used in Bt cotton |
| 3 | Biocontrol with fungi and viruses | Trichoderma against soil fungi; baculovirus (NPV) against insect larvae |
| 4 | Biocontrol with predator insects | Ladybird beetle eats aphids; dragonflies eat mosquitoes |
| 5 | Biofertilizers — symbiotic N fixers | Rhizobium in legume root nodules; Azolla-Anabaena in rice paddies |
| 6 | Biofertilizers — free-living and fungal | Azotobacter, Azospirillum; mycorrhiza (Glomus) improves water and phosphorus uptake |

**Biocontrol agents — who kills what**

| Agent | Type | Target pest | How it works |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) | Soil bacterium | Caterpillars, beetle larvae, fly larvae | Produces Bt toxin crystals; alkaline insect gut dissolves them, toxin kills gut cells |
| Bt cotton (transgenic) | Crop carrying the Bt gene | Bollworm | Plant itself produces the toxin |
| Trichoderma viride | Fungus | Root-rot and wilt fungi | Antagonistic — parasitises and outcompetes pathogenic fungi |
| Baculovirus (NPV) | Insect virus | Lepidopteran larvae (moth, butterfly caterpillars) | Infects and liquefies larvae; harmless to plants, birds, mammals |
| Ladybird beetle | Predatory insect | Aphids (plant lice) | Eats large numbers of aphids |
| Dragonflies | Predatory insect | Mosquitoes | Eats mosquito larvae and adults |

**Biofertilizers — classified by how they fix or supply nutrients**

| Biofertilizer | Type | Host / habitat | What it supplies |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rhizobium | Symbiotic bacterium | Root nodules of legumes (pea, beans, pulses) | Fixed atmospheric nitrogen to the plant |
| Frankia | Symbiotic actinomycete | Root nodules of Alnus (alder) | Nitrogen fixation in non-legumes |
| Azolla + Anabaena | Symbiosis: fern + cyanobacterium | Rice paddies | Anabaena fixes nitrogen in Azolla leaf cavities — green manure for rice |
| Azotobacter / Azospirillum | Free-living aerobic bacteria | Soil around roots (rhizosphere) | Fix nitrogen without a host |
| Glomus (mycorrhiza) | Symbiotic fungus | Roots of most plants | Huge surface area: better phosphorus and water uptake, disease resistance |

≥ 6 worked examples with solved steps, live examples and Nepal-context applications (biology-plan.md §3.1, block V) — written in the unit fill pass.

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example — why Bt cotton works.** The caterpillar bites the leaf; the plant's own cells now carry the *cry* gene from *Bacillus thuringiensis* and produce an inactive protoxin. The insect's alkaline gut juice dissolves it, the toxin is activated, gut cells rupture and the larva dies within days. Humans and birds have acidic guts — the toxin is inactive for us. One gene moved the pesticide from the spray can into the plant.

(4) Classify biofertilizers: symbiotic (Rhizobium, Frankia, Azolla-Anabaena) vs free-living (Azotobacter) vs fungal (mycorrhiza). (5) What does mycorrhiza give the plant besides nutrients?

## 8. Summary and self-check
5–10 line chapter summary, self-check questions and the common-confusions list (block VIII) — completed in the unit fill pass.

**Summary.** Biocontrol replaces poison with predators, pathogens and toxins aimed at pests; biofertilizers replace bagged fertiliser with nitrogen-fixing and phosphorus-scavenging microbes. # Bioremediation, biogas

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Bioremediation** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Microbes in Human Welfare fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Bioremediation
### biogas

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

Microbes can be put to work on our waste. **Bioremediation** uses microorganisms to break pollutants down into harmless substances — oil-eating bacteria (*Pseudomonas*) after spills, microbes cleaning sewage in treatment plants. **Biogas** is the fuel side of the same idea: anaerobic methanogen bacteria digest animal dung and plant waste and release methane-rich gas for cooking and lighting.

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 2 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 3 — Summary and marks map**

| Sub-topic | One-line essence | NEB marks trend |
| --- | --- | --- |

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — waste in, energy and clean water out (study in this order)**

| Step | Concept | Key organism / part |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sewage treatment — aerobic stage | Floc of bacteria and fungi in the aeration tank eats organic matter |
| 2 | Sewage treatment — anaerobic stage | Sludge digested by anaerobic bacteria; methane released |
| 3 | Bioremediation of oil spills | Pseudomonas putida and marine bacteria digest hydrocarbons |
| 4 | Biogas production | Methanogens (e.g. Methanobacterium) under anaerobic conditions |
| 5 | Biogas composition | ~50–70% methane + CO2 + traces; burns without smoke |
| 6 | By-product | Spent slurry = excellent nitrogen-rich fertiliser |

**Bioremediation and biogas — classified summary**

| Application | Microbe | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sewage treatment (aerobic) | Mixed bacterial-fungal floc | Waste water organic matter | Cleaner water + microbial floc |
| Sludge digestion (anaerobic) | Anaerobic bacteria + methanogens | Settled sludge | Methane + stabilised sludge |
| Oil-spill cleanup | Pseudomonas putida and marine hydrocarbon degraders | Petroleum hydrocarbons | CO2 + water + biomass |
| Biogas plant (gobar gas) | Methanobacterium (methanogen) | Cattle dung + water, anaerobic | Biogas (CH4-rich) + fertiliser slurry |
| Key condition | Methanogens are strict anaerobes | Sealed, oxygen-free digester | — |

**Parts of a floating-dome biogas plant and their jobs**

| Part | Job |
|---|---|
| Mixing tank / inlet | Dung + water slurry enters here |
| Digester (well) | Sealed underground tank where anaerobic digestion happens |
| Floating gas holder dome | Rises as gas collects; keeps constant pressure |
| Gas outlet pipe | Carries biogas to the kitchen / lamp |
| Overflow / sludge outlet | Spent slurry exits — used as fertiliser |
| Why the dome floats | It moves up and down with gas volume, so supply pressure stays steady |

Two problems, one plant.</text></svg>

## 5. Worked examples and applications
≥ 6 worked examples with solved steps, live examples and Nepal-context applications (biology-plan.md §3.1, block V) — written in the unit fill pass.

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example — why the digester must be airtight.** Methanogens are **obligate anaerobes**: oxygen poisons them. A cracked dome lets air in, the methane producers stop, acid-formers take over, and gas output collapses while the slurry turns sour. The floating dome is not decoration — it seals the digester while letting gas volume change. This single fact explains the whole engineering of the plant.

## 7. Exam Zone
NEB past-question map (long/short), topic-wise MCQs with explanations, and short tricks (block VII). Existing entrance-exam (CEE) material stays where it is; this zone grows around it — see the seeded exam fields of this file when present.

**Most-asked points (NEB).** (1) Define bioremediation with one example (oil-eating Pseudomonas). (2) Name the methanogen and state why anaerobic conditions are essential. (3) Give the composition of biogas and its two products (gas + slurry fertiliser). (4) Draw and label the floating-dome plant. (5) Name the two stages of sewage treatment and the role of the floc.

## 8. Summary and self-check
5–10 line chapter summary, self-check questions and the common-confusions list (block VIII) — completed in the unit fill pass.

**Summary.** Microbes convert waste to value: aerobic flocs clean sewage, Pseudomonas eats oil spills, and sealed digesters of methanogens turn dung into methane plus fertiliser. The binding condition is anaerobiosis. **Self-check:** can you label the six parts of the biogas plant and explain why the dome floats?

# Adaptations of organisms to environmental conditions

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Adaptations of organisms to environmental conditions** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Organisms and Environment fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Adaptations of organisms to environmental conditions

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

An **adaptation** is any heritable trait — structural, physiological or behavioural — that improves an organism's survival and reproduction in its habitat. Natural selection builds them over generations: desert plants, high-altitude humans and deep-sea fish all carry solutions to the same problem (living where conditions are harsh) reached by different routes.

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Characteristics**

| Part | Structure | Function | Exam note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 2 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |

| Sub-topic | One-line essence | NEB marks trend |
| --- | --- | --- |

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — how organisms cope with their habitat (study in this order)**

| Step | Concept | Classic example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Habitat sets the problems | Desert: heat + water scarcity; altitude: low O2 |
| 2 | Morphological adaptation | Cactus leaves reduced to spines; thick cuticle |
| 3 | Physiological adaptation | Kangaroo rat makes metabolic water; haemoglobin count rises at altitude |
| 4 | Behavioural adaptation | Desert lizards bask in sun when cold, hide in shade when hot |
| 5 | Photosynthetic specialisation | CAM plants open stomata at night (Opuntia, pineapple) |
| 6 | Mimicry and escape | Moths camouflaged on bark; desert animals active at night |

**Adaptations classified by type — with the exam examples**

| Type | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Morphological (structural) | Body form and parts | Xerophytes: thick cuticle, sunken stomata, spines; hydrophytes: flat floating leaves, aerenchyma |
| Physiological (functional) | Internal chemistry and metabolism | CAM photosynthesis (stomata open at night); kangaroo rat's concentrated urine; increased RBC count at altitude |
| Behavioural | What the animal does | Nocturnality in desert animals; lizard thermoregulation; migration of birds |
| Reproductive | Timing and mode of breeding | Desert plants bloom after rare rains; bamboo's mass flowering |

**Worked example — the kangaroo rat.** It lives in deserts without drinking water. Solutions: (1) physiological — its kidneys produce urine far more concentrated than ours; (2) metabolic — water released when fats are oxidised covers its needs; (3) behavioural — it stays in a cool burrow by day and feeds at night, cutting evaporative loss. One animal, three adaptation types: exactly the classification the exam asks for.

**Summary.** Adaptations are heritable solutions to habitat problems, classified as morphological, physiological or behavioural. The same environmental pressure can produce different answers in different lineages. **Self-check:** for cactus, kangaroo rat and mountain human, can you name the adaptation type each example illustrates?
