# Population ecology — growth, regulation, interactions

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Population ecology — growth** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Organisms and Environment fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Population ecology — growth
### regulation
### interactions

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

A **population** is a group of individuals of one species in one place and time. Its size (N) changes by four processes: natality (+), mortality (−), immigration (+), emigration (−). Growth follows two models — unlimited **exponential** growth or **logistic** growth limited by carrying capacity (K). Populations also interact: competition, predation, parasitism, commensalism, mutualism and amensalism.

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 2 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 3 — Summary and marks map**

| Sub-topic | One-line essence | NEB marks trend |
| --- | --- | --- |

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — from population size to interaction types (study in this order)**

| Step | Concept | Key equation / example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Population attributes | N = size; density; birth rate, death rate; sex ratio; age pyramids |
| 2 | Four processes change N | Natality + immigration − mortality − emigration |
| 3 | Exponential growth (unlimited resources) | dN/dt = rN; J-shaped curve |
| 4 | Logistic growth (real world) | dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K; S-shaped curve |
| 5 | Carrying capacity K | Maximum sustainable population for the habitat |
| 6 | Regulation | Density-dependent factors (disease, competition) pull N back toward K |
| 7 | Interspecific interactions | Six pairs — see the classified table below |

**Population interactions — who wins and who loses**

| Interaction | Species A | Species B | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mutualism | + | + | Mycorrhiza and plant; lichen alga + fungus; fig and wasp |
| Commensalism | + | 0 | Cattle egret and cattle; barnacles on whale |
| Predation | + | − | Tiger and deer; also herbivores on plants |
| Parasitism | + | − | Flea on dog; Plasmodium in human; cuckoo brood parasitism |
| Competition | − | − | Gause's Paramecium experiment; invasive species ousting natives |
| Amensalism | 0 | − | Penicillium inhibits bacteria; shading by a large tree |

**Exponential vs logistic growth; r- vs K-strategists**

| Feature | Exponential (J-curve) | Logistic (S-curve) |
|---|---|---|
| Resources | Unlimited (never true for long) | Limited — the real world |
| Equation | dN/dt = rN | dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K |
| Final outcome | Explosion, then crash | Stabilises at carrying capacity K |
| Example | Bacteria in fresh broth; reindeer introduced to island |

## 4. Diagrams and figures
- **D1** — Growth curves / cause–effect–control diagrams (authored SVG — English labels, viewBox 900×640)
- **D2** — Population ecology — growth — process or life-cycle flow (authored SVG — English labels)

## 5. Worked examples and applications
≥ 6 worked examples with solved steps, live examples and Nepal-context applications (biology-plan.md §3.1, block V) — written in the unit fill pass.

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example — Gause's competition.** Two *Paramecium* species grown together in one tube: *P. aurelia* outgrows *P. caudatum*, which dies out — **competitive exclusion**: two species with the same niche cannot coexist. In nature the loser survives by **resource partitioning** (different microhabitat, different feeding time). This one experiment explains why invasive species are so destructive: they occupy the native species' niche without its predators.

NEB past-question map (long/short), topic-wise MCQs with explanations, and short tricks (block VII). Existing entrance-exam (CEE) material stays where it is; this zone grows around it — see the seeded exam fields of this file when present.

# Ecosystem structure and function — productivity, decomposition

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Ecosystem structure and function — productivity** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Organisms and Environment fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Ecosystem structure and function — productivity
### decomposition

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

An **ecosystem** is the functional unit combining the living community and its non-living environment, with energy flow and nutrient cycling linking them. Four functional processes run it: productivity, decomposition, energy flow and nutrient cycling. Energy enters as sunlight, flows one way, and is lost as heat at every transfer — which is why nutrients must be recycled but energy never is.

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Characteristics**

| Part | Structure | Function | Exam note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 2 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 3 — Summary and marks map**

| Sub-topic | One-line essence | NEB marks trend |
| --- | --- | --- |

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — the four functions of an ecosystem (study in this order)**

| Step | Function | Essence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Productivity | Producers fix solar energy as organic matter (GPP → NPP) |
| 2 | Decomposition | Dead matter broken back into minerals — the recycling step |
| 3 | Energy flow | One-way: sun → producers → consumers, 10% transferred per level |
| 4 | Nutrient cycling | Minerals return to the soil and are reused — cyclic, unlike energy |

**Ecosystem components and productivity — classified**

| Category | Members | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Producers (autotrophs) | Plants, algae, cyanobacteria | Fix solar energy into organic matter |
| Consumers | Herbivores (primary), carnivores (secondary/tertiary) | Eat other organisms for energy |
| Decomposers | Bacteria, fungi | Break dead matter into minerals — complete the cycle |
| Abiotic components | Light, temperature, water, soil, minerals | Physical setting and material reservoir |
| GPP (gross primary productivity) | Total fixed by producers | All the energy captured |
| NPP (net primary productivity) | GPP − respiration (R) | What is actually available to consumers; NPP = GPP − R |
| Secondary productivity | Consumers' new biomass | Energy converted into consumer tissue |

**Decomposition — the five steps in order**

| Step | What happens | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Fragmentation | Detritivores break litter into small particles | Earthworms, termites chew leaf litter |
| 2. Leaching | Water dissolves soluble compounds downward | Sugars washed out of litter into soil |
| 3. Catabolism | Microbial enzymes chemically degrade the matter | Fungal and bacterial secretions |
| 4. Humification | Dark amorphous humus forms | Resistant, slow-decomposing store |
| 5. Mineralisation | Humus further degraded to simple minerals | NH4+, PO4 3−, CO2 released for plants |

# Ecological succession

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Ecological succession** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Organisms and Environment fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Ecological succession

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

**Ecological succession** is the predictable, directional change in the species composition of a community over time, ending in a stable **climax community** matched to the climate. It starts from bare rock (primary) or from a disturbed site with soil intact (secondary). The sequence of temporary communities is the **sere**; the first colonisers are **pioneers**.

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Process steps**

| Step | What happens | Where | Key enzyme or number |

**Table 3 — Summary and marks map**

| Sub-topic | One-line essence | NEB marks trend |
| --- | --- | --- |

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — from bare ground to climax (study in this order)**

| Step | Stage | What changes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Nudation | Disturbance creates a bare area (lava, flood, fire, landslide) |
| 2 | Pioneer colonisation | Lichens (rock) or hardy weeds (soil) arrive; soil begins to form |
| 3 | Sere progression | Moss → grass → shrub → young forest: each stage modifies the habitat for the next |
| 4 | Climax community | Stable, self-perpetuating community set by the climate (e.g. forest) |
| 5 | Trends throughout | Biomass, species diversity and niche specialisation all increase; net productivity rises then stabilises |

**Primary vs secondary succession; hydrarch vs xerarch**

| Feature | Primary succession | Secondary succession |
|---|---|---|
| Starting point | Bare rock, lava, sand — no soil | Disturbed site with soil intact (burnt forest, abandoned field) |
| Pioneers | Lichens, mosses | Grasses, weeds from surviving seeds |
| Speed | Very slow (thousands of years — soil must form) | Fast (decades — soil already there) |
| Example | Lava flow colonised on Hawaii | Farmland abandoned in Nepal's middle hills |

## 6. Key terms and statements

**Worked example.** A lava flow cools to bare basalt. Lichens secrete acids, etching the rock and trapping dust — the first soil. Mosses follow, then grasses, then shrubs, then trees; each stage adds organic matter and holds more water, making the site habitable for the next, larger species. # Nutrient cycling — carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Nutrient cycling — carbon** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Organisms and Environment fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Nutrient cycling — carbon
### nitrogen
### phosphorus

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

Nutrient cycling (biogeochemical cycling) returns matter from organisms to the environment and back. Cycles are **gaseous** (reservoir in the atmosphere — carbon, nitrogen) or **sedimentary** (reservoir in rocks and soil — phosphorus, sulphur). The nitrogen cycle is the one with named bacterial specialists; the carbon cycle is the one we are now disturbing; the phosphorus cycle has no gas phase at all.

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Key ideas and worked angles**

**Table 2 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Sub-topic | One-line essence | NEB marks trend |

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — how any nutrient cycle is read (study in this order)**

| Step | Question to ask | Nitrogen example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Where is the main reservoir? | Atmosphere (78% N2) |
| 2 | How does it enter living systems? | Nitrogen fixation by bacteria |
| 3 | How does it move through the food web? | Assimilation → plants → animals |
| 4 | How is it returned? | Ammonification from dead matter and excreta |
| 5 | How is it made reusable? | Nitrification to nitrate — the form plants take up |
| 6 | How does it leave the biosphere? | Denitrification back to N2 gas |

**Carbon vs nitrogen vs phosphorus — the three cycles compared**

| Feature | Carbon cycle | Nitrogen cycle | Phosphorus cycle |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reservoir | Atmosphere CO2 + fossil fuels + limestone | Atmosphere N2 (78%) | Rocks and phosphate ores — SEDIMENTARY |
| Gas phase | Yes (CO2, CH4) | Yes (N2) | None — no gaseous form |
| Entry to life | Photosynthesis fixes CO2 | Nitrogen fixation by bacteria | Weathering releases phosphate to soil |
| Key microbes | — | Rhizobium, Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter, Pseudomonas | Mycorrhiza helps uptake |
| Human disturbance | Fossil fuel burning → rising CO2 | Fertiliser overuse → eutrophication | Mining + detergent runoff → algal blooms |
| Speed | Fast (living) + slow (fossil) | Fast through life, slow in soil pools | Slowest of the three |

**The nitrogen cycle — each step and its named bacterium**

| Step | Change | Organism |
|---|---|---|
| Nitrogen fixation | N2 → NH3 / NH4+ | Rhizobium (nodules), Azotobacter (free-living), cyanobacteria |
| Assimilation | NH4+ / NO3− built into amino acids | Plants, then animals via food |
| Ammonification | Proteins of dead matter and urea → NH3 | Decomposer bacteria and fungi |
| Nitrification (1) | NH3 / NH4+ → NO2− | Nitrosomonas |
| Nitrification (2) | NO2− → NO3− | Nitrobacter |
| Denitrification | NO3− → N2 gas (lost to air) | Pseudomonas and anaerobic bacteria |

# Ecological pyramids and energy flow

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Ecological pyramids and energy flow** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Organisms and Environment fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Ecological pyramids and energy flow

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

An **ecological pyramid** graphs a trophic property — number, biomass or energy — level by level, with producers at the base. The **10% law** (Lindeman): only about a tenth of the energy at one trophic level reaches the next; the rest is lost to respiration, waste and uneaten parts. Energy pyramids are always upright; the other two can sometimes invert.

## 3. Classified tables

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — from trophic levels to the 10% law (study in this order)**

| Step | Concept | Key point |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Trophic levels | T1 producers → T2 herbivores → T3 carnivores → T4 top carnivores |
| 2 | Energy transfer | Only ~10% passes up; 90% lost to respiration, heat, waste |
| 3 | Pyramid of energy | ALWAYS upright — energy must shrink upward (2nd law of thermodynamics) |
| 4 | Pyramid of biomass | Usually upright; inverted in the open ocean (phytoplankton stand small but turn over fast) |
| 5 | Pyramid of numbers | Usually upright; inverted for one tree → many insects → parasites |
| 6 | Implication | Top predators need vast territories — the reason they are rare and vulnerable |

**The three pyramids — which can invert and why**

| Pyramid | Units | Can it invert? | Classic inversion example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Energy | kJ/m²/time | NEVER — always upright | — (energy is lost at every transfer) |
| Biomass | g/m² (dry weight) | Sometimes | Ocean: few phytoplankton grams support more zooplankton — fast turnover |
| Numbers | count of individuals | Often | One large tree feeds thousands of insects, which feed thousands of parasites |

## 5. Worked examples and applications
≥ 6 worked examples with solved steps, live examples and Nepal-context applications (biology-plan.md §3.1, block V) — written in the unit fill pass.

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example.** Producers fix 100,000 kJ/m²/yr. By the 10% law: herbivores get 10,000, first carnivores 1,000, top carnivores 100. To support one 200-kg tiger, the ecosystem must fix energy for tonnes of deer and hectares of grass. **Why it matters:** this arithmetic is why top predators need huge home ranges, why food chains rarely exceed 4–5 levels, and why eating lower on the chain (plants) feeds more people per hectare.

## 7. Exam Zone
NEB past-question map (long/short), topic-wise MCQs with explanations, and short tricks (block VII). Existing entrance-exam (CEE) material stays where it is; this zone grows around it — see the seeded exam fields of this file when present.

**Most-asked points (NEB).** (1) State the 10% law and name Lindeman. (2) Draw the energy pyramid with numbers. (3) Which pyramids can invert, and give the ocean and tree-insect examples. (4) Why can the energy pyramid never invert? (5) Why are food chains limited to 4–5 trophic levels?

## 8. Summary and self-check
5–10 line chapter summary, self-check questions and the common-confusions list (block VIII) — completed in the unit fill pass.

**Summary.** Energy shrinks ~10× at every step; the energy pyramid is always upright, biomass and number pyramids sometimes are not. The consequence: few top predators, short chains, and plants as the energy base of everything. **Self-check:** starting from 200,000 kJ at T1, can you compute T2, T3 and T4?

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Three pyramid types — number, biomass, energy; energy pyramid is ALWAYS upright (Lindeman 10% law); biomass inverted in the ocean (phytoplankton < fish standing crop at a moment); number inverted for a single tree's insects.
Trick 2: 10% law numerical: 10,000 J producers → 1,000 J herbivore → 100 J carnivore → 10 J top — one chain calculation earns the numerical mark.
Trick 3: Trophic level rule: an organism can occupy more than one level (human: primary + secondary consumer); only ~4–5 levels possible because energy dies out.
Trick 4: Standing crop = biomass at a given time; pyramids of biomass use standing crop — the definition line.

# Plant breeding — methods and examples

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Plant breeding — methods and examples** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Plant breeding — methods and examples

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

**Plant breeding** is the purposeful genetic improvement of crop plants: cross parents carrying desirable traits, select the best offspring over generations, and release a stable, superior variety. The classic steps: collection of germplasm → hybridisation → selection → testing → release. Success stories: high-yielding wheat and rice of the Green Revolution, and fortified crops like iron-rich spinach varieties.

## 3. Classified tables

**Table 1 — Process steps**

| Step | What happens | Where | Key enzyme or number |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 2 — Key ideas and worked angles**

| Idea | Statement | Where used | Worked example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

**Table 3 — Summary and marks map**

| Sub-topic | One-line essence | NEB marks trend |
| --- | --- | --- |

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — the five steps of classical plant breeding (study in this order)**

| Step | Stage | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Germplasm collection | Gather all available wild relatives, landraces and improved varieties — the raw material |
| 2 | Hybridisation | Cross selected parents carrying complementary traits (emasculation + bagging for controlled pollination) |
| 3 | Selection | Over generations, keep only the progeny with the best combination of traits |
| 4 | Testing and evaluation | Grow candidates in multi-location field trials vs the best existing varieties |
| 5 | Release and distribution | Officially released variety; seed multiplied and sold to farmers |

**Breeding achievements — the classic examples**

# Single cell protein (SCP)

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Single cell protein (SCP)** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Single cell protein (SCP)

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

**Single cell protein** is edible protein from microbes — bacteria, yeast, fungi, algae — grown on cheap substrates (whey, molasses, straw, even petroleum wastes). The name is a marketing choice: 'microbial protein' sounded unappetising. SCP can supply protein without farmland: a 250-kg cow gains ~200 g of protein per day; the same mass of microbes can produce tonnes of protein in hours.

| 1 | The protein gap | Growing population vs limited cropland and pasture |
| 2 | Microbes' speed | Doubling in minutes-hours vs months for animals; huge biomass fast |
| 3 | Cheap substrates | Whey, molasses, waste starch, methanol — value added to waste |
| 4 | Product | Protein-rich biomass (60–80% protein dry weight) with vitamins and minerals |
| 5 | Uses | Human food supplements, animal feed (e.g. Spirulina, Quorn mycoprotein) |
| 6 | Limitations | Consumer acceptance, nucleic-acid content, quality control |

**SCP sources — microbe, substrate and product**

| Microbe | Type | Substrate | Product / use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Spirulina | Cyanobacterium (blue-green alga) | Open ponds, alkaline water | Health-food supplement; traditional food (Chad dihe) |
| Chlorella | Green alga | Sunlight + CO2 in ponds | Protein and vitamin supplement |
| Saccharomyces / Candida | Yeasts | Molasses, whey, petroleum fractions | Animal feed, baker's/brewer's yeast biomass |
| Fusarium venenatum | Filamentous fungus | Glucose syrup | Quorn mycoprotein — the commercial SCP success |
| Methylophilus | Methylotrophic bacterium | Methanol | High-protein feed; ~25 g protein per 100 g growth in hours |

# Animal husbandry — breeds and management

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Animal husbandry — breeds and management** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). ## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Animal husbandry — breeds and management

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

**Animal husbandry** is the scientific management of livestock — cattle, poultry, fish (pisciculture), bees (apiculture) — for food and products. Modern strategies: improved breeds by **cross-breeding** (e.g. the sunflower-in-chapter example of Karan Swiss cattle), better feed and housing, disease control, and managed fisheries and apiculture. The goal is more milk, eggs, meat and honey per animal with less loss to disease.

# Biofertilizers and sustainable agriculture

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Biofertilizers and sustainable agriculture** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Biofertilizers and sustainable agriculture

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

**Sustainable agriculture** meets today's food needs without destroying the resource base — soil, water and biodiversity. **Biofertilizers** are its nutrient corner-stone: living microbes that fix nitrogen, solubilise phosphorus or decompose organic matter, replacing part of the chemical fertiliser load. Combined with organic manure, crop rotation, IPM and water-wise irrigation, they keep the farm productive without mining the soil.

**Concept flow — the sustainable toolkit (study in this order)**

| Step | Component | What it replaces / saves |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Biofertilizers (Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Azolla, mycorrhiza) | Part of nitrogen and phosphorus fertiliser |
| 2 | Organic manure and compost | Chemical fertiliser; builds soil organic matter |
| 3 | Crop rotation and legume intercropping | Continuous monoculture; natural N input |
| 4 | Integrated Pest Management (IPM) | Calendar spraying — uses biocontrol, traps, resistant varieties first |
| 5 | Water-wise irrigation (drip, rainwater) | Flood irrigation — cuts water use dramatically |
| 6 | Why it matters | Chemical overuse degrades soil, pollutes water and costs money; sustainability keeps the farm farming for the next generation |

**Biofertilizers in the sustainable farm — who does what**

| Biofertilizer | Type | Contribution |
|---|---|---|
| Rhizobium | Symbiotic bacterium in legume nodules | Fixes atmospheric N for the crop; rotation leaves N for the next crop |
| Azotobacter / Azospirillum | Free-living bacteria in the rhizosphere | Fix N without a host; stimulate growth hormones |
| Azolla + Anabaena | Fern-cyanobacterium symbiosis in rice paddies | Green manure for rice — traditional and effective |
| Mycorrhiza (Glomus) | Root fungus | Vast hyphal surface: phosphorus and water uptake, disease resistance |
| Cyanobacteria (Nostoc, Anabaena) | Autotrophic fixers | Add N and organic matter to paddy soils |

## 5. Worked examples and applications
≥ 6 worked examples with solved steps, live examples and Nepal-context applications (biology-plan.md §3.1, block V) — written in the unit fill pass.

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example — the rice paddy that fertilises itself.** A farmer floods his paddy and lets *Azolla* fern cover the water surface. Inside every Azolla leaf lives *Anabaena*, a cyanobacterium that fixes atmospheric nitrogen. As the fern multiplies and then decomposes into the paddy, it releases that nitrogen to the rice — a green manure the farm grows itself. Farmers in Vietnam and China have used this for centuries; it is the neatest biofertilizer package nature offers.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Diazotisation: ArNH2 + NaNO2/HCl at 0–5 °C → ArN2+Cl− — keep it COLD; above 5 °C the diazonium salt decomposes.
Trick 2: Sandmeyer (Cu2Cl2/Cu2Br2/CuCN) replaces N2+ by Cl/Br/CN; warm water gives phenol; H3PO2 gives benzene — the N2 group is the best leaving group, hence the whole synthetic toolbox.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Structure ladder in one line each: primary = amino-acid sequence; secondary = H-bonded α-helix/β-sheet; tertiary = full 3-D fold (disulphide, ionic, H-bonds); quaternary = several subunits (haemoglobin: 4).
Trick 2: Zwitterion: at the isoelectric point the amino acid carries both NH3+ and COO− — explains high melting points and amphoteric behaviour.
Trick 3: Essential amino acids: cannot be synthesised by the body (valine, leucine, lysine...) — quote 3 names for the 1-marker.
Trick 4: Denaturation destroys secondary/tertiary structure (heat, acid, urea) but NOT the primary sequence — coagulation of egg white is the example.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Enzyme = globular protein biocatalyst; features in three lines: enormous rate enhancement, high specificity (lock and key / induced fit), work under mild conditions (T ~37 °C, near-neutral pH).
Trick 2: Classification by reaction: oxidoreductase, transferase, hydrolase, lyase, isomerase, ligase — quote the six names for the classification mark.

Trick 2: Types: steroids (cortisol, sex hormones), proteins/peptides (insulin, growth hormone), amines (adrenaline, thyroxine) — one example each.

data.title: Integrated Rate Equations
notes: **Indefinite integral:** ∫f(x)dx = F(x) + C where F'(x) = f(x). C is the constant of integration.
**Basic integrals:** ∫xⁿdx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)+C (n≠-1), ∫1/x dx = ln|x|+C, ∫eˣdx = eˣ+C, ∫sin x dx = -cos x+C.
**Integration by substitution:** ∫f(g(x))g'(x)dx = ∫f(u)du where u=g(x).
**Integration by parts:** ∫u dv = uv - ∫v du.
**Definite integral:** ∫[a to b] f(x)dx = F(b)-F(a) where F'=f (Fundamental Theorem of Calculus).
**Properties:** ∫[a to b] f(x)dx = -∫[b to a] f(x)dx, ∫[a to a] f(x)dx = 0, ∫[a to b] f(x)dx = ∫[a to c] + ∫[c to b].

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Zero order: [A] = [A]0 − kt, half-life t½ = [A]0/2k (depends on initial concentration); first order: ln[A]0/[A] = kt, t½ = 0.693/k (independent of concentration) — the half-life contrast is THE exam discriminator.
Trick 2: Identify order from data: successive half-lives equal → first order; doubling time with concentration halves → zero order.
Trick 3: First-order numericals: k = (2.303/t)·log(a/(a−x)) — substitute a, a−x, t directly; the 2.303 converts ln to log10.
Trick 4: Pseudo-first order: ester hydrolysis with excess water — water's concentration is constant, so the bimolecular reaction follows first-order kinetics.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: k = Ae^(−Ea/RT); log(k2/k1) = Ea(T2−T1)/(2.303R·T1T2) — the two-temperature form is the numerical workhorse; R = 8.314 J.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Classify by action — analgesics kill pain (aspirin, morphine: narcotic vs non-narcotic), antipyretics lower fever (paracetamol), tranquilizers treat mental stress (barbiturates, diazepam), antihistamines block H1 receptors (cetrizine), antibiotics kill microbes (penicillin, streptomycin).

Trick 4: Antibiotics do NOT work on viruses — the classic misconception question.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Soap making (saponification): fat + NaOH → glycerol + sodium stearate; soap = RCOO−Na+ with hydrophobic tail + hydrophilic head — draw the micelle.
Trick 2: Soap fails in hard water: Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ form insoluble scum (RCOO)2Ca — this single line is WHY detergents were invented.
Trick 3: Detergents = sodium alkyl benzene sulphonates (anionic); work in hard water but are non-biodegradable → water pollution — the merit/demerit pair.
Trick 4: Cleansing mechanism: hydrophobic tails embed in grease, heads face water; agitation lifts micelles away — describe the micelle for the mechanism mark.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Werner's postulates: two valencies — primary (ionisable, satisfied by anions) and secondary (coordination, satisfied by ligands); test with AgCl precipitation counts (one vs three Cl− outside the sphere).

Trick 2: Nomenclature order: ligands (alphabetical, di/tri/tetra) → metal → oxidation state in Roman numerals → anion last; anionic ligands end in −o (chlorido, cyanido); neutral ligands keep names (aqua, ammine).
Trick 3: VBT: inner-orbital (d²sp³, low spin) vs outer-orbital (sp³d², high spin) — count unpaired electrons to decide; [Fe(CN)6]³⁻ has 1 unpaired (low spin), [FeF6]³⁻ has 5 (high spin).
Trick 4: CFT: d orbitals split into t2g and eg by Δo; strong-field ligands (CN−, NH3) pair electrons; weak-field (F−, H2O) don't — spectrochemical series snippet earns the mark.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Chain of definitions: G = 1/R; κ = G·(l/A); Λm = κ·1000/M — each step multiplies by a cell constant or dilution factor; quote units: S m⁻¹ and S cm² mol⁻¹.

Trick 4: Λ°m of weak electrolyte = sum of Λ° of ion pairs, e.g. Λ°(CH3COOH) = Λ°(HCl) + Λ°(CH3COONa) − Λ°(NaCl) — the classic combination numerical.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Inductive effect: permanent polarisation through σ bonds, dies out by C3–C4 (−I: NO2, X, COOH; +I: alkyl) — 'through sigma, distance-limited' is the definition mark.
Trick 2: Resonance: delocalisation through π bonds/ lone pairs; stability order: resonance structures with full octets and least charge separation dominate.
Trick 3: Hyperconjugation: 'no-bond resonance' — α-C–H σ electrons delocalise into an adjacent p-orbital; more α-H → more stable alkene/carbocation (Saytzeff and Markovnikov both rest on this).
Trick 4: Carbocation stability: benzylic/allylic (resonance) > 3° (hyperconjugation + I) > 2° > 1° > methyl — the ordering question is a favourite.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Oxidising agents ladder: KMnO4 (cold dilute = mild; hot alkaline = strong), K2Cr2O7/H+ (1° alcohol → acid), O3 (cleaves C=C), Cu/573 K (1°→aldehyde, 2°→ketone).
Trick 2: Reducing agents: LiAlH4 (reduces everything incl. acids), NaBH4 (aldehydes/ketones only), H2/Ni (C=C, C≡C), Sn/HCl (NO2 → NH2) — one line each.

Trick 4: Addition: markovnikov for HX; hydration gives Markovnikov alcohol; hydroboration-oxidation is the anti-Markovnikov hydration route.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Henry's law one line: p = KH·x — gas solubility DECREASES with temperature, INCREASES with pressure; scuba diving and soda bottles are the standard applications.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Raoult for both components: p1 = x1 p1°, p2 = x2 p2°; total P = x1p1° + x2p2° — a straight line in x1; ideal solutions obey it exactly.
Trick 2: Positive deviation (P > ideal): A–B attraction weaker than A–A/B–B (ethanol+acetone); negative deviation: stronger (chloroform+acetone H-bond) — one example each is the standard answer.
Trick 3: Ideal-solution conditions: ΔHmix = 0, ΔVmix = 0, identical A–A, B–B and A–B interactions.
Trick 4: Azeotropes form at deviation maxima/minima where vapour and liquid have the same composition — cannot be separated by fractional distillation.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Colligative = depends on the NUMBER of solute particles, not their nature — say the definition first; then the four: Δp/p° = x2, ΔTb = Kb·m, ΔTf = Kf·m, π = CRT.

data.topicTitle: Essay writing — argumentative, descriptive, narrative, expository
notes: **What it is:** an essay argues, describes, narrates or explains a topic in organised paragraphs. The examiner marks STANCE + STRUCTURE + evidence, not length.

**Universal skeleton:** Introduction (hook + thesis) → Body paragraphs (ONE reason each: topic sentence → explanation → example) → optional counter-argument (acknowledge, then rebut) → Conclusion (restate thesis + consequence).

**Four types:** *Argumentative* (clear side, reasons, admit the other side), *Descriptive* (5 senses, spatial order, show-don't-tell), *Narrative* (one incident: setup → conflict → climax → reflection), *Expository* (explain causes/process in numbered factors, no opinion).
**Tense logic:** essays live in PRESENT for general truths; past only inside narrative examples; predictions use will/would.

data.title: Letter writing — formal and informal
notes: **What it is:** a letter to someone you do NOT know (editor, manager, office). Half the marks are the fixed BLOCK LAYOUT; the other half is polite business tone.

**Block order:** Sender's address → Date → Recipient's designation + address → Subject line → Salutation ('Dear Sir/Madam') → Body (3 short paragraphs: who you are + purpose / details / polite request) → Complimentary close → Signature + full name in capitals.
**The pairing rule that trips everyone:** 'Dear Sir/Madam' → end **Yours faithfully**; 'Dear Mr/Ms Sharma' (real name) → end **Yours sincerely**.
**Tone grammar:** no contractions (*do not*, *I am*); polite modals (*would*, *could*, *may*); passive voice for formality ('the matter is being investigated').

**Variants:** *Editor* (public issue + call for action), *Job application* (post + skills + 'Enclosure: CV'), *Complaint* (what, when, defect + remedy + deadline), *Inquiry/Order* (price/availability/terms).
Class 12 twist: expect combined tasks (application + CV, editor + solutions). Keep the SAME block layout; extend the body with a second developed paragraph rather than a new layout.
CV essentials (when asked): Name & contact → Career objective → Academic qualifications (table: exam, board, year, marks) → Skills → Experience → References. Noun phrases, no full sentences.

data.title: Email writing
notes: **What it is:** a letter sent digitally — block format plus To/Subject fields. The examiner mainly checks the SUBJECT line and whether tone matches the receiver.

**Structure:** To → Subject (short phrase, not a sentence) → Salutation matched to receiver ('Dear Principal,' vs 'Hi Anisha,') → 1–2 short paragraphs (purpose → details → courteous close) → Sign-off (formal: Yours faithfully + full name; informal: Best wishes + first name).
**Register decides grammar:** the same message shifts — 'could you please' vs 'can you', 'I require' vs 'I need'. Present perfect introduces news ('I have prepared…').
**Never write a lazy subject** ('Queries') — a precise subject is itself worth marks.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

data.title: Report writing and summarisation
notes: **What it is:** factual, third-person, past-tense reporting of an event (sports day, blood donation camp) — not a story, not an opinion.

**Structure:** Headline (short, factual) → Byline ('By a Staff Reporter') + dateline ('Kathmandu, 12 May:') → Lead paragraph answering WHO did WHAT, WHERE, WHEN, WHY in 2–3 sentences → Body in chronological order → a short quotation from the chief guest → closing outcome.
**Tense/voice grammar:** past simple for every event; passive voice is standard for ceremony facts ('trophies were distributed'); reported speech for quotes; third person only — never 'I'.
**Summarisation partner skill:** compress any passage into its core idea in your own words within the word limit — keep the author's viewpoint, drop examples and repetition.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

data.title: Note-making and summary
notes: **Summary:** read for gist → underline key ideas → draft (author's main idea first, then 2–4 key supports) → cut modifiers/examples to fit the word limit → verify meaning is unchanged and nothing is copied.

**Summary grammar:** four paraphrase moves — synonym swap (threat→danger), word-class change (pollute→pollution), voice change (active↔passive), sentence merge; report verbs frame it ('the passage argues…'). Never add your own opinion.

**Note-making:** TITLE in caps → numbered sub-headings (1, 2, 3 — noun phrases, one per paragraph) → compact key-phrase points (a, b, c) → abbreviations (&, →, e.g.) with an 'Abbreviations used' note.
**Note grammar:** nominalise verbs for headings ('agricultural expansion'); drop articles/auxiliaries in points; every point under 7 words.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

data.title: Story writing
notes: **What it is:** a COMPLETE narrative arc judged on plot — situation → problem → turning point → resolution → (often) a quiet moral.

**Structure:** Opening (if the prompt gives a first line, USE it verbatim and continue) → Complication → Rising action → Climax (the decisive moment — slow down here) → Resolution + realisation/moral.

**Tense machinery:** past simple drives the plot; past continuous paints background ('I was dawdling home'); past perfect marks earlier events ('which she had lost'); direct speech at the climax adds life.
**Keep ONE tense zone and ONE narrator** — drifting between present and past, or I/he, breaks the story.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

data.title: Speech and dialogue writing
notes: **What it is:** writing meant to be SPOKEN — short sentences, rhythm, direct address. The examiner checks 'speakability'.

**Structure:** Salutation in order of seniority ('Respected Chairperson, judges, teachers, and my dear friends —') → Self-intro (if required) → Hook (question/fact/quotation) → 2–3 clear points ('First… Second… Finally…') → Persuasive devices (triads, repetition, rhetorical questions) → Strong closing appeal + 'Thank you.'
**Grammar for the ear:** imperatives command action ('Let us pledge…'); rhetorical questions make the audience answer mentally; triads create rhythm.
**Test:** read your draft aloud — where you gasp, rewrite. Repeat your core phrase 2–3 times.
Dialogue pairing (Class 12 often bundles both): keep turns short and purposeful; use speaker names + colons; contractions, fillers and question tags for naturalness; resolve the exchange explicitly.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

data.title: Review writing — book and film
notes: **What it is:** a balanced critical evaluation — what the work is, what it does well, what falls short, and whether it is worth the reader's time.

**Structure:** Title + basic details (title, author/director, year, genre) → Brief SPOILER-FREE summary (2–3 sentences) → Strengths (one concrete example/quote) → Weaknesses (fair, with why it matters) → Recommendation + verdict/rating.

**Review grammar:** present simple dominates ('the story follows…'); evaluative adjectives (compelling, uneven, luminous); concessive fairness ('although the plot is thin, the philosophy is profound'); soft hedging ('readers may find…').
**Never spoil the ending** — restraint reads as mature judgement.
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

data.title: Comprehension and paraphrasing
notes: **What it is:** extracting and restating passage information — the trap is copying whole sentences; the skill is locate-then-restate.

**Method:** skim for gist → scan for the question's keywords (the answer lives nearby) → answer in complete sentences with synonyms → match the question type (WH → answer the WH; 'Why' → 'Because…'; true/false → quote evidence) → verify against the text.

**Grammar of answers:** convert passage nouns into clauses ('its existence' → 'that it exists'); use report frames ('the passage states that…'); keep the passage's tense zone; quote marks ONLY when demanded.
**Length discipline:** 1-mark answers = one sentence; 2-mark answers = answer + reason/evidence.

data.title: Grammar for writing — sentences, clauses, punctuation
data.topicTitle: Grammar for writing — sentences, clauses, punctuation
notes: **Sentence types as tools:** simple (one clause — POWER), compound (two main clauses via and/but/so or a semicolon — equal weight), complex (main + subordinate clause via because/although/when/if — shows the relation between ideas). Mix them: examiners reward rhythm.

**Clauses vs phrases:** a phrase has no subject-verb pair and cannot stand alone; a dependent clause has one but leans on the main clause ('Because it rained.' alone is a fragment). Relative clauses (who/which/that) add noun detail — commas only for extra information.

**Punctuation logic:** full stop ends a thought; comma separates list items, follows openers, precedes and/but/so between full sentences; semicolon joins balanced sentences; colon introduces; apostrophe = possession or contraction (its vs it's is the classic trap). Comma splice = two full sentences joined by only a comma — fix it.

**Tense + agreement discipline:** pick a tense zone per paragraph (essays: present; reports: past); subjects agree with verbs ('Each of the students WAS present'); a/an by SOUND ('an hour', 'a university').
**Full guide:** Full model answers, starting-line banks and exam tips: [/knowledge/writing](/knowledge/writing).

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Classifier — can you write g(y)dy = f(x)dx? → variable separable; M dx + N dy with M, N homogeneous of same degree → put y = vx; dy/dx + Py = Q → linear (integrating factor e^{∫P dx}).
Trick 2: Linear equation answer template: y·IF = ∫Q·IF dx + C — write it immediately after finding the IF.
Trick 3: For homogeneous equations, the substitution y = vx ALWAYS ends in a separable equation; back-substitute v = y/x at the end.
Trick 4: Initial conditions determine C — substitute the point BEFORE simplifying the general solution to avoid algebra errors.

data.topicTitle: Derivatives of Algebraic and Trig Functions
notes: **Derivative definition:** f'(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h)-f(x)]/h = lim(Δx→0) Δy/Δx.
**Geometric meaning:** f'(a) is the slope of the tangent line to y=f(x) at x=a.
**Basic derivatives:** d/dx(xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹, d/dx(sin x) = cos x, d/dx(cos x) = -sin x, d/dx(eˣ) = eˣ, d/dx(ln x) = 1/x.
**Product rule:** (fg)' = f'g + fg'.
**Quotient rule:** (f/g)' = (f'g - fg')/g².
**Chain rule:** d/dx[f(g(x))] = f'(g(x))·g'(x).
**Higher order derivatives:** f''(x) = d/dx[f'(x)], f'''(x) = d/dx[f''(x)], etc.
confusion: ❌ 'd/dx(sin x) = cos x means the slope of sin at x=0 is 0.' ✅ At x = 0, sin(0) = 0, but d/dx(sin 0) = cos 0 = 1 — the tangent is steep, not flat.
❌ 'The derivative of a product is the product of the derivatives.' ✅ No! (fg)' = f'g + fg'. The 'product rule' is NOT 'differentiate each and multiply.'

❌ 'If f(x) = sin²x, then f'(x) = cos²x.' ✅ f'(x) = 2 sin x cos x = sin 2x. You must apply the Chain Rule: derivative of the *outer* function (u² → 2u) times the derivative of the *inner* function (sin x → cos x).
❌ 'd/dx(eˣ) = x·eˣ⁻¹ (power rule).' ✅ No — the power rule is for xⁿ where n is constant. For eˣ (constant base, variable exponent), d/dx(eˣ) = eˣ.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Inverse-trig derivatives are the exam core: d(sin^-1 u) = u′/√(1−u²); d(tan^-1 u) = u′/(1+u²); d(sec^-1 u) = u′/(|u|√(u²−1)).
Trick 2: Logarithmic differentiation for f(x)^{g(x)}: take ln both sides, differentiate, multiply back — works for x^x, x^(sin x).
Trick 3: Simplify BEFORE differentiating: expand products, split fractions, apply log laws — half the algebra work disappears.
Trick 4: Chain-rule discipline: differentiate the outer function first, multiply by the derivative of the inner — write the layers explicitly for long composites.

data.title: Higher Order Derivatives
notes: **Derivative definition:** f'(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h)-f(x)]/h = lim(Δx→0) Δy/Δx.
**Geometric meaning:** f'(a) is the slope of the tangent line to y=f(x) at x=a.
**Basic derivatives:** d/dx(xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹, d/dx(sin x) = cos x, d/dx(cos x) = -sin x, d/dx(eˣ) = eˣ, d/dx(ln x) = 1/x.
**Product rule:** (fg)' = f'g + fg'.
**Quotient rule:** (f/g)' = (f'g - fg')/g².
**Chain rule:** d/dx[f(g(x))] = f'(g(x))·g'(x).
**Higher order derivatives:** f''(x) = d/dx[f'(x)], f'''(x) = d/dx[f''(x)], etc.
**Fact.** Derivative f'(x) = lim_{h→0} [f(x+h) − f(x)]/h = tangent slope; rules: sum, product, quotient, chain.
**Fact.** d/dx xⁿ = nx^{n−1}; d/dx sin x = cos x; d/dx e^x = e^x; d/dx ln x = 1/x.

data.title: Applications of Derivatives
notes: **Derivative definition:** f'(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h)-f(x)]/h = lim(Δx→0) Δy/Δx.
**Geometric meaning:** f'(a) is the slope of the tangent line to y=f(x) at x=a.
**Basic derivatives:** d/dx(xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹, d/dx(sin x) = cos x, d/dx(cos x) = -sin x, d/dx(eˣ) = eˣ, d/dx(ln x) = 1/x.
**Product rule:** (fg)' = f'g + fg'.
**Quotient rule:** (f/g)' = (f'g - fg')/g².
**Chain rule:** d/dx[f(g(x))] = f'(g(x))·g'(x).
**Higher order derivatives:** f''(x) = d/dx[f'(x)], f'''(x) = d/dx[f''(x)], etc.

notes: **Indefinite integral:** ∫f(x)dx = F(x) + C where F'(x) = f(x). C is the constant of integration.

**Integration by parts:** ∫u dv = uv - ∫v du.
**Definite integral:** ∫[a to b] f(x)dx = F(b)-F(a) where F'=f (Fundamental Theorem of Calculus).
**Properties:** ∫[a to b] f(x)dx = -∫[b to a] f(x)dx, ∫[a to a] f(x)dx = 0, ∫[a to b] f(x)dx = ∫[a to c] + ∫[c to b].

data.title: Integration of Trigonometric Functions
notes: **Indefinite integral:** ∫f(x)dx = F(x) + C where F'(x) = f(x). C is the constant of integration.
**Basic integrals:** ∫xⁿdx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)+C (n≠-1), ∫1/x dx = ln|x|+C, ∫eˣdx = eˣ+C, ∫sin x dx = -cos x+C.
**Integration by substitution:** ∫f(g(x))g'(x)dx = ∫f(u)du where u=g(x).
**Integration by parts:** ∫u dv = uv - ∫v du.
**Definite integral:** ∫[a to b] f(x)dx = F(b)-F(a) where F'=f (Fundamental Theorem of Calculus).
**Properties:** ∫[a to b] f(x)dx = -∫[b to a] f(x)dx, ∫[a to a] f(x)dx = 0, ∫[a to b] f(x)dx = ∫[a to c] + ∫[c to b].

data.title: Concept of Limit
notes: **Limit concept:** The limit of f(x) as x approaches a describes the value that f(x) approaches as x gets arbitrarily close to a (but not equal to a).
**Notation:** lim(x→a) f(x) = L means f(x) gets arbitrarily close to L as x approaches a.
**Direct substitution:** If f is continuous at a, then lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a).
**Indeterminate forms:** 0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞, ∞-∞, 0⁰, 1^∞, ∞⁰ require special techniques.
**Standard limits:** lim(x→0) sin(x)/x = 1, lim(x→0) (1-cos x)/x = 0, lim(x→0) (eˣ-1)/x = 1, lim(x→0) ln(1+x)/x = 1.
**Algebraic properties:** lim[f±g] = lim f ± lim g, lim[f·g] = lim f · lim g, lim[f/g] = lim f / lim g (denominator ≠ 0).
**Continuity connection:** f is continuous at a if lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a).
confusion: ❌ 'The limit of a function at a point is always its value at that point' ✅ The limit only concerns values *near* a, not *at* a; f(a) might not even be defined.
❌ 'If the limit doesn't exist, the function is undefined' ✅ A function can be well-defined at a point, but the limit might not exist (e.g., jump discontinuities or oscillations).
❌ 'Indeterminate form 0/0 means the result is 0 or undefined' ✅ 0/0 is a signal to apply algebraic manipulation or L'Hôpital's Rule to find the limit, which may be a finite number.

data.title: Indeterminate Forms
notes: **Indeterminate Forms:** Limits that cannot be directly evaluated (0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞, ∞-∞, 0⁰, 1^∞, ∞⁰).
**L'Hopital's Rule:** For 0/0 or ∞/∞ forms: lim f/g = lim f'/g' if limit of derivatives exists.
**0/0 form:** Requires factoring, rationalization, or L'Hopital's rule.
**∞/∞ form:** Same techniques apply; divide by highest power of variable.
**0·∞ form:** Convert to 0/0 or ∞/∞ by rewriting as fraction.
**∞-∞ form:** Combine fractions or factor to resolve.
**Exponential forms (0⁰, 1^∞, ∞⁰):** Use logarithms: y = f^g → ln y = g·ln f.
confusion: ❌ Applying L'Hopital's rule to 0/1 or 1/0 forms ✅ L'Hopital only applies to 0/0 or ∞/∞ indeterminate forms.
❌ Forgetting to check indeterminate form before using L'Hopital ✅ Direct substitution first; only use L'Hopital if result is 0/0 or ∞/∞.

data.title: Continuity of Functions
notes: **Continuity at a point:** f is continuous at x=a if: (1) f(a) exists, (2) lim(x→a) f(x) exists, (3) lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a).
**Continuous on an interval:** f is continuous on [a,b] if continuous at every point in (a,b), right-continuous at a, left-continuous at b.
**Polynomial functions:** Continuous everywhere on ℝ.
**Rational functions:** Continuous everywhere except where denominator = 0.
**Trigonometric functions:** sin x, cos x continuous everywhere; tan x continuous except at x = (2n+1)π/2.
**Exponential and logarithmic:** eˣ continuous everywhere; ln x continuous for x>0.
**Intermediate Value Theorem:** If f is continuous on [a,b] and k is between f(a) and f(b), then there exists c∈(a,b) such that f(c)=k.
confusion: ❌ Assuming all functions with a hole are continuous ✅ A function is discontinuous at a point if f(a) doesn't exist or doesn't equal the limit.
❌ Continuity means the graph has no breaks ✅ Also requires f(a) to equal the limit value; removable discontinuity exists.

data.title: Differentiability
notes: **Differentiability at a point:** f is differentiable at x=a if f'(a) exists, i.e., lim(h→0) [f(a+h)-f(a)]/h exists.
**Differentiable implies continuous:** If f is differentiable at a, then f is continuous at a.
**Continuous does not imply differentiable:** |x| is continuous at x=0 but not differentiable.
**Smooth functions:** Differentiable everywhere (e.g., polynomials, sin x, cos x, eˣ).
**Corner/cusp points:** Non-differentiable points where left derivative ≠ right derivative.
**Vertical tangent:** Point where derivative approaches infinity (not differentiable).
**Fact.** Indeterminate forms 0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞ → L'Hôpital: lim f/g = lim f'/g' (when applicable).
**Fact.** Standard limits: lim_{x→0} sin x / x = 1; lim_{x→0} (1 + x)^{1/x} = e; lim_{x→∞} (1 + a/x)^x = e^a.
**Fact.** Continuity: f continuous at c iff lim_{x→c}f(x) = f(c). Types of discontinuity: removable, jump, infinite.
confusion: ❌ Assuming continuous functions are always differentiable ✅ |x| at x=0 is continuous but has a corner (not differentiable).
❌ Differentiable implies the function is smooth ✅ Differentiable means derivative exists at that point; corners still exist elsewhere.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Protocol: convert constraints to lines → shade the feasible region (test with origin) → find corner points → evaluate Z at each → optimum. Corner-point evaluation IS the method mark.
Trick 2: Feasible-region test: substitute (0,0) into each inequality; if true, shade toward the origin, else away — do this aloud in working.
Trick 3: If the region is unbounded, Z may not attain an optimum — check with an open half-plane test before declaring max/min.
Trick 4: For 'minimum cost' problems the optimum is usually at the intersection of two binding constraints — solve the pair simultaneously to get the exact point.

data.title: Conditional Probability
notes: **Probability definition:** P(E) = n(E)/n(S) for classical probability, where n(E) = favorable outcomes, n(S) = total outcomes.
**Axiomatic definition:** P(E)≥0, P(S)=1, P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B) for disjoint events.
**Complement rule:** P(E') = 1 - P(E).
**Addition rule:** P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B)-P(A∩B).
**Conditional probability:** P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B), provided P(B)>0.
**Independent events:** A and B are independent if P(A∩B) = P(A)·P(B).
**Multiplication theorem:** P(A∩B) = P(A)·P(B|A) = P(B)·P(A|B).
**Bayes' theorem:** P(Aᵢ|B) = P(Aᵢ)·P(B|Aᵢ) / ΣP(Aⱼ)·P(B|Aⱼ).
**Fact.** P(E) = favourable/total. Additive law: P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B). If mutually exclusive, P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B).
**Fact.** Multiplicative: P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B|A); independence: P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B).
**Fact.** Complement: P(A') = 1 − P(A). For discrete: ΣP = 1; expected value E(X) = Σxᵢpᵢ.

confusion: ❌ 'Direction cosines are arbitrary' ✅ Direction cosines l, m, n are *fixed* values for a given vector: l = cos α, m = cos β, n = cos γ.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: All three angles are cos formulas on direction data — lines: cos θ = |b1·b2|/(|b1||b2|); planes: cos θ = |n1·n2|/(|n1||n2|); line-plane: sin θ = |b·n|/(|b||n|).
Trick 2: Perpendicular/parallel tests: lines ⊥ ⇔ b1·b2 = 0; planes ∥ ⇔ n1 = λn2; line ∥ plane ⇔ b·n = 0 — the dot-product zero is the fastest test.
Trick 3: For line-plane angle, remember it is SIN (the line's angle with the plane is the complement of its angle with the normal) — the classic trap.

data.title: Vector Quantities and Types
notes: **Vector:** A quantity having both magnitude and direction. Represented as arrow or bold letter: **a** or a⃗.
**Scalar:** A quantity with magnitude only (mass, temperature, time).
**Vector addition:** Triangle law: place tail of b at head of a; resultant closes triangle. Parallelogram law: diagonal from common tail.
**Scalar multiplication:** ka has magnitude |k|·|a|. Direction same as a if k>0, opposite if k<0.
**Dot product:** **a**·**b** = |a||b|cosθ = a₁b₁+a₂b₂+a₃b₃. Result is scalar.
**Cross product:** **a**×**b** = |a||b|sinθ · n̂. Result is vector perpendicular to both a and b.
**Unit vector:** â = **a**/|**a**|. Standard unit vectors: î, ĵ, k̂ along x,y,z axes.
**Direction cosines:** cosα=a₁/|a|, cosβ=a₂/|a|, cosγ=a₃/|a|, where α,β,γ are angles with axes.
confusion: ❌ 'Vector magnitude can be negative' ✅ Magnitude is defined as the absolute length, so it is always ≥ 0.
❌ 'Adding vectors is same as adding scalar magnitudes' ✅ Vector addition must account for direction using head-to-tail or component methods; only scalar magnitudes can be added algebraically.
❌ 'A vector with zero magnitude points in a specific direction' ✅ A zero vector (null vector) has undefined direction because it doesn't have a distinct displacement.

data.title: Addition and Subtraction
notes: **Vector:** A quantity having both magnitude and direction. Represented as arrow or bold letter: **a** or a⃗.
**Scalar:** A quantity with magnitude only (mass, temperature, time).
**Vector addition:** Triangle law: place tail of b at head of a; resultant closes triangle. Parallelogram law: diagonal from common tail.
**Scalar multiplication:** ka has magnitude |k|·|a|. Direction same as a if k>0, opposite if k<0.
**Dot product:** **a**·**b** = |a||b|cosθ = a₁b₁+a₂b₂+a₃b₃. Result is scalar.
**Cross product:** **a**×**b** = |a||b|sinθ · n̂. Result is vector perpendicular to both a and b.
**Unit vector:** â = **a**/|**a**|. Standard unit vectors: î, ĵ, k̂ along x,y,z axes.
**Direction cosines:** cosα=a₁/|a|, cosβ=a₂/|a|, cosγ=a₃/|a|, where α,β,γ are angles with axes.
confusion: ❌ 'Vector addition is simply adding components' ✅ While true for components, the *geometric* interpretation requires head-to-tail placement; you must not just add scalar magnitudes.
❌ 'Subtraction is same as addition' ✅ Subtraction is vector addition of the first vector and the negative (reversed direction) of the second vector: A - B = A + (-B).
❌ 'The resultant vector's direction is always the average of the two vectors' ✅ The resultant depends on the relative magnitudes and directions (angles between vectors); it is not a simple average.

notes: **Cross Product Applications:** This topic covers the fundamental concepts of cross product applications in the mathematics curriculum.
Understanding cross product applications is essential for solving problems and building higher-level mathematical skills.

confusion: ❌ 'Cross product results in a scalar' ✅ Cross product (vector product) *always* results in a vector, which is perpendicular to the plane of the two operand vectors.
❌ 'Cross product order doesn't matter' ✅ The cross product is *anti-commutative*: A × B = -(B × A). Swapping the order reverses the direction.
❌ 'Cross product of parallel vectors is max' ✅ The cross product of parallel vectors is *zero* (sin 0° = 0), because they enclose no area.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Scalar triple product [a b c] = a·(b×c) = determinant of the component rows — volume of the parallelepiped; zero ⇔ coplanar.
Trick 2: Vector triple product: a×(b×c) = b(a·c) − c(a·b) — the 'bac − cab' rule; it is NOT associative, so bracket order matters.

Trick 4: [a b c] changes sign on swapping two vectors; cyclic permutations preserve it — quote for sign questions.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Work as a dot product: W = F·d = Fd cos θ — zero work when force ⊥ displacement; quote the condition.
Trick 2: Torque as a cross product: τ = r × F, magnitude rF sin θ, direction by the right-hand rule — state both magnitude and direction for full marks.
Trick 3: Angular momentum L = r × p = r × mv; conservation when τ = 0 — the link line earns the concept mark.
Trick 4: Numericals are one substitution each — keep vectors in component form and use the 3×3 determinant for cross products.

data.topicTitle: AC voltage applied to resistor, inductor, and capacitor
notes: When a sinusoidal voltage is applied to a pure resistor, the current follows the voltage with no delay. The rms current is the rms voltage divided by R, and the average power is the heating I_rms squared times R.

A pure inductor opposes a changing current. Its reactance is X_L = 2πfL, so a higher frequency or a larger inductance means a smaller current. The voltage leads the current by a quarter of a cycle, and the average power is zero.

A pure capacitor opposes a change of voltage. Its reactance is X_C = 1/(2πfC), which is large at low frequency and small at high frequency. The current leads the voltage by a quarter cycle, and again the average power is zero.
The three elements are drawn as phasors. The resistor voltage lies along the current. The inductor voltage is drawn 90° ahead of the current. The capacitor voltage is drawn 90° behind the current.
Household meters read rms values. A peak of 10√2 volts has an rms value of 10 V. Mixing a peak voltage with an rms current gives a wrong power.
A real coil is an inductor with resistance in series. The pure cases on this page are the pieces used later to build the impedance of an LCR circuit.

data.title: AC through R, L, C
notes: **AC through R, L, C:** This topic covers the behavior of AC circuits containing Resistors (R), Inductors (L), and Capacitors (C).
Understanding the phase relationships between voltage and current in R, L, and C components is essential for analyzing complex AC circuits.
Key concepts include impedance, reactance, and the conditions for electrical resonance.
An alternating voltage can be written v = V_0 sin ωt. In a pure resistor the current is i = (V_0/R) sin ωt, so voltage and current reach their peaks together and the average power is I_rms^2 R.

In a pure inductor the current lags the voltage by 90°. The opposition is the inductive reactance X_L = ωL = 2πfL, and it grows with frequency. A pure inductor stores energy in its magnetic field and returns it, so the average power over a cycle is zero.

In a pure capacitor the current leads the voltage by 90°. The capacitive reactance is X_C = 1/(ωC), and it falls as the frequency rises. The average power over a cycle is again zero because energy is stored in the electric field and then returned.
confusion: ❌ 'In an AC circuit, the voltage and current are always in phase' ✅ In a pure resistor, they are in phase. In an inductor, voltage leads current by 90°. In a capacitor, voltage lags current by 90°.
❌ 'Impedance (Z) is the algebraic sum of resistance (R) and reactance (X)' ✅ Impedance is the vector sum: Z = √(R² + (X_L - X_C)²).
❌ 'Resonance occurs when resistance is maximum' ✅ Resonance occurs when inductive reactance equals capacitive reactance (X_L = X_C), which minimizes impedance in a series circuit.
Voltage does not lead the current in a resistor.
X_L rises with frequency. X_C falls.
A pure inductor does not consume average power.
Peak and rms differ by √2. Do not mix them in one formula.

data.title: LC Oscillations
notes: **LC Oscillations:** This topic covers the oscillatory exchange of energy between a capacitor (storing electric field energy) and an inductor (storing magnetic field energy).
In an ideal LC circuit, electrical oscillations occur at a natural frequency determined by the values of L and C.
This is an analogy to a mechanical simple harmonic oscillator (mass-spring system).

If a charged capacitor is connected to a pure inductor, the capacitor discharges through the coil, the current builds a magnetic field, and that field then pushes charge back onto the capacitor with the opposite sign.
The charge on the capacitor is of the form Q = Q_0 cos ωt when it starts from rest at maximum charge. The current is the derivative and is maximum when the charge is zero.
The angular frequency of this exchange is ω = 1/√(LC). The frequency in hertz is f = 1/(2π√(LC)). It does not depend on the starting charge.
confusion: ❌ Thinking LC circuits lose energy immediately without resistance ✅ An ideal LC circuit (zero resistance) oscillates indefinitely; only practical circuits lose energy due to resistance (damped oscillations).

❌ Current is maximum when charge on capacitor is maximum ✅ When charge on the capacitor is maximum, the potential energy is maximum and the current is zero. When the current is maximum, the magnetic energy is maximum and charge is zero (energy transfer).
❌ Misinterpreting the oscillation frequency ✅ The angular frequency is ω = 1/√(LC), and the frequency is f = 1 / (2π√(LC)).
The frequency does not depend on the initial charge.
Maximum current and maximum charge do not happen together.
Energy is not lost in the ideal LC circuit.
ω here is 1/√(LC), not √(LC).

data.title: LCR Series Circuit
notes: **LCR Series Circuit:** An AC circuit containing a resistor (R), inductor (L), and capacitor (C) connected in series.
The behavior is determined by the combination of resistance and reactance (inductive and capacitive).
It exhibits resonance when the net reactance is zero.
A series LCR circuit has one current through R, L and C. The resistor voltage is in phase with the current, the inductor voltage leads by 90°, and the capacitor voltage lags by 90°.

The two reactance voltages are opposite, so the net reactive voltage has size I|X_L − X_C|. With the resistor voltage IR, Pythagoras gives the supply voltage V = I Z, where Z = √(R^2 + (X_L − X_C)^2).
The phase angle satisfies tanφ = (X_L − X_C)/R. If X_L is larger, the current lags the supply voltage. If X_C is larger, the current leads.
At resonance X_L = X_C, Z falls to R, and the current is V/R, the largest series current for that supply. The frequency is f_0 = 1/(2π√(LC)), the same expression as the LC oscillation.
confusion: ❌ Believing resonance occurs at all frequencies ✅ Resonance occurs only at a specific frequency (f_r = 1 / (2π√LC)) where inductive reactance equals capacitive reactance (X_L = X_C).
❌ Misinterpreting phase angle as constant ✅ The phase angle φ (where tan φ = (X_L - X_C) / R) depends on the frequency of the AC source; it is zero at resonance.

❌ Assuming voltage across L and C is zero at resonance ✅ While the net voltage across the L-C combination is zero (because they are 180° out of phase), individual voltages across L and C can be non-zero and large.
Z is not R + X_L + X_C.
Resonance is not maximum resistance.
A lagging current means the circuit is inductive, not capacitive.
The large voltages on L and C are not added arithmetically to get the supply.

data.title: LCR series circuit and power factor
data.topicTitle: LCR series circuit and power factor
notes: The average power in a series LCR circuit is V_rms I_rms cosφ, not the product of the rms voltage and current alone. The extra factor cosφ is the power factor.
From the impedance triangle, cosφ = R/Z. A circuit that is almost a pure resistor has Z near R and a power factor near 1. A circuit dominated by reactance has a small power factor.

At resonance X_L = X_C, φ = 0 and the power factor is 1. All of the average power is then the heating I_rms^2 R in the resistor. The inductor and capacitor still exchange energy, but their average contribution is zero.
A power factor of zero means the current is 90° out of phase with the voltage, as in a pure inductor or a pure capacitor. Energy sloshes back to the source.
A lagging power factor is the inductive case, common with motors. Capacitors are added in industry to pull the power factor back toward 1 so that the current, for a given useful power, is smaller.
The instantaneous power oscillates. The average is what the meter records. Quoting V I without cosφ overstates the power whenever the phase is not zero.

data.title: Transformer
notes: **Transformer:** An electrical device based on mutual induction that changes the voltage level of an AC supply.
It works on the principle of electromagnetic induction: a varying current in the primary coil induces an EMF in the secondary coil via a common magnetic core.
Transformers can be step-up (increase voltage) or step-down (decrease voltage).

A transformer has two coils on an iron core. An alternating current in the primary changes the flux, and that changing flux induces an emf in the secondary. A steady direct current does not keep inducing a secondary emf.
If leakage is ignored, the voltage ratio equals the turns ratio: V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p. More turns on the secondary means a step-up of voltage. Fewer turns means a step-down.
An ideal transformer wastes no power, so V_p I_p = V_s I_s. A step-up of voltage is a step-down of current. Energy is not created.
The core is laminated so that eddy currents have short paths and less heating. A solid iron core would waste power as heat.
confusion: ❌ Assuming transformer works on DC ✅ Transformer only operates on AC as it requires a *changing* magnetic flux to induce EMF (DC has constant flux).

❌ Thinking voltage ratio is independent of current ratio ✅ According to the law of conservation of energy (P_in = P_out for an ideal transformer), voltage and current are inversely proportional: V_p/V_s = I_s/I_p.
❌ Forgetting eddy currents exist in the core ✅ Eddy currents are circular induced currents in the core that cause energy loss as heat; they are minimized by using laminated iron cores.
A transformer does not change DC.
Step-up voltage does not step up current.
The turns ratio is not the current ratio. The current ratio is inverted.
Laminations are about eddy currents, not about the turns ratio.

data.title: Elements of Communication
notes: A communication system moves a message from one place to another. The information source produces the message, which may be speech, music or data.
The transmitter converts that message into a signal that can travel. For radio this includes modulation, placing the message onto a high-frequency carrier so that the antenna can be a practical size.
The channel is the path: a wire, an optical fibre, or free space. Noise, which is unwanted electrical energy, is added along the channel and is not part of the message.
The receiver undoes the transmitter's work. It amplifies the weak signal and demodulates it, recovering a copy of the original message for the listener or the display.
Attenuation is the weakening of the signal with distance. Amplifiers along a long channel restore the level, but they cannot perfectly remove noise that was added earlier.
Bandwidth is the range of frequencies the message or the channel occupies. A wider message, such as video, needs a wider channel than speech.

data.title: Elements of a communication system
notes: The elements can be named as transducer, modulator and transmitter, medium, and receiver plus output transducer. This is the same chain as source, transmitter, channel and receiver, with the transducers made explicit.
A microphone is an input transducer: sound pressure becomes a voltage. A loudspeaker is an output transducer: the recovered voltage becomes sound again.
The message signal is often low frequency. Multiplying it with a carrier, or varying the carrier's amplitude or frequency, produces the modulated wave that the antenna launches.

The medium decides the loss. A copper pair, a fibre and a radio path have different attenuation and different noise. The link budget is the comparison of transmitted power with the power the receiver needs.
At the receiver a tuner selects the carrier, a demodulator strips it, and an amplifier raises the message to a useful level. Selecting the wrong carrier selects a different message.
Two-way radio uses the same elements in both directions. Each station is sometimes the source and sometimes the destination.

data.title: Modulation
notes: A speech or music signal changes too slowly to be radiated from a practical antenna. Modulation copies that message onto a high-frequency carrier so the antenna can be a reasonable length.

In amplitude modulation the carrier frequency stays constant and the amplitude rises and falls with the message. A louder message makes a deeper variation, up to the point where the envelope would cross zero.
The modulated wave contains the carrier and two sidebands, one at f_c + f_m and one at f_c − f_m. If the highest message frequency is f_m, the bandwidth occupied is 2 f_m.
Frequency modulation keeps the amplitude constant and shifts the carrier frequency with the message. It uses a wider band than AM and is less bothered by amplitude noise.
The modulation index in AM is the fractional change in amplitude. An index above 1 means overmodulation: the envelope no longer matches the message and the receiver distorts it.
Demodulation at the receiver strips the carrier and returns the message. A diode detector followed by a filter is the simple AM method taught with this page.

data.title: Bandwidth and propagation of electromagnetic waves
data.topicTitle: Bandwidth and propagation of electromagnetic waves
notes: Bandwidth is the range of frequencies a signal or a channel occupies. A wider message, such as television, needs a wider channel than speech. Two stations must be separated by at least their bandwidths or they overlap.

A ground wave travels along the surface of the Earth. The ground absorbs more energy at higher frequency, so ground-wave broadcast is used for the lower radio frequencies and does not reach around the world.

A sky wave is sent upward and can be returned by the ionosphere. That is how short-wave radio crosses long distances. The ionosphere is not a metal mirror at every frequency: above a critical frequency the wave passes through.
A space wave travels in a straight line from a high transmitting antenna to the receiver. Television and FM use it. The Earth's curve limits the range to a little beyond the geometric horizon.
For an antenna at height h above a spherical Earth of radius R, the horizon distance is about √(2 R h) when h is much smaller than R. A higher mast sees farther.
The same information can be sent in a narrow band by slowing it down, or in a wide band by sending it quickly. The channel must be at least as wide as the signal.

data.title: Electric Current and Drift Velocity
notes: Electric current is the rate at which charge passes a point. One ampere is one coulomb per second. In a metal the moving charges are electrons, but the conventional current is drawn in the direction positive charge would move.

Free electrons move fast in random directions. An electric field adds a small average velocity along the wire, the drift velocity. The random speed is kilometres per second. The drift speed is often a fraction of a millimetre per second.
If n electrons per unit volume, each of charge e, drift at v_d through area A, the current is I = n e A v_d. A larger density, a wider wire or a faster drift means a larger current.
The drift speed is e E τ / m, where τ is the average time between collisions. A stronger field or a longer free time means a faster drift. Collisions turn the ordered drift energy into heat.

The signal travels along the wire at a speed set by the electromagnetic field, close to the speed of light. That is not the drift speed of the electrons. A lamp comes on at once even though each electron drifts slowly.
Current density J is I/A, and J = n e v_d. Resistivity connects J to the field by E = ρ J in an ohmic metal.
confusion: ❌ 'Electrons move at the speed of light in a wire.' ✅ Electrons move at a very slow *drift velocity* (mm/s); the *electric field* (the signal) travels near the speed of light.

❌ 'Electric current is the flow of electrons only.' ✅ By convention, current is defined as the *flow of positive charge*. In many cases (like electrolytes), negative charges also flow, but current is still in the opposite direction of electron flow.

❌ 'Drift velocity is the average velocity of all electrons at all times.' ✅ It is the *net average velocity* of the electrons due to an applied electric field, superimposed on their random thermal motion.
❌ skip the key fact → ✅ ohm's law: v = ir; r = ρl/a (resistivity ρ depends on material)..

data.title: Ohm's law and its limitations
notes: Ohm's law says that the current in a metallic conductor is proportional to the potential difference across it, if the temperature and the physical state stay constant. The constant ratio V/I is the resistance.
Plotted with current vertical and voltage horizontal, an ohmic resistor is a straight line through the origin. The slope is 1/R. A steeper line is a smaller resistance.
The law is a limited description. A filament lamp heats as the current rises, its resistance increases, and the graph bends. You cannot take one R from a cold measurement and use it at white heat.
A semiconductor diode is non-ohmic in a stronger way. It conducts easily in forward bias and almost not at all in reverse bias. No single R describes it.
A thermistor and an electrolyte can also leave the straight line. Quoting V = I R for them without a stated temperature and a stated operating point is not justified.

Inside the range where the metal stays ohmic, the law is still the working tool for series and parallel circuits. The limitation is the range, not a reason to abandon the law for a carbon resistor at a steady temperature.

data.title: Ohm's Law
notes: Ohm's law says that the current through a metallic conductor is proportional to the potential difference across it, provided the temperature and other physical conditions stay constant. The constant of proportionality is 1/R.
The working form is V = IR. R is the resistance. A steeper I–V line means a smaller resistance if I is plotted vertically, because the slope is 1/R.

The law is empirical for ohmic materials. A filament lamp's resistance rises as it heats, so its I–V graph curves. A semiconductor diode conducts very differently in the two directions and is non-ohmic.
Resistivity ρ is the material property in R = ρL/A. Ohm's law can hold while R still changes if the piece is stretched, because L and A change.
The ohm is the resistance that passes 1 A when 1 V is applied. Power in a resistor is I^2 R, or V^2/R, or V I, and that power becomes heat.
A circuit calculation uses Ohm's law on each ohmic element after the currents have been chosen. It is not a law of the battery's internal chemistry.
confusion: ❌ 'Ohm's Law applies to all conductors.' ✅ It is valid only for *ohmic conductors* (where V is proportional to I, like metallic resistors), not for non-ohmic devices like diodes or transistors.
❌ 'Ohm's Law defines Resistance (R=V/I).' ✅ Resistance is a *property* of the conductor (geometry/material); Ohm's law states that *for some materials*, R remains constant regardless of V or I.
❌ 'V is always proportional to I.' ✅ This holds true only when *temperature and other physical conditions* are kept constant.
Ohm's law is not true for every device.
The temperature condition is part of the statement.
Slope of I against V is 1/R, not R, in that plotting choice.
Resistivity and resistance are different.

data.title: Resistance and resistivity — temperature dependence
notes: Resistance is R = ρ L / A. A longer wire has more resistance. A thicker wire has less. Resistivity ρ is the material property, independent of the particular length and area.
The unit of resistivity is the ohm metre. A good conductor has a small resistivity. Glass and rubber have very large resistivities and are used as insulators.

For a metal over a moderate range, ρ = ρ_0 (1 + α ΔT), where α is the temperature coefficient. α is positive for metals, so heating raises the resistivity. More violent lattice vibrations scatter the electrons more often.
The same linear form is used for resistance if the size does not change: R = R_0 (1 + α ΔT). A copper winding in a hot motor has a higher resistance than the cold value on the label.

A semiconductor has a negative temperature coefficient. Heating frees more carriers, and the resistivity falls. That is why a thermistor can be used as a thermometer and why a semiconductor is not described by the metal formula with a positive α.

Alloys such as manganin are made so that α is nearly zero. They are used for standard resistors. Superconductors drop to zero resistance below a critical temperature, which is outside this linear formula.
