subtopics.name: Micromolecules vs macromolecules
points: Micromolecules: small, low molecular weight, soluble — sugars, amino acids, nucleotides, minerals, water
Macromolecules: large, high molecular weight — polysaccharides, proteins, nucleic acids
Acid-insoluble pool (macromolecules) vs acid-soluble pool (micromolecules) is the classical operational split

subtopics.name: Elemental composition
points: C, H, O, N are the dominant elements of life; S and P are next
Carbon is tetravalent and forms stable chains and rings — the backbone of organic chemistry
Water is the most abundant molecule in any cell (60-90% of fresh mass)

subtopics.name: Enzyme fundamentals
points: Almost all enzymes are proteins; ribozymes are catalytic RNA exceptions
They lower activation energy without changing the equilibrium position
Specificity comes from active site complementarity to the substrate

subtopics.name: Factors affecting enzyme activity
points: Temperature: rate rises to an optimum then falls sharply as denaturation begins
pH: each enzyme has an optimum; extremes denature
Substrate concentration saturates at Vmax; inhibitors (competitive, non-competitive) change Km or Vmax differently

subtopics.name: Coenzymes and cofactors
points: Cofactors are non-protein helpers: metal ions (Mg2+, Zn2+, Fe2+) or organic coenzymes
NAD, FAD and coenzyme A are organic coenzymes derived from vitamins
Apoenzyme + cofactor = holoenzyme (the active form)

subtopics.name: Beyond the lock-and-key
points: Induced fit: the active site reshapes on binding, explaining broad substrate tolerance
Allosteric regulation lets a distant site control activity — the basis of metabolic feedback
Enzyme cascades amplify signals (blood clotting, complement, hormone action)

subtopics.name: Water as a biomolecule
points: High specific heat stabilises body temperature; high latent heat of vaporisation powers cooling
Cohesion and adhesion drive transpiration pull in xylem
Water is the medium for every biochemical reaction and a reactant in hydrolysis

data.title: Cell: Introduction of cell, concepts of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells
data.topicTitle: Cell: Introduction of cell, concepts of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Why Start Biology With the Cell?

Everything you study after this topic — tissues, organs, digestion, heredity, evolution — is built on one organising idea: **the cell is the smallest unit of life**. Nothing smaller than a cell is alive; everything alive is made of one or more cells.

- **Why it matters:** every biomolecule you studied in Topic 1 exists *inside* cells, organised into compartments (organelles) that separate reactions and make complex life possible.
- **Where it leads:** Topic 3 dissects the eukaryotic cell organelle-by-organelle; Topic 4 explains how cells reproduce. Prokaryote vs eukaryote is the single most-asked comparison in this unit's NEB papers.
- **Historical thread:** cells were invisible until instruments made them visible — the story of cell discovery is the story of the microscope.

## 2. Fundamental Conceptual Understanding — What a Cell Actually Is

### 2.1 Definition and the essential idea

A **cell** is the smallest, basic **structural, functional and biological unit** of all living organisms — a mass of cytoplasm bound by a membrane, containing genetic material and capable of independent existence and reproduction. Two words carry the whole concept:

- **Structural unit** — every organism is *built* of cells (bricks of a building).
- **Functional unit** — every property of life (metabolism, growth, response, reproduction) happens *inside* cells, not between them.

An organism can be **unicellular** (the single cell does every job — Amoeba, Chlamydomonas, bacteria) or **multicellular** (cells specialise and divide the labour — muscle cell, nerve cell, guard cell). Specialisation is possible only because all cells carry the same complete genome.

### 2.2 The history of cell discovery — who saw what, and when

| Year | Scientist | Discovery | Significance |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1665 | **Robert Hooke** (England) | Saw dead cork cells with his crude microscope; named them "cells" (little rooms) | First description of cells — but only the empty cell *walls* |
| 1674 | **Anton van Leeuwenhoek** (Holland) | First to see **living** cells — bacteria, protozoa, sperm ("animalcules") | First observation of living cells |
| 1831 | **Robert Brown** (Scotland) | Discovered the **nucleus** in orchid cells | Identified the control centre |
| 1838–39 | **Schleiden & Schwann** (Germany) | Cell theory for plants (Schleiden) and animals (Schwann) | Cells as the universal unit of life |
| 1855 | **Rudolf Virchow** | *Omnis cellula e cellula* — all cells arise from pre-existing cells | Completed cell theory; killed spontaneous generation |
| 1931–present | Electron microscopy | Ultrastructure — organelles, membranes, ribosomes revealed | Modern cell biology |

**Conceptual point:** Hooke saw cell *walls* of dead cork; Leeuwenhoek saw living contents. The cell *theory* came two centuries later because theory needed better microscopes and comparative study.

### 2.3 Cell theory — statement and exceptions

**Cell theory (Schleiden 1838, Schwann 1839, Virchow 1855):**

1. All living organisms are composed of one or more cells.
2. The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.
3. All cells arise from pre-existing cells by division.

**Modern additions:** hereditary information passes from cell to cell (DNA); all cells are fundamentally alike in chemistry; energy flow occurs within cells.

**Exceptions / limitations (asked in NEB 2024):**

| Exception | Why it is an exception |
|---|---|
| Viruses | Acellular — no cell membrane, no cytoplasm, no metabolism of their own; alive only inside a host |
| Viroids and prions | Even simpler — naked RNA (viroids) or only protein (prions) |
| Coenocytes / syncytia | Some "cells" are multinucleate masses (fungal hyphae, muscle fibres) — one body, many nuclei |
| Mitochondria and chloroplasts | Contain their own DNA and ribosomes and arise only by division of pre-existing organelles (endosymbiotic origin) |

### 2.4 Cell size, shape and number — why cells are small

Cells vary enormously in size and shape, always matched to function:

| Cell | Size | Why this size/shape |
|---|---|---|
| Mycoplasma (PPLO) | ~0.1–0.3 µm | Smallest known cell |
| Human red blood cell | ~7–8 µm | Small + biconcave = maximum O₂ diffusion surface |
| Amoeba | ~1 mm | Irregular — pseudopodia for movement |
| Ostrich egg | ~15–18 cm | Largest single cell (yolk = stored food) |
| Nerve cell | up to ~1 m long | Long processes carry impulses across the body |

**Why are cells so small? (surface-area-to-volume reasoning — a favourite conceptual question):** as a cell grows, its **volume grows faster than its surface area** (volume ∝ length³, surface ∝ length²). A large cell could not absorb nutrients or expel wastes fast enough through its membrane for its interior. Small size keeps every part of the cytoplasm close to the surface and keeps diffusion fast. Large organisms solve the problem by having **many small cells**, not few big ones.

### 2.5 Basic components every cell shares

Whatever its type, every living cell has:

1. **Cell membrane** — the selective boundary (plasma lemma).
2. **Cytoplasm** — aqueous colloidal medium (cytosol + organelles) where metabolism happens.
3. **Genetic material** — DNA organised as nucleoid (prokaryote) or nucleus (eukaryote).
4. **Ribosomes** — protein synthesis machinery (universal: 70S in prokaryotes, 80S in eukaryote cytoplasm).

Everything else — cell wall, plastids, mitochondria, ER, Golgi — differs between groups, and those differences are exactly what the next sections classify.

## 3. Prokaryotic Cells — Life Before Organelles

### 3.1 Definition and who the prokaryotes are

**Prokaryotes** (Greek *pro* = primitive, *karyon* = nucleus) are cells that **lack a true nucleus and any membrane-bound organelles**. Their genetic material lies naked in the cytoplasm in a region called the **nucleoid**. Domain Bacteria (and Archaea) — bacteria, cyanobacteria (blue-green algae), mycoplasma — are all prokaryotes. They appeared ~3.5 billion years ago, the earliest forms of life.

### 3.2 Structure of a prokaryotic (bacterial) cell — component by component

| Structure | Nature | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Cell wall | Rigid, of **peptidoglycan** (murin) — NOT cellulose | Shape, protection, prevents bursting in hypotonic media |
| Plasma membrane | Lipoprotein bilayer with **mesosomes** (infoldings) | Permeability; mesosomes aid respiration and cell division |
| Nucleoid | Single circular **DNA, naked** (no histones, no nuclear envelope) | Heredity; replication by binary fission |
| Plasmids | Small circular extra DNA | Extra genes (antibiotic resistance); used in genetic engineering |
| **70S ribosomes** | Free in cytoplasm (70S = 50S + 30S subunits) | Protein synthesis |
| Gas vacuoles / inclusion bodies | Storage granules (glycogen, PHB), gas vesicles | Storage; buoyancy in aquatic bacteria |
| Flagella | Protein (flagellin) filaments, no 9+2 arrangement | Locomotion |
| Pili and fimbriae | Surface protein filaments | Attachment; conjugation (gene transfer) |
| Photosynthetic membranes (cyanobacteria) | Thylakoid-like lamellae, **no chloroplast** | Photosynthesis with chlorophyll *a* |

**Key conceptual idea:** prokaryotes achieve *compartmentalisation by invagination and inclusion*, not by membrane-bound organelles. Respiration happens on mesosomes/plasma membrane; photosynthesis on internal lamellae — the same chemistry as eukaryotes, at the membrane surface instead of inside organelles.

### 3.3 Prokaryotic special features (exam list)

- **No true nucleus** — no nuclear envelope, no nucleolus.
- **No membrane-bound organelles** — no mitochondria, ER, Golgi, lysosomes, plastids.
- **70S ribosomes** (eukaryote cytoplasm has 80S) — this difference is why many antibiotics (streptomycin, tetracycline) attack bacterial ribosomes but not ours.
- **Circular naked DNA** + plasmids.
- **Peptidoglycan cell wall** (mycoplasma lacks even the wall — smallest cells).
- **Binary fission** — no mitosis/meiosis, no spindle.
- **Coupled transcription–translation:** mRNA is translated while still being transcribed — possible only because there is no nuclear envelope separating the two.

**Prokaryote essentials — classified**

| Feature | Detail | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Nucleus | Naked circular DNA in a nucleoid region | No nuclear envelope; transcription and translation simultaneous |
| Ribosomes | 70S type | Target of several antibiotics that spare eukaryotic 80S |
| Cell wall | Peptidoglycan (murein) | Lysozyme and penicillin attack this wall |
| Organelles | No membrane-bound organelles | Respiration across the plasma membrane, not mitochondria |
| Size | 1–10 µm typically | High surface-to-volume ratio — fast exchange |
| Reproduction | Binary fission | Exponential growth; no mitosis apparatus |

## 4. Eukaryotic Cells — The Compartmentalised Cell

### 4.1 Definition and who the eukaryotes are

**Eukaryotes** (Greek *eu* = true) have a **true nucleus** — DNA enclosed in a double nuclear envelope with a nucleolus — plus **membrane-bound organelles** (mitochondria, ER, Golgi, lysosomes, plastids). Protists, fungi, plants and animals are eukaryotes; they appeared ~1.5–2 billion years ago.

### 4.2 The compartmentalisation principle (the deep idea of this topic)

Eukaryotic life is organised around **division of labour inside the cell**:

- Membrane-bound compartments allow **incompatible chemistries to coexist** — lysosomes digest at pH ~5 while the cytosol works at pH ~7.2.
- The **nuclear envelope** separates transcription from translation, enabling RNA processing and complex gene regulation.
- **Endomembrane system** (ER → Golgi → vesicles → membrane) manufactures and ships proteins.
- **Endosymbiotic theory:** mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living prokaryotes engulfed by a host cell — evidence: their own circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, double membranes and fission-style division. This theory is the conceptual bridge between the two cell types.

### 4.3 Plant cell vs animal cell — the second guaranteed comparison

| Basis | Plant cell | Animal cell |
|---|---|---|
| Cell wall | Present — cellulose (outside the membrane) | Absent |
| Plastids | Present (chloroplasts, chromoplasts, leucoplasts) | Absent |
| Central vacuole | Large, permanent, tonoplast-bound (up to 90% of volume) | Small, temporary vesicles |
| Centrosome / centrioles | Absent (higher plants) | Present, forms spindle |
| Mitochondria | Fewer, less active | Numerous, very active |
| Lysosomes | Rare (vacuole does the digesting) | Numerous |
| Glyoxysomes | Common (fat metabolism in seeds) | Absent |
| Reserve carbohydrate | Starch | Glycogen |
| Shape | Fixed, often angular (wall) | Flexible, irregular |
| Plasmodesmata | Present (intercellular connections) | Absent (gap junctions instead) |

## 5. Master Comparison — Prokaryotic vs Eukaryotic Cell (the NEB classic)

| Basis | Prokaryotic cell | Eukaryotic cell |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | Cell without a true nucleus; DNA naked in the nucleoid | Cell with a true nucleus enclosed by a nuclear envelope |
| Size | Small — 0.1–5 µm | Large — 10–100 µm |
| Organisms | Bacteria, cyanobacteria, mycoplasma, archaea | Protists, fungi, plants, animals |
| Nuclear envelope | Absent | Present (double membrane with pores) |
| Nucleolus | Absent | Present |
| Genetic material | Single circular DNA, **naked (no histones)** | Linear chromosomes, DNA + **histone proteins** |
| Number of chromosomes | One (plus plasmids) | Two or more (diploid sets) |
| Membrane-bound organelles | **Absent** | Mitochondria, ER, Golgi, lysosomes, plastids |
| Ribosomes | **70S** (50S + 30S) | **80S** (60S + 40S) in cytoplasm; 70S inside organelles |
| Cell wall | Peptidoglycan (bacteria); absent in mycoplasma | Cellulose (plants), chitin (fungi); absent in animals |
| Mesosomes | Present (some) | Absent |
| Respiration site | Plasma membrane / mesosomes | Mitochondria (+ cytosol for glycolysis) |
| Photosynthesis site | Internal thylakoid lamellae, no chloroplast | Chloroplasts |
| Cell division | **Binary fission** (no spindle, no mitosis) | **Mitosis / meiosis** with spindle |
| Transcription–translation | Coupled (same compartment) | Separated (nucleus vs cytoplasm) |
| Cytoskeleton | Primitive (no tubulin/actin system) | Well-developed (microtubules, microfilaments) |
| Examples | *E. coli*, *Anabaena*, *Mycoplasma* | *Amoeba*, mango leaf cell, human liver cell |

**Memory hooks:** "Pro = primitive (no nucleus, no organelles, 70S, binary fission)"; "Eu = true (envelope, organelles, 80S, mitosis)".

### 5.1 Similarities (never forget the shared core)

Both have: plasma membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes (protein synthesis), DNA as genetic material, and the same genetic code — which is why genetic engineering can make bacteria express human genes.

## 6. Conceptual Relationships

- **Topic 1 → here:** all the biomolecules are now seen *in place* — phospholipids build the membrane, DNA sits in the nucleoid/nucleus, enzymes float in the cytosol.
- **Here → Topic 3:** the eukaryotic organelles mentioned by name here (mitochondria, plastids, ER, Golgi, lysosomes, ribosomes, nucleus) are dissected in detail next.
- **Here → Topic 4:** prokaryotes divide by binary fission; eukaryotes by the cell cycle, mitosis and meiosis.
- **Endosymbiosis → evolution (Unit 7):** the prokaryote→eukaryote transition is the deepest example of cooperation in evolution.
- **Antibiotics:** the 70S vs 80S ribosome difference is the molecular reason selective toxicity is possible — a direct health application.
- **Viruses (Unit 3):** viruses are not cells at all — they expose the boundary of cell theory.

**Deep dive — why compartmentalisation changed everything.** A eukaryote can run incompatible chemistries at once: lysosomes digest at pH ~5 while the cytosol stays near pH 7; the mitochondrion keeps its own proton gradient. A prokaryote must keep all reactions in one compartment, which caps its complexity. That single architectural difference — membranes inside membranes — is why eukaryotes could grow large, specialise into tissues, and ultimately build multicellular life.

### 7.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

| Year | Unit | Topic | Question | Marks | Type |

| 2077/2021 | Biomolecules & Cell Biology | Cell | Differentiate between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells (any three points). | 3 | Difference |

### 7.2 Model answers

**Q1 (3m) — Differentiate prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells (any three points).**
Answer as a table:

| Basis | Prokaryotic cell | Eukaryotic cell |
|---|---|---|
| Nucleus | No true nucleus; naked circular DNA in the nucleoid | True nucleus; DNA + histones inside a nuclear envelope |
| Organelles | No membrane-bound organelles; 70S ribosomes | Membrane-bound organelles (mitochondria, ER, Golgi); 80S ribosomes |
| Cell division | Binary fission | Mitosis and meiosis with spindle |

*(Any three clear bases with both sides stated = full marks.)*

**Q2 (3m) — Cell theory, proposers, exceptions.**
Answer: **Schleiden (1838) and Schwann (1839)** proposed that all organisms are made of cells, the cell being the structural and functional unit of life; **Virchow (1855)** added that all cells arise from pre-existing cells (*omnis cellula e cellula*). **Exceptions:** viruses (acellular, no metabolism), viroids/prions, multinucleate coenocytes/syncytia, and mitochondria/chloroplasts (own DNA, arise by fission).

**Q3 (2m) — Why is the mitochondrion the powerhouse of the cell?**
Answer: Because it is the site of **aerobic respiration** — the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation on its cristae generate most of the cell's **ATP** (the energy currency), which powers all cellular work. Cells with high energy demand (muscle, liver) have many mitochondria.

### 7.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Saying prokaryotes have "no nucleus" without adding **no nuclear envelope / nucleoid** — the precise statement scores.
2. Confusing 70S/80S ribosomes or writing "prokaryotes have no ribosomes" (they do — 70S).
3. Calling the bacterial wall cellulose — it is **peptidoglycan**.
4. Listing viruses as prokaryotes — viruses are **acellular**, outside the cell concept entirely.
5. Forgetting similarities (membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, DNA, genetic code) when a question asks "compare".

practiceQuestions:
**Short answer (2m):** Define a cell.

**Answer.** The **cell is the smallest basic structural, functional and biological unit of all living organisms** — a mass of cytoplasm surrounded by a membrane, containing genetic material, capable of independent existence and reproduction. Unicellular organisms perform every life function with a single cell.

**Short answer (2m):** Name the scientists associated with the cell theory and their contributions.

**Answer.** - **Robert Hooke (1665)** — first saw and **named “cells”** in dead cork (though the cell theory came later).
- **Schleiden (1838)** — all **plants** are made of cells.
- **Schwann (1839)** — all **animals** are made of cells.
- **Virchow (1855)** — all cells arise **from pre-existing cells** (*Omnis cellula e cellula*).

**Short answer (2m):** What are plasmids and why are they important?

**Answer.** **Small, self-replicating circular DNA molecules** in prokaryotes, separate from the main chromosome. They carry **accessory genes** — antibiotic resistance, fertility factors — and, because they can be cut and re-ligated, they are the standard **vectors of genetic engineering** (e.g. insulin production in *E. coli*).

**Short answer (2m):** What is a nucleoid?

**Answer.** The **irregular, non-membrane-bound region** of a prokaryotic cytoplasm where the single **circular, naked DNA chromosome** lies — no nuclear envelope separates it from the cytoplasm, which is why transcription and translation can be coupled.

**Long answer (5m):** Differentiate between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.

**Answer.** | Basis | Prokaryotic cell | Eukaryotic cell |
|---|---|---|
| **Nucleus** | No nuclear envelope; **nucleoid** with naked circular DNA | True nucleus; double envelope, nucleolus, pores |
| **Chromosomes** | Single circular DNA + plasmids, **no histones** | Multiple **linear chromosomes with histones** |
| **Membrane-bound organelles** | **Absent** (no mitochondria, ER, Golgi, plastids) | **Present** |
| **Ribosomes** | **70S** (50S + 30S) | **80S** (60S + 40S); 70S inside organelles |
| **Cell wall** | **Peptidoglycan** (bacteria) | Cellulose (plants), chitin (fungi), or none (animals) |
| **Cell division** | **Binary fission** (~20 min) | **Mitosis / meiosis** |
| **Transcription–translation** | **Coupled** — both in cytoplasm simultaneously | Separated — transcription in nucleus, translation in cytoplasm |
| **Size** | 0.5–5 µm | 10–100 µm |
| **Respiration site** | Plasma membrane (mesosomes) | Mitochondria |
| **Examples** | Bacteria, cyanobacteria | Protists, fungi, plants, animals |

**Similarities (the point of continuity):** plasma membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, DNA as genetic material, and the **same genetic code** — all life shares one chemistry.

**Long answer (5m):** Describe the structure of a bacterial cell with a labelled diagram.

**Answer.** **From outside in:**

1. **Cell wall — peptidoglycan (murein)**: rigid, gives shape and osmotic protection; attacked by lysozyme and penicillin. (A slime capsule may lie outside it.)
2. **Plasma membrane**: typical phospholipid bilayer; carries respiratory enzymes (no mitochondria); may fold in as **mesosomes**.
3. **Nucleoid**: one **circular naked DNA** chromosome, no nuclear envelope; plus small **plasmids** (resistance, fertility genes).
4. **Ribosomes — 70S** (50S + 30S), thousands, free in cytoplasm; protein synthesis (and antibiotic target).
5. **Inclusion bodies / gas vacuoles**: stored glycogen, lipid, phosphate granules; buoyancy in aquatic forms.
6. **Flagellum** — simple rotary organ of locomotion made of **flagellin** (no 9+2 arrangement).
7. **Pili and fimbriae** — protein threads: **pili** for conjugation (gene transfer), **fimbriae** for attachment.

*Labelled diagram:* capsule (if drawn), wall, membrane with mesosome, nucleoid loop + plasmid ring, ribosome dots, flagellum and pili.

**Conceptual (3m):** "The eukaryotic cell is a compartmentalised cell." Explain.

**Answer.** Membrane-bound organelles wall off **separate chemical environments** inside one cell:

- **Lysosomes** hold acid hydrolases at **pH ~5** while the **cytosol runs at pH ~7.2** — the same cell hosts two incompatible chemistries side by side.
- The **nuclear envelope** separates transcription (nucleus) from translation (cytoplasm), allowing RNA processing bacteria cannot do.
- **Mitochondria** concentrate respiration enzymes and proton gradients; the **ER/Golgi** run a dedicated export assembly line.

Compartmentalisation prevents interference between processes, raises local enzyme and substrate concentrations, and permits **larger cells and specialisation** — the structural basis of eukaryotic complexity.

**Conceptual (3m):** Why do cells remain small even in large organisms?

**Answer.** **Geometry and diffusion.** When a cell's linear size doubles, its **volume grows 8× (cube)** but its **surface only 4× (square)** — the surface-area-to-volume ratio falls. Every nutrient and waste molecule must cross the membrane, and inside a large cell **diffusion is far too slow** over long distances. A big cell would starve in the middle and poison itself. Large organisms therefore multiply **small, specialised cells** instead of enlarging individual ones — size comes from cell number, not cell size.

**Application (3m):** A new antibiotic inhibits 70S ribosomes. Why is it likely safe for humans, and what limitation must it have?

**Answer.** **Why safe:** human cytoplasmic ribosomes are **80S** (60S + 40S), so a drug that binds only **70S** ribosomes selectively blocks **bacterial protein synthesis** while leaving the patient's own cytoplasmic translation untouched — selective toxicity on a real structural difference.

**Limitation:** human **mitochondria carry 70S ribosomes** (an endosymbiotic relic), so at high dose or long duration the drug can also hit mitochondrial translation — harming mitochondria-rich tissues (liver, kidney, bone marrow, inner ear). That mitochondrial overlap is the basis of several antibiotic side effects.
practice:
Why can mRNA be translated while it is still being transcribed in bacteria but not in humans?

**Answer.** In bacteria there is **no nuclear envelope**: transcription and translation happen in the same compartment, so ribosomes can attach to the growing mRNA and start making protein **before RNA polymerase has finished** — a genuine speed advantage for a 20-minute life cycle. In humans the **nuclear envelope separates the two processes**: mRNA must first be transcribed, **capped, spliced (introns out) and polyadenylated** inside the nucleus, then exported through pores before cytoplasmic ribosomes can read it. Coupling is impossible — and the processing step is precisely why it must be.

Why do antibiotics like streptomycin not stop human protein synthesis?

**Answer.** **Ribosome architecture.** Streptomycin binds specific sites on the **70S bacterial ribosome** (30S subunit) that the **80S human cytoplasmic ribosome** does not possess — different proteins, different shapes, different drug-binding pockets. The antibiotic therefore freezes bacterial initiation and misreads bacterial mRNA while our cytoplasmic translation runs on. The one human structure that *is* 70S — the **mitochondrion** — explains the side effects at high doses, but ordinary doses spare human protein synthesis: selective toxicity from a structural difference.

A cell grows to twice its linear size. What happens to its surface-area-to-volume ratio and why does this limit cell size?

**Answer.** Surface area scales with **length²**, volume with **length³**. Doubling the linear size:

- surface area × 4
- volume × 8
- **SA:V ratio falls to half** (from, say, 6:1 to 3:1).

The membrane is the cell's only exchange surface, so a doubled cell has **half the import/export capacity per unit of living matter**. Diffusion across the interior also slows proportionally more than demand grows — the centre starves and drowns in its own waste before the membrane can service it. This is the mathematical ceiling on cell size, and why large organisms add cells instead of enlarging them.

Why are mitochondria and chloroplasts considered evidence for endosymbiosis?

**Answer.** Both organelles behave like **captured bacteria**:

1. **Own circular DNA**, naked and bacteria-like — separate from nuclear chromosomes.
2. **70S ribosomes** (not the eukaryotic 80S) — and sensitive to the same antibiotics that hit bacteria.
3. **Double membrane** — the outer from the host's engulfing vacuole, the inner the original bacterial membrane.
4. **Binary fission** — they divide independently, like bacteria, never built *de novo*.
5. **Genetic similarity** — their rRNA sequences match *Rickettsia*-like bacteria (mitochondria) and cyanobacteria (chloroplasts).

An ancestral eukaryote engulfed an aerobic bacterium (→ mitochondrion) and, later, a photosynthetic cyanobacterium (→ chloroplast); instead of digesting them, it kept them — and the guests kept their bacterial machinery as the receipt.

confusion: **"Prokaryotes have no nucleus" vs "no DNA":** prokaryotes have DNA — just no nuclear envelope around it. The nucleoid is DNA + cytoplasm, not a membrane compartment.
**Viruses are NOT prokaryotes:** viruses are acellular (no membrane, no cytoplasm, no ribosomes); prokaryotes are complete living cells. This is also why viruses are exceptions to cell theory.
**70S vs 80S:** the S (Svedberg) unit measures sedimentation rate, not size — 70S ribosomes are not "smaller than 80S by 10"; they differ in subunit composition (50S+30S vs 60S+40S).
**Cell wall vs cell membrane:** every cell has a membrane; only some have a wall. The wall is outside the membrane, fully permeable; the membrane is the selective barrier.
**Binary fission vs mitosis:** binary fission has no spindle, no chromosome condensation, no nuclear envelope breakdown — it is simpler DNA replication + splitting.

data.summary: The cell is the smallest structural and functional unit of life — discovered by Hooke (1665), theorised by Schleiden, Schwann and Virchow, and limited in size by the surface-area-to-volume ratio. Every cell shares a membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and DNA, but two great designs exist: prokaryotic cells (bacteria, cyanobacteria) keep their naked circular DNA in a nucleoid, have no membrane-bound organelles, use 70S ribosomes and divide by binary fission; eukaryotic cells enclose their histone-bound chromosomes in a true nucleus, run their chemistry inside membrane-bound organelles (endosymbiotic mitochondria and chloroplasts), use 80S ribosomes and divide by mitosis and meiosis. Plant and animal eukaryotic cells differ mainly in cell wall, plastids, central vacuole and centrioles. These differences — especially 70S vs 80S ribosomes — are the molecular basis of selective antibiotic action.

subtopics.name: Historical development
points: Robert Hooke (1665) coined 'cell' after observing cork under a compound microscope
Anton van Leeuwenhoek first saw living cells (bacteria, protozoa)
Schleiden and Schwann (1838-39) proposed that plants and animals are made of cells; Virchow (1855) added omnis cellula e cellula

subtopics.name: Modern cell theory
points: All living organisms are composed of one or more cells
The cell is the basic unit of structure and function
All cells arise from pre-existing cells by division
Cells contain hereditary material passed to daughter cells

subtopics.name: Prokaryotic cell
points: No membrane-bound nucleus; DNA is a single circular chromosome in the nucleoid
No membrane-bound organelles; ribosomes are 70S
Cell wall usually present (peptidoglycan in bacteria); may have capsule, flagella, pili, plasmids

subtopics.name: Eukaryotic cell
points: True nucleus bounded by a double membrane with pores
Membrane-bound organelles: mitochondria, ER, Golgi, lysosomes, plastids
Ribosomes are 80S; extensive internal membrane system allows compartmentalised chemistry

branches.topic: Level 3 — Upgraded: size, shape and scale

subtopics.name: Dimensions
points: Typical prokaryote 1-10 micrometre; typical eukaryote 10-100 micrometre
Surface area to volume ratio limits cell size — larger cells must divide or become flattened
Human red blood cell ~7 micrometre; a frog egg ~1 mm is near the practical single-cell ceiling

subtopics.name: Cell as an open system
points: Cells exchange matter and energy continuously with the environment
Compartmentalisation lets incompatible reactions run simultaneously
The endosymbiotic theory explains mitochondria and chloroplasts as captured prokaryotes

subtopics.name: Frequently missed
points: Prokaryotes DO have ribosomes — they lack membrane-bound organelles, not all organelles
Viruses are not cells: no cytoplasm, no metabolism, no independent reproduction
Cell theory's classical form predates the discovery of viruses and does not cover them

notes: DETAILED ORGANELLE ANALYSIS (plant + animal cell).

Plasma membrane: phospholipid bilayer (heads out, tails in) + integral proteins (channels, pumps, receptors) + peripheral proteins + cholesterol + glycocalyx (cell recognition). Fluid-mosaic model (Singer & Nicolson, 1972).

Mitochondrion: double membrane; outer smooth, inner folded into cristae; matrix with Krebs enzymes; own DNA + 70S ribosomes (endosymbiosis); aerobic respiration: glycolysis (cytoplasm) → Krebs (matrix) → ETS (cristae) → ~34 ATP.

Chloroplast: double membrane; thylakoids stacked into grana; stroma with Calvin-cycle enzymes; chlorophyll a + b; own DNA + 70S ribosomes; light reactions (grana → ATP, NADPH, O2) + Calvin cycle (stroma → glucose).

Nucleus: nuclear envelope (4 nm, two membranes, pores); nucleoplasm; chromatin (DNA + histone proteins); nucleolus (rRNA + ribosome assembly).
Rough ER (RER): ribosomes on outer surface → protein synthesis (secretory + membrane proteins); continuous with nuclear envelope.
Smooth ER (SER): lipid synthesis, carbohydrate metabolism, detoxification (liver), Ca2+ storage (muscle — sarcoplasmic reticulum).
Golgi apparatus: cisternae + vesicles; modifies (glycosylation), packages, sorts, and secretes proteins; forms lysosomes + cell plate (plants).
Lysosomes: 8–12 nm vesicle, hydrolytic enzymes (acidic pH); digest food particles, worn organelles (autophagy); "suicide bags" when damaged.

**Organelle specialisations — who has what (highly classified)**

| Organelle | Plant cell | Animal cell | Why the difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cell wall | Present (cellulose) | Absent | Turgor pressure needs a rigid box |
| Plastids | Present | Absent | Plants make their own food |
| Large central vacuole | Present (up to 90% volume) | Small vesicles only | Water storage + turgor |
| Centrioles | Absent (higher plants) | Present | Spindle forms differently in plants |
| Lysosomes | Few (vacuole takes the role) | Many | Animals ingest whole particles |
| Mitochondria + ER + Golgi | Present | Present | Core eukaryote machinery shared |
Vacuole: plant — large central (turgor, storage); animal — small (excretion, osmoregulation, contractile in protozoa).
Cytoskeleton: microfilaments (actin), intermediate filaments, microtubules (tubulin); shape, movement, intracellular transport, division (spindle).
Centrioles (animal): microtubule rings; form the spindle during mitosis; absent in most plants.
Cell inclusions: storage granules (starch, fat, glycogen), pigments (leuco-, chro-, heterochromoplasts), crystalloids.
Cell wall (plant): cellulose microfibrils (primary wall) + pectin; secondary wall with lignin; fully permeable; provides rigidity + protection.

**Deep dive — the plasma membrane as a gatekeeper.** The phospholipid bilayer is hydrophobic in its core, so only small non-polar molecules cross freely. Everything else needs help: channels and carriers for ions and sugars (facilitated diffusion), and ATP-driven pumps against gradients (active transport — the sodium-potassium pump is the classic). Fluid-mosaic is the name because proteins drift in a fluid lipid sea, and the mosaic of glycoproteins is how cells recognise each other.
confusion: RER makes PROTEIN; SER makes LIPID. A cell secreting lots of protein has abundant RER + Golgi (e.g., pancreatic acinar cell).
The Golgi does NOT synthesise proteins; it MODIFIES, SORTS, and PACKAGES what the RER made.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their OWN DNA + 70S ribosomes — the key endosymbiosis evidence.
Lysosomes are animal-cell organelles; plants use the large vacuole for hydrolytic digestion.
Cilia and flagella share the 9+2 axonemal microtubule structure; centrioles (9+0) are related but lack the central pair.
The nucleus is NOT the only place with DNA: mitochondria + chloroplasts carry their own genomes.

enrichedContent.summary: A detailed examination of the eukaryotic cell shows how each membrane-bound organelle specialises a metabolic function. The fluid-mosaic plasma membrane controls transport; mitochondria and chloroplasts convert energy (and carry their own DNA, evidence of endosymbiosis); RER makes protein while SER makes lipid; the Golgi modifies and packages; lysosomes digest; the nucleus and nucleolus control heredity; and the cytoskeleton (microfilaments, microtubules) maintains shape and drives division. The protein-secretion pathway (ribosome → RER → Golgi → vesicle → membrane) and the plant/animal cell contrast are core NEB written-answer topics.

data.title: Cell Division — Cycle, Mitosis and Meiosis
data.topicTitle: Cell division: concept of cell cycle, types of cell division (amitosis, mitosis and meiosis) and significances

mcqs.question: DNA replication occurs during which phase of the cell cycle?
mcqs.explanation: The synthesis (S) phase replicates DNA so each chromosome becomes two sister chromatids; G₁ grows, G₂ prepares for division.

mcqs.question: Chromosomes align on the equatorial plate during:
mcqs.explanation: Metaphase lines chromosomes at the equator with spindle fibres attached — the best stage for chromosome counting/karyotyping.

mcqs.question: During anaphase I of meiosis, what separates?
mcqs.explanation: Anaphase I pulls whole homologous chromosomes to opposite poles; centromeres do NOT split until anaphase II.

mcqs.question: Crossing over occurs during which substage of prophase I?
mcqs.explanation: Pachytene: recombination nodules appear and non-sister chromatids exchange segments; chiasmata become visible at diplotene.

mcqs.question: Synapsis of homologous chromosomes occurs during:
mcqs.explanation: Zygotene pairs homologs (synapsis) with formation of the synaptonemal complex, creating bivalents.

mcqs.question: Plant cytokinesis differs from animal cytokinesis because plants form:
options: A cell plate from Golgi vesicles
mcqs.explanation: Golgi vesicles fuse at the equator forming the cell plate, growing outward to become the new wall; the rigid wall cannot be pinched like an animal membrane.

mcqs.question: How many cells result from one meiotic event?
mcqs.explanation: One replication + two divisions yield four haploid cells, each genetically unique because of crossing over and independent assortment.

mcqs.question: Interkinesis is the stage between:
mcqs.explanation: Interkinesis (with no DNA replication) separates meiosis I from meiosis II.

mcqs.question: Which cells typically remain in G₀ and rarely divide?
mcqs.explanation: Mature neurons and cardiac muscle cells are permanent G₀ cells; skin, marrow and gut lining divide constantly.

mcqs.question: Amitosis differs from mitosis because it:
options: Divides the nucleus by simple constriction
mcqs.explanation: Amitosis (Remak, 1841) is direct nuclear constriction without spindle or precise chromosome behaviour — chromatin distribution is unequal.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — How Life Copies Itself at the Cellular Level

A cell's life is a cycle of growth, DNA copying and division. Every scar that heals, every root that grows, every sperm and egg that carries your genes to the next generation is the result of **cell division**.

- **Why it matters:** growth, repair, reproduction and heredity all pass through this topic; it also explains cancer (uncontrolled division) and genetic variation (crossing over).
- **The one-sentence core:** **mitosis copies a cell exactly; meiosis halves the chromosome number and shuffles genes.**
- **Connections:** chromosomes from Topic 3 are the actors here; meiosis connects directly to heredity and evolution (variation), and mitosis to growth and healing.

## 2. The Cell Cycle — The Cell's Life Story

### 2.1 Definition and the grand division

The **cell cycle** (Howard and Pelc, 1953) is the sequence of events from the formation of a cell to its own division into two daughter cells. It has two great phases:

$$\text{Cell cycle} = \underbrace{I_1 + S + I_2}_{\text{Interphase (I-phase)}} + \underbrace{\text{M phase}}_{\text{Division}} + C \text{(cytokinesis)}$$

| Phase | Name | Duration (typical 24 h human cell) | What happens |
|---|---|---|---|
| **G₁** | First gap (post-mitotic) | ~11 h | Growth; RNA and proteins synthesised; organelles multiply; cell decides to divide or exit (G₀) |
| **S** | Synthesis | ~8 h | **DNA replication** — each chromosome is duplicated into two sister chromatids; histones synthesised |
| **G₂** | Second gap (pre-mitotic) | ~4 h | Further growth; spindle proteins, microtubules and RNA made; cell checks DNA for errors |
| **M** | Mitotic phase | ~1 h | Karyokinesis (nuclear division): prophase → metaphase → anaphase → telophase, then **cytokinesis** |

**Interphase misconception:** interphase is NOT a resting phase — it is the most metabolically active period (DNA replication and growth happen here); only *division* is absent.

### 2.2 Checkpoints and G₀

- **Checkpoints** (G₁/S, G2/M, spindle checkpoint) verify that DNA is intact and complete before the next step — the cell's quality control.
- Cells that permanently leave the cycle enter **G₀** (quiescent phase): mature neurons and muscle cells stay in G₀; liver cells can re-enter the cycle on injury.
- **Cancer = checkpoint failure:** cells escape control and divide endlessly. This single sentence is the conceptual bridge between cell division and oncology.

## 3. Amitosis — Direct Division

**Definition:** direct, simple splitting of the nucleus (and then cytoplasm) **without spindle formation, without chromosome condensation** — described by Remak (1841).

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Where | Prokaryotes, some yeast, degenerating/old cells, foetal membranes, cartilage cells |
| Mechanism | Nucleus elongates, constricts in the middle; cytoplasm divides; two nuclei form |
| Result | Two cells with roughly equal but imprecisely distributed nuclear material |
| Significance | Fast, low-cost division for simple/fast-growing or dying tissues |
| Drawback | Unequal distribution of chromatin; no genetic precision |

## 4. Mitosis — Equational Division

### 4.1 Definition

**Mitosis** (Flemming, 1882; Greek *mitos* = thread) is the division of a somatic cell into **two daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent** (2n → 2n). It has **karyokinesis** (nuclear division) followed by **cytokinesis** (cytoplasmic division).

### 4.2 The four stages — what happens and why

| Stage | Key events | Structures to name |
|---|---|---|
| **Prophase** | Chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes (each = 2 sister chromatids joined at the centromere); nucleolus disappears; nuclear envelope breaks down; spindle begins; centrioles move to poles (animals) | Sister chromatids, centromere, spindle |
| **Metaphase** | Chromosomes line up on the **equatorial (metaphase) plate**; spindle fibres from both poles attach to kinetochores; the best stage to count and study chromosomes (karyotyping) | Equatorial plate, kinetochore fibres, polar fibres |
| **Anaphase** | **Centromeres split**; sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles (appears V-, J- or L-shaped by centromere position); poles move apart | Daughter chromosomes, spindle elongation |
| **Telophase** | Chromosomes decondense; nuclear envelopes reform around each set; nucleoli reappear; spindle dissolves | Two daughter nuclei |

### 4.3 Cytokinesis — two different solutions

| Basis | Plant cytokinesis | Animal cytokinesis |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | **Cell plate** forms from Golgi vesicles at the equator, growing outward until it fuses with the wall | **Cleavage furrow**: actin–myosin ring contracts, pinching the membrane inward |
| Direction | Centripetal (inside → outside) | Centripetal (outside → inside) |
| Why the difference | Rigid wall cannot be pinched | No wall, flexible membrane |

### 4.4 Significance of mitosis (exam list — give the reason with each)

1. **Growth** of multicellular organisms (zygote → body by repeated mitosis).
2. **Repair and healing** — replacement of worn-out and wounded cells.
3. **Genetic stability** — exact copies: daughter cells keep the same chromosome number and gene set.
4. **Asexual reproduction** — binary fission, budding, vegetative propagation are mitotic.
5. **Regeneration** — replacement of lost parts (lizard tail, planaria).
6. **Maintains the surface-area-to-volume ratio** of tissues by renewing cells.

## 5. Meiosis — Reductional Division

### 5.1 Definition

**Meiosis** (Farmer and Moore, 1905; Greek *meion* = to lessen) is a **single DNA replication followed by two divisions**, producing **four haploid (n) cells** from one diploid (2n) cell. It occurs only in **germ (reproductive) cells** — sporocytes in plants, gamete-forming cells in animals. It consists of **meiosis I (reductional)** and **meiosis II (equational)**, with a brief **interkinesis** between them (no DNA replication in interkinesis — key point).

### 5.2 Meiosis I — the reduction

| Stage | Key events |
|---|---|
| **Prophase I** (longest, most complex — 5 substages) | See below |
| **Metaphase I** | **Homologous pairs (bivalents/tetrads)** align on the equatorial plate in **two rows**; spindle attaches to kinetochores of homologs (not sister chromatids) |
| **Anaphase I** | **Whole homologous chromosomes separate** to opposite poles — **centromeres do NOT split**; sister chromatids stay together |
| **Telophase I** | Haploid set (each chromosome still double-stranded) reaches each pole; nuclear envelope may re-form; cytokinesis follows |

**Prophase I substages (the most examined sequence in this topic):**

| Substage | Events |
|---|---|
| **Leptotene** | Chromosomes condense and become visible |
| **Zygotene** | **Synapsis** — homologous chromosomes pair; a **synaptonemal complex** forms |
| **Pachytene** | **Crossing over** — non-sister chromatids of the bivalent exchange segments at **recombination nodules**; visible **chiasmata** appear; recombinase (Reca) enzymes act |
| **Diplotene** | Synaptonemal complex dissolves; chiasmata clearly visible; homologs begin to separate (oocytes of some vertebrates stay here for years — dictyotene) |
| **Diakinesis** | Terminalisation of chiasmata; chromosomes fully condensed; nucleolus and envelope disappear; spindle forms |

### 5.3 Meiosis II — the equational division

After interkinesis (no DNA replication), each haploid cell divides like a mitosis: **prophase II → metaphase II (chromosomes in single row) → anaphase II (centromeres split, sister chromatids separate) → telophase II**. Result: **four haploid cells**.

### 5.4 Significance of meiosis (exam list)

1. **Maintains the chromosome number constant** across generations — 2n gamete-forming cells → n gametes; fertilisation restores 2n.
2. **Creates genetic variation** by crossing over (pachytene) and independent assortment (metaphase I orientation) — the raw material of evolution.
3. **Forms gametes/spores** for sexual reproduction.
4. **Repairs defects and aids adaptation** through recombination.
5. **Aids speciation** — variation on which natural selection acts.

### 5.5 Mitosis vs Meiosis — the guaranteed master table

| Basis | Mitosis | Meiosis |
|---|---|---|
| Occurrence | Somatic (body) cells, throughout life | Germ cells, only at reproduction |
| Divisions | One (DNA replicated once, divided once) | Two (DNA replicated once, divided twice) |
| Daughter cells | 2 | 4 |
| Chromosome number | Conserved (2n → 2n) — equational | Halved (2n → n) — reductional |
| Pairing of homologs | No synapsis | Synapsis and bivalent formation |
| Crossing over | Absent | Present (pachytene) — variation |
| Metaphase arrangement | Chromosomes in one row | Meiosis I: pairs in two rows; Meiosis II: one row |
| Anaphase separation | Sister chromatids (centromere splits) | I: homologs (centromere intact); II: sister chromatids |
| Duration of prophase | Short, simple | Long, five substages |
| Genetic result | Identical daughter cells | Genetically different haploid cells |
| Role | Growth, repair, asexual reproduction | Gamete/spore formation, variation |

## 6. Conceptual Relationships

- **Topic 3 → here:** the spindle is built from microtubules; the Golgi makes the plant cell plate; chromosomes come from nuclear chromatin.
- **Here → heredity (Class 12):** segregation of homologs (meiosis I) and independent assortment are the physical basis of Mendel's laws.
- **Here → evolution:** crossing over and independent assortment generate the variation natural selection acts on.
- **Here → health:** loss of mitotic control = cancer; failure of meiotic segregation (nondisjunction) = chromosomal disorders (Down syndrome, trisomy 21).
- **Here → reproduction:** gametogenesis in animals and sporogenesis in plants are meiotic; fertilisation reverses the reduction.

## 7. Exam Orientation

### 7.1 Previous year questions

No cell-division question is present in the authored solved-paper bank for class 11 biology (the 2021–2024 bank questions for this unit cover biomolecules, cells and enzymes). The questions below are **NEB-style practice questions, not verified PYQs** — clearly distinguished as required.

### 7.2 NEB-style practice questions with model answers

**Q1 (3m) — Define the cell cycle. Describe the events of interphase.**
Answer: The cell cycle is the sequence of changes a cell undergoes from its formation to its own division. **Interphase** (the metabolically active "resting" phase, ~23 h of a 24 h cycle) has three sub-phases: **G₁** — growth, RNA/protein synthesis, organelle multiplication; **S** — DNA replication, producing two sister chromatids per chromosome; **G₂** — spindle-protein synthesis and final preparation for mitosis.

**Q2 (5m) — Describe the stages of mitosis with diagrams.**
Answer: Draw the four stages. **Prophase:** condensation into two-chromatid chromosomes, nuclear envelope and nucleolus disappear, spindle forms. **Metaphase:** chromosomes align on the equatorial plate, kinetochore fibres from both poles attach. **Anaphase:** centromeres split, sister chromatids move to opposite poles. **Telophase:** envelopes and nucleoli reform, chromosomes decondense. End with cytokinesis: cell plate (plants) vs cleavage furrow (animals).

**Q3 (5m) — Describe prophase I of meiosis and state its significance.**
Answer: Five substages — **leptotene** (chromosomes visible), **zygotene** (synapsis of homologs, synaptonemal complex), **pachytene** (crossing over at recombination nodules, chiasmata appear), **diplotene** (complex dissolves, chiasmata visible), **diakinesis** (terminalisation, spindle forms). Significance: crossing over produces new gene combinations — the source of genetic variation.

**Q4 (3m) — Give four differences between mitosis and meiosis.**
Answer: Any four table rows — occurrence (somatic vs germ cells), divisions (one vs two), products (2 identical 2n vs 4 varied n cells), crossing over (absent vs present), metaphase arrangement (one row vs pairs in two rows).

**Q5 (3m) — Why is meiosis significant for a species?**
Answer: (1) It halves the chromosome number so fertilisation can restore it — chromosome constancy across generations; (2) crossing over and independent assortment create genetic variation; (3) variation gives natural selection material to act on, enabling adaptation and evolution.

**Q6 (2m) — Why is interphase not a "resting phase"?**
Answer: Because DNA replication (S phase), massive protein/RNA synthesis and growth (G₁, G₂) all occur then — the cell is metabolically at its busiest; only nuclear division is absent.

**Q7 (2m) — How does cytokinesis differ in plant and animal cells?**
Answer: Plants: a **cell plate** of Golgi vesicles forms at the equator and grows outward (centripetal) to become the middle lamella + wall. Animals: an **actin–myosin contractile ring** pinches the membrane inward as a cleavage furrow.

### 7.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Saying DNA replicates "before meiosis II" — replication happens **only before meiosis I**; interkinesis has none.
2. Splitting centromeres in anaphase I — homologs separate whole; centromeres split only in anaphase II (and mitosis).
3. Drawing metaphase I chromosomes in a single row — they align as **pairs in two rows**.
4. Confusing **chiasmata** (visible X-shaped contact points) with **crossing over** (the exchange event at pachytene).
5. Writing "meiosis produces gametes" for plants without mentioning **spores** (meiosis makes spores in plants; gametes form by mitosis in the gametophyte).
6. Calling amitosis the main division of prokaryotes without noting its imprecision (unequal chromatin distribution).
confusion: **Chromatid vs chromosome:** after S phase, each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids joined at one centromere — it is still ONE chromosome. The count changes only when centromeres split (anaphase).
**Mitosis vs meiosis II:** both split centromeres and separate sister chromatids, but meiosis II starts from haploid, recombined cells and follows meiosis I without new DNA replication.

**Crossing over vs independent assortment:** crossing over = physical exchange between non-sister chromatids (pachytene); independent assortment = random orientation of bivalents at metaphase I. Both create variation, by different mechanisms.
**Interkinesis vs interphase:** interkinesis between meiosis I and II has NO DNA replication; interphase of the cell cycle always includes S phase.

**Amitosis vs binary fission:** related but not identical — amitosis is the imprecise direct nuclear division seen in some eukaryotic cells; bacterial binary fission is precise DNA replication followed by septation.

practiceQuestions: **Short answer (2m): Define cell cycle.** — The sequence of events by which a cell grows, replicates its DNA and divides into two daughter cells; it comprises interphase (G₁, S, G₂) and the M phase with cytokinesis.

**Short answer (2m): What is crossing over?** — The exchange of corresponding segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during pachytene of prophase I, producing recombined chromosomes and genetic variation.
**Short answer (2m): What is a bivalent?** — The pair of homologous chromosomes (four chromatids, hence "tetrad") formed by synapsis during zygotene of prophase I.

**Short answer (2m): What is the G₀ phase?** — A quiescent state outside the active cycle into which cells withdraw after mitosis (e.g. mature neurons); they remain metabolically active but do not divide, though some can re-enter the cycle on stimulus.

**Long answer (5m): Describe the stages of mitosis with labelled diagrams and state its significance.** — Prophase (condensation, spindle, envelope loss) → metaphase (equatorial plate, spindle attachment) → anaphase (centromere split, chromatids to poles) → telophase (re-formation of nuclei) → cytokinesis (cell plate vs furrow). Significance: growth, repair, genetic stability, asexual reproduction, regeneration.

**Long answer (5m): Describe meiosis I with diagrams and state how it reduces the chromosome number.** — Prophase I with five substages (synapsis, crossing over), metaphase I (bivalents in two rows), anaphase I (whole homologs separate — centromere intact), telophase I (haploid nuclei). Reduction happens because each pole receives one chromosome of every homologous pair, while each chromosome still has two chromatids.

**Conceptual (3m): Why does meiosis create variation while mitosis does not?** — Mitosis copies an existing genome exactly (no pairing, no exchange). Meiosis adds two sources of novelty: crossing over recombines maternal and paternal alleles within chromosomes (pachytene), and independent assortment randomises which homolog of each pair reaches which pole (metaphase I). Each gamete therefore carries a unique combination.

**Conceptual (3m): "Cancer is a disease of the cell cycle." Explain.** — Normal division is stopped at checkpoints by control genes (proto-oncogenes, tumour suppressors such as p53). When mutations disable these brakes, cells skip G₁/S and spindle checkpoints and divide without restraint, invading tissues — uncontrolled mitosis is the mechanism of tumour growth.

**Application (2m): Why do antibiotics/chemotherapy drugs that block spindle formation stop tumour growth?** — Drugs like colchicine and vinblastine prevent microtubule assembly, so the mitotic spindle cannot form; cells arrest in metaphase and cannot complete division. Rapidly dividing tumour cells are hit hardest.

enrichedContent.summary: The cell cycle runs through interphase — G₁ growth, S DNA replication, G₂ preparation — into the M phase. Amitosis is a rare, imprecise direct splitting. Mitosis (prophase → metaphase → anaphase → telophase, then cytokinesis by cell plate in plants or cleavage furrow in animals) produces two genetically identical diploid cells for growth, repair and asexual reproduction. Meiosis — one replication followed by two divisions — produces four genetically unique haploid cells: prophase I (leptotene, zygotene synapsis, pachytene crossing over, diplotene, diakinesis), metaphase I with bivalents in two rows, anaphase I separating whole homologs, then the equational meiosis II. Meiosis keeps chromosome numbers constant across generations and generates the variation on which evolution acts; its failure (nondisjunction) and mitosis's failure (checkpoint loss → cancer) show why precise division matters.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — How Life Copies Itself at the Cellular Level

A cell's life is a cycle of growth, DNA copying and division. Every scar that heals, every root that grows, every sperm and egg that carries your genes to the next generation is the result of **cell division**.

- **Why it matters:** growth, repair, reproduction and heredity all pass through this topic; it also explains cancer (uncontrolled division) and genetic variation (crossing over).
- **The one-sentence core:** **mitosis copies a cell exactly; meiosis halves the chromosome number and shuffles genes.**
- **Connections:** chromosomes from Topic 3 are the actors here; meiosis connects directly to heredity and evolution (variation), and mitosis to growth and healing.

## 2. The Cell Cycle — The Cell's Life Story

### 2.1 Definition and the grand division

The **cell cycle** (Howard and Pelc, 1953) is the sequence of events from the formation of a cell to its own division into two daughter cells. It has two great phases:

$$\text{Cell cycle} = \underbrace{I_1 + S + I_2}_{\text{Interphase (I-phase)}} + \underbrace{\text{M phase}}_{\text{Division}} + C \text{(cytokinesis)}$$

| Phase | Name | Duration (typical 24 h human cell) | What happens |
|---|---|---|---|
| **G₁** | First gap (post-mitotic) | ~11 h | Growth; RNA and proteins synthesised; organelles multiply; cell decides to divide or exit (G₀) |
| **S** | Synthesis | ~8 h | **DNA replication** — each chromosome is duplicated into two sister chromatids; histones synthesised |
| **G₂** | Second gap (pre-mitotic) | ~4 h | Further growth; spindle proteins, microtubules and RNA made; cell checks DNA for errors |
| **M** | Mitotic phase | ~1 h | Karyokinesis (nuclear division): prophase → metaphase → anaphase → telophase, then **cytokinesis** |

**Interphase misconception:** interphase is NOT a resting phase — it is the most metabolically active period (DNA replication and growth happen here); only *division* is absent.

### 2.2 Checkpoints and G₀

- **Checkpoints** (G₁/S, G2/M, spindle checkpoint) verify that DNA is intact and complete before the next step — the cell's quality control.
- Cells that permanently leave the cycle enter **G₀** (quiescent phase): mature neurons and muscle cells stay in G₀; liver cells can re-enter the cycle on injury.
- **Cancer = checkpoint failure:** cells escape control and divide endlessly. This single sentence is the conceptual bridge between cell division and oncology.

## 3. Amitosis — Direct Division

**Definition:** direct, simple splitting of the nucleus (and then cytoplasm) **without spindle formation, without chromosome condensation** — described by Remak (1841).

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Where | Prokaryotes, some yeast, degenerating/old cells, foetal membranes, cartilage cells |
| Mechanism | Nucleus elongates, constricts in the middle; cytoplasm divides; two nuclei form |
| Result | Two cells with roughly equal but imprecisely distributed nuclear material |
| Significance | Fast, low-cost division for simple/fast-growing or dying tissues |
| Drawback | Unequal distribution of chromatin; no genetic precision |

## 4. Mitosis — Equational Division

### 4.1 Definition

**Mitosis** (Flemming, 1882; Greek *mitos* = thread) is the division of a somatic cell into **two daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent** (2n → 2n). It has **karyokinesis** (nuclear division) followed by **cytokinesis** (cytoplasmic division).

### 4.2 The four stages — what happens and why

| Stage | Key events | Structures to name |
|---|---|---|
| **Prophase** | Chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes (each = 2 sister chromatids joined at the centromere); nucleolus disappears; nuclear envelope breaks down; spindle begins; centrioles move to poles (animals) | Sister chromatids, centromere, spindle |
| **Metaphase** | Chromosomes line up on the **equatorial (metaphase) plate**; spindle fibres from both poles attach to kinetochores; the best stage to count and study chromosomes (karyotyping) | Equatorial plate, kinetochore fibres, polar fibres |
| **Anaphase** | **Centromeres split**; sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles (appears V-, J- or L-shaped by centromere position); poles move apart | Daughter chromosomes, spindle elongation |
| **Telophase** | Chromosomes decondense; nuclear envelopes reform around each set; nucleoli reappear; spindle dissolves | Two daughter nuclei |

### 4.3 Cytokinesis — two different solutions

| Basis | Plant cytokinesis | Animal cytokinesis |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | **Cell plate** forms from Golgi vesicles at the equator, growing outward until it fuses with the wall | **Cleavage furrow**: actin–myosin ring contracts, pinching the membrane inward |
| Direction | Centripetal (inside → outside) | Centripetal (outside → inside) |
| Why the difference | Rigid wall cannot be pinched | No wall, flexible membrane |

### 4.4 Significance of mitosis (exam list — give the reason with each)

1. **Growth** of multicellular organisms (zygote → body by repeated mitosis).
2. **Repair and healing** — replacement of worn-out and wounded cells.
3. **Genetic stability** — exact copies: daughter cells keep the same chromosome number and gene set.
4. **Asexual reproduction** — binary fission, budding, vegetative propagation are mitotic.
5. **Regeneration** — replacement of lost parts (lizard tail, planaria).
6. **Maintains the surface-area-to-volume ratio** of tissues by renewing cells.

## 5. Meiosis — Reductional Division

### 5.1 Definition

**Meiosis** (Farmer and Moore, 1905; Greek *meion* = to lessen) is a **single DNA replication followed by two divisions**, producing **four haploid (n) cells** from one diploid (2n) cell. It occurs only in **germ (reproductive) cells** — sporocytes in plants, gamete-forming cells in animals. It consists of **meiosis I (reductional)** and **meiosis II (equational)**, with a brief **interkinesis** between them (no DNA replication in interkinesis — key point).

### 5.2 Meiosis I — the reduction

| Stage | Key events |
|---|---|
| **Prophase I** (longest, most complex — 5 substages) | See below |
| **Metaphase I** | **Homologous pairs (bivalents/tetrads)** align on the equatorial plate in **two rows**; spindle attaches to kinetochores of homologs (not sister chromatids) |
| **Anaphase I** | **Whole homologous chromosomes separate** to opposite poles — **centromeres do NOT split**; sister chromatids stay together |
| **Telophase I** | Haploid set (each chromosome still double-stranded) reaches each pole; nuclear envelope may re-form; cytokinesis follows |

**Prophase I substages (the most examined sequence in this topic):**

| Substage | Events |
|---|---|
| **Leptotene** | Chromosomes condense and become visible |
| **Zygotene** | **Synapsis** — homologous chromosomes pair; a **synaptonemal complex** forms |
| **Pachytene** | **Crossing over** — non-sister chromatids of the bivalent exchange segments at **recombination nodules**; visible **chiasmata** appear; recombinase (Reca) enzymes act |
| **Diplotene** | Synaptonemal complex dissolves; chiasmata clearly visible; homologs begin to separate (oocytes of some vertebrates stay here for years — dictyotene) |
| **Diakinesis** | Terminalisation of chiasmata; chromosomes fully condensed; nucleolus and envelope disappear; spindle forms |

### 5.3 Meiosis II — the equational division

After interkinesis (no DNA replication), each haploid cell divides like a mitosis: **prophase II → metaphase II (chromosomes in single row) → anaphase II (centromeres split, sister chromatids separate) → telophase II**. Result: **four haploid cells**.

### 5.4 Significance of meiosis (exam list)

1. **Maintains the chromosome number constant** across generations — 2n gamete-forming cells → n gametes; fertilisation restores 2n.
2. **Creates genetic variation** by crossing over (pachytene) and independent assortment (metaphase I orientation) — the raw material of evolution.
3. **Forms gametes/spores** for sexual reproduction.
4. **Repairs defects and aids adaptation** through recombination.
5. **Aids speciation** — variation on which natural selection acts.

### 5.5 Mitosis vs Meiosis — the guaranteed master table

| Basis | Mitosis | Meiosis |
|---|---|---|
| Occurrence | Somatic (body) cells, throughout life | Germ cells, only at reproduction |
| Divisions | One (DNA replicated once, divided once) | Two (DNA replicated once, divided twice) |
| Daughter cells | 2 | 4 |
| Chromosome number | Conserved (2n → 2n) — equational | Halved (2n → n) — reductional |
| Pairing of homologs | No synapsis | Synapsis and bivalent formation |
| Crossing over | Absent | Present (pachytene) — variation |
| Metaphase arrangement | Chromosomes in one row | Meiosis I: pairs in two rows; Meiosis II: one row |
| Anaphase separation | Sister chromatids (centromere splits) | I: homologs (centromere intact); II: sister chromatids |
| Duration of prophase | Short, simple | Long, five substages |
| Genetic result | Identical daughter cells | Genetically different haploid cells |
| Role | Growth, repair, asexual reproduction | Gamete/spore formation, variation |

## 6. Conceptual Relationships

- **Topic 3 → here:** the spindle is built from microtubules; the Golgi makes the plant cell plate; chromosomes come from nuclear chromatin.
- **Here → heredity (Class 12):** segregation of homologs (meiosis I) and independent assortment are the physical basis of Mendel's laws.
- **Here → evolution:** crossing over and independent assortment generate the variation natural selection acts on.
- **Here → health:** loss of mitotic control = cancer; failure of meiotic segregation (nondisjunction) = chromosomal disorders (Down syndrome, trisomy 21).
- **Here → reproduction:** gametogenesis in animals and sporogenesis in plants are meiotic; fertilisation reverses the reduction.

## 7. Exam Orientation

### 7.1 Previous year questions

No cell-division question is present in the authored solved-paper bank for class 11 biology (the 2021–2024 bank questions for this unit cover biomolecules, cells and enzymes). The questions below are **NEB-style practice questions, not verified PYQs** — clearly distinguished as required.

### 7.2 NEB-style practice questions with model answers

**Q1 (3m) — Define the cell cycle. Describe the events of interphase.**
Answer: The cell cycle is the sequence of changes a cell undergoes from its formation to its own division. **Interphase** (the metabolically active "resting" phase, ~23 h of a 24 h cycle) has three sub-phases: **G₁** — growth, RNA/protein synthesis, organelle multiplication; **S** — DNA replication, producing two sister chromatids per chromosome; **G₂** — spindle-protein synthesis and final preparation for mitosis.

**Q2 (5m) — Describe the stages of mitosis with diagrams.**
Answer: Draw the four stages. **Prophase:** condensation into two-chromatid chromosomes, nuclear envelope and nucleolus disappear, spindle forms. **Metaphase:** chromosomes align on the equatorial plate, kinetochore fibres from both poles attach. **Anaphase:** centromeres split, sister chromatids move to opposite poles. **Telophase:** envelopes and nucleoli reform, chromosomes decondense. End with cytokinesis: cell plate (plants) vs cleavage furrow (animals).

**Q3 (5m) — Describe prophase I of meiosis and state its significance.**
Answer: Five substages — **leptotene** (chromosomes visible), **zygotene** (synapsis of homologs, synaptonemal complex), **pachytene** (crossing over at recombination nodules, chiasmata appear), **diplotene** (complex dissolves, chiasmata visible), **diakinesis** (terminalisation, spindle forms). Significance: crossing over produces new gene combinations — the source of genetic variation.

**Q4 (3m) — Give four differences between mitosis and meiosis.**
Answer: Any four table rows — occurrence (somatic vs germ cells), divisions (one vs two), products (2 identical 2n vs 4 varied n cells), crossing over (absent vs present), metaphase arrangement (one row vs pairs in two rows).

**Q5 (3m) — Why is meiosis significant for a species?**
Answer: (1) It halves the chromosome number so fertilisation can restore it — chromosome constancy across generations; (2) crossing over and independent assortment create genetic variation; (3) variation gives natural selection material to act on, enabling adaptation and evolution.

**Q6 (2m) — Why is interphase not a "resting phase"?**
Answer: Because DNA replication (S phase), massive protein/RNA synthesis and growth (G₁, G₂) all occur then — the cell is metabolically at its busiest; only nuclear division is absent.

**Q7 (2m) — How does cytokinesis differ in plant and animal cells?**
Answer: Plants: a **cell plate** of Golgi vesicles forms at the equator and grows outward (centripetal) to become the middle lamella + wall. Animals: an **actin–myosin contractile ring** pinches the membrane inward as a cleavage furrow.

### 7.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Saying DNA replicates "before meiosis II" — replication happens **only before meiosis I**; interkinesis has none.
2. Splitting centromeres in anaphase I — homologs separate whole; centromeres split only in anaphase II (and mitosis).
3. Drawing metaphase I chromosomes in a single row — they align as **pairs in two rows**.
4. Confusing **chiasmata** (visible X-shaped contact points) with **crossing over** (the exchange event at pachytene).
5. Writing "meiosis produces gametes" for plants without mentioning **spores** (meiosis makes spores in plants; gametes form by mitosis in the gametophyte).
6. Calling amitosis the main division of prokaryotes without noting its imprecision (unequal chromatin distribution).

practiceQuestions: **Short answer (2m): Define cell cycle.** — The sequence of events by which a cell grows, replicates its DNA and divides into two daughter cells; it comprises interphase (G₁, S, G₂) and the M phase with cytokinesis.

**Short answer (2m): What is crossing over?** — The exchange of corresponding segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during pachytene of prophase I, producing recombined chromosomes and genetic variation.
**Short answer (2m): What is a bivalent?** — The pair of homologous chromosomes (four chromatids, hence "tetrad") formed by synapsis during zygotene of prophase I.

**Short answer (2m): What is the G₀ phase?** — A quiescent state outside the active cycle into which cells withdraw after mitosis (e.g. mature neurons); they remain metabolically active but do not divide, though some can re-enter the cycle on stimulus.

**Long answer (5m): Describe the stages of mitosis with labelled diagrams and state its significance.** — Prophase (condensation, spindle, envelope loss) → metaphase (equatorial plate, spindle attachment) → anaphase (centromere split, chromatids to poles) → telophase (re-formation of nuclei) → cytokinesis (cell plate vs furrow). Significance: growth, repair, genetic stability, asexual reproduction, regeneration.

**Long answer (5m): Describe meiosis I with diagrams and state how it reduces the chromosome number.** — Prophase I with five substages (synapsis, crossing over), metaphase I (bivalents in two rows), anaphase I (whole homologs separate — centromere intact), telophase I (haploid nuclei). Reduction happens because each pole receives one chromosome of every homologous pair, while each chromosome still has two chromatids.

**Conceptual (3m): Why does meiosis create variation while mitosis does not?** — Mitosis copies an existing genome exactly (no pairing, no exchange). Meiosis adds two sources of novelty: crossing over recombines maternal and paternal alleles within chromosomes (pachytene), and independent assortment randomises which homolog of each pair reaches which pole (metaphase I). Each gamete therefore carries a unique combination.

**Conceptual (3m): "Cancer is a disease of the cell cycle." Explain.** — Normal division is stopped at checkpoints by control genes (proto-oncogenes, tumour suppressors such as p53). When mutations disable these brakes, cells skip G₁/S and spindle checkpoints and divide without restraint, invading tissues — uncontrolled mitosis is the mechanism of tumour growth.

**Application (2m): Why do antibiotics/chemotherapy drugs that block spindle formation stop tumour growth?** — Drugs like colchicine and vinblastine prevent microtubule assembly, so the mitotic spindle cannot form; cells arrest in metaphase and cannot complete division. Rapidly dividing tumour cells are hit hardest.
