A projectile has range 100 m and time of flight 4 s. Find its horizontal velocity and launch angle. — $v_x = 25$ m/s; $u_y = gt/2 = 20$ m/s → $\theta = \tan^{-1}(20/25) = 38.7°$.
Two projectiles are fired at 30° and 60° with the same speed 40 m/s. Show both have $R = 141$ m, and compare their maximum heights (1 : 3).

From a 45 m cliff a stone is thrown horizontally at 10 m/s. When and where does it land? — fall time $t = 3$ s; horizontal landing distance $= 30$ m; impact speed $= \sqrt{10^2 + 30^2} \approx 31.6$ m/s.
universalFacts: Galileo's *Dialogues* (1638) first showed projectile motion is a parabola by superposing uniform horizontal motion with vertical fall — the first known composition of motions.
Artillery fire above ~30 km (Paris Gun, WWI) deviates from the parabola: thin air changes drag and $g$'s direction varies — ideal parabolic flight is a near-Earth, no-air model.
Long-jump athletes take off near 21°, not 45°, because take-off speed itself drops with steeper angles — the real optimum balances range angle against speed loss.
Basketball free throws exploit the high-arc (complementary-angle) region: a steep entry angle enlarges the effective hoop target, even though the flatter shot travels the same distance.
examples: Example 1 (horizontal launch): a stone thrown horizontally at 15 m/s from a 20 m tower: $t = \sqrt{2 \times 20/10} = 2$ s; lands 30 m out — vertical fall sets the TIME, horizontal speed sets the DISTANCE.
Example 2 (full trajectory): $u = 25$ m/s at $\theta = 37°$ ($\sin 37° = 0.6$, $\cos 37° = 0.8$): $T = 3$ s, $H = 11.25$ m, $R = 60$ m — the classic 3-4-5 projectile.
Example 3 (velocity at top): speed at the top $= u\cos\theta = 20$ m/s for the previous shot — the projectile is never at rest.
Example 4 (45° range): maximum range with $u = 30$ m/s is $R_{max} = u^2/g = 90$ m at 45°, with $H = R/4 = 22.5$ m — note $R_{max} = 4H$.
Example 5 (bomb release): a plane at 500 m flying level at 100 m/s releases a bomb — it lands after $t = 10$ s, $500$ m ahead of the release point (it keeps the plane's horizontal velocity).

Time of flight: $T = \dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$
Maximum height: $H = \dfrac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$
Range: $R = \dfrac{u^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$; $R_{max} = \dfrac{u^2}{g}$ at $\theta = 45°$
Trajectory: $y = x\tan\theta - \dfrac{gx^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}$ (parabola); $R = 4H\cot\theta$
keyPoints: Horizontal and vertical motions are independent; they share only TIME.
$v_x$ is constant; $v_y$ changes by $g$ every second; the path is a parabola.
At the top: $v_y = 0$, speed $= u\cos\theta$ (minimum), $a = g$ downward.
Landing speed equals launch speed; landing angle equals −launch angle (symmetry).
$R$ is maximum at 45°; complementary angles give equal ranges but different heights.
$R \propto u^2$ and $H \propto u^2$ — doubling launch speed quadruples both.
data.summary: Projectile motion is the superposition of constant horizontal velocity and vertical free fall, giving a parabolic path. The three headline results — $T = 2u\sin\theta/g$, $H = u^2\sin^2\theta/2g$, $R = u^2\sin2\theta/g$ — all follow from the component equations, with maximum range at 45° and equal ranges at complementary angles. Speed at the top is $u\cos\theta$ (never zero), landing speed equals launch speed, and horizontal-launch problems are handled by letting the vertical fall set the time. These results assume no air resistance and constant $g$.
specialNotes: Note 1: In horizontal-launch problems, get the time from the VERTICAL fall first, then multiply by $v_x$.
Note 2: Memorise $\sin 37° = 0.6$, $\cos 37° = 0.8$ and $\sin 2\theta$ values for 30°/45°/60° — NEB numericals use them constantly.
Note 3: 'Same range' pairs: compare heights as $\sin^2\theta : \sin^2(90°-\theta)$ — the steeper shot rises 3× higher for the 30°/60° pair.
Note 4: State the assumptions (no air resistance, constant $g$, flat ground) in theory answers — they define the model.
importantStatements: Statement 1: A projectile's horizontal and vertical motions are completely independent; gravity acts only on the vertical component.
Statement 2: The horizontal velocity of a projectile remains constant throughout the flight (no air resistance).
Statement 3: The trajectory of an ideal projectile is a parabola.
Statement 4: The horizontal range is maximum at 45° and equal for complementary angles of projection.
importantNotes: Note 1: At the highest point the velocity is purely horizontal: $v = u\cos\theta$ — not zero.
Note 2: Landing speed equals launch speed and the landing angle mirrors the launch angle (energy/symmetry).
Note 3: $R \propto u^2$: small speed increases at launch produce large range gains.
Note 4: For horizontal projection from a height, time of flight depends ONLY on the height: $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$.
examShortTricks: Trick 1: $R = u^2\sin2\theta/g$ — for 30° and 60°, $\sin 2\theta = \sin 60° = 0.866$; write the common range instantly.
Trick 2: At 45°, $R = 4H$ — if a question gives one, the other is a division away.
Trick 3: Horizontal launch from height $h$: time $= \sqrt{2h/g}$, landing speed $= \sqrt{v_x^2 + 2gh}$.
Trick 4: Velocity direction at time $t$: $\tan\phi = \dfrac{u\sin\theta - gt}{u\cos\theta}$ — positive above the horizontal, negative below.
Trick 5: In 'bomb released from plane' questions, the bomb retains the plane's horizontal speed — range = plane speed × fall time.
examNotes: Exam Tip 1: Derivations of $T$, $H$ and $R$ from components are standard 4-mark questions — write the two component tables first.
Exam Tip 2: Draw the trajectory with $v_x$ arrows equal everywhere and $v_y$ arrows shrinking/rising — examiners look for the independence idea.

data.title: Lens Maker's Formula
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Designing a Lens on Paper

Given two spherical surfaces and a glass of known refractive index, the lens maker's formula tells you the focal length before the lens is even ground. NEB 2024 asked for it twice — a 5-mark derivation and a 3-mark numerical.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2022, 2024)

### 2.1 Statement

For a thin lens in air:
$$\frac{1}{f} = (n - 1)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right)$$
- n = refractive index of the lens material (relative to surroundings).
- R₁, R₂ = radii of curvature of the first and second surfaces (Cartesian signs: convex towards the incident light → positive).
- f depends on the **material (n)** and the **geometry (R₁, R₂)** — not on where the object is.

### 2.2 Derivation sketch (NEB 2022, 2024, 5m)

Refraction at a single spherical surface: $\frac{n_2}{v} - \frac{n_1}{u} = \frac{n_2 - n_1}{R}$.

1. **First surface:** light from air (n₁ = 1) into glass (n₂ = n) forms an intermediate image at distance v′:
$$\frac{n}{v'} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{n - 1}{R_1}$$
2. **Second surface:** the intermediate image acts as the object; light leaves glass into air:
$$\frac{1}{v} - \frac{n}{v'} = \frac{1 - n}{R_2} = -\frac{(n-1)}{R_2}$$
3. **Adding** the two equations eliminates v′:
$$\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = (n-1)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right) = \frac{1}{f}$$
using $\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$ for a thin lens.

### 2.3 Worked numericals

**Q (3m, 2024):** A convex lens has surfaces of radii 20 cm and −20 cm and n = 1.5. Calculate its focal length.
$$\frac{1}{f} = (1.5 - 1)\left(\frac{1}{20} - \frac{1}{-20}\right) = 0.5 \times \left(\frac{1}{20} + \frac{1}{20}\right) = 0.5 \times 0.1 = 0.05$$
$$f = 20 \text{ cm}$$

**Q (NEB-style):** A biconvex lens of equal radii 25 cm has f = 20 cm in air. Find n.
$\frac{1}{f} = (n-1)\times\frac{2}{25}$ → $0.05 = (n-1)\times 0.08$ → $n = 1.625$.

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 77:** the formula's right side *is* the lens formula's 1/f.
- **To Topic 79:** with f known, P = 1/f follows immediately.
- **To immersion:** surrounded by liquid (n_medium > 1), the effective (n−1) shrinks and f grows — a lens loses power in water.

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Designing a Lens on Paper

Given two spherical surfaces and a glass of known refractive index, the lens maker's formula tells you the focal length before the lens is even ground. NEB 2024 asked for it twice — a 5-mark derivation and a 3-mark numerical.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2022, 2024)

### 2.1 Statement

For a thin lens in air:
$$\frac{1}{f} = (n - 1)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right)$$
- n = refractive index of the lens material (relative to surroundings).
- R₁, R₂ = radii of curvature of the first and second surfaces (Cartesian signs: convex towards the incident light → positive).
- f depends on the **material (n)** and the **geometry (R₁, R₂)** — not on where the object is.

### 2.2 Derivation sketch (NEB 2022, 2024, 5m)

Refraction at a single spherical surface: $\frac{n_2}{v} - \frac{n_1}{u} = \frac{n_2 - n_1}{R}$.

1. **First surface:** light from air (n₁ = 1) into glass (n₂ = n) forms an intermediate image at distance v′:
$$\frac{n}{v'} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{n - 1}{R_1}$$
2. **Second surface:** the intermediate image acts as the object; light leaves glass into air:
$$\frac{1}{v} - \frac{n}{v'} = \frac{1 - n}{R_2} = -\frac{(n-1)}{R_2}$$
3. **Adding** the two equations eliminates v′:
$$\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = (n-1)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right) = \frac{1}{f}$$
using $\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$ for a thin lens.

### 2.3 Worked numericals

**Q (3m, 2024):** A convex lens has surfaces of radii 20 cm and −20 cm and n = 1.5. Calculate its focal length.
$$\frac{1}{f} = (1.5 - 1)\left(\frac{1}{20} - \frac{1}{-20}\right) = 0.5 \times \left(\frac{1}{20} + \frac{1}{20}\right) = 0.5 \times 0.1 = 0.05$$
$$f = 20 \text{ cm}$$

**Q (NEB-style):** A biconvex lens of equal radii 25 cm has f = 20 cm in air. Find n.
$\frac{1}{f} = (n-1)\times\frac{2}{25}$ → $0.05 = (n-1)\times 0.08$ → $n = 1.625$.

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 77:** the formula's right side *is* the lens formula's 1/f.
- **To Topic 79:** with f known, P = 1/f follows immediately.
- **To immersion:** surrounded by liquid (n_medium > 1), the effective (n−1) shrinks and f grows — a lens loses power in water.

data.title: Power of a Lens
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Measuring a Lens in Dioptres

Opticians never quote focal lengths; they quote **power** — the reciprocal of focal length in dioptres. A +3 D lens bends light three times as strongly as a +1 D lens, and contact prescriptions, camera lenses and spectacles all speak this language.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2024)

### 2.1 Power of a lens

$$P = \frac{1}{f} \quad \text{(f in metres)}, \qquad \text{unit: dioptre (D)} = \text{m}^{-1}$$
- Convex (converging) lens → **positive** power; concave (diverging) → **negative**.
- A shorter focal length means a **stronger** lens: f = 25 cm → P = +4 D; f = 50 cm → P = +2 D.
- Physically, power measures the angle through which the lens bends a ray at height h from the axis.

### 2.2 Combination of thin lenses in contact

For two or more thin lenses touching, powers simply **add**:
$$P = P_1 + P_2 + \cdots \qquad \frac{1}{F} = \frac{1}{f_1} + \frac{1}{f_2}$$
— the reason optometrists can stack lens powers in a trial frame.

### 2.3 Vision correction (NEB 2024, 3m)

- **Myopia (near-sight):** eyeball too long — distant objects focus **in front of** the retina. Corrected with a **concave (diverging)** lens of negative power, pushing the image back onto the retina.
- **Hypermetropia (far-sight):** eyeball too short — near objects focus **behind** the retina. Corrected with a **convex (converging)** lens of positive power, pulling the focus forward.

### 2.4 Worked numericals

**Q (2m, 2024):** Two thin lenses of powers +5 D and −2 D are placed in contact. Find the power and focal length of the combination.
$$P = +5 + (-2) = +3 \text{ D (net converging)} \qquad f = \frac{100}{P(\text{in D})} = \frac{100}{3} ≈ 33.3 \text{ cm}$$

**Q (NEB-style):** A person needs glasses of power −2.5 D. What defect do they have and what is the focal length?
Negative power → concave lens → **myopia**; f = −100/2.5 = −40 cm.

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 77:** P = 1/f converts between the two lens "currencies".
- **To Topic 78:** the lens maker's formula gives f, hence P, at design time.
- **To combinations:** adding powers is the optical analogue of adding conductances in parallel.

specificConditions: **Lens Power Definition:** Power $P = 1/f$ (in meters) measured in diopters (D). A converging lens has $P > 0$, a diverging lens has $P < 0$. Power is additive for thin lenses in contact: $P_{total} = \sum P_i$.

**Combination of Thin Lenses:** For thin lenses in contact, the total focal length is given by $1/f_{total} = \sum 1/f_i$, or equivalently $P_{total} = \sum P_i$. This assumes negligible separation between lenses. For separated lenses, use the equivalent focal length formula including the separation $d$.

**Power vs Magnification:** Lens power $P = 1/f$ relates to focal length, not directly to magnification. Magnification $m = v/u = f/(f-u)$ depends on object distance. A high-power lens (short $f$) gives larger magnification for a given object distance, but $m$ is not simply proportional to $P$.

data.title: Dimensions
notes: Dimensions express a quantity using base quantities. In mechanics, mass M, length L and time T give velocity [v]=LT⁻¹, acceleration [a]=LT⁻² and force [F]=MLT⁻².
Find dimensions from definitions: work W=Fs gives [W]=ML²T⁻²; power P=W/t gives [P]=ML²T⁻³. Pressure is force per area, [p]=ML⁻¹T⁻².
Dimensional homogeneity requires every term added in an equation to have the same dimensions. In s=ut+(1/2)at², both ut and at² have dimension L.
Worked check: in v²=u²+2as, v² and u² are L²T⁻²; as is (LT⁻²)L=L²T⁻². The equation is dimensionally possible, though this test cannot prove it is correct.
Dimensional analysis can check units and infer powers in a relation, but cannot determine dimensionless constants such as 1/2 or functions involving dimensionless variables.

A dimensional check can reject an impossible equation and can suggest the powers in a relation, but it cannot find a dimensionless number such as 1/2 or 2π. An equation that survives the check may still be wrong.

A dimensionally correct equation may still be physically wrong.
A symbol is not a number until the unit is named.
A proportional relation is not an equality until the constant is included.
A vector answer needs a direction as well as a magnitude.
A special case, such as a right angle or a steady temperature, has to be stated before it is used.

data.title: Errors
notes: Random errors vary unpredictably between readings; repeated measurements and averaging reduce their influence. Systematic errors shift results consistently because of calibration, zero offset or method and are not removed by simple repetition.
Accuracy is closeness to an accepted value; precision is agreement among repeated readings. A set can be precise but inaccurate if a systematic offset is present.
If a true value is known, absolute error is |xmeasured−xtrue|; relative error is absolute error divided by the reference value; percentage error is 100 times relative error.
Example: readings 10.2, 10.3 and 10.1 cm average to 10.2 cm. Compared with accepted 10.0 cm, absolute error is 0.2 cm and percentage error is 2%.
Check an instrument’s zero before use, repeat readings where possible, report units and uncertainty, and avoid unsupported digits beyond the instrument resolution.

A random error scatters readings both ways and shrinks when you average more of them. A systematic error, such as a zero offset, shifts every reading the same way and survives the average. You remove it by calibrating or by changing the method, not by repeating the same faulty procedure.
confusion: A small spread does not prove accuracy.
Do not report more digits than the instrument supports.
A symbol is not a number until the unit is named.
A proportional relation is not an equality until the constant is included.
A vector answer needs a direction as well as a magnitude.
A special case, such as a right angle or a steady temperature, has to be stated before it is used.

notes: Repeated readings have a mean value and a spread. A common school estimate of mean absolute error is the average of |xi−x̄|; probable error is sometimes defined as 0.6745 times the mean absolute error for normally distributed random errors.

data.title: Error Propagation & Significant Figures Rules
notes: Significant figures show how precise a measurement is. In 0.00450 m the figures that count are 4, 5 and the trailing zero; the zeros before 4 only locate the decimal point.
For multiplication or division, round the final result to the fewest significant figures among the measured inputs. For addition or subtraction, round to the least precise decimal place.
Worked case: 2.34×1.2 equals 2.808 and rounds to 2.8, because 1.2 has two significant figures. The sum 12.11+0.3 equals 12.41 and rounds to 12.4, because 0.3 is known only to tenths.
Keep guard digits through intermediate steps and round once at the end. Exact counts and defined conversion factors, such as 1 m = 100 cm, do not limit the significant figures of a result.
Relative uncertainty scales with a power. If A=πr² and r is uncertain by 1%, A is uncertain by about 2%, because the power 2 doubles the relative uncertainty before the final rounding.

data.title: Discovery of Nucleus
notes: Rutherford, Geiger and Marsden directed alpha particles at thin gold foil. Most passed almost straight through; a small fraction deflected sharply and very few returned. These observations could not be explained by positive charge spread uniformly through the atom.

Rutherford inferred a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus containing nearly all atomic mass, surrounded by electrons; most atomic volume is empty space. Nuclear radius is about 10⁻¹⁵ m versus atomic radius about 10⁻¹⁰ m.

For a head-on alpha particle, its kinetic energy converts to electrostatic potential energy at closest approach: Eα=(1/4πε₀)(2Ze²/rmin). Thus rmin=(1/4πε₀)(2Ze²/Eα), under the Coulomb-scattering model.
Nuclear notation ᴬ_ZX gives proton number Z, nucleon number A and neutron number N=A−Z. Isotopes share Z but have different A; isobars share A but have different Z.
Example: uranium-235 has Z=92, A=235 and N=143. Its nuclear charge is +92e.

data.title: Nuclear Fission and Fusion
notes: **Particle creation (pair production):** A high-energy photon (γ-ray) with energy hν ≥ 2mc² can create a particle-antiparticle pair. For electron-positron: γ → e⁺ + e⁻. The minimum photon energy is 2m_e c² = 1.022 MeV. Both rest mass energy (2mc²) and momentum must be conserved, requiring a nearby nucleus to absorb recoil.

**Pair production threshold:** For a photon to create a particle of mass m at rest, the photon must have energy at least E_min = 2mc² (for pair production). In the center-of-mass frame, the threshold is exactly 2mc². At rest, the created particles have zero kinetic energy.

**Annihilation:** When a particle meets its antiparticle, they annihilate, converting their entire rest mass into energy. e⁺ + e⁻ → γ + γ (two photons to conserve momentum). Total energy released = 2m_e c² = 1.022 MeV.

**Nuclear fission:** A heavy nucleus splits into two (or more) lighter nuclei plus neutrons, releasing large amounts of energy. Example: ²³⁵U + n → ⁹²Kr + ¹⁴¹Ba + 3n + 200 MeV. The neutrons released trigger a chain reaction.

**Chain reaction and criticality:** In ²³⁵U fission, an average of 2-3 neutrons are released per fission. If, on average, exactly one neutron causes another fission, the reaction is critical. More than one → supercritical (exponential growth). Less than one → subcritical (reaction dies out).

**Nuclear fusion:** Light nuclei combine to form heavier nuclei, releasing energy when the product has higher binding energy per nucleon. Example: ²H + ³H → ⁴He + n + 17.6 MeV. Fusion powers stars (proton-proton chain, CNO cycle) and hydrogen bombs.

**Coulomb barrier in fusion:** Positively charged nuclei repel each other (Coulomb force). To overcome this and fuse, particles need high kinetic energy (high temperature) to approach within the nuclear force range (< 10⁻¹⁵ m). This requires temperatures of 10⁷-10⁸ K.

**Deuterium-tritium (D-T) fusion:** The easiest fusion reaction to achieve on Earth. ²H + ³H → ⁴He (3.5 MeV) + n (14.1 MeV) + 17.6 MeV total. The neutron can be captured to generate heat for electricity. Requires ~100 million K.

**Proton-proton chain (solar fusion):** The dominant fusion process in stars like the Sun. 4p → ⁴He + 2e⁺ + 2ν_e + 26.7 MeV. Involves proton to neutron conversion via weak interaction (beta-plus decay).

**Fusion vs. fission energy per event:** A single U-235 fission releases ~200 MeV. A D-T fusion event releases ~17.6 MeV. However, fusion releases about 3-4 times more energy PER UNIT MASS because lighter nuclei have more nucleons.

**Controlled vs. uncontrolled reactions:** Nuclear reactors use control rods (boron, cadmium) and moderators (water, graphite) to absorb excess neutrons and control the reaction. Nuclear weapons allow uncontrolled supercritical chain reactions producing massive energy release.

**Binding energy perspective:** Fusion increases binding energy (releases energy) for nuclei lighter than iron (~8.8 MeV/nucleon). Fission increases binding energy for nuclei heavier than iron. Iron itself is the most stable — neither fission nor fusion releases energy.
confusion: Pair production requires a nucleus to conserve momentum — a photon alone cannot produce a particle-antiparticle pair even if it has enough energy, because momentum conservation would be violated if the particles are at rest.

Fusion does NOT occur in ordinary stars like the Sun because the 'fusion' of everyday materials involves atomic (electron) interactions, not nuclear. Fusion requires overcoming the Coulomb barrier at 10⁷-10⁸ K, far hotter than any chemical reaction.
Nuclear fission is NOT the same as radioactive decay. Fission requires a neutron to trigger the split; decay is spontaneous. Fission releases ∼200 MeV; decay releases typically 1-5 MeV.

The energy in nuclear reactions comes from the binding energy difference (mass defect), NOT from the rest mass of the fuel itself being 'converted.' Only Δm (the mass difference between reactants and products) converts, not the entire fuel mass.

Antimatter annihilation produces energy (E = mc²), but creating antimatter requires MORE energy than it produces. It is never an energy source on Earth — antimatter is produced in particle accelerators at enormous energy cost.

Nuclear fusion and fission are NOT just 'bigger bombs' — fusion is the opposite of fission in terms of the binding energy curve. Fusion moves nuclei toward the peak (iron); fission moves heavy nuclei toward the peak too. Both release energy by moving toward greater stability.
practice: A 1 kg block of uranium contains ³²³²U (natural uranium). How much energy is released if 0.1% of it undergoes fission, with each fission releasing 200 MeV? Solution: Number of U atoms = (1000 g/mol)/(238 g/mol) × 6.02×10²³ = 2.53×10²¹ atoms. 0.1% undergoing fission = 2.53×10¹⁸ atoms. Total energy = 2.53×10¹⁸ × 200 × 1.602×10⁻¹³ = 8.11×10⁷ J ≈ 81 MJ (enough to power a 100 W bulb for 2.3 years).

A particle accelerator produces a photon of energy 3.0 MeV. Can this photon create an electron-positron pair? Solution: Threshold for e⁺e⁻ pair production is 2m_e c² = 2 × 0.511 MeV = 1.022 MeV. Since 3.0 MeV > 1.022 MeV, YES it can. The excess energy (3.0 - 1.022 = 1.978 MeV) becomes kinetic energy of the e⁺ and e⁻.

The Sun emits energy at 3.8 × 10²⁶ W. If this comes from fusion of hydrogen into helium (4H → He + 2ν + 26.7 MeV), how many kg of hydrogen are converted to energy per second? Solution: Energy per fusion = 6.7 MeV = 6.7 × 1.602×10⁻¹³ = 1.073×10⁻¹² J. Number of fusions per second = 3.8×10²⁶ / 1.073×10⁻¹² ≈ 3.54×10³⁸. Mass per fusion = 4 × 1.67×10⁻²⁷ = 6.68×10⁻²⁷ kg. Mass to energy per second = 3.54×10³⁸ × 6.68×10⁻²⁷ = 2.37 kg. About 600 million tons of hydrogen fuse per second in the Sun.

A D-T fusion reactor produces 1 GW (10⁹ W) of power. How much fuel (in grams/year) is needed if the reactor is 50% efficient? Each D-T fusion releases 17.6 MeV. Solution: Each fusion = 17.6 × 1.602×10⁻¹³ = 2.82×10⁻¹² J. Fusions needed per second = 10⁹/(0.5 × 2.82×10⁻¹²) = 7.09×10²⁰. Mass of D+T = 2+3 = 5 u = 5×1.66×10⁻²⁷ = 8.3×10⁻²⁷ kg. Mass per second = 7.09×10²⁰ × 8.3×10⁻²⁷ = 5.88×10⁻⁶ kg/s. Per year: 5.88×10⁻⁶ × 365 × 24 × 3600 = 185 g/year.

A typical nuclear reactor uses 100 tons of uranium enriched to 3.5% U-235. How much energy is released from 1 year of full operation at 2000 MW thermal? Solution: If all 100 tons (0.035×100 = 3.5 tons of U-235) fissions: Number = 3500/238 × 6.022×10²³ = 8.83×10²⁴ atoms. Energy = 8.83×10²⁴ × 200 MeV = 8.83×10²⁴ × 200 × 1.602×10⁻¹³ J = 2.83×10¹⁴ J. Power = energy/year = 2.83×10¹⁴/(365×24×3600) ≈ 8.96×10⁶ W ≈ 9 MW (reactor does not fission all fuel in one year — fuel stays in core for years).
universalFacts: Einstein's E = mc² is a special case of the full equation E² = (mc²)² + (pc)², which applies to moving particles. At rest (p=0), this reduces to E = mc².

The binding energy curve peaks at iron-56. This is why stars stop producing energy via fusion once they form iron — fusing iron consumes energy instead of releasing it, which is the trigger for stellar collapse and supernova.

The Q-value of a nuclear reaction equals the difference in total rest mass energy (binding energy) of reactants and products: Q = (Σm_reactants - Σm_products)c². This is ALWAYS computed using the full relativistic mass-energy relation.

Pair production is not just a laboratory curiosity — it is how high-energy photons (gamma rays) interact with matter. Medical X-ray and PET imaging relies on understanding these particle creation and annihilation processes.

Both fission and fusion convert mass-energy (Δmc²) to kinetic energy of products. The energy density of nuclear fuel is millions of times greater than chemical fuel precisely because nuclear binding energies (MeV) dwarf chemical energies (eV).

data.title: Nuclear Fission and Fusion
notes: Fission splits a heavy nucleus into medium-mass fragments, often after neutron absorption. Fusion combines light nuclei. Either can release energy when products have greater total binding energy than reactants.
Reaction energy follows mass-energy conservation: Q=(mi−mf)c². Positive Q means the final rest mass is lower and the difference appears as kinetic energy, radiation or excitation.

Uranium-235 fission can release several neutrons. A sustained chain reaction requires, on average, enough neutrons to induce further fissions; a reactor controls this multiplication with neutron absorbers and moderators.

Deuterium–tritium fusion can form helium-4 and a neutron, releasing about 17.6 MeV. The positively charged nuclei must approach closely despite Coulomb repulsion, requiring high temperature and adequate confinement.
Fission is used in nuclear power stations; fusion powers stars. Practical fusion requires maintaining a hot dense plasma long enough for reaction energy to exceed losses.

Fission and fusion release energy for the same structural reason: the products sit higher on the curve of binding energy per nucleon. Fission starts from a very heavy nucleus. Fusion starts from very light ones. A typical fission releases about 200 MeV, carried by the fragments, neutrons and radiation.

specificConditions: **Fission vs Fusion Energy Release:** Both release energy by moving toward higher $BE/A$ (iron peak). Fission splits heavy nuclei ($A > 56$) into medium fragments. Fusion combines light nuclei ($A < 56$) into heavier ones. Both increase the average $BE/A$ of the system.

**Chain Reaction Requirement:** Fission of $^{235}$U by thermal neutrons produces ~2.4 fast neutrons/fission. A sustained chain reaction requires at least 1 neutron to cause another fission ($k \ge 1$). Critical mass is the minimum mass where neutron losses are balanced by productions. Moderators (graphite, water) slow neutrons to thermal energies to increase capture probability.

**Fusion Conditions:** Requires extreme temperature ($T \sim 10^7-10^8$ K) for nuclei to overcome Coulomb barrier ($kT \sim 1$ keV vs barrier $\sim 1$ MeV). data.title: Precision and Significant Figures
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Measurement Is Where Physics Begins

Physics is a quantitative science: every law is a statement about measured quantities. This topic fixes the vocabulary of measurement — SI base units, accuracy vs precision, significant figures, scientific notation, and the errors that limit every measurement. NEB asks it as short definitional questions and small numericals.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Physical quantity** | A property that can be measured, expressed as a number times a unit |
| **Fundamental (base) quantities** | Seven independent quantities: length (m), mass (kg), time (s), electric current (A), thermodynamic temperature (K), amount of substance (mol), luminous intensity (cd) |
| **Derived quantities** | Built from base quantities: velocity (m/s), force (kg·m/s² = N), etc. |
| **Accuracy** | How close a measurement is to the **true value** |
| **Precision** | How close **repeated measurements** are to each other (and the smallest step the instrument resolves) |
| **Error** | The difference between the measured value and the true value |

**Accuracy vs precision (NEB 2024):** a shooter hitting near the bull's-eye (accurate) is different from hitting the same off-centre spot every time (precise but inaccurate). Good measurement needs both.

## 3. Significant Figures — The Rules

Significant figures are the digits in a number that carry meaning — all certain digits plus one uncertain digit.

| Rule | Example |
|---|---|
| All non-zero digits are significant | 247.5 → 4 s.f. |
| Zeros between non-zero digits are significant | 2004 → 4 s.f. |
| Leading zeros are **not** significant | 0.00320 → 3 s.f. (3, 2, 0) |
| Trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant | 2.300 → 4 s.f. |
| Trailing zeros without a decimal point are ambiguous — use scientific notation | 1200 → write $1.2 \times 10^3$ (2 s.f.) or $1.200 \times 10^3$ (4 s.f.) |
| Exact counts (2 apples, 100 in a definition) have unlimited s.f. | — |

**NEB 2014:** 0.00320 m has **3 significant figures** — the leading zeros only locate the decimal point; the trailing zero after the 2 is significant.

### 3.1 Rounding rules

- Digit to drop < 5 → drop (2.34 → 2.3); > 5 → round up (2.36 → 2.4); exactly 5 → round so the last kept digit is even (2.35 → 2.4, 2.45 → 2.4).

### 3.2 Arithmetic with significant figures

| Operation | Rule |
|---|---|
| Multiplication / division | Result keeps the **fewest significant figures** of any factor: $4.2 \times 1.31 = 5.5$ (2 s.f.) |
| Addition / subtraction | Result keeps the **fewest decimal places**: $12.11 + 1.2 = 13.3$ |

## 4. Errors of Measurement

| Error type | Definition | Expression |
|---|---|---|
| **Absolute error** | Difference between a measurement and the mean (or true) value | $\Delta a = \lvert a_i - \bar a\rvert$ |
| **Relative error** | Absolute error divided by the mean value | $\Delta a / \bar a$ |
| **Percentage error** | Relative error × 100 | $(\Delta a/\bar a) \times 100\%$ |
| **Systematic error** | Repeats in one direction — faulty zero, calibration, parallax | Reduce by calibration and better technique |
| **Random error** | Scatters both ways — fluctuations | Reduce by repeating and averaging |
| **Least count error** | Half the smallest division of the instrument | Instrument-limited |

### 4.1 Propagation of errors

| Operation | Error rule |
|---|---|
| Sum/difference $Z = A \pm B$ | $\Delta Z = \Delta A + \Delta B$ (absolute errors add) |
| Product $Z = AB$ | $\Delta Z/Z = \Delta A/A + \Delta B/B$ (relative errors add) |
| Quotient $Z = A/B$ | same as product |
| Power $Z = A^n$ | $\Delta Z/Z = n\,\Delta A/A$ |

**Worked numerical (NEB 2022 style):** How many seconds in a leap year (366 days)?
$366 \times 24 \times 3600 = 3.16 \times 10^7$ s. (366 × 24 = 8,784 h; 8,784 × 3,600 = 31,622,400 s ≈ $3.16 \times 10^7$ s.)

**Worked numerical:** The length of a rod is measured as 25.0 cm with least count 0.1 cm. Express the percentage error.
Percentage error = (0.1/25.0) × 100% = **0.4%**; the length is recorded as 25.0 ± 0.1 cm.

## 5. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 2 (dimensions):** units and dimensions are the bookkeeping of measurement — dimensional analysis checks the equations that relate measured quantities.
- **To Kinematics:** every motion numerical ends with a properly rounded, properly united answer.
- **To experiments throughout:** least count, zero error and error propagation apply to every lab measurement (simple pendulum, Young's modulus, specific heat).
- **To real life:** drug dosages, engineering tolerances and weather data all carry stated uncertainties.

## 6. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 6.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

| Year | Unit | Topic | Question | Marks | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2080/2024 | Physical Quantities | Precision | What is the difference between accuracy and precision? Illustrate with an example. | 2 | Difference |
| 2071/2014 | Physical Quantities | Significant figures | Define significant figures. How many significant figures are there in 0.00320 m? | 2 | Short answer |
| 2078/2022 | Physical Quantities | Numerical | How many seconds are there in a leap year (366 days)? | 1 | Numerical |

### 6.2 Model answers

**Q1 (2m, 2024) — Accuracy vs precision with example.**
Answer: **Accuracy** is how close a measurement lies to the true value; **precision** is how closely repeated measurements agree with one another (and how fine the instrument's least count is). Example: if the true length of a rod is 25.00 cm, readings of 24.98, 24.99 and 25.01 cm are both accurate and precise; readings of 26.10, 26.11 and 26.09 cm are precise but not accurate (a systematic error); readings of 24.5, 26.0 and 25.4 cm are neither.

**Q2 (2m, 2014) — Significant figures; count in 0.00320 m.**
Answer: Significant figures are the digits in a measured quantity that are reliably known — all certain digits plus one uncertain (estimated) digit. In **0.00320 m** the leading zeros only fix the decimal point and are not significant; the digits 3, 2 and the trailing 0 are significant — so it has **3 significant figures**.

**Q3 (1m, 2022) — Seconds in a leap year.**
Answer: 366 days × 24 h/day × 3,600 s/h = 31,622,400 s ≈ **$3.16 \times 10^7$ s**.

### 6.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Counting leading zeros as significant (0.00320 has 3, not 5).
2. Confusing accuracy with precision — accuracy needs the true value; precision needs only repeatability.
3. Keeping too many digits in a numerical answer — round to the least precise factor.
4. Writing percentage error without units of the quantity or without the ± notation.
5. Mixing up systematic (one-directional) and random (scattering) errors.
confusion: **Accuracy vs precision:** accuracy compares with the true value; precision compares repeated measurements with each other — a precise instrument can be inaccurate if mis-calibrated.
**Least count vs error:** the least count is the smallest step the instrument can read; the least-count error is half of it.

The uncertainty comes from the least count of the instrument, and the answer keeps two significant figures consistent with the measurement.

data.summary: Measurement is the foundation of physics: seven SI base units (m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd) generate every derived unit. **Accuracy** is closeness to the true value; **precision** is agreement among repeats — an instrument can be precise yet inaccurate. Significant figures carry the reliability of a number: leading zeros never count (0.00320 m has 3 s.f.), trailing zeros after a decimal point do; multiplication keeps the fewest significant figures, addition the fewest decimal places. Errors come as absolute, relative and percentage, split into systematic (one-directional, fixable by calibration) and random (scattering, reduced by averaging), and propagate through calculations — powers multiply relative error by the exponent. Every measured answer must end rounded, united and honest about its uncertainty.

Note 2: In NEB numericals, always carry one extra guard digit through the working and round only the FINAL answer.
Note 3: Angular measure in radians is dimensionless but its precision still limits results in formulas like $s = r\theta$.
Note 4: Instruments: vernier callipers (0.01 cm) and screw gauge (0.001 cm) reduce least count — the practical way to gain significant figures.

data.topicTitle: Dimensions and uses of dimensional analysis
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Grammar of Physical Equations

Dimensions express every physical quantity in terms of the base quantities M, L, T (and I, Θ, N, J when needed). Dimensional analysis is the grammar check of physics: it tests whether an equation can be correct, derives relations, converts units and finds the units of unknown constants — the working tool behind every formula in this course.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Dimensional formula** | A quantity written as powers of base dimensions, e.g. force = $[MLT^{-2}]$ |
| **Dimensional equation** | The equation equating a quantity to its dimensional formula: $[F] = MLT^{-2}$ |
| **Dimensional vs dimensionless** | Angle, strain, relative density, refractive index, coefficient of friction have **no dimensions** |
| **Principle of homogeneity** | A physically correct equation must have the **same dimensions in every term** — you cannot add length to time |

### 2.1 Dimensional formulas to memorise

| Quantity | Formula | SI unit |
|---|---|---|
| Velocity | $LT^{-1}$ | m/s |
| Acceleration | $LT^{-2}$ | m/s² |
| Force | $MLT^{-2}$ | N |
| Work / energy / torque* | $ML^2T^{-2}$ | J (torque: N·m, same dimensions) |
| Power | $ML^2T^{-3}$ | W |
| Pressure / stress | $ML^{-1}T^{-2}$ | Pa |
| Momentum / impulse | $MLT^{-1}$ | kg·m/s |
| Gravitational constant G | $M^{-1}L^3T^{-2}$ | N·m²/kg² |
| Planck's constant h | $ML^2T^{-1}$ | J·s |
| Surface tension | $MT^{-2}$ | N/m |

*Work and torque share dimensions but are different quantities — dimensional analysis cannot distinguish them.

## 3. Uses of Dimensional Analysis

1. **Checking (verifying) equations — homogeneity test.** Every term must share dimensions.
2. **Deriving relations.** If $T \propto l^a m^b g^c$ for a pendulum, dimensional balance gives $a = 1/2$, $b = 0$, $c = -1/2$ → $T = k\sqrt{l/g}$.
3. **Converting units** between systems: $n_2 = n_1 (M_1/M_2)^a (L_1/L_2)^b (T_1/T_2)^c$ for a quantity with dimensions $M^aL^bT^c$.
4. **Finding dimensions/units of unknown constants** in given equations.
5. **Order-of-magnitude checks** of formulas.

### 3.1 Limitations

- Cannot determine **dimensionless constants** ($k$, $1/2$, $2\pi$).
- Cannot derive equations containing **added** dimensionally different terms or trigonometric/exponential/log functions of angles.
- Cannot distinguish quantities with identical dimensions (work vs torque; speed vs emf-like ratios).

### 3.2 Verifying equations (NEB 2017, 2023)

**Check $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$:**
- LHS: $[s] = L$.
- $[ut] = LT^{-1} \cdot T = L$ ✓
- $[\frac{1}{2}at^2] = LT^{-2} \cdot T^2 = L$ ✓ (the factor ½ is dimensionless)
All terms have dimension L — **dimensionally correct**.

**Check $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$:**
- LHS: $[v^2] = L^2T^{-2}$.
- $[u^2] = L^2T^{-2}$ ✓; $[2as] = LT^{-2} \cdot L = L^2T^{-2}$ ✓ — **dimensionally correct**.

**Convert 5 kg into grams by dimensional analysis (NEB 2015):**
Mass has dimension M. With $n_1 = 5$ kg, $M_1 = 1$ kg, $M_2 = 1$ g: $n_2 = n_1(M_1/M_2)^1 = 5 \times (1000\,\text{g}/1\,\text{g}) = 5000$ g. The **principle of homogeneity/consistency of dimensions** — the physical quantity is unchanged when its unit changes; only the numerical value compensates.

**NEB 2022 MCQ:** kg m² s⁻² = $ML^2T^{-2}$ = **work** (also energy/torque's dimensions — of the options, work).

## 4. Conceptual Relationships

notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Grammar of Physical Equations

Dimensions express every physical quantity in terms of the base quantities M, L, T (and I, Θ, N, J when needed). Dimensional analysis is the grammar check of physics: it tests whether an equation can be correct, derives relations, converts units and finds the units of unknown constants — the working tool behind every formula in this course.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Dimensional formula** | A quantity written as powers of base dimensions, e.g. force = $[MLT^{-2}]$ |
| **Dimensional equation** | The equation equating a quantity to its dimensional formula: $[F] = MLT^{-2}$ |
| **Dimensional vs dimensionless** | Angle, strain, relative density, refractive index, coefficient of friction have **no dimensions** |
| **Principle of homogeneity** | A physically correct equation must have the **same dimensions in every term** — you cannot add length to time |

### 2.1 Dimensional formulas to memorise

| Quantity | Formula | SI unit |
|---|---|---|
| Velocity | $LT^{-1}$ | m/s |
| Acceleration | $LT^{-2}$ | m/s² |
| Force | $MLT^{-2}$ | N |
| Work / energy / torque* | $ML^2T^{-2}$ | J (torque: N·m, same dimensions) |
| Power | $ML^2T^{-3}$ | W |
| Pressure / stress | $ML^{-1}T^{-2}$ | Pa |
| Momentum / impulse | $MLT^{-1}$ | kg·m/s |
| Gravitational constant G | $M^{-1}L^3T^{-2}$ | N·m²/kg² |
| Planck's constant h | $ML^2T^{-1}$ | J·s |
| Surface tension | $MT^{-2}$ | N/m |

*Work and torque share dimensions but are different quantities — dimensional analysis cannot distinguish them.

## 3. Uses of Dimensional Analysis

1. **Checking (verifying) equations — homogeneity test.** Every term must share dimensions.
2. **Deriving relations.** If $T \propto l^a m^b g^c$ for a pendulum, dimensional balance gives $a = 1/2$, $b = 0$, $c = -1/2$ → $T = k\sqrt{l/g}$.
3. **Converting units** between systems: $n_2 = n_1 (M_1/M_2)^a (L_1/L_2)^b (T_1/T_2)^c$ for a quantity with dimensions $M^aL^bT^c$.
4. **Finding dimensions/units of unknown constants** in given equations.
5. **Order-of-magnitude checks** of formulas.

### 3.1 Limitations

- Cannot determine **dimensionless constants** ($k$, $1/2$, $2\pi$).
- Cannot derive equations containing **added** dimensionally different terms or trigonometric/exponential/log functions of angles.
- Cannot distinguish quantities with identical dimensions (work vs torque; speed vs emf-like ratios).

### 3.2 Verifying equations (NEB 2017, 2023)

**Check $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$:**
- LHS: $[s] = L$.
- $[ut] = LT^{-1} \cdot T = L$ ✓
- $[\frac{1}{2}at^2] = LT^{-2} \cdot T^2 = L$ ✓ (the factor ½ is dimensionless)
All terms have dimension L — **dimensionally correct**.

**Check $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$:**
- LHS: $[v^2] = L^2T^{-2}$.
- $[u^2] = L^2T^{-2}$ ✓; $[2as] = LT^{-2} \cdot L = L^2T^{-2}$ ✓ — **dimensionally correct**.

**Convert 5 kg into grams by dimensional analysis (NEB 2015):**
Mass has dimension M. With $n_1 = 5$ kg, $M_1 = 1$ kg, $M_2 = 1$ g: $n_2 = n_1(M_1/M_2)^1 = 5 \times (1000\,\text{g}/1\,\text{g}) = 5000$ g. The **principle of homogeneity/consistency of dimensions** — the physical quantity is unchanged when its unit changes; only the numerical value compensates.

**NEB 2022 MCQ:** kg m² s⁻² = $ML^2T^{-2}$ = **work** (also energy/torque's dimensions — of the options, work).

data.title: Potential Difference, Potential Due to a Point Charge, Potential Energy and Electron Volt
data.topicTitle: Potential difference, potential due to point charge, potential energy and electron volt
notes: **Electrostatic Potential & Potential Difference:** Electric potential at a point P is defined as the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a test charge q₀ from infinity to P against the electrostatic force of the source distribution, without altering the field: $V = \frac{W}{q_0} = -\int_\infty^P \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{r}$. Potential difference between two points A and B is $\Delta V = V_B - V_A = -\int_A^B \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{r}$. Both V and ΔV are scalars, have SI unit volt (V), where $1\,\text{V} = 1\,\text{J/C}$, and are path-independent because the electrostatic field is conservative ($\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{r} = 0$).

**Potential due to an Isolated Point Charge:** For a source charge Q at the origin, the work done in bringing q₀ from infinity to distance r is $W = -\int_\infty^r \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 x^2} dx = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{Q q_0}{r}$. Dividing by q₀ gives the potential: $V(r) = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q}{r} = k\frac{Q}{r}$. Unlike electric field (which is a vector falling off as 1/r²), potential is a scalar that falls off only as 1/r. For an ensemble of point charges, superposition applies algebraically: $V = k \sum_i \frac{q_i}{r_i}$.

**Relation between Electric Field and Potential Gradient:** The electric field and potential are intrinsically related. Since $V = -\int \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{r}$, we obtain $\vec{E} = -\vec{\nabla}V$. For a uniform field directed along the x-axis: $E = -\frac{dV}{dx}$. This is the foundational link that converts every electrostatic field formula into a corresponding potential formula, always by substituting $E \propto 1/r^2$ with $V \propto 1/r$.

**Potential of Standard Charge Distributions:** (1) **Line charge:** $V = -\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0}\ln(r/r_0)$; (2) **Infinite plane sheet:** $V = -\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}x$ (linear decrease, since E is constant); (3) **Charged conducting shell (radius R, charge Q):** $V = kQ/R$ everywhere inside and on the surface, jumping to $V = kQ/r$ outside — a discontinuity of exactly $E R = \sigma R/\varepsilon_0$; (4) **Two parallel plates separated by d:** $E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$ and $V_{AB} = -Ed = -\frac{\sigma d}{\varepsilon_0}$.

**Potential Energy of a System of Charges:** The potential energy of a charge q brought from infinity into the field of source charge Q is $U = qV = k\frac{qQ}{r}$. For two like charges ($qQ > 0$), U is positive, meaning work must be done against repulsion; for two unlike charges ($qQ < 0$), U is negative, indicating the system is bound and energy is released on assembly. For multiple charges, the total energy is the sum over all distinct pairs: $U = k \sum_{i<j} \frac{q_i q_j}{r_{ij}}$. Energy is a scalar and must never be computed by summing $\vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r}$ naively over individual pairs for conservative systems.

**Equivalence of Potential Energy and Force:** By the work-energy theorem, the work done by the electrostatic force in moving a charge slowly from A to B is $W = q(V_A - V_B) = -\Delta U$. Therefore $\Delta U = -W_{electric}$, proving that $\Delta U = -\int \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r}$. This means a force always acts to reduce potential energy: a positive charge accelerates toward lower V, and a negative charge accelerates toward higher V.

**Electron Volt (eV) — Energy Unit Conversion:** The electron volt is the energy gained by a particle of charge e when accelerated through a potential difference of one volt: $1\,\text{eV} = e \times 1\,\text{V} = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C} \times 1\,\text{J/C} = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$. Convenient conversion factors: $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$ and $1\,\text{J} = 6.242 \times 10^{18}\,\text{eV}$. Multiples are commonly used: $1\,\text{keV} = 10^3\,\text{eV}$ (X-rays), $1\,\text{MeV} = 10^6\,\text{eV}$ (particle accelerators, nuclear binding), and $1\,\text{GeV} = 10^9\,\text{eV}$ (collider experiments). Note that electron volt is an energy unit, not a charge or potential unit.
confusion: Treating potential as a vector and adding components: Potential V is a scalar. Only in a region with a clear directional symmetry (e.g. along the axis of a line charge) is it meaningful to write $V = -Ex$; you must never resolve V into vector components like x, y, z components.

Confusing potential difference with potential: Potential difference is a change $\Delta V = V_B - V_A$ between two points and can be positive or negative. Potential V itself is defined relative to infinity ($V_\infty = 0$), so a positive charge gives positive V while an electron gives negative V.

Believing the electron volt is a unit of charge or potential: The electron volt (eV) is a unit of ENERGY, defined as the energy of a charge of magnitude e accelerated through 1 V. 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

Computing total potential energy by summing over all ordered pairs (i, j) instead of distinct pairs (i < j): Every interaction must be counted exactly once; summing both $q_i q_j$ and $q_j q_i$ double-counts each pair energy.
practice: Two charges $q_1 = +2\,\mu\text{C}$ and $q_2 = -3\,\mu\text{C}$ are separated by $30\,\text{cm}$ in vacuum. (a) Find the potential at the midpoint. (b) Find the potential energy of the system. Solution: (a) At the midpoint, $r_1 = r_2 = 0.15\,\text{m}$, so $V = k\left(\frac{q_1}{r_1} + \frac{q_2}{r_2}\right) = (9 \times 10^9)\left(\frac{2 \times 10^{-6} - 3 \times 10^{-6}}{0.15}\right) = (9 \times 10^9)\left(\frac{-1 \times 10^{-6}}{0.15}\right) = (9 \times 10^9)(-6.67 \times 10^{-6}) = -6.0 \times 10^4\,\text{V}$. (b) $U = k\frac{q_1 q_2}{r} = (9 \times 10^9)\frac{(2 \times 10^{-6})(-3 \times 10^{-6})}{0.30} = (9 \times 10^9)(-2 \times 10^{-11}) = -1.8 \times 10^{-1}\,\text{J} = -0.18\,\text{J}$.
universalFacts: The electron volt is named after the electron but is a universal energy unit: an alpha particle with charge +2e accelerated through 1 V gains 2 eV, while a proton accelerated through the same 1 V gains 1 eV.

The resting membrane potential of a human nerve axon (about −70 mV measured inside relative to outside) corresponds to a stored energy of roughly 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰ J per ion crossing the membrane, which is the physical basis of neural signaling.
examples: Electron gun in a cathode ray tube: Electrons accelerated through a potential difference V gain kinetic energy eV. For V = 10 kV, each electron gains 10 keV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ J, which determines the spot size on the fluorescent screen.

Photocell and photoelectric effect: Incoming photons with energies quoted in electron volts (visible light ≈ 1.5–3 eV, UV up to tens of eV) eject photoelectrons only if the photon energy exceeds the work function, the basis of all photoelectric devices.

Nucleosome-free grounding of tall buildings: Lightning-induced potential differences of 10⁸ V are bled harmlessly to earth through lightning rods and thick grounding strips, since $W = qV$ for a large charge at huge potential would otherwise be catastrophic.
practiceQuestions: Q1. Define electrostatic potential at a point. State its SI unit and dimensional formula, and explain why electric potential is a scalar while electric field is a vector.
Q2. Derive an expression for the potential at a point due to a point charge Q, and compare its distance dependence with that of the electric field.
Q3. A charge q is brought from infinity to a point in the field of a dipole of moment p placed along the x-axis. Show that the potential energy is $U = -kq p \cos\theta / r^2$.

Q4. An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 500 V. Calculate the energy gained in joules and in electron volts, and the resulting speed. (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg)
formulas: Potential: $V = \frac{W}{q_0} = -\int_\infty^P \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{r}$
Potential difference: $\Delta V = V_B - V_A = -\int_A^B \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{r}$
Potential due to point charge: $V = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{Q}{r} = k\frac{Q}{r}$
Field–potential link: $\vec{E} = -\vec{\nabla}V$
Potential energy of two charges: $U = k\frac{q_1 q_2}{r}$
System potential energy: $U = k\sum_{i<j} \frac{q_i q_j}{r_{ij}}$
Energy–work relation: $\Delta U = -W_{electric}$
Electron volt: $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$
keyPoints: Potential V is work done per unit positive charge; SI unit is volt (1 V = 1 J/C).
Potential is a path-independent scalar; electric field is a vector with direction given by -∇V.
Potential due to a point charge falls as 1/r, while its electric field falls as 1/r².
Like charges give positive U (repulsive, unbound); unlike charges give negative U (attractive, bound).
1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, an energy unit; 1 MeV = 10⁶ eV is standard in nuclear physics.
data.summary: Electrostatic potential V is the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a test charge from infinity, given by V = -∫E·dr, with SI unit the volt. A point charge Q produces V = kQ/r, falling as 1/r (compared with the field's 1/r²), and fields and potentials are linked by E = -∇V. The potential energy of a charge system is U = kΣqᵢqⱼ/rᵢⱼ, positive for like charges and negative for unlike charges, with ΔU = -W_electric. The electron volt is an energy unit where 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
specialNotes: Electric potential can be zero at a point even where the field is non-zero (the equatorial point of a dipole, and the null point of a dipole field). Only the electric field is guaranteed to be non-zero wherever a charge feels a force.
Inside a hollow charged conductor the potential is constant (not zero): V = kQ/R, whereas the electric field there is zero. Zero field does not imply zero potential.

Because V depends on position but not on the path taken, a charge can reach a point via any route with identical work done, which is why parallel-plate capacitor calculations ignore the fringing geometry at the edges.
importantStatements: Statement 1: Electric potential at a point is defined as the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a test charge from infinity to that point.
Statement 2: The potential due to a point charge varies inversely with distance (V ∝ 1/r), whereas the electric field varies inversely with distance squared (E ∝ 1/r²).
Statement 3: The electric field at any point is the negative gradient of the potential at that point (E = -∇V).

Statement 4: The potential energy of two like charges is positive, indicating a repulsive, unbound configuration, whereas for two unlike charges it is negative, indicating an attractive, bound configuration.
Statement 5: One electron volt is the energy gained by an electron accelerated through a potential difference of one volt, equal to 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
importantNotes: The SI unit of potential is the volt (V), where 1 V = 1 J/C, and its dimensional formula is [M L² T⁻³ I⁻¹], identical to that of energy per unit charge.
examShortTricks: Field-to-potential conversion trick: whenever E ∝ 1/r², the corresponding potential is V ∝ 1/r; whenever E ∝ 1/r, the potential is V ∝ ln r.
Sign check: a positive charge always moves toward lower V, while a negative charge moves toward higher V, since force always acts to reduce potential energy.
eV conversion: multiply eV by 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ to get joules, or divide joules by 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ to get eV.
examNotes: Derivation of potential due to a point charge and of potential energy of a charge system, together with the eV-J conversion, forms a frequently asked 5-mark long question in NEB Class 11 Physics.

mcs.question: An electron is accelerated through a potential difference of 100 V. The energy gained in joules is:
mcs.explanation: Energy gained = qV = (1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)(100 V) = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁷ J, which is equivalent to 100 eV.

mcs.question: Two charges +2 μC and -2 μC are separated by 1 m. The potential energy of the system is:
mcs.explanation: U = kq₁q₂/r. Since q₁q₂ = (2 × 10⁻⁶)(−2 × 10⁻⁶) < 0, the product is negative, so U is negative, corresponding to an attractive and bound configuration.

mcs.explanation: E = 0 means the field has no local variation of potential, but the potential itself can take any value. At the midpoint between two equal positive charges, E = 0 yet V = 2kQ/r ≠ 0.

data.title: Equipotential Lines and Surfaces
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Walking Uphill Without Effort

Move a charge along an equipotential surface and you do no work — like walking along a contour line at constant altitude. Equipotentials turn energy thinking into geometry: where surfaces crowd, fields are strong; where they are flat, nothing pushes.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2024)

### 2.1 Definition

**Equipotential surfaces** are surfaces (real or imaginary) over which the electric potential is constant. Every point on one has the same V — a contour map of the electric landscape.

### 2.2 Properties (NEB 2024, 3m)

1. **No work** is done in moving a charge along an equipotential surface ($W = q\,\Delta V = 0$).
2. **Field lines always cross equipotential surfaces at right angles** — the field has no component along the surface.
3. **Two equipotential surfaces never intersect** — one point cannot have two potential values.
4. Surfaces are **crowded where the field is strong**, widely spaced where weak.
5. A conductor's surface in equilibrium is an equipotential; the whole interior is at one potential.

### 2.3 Standard pictures

- **Point charge:** concentric spheres (V = kq/r), field radial.
- **Uniform field (parallel plates):** equally spaced parallel planes perpendicular to E.
- **Dipole:** lobed surfaces symmetric about the axis.

### 2.4 Worked reasoning

**Q (3m, 2024):** What are equipotential surfaces? Write any three of their properties.
— Definition + any three properties from §2.2.

**Q (NEB-style):** Why must field lines meet equipotential surfaces at 90°?
If a field line had a component along the surface, moving a charge along that component would change potential — contradicting the surface being equipotential. Hence E ⊥ surface.

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 90:** the surface is the locus V = constant of the potential field.
- **To Topic 92:** E = −dV/dr — zero component along the surface is the same statement geometrically.
- **To conductors:** the entire conductor in equilibrium is one equipotential region.

## 4. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 4.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

| Year | Unit | Topic | Question | Marks | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2080/2024 | Electricity | Potential | What are equipotential surfaces? Write any three of their properties. | 3 | Definition + properties |

### 4.2 Likely additional forms (NEB-style)

1. Draw equipotentials for a point charge and for parallel plates (2m).
2. Why is no work done moving along an equipotential? (2m)
3. Sketch field lines and equipotentials together (3m).

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Saying work is "small" along an equipotential — it is exactly **zero**.
2. Drawing field lines parallel to equipotential surfaces instead of perpendicular.
3. Forgetting that intersecting surfaces would force two potentials at one point.

mcs.question: The work done in moving a charge q from one equipotential surface to another surface at a higher potential is:
mcs.explanation: W = qΔV where ΔV is the potential difference between the two surfaces. This is non-zero because the surfaces are not equipotential with each other.

mcs.explanation: Since V = kQ/r, V is constant for a fixed value of r, which is the equation of a sphere centred on the charge. Hence equipotentials are concentric spheres.

data.title: Newton's law of cooling
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — Cooling by the Clock

Hot tea cools fast at first, then slowly — the rate of heat loss is proportional to how much hotter it is than the room. Newton's law of cooling turns that observation into an exponential law, the basis of calorimetry corrections and forensic time-of-death estimates.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Statement

**The rate of loss of heat of a body is directly proportional to the difference between its temperature and the temperature of the surroundings** (for small temperature differences):
$$-\frac{dQ}{dt} \propto (T - T_s) \Rightarrow -\frac{dQ}{dt} = k(T - T_s)$$

With $dQ = mc\,dT$:
$$\frac{dT}{dt} = -\frac{k}{mc}(T - T_s) \Rightarrow T - T_s = (T_0 - T_s)\,e^{-kt/mc}$$
— the excess temperature decays **exponentially**.

### 2.2 Conditions and limitations

- Valid for **small excess temperatures** (ΔT ≲ 20–30 K) where heat loss is mainly by convection/draught.
- Surroundings temperature $T_s$ must stay constant.
- Fails for large ΔT where radiation (∝ T⁴, Stefan–Boltzmann) dominates.

### 2.3 Cooling-curve method for specific heat

Plot temperature vs time; the **slope** $dT/dt$ at any temperature gives the cooling rate. Comparing two liquids in identical calorimeters under identical conditions:
$$\frac{(mc)_{liquid}}{(mc)_{water}} = \frac{(dT/dt)_{liquid}}{(dT/dt)_{water}} \quad \text{(at the same mean temperature)}$$
— the basis of the "cooling rates" method for unknown specific heat.

### 2.4 Worked numericals

**Q (NEB-style):** A body at 80 °C cools to 70 °C in 2 minutes with surroundings at 30 °C. Estimate the time to cool from 70 °C to 60 °C (Newton's law, average-excess method).
- Average excess 1st interval: 75−30 = 45; rate ∝ 45 → cooling rate 5 °C/2 min.
- 2nd interval average excess: 65−30 = 35; rate ∝ 35 → rate = 5×(35/45) = 3.9 °C per 2 min → time = 2×(45/35) = **2.6 min**.

**Q (NEB-style):** Water at 90 °C cools to 60 °C in 10 min with room at 20 °C. Using T − T_s = (T₀ − T_s)e^(−kt/mc), find the constant.
- (60−20)/(90−20) = 4/7 = e^(−10k') → k' = ln(7/4)/10 = 0.0561 min⁻¹ (where k' = k/mc).
- Temperature after another 10 min: 20 + 40×e^(−1.122) = 20 + 13.1 = 33.1 °C.

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 51:** cooling-curve comparison determines specific heat.
- **To Stefan–Boltzmann (Unit 12):** the law is the small-ΔT approximation of radiative+convective loss.
- **To exponential decay:** same mathematics as RC discharge and radioactive decay.

## 4. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 4.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

No verified PYQ for this exact topic in the bank. Practise the statement, the exponential form and cooling-rate numericals as **NEB-style practice**.

### 4.2 Likely question forms

1. State Newton's law of cooling (2m).
2. Derive the exponential cooling equation (4m).
3. Two-interval cooling numerical (3m).

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Applying the law at large temperature differences.
2. Forgetting the surrounding temperature in the exponential.
3. Confusing rate of heat loss (J/s) with rate of temperature fall (K/s) — related by mc.

data.summary: **Newton's law of cooling**: the rate of heat loss is proportional to the excess temperature over the surroundings, $-dQ/dt = k(T - T_s)$, valid for small ΔT. With $dQ = mc\,dT$ it integrates to $T - T_s = (T_0 - T_s)e^{-kt/mc}$ — excess temperature decays exponentially, which is why hot tea cools fast then slowly. Comparing cooling slopes of two liquids in identical calorimeters at the same mean temperature yields the unknown specific heat. Beyond small ΔT, radiation (Stefan–Boltzmann) takes over and the law fails; forensic time-of-death estimates still use it as the working approximation.

data.title: Specific Heat Capacity
notes: **Specific Heat Capacity:** This topic covers the fundamental concepts of specific heat capacity in the physics curriculum.
Understanding specific heat capacity is essential for solving problems and building higher-level mathematical skills.
Key definitions and theorems related to specific heat capacity should be memorized and practiced regularly.

**Definition:** Specific heat capacity ($c$) is the amount of heat energy required to raise the temperature of **1 kg** (SI) or **1 g** (CGS) of a substance by **1 K** (or 1°C). It is an intrinsic property of the material.
**Formula:** From $H = mc\Delta\theta$, solving for $c$: **$c = \frac{H}{m \cdot \Delta\theta}$**. This shows $c$ is the heat per unit mass per unit temperature change.

**Water - the benchmark:** $c_{water} = 4186\text{ J/kg·K}$ (more precisely 4181.3 J/kg·K at 15°C, but 4200 J/kg·K is standard for exam work). This is unusually high compared to most substances, making water an excellent thermal buffer.

**Ice vs. liquid water:** $c_{ice} \approx 2100\text{ J/kg·K}$ - about HALF of liquid water's specific heat. This means ice heats up twice as fast as liquid water for the same mass. During melting, the $c$ changes discontinuously.

**Metals - low specific heats:** Copper: $c = 390\text{ J/kg·K}$, Aluminum: $c = 900\text{ J/kg·K}$, Iron: $c = 450\text{ J/kg·K}$, Lead: $c = 130\text{ J/kg·K}$, Gold: $c = 129\text{ J/kg·K}$. Low $c$ means metals respond quickly to heating - useful for cookware, bad for thermal storage.

**Solids (Dulong-Petit Law):** For most solid elements at room temperature, $c \times M \approx 25\text{ J/mol·K}$ (molar heat capacity). So $c \approx 25/M$ where $M$ is molar mass in kg/mol. Heavy atoms → low $c$ per kg; light atoms → high $c$ per kg.

**Liquids:** Water: 4186, Ethanol: 2440, Mercury: 140, Glycerin: 2430, Ammonia (liquid): 4700. Gases have two specific heats ($c_p$ and $c_v$); most liquids have only one since they don't expand significantly.

**Gases - two specific heats:** For gases, $c_p > c_v$ always. At constant pressure, gas expands and does work, needing MORE heat for the same temperature rise. For air: $c_p = 1005\text{ J/kg·K}$, $c_v = 718\text{ J/kg·K}$. Ratio $\gamma = c_p/c_v \approx 1.4$.

**Temperature dependence:** Specific heat capacity is NOT truly constant - it varies with temperature. For water, $c$ changes from 4217 J/kg·K at 0°C to 4181 J/kg·K at 15°C to 4219 J/kg·K at 100°C. For most school problems, treat $c$ as constant.

**Molar heat capacity vs. specific heat:** Molar heat capacity $C_m = c \times M$ (where $M$ = molar mass). For water: $C_m = 4186 \times 0.018 = 75.3\text{ J/mol·K}$. This is useful for comparing substances on a per-molecule basis.

**Why specific heat differs:** The specific heat depends on how energy is distributed among molecular degrees of freedom. Monatomic gases store energy only in translation (3 DOF). Diatomic gases also store in rotation (2 DOF). Polyatomic molecules add vibration. More ways to store energy → higher $c$.

**Water's anomalous value:** Water's $c = 4186$ is about 5× that of copper and 10× that of lead. This is because water molecules form hydrogen bonds that must be partially broken before molecules can move faster (higher temperature). This "hidden" energy cost makes $c$ high.

**Practical - mixing two substances:** When a hot substance (mass $m_1$, $c_1$, $T_1$) is mixed with a cold substance ($m_2$, $c_2$, $T_2$), the equilibrium temperature is: $T_{eq} = \frac{m_1 c_1 T_1 + m_2 c_2 T_2}{m_1 c_1 + m_2 c_2}$. This is a weighted average by heat capacity.

**NEB focus:** Know the formula $H = mc\Delta\theta$, the values of $c$ for water and common metals, the distinction between $c$ and heat capacity ($C = mc$), and unit conversion between J/kg·K and cal/g·°C ($1\text{ J/kg·K} = 0.000239\text{ cal/g·°C}$).

**Common misconception:** "Specific" means "per unit mass" - it does NOT mean "typical" or "usual." Specific heat capacity is a very specific property that varies enormously between materials. Gold ($c=129$) and water ($c=4186$) differ by a factor of 32.

**SI unit:** $\text{J} \cdot \text{kg}^{-1} \cdot \text{K}^{-1}$ (joule per kilogram per kelvin). Since a temperature INTERVAL of 1 K equals 1°C, this is also written as $\text{J} \cdot \text{kg}^{-1} \cdot \text{°C}^{-1}$.

**CGS unit:** $\text{cal} \cdot \text{g}^{-1} \cdot \text{°C}^{-1}$ (calorie per gram per degree Celsius). Numerically, water has $c = 1\text{ cal/g·°C}$ in CGS, making calculations simpler in this system.

**Conversion between systems:** $1\text{ J/kg·K} = 0.000239\text{ cal/g·°C}$. Conversely, $1\text{ cal/g·°C} = 4184\text{ J/kg·K}$. The factor 4184 comes from $1\text{ cal} = 4.184\text{ J}$ and $1\text{ g} = 0.001\text{ kg}$.

**Dimensional formula derivation:** $c = \frac{H}{m \cdot \Delta\theta}$. Heat $H$ has the same dimensions as energy: $[ML^2T^{-2}]$. Mass: $[M]$. Temperature: $[\Theta]$ (or $[K]$). Therefore: **$[c] = [M^0 L^2 T^{-2} \Theta^{-1}]$**.
**Dimensionless mass:** Notice $[M^0]$ - mass cancels out. This reflects that specific heat is an INTENSIVE property. Two objects of the same material but different masses have the same $c$.
**Alternative form using force:** Since work = force × distance, $[H] = [MLT^{-2}] \cdot [L] = [ML^2T^{-2}]$. So $[c] = [ML^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}] / ([M][\Theta]) = [L^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}]$.

**Common values in both systems:** Water: $1\text{ cal/g·°C} = 4186\text{ J/kg·K}$. Ice: $0.5\text{ cal/g·°C} = 2100\text{ J/kg·K}$. Copper: $0.093\text{ cal/g·°C} = 390\text{ J/kg·K}$. Aluminum: $0.215\text{ cal/g·°C} = 900\text{ J/kg·K}$.
**Dimensional check example:** For $H = mc\Delta\theta$: $[H] = [M] \cdot [L^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}] \cdot [\Theta] = [ML^2T^{-2}]$. This matches the dimension of energy. ✓
**Heat capacity dimensional formula:** $C = mc$, so $[C] = [M] \cdot [L^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}] = [ML^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}]$. Unlike specific heat, heat capacity DOES depend on mass (it's extensive).

**Molar heat capacity dimensions:** $C_m = c \times M$ (molar mass), so $[C_m] = [L^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}] \cdot [M] = [ML^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}]$. Same dimensions as specific heat, but per mole instead of per kg.
**In terms of base SI units:** $[c] = [kg^0 \cdot m^2 \cdot s^{-2} \cdot K^{-1}] = [m^2 \cdot s^{-2} \cdot K^{-1}]$. This is the simplest form - just length-squared per time-squared per kelvin.

**Why $\Theta$ appears in the denominator:** Specific heat is defined PER UNIT TEMPERATURE CHANGE. If $\Delta\theta$ doubles, $H$ doubles. The $\Theta^{-1}$ dimension captures this inverse proportionality.

**Practical importance of correct units:** In $H = mc\Delta\theta$, if $m$ is in kg and $c$ in J/kg·K, then $H$ is in joules. If $m$ is in g and $c$ in cal/g·°C, then $H$ is in calories. Mixing systems (e.g., kg with cal/g·°C) gives WRONG answers.
**NEB exam focus:** Be able to derive $[c] = [M^0L^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}]$, convert between J/kg·K and cal/g·°C, and use the correct units consistently in numerical problems.

**Dimensional homogeneity test:** Any correct formula for heat must have $[H] = [ML^2T^{-2}]$ on both sides. If a proposed formula gives different dimensions, it is immediately wrong - no calculation needed.
confusion: Carefully distinguish between similar-looking concepts in specific heat capacity.
Pay attention to the conditions under which formulas and theorems apply.
Practice with multiple examples to solidify your understanding.

❌ Specific heat capacity is the same for all states of a substance. ✅ Ice ($c=2100$), liquid water ($c=4186$), and steam ($c=2010$) all have different specific heats. The value changes at phase transitions.

❌ Specific heat depends on the shape/size of the object. ✅ Specific heat is an INTENSIVE property - it depends only on the material, not on the object's shape, size, or mass. A gold ring and a gold bar have the same $c$.

❌ $c_p$ and $c_v$ are the same for all substances. ✅ For solids and liquids, $c_p \approx c_v$ because they barely expand. For gases, $c_p > c_v$ significantly because gases expand and do work. The difference is $c_p - c_v = R/M$ (per kg) or $R$ (per mole).

❌ A substance with high specific heat is always "hotter." ✅ High $c$ means the substance RESISTS temperature change - it takes a lot of heat to raise its temperature. Water at 20°C has high $c$ but isn't "hot" - it just requires a lot of energy to change its temperature.

❌ The specific heat of water is 1 cal/g·°C everywhere. ✅ The calorie is DEFINED using water's specific heat, but that specific heat varies slightly with temperature. At 15°C, $c = 4.1855\text{ J/g·K}$ (giving 1 cal = 4.1855 J). The modern exact value is $1\text{ cal} = 4.184\text{ J}$ (thermochemical calorie).

❌ Gases have only one specific heat capacity. ✅ Gases have TWO: $c_p$ (constant pressure) and $c_v$ (constant volume). $c_p - c_v = R$ per mole, or $c_p - c_v = R/M$ per unit mass. For air, $c_p = 1005$ and $c_v = 718\text{ J/kg·K}$.

❌ Metals always have low specific heat. ✅ While most metals do have low $c$ (because they're dense and atoms are heavy), beryllium ($c = 1825$) and lithium ($c = 3580$) are exceptions - they have low atomic mass, so per kg they have many atoms and high heat capacity.

❌ $c$ has dimensions of $[ML^2T^{-2}]$. ✅ $c = H/(m\Delta\theta)$, so $[c] = [ML^2T^{-2}] / ([M][\Theta]) = [L^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}]$. Mass dimension CANCELS. The $[M^0]$ is the key difference from heat capacity.
❌ J/kg·K and J/kg·°C are different units. ✅ Since these units involve a TEMPERATURE INTERVAL (Δθ), and 1 K = 1°C in size, J/kg·K and J/kg·°C are EXACTLY the same. Only absolute temperatures differ.

❌ The dimensional formula depends on the system of units. ✅ Dimensional formulas are system-independent. Whether you use SI or CGS, $[c] = [L^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}]$. Only the numerical VALUES change, not the dimensions.

❌ Heat capacity has the same dimensions as specific heat. ✅ Heat capacity $C = mc$ has $[C] = [ML^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}]$ - it includes the mass dimension $[M]$ because it depends on the amount of substance.

❌ $c$ can have negative dimensions. ✅ Specific heat is always positive for normal materials. Negative $c$ would mean adding heat lowers temperature, which violates thermodynamics (except in exotic gravitational systems like stars).

❌ $1\text{ cal/g·°C} = 1\text{ J/kg·K}$. ✅ They differ by a factor of 4184. The calorie is about 4184 times larger than the joule, and the gram is 1/1000 of a kilogram, so the ratio is $4184 \times 1000 / 1000 = 4184$.

What is the specific heat capacity of a metal if 500 J raises 0.2 kg by 10°C? $c = H/(m\Delta\theta) = 500/(0.2 \times 10) = 500/2 = 250\text{ J/kg·K}$. This matches lead or gold.

How much heat is needed to raise 3 kg of aluminum from 20°C to 100°C? $H = mc\Delta\theta = 3 \times 900 \times 80 = 216{,}000\text{ J} = 216\text{ kJ}$. Compare: same mass of water would need $3 \times 4200 \times 80 = 1{,}008{,}000\text{ J}$ - nearly 5× more!

Find the equilibrium temperature when 0.5 kg of copper ($c=390$) at 90°C is mixed with 0.2 kg of water ($c=4200$) at 20°C. $0.5 \times 390 \times (90-T) = 0.2 \times 4200 \times (T-20)$. $195(90-T) = 840(T-20)$. $17550 - 195T = 840T - 16800$. $1035T = 34350 \Rightarrow T \approx 33.2°\text{C}$.

A 0.1 kg metal at 100°C is dropped into 0.3 kg of water at 15°C. The equilibrium is 18°C. Find the metal's specific heat. Heat lost by metal: $0.1 \times c \times 82 = 8.2c$. Heat gained by water: $0.3 \times 4200 \times 3 = 3780$. $8.2c = 3780 \Rightarrow c \approx 461\text{ J/kg·K}$ (close to iron).

Why does a coastal city have smaller temperature swings than an inland city? Water has $c = 4186\text{ J/kg·K}$ - about 5× that of sand/rock ($\sim 800$). The ocean absorbs/releases enormous heat with minimal temperature change, moderating the nearby air temperature through convection and wind.
Convert 0.5 cal/g·°C to J/kg·K. $0.5\text{ cal/g·°C} \times 4.184\text{ J/cal} \times 1000\text{ g/kg} = 2092\text{ J/kg·K}$. The factor 1000 comes from g→kg; the factor 4.184 from cal→J.

Derive the dimensional formula of specific heat capacity from $c = H/(m\Delta\theta)$. $[H] = [ML^2T^{-2}]$, $[m] = [M]$, $[\Delta\theta] = [\Theta]$. Therefore $[c] = [ML^2T^{-2}] / ([M][\Theta]) = [M^0L^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}]$.
Convert 0.215 cal/g·°C (aluminum) to J/kg·K. $0.215 \times 4184 = 900\text{ J/kg·K}$. ✓ This matches the standard value.
Check dimensional homogeneity of $H = mc\Delta\theta$. LHS: $[H] = [ML^2T^{-2}]$. RHS: $[m][c][\Delta\theta] = [M] \cdot [L^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}] \cdot [\Theta] = [ML^2T^{-2}]$. ✓ LHS = RHS.
A substance has $c = 390\text{ J/kg·K}$. Express this in cal/g·°C. $390 / 4184 = 0.0932\text{ cal/g·°C}$. This is copper.
What are the dimensions of molar heat capacity $C_m$? $C_m = c \times M$ (molar mass). $[C_m] = [L^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}] \cdot [M] = [ML^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}]$.

Use dimensional analysis to show that $H = mc\Delta\theta$ is the only possible form (given $H$ depends on $m$, $c$, and $\Delta\theta$). $[H] = [M]^a [L^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}]^b [\Theta]^c = [ML^2T^{-2}]$. Equating powers: $M$: $a=1$; $L$: $2b=2 \Rightarrow b=1$; $T$: $-2b=-2 \Rightarrow b=1$; $\Theta$: $-b+c=0 \Rightarrow c=1$. So $H \propto m^1 c^1 \Delta\theta^1$. ✓
universalFacts: This topic is a cornerstone of the physics curriculum and appears consistently in examinations.
Understanding specific heat capacity builds the foundation for more advanced topics in mathematics.
Real-world applications of specific heat capacity span engineering, physics, economics, and computer science.

The Dulong-Petit law (1819) states that molar heat capacity of most solid elements is approximately $3R = 24.9\text{ J/mol·K}$ at room temperature. This arises because each atom in a solid has 6 quadratic degrees of freedom (3 kinetic + 3 potential), each contributing $\frac{1}{2}k_BT$.

Water's specific heat is the highest of any common liquid. This is due to hydrogen bonding - energy goes into partially breaking H-bonds before molecules can move faster. This property is why Earth's oceans store vast amounts of solar energy.

Mercury has one of the lowest specific heats among liquids ($c = 140\text{ J/kg·K}$). This is why mercury thermometers respond quickly to temperature changes - they need very little heat to change temperature.

The concept of "thermal inertia" in climate science comes directly from specific heat. Land has lower thermal inertia than ocean, so continents heat and cool faster. This drives monsoon patterns and sea breezes.
Historical note: The word "calorimeter" comes from Latin "calor
(heat). Antoine Lavoisier built the first ice calorimeter in 1780
measuring heat by the amount of ice melted. This was the first quantitative calorimetry.
The dimensional formula $[L^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}]$ is the same as "specific energy per kelvin" - it tells you how much energy per unit mass is needed per degree of temperature change.
In the CGS system, specific heat of water is exactly 1 cal/g·°C by definition. This makes the calorie a "natural" unit for heat calculations, though the SI joule is the standard in modern physics.
Dimensional analysis is a powerful check: if you derive a formula for $c$ and it has wrong dimensions, you know immediately that an error was made - even before plugging in numbers.

The specific heat's dimensions $[L^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}]$ are the same as "velocity squared per kelvin." This reflects that temperature is fundamentally a measure of molecular kinetic energy (velocity).
The dimensional formula is independent of the substance. Whether it's water, iron, or helium, $[c] = [M^0L^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}]$. Only the numerical value changes from material to material.
