data.title: Law of Parallelogram of Vectors
data.topicTitle: Triangle, parallelogram and polygon laws of vectors
notes: **Statement**: If two vectors acting at a point are represented in magnitude and direction by the two adjacent sides of a parallelogram drawn from that point, their resultant is represented in magnitude and direction by the diagonal of the parallelogram passing through the same point.

**Setup**: let $\vec{P}$ and $\vec{Q}$ be two vectors acting at point $A$, represented by adjacent sides $\vec{AB}$ and $\vec{AD}$ of parallelogram $ABCD$. The diagonal $\vec{AC}$ represents the resultant $\vec{R}$. The angle between $\vec{P}$ and $\vec{Q}$ is $\theta$.
**Derivation of magnitude**: draw $CE$ perpendicular to $AB$ extended. In right triangle $BCE$: $CE = Q\sin\theta$ and $BE = Q\cos\theta$. Then $AE = AB + BE = P + Q\cos\theta$.
In right triangle $ACE$: $AC^2 = AE^2 + CE^2 = (P+Q\cos\theta)^2 + (Q\sin\theta)^2 = P^2 + 2PQ\cos\theta + Q^2\cos^2\theta + Q^2\sin^2\theta$.
**Simplifying with $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$**: $R^2 = P^2 + Q^2 + 2PQ\cos\theta$, so $R = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2 + 2PQ\cos\theta}$.

**Derivation of direction**: in triangle $ACE$, $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{CE}{AE} = \dfrac{Q\sin\theta}{P + Q\cos\theta}$, giving $\alpha = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{Q\sin\theta}{P+Q\cos\theta}\right)$, where $\alpha$ is the angle between $\vec{R}$ and $\vec{P}$.
**Special case $\theta = 0°$**: $R = \sqrt{P^2+Q^2+2PQ} = P+Q$, $\alpha = 0°$. Maximum resultant — vectors reinforce each other completely.
**Special case $\theta = 90°$**: $R = \sqrt{P^2+Q^2}$, $\alpha = \tan^{-1}(Q/P)$. The Pythagorean result — the most frequently tested case.
**Special case $\theta = 180°$**: $R = \sqrt{P^2+Q^2-2PQ} = |P-Q|$, $\alpha = 0°$ or $180°$. Minimum resultant — vectors oppose each other.
**Special case $P = Q$**: $R = 2P\cos(\theta/2)$ and $\alpha = \theta/2$. The resultant bisects the angle between two equal vectors. This is a key result for equilibrium problems.
**Special case $P = Q$ and $R = P$**: this occurs when $\theta = 120°$, since $R = 2P\cos(60°) = 2P(1/2) = P$. Three equal forces at 120° to each other are in equilibrium.

**Equivalence to triangle law**: the parallelogram and triangle laws are mathematically equivalent. The diagonal $AC$ of the parallelogram is also the third side of triangle $ABC$, confirming both methods yield identical results.

**Diagonals of a parallelogram**: the two diagonals represent $\vec{P}+\vec{Q}$ and $\vec{P}-\vec{Q}$. Their magnitudes satisfy: $|\vec{P}+\vec{Q}|^2 + |\vec{P}-\vec{Q}|^2 = 2(P^2+Q^2)$ — this is the **parallelogram law of geometry**.

The parallelogram law is the foundation of **statics** — the branch of mechanics dealing with forces in equilibrium. Every force analysis in engineering begins with constructing a parallelogram of forces.

**Graphical method**: to find the resultant graphically, draw the two vectors to scale from a common point, complete the parallelogram, and measure the diagonal. This is how structural engineers historically solved problems before calculators.
The parallelogram law applies to all vector quantities equally: forces, velocities, displacements, accelerations, electric fields, magnetic fields, and momenta. The mathematical form is universal.

**Verification experiment**: suspend two spring balances from a ring, attach a third balance downward. The readings on the two upper balances (vectors $\vec{P}$ and $\vec{Q}$) and the lower balance (weight $\vec{W}$) should satisfy the parallelogram law with $\vec{R} = -\vec{W}$.
In the parallelogram construction, the angle $\theta$ must be measured between the vectors when they are **tail-to-tail** (at the common origin point), not the interior angle of the parallelogram.
The parallelogram law was formalized by **Isaac Newton** in his *Principia* (1687) as the 'parallelogram of forces', making it one of the foundational principles of classical mechanics.
If $\vec{P} \perp \vec{Q}$, the parallelogram becomes a **rectangle**, and the diagonal is easily found using Pythagoras: $R = \sqrt{P^2+Q^2}$. This simplification is heavily tested.

**Parallelogram law with unequal sides**: when $P \neq Q$, the diagonal does not bisect the angle. The angle $\alpha$ from $\vec{P}$ is $\alpha = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{Q\sin\theta}{P+Q\cos\theta}\right)$, which equals $\theta/2$ only when $P = Q$.

**The second diagonal**: the diagonal from B to D (the other diagonal) represents $\vec{P}-\vec{Q}$ (or $\vec{Q}-\vec{P}$ depending on orientation). Its magnitude is $d_2 = \sqrt{P^2+Q^2-2PQ\cos\theta}$.
**Sum of squares of diagonals**: $d_1^2 + d_2^2 = (P^2+Q^2+2PQ\cos\theta) + (P^2+Q^2-2PQ\cos\theta) = 2(P^2+Q^2)$. This identity is useful in many geometry and physics problems.

**When the resultant equals one component**: if $R = P$, then $P^2 = P^2+Q^2+2PQ\cos\theta$, giving $\cos\theta = -Q/(2P)$. This requires $Q \leq 2P$. A special case: if $P = Q$ and $R = P$, then $\theta = 120°$.

**Graphical precision**: the graphical method is limited by drawing accuracy. For NEB exams, analytical methods using the formula are preferred. Graphical methods are for verification and intuition only.

**Statement**: When two non-zero vectors are represented by two sides of a triangle taken in the same order (head-to-tail), their resultant is represented by the third side of the triangle taken in the opposite order.

**Setup for derivation**: let $\vec{P}$ and $\vec{Q}$ act at point $A$, represented by sides $\vec{AB} = \vec{P}$ and $\vec{BC} = \vec{Q}$ of triangle $ABC$. The resultant is $\vec{AC} = \vec{R}$ (the third side taken from $A$ to $C$, opposite to the order $B$ to $C$). Let $\theta$ be the angle between $\vec{P}$ and $\vec{Q}$ when placed tail-to-tail.
**Geometric construction**: from $C$ drop a perpendicular $CD$ to the line $AB$ extended. In right triangle $BCD$: $CD = BC\sin\theta = Q\sin\theta$ and $BD = BC\cos\theta = Q\cos\theta$.
**Applying Pythagoras to triangle $ACD$**: $AC^2 = AD^2 + CD^2 = (AB + BD)^2 + CD^2 = (P + Q\cos\theta)^2 + (Q\sin\theta)^2$.
**Expanding**: $R^2 = P^2 + 2PQ\cos\theta + Q^2\cos^2\theta + Q^2\sin^2\theta = P^2 + Q^2 + 2PQ\cos\theta(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta)$.
**Using $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$**: we get the fundamental result $R = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2 + 2PQ\cos\theta}$.

**Direction of resultant**: in right triangle $ADC$, $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{CD}{AD} = \dfrac{Q\sin\theta}{P + Q\cos\theta}$, so $\alpha = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{Q\sin\theta}{P + Q\cos\theta}\right)$, where $\alpha$ is the angle between $\vec{R}$ and $\vec{P}$.
**Special case $\theta = 0°$** (same direction): $R = \sqrt{P^2+Q^2+2PQ} = P+Q$, $\alpha = 0°$. The vectors add algebraically — maximum resultant.
**Special case $\theta = 90°$** (perpendicular): $R = \sqrt{P^2+Q^2}$, $\tan\alpha = Q/P$. This is the Pythagorean result — the most tested case in NEB.
**Special case $\theta = 180°$** (opposite direction): $R = \sqrt{P^2+Q^2-2PQ} = |P-Q|$, $\alpha = 0°$ or $180°$. The resultant acts along the larger vector — minimum resultant.
**Special case $P = Q$**: $R = \sqrt{2P^2(1+\cos\theta)} = 2P\cos(\theta/2)$ and $\alpha = \theta/2$. The resultant bisects the angle between two equal vectors.
**Minimum and maximum resultant**: $R_{max} = P + Q$ (when $\theta = 0°$) and $R_{min} = |P - Q|$ (when $\theta = 180°$). For any angle, $|P - Q| \leq R \leq P + Q$.

**Lami's theorem connection**: for three forces in equilibrium, each force is proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two: $\frac{F_1}{\sin\alpha} = \frac{F_2}{\sin\beta} = \frac{F_3}{\sin\gamma}$. This follows from the triangle law applied to the force triangle.

The triangle law is equivalent to the parallelogram law — the diagonal of the parallelogram is the third side of the triangle formed by completing half the parallelogram. Both yield identical results.

**Graphical construction steps**: (1) Draw $\vec{P}$ to scale from a point. (2) From the head of $\vec{P}$, draw $\vec{Q}$ at angle $\theta$. (3) The resultant $\vec{R}$ is the line from the tail of $\vec{P}$ to the head of $\vec{Q}$. (4) Measure length and angle.

**Application to equilibrium**: if three vectors form a closed triangle when placed head-to-tail, their resultant is zero and the system is in equilibrium. This is the **triangle of forces** condition.

The triangle law works for ANY vector quantities — forces, velocities, displacements, accelerations, electric fields. The mathematical structure is identical regardless of the physical nature of the vectors.
When $\theta = 120°$ and $P = Q$, the resultant equals each component: $R = \sqrt{P^2+P^2+2P^2(-1/2)} = \sqrt{P^2} = P$. This is a neat result often tested in NEB exams.
The derivation assumes a Euclidean (flat) plane. In curved spaces (general relativity), vector addition follows different rules, but for all Class 11 physics, the flat-plane derivation is exact.

**Law of sines for vectors**: from the triangle formed by $\vec{P}$, $\vec{Q}$, $\vec{R}$, the sine rule gives $\frac{P}{\sin\beta} = \frac{Q}{\sin\alpha} = \frac{R}{\sin\theta}$ where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the angles opposite $\vec{Q}$ and $\vec{P}$ respectively.

**Finding the unknown angle**: if three sides of the triangle are known (magnitudes of $\vec{P}$, $\vec{Q}$, $\vec{R}$), the angle between $\vec{P}$ and $\vec{Q}$ is $\theta = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{R^2-P^2-Q^2}{2PQ}\right)$.

**Application to navigation**: a ship sailing 30 km on a bearing of 60° then 40 km on a bearing of 150° — the resultant displacement is found using the triangle law with the exterior angle being the change in bearing.

**Three concurrent forces in equilibrium**: if three forces $\vec{F}_1$, $\vec{F}_2$, $\vec{F}_3$ act at a point in equilibrium, they form a closed triangle when drawn head-to-tail. Each side represents the magnitude, and each angle inside the triangle relates to the angle between the corresponding force directions.

**Minimum force to maintain equilibrium**: when a weight $W$ is suspended by two strings making angles $\alpha$ and $\beta$ with the horizontal, the tensions can be found from the force triangle. The tension is minimum when the strings are perpendicular to each other.

**Statement**: If a number of vectors are represented in magnitude and direction by the sides of a polygon taken in the same order (head-to-tail), their resultant is represented in magnitude and direction by the closing side of the polygon taken in the opposite order.

**Mathematical form**: for $n$ vectors $\vec{A_1}, \vec{A_2}, \ldots, \vec{A_n}$ placed head-to-tail: $\vec{R} = \vec{A_1} + \vec{A_2} + \vec{A_3} + \cdots + \vec{A_n}$. The closing side (from the tail of the first to the head of the last) represents $\vec{R}$.

**Derivation from triangle law**: applying the triangle law successively: $\vec{OB} = \vec{A_1} + \vec{A_2}$, then $\vec{OC} = \vec{OB} + \vec{A_3} = \vec{A_1} + \vec{A_2} + \vec{A_3}$, continuing until $\vec{R} = \vec{A_1} + \vec{A_2} + \cdots + \vec{A_n}$. Each step uses the triangle law.

**Closed polygon ($\vec{R} = \vec{0}$)**: if the polygon closes (the last head meets the first tail), the resultant is zero and the system is in equilibrium. This is the **polygon of forces** condition for equilibrium.

**For three vectors in equilibrium**: the vectors form a closed triangle. This is the **triangle of forces** theorem: if three forces keep a particle in equilibrium, they can be represented by the sides of a triangle taken in order.

**Lami's theorem** (special case for three forces): if three forces $\vec{F_1}, \vec{F_2}, \vec{F_3}$ act at a point in equilibrium: $\frac{F_1}{\sin\alpha} = \frac{F_2}{\sin\beta} = \frac{F_3}{\sin\gamma}$, where $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are the angles opposite to each force respectively.

**Any number of vectors**: the polygon law generalizes to any number of coplanar vectors. For 4 vectors, you get a quadrilateral; for 5, a pentagon; and so on. The closing side is always the resultant.

**Component method alternative**: for many vectors, it is more efficient to resolve each into components: $R_x = \sum A_{ix}$ and $R_y = \sum A_{iy}$, then $R = \sqrt{R_x^2+R_y^2}$ and $\alpha = \tan^{-1}(R_y/R_x)$.

**Graphical construction**: (1) Draw the first vector to scale. (2) From its head, draw the second vector to scale at the correct angle. (3) Continue for all vectors. (4) The closing side from the start to the end is the resultant. (5) Measure its length and angle.

**Order independence**: vector addition is commutative and associative, so the polygon can be drawn in any order — the resultant is the same. $\vec{A}+\vec{B}+\vec{C} = \vec{B}+\vec{A}+\vec{C} = \vec{C}+\vec{B}+\vec{A}$.
**Equilibrium condition**: a system of coplanar forces is in equilibrium if and only if their vector polygon closes (forms a closed polygon). This means $\sum \vec{F} = \vec{0}$.
**Resolution method for polygon**: resolve all vectors along two perpendicular axes. For equilibrium: $\sum F_x = 0$ and $\sum F_y = 0$. These two equations allow solving for two unknowns.
The polygon law is essential in **structural analysis** of trusses and frames. Each joint is treated as a point where multiple force vectors meet, and the polygon must close for static equilibrium.
**Real-world application**: surveyors use the polygon method (called the 'traverse method') to check the accuracy of measured angles and distances. Any closure error indicates measurement mistakes.

For a regular polygon with $n$ equal forces acting along its sides, the resultant is zero if the forces are arranged symmetrically. This is because the vectors are equally spaced in direction around the circle.

**Special case — three equal forces**: three equal forces in equilibrium must be at 120° to each other. This follows from the force triangle being equilateral, which requires all angles to be 60° (exterior angles of 120°).
The polygon law applies to **non-coplanar vectors** as well — in 3D, the polygon becomes a spatial polygon. The component method ($R_x, R_y, R_z$) is preferred for 3D problems.
In **electrostatics**, the polygon law is used to find the net electric field at a point due to multiple charges. Each field vector is drawn head-to-tail, and the resultant gives the total field.

When the polygon does not close, the **closing side** (from endpoint back to starting point) represents the **equilibrant** — the force needed to bring the system into equilibrium. The equilibrant is equal in magnitude but opposite in direction to the resultant.

**Equilibrant vs resultant**: the resultant $\vec{R}$ is the single vector that replaces all vectors; the equilibrant $\vec{E} = -\vec{R}$ is the vector that balances them to produce equilibrium. They have equal magnitude but opposite direction.

**Sequential application**: for $n$ vectors, apply the triangle law successively: $\vec{R}_2 = \vec{A}_1 + \vec{A}_2$, then $\vec{R}_3 = \vec{R}_2 + \vec{A}_3$, and so on. The final $\vec{R}_n$ is the resultant of all vectors.

**Polygon for non-coplanar vectors**: in 3D, the polygon law still holds but the polygon is now a spatial (non-planar) polygon. The component method is more practical for 3D: $R_x = \sum A_{ix}$, $R_y = \sum A_{iy}$, $R_z = \sum A_{iz}$.

**Regular polygon equilibrium**: $n$ equal forces acting along the sides of a regular $n$-gon in order have a zero resultant. The vectors are equally spaced by angle $2\pi/n$ around the circle, and their sum cancels by symmetry.

**Polygon of velocities**: just as force polygons check equilibrium, velocity polygons check relative motion. A swimmer crossing a river: $\vec{v}_{ground} = \vec{v}_{swimmer} + \vec{v}_{river}$ forms a velocity triangle.
confusion: The parallelogram law gives a different result from the triangle law — They give identical results. The triangle is simply half the parallelogram. The diagonal of the parallelogram is the third side of the triangle.

The angle in the formula is the interior angle of the parallelogram — The angle $\theta$ in $R = \sqrt{P^2+Q^2+2PQ\cos\theta}$ is the angle between the two vectors when placed tail-to-tail, which equals the interior angle at the common vertex.

Only forces obey the parallelogram law — All vectors obey it: velocity, displacement, acceleration, electric field, magnetic field, momentum. Any quantity with magnitude and direction that follows vector addition rules obeys this law.

The resultant is always the longer diagonal — No. The resultant is specifically the diagonal drawn from the common origin point (where the two vectors start). The other diagonal represents $\vec{P}-\vec{Q}$.
If $\theta = 90°$, the parallelogram becomes a square — It becomes a **rectangle**, not necessarily a square. It is a square only if $P = Q$ as well.

The direction formula changes between the two laws — The direction formula $\alpha = \tan^{-1}(Q\sin\theta/(P+Q\cos\theta))$ is identical for both the triangle and parallelogram laws, since they are geometrically equivalent.

You need to draw a full parallelogram to use the law — No. You can use just the triangle (half the parallelogram) for calculations. The full parallelogram is helpful for visualization but not required for computation.
The parallelogram law and triangle law are different — They are mathematically identical. The triangle is exactly half the parallelogram. Both give the same $R$ and $\alpha$.

The parallelogram law fails for three or more vectors — It extends naturally: for three vectors, first find $\vec{R}_{12} = \vec{P}+\vec{Q}$ using the parallelogram, then combine $\vec{R}_{12}$ with $\vec{R}$ using the law again. Or use the polygon law for 3+ vectors directly.

The angle $\theta$ in the formula is the angle inside the triangle — $\theta$ is the angle between the two vectors when placed tail-to-tail, NOT the interior angle of the triangle. If the interior angle is $\phi$, then $\theta = 180° - \phi$.

The resultant always points between the two vectors — This is only true for $0° < \theta < 180°$. When vectors are opposite ($\theta=180°$), the resultant lies along the larger vector, not between them.
Triangle law only works for forces — Triangle law applies to ALL vectors: displacement, velocity, acceleration, electric field, magnetic field, momentum. Any quantity that is a vector obeys this law.

If the triangle doesn't close, the vectors are wrong — An open triangle means the resultant is the closing side. The triangle law says the resultant IS the third side taken in the opposite order — the triangle is open by design.

The direction formula $\tan\alpha = Q\sin\theta/(P+Q\cos\theta)$ is only for the triangle law — This formula is actually derived from the triangle law but is identical to the one from the parallelogram law. Both methods give the same $\alpha$.

A zero resultant means the triangle has no area — A zero resultant means the two vectors are equal and opposite ($P=Q$, $\theta=180°$), forming a degenerate triangle (a line segment), not a triangle with zero area in the usual sense.

You can use the triangle law for more than two vectors directly — The triangle law is specifically for two vectors. For three or more, you apply it successively or use the polygon law. $\vec{A}+\vec{B}+\vec{C}$ requires two applications of the triangle law.

The order of vectors in the triangle matters for the resultant's direction — The triangle law is commutative: $\vec{P}+\vec{Q} = \vec{Q}+\vec{P}$. Swapping the order just reflects the triangle but gives the same resultant vector.

The interior angles of the force triangle are the same as the angles between the force vectors — No. The interior angle of the triangle at a vertex equals $180°$ minus the angle between the two forces meeting at that point (when drawn head-to-tail).

If three vectors form a triangle, they are automatically in equilibrium — Only if they are drawn head-to-tail AND the polygon closes (head of last meets tail of first). If they simply form a geometric triangle but are all pointing in the same rotational direction around the triangle, their resultant is not zero.

The polygon law is a different law from the triangle and parallelogram laws — It is the generalization of both. The triangle law is the polygon law for 2 vectors; the polygon law extends this to any number of vectors.

If the polygon doesn't close, the system is in equilibrium — A closed polygon means equilibrium (resultant = 0). An open polygon means the resultant is the closing side. Only a closed polygon indicates equilibrium.
The order of vectors in the polygon matters — No. Vector addition is commutative: $\vec{A}+\vec{B}+\vec{C}$ gives the same resultant regardless of order. You can rearrange the polygon sides freely.
Lami's theorem applies to any number of forces — Lami's theorem applies ONLY to three forces in equilibrium. For more than three forces, use the polygon law or component resolution.

The closing side is the resultant — The closing side TAKEN FROM the tail of the first to the head of the last is the resultant. The closing side TAKEN FROM the head back to the tail is the equilibrant (opposite to the resultant).
Polygon law only works for forces — It works for all vectors: displacements, velocities, accelerations, electric fields, magnetic fields. Any vector quantity obeys the polygon law.

A regular polygon of forces always means equilibrium — Only if the forces are equal in magnitude and equally spaced in direction. Unequal forces along the sides of a regular polygon generally do not produce equilibrium.

You must draw the polygon to scale to get the answer — No. The polygon law is a mathematical principle. You can solve problems analytically using components without any drawing. Graphical methods are for verification and visualization.
practice: Two forces of 5 N and 12 N act at a point with an angle of 90° between them. Find the resultant using the parallelogram law. [Solution: $R = \sqrt{25+144} = \sqrt{169} = 13\,\text{N}$. $\alpha = \tan^{-1}(12/5) \approx 67.4°$ from the 5 N force.]

Two forces of 10 N and 8 N act at a point with an angle of 60° between them. Find the resultant and its direction. [Solution: $R = \sqrt{100+64+160\cos60°} = \sqrt{164+80} = \sqrt{244} \approx 15.62\,\text{N}$. $\alpha = \tan^{-1}(8\sin60°/(10+8\cos60°)) = \tan^{-1}(6.928/14) \approx 26.3°$.]

Show that if two equal forces each of magnitude $F$ have a resultant of magnitude $F$, then the angle between them is 120°. [Solution: $F = \sqrt{F^2+F^2+2F^2\cos\theta} = F\sqrt{2+2\cos\theta}$. So $1 = \sqrt{2+2\cos\theta}$, giving $1 = 2+2\cos\theta$, hence $\cos\theta = -1/2$ and $\theta = 120°$.]

Two forces of 3 N and 4 N act at a point. What angle between them gives a resultant of 5 N? [Solution: $25 = 9+16+24\cos\theta$, so $25 = 25+24\cos\theta$, giving $\cos\theta = 0$ and $\theta = 90°$. The forces are perpendicular.]

Find the resultant of two vectors $\vec{A} = 6\hat{i} + 8\hat{j}$ and $\vec{B} = 3\hat{i} - 4\hat{j}$ using component method. [Solution: $\vec{R} = 9\hat{i} + 4\hat{j}$. $R = \sqrt{81+16} = \sqrt{97} \approx 9.85$. $\alpha = \tan^{-1}(4/9) \approx 24.0°$.]

Two forces $\vec{P}$ and $\vec{Q}$ have a resultant of 26 N. If $\vec{Q}$ is doubled, the resultant becomes 54 N. Find $P$ and $Q$. [Solution: $P^2+Q^2+2PQ\cos\theta = 676$ and $P^2+4Q^2+4PQ\cos\theta = 2916$. Subtracting: $3Q^2+2PQ\cos\theta = 2240$. This requires additional info; assume $\theta=90°$: then $P^2+Q^2=676$ and $P^2+4Q^2=2916$. Subtracting: $3Q^2=2240$, $Q^2=746.67$, $Q\approx27.3$. Then $P^2=676-746.67<0$ — inconsistent. Try solving simultaneously with $\cos\theta$: need third equation.]

Prove that the sum of the squares of the diagonals of a parallelogram equals the sum of the squares of its four sides. [Solution: Diagonals: $d_1^2 = P^2+Q^2+2PQ\cos\theta$, $d_2^2 = P^2+Q^2-2PQ\cos\theta$. Sum: $d_1^2+d_2^2 = 2P^2+2Q^2 = 2(P^2+Q^2)$. Four sides: $2P^2+2Q^2$. Hence $d_1^2+d_2^2 = 2P^2+2Q^2$. Proven.]

Two forces act at a point: one is twice the other. If the resultant is perpendicular to the smaller force, find the angle between them. [Solution: Let forces be $F$ and $2F$. Resultant $\vec{R}\perp\vec{F}$ means $\alpha = 90°$. From $\tan\alpha = \frac{2F\sin\theta}{F+2F\cos\theta} = \infty$, the denominator must be zero: $F+2F\cos\theta=0$, so $\cos\theta=-1/2$, giving $\theta=120°$.]

Two forces of 10 N and 15 N act at a point with an angle of 90° between them. Find the resultant and the angle it makes with the 15 N force. [Solution: $R = \sqrt{100+225} = \sqrt{325} \approx 18.03\,\text{N}$. $\alpha = \tan^{-1}(10/15) = \tan^{-1}(2/3) \approx 33.7°$ from the 15 N force.]

Two vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ with $|\vec{A}|=6$, $|\vec{B}|=8$, and angle 60° between them. Find the magnitude of their resultant and the angle it makes with $\vec{A}$. [Solution: $R = \sqrt{36+64+96\cos60°} = \sqrt{100+48} = \sqrt{148} \approx 12.17$. $\alpha = \tan^{-1}(8\sin60°/(6+8\cos60°)) = \tan^{-1}(6.928/10) \approx 34.7°$.]

Two forces of 5 N and 12 N act at a point with an angle of 90° between them. Find the resultant and its direction. [Solution: $R = \sqrt{25+144} = \sqrt{169} = 13\,\text{N}$. $\tan\alpha = 12/5$, so $\alpha = \tan^{-1}(2.4) \approx 67.4°$ from the 5 N force.]

Two forces of 10 N each act at a point with an angle of 60° between them. Find the resultant. [Solution: $R = \sqrt{100+100+200\cos60°} = \sqrt{200+100} = \sqrt{300} = 10\sqrt{3} \approx 17.32\,\text{N}$. $\alpha = \tan^{-1}(10\sin60°/(10+10\cos60°)) = \tan^{-1}(8.66/15) \approx 30°$. The resultant bisects the angle.]

Find the resultant of two forces 8 N and 6 N acting at an angle of 120°. [Solution: $R = \sqrt{64+36+96\cos120°} = \sqrt{100-48} = \sqrt{52} \approx 7.21\,\text{N}$. $\tan\alpha = \frac{6\sin120°}{8+6\cos120°} = \frac{5.20}{5} \approx 1.04$, so $\alpha \approx 46.1°$.]

Three forces of 3 N, 4 N, and 5 N act at a point. If the 3 N and 4 N forces are perpendicular, show that the system is in equilibrium when the 5 N force is opposite to their resultant. [Solution: Resultant of 3 N and 4 N at 90°: $R = \sqrt{9+16} = 5\,\text{N}$. The 5 N force acting in the opposite direction gives $\vec{R}_{total} = 5 - 5 = 0$. Equilibrium confirmed.]

Two vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ have magnitudes 7 N and 9 N. What is the range of possible resultant magnitudes? [Solution: $R_{min} = |9-7| = 2\,\text{N}$ (when opposite), $R_{max} = 9+7 = 16\,\text{N}$ (when same direction). Range: $2\,\text{N} \leq R \leq 16\,\text{N}$.]

Two equal forces $F$ each have a resultant of $F\sqrt{3}$. Find the angle between them. [Solution: $R = 2F\cos(\theta/2)$, so $F\sqrt{3} = 2F\cos(\theta/2)$, giving $\cos(\theta/2) = \sqrt{3}/2$, so $\theta/2 = 30°$ and $\theta = 60°$.]

A displacement of 3 km is made east, then 4 km at 60° north of east. Find the resultant displacement using the triangle law. [Solution: $R^2 = 9+16+24\cos60° = 25+12 = 37$, so $R = \sqrt{37} \approx 6.08\,\text{km}$. $\tan\alpha = \frac{4\sin60°}{3+4\cos60°} = \frac{3.464}{5} \approx 0.693$, $\alpha \approx 34.7°$ north of east.]

If the resultant of two vectors $\vec{P}$ and $\vec{Q}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{P}$, show that $Q\cos\theta = -P$ where $\theta$ is the angle between them. [Solution: If $\vec{R} \perp \vec{P}$, then $\alpha = 90°$ and $\tan\alpha$ is undefined. From $\tan\alpha = Q\sin\theta/(P+Q\cos\theta)$, the denominator must be zero: $P+Q\cos\theta=0$, giving $\cos\theta = -P/Q$. This requires $Q > P$.]

Two forces of 15 N and 20 N act at a point. The resultant is 25 N. Find the angle between the forces. [Solution: $R^2 = P^2+Q^2+2PQ\cos\theta$. $625 = 225+400+600\cos\theta$. $625 = 625+600\cos\theta$, so $\cos\theta = 0$ and $\theta = 90°$. The forces are perpendicular.]

A force of 10 N is resolved into two components along directions that make angles of 30° and 60° with the force. Find the magnitudes of the components. [Solution: Using the law of sines in the force triangle: $\frac{F}{\sin90°} = \frac{F_1}{\sin60°} = \frac{F_2}{\sin30°}$. So $F_1 = 10\sin60° = 8.66\,\text{N}$ and $F_2 = 10\sin30° = 5\,\text{N}$.]

Four forces of 10 N, 20 N, 25 N, and 15 N act along the sides of a quadrilateral taken in order. If the quadrilateral closes, show the system is in equilibrium. [Solution: A closed quadrilateral means the vector polygon closes, so $\vec{R} = \vec{0}$. The system is in equilibrium by the polygon law.]

Three forces of 5 N, 7 N, and 8 N act at a point and keep it in equilibrium. Find the angles between the forces. [Solution: The forces form a triangle with sides 5, 7, 8. Using cosine rule: $\cos A = (49+64-25)/(2\cdot7\cdot8) = 88/112 = 0.7857$, so angle opposite 5 N is $\approx 38.2°$. Similarly, angle opposite 7 N $\approx 61.0°$, angle opposite 8 N $\approx 80.8°$. The angles BETWEEN the forces are the supplements: $180°-38.2°=141.8°$, $180°-61.0°=119.0°$, $180°-80.8°=99.2°$.]

A body is acted upon by three forces: 3 N east, 4 N north, and 5 N at 53° south of west. Show whether the body is in equilibrium. [Solution: Resolve: $F_x = 3 + 0 + 5\cos(180°-53°) = 3 - 5(0.6018) = 3 - 3.009 \approx 0$. $F_y = 0 + 4 + 5\sin(180°-53°)(-1) = 4 - 5(0.7986) = 4 - 3.993 \approx 0$. Both components $\approx 0$, so the body is in equilibrium.]

Five equal forces act at a point with consecutive angles of 60° between them. Find the resultant. [Solution: The forces are at 0°, 60°, 120°, 180°, 240°. $R_x = F(\cos0°+\cos60°+\cos120°+\cos180°+\cos240°) = F(1+0.5-0.5-1-0.5) = -0.5F$. $R_y = F(\sin0°+\sin60°+\sin120°+\sin180°+\sin240°) = F(0+0.866+0.866+0-0.866) = 0.866F$. $R = F\sqrt{0.25+0.75} = F$. The resultant has magnitude $F$.]

Using Lami's theorem, find the tension in two strings supporting a 100 N weight, if the strings make angles of 30° and 60° with the vertical. [Solution: The angles between forces: between T1 and T2 is $180°-30°-60°=90°$, between T1 and W is $180°-60°=120°$, between T2 and W is $180°-30°=150°$. By Lami: $T_1/\sin120° = T_2/\sin150° = 100/\sin90°$. $T_1 = 100\cdot\sin120°/1 = 86.6\,\text{N}$. $T_2 = 100\cdot\sin150°/1 = 50\,\text{N}$.]

Three concurrent forces are in equilibrium. The angles between them are 150°, 120°, and 90°. If the smallest force is 20 N, find the other two. [Solution: Smallest force is opposite the largest angle (150°). By Lami's theorem: $F_1/\sin150° = F_2/\sin120° = F_3/\sin90°$. With $F_1 = 20$: $20/0.5 = 40$. So $F_2 = 40\sin120° = 34.64\,\text{N}$, $F_3 = 40\sin90° = 40\,\text{N}$.]

A force polygon has sides representing forces of 5 N, 12 N, and 13 N. Show that these forces can be in equilibrium and find the angles between them. [Solution: $5^2+12^2 = 25+144 = 169 = 13^2$. This is a right triangle. For equilibrium, the angles between forces are the supplements of the triangle angles: $90°\to90°$, $\tan^{-1}(12/5)\approx67.4°\to112.6°$, $\tan^{-1}(5/12)\approx22.6°\to157.4°$.]

Four forces of magnitudes 1 N, 2 N, 3 N, and 4 N act along the sides of a rectangle taken in order. Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant. [Solution: Along the rectangle sides (say, 2 units by 1 unit): $\vec{F}_1=1\hat{i}$, $\vec{F}_2=2\hat{j}$, $\vec{F}_3=-3\hat{i}$, $\vec{F}_4=-4\hat{j}$. $\vec{R} = (1-3)\hat{i}+(2-4)\hat{j} = -2\hat{i}-2\hat{j}$. $R = \sqrt{4+4} = \sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2} \approx 2.83\,\text{N}$. Direction: $225°$ from positive x-axis (southwest).]

Five forces of 1 N, 2 N, 3 N, 4 N, and 5 N act along the five sides of a regular pentagon taken in order. Find the resultant. [Solution: For a regular pentagon, the exterior angle is 72°. Taking the first side along the x-axis, the five forces are at angles 0°, 72°, 144°, 216°, 288°. $R_x = 1+2\cos72°+3\cos144°+4\cos216°+5\cos288° = 1+0.618-2.427-3.236+1.545 = -2.5$. $R_y = 0+2\sin72°+3\sin144°+4\sin216°+5\sin288° = 0+1.902+1.754-2.351-4.755 = -3.45$. $R = \sqrt{6.25+11.9} \approx 4.26\,\text{N}$. Direction: $\tan^{-1}(3.45/2.5) \approx 54.1°$ below negative x-axis, or $234.1°$ from positive x-axis.]

Three forces of 3 N, 4 N, and 5 N act at a point. The angle between the 3 N and 4 N forces is 90°. Find the angle between the 5 N force and the resultant of the other two. [Solution: Resultant of 3 N and 4 N at 90° is $R_{34} = 5\,\text{N}$. Since the third force is also 5 N and the three are in equilibrium, the 5 N force must be opposite to the resultant of the other two. Therefore the angle between the 5 N force and the resultant of 3 N and 4 N is 180° — they are anti-parallel.]
universalFacts: Newton's **second law of motion** ($\vec{F}_{net} = m\vec{a}$) implicitly relies on the parallelogram law: the net force is the vector sum of all individual forces, found by successive application of the parallelogram law.

The **parallelogram identity** ($|\vec{A}+\vec{B}|^2 + |\vec{A}-\vec{B}|^2 = 2|\vec{A}|^2 + 2|\vec{B}|^2$) is a fundamental property of inner product spaces and holds in any number of dimensions, not just 2D.
NEB exam frequency: parallelogram law numerical problems appear in almost every year's physics paper, typically 3-5 marks. The 90° special case (Pythagorean) is the most common variant.

The parallelogram law of forces was experimentally verified by **Pierre Varignon** (1654-1722), who showed that the moment of a resultant force equals the sum of the moments of its components — a direct consequence of the parallelogram law.
In **aerodynamics**, the parallelogram law explains how wind affects an aircraft's ground track. The airspeed vector plus the wind vector gives the ground velocity vector (the resultant).

The term 'resultant' comes from the Latin *resultare* meaning 'to leap back' or 'to result'. In physics, it specifically means the single vector that has the same effect as all the original vectors combined.
Engineering structures like **bridge trusses** are analyzed using the parallelogram law at each joint. Every joint must be in equilibrium, so the force vectors at each joint form closed polygons.

When $\theta = 120°$ and $P = Q$, the resultant equals each component. This is why **tripods** are stable: the three leg forces are typically arranged at approximately 120° to each other, giving balanced resultant forces.

The **parallelogram law** is the geometric foundation for the **component method**. Resolving vectors into x and y components and adding them is mathematically equivalent to repeatedly applying the parallelogram law.
In **electrostatics**, the net force on a charge due to multiple other charges is found by applying the parallelogram law successively (or using components), since electric forces are vectors.

The triangle law of vectors is one of the oldest results in mechanics. It appears in **Euclid's Elements** (Book I, Proposition 26) in geometric form, and was adapted to physics by **Stevin** in 1586 for analyzing forces on inclined planes.

NEB exam pattern: triangle law derivation + numerical resultant problems account for approximately 8-12 marks in the physics paper. Students who can derive $R = \sqrt{P^2+Q^2+2PQ\cos\theta}$ from first principles typically score full marks.

The law of cosines in trigonometry ($c^2 = a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C$) is the mathematical backbone of the triangle law. The only difference is the sign: in the triangle law, the interior angle is $180°-\theta$, and $\cos(180°-\theta) = -\cos\theta$, flipping the sign.
In structural engineering, triangle law is used to analyze **trusses** — frameworks of triangles that distribute loads. Each joint is in equilibrium, so the forces form closed triangles.

The triangle law is directly related to **Lami's theorem**, which states: if three forces keep a particle in equilibrium, each force is proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two. This is derived by applying the sine rule to the force triangle.
When two vectors are perpendicular ($\theta=90°$), the triangle law reduces to the Pythagorean theorem. This special case is so common in NEB problems that students should recognize it instantly.

Vector addition via the triangle law is how **GPS systems** calculate your position: combining the satellite signal vectors (displacement from each satellite) gives your position vector relative to Earth's center.

The triangle law fails only when vectors are not free vectors (bound vectors tied to specific points) or in non-Euclidean geometries. For all Class 11 physics problems in flat space, it is universally valid.

The **sine rule** for any triangle: $\frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{c}{\sin C} = 2R_{circum}$, where $R_{circum}$ is the circumradius. In vector triangles, this relates force magnitudes to the angles between them.

In **statics of rigid bodies**, the triangle law combined with Lami's theorem provides a complete solution for any three-force system in equilibrium, eliminating the need for component resolution in simple cases.

The polygon law of forces is the basis of **graphical statics**, a method developed in the 19th century by engineers like **James Clerk Maxwell** and **Karl Culmann** to analyze structures before the advent of computer-aided design.

NEB exam tip: questions on the polygon law often appear as 'show that these forces are in equilibrium' problems. The key is to check if the vector polygon closes (sum of components in both directions equals zero).

The concept of a **force polygon** is used in the graphical analysis of **trusses** (bridge frameworks). Each joint's forces form a closed polygon, allowing engineers to determine internal forces in each member visually.
In navigation, the **dead reckoning** method uses the polygon law: a ship's position is found by adding successive displacement vectors (course and distance segments) head-to-tail.

The **closure error** in a surveying traverse is a direct application of the polygon law. If the measured sides and angles don't form a closed polygon, the error is distributed among the measurements.

Lami's theorem (a corollary of the polygon law for three forces) is named after **Bernard Lami** (1640-1715), a French mathematician and engineer. It provides a quick shortcut for three-force equilibrium problems.

The polygon law extends to **three dimensions** — spatial force polygons are used in 3D truss analysis. The component method ($\sum F_x=0$, $\sum F_y=0$, $\sum F_z=0$) is the algebraic version of the 3D polygon law.

When forces are in equilibrium, the polygon closes — this means the work done by the forces in any closed path is also zero (for conservative forces). This connects the polygon law to the concept of conservative force fields.

The **polygon law** is the foundation of **finite element analysis** (FEA). In FEA, complex structures are broken into simple elements (triangles), and equilibrium at each node is checked using polygon laws.
A **vector loop** in kinematics (e.g., four-bar linkages) uses the polygon law: the sum of displacement vectors around a closed loop equals zero. This is fundamental in mechanism analysis.

data.title: Resolution of a Vector
notes: **Definition**: the process of splitting (breaking) a vector into its constituent parts is known as **resolution of a vector**. Each constituent is called a **component** of the vector along the chosen direction.

**Rectangular (perpendicular) resolution**: when a vector is resolved along two mutually perpendicular directions (typically x and y axes), the components are $R_x = R\cos\theta$ and $R_y = R\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle the vector makes with the x-axis.

**Inverse operation of addition**: resolution is the reverse of vector addition. If two perpendicular components $\vec{R}_x$ and $\vec{R}_y$ add to give $\vec{R}$, then resolving $\vec{R}$ recovers these components.

**Derivation setup**: let $\vec{R}$ act at origin $O$ making angle $\theta$ with the x-axis. Construct parallelogram $OACB$ where $OA$ lies on the x-axis and $OC$ lies on the y-axis. The diagonal $OB$ represents $\vec{R}$.
**By the parallelogram law**: $\vec{OA} + \vec{OC} = \vec{OB}$, i.e., $\vec{R}_x + \vec{R}_y = \vec{R}$. This means $\vec{R}$ is completely determined by its two perpendicular components.
**Deriving the components**: in right triangle $OAB$, $\cos\theta = OA/OB = R_x/R$, so $R_x = R\cos\theta$. Similarly, $\sin\theta = OC/OB = R_y/R$, so $R_y = R\sin\theta$.
**Combining components**: $R = \sqrt{R_x^2 + R_y^2}$ (magnitude) and $\tan\theta = R_y/R_x$ (direction). The original vector is $\vec{R} = R_x\hat{i} + R_y\hat{j}$ in unit vector notation.

**Sign convention**: $R_x$ is positive if $\vec{R}_x$ is along $+x$ direction, negative if along $-x$. Same for $R_y$. This sign convention allows vectors in any quadrant to be handled systematically.

**Vector form**: $\vec{R} = R_x\hat{i} + R_y\hat{j} + R_z\hat{k}$ for a 3D vector, where $R_x = R\cos\alpha$, $R_y = R\cos\beta$, $R_z = R\cos\gamma$ and $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are the angles with x, y, z axes.
**Direction cosines**: for 3D vectors, $\cos\alpha$, $\cos\beta$, $\cos\gamma$ are called direction cosines, and they satisfy $\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1$.
**Why resolution is useful**: a single vector makes solving equilibrium problems difficult. Resolving into components turns a vector problem into multiple scalar problems, which are easier to solve.

**Resolution in any two directions**: a vector can be resolved along ANY two non-parallel directions, not just perpendicular ones. Rectangular resolution is the most common because it gives independent components.
**Resolution and addition are inverse operations**: $\vec{R}_x + \vec{R}_y = \vec{R}$ (addition) and $\vec{R} = \vec{R}_x + \vec{R}_y$ (resolution). The same equation, viewed in two directions.

**Applications**: inclined plane problems (gravity resolved into parallel and perpendicular components), projectile motion (initial velocity into horizontal and vertical), forces at angles (along and perpendicular to surfaces).

**On an inclined plane at angle $\phi$**: weight $mg$ is resolved into $mg\sin\phi$ parallel to plane (causing sliding) and $mg\cos\phi$ perpendicular to plane (causing normal reaction). This is a classic NEB application.

**For a vector along an arbitrary direction $\hat{u}$**: the component of $\vec{A}$ along $\hat{u}$ is $A_u = \vec{A}\cdot\hat{u} = |\vec{A}|\cos\alpha$, where $\alpha$ is the angle between $\vec{A}$ and $\hat{u}$.

**Resolution in 3D**: $\vec{R} = R_x\hat{i} + R_y\hat{j} + R_z\hat{k}$ where $R_x = R\cos\alpha$, $R_y = R\cos\beta$, $R_z = R\cos\gamma$, and $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are angles with x, y, z axes respectively.

**Equivalence with triangle law**: the resolution of $\vec{R}$ into $\vec{R}_x$ and $\vec{R}_y$ is essentially constructing a right triangle with hypotenuse $R$ and legs $R_x, R_y$. The Pythagorean theorem gives $R = \sqrt{R_x^2+R_y^2}$.
**Inverse problem**: given components $R_x$ and $R_y$, the original vector is $\vec{R} = R_x\hat{i} + R_y\hat{j}$ with $R = \sqrt{R_x^2+R_y^2}$ and $\theta = \tan^{-1}(R_y/R_x)$.

The angle in the formula $\theta$ must be measured from the axis the component is along. For $R_x = R\cos\theta$, $\theta$ is measured from the x-axis. The component along any other axis at angle $\phi$ is $R\cos(\theta-\phi)$.

**Oblique resolution**: a vector can be resolved along ANY two non-parallel directions, not just perpendicular ones. If resolved along directions making angles $\alpha$ and $\beta$ with the vector, the components are found using the sine rule: $\frac{R}{\sin(180°-(\alpha+\beta))} = \frac{R_1}{\sin\beta} = \frac{R_2}{\sin\alpha}$.

**Resolution along a non-perpendicular axis**: the component of $\vec{R}$ along a direction making angle $\phi$ with the x-axis is $R\cos(\theta-\phi)$, where $\theta$ is the angle of $\vec{R}$ with the x-axis.

**Projection vs component**: the projection of $\vec{A}$ on $\vec{B}$ is the scalar $\vec{A}\cdot\hat{B} = A\cos\alpha$. The component of $\vec{A}$ along $\vec{B}$ is the vector $(\vec{A}\cdot\hat{B})\hat{B}$. The projection is the magnitude (with sign); the component is the full vector.

**Resolution in physics problems**: in projectile motion, $v_0$ is resolved into $v_{0x}=v_0\cos\theta$ and $v_{0y}=v_0\sin\theta$. In inclined planes, weight is resolved into $mg\sin\theta$ (parallel) and $mg\cos\theta$ (perpendicular). The choice of axes determines the complexity of the problem.
confusion: Resolution is the same as addition — Resolution BREAKS a vector INTO components; addition COMBINES components INTO a vector. They are inverse operations. $\vec{R}_x+\vec{R}_y=\vec{R}$ is addition; given $\vec{R}$, find $\vec{R}_x, \vec{R}_y$ is resolution.

Components can be in any two directions — Components can be in ANY two non-parallel directions, but rectangular (perpendicular) resolution is most common because the components are independent. Oblique components can be converted to rectangular using transformation formulas.

The angle in $R_x = R\cos\theta$ is the angle between $R$ and $R_y$ — No, it is the angle between $R$ and the x-axis (the direction of $R_x$). The component $R_y = R\sin\theta$ uses the same $\theta$ because $\theta_x + \theta_y = 90°$ for perpendicular components.

A larger component means a larger vector — A larger component does not mean a larger vector if the components are along different directions. $R = \sqrt{R_x^2+R_y^2}$ is the actual magnitude, considering both components.

Resolution gives the magnitudes of sub-vectors only — Resolution gives the FULL components as vectors: $\vec{R}_x$ (with direction) and $\vec{R}_y$ (with direction). Magnitudes alone are $R_x$ and $R_y$, but each is along a specific axis.

The angle in the formulas must be from the x-axis always — The angle can be measured from any axis, but you must use the correct trigonometric function: $R_x = R\cos\theta$ if $\theta$ is from x-axis, $R_y = R\sin\theta$. If $\theta$ is from y-axis, swap the roles.

Resolution into more than two components is impossible — A vector can be resolved into any number of components, as long as their vector sum equals the original. In 3D, we typically use three perpendicular components.
You can resolve a vector into components without specifying axes — To resolve a vector, you must specify the directions of resolution. Without axes, there are infinitely many possible resolutions.

Resolution changes the physical meaning of the vector — No. Resolution gives an EQUIVALENT description. The vector's physical effect is unchanged; we've just broken it into parts that are easier to work with.

A vector can have more than one set of components — Yes! Any vector has infinitely many component representations depending on the choice of axes. However, the rectangular (perpendicular) components are unique for a given choice of axes.
practice: A force of 100 N acts at 30° to the horizontal. Find its horizontal and vertical components. [Solution: $F_x = 100\cos30° = 100\cdot(0.866) = 86.6\,\text{N}$. $F_y = 100\sin30° = 100\cdot(0.5) = 50\,\text{N}$.]

A block of 10 kg rests on a smooth inclined plane at 30° to the horizontal. Find the components of weight along and perpendicular to the plane. [Solution: $W = mg = 10\cdot9.8 = 98\,\text{N}$. Along plane: $W\sin30° = 98\cdot0.5 = 49\,\text{N}$ (down the slope). Perpendicular: $W\cos30° = 98\cdot0.866 = 84.87\,\text{N}$ (into the plane).]

Resolve a vector of magnitude 20 N along two perpendicular axes such that the component along one axis is 12 N. Find the other component and the angle. [Solution: $R^2 = R_x^2 + R_y^2$, so $R_y = \sqrt{20^2-12^2} = \sqrt{400-144} = \sqrt{256} = 16\,\text{N}$. $\theta = \cos^{-1}(12/20) = 53.1°$.]

A body moves with velocity 50 m/s at 60° north of east. Find its eastward and northward components. [Solution: $v_x = 50\cos60° = 25\,\text{m/s}$ (east). $v_y = 50\sin60° = 50\cdot0.866 = 43.3\,\text{m/s}$ (north).]

If $\vec{A} = 4\hat{i} + 3\hat{j}$ and $\vec{B} = 5\hat{i} - 12\hat{j}$, find the resultant. [Solution: $\vec{R} = \vec{A}+\vec{B} = 9\hat{i} - 9\hat{j}$. $R = \sqrt{81+81} = \sqrt{162} = 9\sqrt{2} \approx 12.73$. $\alpha = \tan^{-1}(-9/9) = -45°$ (below x-axis).]

Show that the resultant of two perpendicular vectors of magnitudes 5 and 12 is 13, and find the angle it makes with the 12-unit vector. [Solution: $R = \sqrt{25+144} = \sqrt{169} = 13$. $\theta = \tan^{-1}(5/12) = 22.6°$ from the 12-unit vector. By the 5-12-13 right triangle, this is the famous 3-4-5 triple scaled up.]

A force has components $F_x = -6\,\text{N}$ and $F_y = 8\,\text{N}$. Find the magnitude of the force and the angle it makes with the positive x-axis. [Solution: $F = \sqrt{36+64} = 10\,\text{N}$. $\theta = \tan^{-1}(8/(-6)) = 180° - 53.1° = 126.9°$ (second quadrant).]

A vector of magnitude 10 units makes equal angles with the x and y axes. Find its components. [Solution: If $\theta_x = \theta_y = \alpha$, then since the components are along the axes, the angle between them is 90°. The vector is along the angle bisector, so $\alpha = 45°$. Components: $R_x = R_y = 10\cos45° = 10/\sqrt{2} = 5\sqrt{2} \approx 7.07$.]

A force of 50 N is resolved into two components along directions making angles of 30° and 45° with the force. Find the magnitudes of the components. [Solution: Using the sine rule in the resolution triangle: $\frac{50}{\sin(180°-30°-45°)} = \frac{F_1}{\sin45°} = \frac{F_2}{\sin30°}$. The angle between the components is $180°-30°-45° = 105°$. $F_1 = 50\sin45°/\sin105° = 50(0.7071)/0.9659 = 36.6\,\text{N}$. $F_2 = 50\sin30°/\sin105° = 50(0.5)/0.9659 = 25.9\,\text{N}$.]

A particle is acted upon by three forces: 10 N along +x, 15 N at 60° from +x, and 20 N at 150° from +x. Find the resultant by resolution. [Solution: $F_{1x}=10$, $F_{1y}=0$. $F_{2x}=15\cos60°=7.5$, $F_{2y}=15\sin60°=12.99$. $F_{3x}=20\cos150°=-17.32$, $F_{3y}=20\sin150°=10$. $R_x=10+7.5-17.32=0.18$, $R_y=0+12.99+10=22.99$. $R=\sqrt{0.03+528.54}=\sqrt{528.57}\approx23.0\,\text{N}$. $\alpha=\tan^{-1}(22.99/0.18)\approx89.6°$ from +x.]
universalFacts: Resolution of vectors is the **inverse operation** of vector addition. Addition combines two or more vectors into a single resultant; resolution decomposes a single vector into two or more components.

NEB exam frequency: resolution problems appear in nearly every physics paper, especially in inclined plane mechanics, projectile motion, and statics. Mastery of the formulas $R_x = R\cos\theta$ and $R_y = R\sin\theta$ is essential.

In **structural engineering**, forces in trusses are resolved into components along the truss members to determine tensions and compressions. The resolution allows solving for multiple unknowns using equilibrium equations.
The choice of coordinate axes in resolution is a **free choice** that affects the simplicity of the solution. For inclined plane problems, axes along and perpendicular to the plane minimize the work.
**Galileo's inclined plane experiments** for studying falling bodies relied on resolution. He resolved gravity into components along and perpendicular to the plane, making the analysis tractable.

Resolution of vectors in **2D** uses two components; in **3D**, three. The number of components equals the dimension of the space — but for any practical purpose, three components suffice for our world.

The result of resolving a vector into components depends on the **choice of axes**. Different axes give different components, but the resultant is the same. Always choose axes that simplify the problem.

In computer graphics and game development, every 3D object is manipulated using resolved vector components along x, y, z axes. This allows efficient calculations for rotation, translation, and lighting.

The **resolution of weight on an inclined plane** is one of the most important applications in Class 11 physics. The component $mg\sin\theta$ causes acceleration down the plane; $mg\cos\theta$ is balanced by the normal reaction.
In **statics**, resolution of forces into components leads to the two equilibrium equations: $\sum F_x = 0$ and $\sum F_y = 0$. These are the algebraic form of the polygon law for coplanar forces.

data.title: Resolution of Vectors — Finding Components
notes: **Standard formulas**: for a vector $\vec{F}$ of magnitude $F$ making angle $\theta$ with the x-axis, the components are $F_x = F\cos\theta$ (along x-axis) and $F_y = F\sin\theta$ (along y-axis). The vector form is $\vec{F} = F_x\hat{i} + F_y\hat{j}$.

**Angle measured from y-axis**: if the angle $\phi$ is measured from the y-axis, the formulas become $F_y = F\cos\phi$ (adjacent to y) and $F_x = F\sin\phi$ (opposite to y). The component adjacent to the angle uses cosine; the opposite uses sine.

**Figure (i) — 10 N at 30° from y-axis**: $F_y = F\cos30° = 10 \cdot (\sqrt{3}/2) = 5\sqrt{3} \approx 8.66\,\text{N}$, $F_x = F\sin30° = 10 \cdot 0.5 = 5\,\text{N}$. The y-component is larger because the angle is closer to the y-axis.

**Figure (ii) — 10 N at 45° from y-axis**: $F_x = F\sin45° = 10 \cdot (1/\sqrt{2}) = 5\sqrt{2} \approx 7.07\,\text{N}$, $F_y = F\cos45° = 5\sqrt{2} \approx 7.07\,\text{N}$. At 45° from y-axis (or from x-axis), both components are equal.

**Why the formulas change**: when the angle is from the x-axis, the x-component is 'adjacent' and uses cosine. When the angle is from the y-axis, the y-component is 'adjacent' and uses cosine. Always identify which axis the angle is measured from.
**SOH-CAH-TOA**: Sine = Opposite/Hypotenuse, Cosine = Adjacent/Hypotenuse, Tangent = Opposite/Adjacent. Apply this to identify which trig function to use for each component.
**Special angle values to memorize**: $\sin30° = \cos60° = 1/2$, $\cos30° = \sin60° = \sqrt{3}/2$, $\sin45° = \cos45° = 1/\sqrt{2}$, $\tan30° = 1/\sqrt{3}$, $\tan60° = \sqrt{3}$.

**Components in 3D**: for a vector $\vec{F}$ in 3D, $F_x = F\cos\alpha$, $F_y = F\cos\beta$, $F_z = F\cos\gamma$ where $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are angles with x, y, z axes. The direction cosines satisfy $\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1$.

**Components for an inclined plane**: for a plane tilted at angle $\theta$, the component of gravity along the plane is $g\sin\theta$ (down the slope) and perpendicular is $g\cos\theta$. This is a standard NEB problem.

**Sign convention for components**: components are positive in the direction of the positive axis. If a force points in the negative x direction, $F_x$ is negative. This is essential for solving equilibrium problems.

**Negative components**: if the angle $\theta$ is between 90° and 180° (second quadrant), $\cos\theta < 0$, so $F_x$ is negative. Similarly, in the third and fourth quadrants, appropriate components become negative.
**Adding resolved components**: to find the resultant of multiple forces, resolve each into x and y components, then add: $R_x = \sum F_{ix}$, $R_y = \sum F_{iy}$, $R = \sqrt{R_x^2 + R_y^2}$.
**Vector magnitude from components**: $F = \sqrt{F_x^2 + F_y^2 + F_z^2}$. This is the 3D extension of the Pythagorean theorem.

**Example 1 (10 N at 60° from x-axis)**: $F_x = 10\cos60° = 5\,\text{N}$, $F_y = 10\sin60° = 5\sqrt{3} \approx 8.66\,\text{N}$. Compared to 30° from y-axis (which equals 60° from x-axis), the components are the same.

**Example 2 (15 N at 37° from x-axis, with $\sin37°\approx0.6$, $\cos37°\approx0.8$)**: $F_x = 15 \cdot 0.8 = 12\,\text{N}$, $F_y = 15 \cdot 0.6 = 9\,\text{N}$. The 3-4-5 triangle appears here, useful in physics problems.

**Component along an arbitrary direction**: to find the component of $\vec{A}$ along a unit vector $\hat{u}$ (any direction), use the dot product: $A_u = \vec{A}\cdot\hat{u} = |\vec{A}|\cos\alpha$, where $\alpha$ is the angle between $\vec{A}$ and $\hat{u}$.
**Two key rules**: (1) Component along an axis = magnitude × cos(angle with axis). (2) If the angle is with the OTHER axis, use sine (since the two axes are perpendicular).

**Practical example — pulling a lawn roller**: pulling with force $F$ at angle $\theta$ to the ground, the effective horizontal force is $F\cos\theta$ and the vertical lift is $F\sin\theta$. Pulling at an angle reduces ground reaction.

**Projectile launch at angle $\theta$**: initial velocity $v_0$ resolves into $v_{0x} = v_0\cos\theta$ (horizontal) and $v_{0y} = v_0\sin\theta$ (vertical). These are the foundation of projectile motion analysis.

**Direction cosines in 3D**: for a vector $\vec{A}$ making angles $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ with the x, y, z axes: $A_x = A\cos\alpha$, $A_y = A\cos\beta$, $A_z = A\cos\gamma$. The direction cosines satisfy $\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1$.

**Unit vector from components**: if $\vec{A} = A_x\hat{i} + A_y\hat{j} + A_z\hat{k}$, then $\hat{A} = \frac{\vec{A}}{|\vec{A}|} = \frac{A_x}{A}\hat{i} + \frac{A_y}{A}\hat{j} + \frac{A_z}{A}\hat{k} = \cos\alpha\,\hat{i} + \cos\beta\,\hat{j} + \cos\gamma\,\hat{k}$.

**Component along a line**: to find the component of $\vec{A}$ along a line with direction cosines $(l, m, n)$, use $A_{\text{line}} = A_x l + A_y m + A_z n = \vec{A}\cdot\hat{u}$, where $\hat{u}$ is the unit vector along the line.

**Vector resolution is unique for rectangular components**: for a given set of perpendicular axes, the rectangular components $R_x$ and $R_y$ are uniquely determined. However, oblique components (along non-perpendicular directions) are not unique without additional constraints.
confusion: Component formula is always $F\cos\theta$ — The component along the axis the angle is measured from uses cosine. The component along the perpendicular axis uses sine. Both formulas change based on reference axis.

The angle 30° means the x-component is $F\sin30°$ — It depends on which axis 30° is measured from. If 30° is from the x-axis, $F_x = F\cos30°$ and $F_y = F\sin30°$. If 30° is from the y-axis, the formulas swap.
Components are always positive — Components can be negative if the vector points in the negative direction of an axis. Sign indicates direction along that axis, not magnitude.
Angle is always from the x-axis — The angle can be from any reference axis. You must state which axis the angle is measured from, or use unambiguous notation (e.g., '30° above the horizontal').

$\cos$ and $\sin$ can be used interchangeably for components — No. The component ALONG the axis the angle is measured from uses $\cos$. The component PERPENDICULAR to that axis uses $\sin$. This is fixed.
A force at 30° above the horizontal has $F_y = F\sin30°$ — Correct if 30° is from horizontal. If 30° is from vertical, $F_y = F\cos30°$. Always verify the reference axis.

Components are independent of the choice of axes — Components DEPEND on the choice of axes. The same vector has different components in different coordinate systems, but the same magnitude and direction.

Resolving a vector into components changes the vector — No, it gives an EQUIVALENT representation. The vector is unchanged; we just describe it in a different way. $\vec{F}$ and $(F_x, F_y)$ are two descriptions of the same vector.

The component along an axis is always $F\cos\theta$ — Only if $\theta$ is measured from that axis. If $\theta$ is measured from the perpendicular axis, the component along the first axis is $F\sin\theta$.

Components and the original vector have different physical dimensions — No. Components and the original vector always have the same dimensions. If $\vec{F}$ is a force, both $F_x$ and $F_y$ are forces.
practice: A force of 20 N acts at 60° above the horizontal. Find its horizontal and vertical components. [Solution: $F_x = 20\cos60° = 10\,\text{N}$. $F_y = 20\sin60° = 20\cdot(\sqrt{3}/2) = 10\sqrt{3} \approx 17.32\,\text{N}$.]

A force of 50 N acts at 30° to the vertical. Resolve it into horizontal and vertical components. [Solution: Vertical (along which 30° is measured): $F_y = 50\cos30° = 50\cdot(0.866) = 43.3\,\text{N}$. Horizontal: $F_x = 50\sin30° = 50\cdot0.5 = 25\,\text{N}$.]

Find the components of a 100 N force at 45° below the horizontal (third quadrant). [Solution: $F_x = 100\cos45° = 70.7\,\text{N}$ (positive, along +x). $F_y = -100\sin45° = -70.7\,\text{N}$ (negative, since below x-axis).]

A vector makes angles 60°, 45°, and 60° with the x, y, and z axes respectively. If its magnitude is 20, find its components. [Solution: $F_x = 20\cos60° = 10$, $F_y = 20\cos45° = 20/\sqrt{2} = 10\sqrt{2} \approx 14.14$, $F_z = 20\cos60° = 10$. Check: $100 + 200 + 100 = 400 = 20^2$ ✓]

A body of 5 kg is pushed with horizontal force 30 N. Find the normal reaction from the ground. [Solution: $W = mg = 5\cdot9.8 = 49\,\text{N}$ (down). $N = W = 49\,\text{N}$ (up). The horizontal force doesn't affect the vertical equilibrium since there is no vertical component.]

Resolve a force of 40 N at 53° above the horizontal into components, using $\sin53°=0.8$ and $\cos53°=0.6$. [Solution: $F_x = 40\cdot0.6 = 24\,\text{N}$, $F_y = 40\cdot0.8 = 32\,\text{N}$. This is a 3-4-5 right triangle scaled by 8.]

A force of 60 N is applied at 30° to the horizontal. Find (a) the horizontal component, (b) the vertical component, and (c) verify that $F^2 = F_x^2 + F_y^2$. [Solution: (a) $F_x = 60\cos30° = 60\cdot(0.866) = 51.96\,\text{N}$. (b) $F_y = 60\sin30° = 30\,\text{N}$. (c) $51.96^2 + 30^2 = 2700 + 900 = 3600 = 60^2$ ✓]

A 2 kg ball is thrown at 30° above the horizontal with speed 20 m/s. Find the initial horizontal and vertical velocity components. [Solution: $v_x = 20\cos30° = 20\cdot(0.866) = 17.32\,\text{m/s}$. $v_y = 20\sin30° = 10\,\text{m/s}$.]

A vector $\vec{A}$ has magnitude 10 and makes angles 60°, 60°, and 90° with the x, y, and z axes respectively. Find its components. [Solution: $A_x = 10\cos60° = 5$, $A_y = 10\cos60° = 5$, $A_z = 10\cos90° = 0$. Check: $25+25+0 = 50 \neq 100$. This is inconsistent — the given angles are impossible for a single vector. Valid angles must satisfy $\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1$.]

Find the components of the vector $\vec{r} = 3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 12\hat{k}$ along the directions of the unit vectors $\hat{u}_1 = \frac{\hat{i}+\hat{j}}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $\hat{u}_2 = \frac{\hat{j}+\hat{k}}{\sqrt{2}}$. [Solution: Component along $\hat{u}_1$: $\vec{r}\cdot\hat{u}_1 = \frac{3+4+0}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{7}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 4.95$. Component along $\hat{u}_2$: $\vec{r}\cdot\hat{u}_2 = \frac{0+4+12}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{16}{\sqrt{2}} = 8\sqrt{2} \approx 11.31$.]

A force of 100 N makes angles of 60° with the x-axis and 45° with the y-axis. Find the angle with the z-axis and the z-component. [Solution: $\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1$. $\cos^260° + \cos^245° + \cos^2\gamma = 1$. $0.25 + 0.5 + \cos^2\gamma = 1$. $\cos^2\gamma = 0.25$, so $\gamma = 60°$ or $120°$. Taking $\gamma = 60°$: $F_z = 100\cos60° = 50\,\text{N}$. The components are $F_x = 50\,\text{N}$, $F_y = 70.7\,\text{N}$, $F_z = 50\,\text{N}$. Check: $2500+5000+2500 = 10000 = 100^2$ ✓]
universalFacts: Resolution of vectors is the **backbone of mechanics**. Almost every NEB problem in vectors, statics, dynamics, and projectile motion requires resolving a vector into perpendicular components.

**NEB exam tip**: when a problem says 'a force of X N at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal' or 'to the vertical', identify the reference axis first. Then use $\cos$ for the axis the angle is from, and $\sin$ for the perpendicular axis.
In engineering, the resolution of forces allows **stress analysis** in materials. Forces along structural members (axial) and perpendicular to them (shear) are determined by resolution.
The famous **3-4-5 right triangle** appears frequently: $\sin37°\approx0.6$, $\cos37°\approx0.8$, $\sin53°\approx0.8$, $\cos53°\approx0.6$. Memorize this to speed up problem-solving in NEB exams.

In **GPS navigation**, the velocity of a vehicle is resolved into north-south and east-west components to track position over time. Position updates are vector additions of resolved velocity components.
The choice of axes in resolution is **strategic**. For inclined plane problems, axes along and perpendicular to the plane minimize the number of forces that need to be considered in each direction.

Resolution and addition are **inverse operations**: resolution takes one vector and gives multiple, addition takes multiple and gives one. The formulas $R_x = R\cos\theta, R_y = R\sin\theta$ and $R = \sqrt{R_x^2+R_y^2}$ are the two sides of the same coin.

**Rope-pulling problems** (like dragging a sled) are classic resolution applications. The pulling force at an angle is resolved into a useful component (horizontal motion) and a wasted component (lifting up).
Direction cosines $(\cos\alpha, \cos\beta, \cos\gamma)$ are the **components of the unit vector** along the given direction. They completely specify the direction of a vector in 3D space.
The **dot product** $\vec{A}\cdot\hat{u}$ gives the component of $\vec{A}$ along $\hat{u}$ — this is the most general way to find a component along any direction, not just the coordinate axes.

data.title: Types of Vectors
notes: **Like (parallel) vectors**: vectors having the same direction, regardless of their magnitudes. They can be written as $\vec{A} = a\vec{B}$ where $a$ is a positive scalar. Like vectors add by ordinary arithmetic: their resultant is also parallel to them.

**Unlike (anti-parallel) vectors**: vectors having exactly opposite directions. If $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are anti-parallel, $\vec{A} = -a\vec{B}$ where $a$ is a positive scalar. The dot product of two anti-parallel vectors is $-|\vec{A}||\vec{B}|$.

**Co-planar vectors**: vectors that lie in the same plane. Any two vectors are always coplanar. Three vectors are coplanar if their vector sum or the scalar triple product $\vec{A}\cdot(\vec{B}\times\vec{C}) = 0$.

**Non-coplanar (skew) vectors**: vectors that do not lie in the same plane. Three vectors are non-coplanar if they span 3D space. The minimum number of non-coplanar vectors needed to span 3D is three.

**Null (zero) vector $\vec{0}$**: a vector with zero magnitude and indeterminate direction. It is the additive identity: $\vec{A} + \vec{0} = \vec{A}$. The zero vector is parallel to every vector, since $0\vec{A} = \vec{0}$.

**Unit vector**: a vector of magnitude 1 in a specified direction, denoted with a hat/circumflex: $\hat{n}$, $\hat{A}$. For any vector $\vec{A}$, the unit vector along it is $\hat{A} = \vec{A}/|\vec{A}|$.

**Standard unit vectors $\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$**: unit vectors along the x, y, and z axes of a Cartesian coordinate system. They are mutually perpendicular: $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{j} = \hat{j}\cdot\hat{k} = \hat{k}\cdot\hat{i} = 0$ and $\hat{i}\times\hat{j} = \hat{k}$ (right-hand rule).

**Position vector**: the vector from the origin to a point, denoted $\vec{r}$. If the point is $(x, y, z)$, then $\vec{r} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$. It specifies the location of a point relative to the origin.

**Equal vectors**: two vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are equal if they have the same magnitude AND the same direction. They can be drawn from different points but are physically equivalent: $\vec{A} = \vec{B}$ implies $|\vec{A}| = |\vec{B}|$ and parallel with same orientation.

**Negative vector**: $-\vec{A}$ is the vector with the same magnitude as $\vec{A}$ but opposite direction. $\vec{A} + (-\vec{A}) = \vec{0}$. Useful in problems like relative velocity and force balance.
**Collinear vectors**: vectors lying along the same line, regardless of direction. They are either parallel or anti-parallel. Collinear vectors add algebraically with appropriate signs.

**Axial vector (pseudovector)**: vectors representing quantities like angular velocity, torque, and magnetic field. They change sign under reflection (mirror inversion). In contrast, **polar vectors** (force, velocity) follow normal vector addition.

**Free vector**: a vector that can be translated parallel to itself without changing its physical meaning. Examples: velocity, force. In contrast, a **bound (localized) vector** is tied to a specific point (e.g., moment of a force about a point).

**Basis vectors**: a set of linearly independent vectors that span the entire vector space. For 3D, $\{\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}\}$ is the standard basis. Any vector in 3D can be written as a linear combination of basis vectors.
**Orthogonal vectors**: vectors that are perpendicular to each other. The dot product of orthogonal vectors is zero: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = 0$ for perpendicular $\vec{A}, \vec{B}$.

**Mutually perpendicular vectors**: a set of vectors where each is perpendicular to every other. $\{\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}\}$ is the canonical example in 3D. The magnitude of any vector is the square root of the sum of squares of components along such a basis.

**Solved example**: two vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are equal if $\vec{A} = \vec{B}$. But 'parallel' only requires same direction, allowing different magnitudes. So parallel does not imply equal, but equal implies parallel.

**Collinear three-vector property**: if $\vec{A}, \vec{B}, \vec{C}$ are collinear, then $\vec{C} = a\vec{A} + b\vec{B}$ for some scalars $a, b$ (and conversely, three collinear vectors are linearly dependent).

**Vector notation distinction**: bold $\mathbf{A}$ and arrow $\vec{A}$ both denote vectors. Magnitude is $|\vec{A}|$, $|\mathbf{A}|$, or simply $A$. Unit vectors are $\hat{a}$ or $\hat{u}$ (with hat).

**Practical applications**: in physics, identifying the type of vector helps in selecting the correct operation. Force is a polar vector (adds via parallelogram law), torque is an axial vector (different rules for reflection).

**Contravariant vs covariant vectors**: in advanced vector analysis, vectors are classified by how their components transform under coordinate changes. Contravariant components transform opposite to basis vectors; covariant components transform the same way. This distinction is crucial in tensor analysis and general relativity.

**Basis-independent definition**: a vector is fundamentally defined as an object that transforms in a specific way under coordinate rotations. The component representation $\vec{A} = A_x\hat{i} + A_y\hat{j} + A_z\hat{k}$ is basis-dependent, but the vector itself is a geometric object independent of coordinates.

**Linear dependence and independence**: a set of vectors is linearly independent if no vector in the set can be written as a linear combination of the others. In 3D, at most 3 vectors can be linearly independent. Four or more vectors in 3D are always linearly dependent.

**Zero vector and linear dependence**: the zero vector is always linearly dependent with any set of vectors (since $0\cdot\vec{A} + 0\cdot\vec{B} + 1\cdot\vec{0} = \vec{0}$). Any set containing the zero vector is linearly dependent.

**Coplanarity test for three vectors**: three vectors $\vec{A}$, $\vec{B}$, $\vec{C}$ are coplanar if and only if their scalar triple product is zero: $\vec{A}\cdot(\vec{B}\times\vec{C}) = 0$. This is equivalent to the volume of the parallelepiped they form being zero.
confusion: Like vectors are equal — Like vectors are parallel (same direction), but their magnitudes can differ. Equal vectors require both same direction and same magnitude. $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i}$ and $\vec{B} = 5\hat{i}$ are like vectors but not equal.
The null vector has no direction at all — The null vector has indeterminate direction, meaning we cannot assign a unique direction to it. By convention, it is treated as parallel to every vector.

All vectors in 3D are coplanar — Any TWO vectors are coplanar, but three vectors can be non-coplanar (skew). Four or more vectors can always be reduced to a set in 3D, with at most 3 linearly independent members.

Unit vectors are unique for each direction — There are infinitely many unit vectors for the same direction (any vector of magnitude 1 in that direction). However, for a given direction, the unit vector is unique up to sign.

Co-planar and parallel mean the same thing — Parallel vectors must lie along the same line (collinear). Coplanar vectors only need to be in the same plane; they can point in different directions within that plane.
Anti-parallel vectors are like vectors with a sign — Anti-parallel vectors point in OPPOSITE directions. Like vectors point in the SAME direction. They are fundamentally different categories.

Equal vectors must start at the same point — No. Free vectors are equal if they have the same magnitude and direction, regardless of position. The position of the vector's tail or head does not affect its equality.

Position vector and displacement vector are the same — Position vector $\vec{r}$ is from origin to a point. Displacement vector $\Delta\vec{r}$ is the change in position from one point to another. They are related but not identical.
The negative of a vector changes its magnitude — No. The negative vector $-\vec{A}$ has the SAME magnitude as $\vec{A}$ but the OPPOSITE direction. Only the direction changes.

All unit vectors are the same — No. Each unit vector points in a different direction. $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$, and $\hat{k}$ are all unit vectors but point in different (mutually perpendicular) directions. There are infinitely many unit vectors, one for each direction.
practice: State which of the following pairs of vectors are like, unlike, coplanar, or equal: (a) $\vec{A} = 3\hat{i}$, $\vec{B} = 7\hat{i}$. (b) $\vec{A} = 4\hat{j}$, $\vec{B} = -6\hat{j}$. (c) $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}$, $\vec{B} = 2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}$. [Solution: (a) like, coplanar, not equal (different magnitudes). (b) unlike, coplanar, not equal. (c) equal (and therefore like, coplanar, parallel).]
Find the unit vector along $\vec{A} = 3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j}$. [Solution: $|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{9+16} = 5$. $\hat{A} = \vec{A}/|\vec{A}| = (3/5)\hat{i} + (4/5)\hat{j}$.]

Are the vectors $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$, $\vec{B} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}$, $\vec{C} = 3\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 5\hat{k}$ coplanar? [Solution: Compute the scalar triple product $\vec{A}\cdot(\vec{B}\times\vec{C})$. First, $\vec{B}\times\vec{C} = \hat{i}((-2)(5)-(1)(1)) - \hat{j}((1)(5)-(1)(3)) + \hat{k}((1)(1)-(-2)(3)) = -11\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 7\hat{k}$. Then $\vec{A}\cdot(\vec{B}\times\vec{C}) = 2(-11) + 3(-2) + 4(7) = -22 - 6 + 28 = 0$. Since the scalar triple product is 0, the vectors are coplanar.]

Show that the zero vector $\vec{0}$ is parallel to every vector. [Solution: For any $\vec{A}$, the zero vector can be written as $\vec{0} = 0\cdot\vec{A}$. The scalar multiplier is 0, which is a non-negative real number. So $\vec{0}$ is parallel to $\vec{A}$ by the definition of parallelism. Also, $\vec{0}$ has no specific direction, so the convention treats it as parallel to all directions.]

If $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are unit vectors making 60° with each other, find $\vec{A}+\vec{B}$. [Solution: $|\vec{A}+\vec{B}| = \sqrt{1+1+2\cos60°} = \sqrt{2+1} = \sqrt{3}$. Direction: bisects the angle, so 30° from each. $\vec{A}+\vec{B} = \sqrt{3}\hat{n}$, where $\hat{n}$ is the unit vector at 30° from both.]

Determine whether the vectors $\vec{A} = 3\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}$, $\vec{B} = \hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 5\hat{k}$, $\vec{C} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$ are coplanar. [Solution: $\vec{B}\times\vec{C} = \hat{i}((-3)(3)-(5)(-1)) - \hat{j}((1)(3)-(5)(2)) + \hat{k}((1)(-1)-(-3)(2)) = -4\hat{i} + 7\hat{j} + 5\hat{k}$. $\vec{A}\cdot(\vec{B}\times\vec{C}) = 3(-4) + (-2)(7) + 1(5) = -12 - 14 + 5 = -21 \neq 0$. Not coplanar.]

Express the vector $\vec{F} = 6\hat{i} + 8\hat{j}$ in terms of its magnitude and a unit vector along it. [Solution: $|\vec{F}| = \sqrt{36+64} = 10$. $\hat{F} = (6/10)\hat{i} + (8/10)\hat{j} = 0.6\hat{i} + 0.8\hat{j}$. $\vec{F} = 10(0.6\hat{i}+0.8\hat{j}) = 10\hat{F}$.]

Given $\vec{A} = 2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j}$ and $\vec{B} = -4\hat{i} + 6\hat{j}$, show that the vectors are anti-parallel. [Solution: $\vec{B} = -2(2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}) = -2\vec{A}$. The negative scalar indicates opposite direction. So $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are anti-parallel. Verify: $B/A = |-4\hat{i}+6\hat{j}|/|2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}| = \sqrt{52}/\sqrt{13} = 2$. The ratio is negative, confirming anti-parallel.]

Find three unit vectors that are mutually perpendicular to each other. [Solution: The standard unit vectors $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$, $\hat{k}$ are mutually perpendicular: $\hat{i}\cdot\hat{j}=0$, $\hat{j}\cdot\hat{k}=0$, $\hat{k}\cdot\hat{i}=0$. Any rotation of this set also gives three mutually perpendicular unit vectors.]

Show that the vectors $\vec{A} = \hat{i} + \hat{j}$, $\vec{B} = -\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$, and $\vec{C} = \vec{B} - \vec{A} = -2\hat{i} + \hat{k}$ form a triangle. Find its type and area. [Solution: $\vec{A}+\vec{C} = \hat{i}+\hat{j}-2\hat{i}+\hat{k} = -\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k} = \vec{B}$, so the triangle closes. Magnitudes: $|\vec{A}|=\sqrt{2}$, $|\vec{B}|=\sqrt{3}$, $|\vec{C}|=\sqrt{5}$. Check: $2+3=5$, so $|\vec{A}|^2+|\vec{B}|^2 = |\vec{C}|^2$ — it is a right-angled triangle with the right angle between $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$. Verify: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = -1+1+0 = 0$. Area $= \frac{1}{2}|\vec{A}||\vec{B}| = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2}\sqrt{3} = \frac{\sqrt{6}}{2} \approx 1.225$.]

If $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are unit vectors with $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = 1/2$, find the angle between them and the magnitude of $\vec{A}+\vec{B}$. [Solution: $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B} = |\vec{A}||\vec{B}|\cos\theta = \cos\theta = 1/2$, so $\theta = 60°$. $|\vec{A}+\vec{B}| = \sqrt{1+1+2\cos60°} = \sqrt{2+1} = \sqrt{3}$.]

Three mutually perpendicular unit vectors $\hat{u}_1$, $\hat{u}_2$, $\hat{u}_3$ form a basis for 3D space. Express an arbitrary vector $\vec{A} = 5\hat{i} + 12\hat{j}$ in terms of this basis. [Solution: The standard basis $\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$ IS a set of three mutually perpendicular unit vectors. $\vec{A}$ is already expressed in this basis: $A_x = 5$, $A_y = 12$, $A_z = 0$. The magnitude is $|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{25+144} = 13$.]
universalFacts: The classification of vectors into types (like/unlike, coplanar/non-coplanar, polar/axial) is essential for choosing the right operation. Like vectors add algebraically; non-coplanar vectors require 3D analysis.
NEB exam pattern: 'types of vectors' questions are usually short answer or fill-in-the-blank format. Common question: 'define and give an example of unit vector/like vector/co-planar vector'.

The **right-hand rule** for unit vectors $\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$ is essential for cross products: $\hat{i}\times\hat{j} = \hat{k}$, $\hat{j}\times\hat{k} = \hat{i}$, $\hat{k}\times\hat{i} = \hat{j}$. This cyclic order defines the orientation of 3D space.

**Polarity** of vectors (polar vs axial) matters in electromagnetism. Electric field $\vec{E}$ is a polar vector, magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is axial. The Lorentz force $\vec{F} = q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$ produces a polar force from the cross product of two vectors of different polarities.

The **zero vector** is unique in that it is the only vector with indeterminate direction. It is the additive identity, and it is parallel to every vector (since $\vec{0} = 0 \cdot \vec{A}$ for any $\vec{A}$).

In **linear algebra**, the concept of basis vectors generalizes $\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$ to any set of linearly independent vectors. The 3D space we work in has dimension 3, requiring exactly 3 linearly independent basis vectors.

The **displacement vector** $\Delta\vec{r} = \vec{r}_f - \vec{r}_i$ is a fundamental concept in kinematics. It depends only on initial and final positions, not on the path taken — this is why the work-energy theorem works.

**Co-planar vectors** simplify problems enormously: any problem with three or more vectors that are coplanar can be analyzed in 2D using x and y components. Non-coplanar vectors require full 3D analysis.

The concept of **linear independence** is fundamental: three non-coplanar vectors form a basis for 3D space. Any vector in 3D can be uniquely expressed as a linear combination of three linearly independent vectors.

**Vector spaces in physics**: the set of all displacement vectors in 3D space forms a vector space. Similarly, the set of all force vectors forms a vector space. Understanding vector types helps identify which vector space a physical quantity belongs to.
