The devices worth carrying into every answer: **exaggeration** ("I was so nervous I could have buttered the ceiling"), **understatement** (after the storm: "the weather has turned slightly breezy"), the **rule of three** ("he packed his books, his pens, and his fear of mathematics"), **anticlimax** ("he fought bravely for justice, honour and the last piece of cake"), and the **clash of registers** — formal words in undignified scenes, which is why "the mortuary-cold water of the bucket bath" is funnier than "the freezing water".

And hear the **tone**: is the writer laughing *with* the fools or *at* them? The same stumble can be written fondly or cruelly, and the tell is in the small words — *poor man, our heroic fool, bless him*. NEB's tone questions are this distinction wearing an examiner's suit.

## Writing humour — craft, not chance

The comic sentence is architecture: **setup** in plain language, **turn** in as few words as possible, and the surprise word at the very end — anything after a punchline is a stumble. "I finally got eight hours of sleep. Four at a time." Twelve words, two frames, one laugh.

Exaggerate the **true**, not the invented: the invigilator patrolling like a border guard, the mother who detects an untidy room through a closed door, the queue for water at break. Shared recognition — *we all do that* — earns the laugh; invented absurdity earns nothing, because the reader has nothing to recognise.

And keep a spine under the jokes: the story of the disastrous picnic is also about optimism, or family, or rain. Write the spine first, then dress it. An essay that is funny *and about something* is literature; an essay that is only funny is a party trick — and party tricks get sober marks.

## The comparison the exam sets

| Basis | Irony | Sarcasm | Satire |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Core move | say the opposite of what is meant | irony aimed at a person | irony organised against a vice |
| Target | situations, fate, oneself | an individual, present | institutions: greed, hypocrisy |
| Tone | gentle to bitter | biting, personal | mock-serious, public |
| Aim | wit and insight | to wound or score | to expose and reform |
| Victim feels it? | not required | required | the powerful, safely absent |
| Example | "Lovely weather" in a downpour | "Nice of you to finally join us." | mock awards for bribe-takers |
| Risk | taken literally | ruins relationships | read as endorsement if too deadpan |

The table is the two-mark question ("distinguish irony and sarcasm") answered in full — but in the exam, say it in prose with the target test: irony plays with situations; sarcasm plays with people; satire plays with the whole system and means to fix it.

## How the exam asks it

**"What makes the passage humorous?"** (4 marks) — two devices, each with a quoted phrase and one line on the turn; never retell the joke, analyse it. **"Distinguish irony and sarcasm"** (2 marks) — the target test in one sentence. **The humorous narrative** ("A funny incident I cannot forget", 6–8 marks) — setup-turn structure per paragraph, one true detail exaggerated one step past sense, the spine stated in the last line. **The short answer** ("Why is humour called a social lubricant?") — it eases tension, bonds strangers, and lets criticism be heard where direct words would be refused: the court jester's licence, still valid.

Hunt first for the opposites — grand words for small things, praise that cannot be sincere, formal dress at a food fight. One quoted phrase per device is evidence enough; quoting whole paragraphs shows everything and proves nothing.
examShortTricks: Trick 1: Name the humour device precisely: irony, pun, hyperbole, situational comedy — precision of device + the quoted instance is the full-mark pair.
Trick 2: 'Why is this funny?' answers must explain the INCONGRUITY (what we expected vs what happened) — expectation violation is the theory to cite.
practiceQuestions: Q. What makes the situation in the text humorous? (2 marks) — the gap between expectation and outcome; cite the moment.
Q. Identify one example of irony in the text. (2 marks) — quote the line and explain the intended vs actual meaning.
keyPoints: Identify humour types: situational, verbal, irony — name the type then explain.
Humour often carries social criticism; state what is being mocked.

data.title: Unit 8 — Human Culture
notes:
## Reading culture with words

Culture is everything a people make and keep — language, food, festivals, dress, beliefs, manners, buildings — and Nepal is the richest classroom for it on earth: dozens of languages, half a dozen calendars, and every street a living museum where a medieval shrine and a mobile-recharge shop share a wall. The unit asks two things of you: describe a festival so a stranger can smell it, and argue about what happens when cultures meet — which they are, everywhere, right now.

## The words that carry the theme

Sort the ideas first. **Material culture** is the visible made thing — dress, food, tools, architecture. **Non-material culture** is the carried invisible — language, values, beliefs, etiquette, the sense of what is polite and what is past. **Heritage** names what is handed down: *custom, ritual, folklore, oral tradition, heirloom, intangible heritage* (the dances, songs and craft knowledge that live only in people), *UNESCO World Heritage Site*. And the verbs of change tell the whole story in miniature: traditions **fade away**, **revive**, are **passed down**, **blend**, are **adopted** — or are **lost**, which is the verb the essays worry about.

The vocabulary of respect matters as much as the vocabulary of description: *sacred, solemn, festive, reverent, vibrant* belong in culture writing; *quaint* and *primitive* do not — they are condescension wearing a compliment's coat. And the idioms: *melting pot*, *a way of life*, *the old country*, *roots* (as in *put down new roots* while keeping the old ones watered).

Grammar's quiet helper here is the **present simple of habit**: "Bhai Tika **seals** the bond between sisters and brothers" — customs live in the tense of always, while your remembered instance lives in the past ("Last Maghe Sankranti, my grandmother **insisted**…"). Descriptions that can hold both — the eternal rite and one particular afternoon — always read as authentic.

## Reading the theme like a writer — the devices of culture writing

**Imagery** is the master device, and it is sensory: a festival described by sight alone is a postcard; described by smell (marigolds and incense), sound (deusi songs at the door), taste (sel roti eaten standing up) and touch (rice paste on the forehead), it becomes a place the reader visits. The exam's descriptive tasks are really imagery tasks with a word count.

**Symbolism** runs the theme: the tika is not a mark but a blessing made visible; jamara is barley and also the wish that growth be golden; a festival is never only a festival — it is a community telling itself its own story once a year. When a passage calls a lamp "a small argument against the dark", the symbol is doing philosophy, and noticing it is the analysis.

**Juxtaposition** — old beside new — is the theme's favourite composition: the dasho coat worn with sneakers, e-greetings travelling beside tika, a drone filming a ritual older than the drone. Writers juxtapose to ask a question without asking it; your essay can answer it: change is not betrayal — every tradition was once an innovation that survived.

And **tone** decides everything, as in the humour unit: affectionate observation reads as love; anthropological distance can read as condescension. The difference is in the small words, again — *we* versus *they*, *our* quiet streets versus *their* customs.

## The debates, held honestly

**"Globalisation is destroying local culture."** Evidence for the prosecution: English crowding mother tongues out of urban playgrounds; festivals compressed into photo opportunities; the same shops, shows and shoes from Kathmandu to Kansas. Evidence for the defence: the same connectivity gave Nepali music, film and food a world audience, and diaspora communities now fund and revive rituals the villages alone could not sustain. The synthesis worth writing: globalisation is a **filter, not a vacuum** — what survives is what communities deliberately transmit. The danger is passive drift; the remedy is deliberate teaching — the language spoken at home, the festival celebrated properly and not merely posted.

**"Tradition versus modernity"** is a false war, and saying so is the top-band move: they are shelves in the same house. A family video-calls a daughter abroad *during* the tika ceremony. Argue practice by practice: does it still serve care, identity, joy? Then retain, reform or retire it — case by case, with reasons.

**"Should tourists pay more at heritage sites?"** Weigh heritage as a public good that needs funding against fairness and access; note the risk of living temples becoming tickets. Land on differentiated pricing with transparent conservation use — policy, not slogan.

## The comparison the exam favours

| Basis | Folk culture | Popular culture |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Origin | anonymous, communal, local | named artists, media industries |
| Transmission | face to face, generation to generation | streaming, trends, algorithms |
| Change rate | slow, stable | fast, seasonal |
| Ownership | the community's | copyright's |
| Nepal example | deuda, lakhe dance, local melas | film hits, global pop covers |
| Function | identity, ritual, continuity | entertainment, shared moment |
| Lifespan | centuries | seasons |
| Relationship | feeds the popular | borrows back, repackages |
| Preservation | needs documentation and practice | markets handle it |

The table's last row is the essay's hinge: folk culture dies quietly unless someone teaches it on purpose — which is why "preserve heritage" essays should end with verbs (teach, practise, document, fund), not adjectives (rich, vibrant, precious).

## How the exam asks it

The **descriptive essay** ("Describe a festival you celebrate") wants one festival, three senses, one sequence, one meaning — depth beats breadth every time. The **argumentative essay** ("Traditional culture is being lost to globalisation") wants both shelves weighed and a deliberate-transmission close. The **short answers** want definitions with pulse: "intangible heritage is what lives in people — language, music, ritual, craft — not in objects; lose the speakers and you lose it all." The **article or letter** (to a tourist board, on protecting heritage) wants one problem, one workable proposal, one polite close.

A worked miniature of the whole method: *"Tihar arrives by smell before sight: marigolds at every gate, oil lamps outnumbering electric ones for one night, the kitchen surrendering to sel roti fried in batches that never reach the plate warm. By the third day the streets ring with deusi songs that ask more than they demand, and even the stingiest householder pays the traditional tax in sweets. What the lights say, quietly, is that darkness loses when the whole lane decides together."* — senses, sequence, meaning, and a last line that argues. That is the unit, folded into four sentences.
examShortTricks: Trick 1: Culture questions expect the visible/invisible split: artefacts and festivals vs values and worldview — answer with one of each.
Trick 2: For culture-change questions, argue preservation THROUGH change (adaptation) rather than freezing culture — the nuanced stance scores.
practiceQuestions: Q. How does culture shape identity? (2 marks) — language, rituals and values give belonging; one example.
Q. Should traditions change with time? (2 marks) — yes, adapt their core values to new contexts; keep the meaning, update the form.
keyPoints: Culture is learned, shared and changing — three adjectives examiners expect.
Compare cultural practices across communities without judging them.

data.title: Unit 9 — Ecology and Environment
notes:
## The theme with a deadline

Environment is where language has consequences: the essays you practise here are rehearsals for arguments citizens must win about the air they breathe and the water they drink. Nepal makes the stakes visible from any window — the world's highest mountains are the source of its rivers, and the cleanest hill air coexists with Kathmandu's winter smog. The unit gives you the vocabulary, the cause-and-effect grammar, and the argument frames; the exam gives you marks for all three.

## The words that carry the theme

The systems first: **ecosystem, biodiversity, habitat, food chain, watershed, carbon footprint**, and the pair every essay should keep straight — **climate** (decades of averages) versus **weather** (one Tuesday). The problems: **pollution** (air, water, soil, noise, plastic), **deforestation, landslides, erosion, extinction, invasive species, waste mismanagement** — and Nepal's own acronym, **GLOF** (glacial lake outburst flood), the mountain's version of a bursting dam. The responses: **conservation, afforestation, recycling, waste segregation, renewable energy, sustainable development, climate adaptation, mitigation, environmental impact assessment**.

One precision worth marks: the **greenhouse effect is not the villain** — it keeps the Earth liveable; the *enhanced* effect from burning fossil fuels is the problem. Candidates who make that distinction sound like readers; candidates who do not sound like headlines.

The phrasal verbs and collocations: to **cut down on** emissions, **phase out** diesel, **run out of** groundwater, **clean up** a river, **wipe out** a species, **set up** a recycling scheme; **heavy traffic, toxic fumes, a blanket of smog, arable land, flash floods**. And the honest hedges: pollution is "a major contributor to" respiratory illness, not its single cause — calibration is credibility.

## Reading the theme like a writer — the devices of environmental writing

Environmental writing is built on **cause and effect chained together**, and the chain is itself a device: "Deforestation removes roots → roots hold soil → soil washes into rivers → rivers silt up → floods deepen downstream." Write the arrows first, then convert them to sentences with *as a result, consequently, which in turn* — the logic becomes unbreakable, and the examiner can see the links.

**Personification** is the theme's most powerful figure: the mountain "bleeds" plastic, the river "chokes", the forest "loses its lungs". It works because it converts statistics into something with a pulse — but it must be earned by facts nearby, or it reads as decoration. **Contrast** structures every serious essay: the green hill station against the grey city; the glacier photograph from 1980 against today's; the village that banned plastic bags against the town that did not. One concrete before-and-after is worth a page of alarm.

Then there is **irony**, the theme's bitterest device: bottled water sold in a country with the world's largest fresh-water reserves; air-conditioners cooling rooms while warming the planet that needs the cooling; the "eco-resort" flying guests in to admire an unspoiled view their flights are spoiling. An essay that catches one such irony and explains its mechanism is doing the analysis NEB's comprehension questions pay for.

## The debates, held honestly

**"Development versus environment"** is the theme's false boxing match, and refusing it is the top-band move. The honest frame is **sustainable development** — meeting present needs without stealing from the future — and it is not a rich-country luxury: hydropower is development *and* low-carbon; community forestry is conservation *and* livelihood; the question is which development, not whether. Concede the real tension (a poor country cannot be lectured into staying poor), then rebut the false choice with the examples.

**"Who is responsible — governments or individuals?"** Concede the comfort of personal virtue; note its ceiling — no amount of personal thrift regulates a coal plant. Land on both at their levels: individuals set norms and markets; governments set rules and infrastructure; and in a democracy the individual's sharpest tool is the demand for policy.

**"What can students actually do?"** wants verbs, not virtues: segregate waste, refuse single-use plastic, walk and share rides, join the school eco-club, audit the school's own bins and bulbs, obey the bag ban and defend it. End each list with a verb — that is the difference between a slogan and a plan.

## Grammar and style: the theme's quiet tests

**Uncountable nouns** rule here and punish the careless: *pollution, deforestation, waste, evidence, information, research* take no plural and no "a" — "much pollution", never "many pollutions"; "a piece of research", never "a research". Quantify with *a rise in, a decline of, a sharp increase in*; compare with *worse than, the worst, twice as much as*.

**Scale language** keeps arguments honest: local, national, regional, global. The litter in your lane is local; the plastic in it joins an ocean-scale current; the climate driver behind the whole story is global. The phrase worth owning: "a global problem with local handles."

And the **modal** calibration from Unit 5 applies with force: "The government **should** enforce kiln standards"; "Cities **might** pilot odd-even traffic days"; "We **must not** confuse a cold winter with a refuted trend." Calibration is style; style is marks.

## How the exam asks it

The **problem–solution essay** ("Air pollution in Kathmandu", "Plastic pollution", 8–10 marks) wants the cause chain first and solutions aimed at causes, at three scales, with one Nepal anchor: brick kilns, vehicle exhaust, road dust, crop burning — each with a handle. The **speech or article** ("Save the environment") wants a strong opening line, three verbs per listener, and a close worth chanting — and no statistics you cannot source. The **short answers** want the distinctions said plainly: weather is mood, climate is statistics; a carbon footprint is the total greenhouse gases an activity causes. The **formal letter** to a municipality wants layout, one problem, one workable proposal, polite insistence.

A worked miniature of the whole method: *"Every winter Kathmandu's air turns toxic, and the causes stack like the smog itself — kilns firing without scrubbers, vehicles idling in unmanaged traffic, dust from unpaved roads, stubble drifting in from the Terai. Each source has a handle: kiln standards, bus lanes, paving, alternative stubble use. 'The pollution is unbearable' is not an analysis until it becomes a list with handles attached."* — chain, handles, close. The unit, folded into three sentences.
examShortTricks: Trick 1: Environment questions: pair every PROBLEM with a SOLUTION — imbalance (all problems, no fixes) loses the band.
Trick 2: Use Nepal anchors: hydropower vs deforestation, plastic bans, community forestry — one local example per answer.
practiceQuestions: Q. Suggest two ways students can protect the environment. (2 marks) — reduce/reuse plastic and plant or protect trees; be specific.
Q. What is climate change doing to Nepal? (2 marks) — glacier melt and erratic rainfall affecting farming and hydropower.
keyPoints: Link human activity to environmental consequence in every answer.
Know terms: ecosystem, sustainability, conservation — use them precisely.

data.title: Unit 10 — Career Opportunities
notes:
## The theme with your name on it

Career is the unit students read most closely, for obvious reasons — the reader is choosing, or about to choose. The honest frame is that a career is neither a lottery nor a ladder but a **portfolio**: education, skills, connections, reputation and luck, built over years. The unit gives you the vocabulary of work, the language of applications and interviews (where marks and jobs share the same rules), and the argument frames for the debates — passion versus security, migration versus staying, degrees versus skills.

## The words that carry the theme

The vocabulary of work sorts into layers. **The search:** vacancy, opening, candidate, applicant, CV (curriculum vitae — the story of your working life in two pages), cover letter, interview, shortlist, appointment. **The working life:** profession, occupation, career path, promotion, increment, resignation, retirement, internship, apprenticeship, freelance, shift. **The economy's moods:** job market, unemployment, self-employment, entrepreneurship, startup, gig work, brain drain (the phrase every Nepal essay needs), remittance (arriving from Unit 6).

The phrasal verbs carry the journey: to **fill in** a form, **send off** an application, **take up** a post, **set up** a business, **take on** staff, **step down** from a role, **branch out** into something new, **get laid off** (the passive voice of bad news). And the idioms the working world actually speaks: *climb the ladder*, *get your foot in the door*, *a dead-end job*, *wear many hats*, *work your way up*, *burn out* — the last one a warning the theme should say honestly.

Register is the hidden test: a **CV** and an interview speak formal English (*I am writing to apply for…; I have three years' experience of…*), while a conversation about careers speaks natural English (*I'm thinking of taking up nursing*). Losing the register — "I wanna apply for the job sir" — costs marks in both worlds.

## Reading the theme like a writer — the language of applications

An application letter is **persuasion with a format**, and the format is the easy half: your address and the date, the employer's address, a salutation (*Dear Sir or Madam* when the name is unknown, *Dear Ms Sharma* when it is not), the purpose in the first line, the evidence in the middle, the polite close (*Yours faithfully* with the unknown name, *Yours sincerely* with the known one). Layout is marks lying on the table; candidates who lose them have nobody to blame but their margins.

The persuasive half is **evidence shaped to the role**. Every claim wants a proof: not "I am hardworking" but "I balanced a full course load with six hours of weekly tutoring". The device at work is **concrete detail** again — the same one that carried the family essays — and it works identically in an interview: stories are remembered; adjectives are not.

**Formal tone** has its own small grammar: no contractions (*I am*, not *I'm*), no slang, modals of polite request (*I would be grateful if…*), and the humble-brag discipline — state achievements as facts, let the reader supply the admiration. And beware the **cliché pile** ("dynamic team player with a proven track record"): every applicant writes it, so it proves nothing. Specific beats impressive; a specific thing you actually did beats an impressive thing nobody believes.

## The debates, held honestly

**"Follow your passion" versus "follow the market".** The romance says passion sustains effort; the pragmatist says passion does not pay in a saturated field. The synthesis worth writing: passion determines *what* you will be good at, the market determines *whether* it pays — and the durable careers find the overlap, or build it (a hobby that becomes a trade, a skill that creates its own demand).

**"Degrees versus skills."** The degree certifies learning; the skill does the work. Nepal's own paradox — thousands of graduates, employer complaints of unemployability — argues for both: the degree opens the door, the skill keeps you in the room. Vocational education, from Unit 5, returns here with evidence.

**"Go abroad or stay?"** The honest version holds both sides: abroad pays in currency and costs in family; staying pays in family and strains in opportunity. The mature close refuses the binary — the question is not where but *doing what*, since a purposeful job at home beats a purposeless one abroad and vice versa. Brain drain is a symptom, as with migration in Unit 19; the cure is an economy that makes staying rational.

## Grammar and style: the tense of your own story

The **present perfect** is the working life's home tense — "I **have completed** my +2", "I **have worked** as a tutor **for** two years" — because it ties the past to the present application. The **simple past** dates the finished chapter ("I **joined** the club in 2079"). Mixing them ("I have joined in 2079") is the theme's signature slip, and interviewers hear it the way musicians hear a flat note.

The **conditional** carries the interview's diplomacy: "I **would** welcome the chance to…", "If selected, I **would** commit to…". And the **formal infinitive** of purpose opens letters the exam loves: "I am writing **to apply for** the position of…".

One style rule above all: **short sentences in the letter**. Nervous writers inflate; confident writers compress. "I am confident that my experience and enthusiasm would make me a valuable addition to your team" — fine; but "I led a team of five volunteers for a year" is finer, because it is a fact and facts do not need adjectives.

## How the exam asks it

The **application letter** (6–8 marks) is near-guaranteed: an advertisement is given, you apply. Checklist the format first (addresses, date, salutation, subject line, close), then purpose in line one, then two proofs shaped to the role. The **CV-writing task** wants reverse-chronological order, action verbs (*led, organised, trained*), no full sentences, no photo-of-your-personality prose. The **essay** ("Unemployment problems among youths", "Self-employment as a career") wants the dialectic frames above with one Nepal anchor. The **short answers** want definitions with pulse: "an internship is supervised work experience that trades salary for learning — worth more than it pays."

And one piece of advice that outlives the exam: the letter you write for marks is practice for the letter that changes your life. Learn the format now, honestly, and the exam has already paid for itself.
examShortTricks: Trick 1: Career questions test FORMAL WRITING: cover letter and CV conventions — follow the fixed format; content must match the advertised post.
Trick 2: Interview answers use the STAR frame: Situation, Task, Action, Result — one compact STAR example beats vague claims.
practiceQuestions: Q. Write a cover letter for a teaching vacancy. (4 marks) — format, post and source, two matching qualifications, availability.
Q. How should you answer 'tell me about yourself' in an interview? (2 marks) — brief education, relevant skills, one achievement — under a minute.
keyPoints: CV and job-application language is tested — revise formal register and format.
Match personal skills to job requirements explicitly in answers.

data.title: Unit 11 — Hobbies
notes:
## The theme that is secretly about time

A hobby is what you do when nobody is making you do anything — which is why the theme, lightly examined, turns out to be about identity, discipline and joy. The exam likes it because every candidate has material: the football at dawn, the guitar with two broken strings, the novel abandoned at page forty. The unit's job is to give that material language — the vocabulary of pastimes, the grammar of habit, and the gentle art of writing about pleasure without sounding like a brochure.

## The words that carry the theme

The verb **to go** splits the theme neatly: you **go swimming, go trekking, go fishing** (go + -ing for activities away from home), but you **play** chess and **collect** stamps and **read** novels — the collocations are fixed, and mixing them ("I go chess") is the theme's signature error. The big families: **sports and games** (from Unit 3's vocabulary), **creative pastimes** (painting, photography, writing, playing an instrument), **collecting** (stamps, coins, stories about strangers), **making** (cooking, knitting, coding), **outdoors** (birdwatching, gardening, hiking — Nepal's hills make this the national hobby whether admitted or not).

The phrasal verbs of pastime: to **take up** a hobby (begin), **give up** (quit), **keep up with** (stay regular), **get into** (become absorbed), **wind down** (relax after work), **brush up on** (polish a rusting skill). And the expressions that carry the theme's philosophy: *variety is the spice of life*, *all work and no play makes Jack a dull boy*, *a change is as good as a rest* — one per essay, placed where it lands.

Grammar's quiet gift here is the **gerund**: hobbies are grammatically activities-as-nouns — "I enjoy **reading**", "**Swimming** keeps me sane", "My hobby is **photographing** old doors". The exam tests the verb patterns that decide what follows: *enjoy, avoid, suggest, mind* take **-ing**; *want, decide, hope, plan* take **to + verb**. "I enjoy **to swim**" is the theme's most common two-mark loss.

## Reading the theme like a writer — writing pleasure well

Writing about a hobby fails in one specific way: **the brochure voice** — "Reading is very interesting and improves knowledge." The cure is the same concrete detail that carried the family and sports units: not "I love trekking" but "the tea house at 4,000 metres, where the owner's daughter does homework by lantern and the fog closes like a curtain at seven". One particular beats three adjectives; the reader must see *your* hobby, not *a* hobby.

**Understatement** is the hobbyist's native tone — the truly devoted downplay: "I've been known to miss a bus or two for a good sunrise" says more than "I am passionate about photography". **Mild irony** keeps it human: the guitar with two broken strings, the stamp collection that cost a fortune in patience. And **anecdote** supplies the spine: one afternoon when the hobby taught you something — patience from fishing, failure from the kiln, silence from birdwatching — is the essay's load-bearing wall.

There is also a serious register hiding in this light theme, and the exam uses it: hobbies in **resumes and interviews** (Unit 10's territory) must sound purposeful — "reading" becomes "wide reading across history and current affairs" — without lying. The difference between the two registers is the difference between a friend asking and an employer asking; knowing which room you are in is the skill.

## The debates, held honestly

**"Are hobbies a waste of time?"** Concede the opportunity cost honestly — an hour of guitar is an hour not studied. Rebut with the evidence of how attention works: a rested, pleased mind learns faster than an exhausted one; the hobby is not theft from study but interest paid on it. Land the synthesis: the waste is not the hobby but the **unstructured excess** — the same phone that reads books can eat evenings.

**"Should hobbies be turned into careers?"** The dream says yes; the economics say carefully. A hobby monetised acquires deadlines, clients and invoices — and sometimes stops being a refuge. The mature answer: turn the hobby into a career only if you love the *work* of it, not the *escape* of it — they are different pleasures, and confusing them ruins both.

**"Screen hobbies versus hands-on hobbies."** Refuse the moral panic: reading on a phone is still reading. The real variable is **making versus consuming** — a screen that helps you draw, code or compose is a workshop; a screen that only scrolls is a slot machine. The distinction, stated once, is the essay.

## Grammar and style: the tense of habit

Hobbies live in the **present simple with adverbs of frequency** — "I **usually** sketch on Saturdays", "We **hardly ever** miss the morning match" — and the exam quietly checks the position of those adverbs (before the main verb, after *be*). The **present perfect continuous** tells the hobby's history with pride: "I **have been playing** the madal **for** six years" — the duration is the devotion.

Comparatives supply the essay's judgements: "Trekking is **more demanding than** gardening, but **less forgiving** of a missed monsoon." And the **used to / would** pair from the family unit returns for abandoned hobbies: "I **used to** collect stickers; I **would** trade three of a kind for one I lacked" — the past tense of who you were is the essay's quiet engine.

## How the exam asks it

The **personal essay** ("My hobby", 6–8 marks) wants one hobby deep, not five hobbies listed: what, when, how it began, one anecdote, what it taught. The **dialogue** (two friends on free time) wants turn-taking, gerunds flying free, and one recommendation with a reason. The **short answers** want the verb-pattern rules said with examples. The **speech** ("The importance of hobbies for students") wants the debate frame above — concede the opportunity cost, then collect the interest.

A worked miniature of the whole method: *"Photography taught me to wait. For a year I chased sunrises up the hill behind our house and came home with nothing twice for every once — until the morning the fog lifted just as the light hit the stupa, and I understood that the picture was never the reward; the waiting was."* — one hobby, one scene, one lesson. That is the unit, folded into two sentences.
examShortTricks: Trick 1: 'Describe your hobby' answers need SPECIFICS: when you started, what you actually do, one skill gained — concrete detail is the band marker.
Trick 2: Argue the value line: hobbies build skills and mental health — connect one hobby to one benefit, not a generic list.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why are hobbies important for students? (2 marks) — stress relief and skill-building; one concrete example.
Q. Describe a hobby of yours and what it has taught you. (3 marks) — specific activity, routine, one lesson learned.
keyPoints: Hobbies develop skills and identity — argue their value beyond entertainment.
Use hobby vocabulary (collecting, crafting, trekking) naturally in sentences.

data.title: Unit 12 — Animal World
notes:
## The theme that tests our vocabulary and our ethics

Animals are the theme where description and conscience share a leash: the same paragraph must name the creature precisely and decide how we owe it. Nepal makes the theme vivid — tigers and rhinos are a census success story here, elephants occasionally attend village meetings uninvited, and every monsoon the streets fill with somebody's abandoned puppies. The unit gives you the naturalist's vocabulary, the grammar of comparison and habit, and the ethics frames the exam sets.

## The words that carry the theme

Precision begins with the **collective nouns** the exam loves: a **pack** of wolves, a **herd** of elephants, a **flock** of birds, a **swarm** of bees, a **pride** of lions, a **school** of fish. Then the family words: **cub, calf, kitten, chick, foal, puppy**; and the gender pairs the paper tests — **lion/lioness, tiger/tigress, bull/cow, ram/ewe, stallion/mare**. The homes: **nest, den, burrow, stable, kennel, hive, aquarium**. The sounds, because English insists: dogs **bark**, cats **meow**, lions **roar**, bees **buzz**, snakes **hiss**, elephants **trumpet** — onomatopoeia is doing the naming, and it is the theme's built-in literary device.

The conservation vocabulary arrives from Unit 9 wearing fur: **endangered, vulnerable, extinct, poaching, habitat loss, wildlife sanctuary, national park, captive breeding, poacher versus ranger, human-wildlife conflict**. Nepal's own evidence is exam-ready: the tiger census doubling, the rhino translocations, the conservation success that tourism pays for — one checkable fact per essay, hedged as always.

And the idioms — animals live deep in English: *let the cat out of the bag*, *hold your horses*, *a fish out of water*, *the elephant in the room*, *crocodile tears*, *a wolf in sheep's clothing*, *busy as a bee*, *kill two birds with one stone*. Each is a small story frozen in a phrase; one, used aptly, shows the examiner a reader.

## Reading the theme like a writer — the devices animals carry

**Personification** is the theme's oldest device — animals in literature think, plot and judge because it lets writers say human things at a safe distance: the crow's persistence in the fable is really a lecture on patience. **Fable and allegory** build whole morals on four legs; when a passage gives a fox cunning or an owl wisdom, the animal is a **symbol**, and naming what it stands for is the analysis.

**Imagery** here is a naturalist's job: not "a big cat" but "shoulders rolling under the coat, the tail's last third flicking like a metronome". Sound imagery matters too — the theme comes with its own orchestra (§1's verbs) — and a description that can be *heard* is half-written.

**Irony and reversal** give the theme its bite: the "guard dog" asleep while the cat investigates the thief; the zoo advertising freedom; humans caging animals to study freedom. And **pathetic fallacy** — weather or animals mirroring mood — waits in every set passage: the dog howling before the bad news. Notice it, name it, and say what mood it carries.

## The debates, held honestly

**"Zoos: prisons or sanctuaries?"** Concede the cage's indictment — pacing predators, concrete enclosures. Rebut with the modern zoo's changed job: breeding programmes for the near-extinct, veterinary care, the child who sees a tiger and grows up to fund its forest. Land the synthesis: the question is not *whether* zoos but **which kind** — the concrete menagerie or the conservation ark.

**"Should animals be used in testing?"** The hardest frame in the theme, and it deserves its difficulty: weigh human medicine saved against suffering caused, then argue the ladder — replace where possible, reduce where not, refine always. The three R's are quotable and calm; slogans are neither.

**"Wildlife versus development."** The road through the forest, the airport near the wetland — Nepal argues these in the papers weekly. The honest frame: costs are real on both sides, mitigation (overpasses, corridors, timing) is the art, and the long ledger says the forest pays the country back in tourism, water and stability. One concrete case — a highway and a rhino corridor — beats a paragraph of principle.

**"Pets versus wildlife."** The quiet frame behind the puppy on the street: a pet is a commitment of years, not a festival purchase; abandonment is the theme's most answerable cruelty. The short essay here almost writes itself — which is why it scores well when told with one specific dog and badly when told with slogans.

## Grammar and style: comparison and habit

Animals invite **comparison**, and the grammar must keep up: "A cheetah runs **faster than** a deer"; "The rhino is **the most heavily built** of them all"; "A cat sleeps **as much as** sixteen hours a day". Watch the double comparatives ("more faster" — the classic slip) and the irregulars (*good/better/best, bad/worse/worst*) that examiners salt into every paper.

**Habit and instinct** live in the **present simple with plural subjects** — "Tigers **hunt** alone; elephants **move** in herds led by a matriarch" — and the agreement slips here (the elephant **move**) are the theme's quiet grammar tax. The **passive** returns for the species' story: "The tiger **was declared** the national animal; habitat **has been lost** to farmland; cubs **are smuggled** across borders." Who did it matters less than what happened — the passive's honest use.

And the **reported speech** of wildlife journalism — "The warden **said that** the herd had moved to the river" — waits for the narration unit; this theme is where it gets its practice sentences.

## How the exam asks it

The **descriptive essay** ("The animal I like most", 6–8 marks) wants one animal, seen precisely: appearance in naturalist detail, habitat and habits in the present simple, one reason for your choice that is not "it is beautiful". The **argumentative essay** ("Zoos should be banned", "Save wildlife") wants the frames above with one Nepal anchor — the tiger census, the community forests. The **story from an animal's point of view** (a favourite creative task) wants consistent personification: the dog narrates, so the dog cannot suddenly become "it". The **short answers** want the collective nouns, the homes, the sounds — the theme's vocabulary table in disguise.

A worked miniature of the whole method: *"The rhino is not aggressive; it is certain. It has survived ice ages, poachers and our fences by refusing to hurry, and there is a lesson in that — but the lesson is ours, not its: the animal did not ask to symbolise anything. It asks only for the tall grass, the river at dusk, and to be left certain."* — precision, personification with a purpose, and an ethics close. The unit, folded into three sentences.
examShortTricks: Trick 1: Animal texts often argue ethics — organise answers as welfare facts (sentience, suffering) + human duty + one practice to change.
Trick 2: Comprehension questions target behaviour details (habitat, diet, instinct) — underline them during reading.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why should humans protect animal habitats? (2 marks) — biodiversity and ecosystem balance; human survival depends on it.
Q. Is keeping animals in zoos justified? (2 marks) — conservation and education vs captivity stress; end with conditions that justify it.
keyPoints: Animal rights vs human use — present both positions before your own.
Note personification of animals in texts and what it reveals about humans.

data.title: Short Story 1 — Neighbours (Tim Winton)
notes:
## The story at a glance

"Neighbours" by Tim Winton is a small story about a large discovery: a young Australian couple move into a new suburb, brace themselves against the noise of their migrant neighbours — the Macedonian family shouting and singing, the Polish widower hammering — and are slowly, embarrassingly, won over. The neighbours turn out to be the community the couple did not know they were missing: they teach the young wife to cook, help butcher the pig, weep at her pregnancy, and celebrate the birth as their own. Winton's theme is the prejudice inside the newcomers — and the warmth that dissolves it.

## The plot, retold with an eye on its turns

The setup is a wall of difference: the young couple regard their street with suspicion — the Macedonians' "strange" cooking smells, the shouting, the visitors at odd hours — and the neighbours' friendliness reads to them as intrusion. The first turn is practical: the Macedonian woman teaches the wife how to cook stuffed peppers and cabbage rolls, and the young man, reluctantly, finds himself helping the Polish widower rebuild his chicken coop and slaughter a rooster — the walls thinning through work rather than words.

The second turn is the pregnancy, and Winton makes it the story's converter: the neighbours respond to the news with an intensity the couple has never met — the Macedonian women touch the young wife's belly, offer names and blessings, and the Polish widower, told of the birth, climbs the fence, holds the baby and weeps. The couple, who began by cataloguing differences, end the story inside a web of affection they did nothing to earn except accept.

The close is the story's quietest and loudest moment: the young husband, holding his child amid the neighbours' joy, finds himself weeping — "My God!" — the sentence that marks his conversion. The people he pitied as backward have taught him what his own culture's suburb had lost: that community is made of presence, food, noise and shared joy.

## The devices, with evidence

- **Contrast** — the story's engine: the couple's reserve against the neighbours' exuberance; the cold professionalism of their own culture against the migrants' noisy intimacy; the opening suspicion against the closing tears.
- **Symbolism** — the fence the Polish widower climbs is the story in one image: the barrier that becomes a threshold. The shared food — peppers, cabbage rolls, the butchered rooster — is culture crossing the border the couple thought they were guarding.
- **Point of view** — third person, close to the couple: we feel their condescension and then their conversion from the inside, which is why the ending's tears land as earned rather than sentimental.
- **Irony** — the couple expected to teach the migrants how to live in Australia; the migrants teach them how to live.
- **Warm detail** — the story's method throughout: specific acts (the belly touched, the rooster, the fence climbed) instead of general claims about community.

The exam question "how does the couple's attitude change?" is answered by the arc above — suspicion, reluctant participation, gratitude, tears — and each stage is anchored in an act, not a feeling.

## The characters worth an essay

**The young couple** are the story's real subjects — the majority-culture newcomers who think they are the mainstream and discover they are the poor ones in the currency that counts. Their arc from judgment to gratitude is the story's moral plot. **The Macedonian family** is generosity as a way of life: cooking, singing, naming, touching — a culture expressed in abundance. **The Polish widower** is the story's most affecting figure: alone, hammering at odd hours, he is the neighbour nobody wanted — and the one who weeps at a stranger's baby. His loneliness and his joy are the same fact: he has love to give and finally somewhere to give it.

## The themes worth an essay

**Prejudice and its cure** — the central theme: the couple's assumptions about migrants dissolve through contact, not argument; the story argues that familiarity is the antidote to bias. **Community versus privacy** — the couple's culture prizes distance; the neighbours' culture prizes presence — and the story sides, gently but firmly, with presence. **Cultural exchange as mutual enrichment** — the migrants give more than they receive, and the giving is food, help and joy. **The universality of family** — a birth in one house becomes a celebration in every house on the street. Write the essay with the fence, the food and the tears as your three anchors.

## NEB short answers, solved

**Q. How did the young couple first regard their neighbours? (2 marks)**
A. With suspicion and condescension: the Macedonian family's cooking smells, shouting and visitors seemed strange and intrusive, and the Polish widower's hammering was a nuisance. They thought of the newcomers as backward and themselves as the standard.

**Q. How did the neighbours treat the young couple? (2 marks)**
A. With open warmth: the Macedonian woman taught the young wife to cook traditional dishes, the women offered blessings and names for the unborn child, and the Polish widower helped with work and wept with joy at the birth. The couple received more friendship than they had ever offered.

**Q. What was the effect of the pregnancy on the neighbourhood? (2 marks)**
A. It converted the street into one family: the Macedonian women touched the young wife's belly and shared their traditions, and when the child was born the neighbours celebrated as if the baby were their own. The pregnancy made the couple's belonging complete.

**Q. Why does the Polish widower weep at the end? (2 marks)**
A. From joy and relief: the birth gives his loneliness somewhere to go. He climbs the fence — the story's symbolic barrier — holds the baby and weeps, because the young couple's family has become his own.

**Q. What does the story suggest about multicultural neighbourhoods? (2 marks)**
A. That difference is a resource, not a threat: the migrants' ways of living — cooking, helping, celebrating together — enrich the community that receives them. Winton suggests the newcomers to a suburb may be the ones who teach belonging.

**Q. How does the story end, and what does the ending mean? (2 marks)**
A. The young husband weeps, saying "My God!", as he holds his child amid the neighbours' joy. The tears mark his conversion: the man who began by judging his neighbours ends by recognising them as the community he had been missing.

## NEB long answers, solved

**Q. "The neighbours taught the couple more than the couple could teach them." Discuss with reference to the story. (8 marks)**
A model answer agrees and builds the evidence in order: the couple arrived with the majority culture's confidence and a list of judgments, while the neighbours arrived with stuffed peppers, help with the coop, blessings for the unborn child and tears for the newborn. It should trace the couple's arc through acts — the reluctant cooking lesson, the shared butchering, the fence climbed — and note Winton's irony: the "backward" neighbours practise the community the locals have lost. The strongest answers close on the ending: the husband's tears are the receipt for what has been given, and the story's verdict is that culture's best currency is presence.

**Q. How does Winton use contrast to carry the story's meaning? (8 marks)**
A model answer organises the analysis around the story's paired opposites: reserve against exuberance, privacy against presence, judgment against generosity, silence against noise — and shows that the couple's culture, not the migrants', is the one found wanting. It should discuss the point of view (the reader lives inside the couple's condescension and watches it dissolve), the fence as the story's symbolic hinge, and the food as culture crossing the border. The strongest answers note that the contrasts are never weaponised: the story's warmth converts rather than condemns, which is why it persuades.
examShortTricks: Trick 1: Theme: overcoming prejudice through neighbourly warmth — the young couple's initial discomfort with migrant neighbours dissolves into community; trace the change in three stages.
Trick 2: Sensory contrast does the work: the Macedonian family's smells, sounds and food first irritate, then charm — link two sensory details to the change of heart.
Trick 3: The ending (the couple weep at the neighbours' gift/expecting a baby) shows acceptance complete — quote the final gesture as evidence.
practiceQuestions: Q. How do the young couple's feelings towards their neighbours change? (3 marks) — suspicion → curiosity → affection; cite one moment for each stage.
Q. What does the story suggest about multicultural neighbourhoods? (2 marks) — differences initially divide but shared kindness builds community.
keyPoints: Theme: overcoming cultural distance — the young couple gradually joins the migrant community.
The final image (the woman weeping at birth) shows belonging achieved; quote it.

data.title: Short Story 2 — A Respectable Woman (Kate Chopin)
data.topicTitle: Short Story 2 — A Respectable Woman (Kate Chopin)
notes:
## The story at a glance

"A Respectable Woman" by Kate Chopin is a short story about a feeling that is never named — which is precisely how such feelings behave. Mrs. Baroda, comfortably married to Gaston, is irritated when her husband's friend Gouvernail comes to stay for weeks on the plantation. Her irritation softens into fascination, and one night on the bench under the live oak, sitting beside the quiet young man, she feels an impulse she does not analyse — and flees to the city. The story's last line, delivered months later, is its confession: she has overcome everything, and Gouvernail may visit again. Chopin writes desire and propriety in the same sentence and lets the reader feel the tug.

## The plot, retold with an eye on its turns

The setup is a wife's announcement: she is not going to like Gouvernail — she has heard he is a cynic and had hoped to leave him off the guest list. Gaston laughs; Gouvernail arrives and turns out to be nothing like the rumour: quiet, courteous, tired, asking nothing. Her dislike, deprived of fuel, has nowhere to go.

The middle is the story's slow burn: she cannot classify the man — he is neither witty nor demanding, and his silence puzzles her more than charm would. She tries to provoke him into conversation and gets gentleness back; she scolds herself for the unreasonable hostility, and the scolding is the story's tell — irritation that needs explaining is not irritation. One evening Gaston suggests she invite Gouvernail back for the summer; she refuses, with a sharpness that surprises even her.

The bench scene is the story's centre, told with Chopin's famous restraint: sitting beside Gouvernail in the silence, listening to his low voice about the old days and his desire to live and die in this bosom of tranquillity, she feels something rising in her that the narrative refuses to name — and she rises with it, leaving abruptly for the city until the visit is over. Gaston is baffled; the reader is not.

The close completes the design: months later, on her husband's repeated suggestion, Mrs. Baroda kisses him and says Gouvernail may come again — she has overcome everything, and this time she will be very nice. The sentence is a riddle with one honest solution: what she overcame was not her dislike.

## The devices, with evidence

- **Third-person limited point of view** — the story's master choice: we live inside Mrs. Baroda's consciousness, which means we know more about her feelings than she admits even to herself — the gap between what she thinks and what she says is the story's space.
- **Restraint (subtext)** — Chopin never names the attraction: the unnamed impulse on the bench, the flight to the city, the "overcoming" — the omission is the technique, and the reader supplies the word.
- **Irony** — layered: the title's "respectable" describes the mask, not the struggle; her stated dislike is the opposite of her actual feeling; and the final promise to be "very nice" is the story's most charged sentence.
- **Contrast** — the rumoured cynic against the gentle reality; her chatter against his silence; the plantation's tranquillity against the disturbance inside its hostess.
- **Symbolism** — the bench under the live oak: the scene of temptation staged in the most innocent of settings; the city as the place of flight and recovery.

The exam question "why does Mrs. Baroda leave for the city?" is answered by reading the omission: she flees the feeling she will not name, and the flight is the confession the story never makes directly.

## The characters worth an essay

**Mrs. Baroda** is the story's whole terrain: intelligent, self-aware enough to notice her own unreasonableness, and respectable enough to refuse her own discovery. Her arc is not a fall but a negotiation — feeling observed, resisted, survived, and finally invited back, which is the most honest ending a story of this kind can have.

**Gouvernail** is the quiet catalyst: he does nothing — that is his role. His gentleness and fatigue disarm her defences precisely because they make no demands; the story's temptation is made of kindness, not seduction. **Gaston** is the blind centre of the triangle: affectionate, oblivious, and delighted at the end without knowing why. His innocence is the story's quietest irony — the person with the least knowledge is the one with the most to lose.

## The themes worth an essay

**Desire versus propriety** — the central theme: a respectable woman's capacity for feeling exceeds what her respectability permits, and the story dramatises the negotiation without judging it. **The limits of self-knowledge** — Mrs. Baroda's narration of her own motives is unreliable, and the story trusts the reader to hear what she will not say. **Marriage and its silences** — Gaston's obliviousness is affectionate and total; the story asks how much a marriage can hold without knowing. **The ambiguity of endings** — the invitation back is either victory over temptation or its scheduling; Chopin leaves the choice to the reader, which is the story's final sophistication. Anchor the essay in the bench scene and the last line, and let the unnamed feeling stay unnamed.

## NEB short answers, solved

**Q. Why was Mrs. Baroda annoyed by Gouvernail's visit? (2 marks)**
A. She had formed a picture of him from rumour — a cynical, tiresome man — and had wanted the summer to herself with Gaston. The annoyance is her stated reason; the story's suggestion is that the dislike was never about who Gouvernail was.

**Q. How did Gouvernail actually behave? (2 marks)**
A. Gently and undemandingly: quiet, courteous, tired from overwork, happy to sit in silence and speak only when spoken to. His mildness disarms her hostility precisely because it gives her nothing to fight.

**Q. What happened on the bench under the live oak? (2 marks)**
A. Sitting beside Gouvernail in the evening quiet, listening to his low voice about the old days and his wish to live and die in that tranquillity, Mrs. Baroda felt an impulse she could not explain — and left abruptly for the city the next day. The story never names what she felt.

**Q. Why did she go to the city? (2 marks)**
A. To escape the feeling she would not examine: the visit to her aunt's is a flight from temptation rather than a social errand. The flight is the story's indirect confession.

**Q. What does Mrs. Baroda say at the end, and what does it mean? (2 marks)**
A. She tells Gaston that Gouvernail may visit again — she has overcome everything and will be very nice this time. The surface meaning is reconciliation; the honest reading is that what she overcame was not dislike but temptation, and the invitation is its careful management.

**Q. How does the title carry the story's irony? (2 marks)**
A. "Respectable" names the social identity Mrs. Baroda must maintain while feeling what the story never names: the word describes the mask that makes the struggle possible. The irony is that her respectability is both her prison and her poise.

## NEB long answers, solved

**Q. "The story never names Mrs. Baroda's feeling, and that is its power." Discuss Chopin's use of restraint. (8 marks)**
A model answer treats the omission as the story's central technique: the unnamed impulse on the bench, the unexplained flight to the city, the "overcoming" in the last line — each silence invites the reader to supply what the narrative withholds, and the supplied word is more powerful than any stated one. It should contrast the period's propriety (why the feeling cannot be named) with the story's honesty (why it cannot be denied), and use the point of view to show the gap between Mrs. Baroda's self-narration and her behaviour. The strongest answers close on the ending's ambiguity: the invitation back is either discipline or desire, and Chopin's refusal to choose is the story's final respect for its heroine's complexity.

**Q. Sketch the character of Mrs. Baroda and trace her change through the story. (8 marks)**
A model answer builds the portrait in stages: the confident hostess who announces her dislike; the puzzled woman whose hostility loses its object; the self-scrutinising wife who scolds her own unreasonableness; the tempted woman on the bench; the flight to the city; and the composed hostess of the final line who has, in her own words, overcome everything. It should argue that the change is not from prudishness to passion but from ignorance of her own heart to a negotiated awareness of it — and that her composure at the end, promising to be "very nice", is the most revealing sentence she says.
examShortTricks: Trick 1: Irony in the title: Mrs Baroda's 'respectability' is tested by suppressed attraction to Gouvernail — the gap between appearance and feeling is the story's engine.
Trick 2: Track her internal conflict in three beats: annoyance → fascination → flight to the city → (final hint of surrender) — the beats are the character-answer skeleton.
Trick 3: Chopin's restraint: nothing 'happens' outwardly; all the drama is psychological — say this when asked about style.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why does Mrs Baroda leave for her aunt's house? (2 marks) — she is troubled by her growing attraction to Gouvernail and fears losing respectability.
Q. What does the ending suggest? (2 marks) — her husband's hope that she will 'invite' Gouvernail again hints she has not fully conquered the feeling.
keyPoints: Mrs Baroda's suppressed attraction to Gouvernail — repressed desire vs social respectability.
Her final decision ('I shall treat him better') is ambiguous; discuss what it implies.

data.title: Short Story 3 — A Devoted Son (Anita Desai)
data.topicTitle: Short Story 3 — A Devoted Son (Anita Desai)
notes:
## The story at a glance

"A Devoted Son" by Anita Desai is a story about love that becomes control without changing its name. Rakesh, the son of poor Varma, rises to the top of the medical school, honours his parents in every traditional way — marries the mother's choice, brings his bride home, touches his father's feet — and then applies his medicine to his father's life: no fried food, no sweets, tonics by the clock, a schedule of care the old man experiences as a cage. The father's rebellion, the son's inflexibility, and the death that ends the argument leave the title standing like a question: devotion to whom — the father, or the son's own idea of duty?

## The plot, retold with an eye on its turns

The rise: Varma, a kerosene-dealer son of a poor family, announces his son's first-place result to the street; Rakesh wins a scholarship to the United States, returns with a degree and American admiration, and — the gesture the neighbourhood applauds — marries a village girl of his mother's choosing rather than an American. The early chapters are triumph: the son who had everything and gave back more.

The turn arrives with the father's health. Rakesh, now chief physician, takes over his father's body as a project: banned fried foods and sweets, vitamins and tonics, walks and schedules, and the father — who wants his sweets and his freedom — finds the love indistinguishable from authority. The comic-sad middle is their war of small rebellions: Varma bribing grandchildren to buy him sweets, complaining that his son's tonics taste of punishment, and announcing, whenever he can, that he is dying.

The endgame deepens the irony: the son's care extends the father's life past the point where the father wants it extended — the widow of the neighbourhood's sympathy, the old man's conviction that his son is keeping him alive against his will. On the last evening Varma pushes away the tonic, and Rakesh, firm and gentle, insists. The father dies; the son's devotion is intact; and the story leaves the reader holding both truths at once — the care was real, and the cage was real too.

## The devices, with evidence

- **Irony of the title** — the master device: "devoted son" is accurate and insufficient at once, since the devotion that feeds the father also imprisons him; the story's argument lives in that double reading.
- **Contrast** — the son's medical authority against the father's personal liberty; the neighbourhood's admiration against the old man's resentment; the young Rakesh who touched his father's feet against the doctor who schedules his life.
- **Point of view** — the narration moves between son and father, so the reader is given both the care and the cage and is never allowed to settle into either camp.
- **Domestic detail** — the sweets smuggled by grandchildren, the tonic's taste, the banned fried food: Desai's argument is carried by household objects, not speeches.
- **Generational conflict as structure** — the story's arc is the classic one inverted: the son who once obeyed now commands, and the reversal is where the pain lives.

The exam question "is Rakesh a good son?" is answered by holding the story's two truths: his devotion is genuine, and genuine devotion can still fail to ask the person it loves what he wants.

## The characters worth an essay

**Rakesh** is duty embodied: brilliant, obedient, grateful — and blind, in the way duty often is, to the difference between caring for a father and managing him. His flaw is not cruelty but certainty: he never doubts that he knows best, and the story's tragedy is that his certainty is medically right and personally wrong.

**Old Varma** is the story's heart: proud of his son's success and furious at its consequences, he wants sweets, respect and the right to die on his own schedule. His rebellions are comic and heartbreaking at once — the smuggled sweets, the announced deaths — and his last refusal of the tonic is the story's clearest sentence. **The mother** and **the wife** frame the household's quiet labour: the mother's early death removes Rakesh's gentler parent; the wife serves the regime the son prescribes. **The neighbourhood** is the story's chorus: it applauds the devotion it never has to live inside.

## The themes worth an essay

**Love as control** — the central theme: care administered without consent becomes authority; the story asks where devotion ends and domination begins. **Generational reversal** — the son who owed everything now governs the man who gave everything; the pain of the story is the role reversal inside a loving family. **Tradition versus modernity** — the traditional duty of the son meets the modern physician's regimen; both claim to honour the father, and neither asks him. **The right to die as one wishes** — the story's most modern question: Varma's last demand is not for sweets but for autonomy. Write the essay from both chairs — the son's and the father's — and refuse to leave either.

## NEB short answers, solved

**Q. How did Rakesh honour his parents after his success? (2 marks)**
A. In every traditional way: he touched his father's feet, married a village girl of his mother's choosing instead of a foreigner, brought his bride into the family home, and cared for his parents with pride and gratitude. The neighbourhood counted him a model son.

**Q. How did Rakesh care for his ailing father? (2 marks)**
A. As a physician as much as a son: banned fried foods and sweets, prescribed tonics and vitamins, scheduled walks and rest, and supervised the diet strictly. The care was professional, tireless — and experienced by the father as control.

**Q. Why did Varma resent his son's care? (2 marks)**
A. Because it took away his freedom along with his disease: he wanted his sweets, his fried food and his own decisions, and the son's regime treated him like a patient rather than a father. The love that prolonged his life also made his life not his own.

**Q. How did Varma try to escape the regime? (2 marks)**
A. Through small rebellions: bribing the grandchildren to buy him sweets from the bazaar, complaining publicly that the tonics tasted of punishment, and announcing his approaching death to anyone who would listen.

**Q. What is the irony of the title? (2 marks)**
A. That the devotion is real and harmful at once: the son's care extends the father's life against the father's wishes, and the title's praise conceals the story's question — devotion to the father, or to the son's own idea of duty?

**Q. What does the story suggest about the relationship between love and control? (2 marks)**
A. That love without consent slides into control: Rakesh's care is genuine, but because it never asks the father what he wants, it becomes authority. Desai suggests that loving someone includes letting them choose, even wrongly.

## NEB long answers, solved

**Q. "Rakesh was a devoted son, but his devotion became a cage." Discuss both sides. (8 marks)**
A model answer holds the two truths in balance: on one side, the evidence of real devotion — the feet touched, the mother's choice honoured, the tireless medical care that extended the father's life; on the other, the evidence of the cage — the banned sweets, the scheduled life, the tonics forced on a man who announces he wants to die. It should use the story's reversals (the obedient son becomes the commanding doctor) and the father's small rebellions as the cage's proof, and close on the story's refusal to convict either party: Desai's point is not that Rakesh was wrong to care but that care which never asks is a form of power.

**Q. Sketch the character of old Varma and justify his rebellion. (8 marks)**
A model answer builds the portrait in stages: the proud father announcing his son's results to the street, the grateful beneficiary of the son's rise, and the rebel whose sweetness-smuggling and death announcements are comic on the surface and desperate underneath. It should argue that Varma's rebellion is a claim to personhood: what he demands is not sugar but the right to be consulted, to be a father rather than a case. The strongest answers use his last evening — the tonic refused, the son insistent — as the scene that proves the story's point: the man's final wish was heard only as a symptom.
examShortTricks: Trick 1: Central irony: Rakesh's devotion (strict diet, medicine) becomes a cage for his father — love imposed becomes control; state this reversal.
Trick 2: Track the power inversion: son obeyed father as a child; father must obey son in old age — structure the answer around the two halves.
Trick 3: The father's final act (refusing medicine, letting death come) asserts autonomy — explain what it says about dignity in old age.
practiceQuestions: Q. How does Dr Rakesh's care become controlling? (2 marks) — he forbids the father's food and treats him like a patient, not a parent.
Q. What does the father's deathbed act mean? (2 marks) — he reclaims his right to choose, dying on his own terms.
keyPoints: Rakesh's devotion turns to control — filial duty vs the father's autonomy.
Irony: the son who saved Varma's life also takes away his joys (sweets, food).

data.title: Short Story 4 — The Treasure in the Forest (H. G. Wells)
data.topicTitle: Short Story 4 — The Treasure in the Forest (H. G. Wells)
notes:
## The story at a glance

"The Treasure in the Forest" by H. G. Wells is an adventure story that turns on its readers: two rough seamen, Evans and Hooker, murder a Chinese man to steal his map of a buried treasure, sail to the island, find the gold — and die of the touch of it. The treasure is guarded, it turns out, by poisoned thorns the Chinese had planted, and the story's final image is of the gold waiting in the sun for the next claimant. Wells's theme is greed as a fatal instrument, and the colonial subtext — Englishmen looting a Chinese find — is the story's quietest indictment.

## The plot, retold with an eye on its turns

The setup is a crime told in flashback: the dying Chinese man on the beach, the map he would not surrender, the two seamen who took it from him — the murder that buys the expedition. Wells gives the victim barely a paragraph, and the economy is the point: the whole imperial drama — a Chinese labourer's discovery, Englishmen's entitlement, a life taken for a piece of paper — is compressed into the story's first minutes.

The voyage and the landing build the atmosphere of a Gothic island: the creek, the dense growth, the silence. The discovery scene is the story's hinge: the gold is there, exactly as the map promised — and around it the ground is ringed with a thorny, creeping plant the two men barely notice. Evans, eager, reaches among the ingots; Hooker, more cautious, watches. The poison works with the quietness of all well-made traps: a pricked finger, a numbness, the sudden understanding that the Chinese had guarded their gold not with walls but with botany.

The ending is swift and cold: Evans dies among the treasure he stole the map for; Hooker, realising the truth too late, dies at the boat's edge — and the final image returns to the gold, untouched, gleaming in the forest's silence, waiting. The story's arithmetic is exact: two lives spent for the treasure, and the treasure has not moved.

## The devices, with evidence

- **Irony of fate** — the master device: the men who murdered for the map die on the very spot the map led to; the treasure is gained and fatal in the same gesture.
- **Foreshadowing** — the dying Chinese man's gestures toward the map, the island's too-quiet growth, the thorns noticed and dismissed: Wells marks the trap in advance and lets greed walk into it anyway.
- **Atmosphere** — the Gothic island: creek, density, silence, heat — a setting that feels wrong before anything goes wrong, priming the reader for the retribution.
- **Symbolism** — the poisoned thorns are the story's thesis in an image: wealth guarded by the violence of those who hid it; the gold that outlives its thieves is greed's own eternity.
- **Economy and restraint** — the murder is told in a breath, the deaths in a page: Wells trusts the idea to carry the horror, and the brevity is the cruelty.

The exam question "why do the treasure hunters die?" is answered in one line: because the treasure was defended — by its owners' poison and by the story's own moral law, which charges greed at full price.

## The characters worth an essay

**Evans and Hooker** are less characters than instruments of greed — but Wells distinguishes them finely: Evans is the eager hand, first to the gold, first to touch the thorns; Hooker is the slower, more cautious intelligence that sees the trap a moment too late. Their difference makes the story's lesson universal: caution does not save the man who is already inside the crime.

**The Chinese man** — barely present, entirely central: the discoverer of the treasure, the keeper of its secret, and the story's first death. His murder is the moral transaction that prices everything after it, and Wells's refusal to name him fully is itself the colonial indifference the story indicts.

## The themes worth an essay

**Greed and retribution** — the central theme: the treasure's price is exact, and the collectors pay it in full; the story is a moral machine. **Colonial greed** — the Englishmen's casual entitlement to a Chinese discovery is the story's historical argument: the poison is only the island's version of the resistance the looters never expected. **The silence of nature as justice** — no avenger appears; the thorns do the work: the theme that the world's traps are patient. **The folly of shortcuts** — a map stolen, a murder committed, and the treasure still out of reach: the theme that what is taken by force is never truly held. Anchor the essay in the final image — the gold waiting — and the theme completes itself.

## NEB short answers, solved

**Q. How did Evans and Hooker get the treasure map? (2 marks)**
A. By murder: the Chinese man who discovered the hoard would not surrender its secret, and the two seamen took the map from him as he lay dying on the beach. The crime is the story's moral first move and the price of everything after.

**Q. What did they find on the island? (2 marks)**
A. Exactly what the map promised: a hoard of gold ingots hidden in the forest's dense growth. But the ground around the treasure was ringed with a thorny, creeping plant the Chinese had planted as a guard — the detail the greedy eye does not stop to read.

**Q. How did the treasure kill them? (2 marks)**
A. Through the thorns: Evans, reaching among the ingots, was poisoned by the plant's touch, and Hooker, realising the truth too late, was poisoned as well before he could escape. The Chinese had defended their gold with poison rather than walls.

**Q. What is the significance of the ending's image? (2 marks)**
A. The gold lies untouched in the sun, waiting for the next claimant: the treasure has outlived its thieves as it outlived its owners. The image delivers the story's verdict — greed's reward is not possession but the grave beside the prize.

**Q. How does the story criticise colonial greed? (2 marks)**
A. In its casting: Englishmen murder a Chinese discoverer to loot his find, assuming the island's wealth is theirs for the taking. The poison that kills them is the colonised world's silent resistance — the story's retribution is both botanical and moral.

**Q. What role does foreshadowing play in the story? (2 marks)**
A. It marks the trap before it springs: the dying man's gestures, the island's unnatural silence, the thorns noticed and ignored. Wells lets greed walk past every warning sign, which is how the story makes its point about the blindness of desire.

## NEB long answers, solved

**Q. "The treasure in the forest is a moral trap as much as a physical one." Discuss. (8 marks)**
A model answer works both senses of trap: the physical — the poisoned thorns planted by the treasure's owners, which kill Evans among the gold and Hooker at the boat — and the moral — the murder that purchased the map, the entitlement that never asked whose treasure it was, and the blindness that ignores every warning sign. It should trace the story's economy (the murder told in a breath, the deaths in a page) and close on the final image: the gold waiting in the sun, the story's statement that the trap resets itself for the next claimant, because greed does not learn from the last set of corpses.

**Q. How does Wells build suspense and atmosphere in the story? (8 marks)**
A model answer organises the analysis by stages: the flashback murder that prices the expedition in blood; the voyage and landing with their Gothic silence and density; the discovery scene's double vision (the gold gleaming, the thorns unnoticed); and the poison's slow, quiet working. It should discuss foreshadowing as the engine of suspense — every warning the men ignore raises the reader's dread — and the restraint of the prose, which lets the horror arrive without commentary. The strongest answers note that the atmosphere is itself a device of justice: the island feels wrong because it is wrong.
examShortTricks: Trick 1: Greed is the mechanism of doom: the treasure is guarded (poisoned by the dead Chinese crew's trap) — the island punishes covetousness; state the moral.
Trick 2: Atmosphere: heat, silence, the dead bodies — the gothic detail foreshadows the ending; connect one detail to the outcome.
Trick 3: The twist: the 'treasure' they take is already lethal — irony of the prize being the poison; name it explicitly.
practiceQuestions: Q. What is the consequence of the men's greed? (2 marks) — one dies from the poisoned environment/guards' trap; the treasure destroys its seekers.
Q. How does Wells build suspense? (2 marks) — ominous setting details and the dead crew foreshadow danger before the climax.
keyPoints: Greed kills — the Spanish treasure's poisoned environment punishes the treasure hunters.
Gothic atmosphere: the dead man, the lethal forest; link setting to theme.

data.title: Short Story 5 — My Old Home (Lu Xun)
data.topicTitle: Short Story 5 — My Old Home (Lu Xun)
notes:
## The story at a glance

"My Old Home" by Lu Xun is a story about going back and finding that home exists only in memory. The narrator, educated and now urban, returns to his hometown after twenty years to move his mother and the household, and meets Runtu — the peasant boy of his childhood, the friend who taught him the countryside's secrets — now a stooped, silent father of many, broken by taxes and famine, who calls his old playmate "Master". The story's sorrow is the wall that has grown between them, and its hope is carried by the children of the next generation — and by the famous closing image: hope is like a road; it exists because people walk it.

## The plot, retold with an eye on its turns

The return is the story's frame: the narrator arrives in cold, grey weather to sell the family property and transport his mother — and the hometown of memory is disappointingly small, dim and unimproved. The melancholy is established before any meeting: the place itself has shrunk.

The memory of Runtu is the story's warm centre: the boy of the golden-necked gull picture, quick and fearless, who showed the young master the snow-ground traps, the shells, the watermelon fields under the moon — the image of a friendship that had no class in it. The reality arrives with the man: grey and wrinkled, hands cracked, red-rimmed eyes, and the voice that changes everything — "Master!" The narrator chokes; the childhood equality has become an adult hierarchy, installed not by law but by need and habit.
